PART TWO 1. The first title of law, known as Non-payment of Debt.
The procedure for the application of wealth; the section on pledges;
the subject matter of pledges concerning a faultless creditor.
The topics concerning a debtor who possesses malice;
the topics concerning the destruction of ownership and so forth regarding the pledge (ādhi); and the topics concerning the establishment of the pledge.
The section on sureties concerns the resolution of disputes regarding pledges and the like, as well as matters relating to the release of such pledges.
The classifications of sureties,

Methods of repayment for those provided by a surety and others;

The rule regarding the limit of increase;

The Procedure for the Repayment of Debts; Matters Concerning Debtors Unable to Pay.

those concerning theft,

[1] Now the section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) begins. Therein, first, the nature of legal procedure is defined. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"In former times, men were devoted to righteousness and non-violent."
The legal procedure is proclaimed for those who are overcome by greed and hatred.
The meaning of this has been explained by Nārada: "When men were solely devoted to dharma and speakers of truth, at that time there was no legal dispute, nor hatred, nor even envy."
"When the dharma of men has perished, legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is proclaimed.
This means that the disputes of men concerning subjects such as the non-payment of debt and so forth are proclaimed as *vyavahāra*. And thus Kātyāyana says:
"When the extensive exposition of justice, known as *dharma*, which is to be accomplished through effort, has been interrupted..."
But that dispute which is rooted in what is to be proven is called a legal proceeding (vyavahāra).

This is the meaning: when the entity called *dharma*—which is to be accomplished through efforts such as "speaking correctly" and "refraining from injury"—is interrupted by the influence of greed, hatred, and so forth, then the detailed exposition of legal reasoning (*nyāyavistara*) is undertaken in cases such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) for the sake of obtaining a means of proof, and in matters concerning conventional law (*samayadharma*) for the sake of avoiding the laws of others. In that context, the dispute among men which is rooted in what is to be proven is called *vyavahāra*. For this very reason, Hārīta says:
"The recovery of one's own property and the avoidance of the property of others..."
That in which legal proceedings are conducted according to justice is called a court of law.

The meaning is that a dispute over the denial of wealth, as well as a dispute among heretics and others concerning their own religious duties and conventions (*svadharma-samaya*), constitutes a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). Nor should it be suspected that disputes such as theft or assault are not legal proceedings; for Yājñavalkya says: "When one who has been oppressed by others through a path deviating from the *smṛtis* and established custom brings the matter before the king, that indeed is a subject of legal procedure."
Kātyāyana also says:
"If a teacher should strike a disciple out of anger without using a cane,
such that excessive pain is caused, the dispute shall belong to the father of the disciple."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"If a master provides wages to servants who are performing their work,
yet the servants do not perform it, then a dispute arises."
Someone may commit violence, or one may fail to give what is owed;
these two are the bases of dispute, and between them, the latter has more consequences.
Uśanas also says:
Whatever matter one might report to the king regarding any business, that ground is proclaimed to be of eighteen kinds in legal disputes. [3]

Thus, the implied meaning of the statements of Yājñavalkya and others—that legal dispute (*vyavahāra*) is a contention concerning any one of the eighteen kinds of subject matters—should be understood. For this very reason, Nārada says: "Recovery of debt, deposits, partnership, the resumption of what has been given, and breach of contract..."
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale without ownership,
non-delivery of what has been sold, and likewise rescission after having purchased;
Non-performance of agreements, disputes, and the son born of the field; the union of man and woman, partition of inheritance, and violence.
Harshness of speech, as well as violence with a staff,
gambling, and miscellaneous matters— these are recorded as the eighteen titles of law.

The meaning is that a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is traditionally defined as having any one of the eighteen titles (*viṣaya*), beginning with the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*). Nor should it be argued that this is contradictory to the traditional teaching that there are "eighteen titles," because other titles such as "deposits" (*nikṣepa*) are also recorded in tradition; for he [the author] himself says:
"Another division of these very [titles] is recorded as one hundred and eight;
due to the diversity of human actions, it is said to have a hundred branches."
Kātyāyana also says:

"Due to the eighteen divisions of legal actions (*kriyā*), they are divided into eight thousand. The meaning is that they are divided according to the differences in legal actions, which is to say, according to the differences in the objects to be proven (*sādhya*). By this, it is stated by implication that legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) are also divided into eight thousand. There is no contradiction between the phrases "one hundred and eight" and "eight thousand," because both are intended to demonstrate a great plurality.
[4] Thus concludes the determination of the nature of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the eighteen titles of law (*aṣṭādaśapada*).
In this regard, Nārada has shown the nature and some of the divisions of the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*):
"That which is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner,
as well as the rules for giving and receiving— that is remembered as *ṛṇādāna*."

A debt contracted by a father or others for the sake of activities other than gambling and similar censurable acts must be paid. A debt contracted by a son or others for the sake of maintaining the family or other necessary duties, as opposed to non-essential matters, must be paid. Furthermore, during the period following the end of childhood and before the attainment of majority, the heirs—sons, grandsons, and so forth—must pay the debt according to the rules regarding doubling the principal (*dvaiguṇya*) and other such methods. All of this, as well as the legal principles governing the lending of money, such as "the seizure of collateral and other rules for the employment of wealth should be applied gradually," and the principles for the recovery of lent capital—all these matters stated within the scope of a particular dispute are what is traditionally known as the title of law *ṛṇādāna* (non-payment of debts). He [Yājñavalkya] himself also states the nature and divisions of the second title of law.
That wherein one deposits one's own property without hesitation due to trust is called "deposit" (nikṣepa), a title of legal dispute, by the wise.
"That which is deposited in an uncounted and unrecognized manner is to be known as *upanidhi*; the wise know *nikṣepa* to be counted.

This means that the distinction between *nikṣepa* and *upanidhi* is based on whether they are counted or uncounted. The meaning of the term "unrecognized" (*avijñāta*) has been elaborated upon by Bṛhaspati.

"That which is given unannounced, at a distance, without a specific number, without being shown, and marked with a seal, is known as *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit). [5] The word "given" implies "into the hand of another. And so says Yājñavalkya:

When an uncounted quantity of goods contained in a vessel is placed in one's hand and handed over, that property is termed *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit); it must be returned in exactly the same manner.

The "container" (*bhājana*) refers to a vessel such as a box or similar receptacle that serves as a support for the deposit; the mention of the "hand" is merely illustrative. Therefore, Nārada states:
"That which is deposited in another's house—whether it be an object separated from other goods or an unmarked item—is known as *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit)."
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says that where an object devoid of specific characteristics is deposited, that is called *nyāsa* (deposit):
"When property is placed in another's house due to fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or because of harassment by heirs, that is proclaimed as a *nyāsa*."
Kātyāyana, however, states an exception to this:
"That which is purchased, left by one who has gone abroad, deposited, lent for use, pledged, requested,
and even that offered as part of a Vaiśya’s trade— that object is known as *upanidhi* (a sealed deposit)."

*Kraya* (purchase) refers to the wealth acquired through buying. In the phrase "deposited by one who has gone abroad" (*proṣitanikṣiptam*), the inclusion of the term *proṣita* (gone abroad) is intended as an illustration for one who is about to depart (*pravatsyat*). *Bandha* means a pledge (*ādhi*). *Anvāhitam* is that which has been entrusted to another for the purpose of giving to someone else. *Yācitam* is an ornament or similar item belonging to another that has been brought [for use]. That which is "entrusted for the sake of livelihood" (*vaiśyavṛttyarpitam*) is that which has been handed over to another for the purpose of subsistence, such as for agricultural work and the like. Nārada states that this aforementioned classification of deposits and so forth is further divided into two types: "That [deposit] is said to be of two kinds: one with witnesses (*sākṣimat*) and likewise the other."
Likewise, its counter-gift (*pratidāna*) would be the condition (*pratyaya*) in the opposite case.
The condition is divine.
Thus, by that very [statement], the two distinct natures of the third term are also shown.
Where merchants and others perform an enterprise collectively,
that is known as the legal subject matter of "partnership" (saṃbhūyasamutthāna).

Merchants [engage in] trade, officiating priests [perform] sacrifice, farmers [practice] agriculture, goldsmiths and the like [exercise] their craft, dancers and the like [perform] dance and so forth, and thieves [commit] theft; when they perform these activities collectively, that is "trade and the like performed in association. Based on the etymology "that by which they rise together (samuttiṣṭhante) and prosper (samedhante)," the meaning is that this is the title of the legal dispute known as *saṃbhūyasamutthāna* (partnership). By the mention of "merchants and the like," these various subdivisions are already indicated. Likewise, the nature and subdivisions of the fourth title of dispute are also shown by that very same [mention].
When one, having given property improperly, desires to take it back again,
that is indeed the legal head of dispute known as "Rescission of a Gift" (dattāpradānika).

The literal meaning (*śrauto ’rtha*) of this legal title (*vyavahārapada*) known as *dattāpradānika* is: that gift in which the substance given is to be taken back from the recipient due to the negligence of the agent (*karmakāra*) and others; for its etymology is: "that in which there exists the non-delivery (*apradāna*) of what has been given. Furthermore, the implied meaning (*ārthiko ’rtha*) is that this very same title is also called *dattānapākarma*, based on the etymology: "that in which there exists the non-removal (*anapākarma*), or non-withdrawal, of what has been given," because there was no negligence on the part of the agent and others. Having thus stated the twofold nature of this title according to the literal and implied meanings, the author himself further states its fourfold division based on the distinctions among the substances that serve as the objects of action, such as those that ought to be given and those that ought not to be given.
Now, that which is to be given and that which is not to be given, as well as what has been given and what has not been given—
these fourfold paths of giving are to be understood in legal proceedings.

That which is "to be given" (*deyam*) is a substance that, being unprohibited, brings about the act of giving; that which is "not to be given" (*adeyam*) does not bring it about. When there is an act of giving, that which has been "given" (*dattam*) cannot be taken back from the recipient; that which is "not given" (*adattam*) can be taken back. By means of these categories—the givable and ungivable, the given and not given—the fourfold path of giving, or the modes of giving, should be understood in legal proceedings. Likewise, the specific nature of the subsequent category is also stated: "But when one, having agreed to service, does not perform it—this is called the title of dispute concerning 'having agreed to non-service' (*aśuśrūṣābhyupetya*)."

The meaning is that the failure to carry out the commands of a teacher or other superior, which has been accepted by one who is a servant such as a disciple, is the title of legal dispute known as *abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā* (non-compliance after undertaking service). Since the word "he" (*yaḥ*) is used as a general term, its fivefold nature—consisting of the five types of servants known as disciples (*śiṣya*), resident pupils (*antevāsin*), hired laborers (*bhṛtaka-karmakṛt*), and slaves (*dāsa*)—is established by implication; therefore, no separate classification is shown by that term. However, Bṛhaspati has shown many divisions: "But they are stated to be of many kinds according to their caste and occupation, and fourfold on account of learning, specialized knowledge, desire, and wealth."
"Furthermore, each of these is subdivided according to the differences in their respective functions.

For the knowledge of the Vedas is the motive for a student (*śiṣya*), technical skill for an apprentice (*antevāsī*), and pleasure and wealth for a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*) and others. However, the distinctions in the essential nature of the subsequent category have been stated by Nārada:
"The rules and procedures for the giving and receiving of wages for servants have been declared."
The non-payment of wages is recorded as that title of dispute. [8]

The procedure for the giving and taking of wages (*vetana*) or hire (*bhṛti*) by those performing work for the sake of their masters—stating what kind of wage should be given, what kind should not be given, how that which has been paid may be recovered from such a person, or in some cases that double should be paid—and so forth, is explained in this legal title (*vivādapada*). The meaning is that it is called the legal title of "Non-payment of Wages" (*vetanānapākarma*), based on the etymological derivation that here there is a non-discharge, non-removal, or non-performance of what is due. By this very [explanation], its manifold nature is stated through the various distinctions of what is to be given and so forth. He states the same regarding the intermediate category (*antarapada*) as well.
When property belonging to another— whether deposited, lost, found, or stolen—
is sold in the absence of the owner, that is to be known as "sale by one who is not the owner" (asvāmivikraya).

"In the absence of the owner"—this is the understood remainder [of the phrase]. And so Vyāsa says: "When property belonging to another—such as that which was borrowed, deposited, or pledged—is sold by someone else in the absence of the owner, that should be known as *asvāmivikraya* (sale by one who is not the owner)."

"In the absence of the owner" means in the absence of the presence of the owner. In this same manner, the essential nature and divisions of the subsequent term should also be understood. And so says Nārada: "When, after selling a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer—that is called the legal dispute of 'non-delivery after sale'."
And since the distinction [of this law] arises from the distinction between types of merchandise, he states that distinction:
"In this world, there are two kinds of property: moving and likewise stationary;
all of that is called 'merchandise' (paṇya) in the rules concerning purchase and sale."
The wise have recorded its method of giving and taking as being sixfold: by calculation, by weighing, by measuring, by action, by form, and by splendor.

[9] The meaning of this is as follows: "by calculation" refers to betel nuts and the like; "by weighing" refers to gold and the like; "by measuring" refers to rice and the like with measures such as the *prastha*; "by action" refers to horses, buffaloes, and the like through actions such as milking; "by form" refers to courtesans and the like; and "by splendor" refers to gems and the like due to their radiance. Thus he has stated the essential nature of each subsequent category as well.
When a purchaser, having bought a commodity for a price, does not value it highly,
this is called the legal subject matter known as "repentance after purchase."
"He does not hold it in high esteem" means that he does not regard it as something to be clung to. Likewise, for the purpose of defining the subsequent category of legal matters, he says:
"The established rule of the heretics, guilds, and so forth is called *samaya*. The failure to carry out that *samaya* is recorded as a subject of dispute (*vivādapada*)."

Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍāḥ*) are the Kṣapaṇakas and others. Merchants (*naigamāḥ*) are caravan-traders and merchants. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), groups of Brāhmaṇas learned in the three Vedas, guilds (*śreṇī*), associations (*pūga*), bands (*vrāta*), corporations (*gaṇa*), clusters (*gulma*), villages (*grāma*), regions (*deśa*), and so on, are included. Their "establishment" (*sthitiḥ*) is the convention (*samayaḥ*) consisting of a formal arrangement according to customary law (*pāribhāṣika-dharma*). The non-transgression (*anapākarma*) of that—that is, its non-violation—is what constitutes the non-transgression of convention (*samayānapākarma*). When that is performed otherwise, it is meaningful through the figure of speech known as "contradiction" (*viruddhalakṣaṇā*). The meaning is that this is recorded in the legal codes (*smṛti*) as a head of dispute (*vivādapada*) called the non-transgression of convention. Its primary alternative name, "violation of agreement" (*saṃvidvyatikrama*), has not been mentioned because it is already well-known as the designation for this subject.
He also explains the subsequent verse:
"Where there are determinations regarding embankments, field boundaries, limits, ploughed land, unploughed land, and ownership over fields—that is known as a dispute concerning fields. [10]

A *setu* is a dam that binds the flow of water. A *kedāra* is a small area demarcated by small embankments, or simply a field. A *maryādā* is the boundary of fields and the like. A *vikṛṣṭa* is a piece of land ploughed with the plow and other implements. An *akṛṣṭa* is fallow, unploughed land. The meaning is that a dispute arising from fields (*kṣetraja*) is one in which there are determinations regarding these matters pertaining to fields. Kātyāyana states that it is of six kinds: "Excess, deficiency, [dispute over] a share, existence and non-existence, possession through enjoyment, and boundaries—these six are the causes of disputes concerning land."

The meaning of this is explained in detail: having accepted a certain portion of land, the dispute based on "there is more land than that" or "there is not" is caused by excess (*ādhikya*). When it is said, "This much land is yours," and [the other replies], "I have this much," such a case is caused by deficiency (*nyūnatā*). When it is said, "I have a share in this land," and [the other replies], "No," such a case is caused by the existence of a share (*aṃśas-titva*). When it is said, "You have no share in this land," and [the other replies], "It exists," such a case is caused by the non-existence of a share (*aṃśa-nāstitva*). When it is said, "My land is being enjoyed by you now, though it was not enjoyed by you before," and [the other replies], "There was enjoyment even before," such a case has its seed in prior possession (*bhoga-bhukti*). When it is said, "This boundary belongs to my land," and [the other replies], "No," such a case arises from a boundary (*sīmā-sambhava*). And Nārada states that this dispute is divided according to the various types of boundaries.
The boundary is recorded as being of five kinds: that marked by a banner, that marked by fish, that established by fire, that free from fear, and that determined by royal decree.

A *dhvajinī* (frontier) is characterized by trees and the like; a *matsyinī* (fishing-ground) by water; a *naidhānī* (burial-ground) by pits, furrows, and so forth. A *bhayavarjitā* (free from fear) is established through mutual agreement between the two disputants. A *rājaśāsananītā* (brought under royal decree) is one created by the king’s will.
[11] Now, he has briefly defined the two preceding terms:
"That in which the rites for marriage and so forth of women and men are proclaimed."
That title of dispute is called "the union of woman and man."
Where the partition of the property of a father or others is effected by the sons,
that is declared by the wise to be the legal head of dispute known as "Inheritance" (Dāyabhāga).

In both instances, the word "etc. (*ādi*) indicates a manifold variety of divisions. The term "by sons" is intended as an illustration for all heirs. As for the subsequent three terms, they have been explained through detailed elaboration.
Whatever act is performed impulsively by those arrogant with power, that is declared to be *sāhasa*; here, *saha* is said to mean strength (*bala*).
The meaning is: "whatever [involves] the seizure of property held in common," and so forth. And thus says Yājñavalkya:
"The forcible seizure of common property is declared to be *sāhasa* (violence).
The mention of "common property" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the killing of human beings and other such acts. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:
"Killing a human, theft, violating another's wife, verbal abuse, and both [physical and verbal] violence— thus violence is recorded as fivefold.
Having thus stated the manifold nature of this category through the word "whatever" occurring in the defining verse, Nārada further declares its threefold division:

Furthermore, that [meditative concentration] is to be known as threefold—namely, the initial, the intermediate, and the superior; their respective characteristics have been stated separately in the treatises.
Thus, its characteristic has also been explained in detail by him.
The first degree of *sāhasa* (violence) is declared to consist of breaking, throwing down, crushing, and so forth, fruits, roots, water, and other such agricultural implements.
In the same manner, the theft of clothing, cooked food, drink, and household utensils is declared to be the middle amercement.
"Malice (vyāpāda) consists of [causing harm] by means of poison, weapons, and the like; violating another's wife;

and whatever else obstructs life—this is declared to be the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa). Here, "malice" (vyāpādana) refers to the infliction of various calamities through poison and other such means. Likewise, he states the nature of verbal abuse (vāk-pāruṣya).
Speech that is contrary in meaning and joined with abuse or disparagement regarding one's country, birth, family, and so forth— that is called harsh speech (*vākpāruṣya*).

Harsh speech (*vākpāruṣya*) is that utterance which conveys a meaning intended to insult the country and so forth, as well as that which has a meaning causing extreme suffering. It is also of three kinds; thus he says:
"It is remembered as being of three types due to its being harsh, vulgar, and intense.
He then states the nature of "harsh" and the other categories:

The wise say that speech accompanied by reproach and harshness is "indecent" (aślīla), while that which is joined with the mention of physical defects and severe censures involving grounds for expulsion is called "fierce" (tīvra).

"Damn you, fool, wretch," and so forth, is speech with reproach (*ākṣepa*). "Defect" (*nyaṅga*) refers to blemishes such as a relationship with one's sister. "Causing a fall" (*patanīya*) refers to [accusations] such as "you are a drinker of liquor. And thus Kātyāyana says: "When one reproaches another at any time with marks designated as false—whether they be non-existent or indeed existent—that is considered by the wise to be harsh speech (*niṣṭhurā vāk*)."
When one, out of anger, uses speech to cause the humiliation of another's livelihood,
country, family, and so forth, that is considered by the wise to be *aślīlā* (obscene or abusive).
That speech which binds one with the noose of great sins, which produces passion and hatred, or which causes the loss of caste— that indeed is known as intense speech.

Bṛhaspati, however, here also states that there are three types— distinguished as minor, middling, and major— similar to [the classification of] rash acts: "The reviling of countries, villages, families, and so forth, by associating them with sin, but without the use of property, is called the first [type of] verbal abuse."
Speaking of a sister, a mother, or their relatives, as well as proclaiming a minor offense (upapātaka),
is declared by those who know the scriptures to be middling verbal abuse.

"The discussion of forbidden foods and drinks, the reviling of those guilty of mortal sins (mahāpātaka), and harshness consisting of piercing the vital points intensely—this is declared to be the highest [degree of] verbal abuse. The phrase "without property" means "without the excellence of property. Kātyāyana, however, mentions other varieties of verbal abuse as well.
Making the sound "huṃ," coughing, and whatever else is censured in the world— if one imitates these or speaks them aloud, it is likewise called verbal abuse.

"Those who, out of anger, proclaim the faults of one who is faultless, or perceive virtue in one who is devoid of virtue, or who apply a different designation [to another], know that man to be corrupt in speech. Vyāsa, however, has described the nature of verbal assault (*vāgdaṇḍapāruṣya*).
The throwing of ashes and other substances, the crushing with the hands and so forth,
and the binding with garments and the like is called verbal and physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). Bṛhaspati also says:
Assault with hands, stones, clubs, ashes, mud, dust,
or weapons is called physical violence (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).

The phrase "striking" refers to [striking] the limbs of another; and thus Nārada says: "Assaulting the limbs of another with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth, as well as injuring them with ashes and the like, is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault)."
Regarding the limbs of others, whether in stationary or moving forms, *daṇḍa* (punishment) is injury, and *pāruṣya* is harshness. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that this category is also threefold:
"Its threefold nature is observed according to the sequence of low, middling, and high, by means of threatening, striking without hesitation, and the sight of blood."

The meaning is that there is a threefold classification—lowest, middling, and highest—based on the degree of the agent’s activity and the degree of distinction in the objects that serve as the karma, due to the transcendence of inferior, middling, and superior substances. Now, one might object: since the two types of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) are specific forms of violence (*sāhasa*), it is improper to mention them as separate categories. This is true; however, that which is committed impulsively is a specific form of violence, whereas that which is committed through deception is indeed a separate category, because it lacks the defining characteristics of violence. Thus it has been stated by that very same author:
Theft is indeed a variety of that [misappropriation], though a distinction therein is now stated:
an *ādhi* (mortgage) involves forceful seizure, whereas theft involves deception.

*Mādhi* means affliction (*kleśa*). When that is carried out by way of seizing property through force, it is *sāhasa* (violence). On the other hand, when it is carried out by way of taking property through fraud, the meaning is that it is *steya* (theft). [Objection: But surely, by this, a distinction of theft has been stated, not of verbal or physical assault (*pāruṣya*). [Reply: True. However, when a distinction is stated even for that which was not mentioned separately, a distinction is all the more clearly perceived for that which was mentioned separately; thus, since this refers to theft in general, there is no contradiction. Therefore, its mention as a separate term is indeed appropriate. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṅgraha* says:
If acts such as the killing of a human being are committed by force, they are called "acts of violence" (sāhasa); otherwise, they are classified differently according to their specific descriptions.

Otherwise, if they are committed without force (*aprasabham*), then they are as previously described—namely, those termed theft (*steya*), adultery (*strī-saṅgrahaṇa*), verbal abuse (*vāk-pāruṣya*), and physical assault (*daṇḍa-pāruṣya*); this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "In that case, adultery and theft should also be mentioned separately from violence (*sāhasa*). True; for that very reason, Manu states:
"Theft, violence, and likewise adultery."

Thus it was listed separately. However, since those two (the two forms of verbal and physical abuse) are committed solely through deception (*chala*), their status as distinct categories is quite clear; thus, Nārada showed at the stage of the initial enumeration that they are actually included within *sāhasa* (outrageous acts). On the other hand, because the two types of *pāruṣya* (assault and defamation) are generally committed by force (*prasabha*), their status as distinct categories is not so obvious; therefore, they were listed separately as well. Thus, everything is faultless. Having stated the distinction between theft (*steya*) and *sāhasa*, Nārada also stated its threefold nature:
"The wise should know that [theft] is also of three kinds, depending on the nature of the object."
But by the theft of goods that are inferior, middling, or superior—
Minor items and so forth have also been shown by that same [author]:
"Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, bones, wood, leather, grass, and the like,
as well as leguminous grains and prepared food— these are declared to be minor items."
Clothing, with the exception of silk; likewise animals, with the exception of cows;
metals, with the exception of gold; and grains such as rice and barley—these constitute the middle [grade of gifts].
[16] Gold, jewels, silk, women, men, cattle, elephants, and horses,
as well as the property of gods, brahmins, and kings, should be known as the highest class of goods.
"Depriving these [of their property] by various means after deceiving them—when they are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless—the wise call this theft.

Shami-dhānya refers to leguminous grains such as mung beans and black gram that are encased in pods. Kauśeya refers to what is produced from threads originating in the cocoons of silkworms. Regarding the threefold nature of sexual intercourse with women, Bṛhaspati says:
Understand that the gathering [of women] for the root of evil is of three kinds:
two are caused by force and the like, while the third arises from passion.

*Saṅgrahaṇa* (adultery) is the connection of a man with another's wife. Thus says Nārada: "Staying together, conversing, and dalliance—these three are the stages of *saṅgrahaṇa* for a man with another's wife, whether at an improper time or in an improper place."

Bṛhaspati states the definition of the three types [of rape] mentioned by himself: "That which is done with a woman who does not consent— whether she be asleep, insane, intoxicated, or babbling— and which is committed in private by force, that indeed is [rape]."
When a union is brought about by bringing a woman to one's house under a pretext or by administering intoxicants or magical charms, that they know as *upādhikṛta* (procured through fraud).
That which is done through mutual passion of the eyes, or by the dispatching of a female messenger,
or out of greed for beauty or wealth, should be known as born of attachment.
The *kārmaṇa* is the act of subjugation. Furthermore, he himself stated that it is characterized by a threefold nature according to its being inferior, middling, or superior:
[17] That, moreover, is declared to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
[These are] a sidelong glance, laughter, and likewise the dispatching of a female messenger (*dūtī*).
The first collection is known as the enjoyment of ornaments and garments;
the second is the sending forth of perfumes, garlands, incense, honey, food, and clothing.
They know that conversation in private constitutes the middling form of seduction;
likewise, sharing a single bed, seat, play, kissing, and embracing [constitute the highest].
"This is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the supreme method of summary.
Vyāsa also says: "The summary is to be known as threefold: the first, the middling, and likewise the lowest."
And as for the "supreme" one, its definition has been stated separately in the scriptures.
Conversation at an improper place or time, or in a secluded spot with another's wife,
as well as side-long glances, staring, and laughter— this is recorded as the first stage of seduction.
The sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the enticing with food and drink, is recorded as the middling means of winning over.

When two people lie down or sit together in a secluded place, or when they take refuge in one another, or when they engage in seizing each other by the hair— this should be known as the highest form of sexual union.

In a secluded, private place; by means of "hair-to-hair" grips—that is, sports preceded by the mutual seizing of each other's hair. Kātyāyana also states the various types of seizing: "If [the lover] employs a messenger, stays at an improper time or place, or seizes the neck, hair, hem of the garment, or the ears, nose, hands, and so forth."
[18] Dwelling in one place, sitting in one place, and eating in one place—this is known as the ninefold practice of restraint (*saṃgraha*).
*Añcala* means the hem of a garment. Likewise:
"One should not converse with another's wife at a sacred ford, in the forest, or even in the house."
And at the confluence of rivers, he shall incur the penalty for adultery.
Intercourse is sexual union. Likewise:
"The act of providing assistance, dalliance, touching ornaments and garments, and even sitting on the same bed—all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery)."
"Doing a favor" (*upakārakriyā*) means performing a service by giving betel leaves and other such items. "Sport" (*keli*) means jesting. And so it is said:
"If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, tolerates it—with mutual consent, all this is recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery)."
"An improper place" refers to locations such as the vicinity of the breasts. Nārada also states:
"If one should seize her by the hand, or by the braid of hair, or even by the hem of her garment;
or if one should say, 'Stay! Stay!', all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse)."
Likewise, in order to clarify the specific nature of the term *dyūtasamāhvaya*, that same author says:
"Gambling (*devana*) conducted with crooked means such as dice, fists, shells, or sticks,
and playing for a stake (*paṇa*) with birds and so forth, is the legal category (*pada*) known as *dyūtasamāhvaya*."

*Vardhra* is a leather strap. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), items such as *kapārdikā* (cowrie shells) are included. Gambling (*devana*) or playing with dice and other implements for a wager (*paṇapūrvaka*), when performed deceitfully—that is, with crookedness—is what is called *dyūta*. Likewise, gambling with living creatures (*vayas*) such as cocks and the like for a wager is called *samāhvaya*. The meaning is that these two combined constitute a single term, *dyūtasamāhvaya*. The mention of "living creatures" (*vayas*) is intended to indicate all sentient beings. Therefore, Manu says: "In this world, that which is performed with non-living things is called *dyūta*."
But that which is performed by living beings is to be known as *samāhvaya* (gambling with animate objects).
Bṛhaspati also says:
"When birds, rams, bulls, and so forth, having staked upon one another,
strike each other after making a wager— that they call *samāhvaya* (gambling)."
However, the definition and classification of the miscellaneous category (prakīrṇaka) were stated by Nārada.
Furthermore, in the miscellaneous section (prakīrṇaka), lawsuits pertaining to the king are to be known;
namely, the obstruction of the king’s commands and likewise the performance of his duties.
The destruction of the city's leaders as well as that of the subjects,
and the subversion of the dharma of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies.
Disputes between father and son, the transgression of penances, the neglect of receiving gifts, and even the abandonment of those belonging to the stages of life;

"The fault of the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), as well as the lack of restriction regarding their livelihoods, and whatever has not been seen among the previous [titles of law]—all that shall be *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous).

The meaning is this: whatever must be adjudicated by the king by taking the position of an opponent when there is a transgression of his own commands and so forth, and whatever was not mentioned in the previously stated titles such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and the rest—all that is the title of law known as *prakīrṇaka*. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
[20] Laziness, causing a breach of trust, collective rising [in revolt], taking wages [without working], refusal to serve, false claims regarding land, and selling what one does not own;
Regret regarding purchase and sale, likewise breach of contract,
union between man and woman, theft, partition of inheritance, and gambling with dice.
These fourteen words, arising from their respective meanings,
are further divided in many ways according to the distinctions of action.
Harsh speech, killing, and likewise the abduction of another's wife—
Bṛhaspati has stated that these four items arise from violence.
Distinguished individually as inferior, middling, and superior,
the specific distinction of these four has been set forth in their proper sequence.
These eighteen points set forth in the Dharmaśāstras are the root of all disputes; those who know them are the true judges.
Thus concludes the determination of the eighteen titles of law in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the divisions of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) are discussed.

It has already been stated that legal procedure is of many kinds due to the diversity of its subject matter inherent in its nature. Now, its classification according to the stakes (*paṇa*) and other factors is being set forth. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:

"If the dispute should be accompanied by a wager (*paṇa*), one should cause the defeated party to pay it. A "wager" (*paṇa*) is that wealth which, out of pride, has been accepted by the defeated party with the thought, "I shall give this much to the king"; a lawsuit together with that is "with a wager" (*sapaṇa*). Because of the word "if" (*cet*), there is also the case "without a wager" (*apaṇa*); thus, legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is of two kinds. As it has been stated by Nārada: "It is to be known as having two characteristics: with a counter-claim (*sottara*) and without a counter-claim (*anuttara*)."
"Sottara" (with a stake) refers to that [legal proceeding] where a wager (*paṇa*) exceeding the fine is involved.

The meaning is that in a lawsuit, prior to the recording of the claim (*pratijñā-vilekhana*), a wager greater than the fine is accepted by both parties or by one of them; that is a "sottara" lawsuit. Other varieties have also been stated by him:
"It has four feet, four bases, and indeed four means of proof."
He is celebrated as the one who possesses the four benefits, who pervades the four, and who performs the four deeds.
"It has eight limbs, eighteen points, and likewise a hundred branches;
it has three origins, two applications, two doors, and likewise two destinations.
Thus he himself explains these various categories.
Dharma, judicial procedure, established custom, and royal edict—
this four-legged system of legal process functions such that each subsequent element overrides the preceding one.

Now, it may be asked: "Is it not the case that the plaint (*pratijñā*), the reply (*uttara*), the means of proof (*pramāṇa*), and the decision (*nirṇaya*) constitute the stages of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*), and not *dharma* and the other factors? Why then has this been said? It is replied: The stage of decision (*nirṇayapāda*) is fourfold according to its conformity with *dharma* and the rest. In that regard, whatever decision follows from whichever factor is designated by that specific term. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that the determination of the fourfold nature [of the lawsuit] is established through *dharma* and the others as well. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "By *dharma*, by legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), by custom (*caritra*), and by the king’s command—thus is the decision regarding a doubtful matter declared to be of four kinds."
Kātyāyana states the definition of all four types of judicial determinations:
"In a dispute where the wrongdoer establishes his authorship and the owner of the wealth recovers his own property, that is a determination made by means of *dharma* alone. [22]

Fault consists of violence and the like; agency is the state of being the performer thereof. As for the Smṛti scripture, whatever has been proclaimed by those who establish dharma, it is indeed known as *vyavahāra* (legal procedure) for the purpose of deciding legal matters.
The meaning is that a decision reached in accordance with the plaint, the reply, and so forth, as established by the *Dharmaśāstra*, is called "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*).
Whatever is constantly practiced by someone, whether it be righteous or unrighteous, on account of the custom of the country, that is proclaimed as "conduct" (*caritra*).

The meaning is that the legal decision (*nirṇaya*) following from that is likewise proclaimed to be of the same nature. Whatever law (*dharma*) the king establishes in accordance with the *Nyāya* treatise, as well as local custom (*deśadṛṣṭi*), that is the just royal edict (*rājaśāsana*).

This is its meaning: a royal decree (*rājaśāsana*) is said to be a determination conceived solely by the king's mind that is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*māna*). Regarding this, Bṛhaspati further states that each type is twofold:
"Each one is declared to be of two kinds by the wise, due to the difference in action.
That twofold nature has been demonstrated by him [Bṛhaspati] himself.
Having thoroughly investigated the matter and deliberated upon it with reason,
and having examined it through oaths— that is to be known as the determination of dharma.
That in which the defendant admits the claim is the first form of decision;
the second is declared to be that which is properly cleared by means of ordeals.

The first determination of legal procedure (*dharmākhyanirṇaya*) is that which is carried out in accordance with the pursuit of truth (*tattvānusaraṇa*). The second is that which is carried out without the pursuit of truth, either by means of an oath (*satyottara*) or by means of divine proof (*divyapramāṇa*); such is the meaning. [23] But that legal procedure which is determined by means of evidence (*pramāṇa*) is called the second; it is proclaimed as following immediately after verbal quibbling (*vākchala*).

In this context, human testimony is intended as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that which is determined by divine means constitutes the ultimate limit of legal decision (*dharmanirṇaya*). Conduct established through inference is called "custom" (*caritra*);
however, the second [type of custom] is cited by those learned in the scriptures (*śāstravid*) as being based on local usage (*deśasthiti*).
Inference is the sign [consisting of] such things as a torch in hand. Furthermore, that which is devoid of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is known as a royal decree;
likewise, another is proclaimed as being in accordance with the method of the scriptures. Thus it is said.
The meaning of the phrase "devoid of means of valid cognition" has been explained in detail by Vyāsa:
"Written documents, witnesses, and possession are remembered as the threefold means of valid cognition;
the wise know inference to be the logical reason, and reasoning (tarka) as well."
The eighty topics previously established have been declared as the conduct;
there are oaths corresponding to the facts, such as those concerning the Smṛtis and the words of truth.
"In their absence, the wise know that the king's command constitutes the final decision.

[Objection: But if this is so, then Nārada’s statement—"The latter sublates the former"—is incoherent; for, by virtue of its greater conformity with the true nature of reality, it is the former itself that should sublate the latter.
[The King] should conduct legal proceedings by setting aside deception and relying on the facts.

And because it has been stated by Yājñavalkya thus: [it is said in reply: True; generally this is so everywhere, but in certain specific cases, the latter indeed sublates the former. And the statement of Nārada refers to such a case. For instance, when a distinguished person, such as a king or the like, out of delusion has somehow committed an act such as touching the wife of a king, and having done so, denies it out of fear for his own life, and there are witnesses who, being questioned by the king, give false testimony saying, "Let there be no execution for him," thinking "he is not the doer of this deed"—then, since the fault is attributed to one who is not the actual doer, *dharma* (the internal moral law) is sublated by *vyavahāra* (legal procedure). And the sublation of *dharma* here is appropriate, because of the injunction for witnesses to speak falsely in the rule: "But where there would be the death of those belonging to the [caste] classes... When, however, someone such as an Ābhīra is accused by another, saying, "This man has committed adultery with another's wife and there are witnesses," and he replies: "It is true that the witnesses have spoken thus, yet I am not to be punished; I did this by the force of my good character (*caritra*), and the king has recorded it in the register"—then *vyavahāra* (the legal record) is sublated by *caritra* (good character), because the punishment obtained through the legal procedure is nullified by the evidence of good character. And the sublation by *caritra* here is appropriate.
O Bṛhaspati, the legal proceedings of those residing in villages, cow-pens, cities, guilds, caravans, and armies must be decided according to established custom.

Because of this statement. Custom (*caritra*) is also sometimes set aside by royal decree: for instance, a custom was established that no royal official should enter within the precincts of a nobleman’s house. Then, when a certain offender was discovered having entered the house, the king commanded a royal official, "Enter even inside the house and bring out that wicked man. In such a case, even custom is set aside by the king's command, because the king's decree is more powerful than custom due to the necessity of suppressing the wicked. Keeping precisely such a case in mind, Bṛhaspati also said:
That legal proceeding in which a decision is made by relying solely upon the treatises should be known as a mere formal dispute; by it, Dharma is lost.

[25] A definitive conclusion is reached there through inference based on local custom and following the common understanding of the people; however, in such a case, the formal legal procedure is set aside.
"Having set aside established custom (*caritrācāra*), where the king might again issue a decision, that indeed is the royal decree (*rājājñā*); by it, custom is superseded.
Thus [it is said]. Now, the subject at hand is stated; he speaks for the purpose of explaining the four bases [of judicial procedure]:
In that regard, dharma is established in truth; legal procedure, however, rests with witnesses;
customary law resides in written records; and royal edict lies in the king's command.

The mention of witnesses is intended as an illustration for all means of proof other than divine ordeals that are established in the *dharmaśāstras*. "Pustaka" refers to written documents (*lekhyam*). He states that it has four means of accomplishment:
it is called "four-means" because it is to be accomplished through the means of conciliation (*sāman*) and the others;

the intention is that it is to be accomplished through the means of conciliation and so forth for both the plaintiff and the defendant who are in dispute. He states that it is beneficial in four ways.

Because he protects the four stages of life (*āśrama*), he is "beneficial to the four. The mention of the *āśramas* is intended to indicate the social classes (*varṇas*) as well. He describes him as "pervading the four":
"the judges, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king himself."
Because it pervades [the body] foot by foot, it is therefore remembered as "four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).

The meaning is that, when correctly or incorrectly perceived, it pervades the agent and the other factors quarter-by-quarter through the fruit of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). He speaks of one who performs fourfold action: "Of merit, of wealth, of fame, and likewise of worldly attachment."
Because she performs these four functions, she is proclaimed as the "Four-Actress."
Attachment to the world means affection for the people. He states the eight components:
"The king, his officers, the members of the court, the legal treatise, the calculator and the scribe, gold, fire, and water—these are declared to be the eight components."

We shall explain their application later on. The commentary on the two sections consisting of one hundred and eighteen topics, as shown in the preceding chapters, should be kept in mind here. He speaks of the three origins: "Since it proceeds from these three—desire, anger, and greed—it is called 'three-origin'; therefore, this triad is the cause of disputes."
The phrase "in all cases as far as possible" is the ellipsis to be supplied. He states the two types of accusation:
"The two-fold accusation, however, should be understood as arising from suspicion and from the accusation of the actual fact.
He provides an illustration for this very point:
But the suspicion regarding the wicked arises from their association, as seen in the case of stolen goods and the like.

Because of association with those who are currently wicked, even a virtuous person may be suspected of theft and other crimes by gamblers. "Observation of stolen goods" refers to the discovery of signs such as a portion of what was taken, or direct observation. This is merely an illustration; for even when the wicked associate, suspicion of deposits and the like may arise when they associate with wealthy virtuous people. Therefore, this is not the definition of an accusation based on suspicion. He states that it has two doors: "It is called 'two-doored' because it is connected to two sides;
of these two, the first side is the plaint, and the counter-plaint is its opposite."
The word "debate" (*vāda*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Gateway" (*dvāra*) refers to the engagement in the commencement of an action. He states its two-fold nature:
"Because it follows both the real (*bhūta*) and the quibble (*chala*), it is declared to be two-fold.
The real is that which is conjoined with the true meaning; the quibble is that which is stated through error. Thus.
Hārīta also mentions certain varieties:
"It has one root, two shoots, two trunks, and likewise two fruits.
Kātyāyana, however, explains these as follows:
The root of the doctrine of what is to be proven (sādhyavāda) is that which has been presented by the proponent;
"non-delivery of what is to be given" and "violence" are said to be the two grounds for challenge (utthāna).
"In the Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra, however, two branches are cited:
victory (*jaya*) and defeat (*avasāya*); these two results are fully described.
Here, *avasāya* means defeat. Furthermore, another distinction has been shown by that same author:

"The plaint (*pūrvapakṣa*), the reply (*uttara*), the judgment (*pratyākalita*), and the stage of proof (*kriyāpāda*)—therefore, this [legal proceeding] is declared to have four parts. *Pratyākalita* refers to the deliberation by the judge and others, following the acceptance of the reply, as to which of the two disputing parties should appropriately present the means of proof (*kriyā*) in this case. *Kriyā* consists of evidence such as written documents; the presentation of that is the "stage of proof" (*kriyāpāda*). Because the stages of judgment and proof also constitute parts of the legal process (*vyavahāra*) that culminates in the resolution of the dispute, it is said that "[the lawsuit] is declared to have four parts."
For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* also stated that even the concluding portion constitutes legal procedure (*vyavahāra*):
"Legal procedure is declared to be the establishment of what is just through verbal statements among humans when they have conflicting claims regarding their own interests."

Some say that *pratyākalita* is the deliberation (*vimarśana*) which, once the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) have been presented, dispels the suspicion of the absence of such means and results in the determination of victory or defeat. In their view, only the number of stages (*pāda*) is intended, not the sequence [of the specific names], because it would follow that the stage of *pratyākalita* would constitute a fourth stage. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"When that [claim] is established, he attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs."

Thus, even there, by the word *siddhi* (success), that which results in success—namely, the judgment (*pratyakalita*)—is meant, and not the determination of victory or defeat; for the latter exists even after the mutual agreement (*saṃpratipatti*), which would lead to a contradiction with the statement, "In cases of mutual agreement, [the case ends] with two steps. Therefore, the meaning of Yājñavalkya’s rule is identical to that of Kātyāyana’s statement. Others, however, interpret this statement as follows:
"By means of the plaint, the reply, the legal proceedings, and the success resulting from them, which proceed in succession..."
But when its four parts are projected [into the performance], it is designated as "four-footed" (catuṣpāda).

Thus they describe it as having the same meaning as the statement in another *smṛti*. Furthermore, they argue that because there is no presentation of a formal proof (*sādhana*) in the case of a response based on agreement (*saṃpratipatti*), and because the matter already asserted cannot be something yet to be proven, there is no "foot" characterized by the establishment of a probandum; consequently, there is no contradiction with the statement, "In cases of agreement, there are two feet. In this view, the sequence of the feet is also shown in another *smṛti*:
"The first foot therein is the *bhāṣā* (the plaint), and the second is likewise the *uttara* (the reply);
the third is the *kriyā* (the proof), and the fourth is known as the *nirṇaya* (the decision)."
Thus ends the section on the various types of legal proceedings in the Smṛticandrikā; now follows the determination of the adjudicators.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"But legal procedure, though proclaimed as manifold by the wise, is of one kind;
its decider is the king and the learned Brāhmaṇa.
Here, "Brāhmaṇa" refers to the one known as the *prāḍvivāka* (judge). And so it is said by that same [author]:

"In a dispute, he asks the question and likewise the counter-question; he speaks first with kindness—therefore he is called a *prāḍvivāka*. The meaning is that his name is etymologically derived (*yaugikī saṃjñā*): he is a *prāṭ* because he asks the plaintiff's and defendant's cases (*pūrvottarapakṣau*), and he is a *vivāka* because he specifically declares the decision (*nirṇaya*).
Nārada also, while elaborating upon the state of being highly learned (*bahuśrutatva*) in a Brāhmaṇa, has shown this designation by means of another method:
"One who is proficient in the eighteen branches of knowledge, who knows the eight thousand divisions thereof,
who is skilled in *ānvīkṣikī* and the other sciences, and who is devoted to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*."
"He who asks about the matter under dispute, the law as it has been heard, and the established opinion, and who discerns [the truth] from that, is traditionally known as the *prāḍvivāka* (judge).
[30] Thus, by the very expression of its etymological derivation, its function is also stated by both [definitions]. And it has also been stated directly by Nārada:

"Just as a physician should extract a splinter from the body by means of an instrument, so should the judge extract the splinter by means of legal procedure. And regarding the phrase "and a Brāhmaṇa," the word "and" (ca) is intended to include other types of judges; for this very reason, Manu says:

"In those places where men most frequently engage in disputes, they should carry out their adjudication by relying upon the eternal Dharma. This means "in those places" refers to the eighteen titles of law (*aṣṭādaśapada*). Kātyāyana also says:
"Accompanied by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), the ministers, the Brahmins and the royal chaplain, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven through righteousness as a witness.

Here, the *prāḍvivāka* has the characteristics previously described; "accompanied by the judge" means existing together with him. Similarly, the analysis of the compounds *sāmātya* and so forth should be understood according to the numbers that will be stated later. Furthermore, the definition of a minister (*amātya*) has been stated by Vyāsa:
"One should appoint as a minister a learned Brahmin who knows the meaning of all treatises, is free from greed, speaks with justice, is wise, and has come down through hereditary succession.

Although the term "Brahmin" (*vipra*) was already used, the further mention of "twice-born" (*dvija*) is intended to show that even in the absence of a Brahmin possessing the aforementioned characteristics, one may appoint a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who possesses those same traits as a minister, but never a Śūdra. For he (the author) says the same:
"He who, setting aside the twice-born, should look after affairs together with the śūdras—
his kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish. In this [verse],
the singular number used for "minister" (amātyam) is merely illustrative, as it resides within the subject of the statement.

"He should enter the assembly hall humbled, accompanied by ministers who are experts in counsel"—since Manu thus prescribes entry into the assembly with many ministers, and because of the inclusion of the qualification "experts in counsel" (*mantrajñaiḥ*), it is established that they are useful here insofar as they deliberate on the counsel necessary for overseeing state affairs. Likewise, plurality is also stated regarding Brahmins by that same author:
"But the king, desiring to see legal proceedings, [should sit] together with Brahmins."

Thus, by the first half [of the verse]. The word "by learned Brāhmaṇas" is to be supplied as the remainder. And so says Yājñavalkya: "The king shall examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas. Although there is no distinction between these [members] and others on account of their learning, their being Brāhmaṇas, their plurality, and their integrity in the assembly, nevertheless, their distinction from them must be determined by the fact that they are not appointed. For they are indeed appointed. Therefore Vasiṣṭha says:
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma is fit to speak;
he who lives by the scriptures speaks the divine word.
As for that which was said by Nārada:
One who has not been appointed must never speak at all in a legal proceeding;
however, one who has been appointed must speak words that are impartial.

Thus, this refers to the appointment of those who have arrived by chance or due to other business; otherwise, it would contradict the previously cited statements and lead to the undesirable consequence that Brāhmaṇas would be compelled to engage in other tasks merely to fulfill their role as assistants. However, there should be only one domestic priest (*purohita*). Accordingly, Vyāsa says:
"The king should appoint a domestic priest who is a Brāhmaṇa from the North (Udīcya), well-disposed toward him, perfected in Vedic learning and study, free from greed, and truthful."

In this context, singularity is intended, because it resides in that which is to be produced, just as in the expression "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*). By saying "beneficial," he shows that the king's unrestrained activity regarding those who should not be punished must be restrained by the domestic priest (*purohita*). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha has prescribed an expiation even for the priest when the king transgresses the purpose of the science of punishment: "Upon the release of one deserving of punishment, the king shall fast for one night, and the priest for three nights; upon failing to punish one who does not deserve punishment, the priest shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance, and the king for three nights. Furthermore, the members of the court (*sabhyāḥ*) are many; and so says Nārada.

"The king, however, should appoint righteous assessors who have been well-tested, who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings like excellent oxen. The phrase "he should appoint assessors" means for the purpose of overseeing legal proceedings; the sense is that he should engage them through such means as providing wealth and honor so that they do not abandon their presence in the court. When it is asked who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings, Yājñavalkya [states]: [33]

"Those who are accomplished in learning and study, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend—these should be appointed by the king as members of the court.
These [members] also must be Brāhmaṇas alone. And so says Kātyāyana:
"But he [the king] should be joined by stable members of the assembly— wise, hereditary, and the best of the twice-born—
who are skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras and proficient in the Arthaśāstra.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states those who are to be excluded:
"Those who are ignorant of local customs, atheists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge,
the insane, the angry, the greedy, and the afflicted— these should not be questioned in a formal legal determination.
Thus he [the same author] also stated the rule regarding their number.
"A council where there sit seven, five, or even three Brahmins who are knowers of the world, the Vedas, their auxiliary sciences, and the Dharma— that assembly is equal to a sacrifice."

In this matter, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) and others are merely assistants, like officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because they seek wealth; they possess no independent authority (*adhikāra*). It should be understood that the authority for the administration of justice belongs to the king alone. For this very reason, in the passage beginning with "together with the judge," he alone is mentioned as the primary subject, not the others; furthermore, the connection with the fruit of the action is stated to belong to him alone, and not to the others. There is a fault in acting otherwise; moreover, by the force of the *smṛti* texts, the king’s authority is perpetual: "Punishing those who should not be punished, and failing to punish those who deserve punishment, the king incurs great infamy and goes to hell."

Thus, because Manu records that the fault belongs specifically to the king, it is for this very reason that the rule regarding the entry of those other than the king into the court has been shown by him alone:
"Either one should not enter the court, or one should speak what is just;
by not speaking or by speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner."
Furthermore, the rule for a king’s entry into the assembly hall was shown by Bṛhaspati:
"The king, surrounded by three virtuous men, should examine the legal cases after entering the foremost assembly hall, whether seated or standing."

The meaning is that he is surrounded by exactly three *sabhyas* (court members), and not by only one or two; therefore, there is no contradiction with the previously stated number of court members. Consequently, it is established that, as in the *Rājasūya*, the king alone has the authority (*adhikāra*) in the administration of justice. By the word "king" (*rājan*) here, one who performs the duties of sovereignty—whether belonging to the Kṣatriya caste or another caste, whether consecrated (*abhiṣikta*) or unconsecrated, and whether protecting the subjects—is denoted through a figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*). This is not because of the etymological rule (*śābdasmṛti*) that "the kingdom (*rājya*) is the act of a king (*rājan*)," nor because the word "king" is primary (*mukhya*) only for the Kṣatriya-born according to the logic of the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice (where "king" refers specifically to a Kṣatriya in the phrase "the king [performs] the Rājasūya"). For it has already been stated in the *Aveṣṭyadhikaraṇa* that the usage of the word "king" by the noble Manu and others in reference to one who performs sovereignty is figurative. Precisely for this reason, Bṛhaspati has declared the admission of any ruler (*nṛpati*) whatsoever into the assembly.
Having risen in the morning and performed purification according to the prescribed rules,
the king [should honor] his gurus, astrologers, physicians, deities, Brahmins, and domestic priests.

"Having honored these [guests] as is fitting with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments, and having paid obeisance to his elders and others, he, being cheerful of countenance, shall enter the assembly hall.

For this very reason, Yājñavalkya also ordained that the investigation of legal cases belongs to him alone: "The king shall examine the legal proceedings. As for that which was stated by Prajāpati: [35]
A king consecrated for his coronation, or a learned Brāhmaṇa,
seated upon the seat of justice, should examine legal cases with impartiality.

Thus—"not haughty" means not arrogant—this too is for the purpose of enjoining that the consecrated king must perform the examination of legal cases, and not for the purpose of prohibiting others; for if that were the case, it would result in a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*). For this very reason, it was stated immediately thereafter by that same author:
"In this manner, the Kṣatriya vassals [should judge] separately in their own respective territories;
however, for other kings, a preeminent Brāhmaṇa should act [as judge]."

The kṣatriya vassals, being gentle and seated upon the Dharma-throne, should oversee legal proceedings. As for other kings—those belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, and other castes—the meaning is that they should always appoint a preeminent Brāhmaṇa as the overseer of legal proceedings in order to fulfill their own authority. As for the alternative view stated by him, namely, "or a Brāhmaṇa who is highly learned," even that is not intended to establish the Brāhmaṇa's exclusive right; rather, it is intended to show that even in the absence of a king, a highly learned person may act as the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) by royal appointment. This is because it has already been demonstrated that the Brāhmaṇa has no inherent right to oversee legal proceedings. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: "In the oversight of legal proceedings, one should appoint a Brāhmaṇa. Bṛhaspati also speaks with this same intention.

"The king, or else a Brahmin acting as the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka), should examine the cases, having placed the constituent elements of justice at the forefront and remaining steadfast in the opinion of the court members and the scriptures. And this is an alternative course only when the king does not personally investigate them; for thus says Manu: [36]...

"When the king himself does not personally conduct the investigation of legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to investigate those cases. Here, "learned" means one who is highly erudite. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"One who studies only a single treatise cannot know how to determine what must be done;
therefore, kings should ensure that those who possess extensive traditional knowledge (*āgama*) are present in legal disputes.
The mention of "extensive traditional knowledge" is intended to indicate other qualities as well. Thus it has been said:
"A man who is not cruel, sweet-tempered, affectionate, hereditary, discerning, energetic, and free from greed— such a person should be appointed by the king to the office of debate.
Thus it was said by Kātyāyana as well.
When the king does not personally carry out the decision of a legal case, he should then appoint a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the scriptures to do so.
"One who is capable, of noble birth, impartial, not causing alarm, steady, fearful of the hereafter, most righteous, diligent, and free from anger.
Thus [it is said]. The phrase "because of a particular other matter" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. And so says Yājñavalkya:

"But by a king who, due to the pressure of business, is unable to oversee legal proceedings, a Brāhmaṇa learned in all the Dharmas should be appointed together with the court members (*sabhyas*). This means that when a king is unable to oversee legal proceedings because he is preoccupied with other more important matters, a judge named *Prāḍvivāka* should be appointed together with exactly three court members, rather than with ministers and others. For this very reason, Manu says:
[37] "Surrounded by exactly three members of the assembly, he should examine his duties, having entered the foremost hall, either seated or standing.
The restriction "by exactly [three]" is for the purpose of excluding others; and "by three" is for the purpose of excluding the numbers five or seven. With this very intention, Vyāsa also says:

"Having observed that a dispute has arisen, he deliberates with diligence together with the members of the court; for this reason, he is known as the *prāḍvivāka* (judge). On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"But where there is no Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the Dharmaśāstras; one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort. Here, "learned" is to be supplied [to the word Brāhmaṇa]. And likewise, that same author says:
"Where there may be no learned Brāhmaṇa, one should employ a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the Dharmaśāstras; but one should not, even with effort, exclude a Śūdra.

By the word "Kṣatriya," it is understood that the term "learned" applies here as well, since it is prescribed as a substitute for a learned Brāhmaṇa. By using the expression "with effort," he shows that a grave loss results from failing to avoid [an unqualified person]. And this has been stated by Manu:
"But the kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow in the mud while [the king] looks on.
Therefore, even when Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas learned in the Dharmaśāstras are unavailable, a Śūdra is to be avoided. And so it has been stated by that same [author]:

"One who lives by his birth alone may indeed be called a 'pseudo-Brāhmaṇa' (brāhmaṇabruva), but he must never, under any circumstances, be a Śūdra acting as a teacher of dharma to the king. Thus, one who lives by his birth alone is not one who lives by learning or vows. Vyāsa, however, speaks of the fault in employing a Śūdra even in positions such as that of a minister.
"He who, setting aside the twice-born, should look after affairs together with Śūdras—his kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish.

Thus, the intention is that for the sake of avoiding such faults, one should exclude Śūdras even from positions such as those of ministers. Likewise, Kātyāyana states that for the purpose of pleasing the kingdom, the king should sit in the assembly together with a few merchants as well.
"It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good character, youth, proper conduct, and wealth, and who are free from envy;
'possessing noble lineage' (kulabhūtaiḥ) means being in a collective body (vṛndabhūtaiḥ). Thus he [the author] also states their duty:
"In that regard, listeners should be made judges according to the principles of justice.
Likewise, Bṛhaspati states that the king should also appoint calculators and scribes:
"Those who know the true nature of words and designations, who are skilled in calculation, and who are pure..."
"The king should appoint as astrologer and scribe two men who are proficient in various scripts. Vyāsa also says:
"One who is an expert in the three branches of astrology and who produces clear, verifiable results..."
The king should appoint an accountant who is perfected in both learning and study.
"One should appoint a clear-writer who is pure, skilled in the casting of words, one with distinct characters, free from anger, non-greedy, and truthful" (39).

"One who is proficient in the three branches of astrology"—the meaning is: one who is expert in the science of astrology consisting of the three branches of *hora*, *gaṇita*, and *saṃhitā*. The qualification "endowed with learning and Vedic study" is for the purpose of indicating that the calculator (*gaṇaka*) must be of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) caste, since that is impossible for a *śūdra* and others. Because of his association with them, the scribe (*lekhaka*) must also be a twice-born. For this very reason, in order to exclude the status of being a twice-born from the *sādhyapāla*, [the text specifies:]...
The king should appoint as the protector of the defendant a person who can prove the case,
who has come down by hereditary succession, who is steadfast, who is a Śūdra, and who abides by the opinion of the members of the court.

Thus, the mention of the *śūdra* was made by that very [author]. The meaning is: regarding the task of summoning the names of the defendant, the plaintiff, witnesses, and so forth for the purpose of the trial (*sādhya*). And so says Bṛhaspati: "In summoning and in protecting the witnesses, the plaintiff, and the defendant, the judge must appoint his own servant as a truthful speaker, who is dependent upon the members of the court."

"Summons without cause" means an invitation. The meaning is that the king must appoint his own official, who has come through hereditary succession, as the presiding judge (*sabhyādhi*). Thus, these have been declared by Manu and others as the superior venues for judicial decision. However, Bhṛgu has also mentioned inferior venues for decision:
"Bhṛgu declared ten and five places of litigation, by which litigants reach a decision once they have entered into a dispute."
And those fifteen locations have been shown by him as follows:
"Forest-dwellers should [use] their own [locations]; those traveling with a caravan are prescribed [to use] those of a caravan;
soldiers [should use] those of soldiers; and even in a village, those who dwell in both [types of places]."
And with the consent of both parties, the clan-chiefs, the leaders of the caravans, and the inhabitants of the cities and villages accept the desired site.
“Village communities, guilds, and corporations; those learned in the four Vedas and organized groups;
families and family heads; appointed officials, and likewise the king. Thus it is said.

In this context, there are five places where legal proceedings may be conducted, specifically for the various classes of people such as forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) and others. When a dispute arises among people living in the form of a village, the decision is reached by those residing nearby. The inhabitants of the place—whether they be heads of families, leaders of caravans, or prominent citizens of towns and villages—take up the case with the consent of the plaintiff and the defendant, provided there is no subsequent regret. The ten types of places, beginning with the village, are common [to all]. A "village" (*grāma*) refers to people settled in the form of a village. A "citizen" (*paura*) is a collective body of town-dwellers. A "guild" (*gaṇa*) is a collection of families; indeed, a multitude of families is proclaimed to be a *gaṇa*.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) of Kātyāyana: "Guilds (śreṇī) consist of the eighteen low-born castes, such as washermen and others; the 'knower of the fourfold science' (cāturvidya) is one endowed with the fourfold knowledge beginning with Ānvīkṣakī. The word 'and' in the phrase 'and the knower of the fourfold science' is intended to include the knower of the fourfold science together with other learned persons; therefore, it should not be said that [the decision] may be made by a single person who knows the rule, for Pitāmaha prohibits the declaration of dharma by a single individual. Guilds (varginaḥ) refer to groups and the like.
Bṛhaspati says that *gaṇas*, groups of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍapūgas*), associations (*vrātas*), guilds (*śreṇis*), and whatever other collective bodies exist, are designated as "corporations" (*vargyas*).

Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana. The mention of Bṛhaspati is intended to show that this designation is already well-established in the context of *gaṇas* and the like; for he himself has stated: "A *vrāta* is a collection of those who bear weapons; those who have assembled as a *vrāta* are said to be those who bear various weapons. "Families" (*kulāni*) refers to the lineages (*sagotra*) of the plaintiff and the defendant. "Family elders" (*kulikāḥ*) are certain elderly members born of the lineages of the plaintiff and the defendant. "Commissioned officials" (*niyuktāḥ*) are the three members of the court (*sabhyāḥ*) together with the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*). The "king" (*nṛpatiḥ*) is accompanied by Brāhmaṇas and others. [41]
On this point, Bṛhaspati says: "The assembly is declared to be of four kinds: established, unestablished, sealed, and likewise learned; and the members of the assembly are of the same types."

The assembly (*sabhā*) located in the three places beginning with the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) is "unestablished" (*apratiṣṭhitā*).
