Whatever custom has been established in a particular region and persists there at all times,
provided it does not contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, that is called a "local practice" (deśadṛṣṭa).
And he himself said that this must be entered into a book:
"The legal settlement determined with the consent of the country shall always be maintained in writing, sealed with the royal seal."
"She must be protected with effort according to the scriptures; having observed her, one should reach a decision.
The word "her" (*tām*) is used for the purpose of indicating that this rule applies even to a settlement approved by the family and others. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says:
"Whatever the best person practices, whether it be righteous or unrighteous..."
That which arises from the customs of one's family and locality is proclaimed as *caritra*.
O Bṛhaspati, the legal proceedings of those residing in villages, cow-pens, cities, guilds, caravans, and armies must be decided according to established custom.

This concerns matters of mutual dispute among those residing in villages and the like; however, in their disputes with others, the decision must be reached solely by means of what is seen in the authoritative scriptures (śāstra). And so says that same [author]:

"For those dwelling in regions, towns, cow-pens, cities, or villages, [the law] is according to their own conventions; in cases other than these, it is together with them [determined] from the Dharmaśāstras."
And where these grounds of proof do not exist, the decision there is based on the word of the king; thus he himself has said:
"Where neither a written document exists, nor possession, nor witnesses, and where there is no application of divine ordeals, the king is the authority there."
"Those discourses which cannot be determined and whose nature is doubtful—
for these, the king shall be the authority, since he is the lord of all.
Thus says Hārīta on this point.

Legal procedure that is consistent with what is declared in the Dharmaśāstras and Arthaśāstras, characterized by the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas), and free from deceit— that is righteous (dhārmika).
"Righteous" means not deviating from the Dharma. Nārada has declared the fruit for a king who perceives things in this way:
"For a self-disciplined king who adjudicates legal cases according to the Dharma, seven virtues arise, like the seven flames of a fire."
The meaning is that seven qualities arise from fire, just as its seven flames do. He [the author] states those qualities himself:
"Virtue, wealth, fame, the ripening of the world, favor, great respect from the subjects, and an eternal station in heaven."

The ripening of the world is the winning of the people's affection; "favor" means being worthy of reliance. By the punishment of the wicked and the gathering together of the virtuous, kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrifices.

Yājñavalkya also says: "The king who punishes those deserving of punishment and properly executes those deserving of death has performed sacrifices accompanied by hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees."
[60] Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his councilors, should personally examine legal cases every day, each yielding a fruit equal to that of a sacrifice.

The expression "every day" refers to days other than the fourteenth, the new moon, the full moon, and the eighth. Thus says Saṃvarta: "On these lunar days—the fourteenth, the new moon, the full moon, and likewise the eighth—one should never engage in legal transactions."
On other lunar days as well, [he should do so] specifically before the turning of the day (āvartana). And so Bṛhaspati says:
"Having occupied that [throne] in the forenoon, together with his aged ministers and dependents, he should look upon and likewise listen to the ancient treatises on dharma and artha."
"The king, surrounded by exactly three members of the court, should examine the legal cases.

This means [he should do so] in that court possessing the characteristics previously described. Even during the forenoon, he should do so only after the first four *ghaṭikās* have passed, because that [initial period] is intended for the performance of the *agnihotra* and other such rites. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"That which follows the third of the eight parts of the day..."
"That time is declared by the scriptures to be the ultimate limit for legal proceedings.
Within this period, measured in three parts, he should constantly examine the case. And so Pitāmaha says:
"The scribe, the calculator, the legal treatise, the bailiff, and the members of the court..."
Gold, fire, and water are recorded as the eightfold instruments [of ordeal];
having sat upon them, he should constantly examine the business reported by the citizens.
The mention of "citizens" (*paura*) is intended as an illustration for all people residing within one's own kingdom. And so says Manu:
"Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects after having greeted them."

"In that assembly" is the meaning. Even among the subjects, he should not personally initiate a dispute and then proceed to hear it. And so says Pitāmaha: "But he should not look [at the case] having himself conjectured it, nor by means of a person. The phrase "or by a person" is a prohibition against a person commissioned by the king or one conjectured by him; it does not, however, refer to a mere person in general. If it were otherwise, even the hearing of a case conjectured by a person related to the plaintiff or the defendant would be prohibited. For this very reason, Manu has specified the nature of the person.
"The king himself, nor his official, shall initiate a legal case on their own behalf"—the phrase "of men who do not litigate" is to be understood as the ellipsis. And so says Nārada:
"But neither by virtue of his authority, nor again out of greed for wealth, shall the king [initiate a suit]."
But he should initiate legal proceedings for those men who do not dispute among themselves.

"Legal matters" (*kāryāṇi*) means disputes (*vivādāni*). Likewise, Manu states that even a matter arising from the subjects themselves must not be accepted by the judge if it has not been reported by the litigant or someone related to them, having been learned of only by some other means:

"And one must never seize a matter not brought forward by another. "Not brought forward" (*aprāpitam*) means not reported; "by any means whatsoever" (*kathaṃcana*) means through passion and so forth. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says:
"A king, while seizing wealth not brought by others, does so neither out of passion, nor greed, nor anger, nor even by his own whim.
(62) "By others" means by accusers. Regarding this, he [the author] states the exception:
A king should himself take cognizance of these— transgressions, offenses, and the legal precedents of kings— even without petitioners.
Regarding that, he himself stated the fallacies:
"One who breaks the paths, one who hurls objects with his hands, one who leaps over the ramparts,
and likewise one who destroys a water reservoir or a sanctuary."
One who fills in the moats and reveals the king's vulnerabilities;
[one who enters] the inner apartments, the bedchamber, the treasury, and the kitchen.
He who enters uninvited and gazes upon the food,
desiring to discharge excrement, urine, phlegm, or wind before the king.
Furthermore, one who enters while sitting cross-legged, obstructing the place of honor,
or wearing attire superior to that of the king, shall be punished.
And whoever should enter through a side door at an improper time,
as well as [climb] onto a bed, a seat, sandals, or a couch;
He who stands nearby on the king's private couch,
or who serves those hostile to the king, or who occupies a seat not granted to him;
He who takes gold from clothing or ornaments,
and he who, having taken betel-leaf by his own hand, should chew it;

One who speaks without being appointed, one who reviles the king, one wearing only a single garment, as well as one who is anointed with oil, one with disheveled hair, and one whose head is wrapped in a cloth;
With his limbs adorned and wearing garlands, shaking his lower garment,
covering his head, and intent on searching for faults.
"One who is attached, one with disheveled hair, one who plucks at the ears or eyes,
one who scrapes the teeth, and one who cleans the ears or nose—
these fifty deceptions occur in the presence of a king. Thus it is said.

Lying upon the king’s bed, sitting upon his seat, and stepping upon his sandals—these are the three forms of deception (*chala*). Regarding the phrase "and likewise of clothes and ornaments," it should be understood that the word "one who takes what is not given" (*adattagrāhaka*) is to be supplied as the subject. The repetition of the term "with disheveled hair" (*muktakeśa*) is for the purpose of including one who is shaven-headed (*muṇḍa*) as well. The remainder is clear in meaning. Nārada states the offenses: "Disobedience of commands, killing a woman, intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṅkara*), adultery with another’s wife, theft, and [abandoning] a fetus without its father."
"Verbal abuse, that which is unspeakable, physical assault, and the causing of an abortion—these indeed are the ten offenses.
The implication is that the king himself should investigate these cases even without a complainant. And so says Saṃvarta:
The king himself, without the litigants, may investigate matters concerning arrest, the obstruction of roads, and a woman pregnant without her husband.
If the acquisition of any visible property is not seen anywhere to have come from a legal source,
the king himself should investigate it, even without a litigant.
The king himself should investigate the destruction of an assembly hall, the cutting down of trees, and damage to crops, even without a litigant.
The king himself shall investigate the crime of abducting a maiden, as well as a fallen Brahmin and one who is engaged in speaking for the sake of another.
One who obstructs the roads for the sake of the sixth-part tax or customs duties,
one who causes fear through theft within his own kingdom, and one who violates another's wife.
The king himself should investigate these ten offenses: the slayer of a cow or a Brahmin, and likewise one who destroys crops.

The meaning is that the king himself shall adjudicate these ten offenses, beginning with obstruction (*āsedha*). Here, the mention of "obstructing the path" (*pathibhaṅga*) is for the purpose of illustrating *chala* (fraudulent pretexts), while the inclusion of some among the ten offenses is for the purpose of illustrating those [other types of *chala*]. The mention of "one who destroys crops" (*sasyaghātuka*), however, is for the purpose of illustrating the *pada*s (categories). And all the *pada*s have been shown by Pitāmaha (Bṛhaspati): "The one who cuts [the crop], the one who destroys the crop, the arsonist, likewise the one who ruins [property], the one who violates a maiden, and the one who guards a hidden treasure."
One who destroys bridges or thorns, one who trespasses upon fields,
one who cuts down groves, and likewise one who administers poison;
One who commits treason against the king, one who breaks his seal,
one who divulges his secret counsel, and one who releases a prisoner who has been bound;
He collects fines for enjoyment and fines for punishment, as well as gifts and even excessive levies; he seizes property that has no owner, such as that proclaimed by the beating of drums.

"Substances licked by the king, and whatever causes the destruction of the body—these twenty-two points, the wise say, are to be known by the king. (65) Thus, having recognized *chala* (fraud) and the other categories either directly or through the statements of informers (*stobhaka*) and spies (*sūcaka*), they should be investigated by the king. It should be understood, however, that other matters are to be known by the litigant or someone connected to them, and not otherwise. Kātyāyana states the definitions of the informer and the spy:
But he who, though primarily motivated by wealth, first reports a matter condemned by the scriptures, being impelled by his own interest, is declared to be a *stobhaka* (an obstructer).
One who is appointed by the king himself to observe the faults of others,
and having learned of them, reports them to the king, is designated as a *sūcaka* (informant).
"Primarily concerned with the welfare of others" means that he has the welfare of others as his main objective. Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"Having understood the treatises, the duties of the social classes, the duties of the various castes, and the nature of legal procedure, the king should carry out all of that."
Furthermore, the *prakṛtis* have been shown by the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the *buruḍa*, the fisherman,
as well as the *mleccha* and the *bhillā*, are to be known [as such]."
Vemara, Sthiravi, Vyādha, Hastalākṣa, Drughaṭṭaka;
Kosedaka, Ābhīra, Padma, Mātaṅga, Aṇḍa, and Upagopa.
"These eighteen constituent elements have been declared by the wise to always stand outside the castes and the stages of life.
Furthermore, the nature of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) has been described in the very first section. Manu also says:
Having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the eternal laws of guilds, and the family laws, he should cause them to be maintained within their respective groups.

The "laws of guilds" (*śreṇīdharma*) refer to such rules as those established for merchants, artisans, and others within their own respective groups, such as: "this item must not be sold on this day," or "this item may be sold only by this specific guild. The "family laws" (*kuladharma*) refer to such traditions as: "in this family, the piercing of the ears must be performed on the fifth day or in the fifth year," and so forth. "He should cause them to be maintained" means he should make them known. And if they do not observe them, he should compel them to do so by force, except in times of distress. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
Having disciplined those who have strayed from their own duty— be they families, subjects, guilds, or even rural districts— the king shall establish them once more on the right path.
Nārada, however, describes the manner of examining the case:
"Placing the treatises on Dharma before him and abiding by the opinion of the presiding judge,
he should examine the legal cases in their proper order with a concentrated mind."
"Successively" means by hearing the statements of the plaintiff in due order; and thus that same [author] says:

"The first stage is the legal tradition (āgama), then the subject matter of the lawsuit (vyavahārapada), then the investigation, and finally the decision; thus the judicial process (darśana) is fourfold."

"Āgama" (the plaintiff's statement) is the hearing of the words of the claimant; that must be performed first. Then, those words must be included within one of the legal titles (*padas*), such as non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth. Following that is the investigation of the plaint, the reply, and the means of proof (*pramāṇa*); thereafter, victory is determined by means of the evidence. Thus it is explained in his commentary (*bhāṣya*). Regarding this, Manu says:
"A lord who seeks his own welfare must always forgive litigants who revile him, as well as children, the elderly, and the sick."
Because he endures insults from those in distress, he is glorified in heaven;
but because he does not endure them out of pride in his power, he goes to hell.
Thus ends the procedure for the audience in the *Smṛticandrikā* [67].
Now follows the procedure for the injunctions (*āsedha*).
In that regard, Nārada says: "The plaintiff shall restrain one who stands silent when a matter must be spoken, or who departs from the court,
by means of legal process until the appearance for summons."

Even when a matter is doubtful, one who disregards the statement of the claimant—such as "one should remain indifferent toward a decision and proceed toward a resolution"—the king shall restrain by royal command; he shall block him up to the point of summoning for the purpose of witnessing the legal proceeding, meaning for the sake of reaching a verdict on the dispute. He states that this restraint is of four kinds: "Restraint of place, restraint by time, likewise restraint from travel, and restraint from activity—restraint is thus fourfold; one who is restrained must not transgress it."

Restriction of place (*sthānāsedha*) is confinement such that one must not move from places like one's home or a temple. Restriction by time (*kālakṛta*) is of this nature: that one must present oneself on the fifth day and so forth, otherwise one has transgressed the king’s command. Restriction from travel (*pravāsād āsedha*) is the prevention of departure. Restriction of activity (*karmaṇa āsedha*) is the prohibition of activities such as the display of merchandise for sale, but not of activities such as inspection. As Kātyāyana says:

"But he who, by restraining the senses or by [stopping] speech, breathing, and so forth, should restrict one who is not subject to restriction, shall be punished; he is not a transgressor [of the law]."

The meaning is that because the restraint of the senses and so forth involves great difficulty (*saṅkaṭa*), the transgression of a royal command in such a case does not bring about fault. For this very reason, Nārada states that there is no offense even in cases of difficulty such as crossing a river:

"In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, difficult terrain, or being beset by calamity, one who has not yet achieved his goal and who bypasses a prohibition shall not be held at fault. (NSm 1.145)

"Crossing a river" refers to the act of crossing a river. A "kāntāra" is a difficult path. A "durdeśa" is a region infested with wicked thieves, tigers, and the like. An "upaplava" is being distressed by enemy forces and so forth. In such circumstances, there is no offense even if one transgresses a command. However, Pitāmaha states that in other cases there is an offense: "He by whom the king's command is transgressed, especially when it ought to be carried out, has committed treachery against the seven-limbed kingdom."

But where there is an offense due to the transgression of an order, Vyāsa states the punishment: "One who is subject to restraint and who, having been restrained, departs, deserves punishment. Nārada also says:
If one who has been placed under restraint at the time of restraint violates that restraint, he should be punished;
otherwise, the one who imposed the restraint shall be liable for a fine.
"Acting otherwise" means restraining one who should not be restrained; and so Vyāsa says:
"But he who restrains those who should not be restrained shall be punished by the king—this is the settled rule.
Kātyāyana states who those are who should not be restrained:
Those who have climbed trees or mountains, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those in difficult positions, should not be interrogated by those seeking to accomplish their purpose.
Those afflicted by disease, those in distress, and likewise those performing sacrifices;

those who have not yet crossed over [to the other side], as well as those intoxicated, insane, or mentally dull—these should not be obstructed. Nor should a farmer at the time of sowing seeds, nor a soldier during the time of military service.
Having made his vow, he set forth, and he did not die prematurely along the way.
A farmer who is diligently engaged with his crops, from the commencement of work until the harvest, shall not be sued during that time, even if water arrives.
The intention is that there is no fixed time limit [for such cases]. Bṛhaspati also says:

"One who has undertaken a sacrificial session (sattra), one intent on marriage, the sick, those afflicted by grief, the insane, children, the intoxicated, the elderly, one who is commissioned, and one engaged in essential work—even if he is under a vow [is not to be summoned]."
A soldier in the midst of battle, a farmer during the harvest, those in a state of distress, and likewise women accompanied by their protectors, must not be obstructed.

In battle or in war; even Nārada says: "One who desires to enter into a contract, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal business [should not be summoned]."
Cowherds [are summoned] when cattle graze; farmers at the beginning of the sowing of crops;
artisans at that time [of need]; and those who bear arms during a conflict.
A messenger, one who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and those in a precarious situation must not be obstructed; nor shall the king summon them.

One desirous of settling [a debt] is one facing marriage. "Pasture for cattle" refers to the entrance of a forest. "Not having attained legal capacity" means being less than sixteen years of age. "Those in distress" are those whose entire property has been seized by thieves and the like. Vyāsa also says: "One who is ill, one desiring to sacrifice, one who is insane, one seeking merit, one engaged in a profession, one observing a vow, or one intent on giving a gift—such a person should not be sued, nor should he be obstructed, nor should he be summoned."

Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the specific rule: "But when the grain has sprouted, a farmer who has sold his merchandise as a merchant, as well as those who were striving in trade and those who have completed their transactions, shall not be liable for the loss. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the section on restraint (*āsedha*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now begins the commencement of the trial (*darśanopakrama*).
Regarding this, Manu says:
Having occupied the Dharma-seat, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should begin the examination of legal cases after bowing to the guardians of the world.
The phrase "at the time prescribed by the scriptures" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"At the proper time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a prostration:
'What is your business? What is your grievance? Do not fear; speak, O man!'"

"What is the matter? is a question for the purpose of knowing whether a gift was withheld; "what is the injury? is for [knowing] violence. Likewise, he states that the presiding judge (sabhāpati) must pose four questions in order to fully ascertain the agent, the place, the time, and the cause of those two: "By whom, where, when, and why?"—thus he should question one who has come before the court.

Thus questioned, the seeker of justice should then inform him of the matter to be stated. And so Yājñavalkya says: "When one who has been oppressed by others through a path contrary to the law and custom brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a ground for legal action."

By this, it is stated by implication that the plaintiff should report the injury inflicted by another. Here, the word "if" (*cet*) is intended to indicate that the reporting should be done out of one's own desire to inform, and not by royal command. [71] The plural form "by others" (*paraiḥ*) is used for the sake of illustration. For this very reason, Kātyāyana demonstrated the question regarding the perpetrator of the offense using the singular form "by whom? (*kena*). The inclusion of the term "assaulted" (*ādharṣita*) is for the purpose of designating the party entitled to litigate in a dispute, and not the actual perpetrator. Whether appointed by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant—
Of two people who dispute for the sake of one another, there is victory and defeat.

Thus, because Kātyāyana states that even one who is appointed [as an agent] in a dispute possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*), the mention of the "appointed" person is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for his [the appointer's] kin as well. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says: "If the father, brother, friend, kinsman, or even a relative should act as the representative (*upasthāna*), one should proceed with the lawsuit there."

"Whatever one may cause another to do by means of any person through an appointment, that should be known as done by that very person; for it is declared to be irrevocable. Thus, it should be understood that the plaint must be filed either by the plaintiff himself or by a person belonging to him, and not by anyone else. For this very reason, Nārada says:
He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under appointment,
yet speaks for the sake of another, shall be punished if he gives false testimony in legal proceedings.
Kātyāyana also says:
"Slaves, laborers, disciples, appointed officials, and likewise kinsmen are not to be punished as litigants; however, anyone other than these shall be subject to punishment."
Likewise, Uśanas states that even one who makes a formal accusation is liable to punishment if he speaks while undisciplined at the time of the accusation:
"One who is armed, one who is without an upper garment, one with disheveled hair, one accompanied by weapons,
or one wearing a garland with his left hand, shall incur punishment for speaking."

Therefore, the intention is that one who is not of such a nature should speak [the truth]. Consequently, the scribe shall write down all those words upon a wooden board or similar surface. And so says Nārada:

"If, provoked by one of the parties through passion or other motives, he should speak during the legal proceeding, he shall write down all of that as 'Om' for the plaintiff upon the wooden board and other such surfaces."

"In the act" means in the presence of the king and others. And that written document—such as "I gave this wealth to him in a previous birth, yet he does not give it back"—if it is not unfit for judicial inquiry, then one should perform acts such as giving a seal to summon the defendant. Thus says Kātyāyana:

"What he says when questioned in this manner, the judges, together with the Brāhmaṇas, should deliberate upon; if the matter is just, then [the summons] follows thereafter for the purpose of calling him."
Or he should place a seal upon it, or he should command a man [to do so].

In that case, regarding the complainant: the person is the guardian of the object to be proven (*sādhyapāla*). "Proper" means suitable. The phrase "for the purpose of summoning" refers to the accused; this is the ellipsis. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"Whether on account of a formal charge or out of suspicion, the king shall cause that very person to be brought by means of a seal or by a messenger."
The intention is that, regarding the giving of a reply, only he has the authority; for this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
"Authority belongs to the one who is accused, and not to another, because of the lack of connection."

The meaning is that for another person who is not formally accused, there is no right to provide a reply because he lacks a connection to that dispute. Therefore, the status of being a respondent (*uttaravādin*) for the other does not arise spontaneously; rather, it occurs because he is made a defendant by the accuser, or because he is handed over to the judge as one who must perform his duty, or because he voluntarily accepts the role of a defendant at the request of the plaintiff. It is not otherwise. As that same author says: "The other is also considered an opponent when he is obstructed by the accused;
or when another person, different from the one [initially named], is handed over by the plaintiff to the judicial authority."
That person who has himself accepted [the opponent's position] should be known as the respondent (prativādin).

This is the meaning: another, though unrelated to the dispute, who has been made an opponent (*pratirodhī*) or a defendant (*prativādī*) by the plaintiff (*abhiyukta*), and who is recognized as the respondent (*uttaravādī*) by Manu and others—that is to be known as the second type. Likewise, there is another, a different one, who is unrelated to the dispute but has been presented to the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), the authority over dharma, by the plaintiff, or who has himself accepted the role of a defendant. This status of being a defendant for one who lacks formal standing (*anadhikārī*) should be understood to apply to cases involving those who are incompetent (*akalya*) and so forth, because in such cases it is difficult for the formally authorized party (*adhikārī*) to act directly. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
In the case of those who are timid, dull-witted, insane, aged, women, children,
or diseased, a kinsman, or another person appointed by the court, shall state the preceding and subsequent facts.
For this very reason, Hārīta and others record a prohibition against summoning them:
"Those who are indisposed, children, the elderly, those engaged in difficult medical treatments,
those preoccupied with urgent business, those addicted to vices, and those occupied with royal affairs or festivals."
A king should not summon servants who are intoxicated, insane, negligent, or afflicted by disease.

One who is "unwell" (*akalya*) is diseased. One who is "in distress" (*viṣamastha*) is one for whom a crisis has arisen. One who is "busy with duties" (*kriyākula*) is preoccupied with performing obligatory and occasional rites. One who "neglects his business" (*kāryātipātī*) is one for whom the loss of more important tasks occurs when he comes [to court]. "Calamity" (*vyasana*) is suffering born from separation from what is desired and so forth; one who possesses that is "one in calamity" (*vyasanī*). "Intoxicated" (*matta*) is one whose intellect is impaired by intoxicants such as *dhattūra* and the like. "Insane" (*unmatta*) is one [afflicted] by planetary influences, bile disorders, and so forth. "Negligent" (*pramatta*) is one lacking attention in all matters. "Afflicted" (*ārta*) is one pained by despair and the like. The mention of "servants" (*bhṛtya*) is intended to include women who are not independent. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
The king should not summon those who are intent on religious duties, those seeking prosperity, the sick, the dull-witted, nor women who are unwell, intoxicated, insane, or afflicted.

In this context, women are intended to be dependent. He [Manu] himself says: "A young woman born of a noble family who has not yet reached her menses, and a maiden of the highest caste—these are declared to have their kinsmen as their masters."

"Those whose wives are dependent on them, wanton women, courtesans, those who have lost their family status, and those who are outcastes—these are declared to be fit for summoning. Here, "of low standing" (*hīnapakṣā*) means belonging to a base family; "young woman" (*yuvatī*) is an epithet of that same [wife]. "Born in a family" (*kule jātā*) means born in a noble family, or else "born in the highest caste" (*sarvavarṇottamā*), meaning of a higher caste than the one being considered. These five previously mentioned [wives] are under the authority of their relatives (*jñātiprabhukāḥ*), being dependent on others; not the others. Therefore, the meaning is that the summoning of those whose wives are dependent on them and so forth is desired by Manu and others. Nārada also prohibits the summoning of certain individuals.
One who desires to settle a debt, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one assailed by another, and likewise one engaged in royal business.
Cowherds [are summoned] at the time of the cattle's grazing; farmers at the commencement of the sowing of crops; artisans at their respective times; and those who bear arms during a conflict.

A messenger who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, a person observing a vow, and those in a precarious situation must not be obstructed; nor should the king summon them.
"One desirous of discharging [a debt] is one intent on marriage. Vyāsa also says:

"One who is ill, one wishing to sacrifice, one who is insane, one seeking dharma, one addicted to vice, one under a vow, or one intent on giving—such a person should not be pressed for payment, nor should he be obstructed, nor should he be made to fight."

Therefore, it is established that the prescription for substitutes applies only in the case of those who are ill and so forth. However, when the purpose is not accomplished by means of a substitute sent on behalf of one who is ill and so forth, then even those who are ill and so forth must be summoned. Thus says Hārīta:
"Having ascertained the place and the time, as well as the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand, the king should have even those who are ill summoned by means of gentle vehicles."
However, when the charge concerns a particularly grave matter, it is necessary to summon the accused himself, because in such cases the use of a representative is prohibited. As Kātyāyana states:
"In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's wife, and other similar indecent accusations, no substitute defendant is permitted."
He himself also uttered these indecent words:
"In the case of killing a human, theft, violating another's wife,
eating what is unfit to be eaten, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden..."
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the defendant shall not be made to pay; this applies to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
The opponent is the representative of the plaintiff and the defendant; he must by no means be accepted for such important matters as these. For this very reason, Hārīta says:

"Even those who, having learned of the legal charge, have gone forth into the forest as ascetics and the like—the king should summon them for important matters, provided he does not cause them offense."

By saying "without provoking anger" here, he indicates that even with harsh words, one may call out to an ordinary person. This has been made clear by Vyāsa: "He who inflicts injury or does not give what is owed when asked due to bad character—such a person may be dragged away by order of the king."
Regarding one who does not come even by the king's command, Bṛhaspati states the punishment:
"If one who has been summoned does not come out of arrogance, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen,
the king shall impose upon him a punishment proportionate to the nature of the legal claim."
Kātyāyana also says:
"If one who is capable should disregard the king's command when summoned,
the king shall inflict upon him punishment according to the procedure prescribed by law."
For a minor offense, the fine shall be fifty; for a middling offense, it shall be no less than two hundred;
and for grave matters, he shall always be fined at least five hundred.
The number of *paṇas* is to be counted. Whatever fine has been prescribed for a particular offense with effort,
there shall be the collection of *paṇas*, or else its equivalent value, from the offender before the king.

This is because it is stated by that very same [author]. The measure of the *paṇa* should be understood from what will be explained later. Because of the word "addicted" (*sakta*), no punishment is to be prescribed in cases such as misfortune; rather, once that addiction has ceased, he should be summoned again. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"In a region ravaged by a foreign army, during a famine, or when afflicted by disease, one should summon [the defendant] again and not impose a fine."
Hārīta also says:
"When a matter pertaining to the gods has been truly investigated by the accused,
whether at the appointed place or in the interim, he who proceeds in this manner incurs no fault."

"In reality" means from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If [the king] punishes one who has not committed an offense against the ultimate truth and subsequently proceeds according to justice, it is as follows:
"That which ought to be established with effort must be done; otherwise, he becomes subject to punishment.
Having punished him first, the king should afterwards proceed according to justice."

Thus, by whatever means possible, once the defendant has been brought forward by the plaintiff, he should be made to stand before the court or in some other designated place. Accordingly, Pitāmaha says: "The defendant should be placed before the court by the plaintiff, or in another desired location; for only there is he a valid witness, and not otherwise."

The meaning is that he should be stationed where it is impossible to conceal his wicked characteristics. Then, when questioned by the king, the defendant (abhiyogin) shall report the facts relevant to his own case; for it is impossible to investigate the truth based solely on the mere statement made by the plaintiff (abhiyoktṛ). For this very reason, Manu has stated regarding the procedure for investigating the truth: "By means of tone, complexion, gestures, facial expressions, the eyes, and speech... [Manu 8.25].

Even in a case involving *chala* (quibble), the account of the accused person—necessary for determining whether he was the one employing *chala* prior to the drafting of the plaintiff's plea (*pūrvapakṣa*)—must be understood through his own testimony. Once it is ascertained that both parties have employed *chala*, the procedure for the judicial investigation follows accordingly. Therefore, it should be understood that even the accused has the right to provide his account. After the determination of which of the two litigants used *chala*, Yājñavalkya states:
"A surety capable of resolving the matter should be taken from both."

The determination of a case consists in the effortless recovery of the proven debt, fine, or property; the judge (*vyavahāradraṣṭṛ*) must accept as a surety (*pratibhū*) someone capable of performing this task for both the plaintiff and the defendant—this is the meaning. Regarding those who are to be excluded from this role, Kātyāyana states:

"One who is not an owner, nor an enemy, nor one appointed by the owner; likewise, one who is imprisoned, one who has been fined, and those who are under suspicion—these are never [to be accepted] anywhere."
Neither an heir nor one who is destitute, nor those who dwell in perpetual residence,
nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants [shall inherit].
One who is incapable of paying the debt to the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king should not be accepted as a surety for the performance of the obligation,
nor should one who is unknown [to the parties] be taken as such.

Those who are under suspicion are those accused. "Those living in perpetual residence" refers to lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*). "Equal to that" means equal to the property that has become the subject of dispute; this is intended to indicate the prescribed punishment. If the plaintiff is unable to provide a surety for the dispute, it has been stated by that same [author]: "If there is no surety for a plaintiff who is fit for a lawsuit, he, being protected, shall pay wages to the messenger at the end of the day."

To the messenger who protects the one to be accomplished; likewise, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that a litigant who has surrendered and then taken back property should be brought before the court: "A person who seizes what has been seized should not be brought before the court by the king;
rather, that property should either be restored to him or deposited for another. [79]
"Of the other," meaning of the neutral party; "in the presence of," is the ellipsis. Likewise, the sequence of speech for the plaintiff and others has also been stated by that same author:
"In that case, the plaintiff shall speak first, and the defendant immediately thereafter;
at the end of those two, however, are the members of the court, and after that, the presiding judge."

"One should speak first" means one should make the formal proposition (*pratijñā*). And so says Nārada: "Whether in the case of a command, a document, a copper-plate grant, a royal edict, a mortgage, a sale, or a purchase, he who makes a prior representation to the king should be recognized by those learned in the law as the plaintiff (*pūrvavādin*)."
The meaning is that in every dispute, the plaintiff alone is the one who states the claim (*pratijñāvādī*). Regarding this, the same author states an exception:

"To whichever party the greater suffering occurs, or for whom the matter (*kārya*) is more significant, to him the right to state the claim (*arthivāda*) should be granted; not to the one who would have reported first."

The *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) refers to the *pūrvapakṣa* (the plaintiff's case). And so says Kātyāyana: "He for whom there is greater suffering or whose legal matter is more significant shall be the *pūrvapakṣa*, and not he who was the first to present his claim."

The meaning is that, in such a case, the examiners must determine the reversal of the status of plaintiff and defendant. Where both parties simultaneously stand as plaintiff and defendant toward one another due to a difference in the matters to be proven (*sādhya*), there the claim of the party of higher caste or the one suffering greater hardship should be examined first. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"When both the plaintiff and the defendant come forward with the cry of 'I first,' the lawsuit should be accepted according to the order of castes, or by considering the degree of suffering."

If the litigants are of equal caste, the decision should be made based on the degree of suffering. However, when several pairs of litigants appear simultaneously, Manu states the order of precedence for their examination:

"Having understood both the purpose and the lack of purpose, as well as the mere nature of dharma and adharma, he should examine all the cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes."
Thus ends the commencement of the section on the examination of evidence in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the section on the plaint (*pratijñāpāda*).
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Then, when he has arrived, the plaintiff shall formulate his claim. This means that once the defendant is present, the plaintiff should have his claim written down. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"The claimant shall have the writing made in the presence of the defendant, exactly as it was stated by him."

The phrase "as it was stated" (*yathāveditam*) is intended to demonstrate that only that which was stated as the matter to be proven (*sādhya*) should be written down, and not any other matter to be proven; it does not mean, however, that everything that was stated must be written down. For this very reason, he [the author] himself states: "It shall be marked with the year, month, half-month, day, name, caste, and so forth," even for those particulars such as the year that were not previously stated, since they must now be recorded.

The year is equal [to twelve months], and it should be recorded as current at the time of the transaction involving wealth and so forth. The month and other units are likewise contemporary with that time. The specific qualifications included by the word "and so forth" (ādi) have been shown by Kātyāyana:
"Having recorded the time, the year, the month, the fortnight, and likewise the lunar day (tithi);
the hour, the region, the district, the location, [the creditor's] caste, appearance, and age."
He [should state] the quantity of the substance to be proven, the number, his own name,
the names of the kings in their proper order, the place of residence, and the name of the person against whom the claim is made.
"One should set forth the names of the ancestors in order, as well as the harasser and the giver, and other signs of forgiveness, after having proclaimed the [defendant's] position. Thus it is said.

*Time* (*kāla*) refers to the time for the investment of wealth and so forth, as characterized by the current king; it includes such terms as "the year" or "the rains. *Season* (*velā*) is time characterized by activities such as eating. *Place* (*pradeśa*) is a specific location, such as a field to be litigated. *District* (*viṣaya*) is a region such as Antarvedī. *Location* (*sthāna*) is the village or similar site where the subject of dispute, such as a house, is situated. *Form* (*ākṛti*) is a particular configuration of parts. *Age* (*vayas*) is youth and so forth. *Measure* (*pramāṇa*) is the dimension, such as a staff, a scale, or a measure (*prastha*). *The self* (*ātman*) refers to the plaintiff. *The kings* refers to those who have been enjoying the fields and so forth. *Dwelling* (*nivāsa*) is the place of residence, such as a house or a cow-pen. *Ancestors* (*pitaraḥ*) are the progenitors of the plaintiff and the defendant. *Injury* (*pīḍā*) is that inflicted by a surety or a creditor. *Acquirer* (*āhartā*) is one who performs the acquisition through gift or other means. *Giver* (*dāyaka*) is the donor. *Signs of intolerance* (*kṣamā-liṅgāni*) are the causes for not tolerating the use of one's own property by another. *Others* refers to additional factors beyond those shown, such as the acquisition of interest. Thus says Bṛhaspati:

One should cause to be written that which is faultless, accompanied by a formal declaration, consistent with valid means of knowledge and traditional authority, and which includes the substance, the number, the origin, the injury, and the signs of forbearance.
He stated those other characteristics as well:
"It consists of few syllables but contains abundant meaning; it is free from doubt and not confused; it is endowed with formulations that prevent contradictions and negates opposing views. [82]

"Having correctly considered such qualities as these and being well-ascertained, a position (*pakṣa*) that is acceptable should be established; otherwise, it is a fallacious position (*pakṣābhāsa*). Thus says the author of the *Saṃgraha* as well.
It should be meaningful, conjoined with the Dharma, complete, and free from confusion;
it should consist of expressive words that are like what is to be established and connected to the subject matter at hand.
It must be well-known, non-contradictory, certain, capable of proving the point,
concise, complete in its meaning, and not in conflict with place or time.
It is endowed with the year, season, month, fortnight, day, time,
place, region, location, dwelling, the name of the person to be accomplished, caste, form, and age.
It should be marked with the names of the defendant, the witnesses, the number of proofs, the self, the adversary,
the ancestors, and the sovereign, as well as one's own name.
"That which, like a self-inflicted wound embraced by patience, reveals the heart of the one who has taken [the property] to the king—that is designated as *bhāṣā* (the plaint). Thus it is said.

"Meaningful" (*arthavat*) means possessing a purpose. "Connected with the law" (*dharmasaṃyukta*) means endowed with qualities such as having few syllables and abundant meaning. "Complete" (*paripūrṇa*) means not requiring ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). "Unconfused" (*anākula*) means having letters that are free from ambiguity. "Possessing the thing to be proved" (*sādhyavat*) means not lacking the matter intended to be established. "Expressive words" (*vācakapada*) means devoid of metaphorical or indicative usage. "Connected with the subject matter" (*prakṛtārthānubandhi*) means not contradicting the matter previously announced. "Well-known" (*prasiddha*) means having as its object things well-established in the world. "Non-contradictory" (*aviruddha*) means not contradicted by the city, the kingdom, the judge, the king, and so forth; likewise, it is not contradicted by what precedes or follows, nor by perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor by conventional law (*vyāvahārikadharma*). "Certain" (*niścita*) means free from suspicion of another meaning. "Capable of proof" (*sādhanakṣama*) means worthy of being proven. "Concise" (*saṃkṣipta*) means not overly prolix. "Containing the whole matter" (*nikhilārtha*) means leaving nothing of what is to be said unexpressed. "Not contradicting place and time" (*deśakālāvirodhi*) means being free from statements such as "there is a betel-nut plantation in the Middle Country" or "a thousand mango fruits were stolen during the autumn season. "Marked by the names of the opponent, oneself, ancestors, and various kings": "the opponent" (*para*) is the defendant; "oneself" (*ātman*) is the plaintiff; "ancestors" (*pūrvajāḥ*) are their fathers and so forth; "various kings" (*anekerājānaḥ*) are those who reigned during the period of possession. Their names are "the names of the opponent, oneself, ancestors, and various kings," and the plaint is marked (*cihnita*) by them. The rest has been explained. The qualities beginning with "meaningfulness" and ending with "not contradicting place and time," when accompanied by the names of the plaintiff and defendant, are useful for all legal pleadings (*bhāṣā*). Therefore, these must necessarily be present in every plea, because without them, it is impossible to easily achieve the establishment of the matter to be proved (*sādhyasiddhi*) in any case. However, all qualifications such as the year and so forth are not useful in every instance, since the establishment of the matter to be proved can occur in various cases even without some of them. Therefore, they should be included only where they are useful, and not elsewhere, due to the lack of purpose. Among these, years and other times are useful in disputes regarding interest, the doubling of wealth, and in disputes concerning the priority of gifts, purchases, mortgages, and so forth. Places, regions, and locations, as well as the names of the opponent, oneself, ancestors, and various kings, and the mention of the acquirer and the donor, are useful in disputes over immovable property. The name of the matter to be proved, the caste, the form, and the age are useful in monetary disputes such as theft or sale without ownership. The number of proofs and the quantity are useful in disputes over measurable, weighable, or counted goods, as well as in theft. Signs of tolerance are useful in disputes regarding neglected property and the like. Personal suffering is useful in disputes with debtors or sureties; this is the general direction. Thus, it should be understood that years and other factors are to be included in various instances along with meaningfulness and the rest, according to their utility. The country, as well as the location, the settlement, the caste,
the designation, the residence, the measurement, and the name of the field.
"One should record these ten—namely, the paternal and ancestral [lineage], and the proclamation of former kings—in disputes concerning immovable property.
The intention is that these are useful in such cases. Hārīta also says:
A seat, a bed, a vehicle, copper,
bell-metal, iron, grain, stone, clothing, bipeds, and quadrupeds.
If there should be a collection of substances such as gems, pearls, corals, diamonds, silver, and gold, their number must likewise be calculated.

"In whatever region, whatever substance is measured by whatever standard, by that [standard] and in that [region] the calculation must be made by those engaged in legal proceedings. Thus he says that the calculation must be made after measuring the diamond (*vajra*) by its own specific standard. And so, since it is impossible to achieve immediate success in a matter where a particular thing is required if that thing is absent, a position devoid of useful items is simply not acceptable. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
A plaint that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number,
and deficient in action and proof, is not accepted as admissible.
The measure of the action is the measure of what is to be accomplished. Likewise, even if it lacks characteristics such as being purposeful, the thesis (pakṣa) is indeed to be rejected.
"A king should avoid a thesis that is unestablished, unassailable, useless, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory. [85]
Among these, the "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) has been defined by Bṛhaspati:
"That which has not been made by anyone is declared to be unestablished.

An example of this is: "A vessel filled with a thousand fruits was taken. The "unobstructed" (*nirābādha*) is that which is free from trouble, such as when one says, "He conducts his affairs in his own house by the light of the lamp situated in our house. The "meaningless" (*nirartha*) and the "purposeless" (*niṣprayojana*) have been shown by Bṛhaspati.
An offense that is very slight and involves very little matter is known as "insignificant" (nirarthaka);
however, one that lacks any obstruction to the accomplishment of the task should be understood as "useless" (niṣprayojana).

In this regard, an example of the *nirarthaka* (meaningless) is: "I was looked at by him with a smile," or "My lac-dye has been stolen by him. An example of the *niṣprayojana* (purposeless) is: "Yajñadatta is reciting boastfully near our house. These two have also been shown by that same author in another manner:
"A legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) lacking terms such as *kusīda* (loan/interest) is to be known as *nirarthaka*;
likewise, one involving [charges of] verbal abuse and the like is to be known as *niṣprayojana*."

A "pointless" (*nirarthaka*) plaint is one that is not included within the eighteen titles of law, beginning with non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*). The meaning is that a claim accompanied by matters such as verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*), which are useless for establishing the point at issue, is purposeless. By that same [author], the "unprovable" (*asādhya*) and the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) have also been shown: "The wise declare that a claim such as 'this person must give me a bow made of a hare's horn' is impossible and unprovable."
"When a case has been stated such that there would be opposition within the court, among the judges, the king, the city, or the kingdom—that is declared to be 'contradictory' (viruddha).
Thus [says the law]; Nārada also demonstrates the defects of the plaint (*bhāṣā*).
A plaint that refers to something other than the actual matter, one that is devoid of substance, one that lacks authoritative sources or traditional transmission,
and one that is deficient or excessive in its written form— these are declared to be defects of the statement.
He explains this himself:
"Even when the subject matter is common [to both parties],

if one person appointed for the plaintiff's case should cause the written statement (*bhāṣā*) to be recorded with a different meaning, the wise know that to be a *anyārthā* (a statement of a different meaning)."

The meaning is that even a single member of the assembly, whether unappointed or not a relative, may cause the document to be written in whatever language is required, whether for the sake of the assembly or for the sake of an individual.
However, he who speaks out of hatred or delusion, saying "this man is a slayer of a Brahmin," should be known as a perjured witness;
and where one causes the defendant to be released, they know that testimony to be devoid of substance.

The meaning is that which was stated by the proponent of the thesis (*sādhyavādin*)— that [objection] in which it is abandoned is "devoid of the meaning of the statement. "In cases of what is to be counted, weighed, or measured, as well as fields, houses, and so forth, where no specific number is indicated, that is 'devoid of proof' (*pramāṇavivarjitā*)."
That which is obtained through learning, inherited, acquired, purchased, or passed down by lineage—
if it is not recorded in writing in this manner, that discourse would be without scriptural authority.
The month, as well as the fortnight, the lunar day, and likewise the day of the week—
if these are not written therein, they know that document to be deficient in its essential elements.

But having caused a statement to be written down as it was specified and as it occurred subsequently, if one should later point to a witness who contradicts it, that prior [testimony] shall be declared superior.
"Where both sides are entirely set forth by the proponent, yet it is written as if doubtful, they know that to be a corrupted form of speech.
This means where both positions in their entirety have been indicated by the proponent alone. Furthermore, he [the same author] states other unacceptable positions as well:
A proposition is considered inadmissible if its sequence is broken, if its meaning is inverted, if its meaning is confused,
if it is meaningless, if it is past its time, or if it is double-faced.
In that regard, the "disordered sequence" has been explained by that very [author]:
"The formulation of a thesis-meaning is not commended when it is placed out of its proper position;
rather, that is cited as a 'disordered sequence' of the thesis."

The meaning is that "disordered arrangement of syllables" refers to a broken sequence. That which conveys meaning through a reversed order or through a disjointed connection is "scattered in meaning" (*prakīrṇārtha*) or "composite in meaning" (*saṃkalitārtha*). He explains those [fallacies] beginning with the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*): "When the root matter is abandoned and its secondary qualities are written down there, that position is indeed 'meaningless' (*nirarthaka*), being devoid of any proof for what has occurred."
Where a document records a substance whose time has passed,
that is considered a "past" plea (atītakāla-pakṣa), even though there may be evidence available.

"That position in which the object of proof is twofold, involving a consideration of different times due to a difference in action—that position is said to be 'dual-situated' (dviṣṭha). Thus [it is said].

*Bhūtasādhana* means the proof of the principal substance that has come into being. *Bhūtakāla* is the time that serves as the limit. This is due to the distinction between actions and the distinction between measures of proof. Furthermore, he (Yājñavalkya) states other fallacious plaints (*pakṣābhāsa*) as well:
"By the insertion of different syllables and by the shifting to a different meaning, a document may become confused, and the legal action itself may likewise become confused. [88]
If, in a debate, one who is capable remains indifferent for twenty or ten years regarding the point to be proven, his position shall be considered false.
Where one might write down a claim along with the matter to be proven,
yet it is devoid of the proper sequence of statements, that plaint also does not succeed.

The action is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and the means is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Hārīta also states: "An object whose means of proof has been introduced, whether it is subsumed under two aspects or is distinct from its own *sādhya*, that too would be a false thesis (*pakṣa*)."

The meaning is this: when a matter that has been set forth and commenced for proof is introduced into the plaint in two ways—either by way of a second claim (*dādhyatā*) or as a different kind of thing than what was stated in the *sādhya* (the object to be proven), or else in a manner contrary to it—that too is a fallacious plaint (*pakṣābhāsa*). Bhṛgu also says:

"Where a matter has been abandoned by the plaintiff, or where one point must be inferred from another, there the plaint is not valid, being devoid of both scriptural authority and established custom."
One should avoid from afar that thesis in which both contradictory and non-contradictory meanings are seen to be established within a single [subject].
By one who is inferior and speaks inferiorly— even the grandfather [of the law] has said:
"The speech of one who composes words that are mutually contradictory does not succeed, for his discourse is muddled by conflicting statements."
Kātyāyana also says: "He who does not wish to act according to justice, or who acts unjustly,
and likewise he who does not cause [the facts] to be recorded— his case is not proven."

The meaning is that one does not cause it to be recorded either in a negative form, such as "having taken my rightfully acquired wealth, she does not give it back," or in a positive form, such as "she seizes my fields and so forth. Likewise: A plaint that is contrary to the city or the kingdom, that which is rejected by the king, and that which is confused by multiple points does not succeed.

A lawsuit that contradicts the customs of the city or the kingdom, or one whose subject matter—such as tolls, shops, and so forth—has been waived by the king, does not succeed at all. However, the meaning is that a case involving several distinct points, such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and others, does not succeed simultaneously because of the diversity of the legal procedures (*kriyā*). Furthermore, it has been stated by him [Yājñavalkya]:
"If a matter in a lawsuit involves many assertions and is well-established, the king may certainly accept it as well, out of a desire to ascertain the truth."

Thus, this is intended to demonstrate that even when a matter involves multiple points (*pada*), it may be accepted as a single claim through a distinction in its parts; or else, it is intended to demonstrate that one should first state the claim by distinguishing between various types of items—such as gold, clothing, cattle, and grain—which fall under a single head like "recovery of debts" (*ṛṇādāna*), and which have been taken with differences in number, quantity, place, time, interest, and so forth, and then conclude that all of it must be returned as a single unit, stating "all that shall be restored. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the earlier statement. Likewise:
Tradition, enjoyment, cessation, and likewise aspiration—these four they declare [to be the means of proof]; however, defects of speech are not valid reasons.

*Āgama* (tradition) refers to the means by which wealth is acquired, such as receiving gifts and so forth. *Paribhoga* (enjoyment) is the non-cessation of utilizing [the wealth] according to one's will. *Vyucchitti* (interruption) is the cessation of enjoyment due to regional upheaval and the like. *Prārthanā* (petition) is the proclamation of the acquisition of enjoyment through logical arguments. These four—*āgama* and the rest—are called the "qualities of speech" (*bhāṣāguṇa*). However, those *āgamas* and so forth that are "unfounded"—that is, those established in speech without a basis for their inclusion—are called "defects of speech" (*bhāṣādoṣa*); this is the meaning. Therefore, in this context, one should exclude what is not required and understand what is required. And thus, he [the author] says:
One should divide excessive amounts and supplement those that are deficient;
one should record them on the ground as long as the matter has not been finalized.

The meaning is that he should cut away or erase. "On the ground" is used as an illustration; for it is said by that same [author]: "The judge should cause the plaintiff's case, as stated naturally, to be inscribed on a board with chalk-dust, and thereafter, once it has been refined, upon a leaf."

"Stated by its own nature" means stated without the qualifications of fear and so forth. "Purified" means neither deficient nor excessive, and free from defects such as being unestablished. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "Those who know the subject matter recognize the *pakṣa* (the thesis) as being free from defects of the proposition, endowed with the probandum and its cause, certain, and established in the world."

The meaning is that it is established in the world and not contradicted by conventional dharma (*vyāvahārika-dharma*); for such a meaning as "well-known in the world" has already been stated by implication through the phrase "free from defects of the thesis. Therefore, Manu says: "The testimony of the court members is not valid, even if it be well-established, if it is spoken outside [the court] regarding dharma, whether fixed or conventional."

The meaning is that even a statement free from all defects must not be accepted by the members of the court if it contradicts the conventional law (*vyāvahārika-dharma*). Thus, Bṛhaspati states that a plaint (*pakṣa*) characterized as described above is of four kinds: "An accusation based on suspicion, a truthful claim, a request for what has been obtained, and a retrial after a previous legal proceeding—these are to be known as the four kinds of plaints. [91]
On this point, Nārada says:
One should examine the plaintiff's claim only until the appearance of the defendant's reply;
once the claim has been countered by the reply, the examination ceases.

Nor should it be suspected here that, according to the analogy of the "conch-shell hour" (*śaṅkhavelā*), the process of purification ceases once the time suitable for delivering a reply has passed; for he himself says:
"The defendant shall not present his answer until the plaintiff has caused the matter intended to be stated to be written down. (NSM 3.2)

Some desire further purification even when an answer has already been given; that should be rejected because it leads to the fallacy of infinite regress and contradicts the previously stated rule. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says: "When the speech is neither deficient nor excessive, one should listen again after having properly formulated [the question], and then [receive] the answer."
Since the defendant has begun his reply, even that which is relevant and spoken by the plaintiff must not be admitted, because its proper occasion has been bypassed.
The meaning is that [the claim] is "given" once the trial has commenced; for even while it is being given, a subsequent rebuttal is accepted. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"Whether spoken by the plaintiff out of delusion or through guile, or even if it is included within the defendant's reply, that must be accepted by both parties."

"Contained within the reply" means that even when the reply is being stated by the plaintiff, it is included; "of both" refers to the plaintiff and the defendant. However, for the defendant, the "stage of proof" (*kriyāpāda*) constitutes the reply. [92] When the judges have accepted the reply without first clarifying the plaint, then, after imposing a fine upon the judges, the case must be examined starting from the plaint. But when the plaintiff is unable to state the plaint immediately, Bṛhaspati says:
"When the accuser, due to lack of confidence, does not venture to speak..."
A period of time should be granted to him, in accordance with his capacity for action.
Thus ends the section on the Plaint (*pratijñāpāda*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now begins the section on the Reply (*uttarapāda*).
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
Once the prima facie case has been determined, distinguished by what is acceptable and what is unacceptable,
and once the meaning of the plaintiff's proposition has become firm, one should then cause the defendant's reply to be written down.

The meaning is that even if a claimant has established his case, once it has been further scrutinized by the judge and others and found to be stable, the defendant should then set down his reply (*uttara*) to that claim. Nārada also says:
"But when such a claim has been formulated by the plaintiff, the defendant should then present his reply connected with that claim."
The meaning of "of such a kind" has been explained by Hārīta:
"It should have few syllables but be rich in meaning, free from defects of the thesis,
supported by witnesses, endowed with logical grounds, irreproachable, and well-ascertained."
When such a plaint has been written by the plaintiff,
the defendant shall then deliver a reply connected to that very position.

One who possesses witnesses is one who has the supervision of the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) and others. However, when he is not such [a person], then he should not grant [the judgment]; this is established by implication. To clarify this, that same author [Yājñavalkya] states, citing one example of a fallacious plea (*pakṣābhāsa*), that no reply should be given to it:
"A wise man should not give a reply to one who requests land that is common property or goods belonging to a corporation (*gaṇa*). (YDh 2.30)
Therefore, Yājñavalkya states that the defendant must submit his reply only after the plaintiff's case has been examined:
"The reply of one who has heard the matter should be written down in the presence of the plaintiff.
The literal meaning is: "of the defendant (pratyarthin) who has heard the meaning of the statement (bhāṣā). The author of the Saṃgraha also says:
It has no other purpose, its meaning is not deficient, it is endowed with logic and scripture,
it is neither lacking nor excessive, it is unseen by others, and it does not arise from any other syllables.

"Immediately after the plaint has been written on the leaf, this is the time for the defendant, having heard the matter, to give his reply. The meaning is: when the plaint has been written in such a way that it possesses the full set of characteristics, such as being "not for another purpose" (*ananyārtha*) and so forth. Furthermore, this rule regarding the time limit applies only to disputes concerning cattle and similar matters. And thus says Nārada:

In cases of theft of cattle, land, gold, or women; in cases of violence, verbal or physical abuse, and urgent matters; and in cases of assault and false accusation, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.

A curse (*abhiśāpa*) is a false accusation of sin. Although it is a form of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), it is mentioned again for the sake of emphasis. Kātyāyana has declared it to be urgent: "Where dignity departs, or where there is ruin or abandonment, one should not delay; for that matter is urgent."
[94] Likewise, regarding other matters as well, he (Yājñavalkya) himself states that a response must be made immediately:
"In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and procreation;
likewise in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and similarly in buying and selling."
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence, embezzlement of a deposit, fraud, and false testimony, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.

*Upadhi* is an admission made under the influence of fear or other such motives. Yājñavalkya also states: "In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations, and the loss of cattle, as well as in matters concerning women, one should litigate immediately; in other matters, the time for litigation is said to depend on the will [of the parties]."
The meaning is: "except in cases such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth. And thus says Nārada:

"Because of the profundity of legal disputes and because of the incapacity of even the traditional law (*smṛti*), one may, out of a desire to discover the truth, allow time to pass in matters such as debts."

"In matters such as debts" means in legal titles of dispute such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says: "In cases of debt, deposits, pledges, gifts, joint undertakings, agreements, and the division of inheritance, the time [of payment or action] must be diligently observed."
In such cases as these, the granting of time occurs when the defendant seeks it for reasons such as forgetfulness; even so, Kātyāyana states:
"If, having heard the matter set forth in writing, the defendant requests time for the dispute due to a valid reason, it should be granted to him without doubt."
Because memory is possible regarding actions performed recently, that same author states that the trial must take place immediately:
"In cases of actions performed recently, the lord should cause a trial to be held immediately;
or, in cases where time has elapsed, he should grant a period of time to the defendant."
[95] The term "the defendant" (*pratyarthin*) is used for the sake of illustration. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"If the mind of one who wishes to speak in a dispute does not have the courage, time must indeed be granted to both the plaintiff (*arthin*) and the defendant (*pratyarthin*)."

And when it is asked how much time should be granted, he himself says: "In cases such as debts, one may obtain [time] immediately, or after one day, five days, three days, a month, three fortnights, or seven days, depending on the gravity or lightness of the matter."

Gautama also states, "One should wait for a year. Regarding this, Kātyāyana declares the settled rule: "Having ascertained the time available and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand, the master [the judge] shall grant a short or long period to the defendant."

Time refers to the connection with the object and so forth; "capacity" refers to that of the agents and of the effects—the objects to be accomplished. The meaning of the verse has been explained in detail by that very [author]:
"In the case of an immediate act, it is immediate; when a month has passed, it shall be one day;
in the case of a six-year-old, it shall be three nights; and in the case of a twelve-year-old, seven days."
In the case of a twenty-year-old, she shall receive [the fee] for ten days or half a month;
when thirty years have passed, it shall be for one month, and beyond that, it shall be for three fortnights.
And he demonstrates the determination according to one's capacity:
"The time [for study] is before a year, as desired by oneself;
however, for one who is dull-witted, insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by disease, it is for a year."
Or when the matter has reached another region, or when the meaning of the object is unknown,
or when the root witnesses or the witnesses themselves are situated in a foreign land.
In that case, the time for men would last until their reunion with their own country.

Within a year, the presiding judge shall determine the deadlines for the various legal proceedings according to their capacity—whether by day, fortnight, three fortnights, or up to a year. "Mūla" refers to the principal sum of money under dispute. Thus, he clarifies the determination based on the nature of the case:
"Whether it be a day, a month, half a month, a season, or even a year;
the defendant must be granted a period of time corresponding to the stability of the matter at hand."

The "stability of action" refers to the determination of the relative importance or insignificance of the matter at hand. Thus, when the appropriate time has arrived as established by these rules, Bṛhaspati states that the defendant must submit a written reply that neither exceeds nor falls short of the literal meaning of the plaintiff's plea: "When the time has been fixed, the defendant, in the presence of the court members, shall then write his reply in accordance with the words of the plaintiff's plea."
In this regard, Kātyāyana says to the king:
"Having considered whatever local custom has been handed down through a succession of tradition, the king should cause a reply to be given according to justice."
Regarding the characteristics of a rejoinder (*uttara*), Prajāpati has said:
"Those who know it recognize a rejoinder as that which pervades the entire position (*pakṣa*), which is essential, unambiguous, unconfused, and not to be understood through mere verbal explanation."

"Comprehensive" (*vyāpaka*) means covering the entire side of the case. "Essential" (*sāra*) means capable of withstanding prior accusations and subsequent rejoinders. "Unambiguous" (*asaṃdigdha*) means free from fragmentation, ellipsis, and the like. "Unconfused" (*anākula*) means having a coherent meaning. "Not requiring explanation" (*avyākhyāgamya*) means easy to understand. Hārīta also says:
"Connected with the meaning of the plaintiff's case, not having multiple meanings, unconfused, not too brief, with words in their proper order, comprehensive, and not excessively long. [97]
Such an answer should be given as is essential, free from doubt, not partial to one side, clearly audible to the plaintiff, and with its meaning unambiguous.

Connected with the meaning of the plaintiff's claim, following upon the accusation, possessing multiple meanings yet extracting a specific point, with unambiguous words preceded by a definite proposition, not falling into one side of the case while leaving no part of one's own position unaddressed, heard from the plaintiff as previously stated, and having its meaning unhidden—being intelligible through straightforward expression and well-known terms—a reply characterized in this way should be known as fourfold;
for the plaint is fourfold, and the counter-plaint is likewise.

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Bṛhaspati. When it is asked, "How, then, is there a fourfold nature of the counter-pleadings (pratipakṣa)? Nārada says: "The reply (uttara) may be of four kinds: by way of denial (mithyā), or by way of admission (saṃpratipatti), or by way of a counter-attack (pratyavaskandana), or by way of establishing a prior judgment (prāṅnyāya)."

This third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). Regarding that, Kātyāyana states the definition of "falsehood" (*mithyā*) and "admission" (*saṃpratipatti*): "If one who is accused should deny the accusation, one should recognize that as 'falsehood' (*mithyā*) as a reply in legal procedure."
"The statement of the truth regarding the matter to be proven is declared to be *pratipatti* (admission).
Furthermore, the definition of *pratyavaskandana* (counter-attack) has been stated by Nārada:
"If the defendant [admits] that very matter which has been written down by the plaintiff..."
"Having entered [the plea], one should state the cause; this is known as *pratyavaskandana*.
Thus [it is said]. Hārīta states the definition of *prāṅnyāya*:
"In this matter, I previously had a dispute with this person; at that time..."
"If he should say, 'He has been defeated,' that reply shall be a *prāṅnyāya*.
Thus, in order to clarify the replies (*uttara*) characterized as described above, it was also stated by Prajāpati:
"Whatever has been alleged here by the plaintiff concerning me..."
To the extent that everything is unreal, it is known as a false rejoinder (mithyottara).
"This very thing must be given by the claimant; it is not a false statement"—this second type of reply is called "admission" (*saṃpratipatti*).
"This was indeed given to me by him;
however, I have given it back to him in turn"—an objection of this kind is known as *pratyavaskandana*.
In this other matter, I was previously initiated by the plaintiff;
since I have won this case, the rule of the prior judgment is declared.
And Kātyāyana states that this plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) is of three kinds:
"I shall prove [my case] by means of family members, witnesses, or a written document;
and this man has already been defeated by me previously"—this is the threefold plea of prior judgment.
The term "by the judges" (*kulikaiḥ*) is intended as an illustration for those who oversee legal proceedings. Likewise, he [the author] himself states that there are four kinds of false [testimony]:
