"This is false: 'I do not know it,' 'I was not present there at that time,' and 'I was not born at that time'—thus is the fourfold falsehood. So it is said.

Thus, regarding "acceptance through agreement," it is true that such distinctions as "it is exactly as he says" and so forth should be inferred according to the circumstances. Regarding "acceptance by way of a counter-attack" (*pratyavaskandana*), the distinctions such as "it was returned" or "it was obtained through a gift" are to be observed. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"The rule for the plaintiff has been declared in the presentation of a coherent case;
now, that which is not to be accepted among the fourfold types is being stated."

One should not write about anything other than the subject at hand, nor that which is irrelevant, deficient, excessive, incoherent, non-pervasive, essence-less, doubtful, or contrary to the opposing position.

That which is other than the subject matter at hand is that which does not resolve the charge written by the plaintiff; it is neutral, lacking the character of a counter-claim, disconnected, and not following from the charge. Kātyāyana also says:
"That which is unestablished, contradictory, too little, or too much;
doubtful, impossible, unclear, irrelevant, or excessively defective [is inadmissible]."
"A response that is non-pervasive, disjointed in its words, of hidden meaning, confused,
requiring interpretation, or devoid of substance is not praised by the wise.
Regarding this, he [the author] himself explains the first five of these fallacious responses.
If, however, one does not understand the sign,
the form, or the convention, or if it is stated in another language, that answer is considered unestablished.

The meaning is that what is stated by one who is ignorant of the insignia, the constituent parts, the configuration, the number, or the time [of the document], and what is stated in a foreign dialect, is "unfamiliar" (*aprasiddha*).
"It was returned by me in my childhood," or "it was certainly not returned by me"—
when one speaks thus, that should be understood as a "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reply in this context.
The meaning is that a contradictory reply (*viruddhottara*) is a statement that contradicts what was said previously.
To say, "I have already defeated him in this matter," [is an example]. That which says, "By me previously... is known as an insufficient reply (*ūna*).

In this context, when one ought to say, "This was formerly won by me," the mere reply "Formerly by me" is too brief; such is the meaning. For what should have been said is: "The task was performed by me;
that object which was formerly seized [by him] is now [mine]. That [omission] is excessive.
The meaning is that when a true answer (*satyottara*) such as "it was taken" ought to be stated, an answer such as "it was done by him" and so forth is excessively prolix.
Similarly, when one ought to say "it must be given by me," saying "it is not to be given by me" is an ambiguous answer (*saṃdigdha*); thus should it be understood by the wise in legal proceedings.

In the case of the phrase *māyādeyam*, since the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a* is possible—resulting in the understanding that it means *adeyam* (not to be paid)—such a response is indeed "ambiguous" (*saṃdigdha*), meaning it is uncertain. An "impossible" (*asaṃbhava*) reply is one such as: "The wealth to be paid by us has already been given by our great-grandson's son. An "unclear" (*avyakta*) reply is one that cannot be easily articulated. These two types of fallacious replies (*uttarābhāsa*) are self-evident and thus were not explained by him [the author]. He explains another type: "And by this [reply], a *sāhasa* (an act of violence or force) previously established through strength and weakness [is refuted]."
They consider this to be unstated; therefore, it is said to be for another purpose.

The meaning is that when a claimant’s statement regarding an improper transaction results in nothing more than a mutual contradiction of words, it is considered "for another purpose. It is "excessively defective" (*atidoṣavat*) because it is defective due to exaggeration (*atyukti*), such as saying "a hundred was to be given" when two hundred were actually given. The fourfold category beginning with "non-pervasive" (*avyāpaka*) has been explained by that same author: "When it is stated, 'I gave this thousand together with him,' but only half of that was actually returned, that is recorded here as 'non-pervasive' (*avyāpaka*). [101]
As long as the proponent has not properly established his case,
that which was previously accepted by me is said to be a "distorted point."
The meaning is that an answer given by a false witness before the determination of the plaintiff's case is called "vyastapada" (a disjointed or misplaced statement).
But will anyone give a lotus without having grasped it?
That answer, however, should be understood as being of hidden meaning according to legal procedure.

The meaning of the apparent answer uttered as "I do not give the lotus because it has not been taken" is as follows: an answer that possesses ambiguity, such as the word *tāmarasa* (which can mean both "lotus" and "conquest of all the earth") used in the context of a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*), and which contains indirect speech (*vakrokti*) and so forth, should be understood as having a hidden meaning—this is the sense of the verse. "Should it be given by him alone, or should it be given by me?"—the experts in this matter know such an answer to be called "confused" (*ākula*).

The meaning is that it is "confused," like a collection of many word-meanings that are not syntactically connected. It is "to be understood through [further] commentary" because it is inherently difficult to comprehend. He stated that such an answer is "substantialless":
"The crow has no teeth, or it does have them," and so forth. "Substantialless" means that, in reality, it is not accepted as a correct answer.

The meaning is that it is useless and insubstantial, like the search for a crow’s teeth, which serves as a standard example of a futile rejoinder (*uttara*). Likewise, he [Yājñavalkya] himself stated that when there are multiple replies—such as "true," "false," and so forth—in relation to a single plea (*bhāṣā*), it is an invalid reply (*anuttara*):

"That which is true in one part of the claim, and contains a legal ground (*kāraṇa*) in another part, and is false in yet another part, is an invalid reply because of its internal inconsistency (*saṃkara*)."

[Objection: But even if there is a confusion [of the two means of proof], since each subsequent [proof] refutes its respective portion, it is possible for the entire collection of subsequent proofs to pervade the whole position; so how can they be considered "not a valid rejoinder" (*anuttara*)? [Reply: True. For this very reason, he himself stated [in the *Ślokavārttika*] to support the fact that they are not a valid rejoinder:
"In a single dispute, there cannot be legal action (*kriyā*) for both disputants.
There can be no establishment of the object for both, nor can there be two legal actions in one case."

This is the meaning: *kriyā* (proof) refers to evidence such as written documents; that belongs only to the defendant (*pratyarthin*) in the case of a plea of denial (*pratyavaskandana*) or a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), but in the case of a plea of falsity (*mithyottara*), it belongs only to the plaintiff (*arthin*). However, it will be stated later that in the case of a plea of truth (*satya*), it belongs to neither. Thus, where there is a mixture of the three types of pleas other than truth, the defendant would have two proofs and the plaintiff would have one. Where there is a mixture of the two—truth and those other than falsity—the defendant alone has two proofs. Furthermore, where there is a mixture of two pleas of falsity, or two pleas of prior judgment, then each of the plaintiff and the defendant has one proof respectively. Nor should it be argued that "let it be exactly as it has occurred," for proof is employed for the purpose of establishing what is to be proven (*sādhya*). In a single legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*), there is only one thing to be proven for only one party; therefore, in that case, it is not possible for both to have proof, nor for one to have two proofs, because there is no second thing to be proven. And since one thing to be proven is established by a single proof, any other would be redundant. As for the case of a mixture involving a plea of truth with the others, although this specific fault does not arise, nevertheless, since the conclusion of a lawsuit occurs either in all four stages or in half of them within a single proceeding, even there it cannot constitute a valid reply (*anuttara*). Therefore, it is rightly said: "Because of this mixture, it is not a valid reply. And thus, in every legal proceeding, only one reply that pervades the entire claim (*pakṣavyāpi*) should be accepted. However, where such a reply is entirely unobtainable, but rather there are multiple replies each covering only a single part, then, having no other recourse, one should make several propositions (*pratijñā*) to avoid the defects of the claim according to the nature of the replies, and accept one reply for each proposition in sequence. Otherwise, there would be a total lack of a final decision (*nirṇaya*) in that case. For this very reason it was said: "Because of this mixture, it is not a valid reply. The intention is that when the mixture is eliminated by the aforementioned method, it indeed becomes a valid reply. For this same reason, regarding this very subject, Hārīta has explained the sequence of accepting replies through a series of questions.
If both a false plea and a plea based on a special cause should occur in one case,
or if a true plea occurs along with another, which of those pleas should be accepted?

The word "previously" is to be supplied [as the object of the verb]. He states what that previously graspable [object] is: "That which has an extensive range of objects, or wherein the fruit of the action resides—that should be known as the subsequent [member]; otherwise, it is not distinct [from the former]."

This is the meaning: when there is a plurality of subsequent replies (*uttara*) among which some are true and others not, that which pertains to multiple objects should be grasped first. When there is a plurality [of replies] including a true one, even if it concerns multiple objects, one should set aside the true one and adopt another subsequent reply at the outset, because there is no fruit of action (*kriyāphala*) in a true [reply]. Nor should it be said that this rule applies only to cases where, after the time [of the initial plea], several subsequent replies pervading the entire claim (*pakṣavyāpaka*) are presented—such as when a certain man, having been accused with the words, "My cow was lost; I saw it in his house," says, "This is false; she was born right here in my own home," and so forth. For it has been stated: "Otherwise, it is confused (*asaṅkīrṇa*). The meaning of this is: a reply is "unmixed" (*asaṅkīrṇa*) in this sequence; otherwise, in the case of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*), it would indeed be "confused. However, in the case of multiple replies pervading the claim—which concern alternative options (*vikalpa*)—there is never an occasion for confusion. Therefore, this statement refers specifically to the subject of "confused" replies. For this very reason, he (the author) has begun another statement regarding the subject of multiple replies pervading the claim.
"Or else, even in the case of two false pleadings, the answer that provides the reason should be accepted. [104]

The intention is that a *kāraṇottara* (a plea of a special cause) is more serious than a false plea (*mithyā*) because it is established as being non-otherwise-possible (*ananyathāsiddha*). Therefore, since the two types of false pleas are merely illustrative examples, it should be inferred that when other types of pleas are combined, the more serious one must be accepted. Furthermore, where there is a plea of confusion (*saṃkarottara*) in which the previously mentioned grounds for the sequence do not exist due to equal strength, the plea should still be accepted according to the order preferred by the litigant, because a definitive decision is necessary. Thus described, the plea must be presented by the defendant himself. And so says Hārīta:
In that case, the defendant’s reply should follow the point of contention,
state the essential meaning clearly, and be free from any designation of faults.
Furthermore, when he himself does not provide an answer and the time for its delivery has passed, that same [author] says:
"When the defendant does not give an answer according to the facts of the plaintiff's case,
he should be made to provide it by means of conciliation and other such methods."

"He should be made to pay by the king"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. And so says Nārada: "One should give a reply according to the facts; if one does not give it, the king should compel him to pay through means such as conciliation, dissension, and so forth, until that debt has been recovered."
The methods beginning with conciliation (*sāman*) have been shown by Hārīta:
conciliation is speech preceded by kindness; dissension is the pointing out of dangers; bribery is the withholding of wealth; and punishment is beating and imprisonment.
Likewise, Vasiṣṭha has also stated:
"Crookedness, conciliation, dissension, and punishment— these four,
along with deception, indifference, and sorcery, are proclaimed as the seven expedients."
Regarding that which cannot be accomplished even by these means, the same [author] says:
"But he who, though exhorted by these means, does not give an answer, when seven nights have passed, he is defeated and must pay. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the latter section in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, some statements regarding the subjects of legal disputes are recorded;
therein, Yājñavalkya says:

"One should not bring a counter-charge against him without having first settled the original charge. Here, "without having settled" means "without having resolved. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the exception to this rule:
"But one may bring a counter-charge in cases of quarrels and acts of violence."

The phrase "the possibility of a counter-charge" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. This means that in a quarrel, there are two types of harshness. He (Nārada) says the same regarding the accuser: "One who is being sued shall not, by another statement, lead the case into a state of contradiction. The meaning is: one who is being sued by a plaintiff shall not sue another plaintiff before the former's charge has been resolved; likewise, having stated what was to be said for the sake of the accusation, one must not speak otherwise. He who speaks otherwise becomes defeated due to his contradictory testimony. And so says Nārada:

"One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the legal procedure, one who does not appear, one who is without a reply, and one who flees when summoned—these are remembered as the five kinds of defeated parties.
Among these, he has been determined to be defeated by virtue of speaking otherwise. [106]
He who abandons his previous argument and takes up another again should be known as a person of inferior debate, due to shifting his position.

The *pūrvavāda* is the formal statement of the claim. And so Kātyāyana says: "Having caused [the defendant] to hear the matter according to the case, if he should abandon it or state something else, that plaintiff has relied upon another side; therefore, he is defeated."
Likewise, he who speaks in contradiction, saying "I do not charge him" after having already charged another, is also defeated because of his inconsistent testimony; thus the same author says:
"One should not say of another that the matter was not stated by me after having charged him.
One who speaks falsely in this manner should likewise be declared defeated."
And likewise, the same author states that one who alters a plaint previously committed to writing—even if he does so by speaking otherwise—is defeated for his false testimony:
"But a plaintiff who, having caused a statement to be written, speaks again of it as either deficient or excessive, shall be defeated; he is not entitled to his accusation."

"Having caused it to be written"—the word "on a document" (*patre*) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence], because the depositing and withdrawing [of such a document] on land and so forth has been stated by that very same author. "The charge" (*abhiyoga*) refers to the plaintiff's case (*pūrvapakṣa*); the meaning is that he is not entitled to make it. And this lack of entitlement is to be understood as applying when the defendant's reply (*uttara*) has been made; however, if the reply has not been made, there is simply defeat (*hīnatā*), not a lack of entitlement, because the clearing of the plaintiff's case is permitted out of necessity in cases such as delusion once the reply has ceased. Likewise, one who is defeated due to hatred of the legal procedure (*kriyādveṣitā*) or for failing to appear is defined by that same author.
The members of the court and the witnesses are to be known by the wise as the "action" (kriyā).
He who, out of delusion, hates that action is called a hater of the action (kriyādveṣī).
[107] “By failing to appear after being summoned, one is defeated immediately.

This means that if one does not arrive immediately following the summons, one becomes defeated at that very moment. Likewise, in order to define defeat by way of silence, the same author says: “Even when told ‘Speak!’, if one does not speak, one deserves immediate confinement.”
On the second day, one should know that the defeat of that evil-minded person is certain.
Defeat is inferiority. For this very reason, Hārīta says:
"To delay the time by making pretexts, remaining silent in the assembly, speaking after one has already spoken, and contradicting what was said—these are the characteristics of one who is losing."

"With a pretext" means with a fraudulent motive. And so says Kātyāyana: "But where one seeks to prolong the matter through a pretext, one should know that as a 'sāpadeśa' [case], which is recorded as a ground for defeat in litigation."

But one who flees when summoned (*āhūtavipalāyī*) is one who, having perceived the summons as a means to avoid the legal charge, moves about in concealment. It is stated that "the defeated party (*hīna*) is of five kinds" in order to indicate that the gravity of the defeat increases for each subsequent category; it is not intended to restrict the defeated parties to exactly five types, since other forms of defeat are also recorded in tradition. Furthermore, the indication of the gravity of the defeat is for the purpose of indicating that the punishment becomes increasingly severe for each subsequent category. And so it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "One who speaks falsely [shall pay] five *paṇas*; one who shows malice toward the legal procedure (*kriyādveṣī*), ten *paṇas*."
The attendants are twenty-two; the unsurpassed one is indeed sixteenfold.
And one who flees after being summoned shall be made to pay a fine of twenty paṇas.
Regarding this, the same author states the specific rule for the application of punishment in the third and fifth cases:
"The king shall punish him who does not come when summoned three times, him who flees after being summoned, or him who has exceeded a period of five nights. [108]
Likewise, he has shown another way in which a party is defeated:
where one should cause a division among those litigants who have been made to hear the case, and should entice the plaintiff with greed— one should designate that person as defeated.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"He who creates fear, or division, or intimidation, or obstruction—
such a litigant loses his case in legal proceedings."

The meaning is that the disputant by whom fear and the other [defeats] have been incurred—either collectively or individually—in the course of the legal proceeding, is defeated. "Terrifying" means the production of fear through another means. Manu also says:
"He who points out what should not be pointed out, he who, having pointed it out, denies it, and he who does not perceive the points of argument as superior or inferior—he is defeated."
Furthermore, he who, having cited an authoritative source, subsequently evades it;
and who, when questioned about a matter properly set forth, does not acknowledge it.
"Having said, 'There are witnesses,' if one who has been told to point them out does not do so, the judge, based on these grounds, shall declare him to be devoid of truth. Thus it is said.

This is the meaning: he who points out a witness who is "unindicatable"—meaning one who could not have been present at the time of the decision; or he who, having pointed out such a person, subsequently denies it, saying, "I did not point him out"; or he who does not acknowledge the internal contradiction in his own statements; or again, he who departs under some pretext, such as claiming, "I am suffering from illness" and so forth; or he who, when asked, "Having restated the matter well-posed and well-stated, what do you say to this?", offers no reply whatsoever; and he who, having said that there are witnesses, fails to name them even when told, "Name them"—such a person is "defeated" (*hīna*). The presiding judge in the court of law (*dharmādhikaraṇa*) should declare him defeated on account of these aforementioned grounds. Even among these defeated parties, a punishment corresponding to the fault must be imposed. And thus says Kātyāyana in the section on the defeated party:

"Having grasped [the case] according to the fault, there is no further debate"—this is the meaning, with the words "for the sake of establishing the matter at hand" as the ellipsis. And this prohibition applies only to disputes arising from anger, since Nārada says:
"In all disputes concerning wealth, one does not fail because of verbal trickery."
In cases concerning cattle, women, land, and the non-payment of debts, even one who deserves punishment does not lose his property.

In disputes concerning all matters such as cattle and the like, even if a quibble of words (*vākchala*) or a statement made through negligence is raised, one does not fail, nor is one utterly defeated; for the meaning is that even for one who is liable to punishment in such cases, there is no loss of the subject matter at hand. Regarding this exception, Kātyāyana says:
"When both parties have committed their statements to writing and the determination of the case has begun, he who speaks something not previously stated is defeated regarding that matter."
Yājñavalkya also says: "He who proves a doubtful matter on his own initiative, he who absconds,
or he who says nothing when summoned— he is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment."

"Independent" means not depending on an investigator. "Should depart" means that without having given what is due, he departs and stays away, or flees. Since the status of being "defeated" (hīna) is already established by the very mention of "punishment," the further mention of "defeated" is for the purpose of making it known that he is defeated in relation to the matter at hand. For this very reason, Nārada says: "But he who proceeds with a disputed matter without reporting it to the king shall be forcibly punished, and that matter shall not be settled."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses,
and one who admits the claim in his own words— these are the four kinds of litigants who lose their case."

"One who has admitted [the claim] by his own statement" means one who has acknowledged it through his own words. Here too, the mention of "fourfold" is intended to indicate that among these, each subsequent one suffers a loss of the case more rapidly than the preceding one; it is not, however, intended as a restriction that only a fourfold loss from the subject matter at hand occurs, since other types of loss have also been mentioned. When it is asked, "In what case and for whom does the loss occur? he himself says: "One who flees loses after three fortnights; one who maintains silence after seven days; one defeated by witnesses at that very moment; and one who admits [the claim] likewise loses."

Regarding those witnesses who have been thus designated, [the author] says that even for one who does not cause them to be examined, such a deficiency arises after a long time: "But if one does not cause those witnesses to be examined within thirty nights or three fortnights after having pointed them out, his case suffers defeat."
The phrase "he shall not cause [the suit] to be heard at will" is the understood remainder [of the sentence]. And so says Kātyāyana:
"But that plaintiff who, having pointed out witnesses, does not cause the suit to be heard at will—he loses his case after thirty nights have passed. Thus it is said.
If one does not fail [to appear] unintentionally, for that very reason Bṛhaspati says:
"When a person has been summoned to a trial by ordeal and has made a firm commitment to appear,
if he does not present himself, one should not allow him to plead a pretext in that matter."
"When a fault caused by fate or the king occurs at that time, he shall not be defeated merely by the abandonment of his plea.

By stating "one should not employ deception therein," [the author] makes it known that even by refuting a deceptive statement that establishes the loss of the claim, the legal proceeding must be carried forward. Thus, it should be understood that in disputes over property, the testimony of the defeated party is to be accepted only where there is no statement regarding the loss of the claim, and not otherwise. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"Because fleeing is not a valid way to conclude, and because of relying on the side of another, the debate of one who is inferior is accepted [as lost], but not that of one defeated by his own words.

This means that even in cases such as fleeing, if the time limit set as the boundary has been exceeded, the debate is accepted [as lost] for the one who fails to appear, since there is no loss of the point at issue. In that regard, if the defeat of the other party occurs through the inferior party, then the distinction has already been shown by him.
"For the wise know that there is a means of rescue for one who has been defeated by a deficient statement;
however, for one who is himself deficient in his own statement, no rescue exists. Thus [it is said].
But Yājñavalkya, for the purpose of identifying a fraudulent litigant, says:
He goes from one place to another, licks the corners of his mouth,
his forehead perspires, and his face turns pale.
With parched mouth and faltering speech, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips.
"One who undergoes a change from his natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body—whether during a legal proceeding or as a witness—is proclaimed to be corrupt. [112] Thus [it is said].

*Sṛkviṇī* refers to the corners of the lips. *Nirbhujati* means he distorts or makes crooked. "He undergoes a change from his natural state" means he proceeds to the opposite of his inherent character; such is the meaning. Manu also says:
"By means of facial expressions, gestures, gait, physical movements, and speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived. Thus it is said.

The word "of the corrupt" (*duṣṭasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Thus, even for one known to have a corrupt internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is neither punishment nor exclusion from the proceeding; for those two [consequences] have not been mentioned by the sages. Furthermore, since it is possible for even one who is not corrupt to possess such signs [of corruption] in some way or another, the statements that designate someone as corrupt are not redundant, as they serve the purpose of enjoining vigilance in protecting him [from being wrongly accused]. However, regarding those who, out of fear of certain defeat, withdraw from the debate either before the evidence is presented or even on their own accord, Bṛhaspati states that they are to be punished.
"When a deliberation is conducted between the plaintiff and the defendant, those who reach a private settlement [without reporting it] shall be made to pay double the fine.
The phrase "they reach a private settlement" implies that they do so by deceiving the king. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
"Those who, having presented their case, reach a settlement between themselves, shall all be fined double [the amount in dispute], for they have deceived the king.
Thus, there is no punishment for those who have settled their dispute without deception; for this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
When the two sides have been drawn out and the decision on the matter has been set in motion,
a reconciliation may occur between the two heated parties, like that of two pieces of iron.
[113] But in that case, there may be a choice between witnesses and assessors for both parties;
those two who are discerning should bring about a settlement while the matter is still wavering.
"Where there is a discrepancy between the treatise and the practice regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a reconciliation of both is praised by royal decree.
This means that those two who would enter into a compromise before one of the disputants suffers an absolute defeat are the ones truly wise.
Thus ends the section on subjects of dispute in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now begins the section on the defendant's reply (*pratyākalita*); regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
But for those who persist in their defense, the members of the court shall investigate;
having stated the case, a proper reply must be given to one of the litigants.

The meaning is that, among those legal proceedings (*dharmādhikaraṇa*), the proof (*vibhāvanā*) or the means of action (*kriyā*) must be determined by the judges for either the plaintiff or the defendant. And so says Kātyāyana:
"When the written statement has been properly scrutinized and found to be faultless, the production of evidence (*kriyākaraṇa*) is required from either the defendant or the plaintiff."

The meaning is that whether one is a plaintiff (*arthin*) or a defendant (*pratyarthin*), whoever has a matter to be proven (*sādhya*) should, for the sake of establishing that proof, submit the evidence (*pramāṇa*) immediately after the formal reply (*saduttara*). Thus says Yājñavalkya: "Thereafter, the plaintiff shall immediately cause the proof of the matter asserted to be written down. The meaning is that the disputant who possesses the matter to be proven should present the evidence immediately upon the establishment of the reply. When it is asked what that evidence is, he himself says: [114]
Written documents, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof;
in the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.
The divine [means of proof] consists of the balance and so forth. And thus says Nārada:
"Legal procedure is declared to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine.
Human procedure is by means of documents and witnesses; the divine is remembered as the balance and so forth."

The meaning is that [evidence] consisting of documents, witnesses, and possession is called "human" (*mānuṣī*), because possession also pertains to human beings. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:
"Evidence by witnesses, documents, and inference is recorded as being threefold.
Here, "inference" (*anumāna*) refers to possession, because it corresponds to ownership. The ordeals such as the balance (*dhaṭa*) and so forth are also shown by that same author.
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation (kośa);
the sixth is said to be rice grains, and the seventh is the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka).
"The eighth is said to be the ordeal by balance, and the ninth shall be that born of dharma (the ordeal of truth).
All these divine [ordeals] have been prescribed by the Self-Existent One.
Other two-fold [ordeals], however, were prescribed by Nārada.
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cows, seeds, gold, the feet of the gods and ancestors, and meritorious deeds [are the oaths].

Here, the word "and" (ca) is intended to include other [oaths] as well, such as touching the head of one's son. These [ordeals], beginning with the balance (dhaṭa), and these [oaths], beginning with truth (satya), possess the two designations "divine" (divya) and "pertaining to the gods" (daivika), because they were established by the gods in heaven. And so says Pitāmaha:
Since they were employed by the gods and the wise for the sake of nourishment and for the sake of mutual purification, they are therefore called "divine" (divya) by name.

In this context, by the force of the introductory statement (*upakrama*), it is understood that they are "divine" by name, because the observation of the cause indicates they were employed by the gods. By the force of the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*), it is understood that they have their origin in heaven, because it has been stated that they are "celestial" (*divya*) by name. Therefore, by this statement, two etymological names are given for the balance and other ordeals—just as the word *ājya* (clarified butter) is used from its arrival at the sacrifice (*ājigamana*)—despite the apparent contradiction with the Vedic text. The name for the oath was also shown by Nārada himself for those very same ordeals:
"The Seven Sages, as well as Indra and the others, rich in asceticism, [performed them] for the sake of the lotus-pond (*puṣkara*)."
"Those who are unperturbed should take an oath for mutual purification," so it is said. Vyāsa also states:
"Oaths corresponding to the value of the matter are recorded as the truth-oath, the ordeal by balance, and so forth."

As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati— "The divine [ordeals] are recorded as ninefold, beginning with the balance (dhaṭa) and ending with the sacred libation (dharmaja)"— in that context, the word "by the Self-born One" (svayambhuva) should be understood as the ellipsis, because in reality the divine ordeals are of many kinds when taken together with the oaths (śapatha) such as truth (satya) and so forth mentioned in the Nārada-smṛti. Furthermore, regarding the statement in the Nārada-smṛti that distinguishes between divine ordeals and oaths:
When no witness is found for men engaged in a dispute,
then one should examine them by means of ordeals or various kinds of oaths.

Thus, it is shown that the term *divya* (divine ordeal) is used for serious matters and the term *śapatha* (oath) for minor ones as a general rule, but not to indicate a difference in their meaning, since in common usage they are synonymous. The phrase "no witness exists" is intended to indicate the absence of the three means of proof beginning with written documents (*likhita*), because Yājñavalkya prescribes divine ordeals only when all human means of proof are absent. For this very reason:
"When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine procedure; but by employing a divine ordeal when witnesses are available, he is defeated thereby. (YDh 2.74)

Thus, even in the statement of Kātyāyana, the mention of "witnesses" (sākṣin) should be understood as an illustration for human evidence (mānuṣa). Likewise: "In the performance of legal procedures in villages and cities during the daytime, when witnesses are available, divine means of proof (daivī kriyā) are not employed."

Thus, even in the statement of Nārada, the mention of the *divākṛta* (oratory) and other human means of proof should be understood as intended to exclude divine ordeals when human evidence is available. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "If a human means of proof exists, even if it covers only a portion [of the case], that is to be accepted; but not a divine one, even if complete, for men who speak [in court]."

The meaning is that when the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is qualified, and human evidence is possible regarding the substantive portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), divine proof (*divya*), even if it establishes the qualified matter, should not be accepted. The intention is that the establishment of the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*), however, should be accomplished either by the maxim of "proving one part" (*vibhāvitaikadeśanyāya*) or by means of a minor oath. Nor should it be argued that, because the term "one part" is stated without qualification, divine proof is prohibited whenever human evidence is possible—whether regarding the qualifying portion or the substantive portion. For he [the author] himself says:
"Leaving aside the essential word, even if there are many non-essential ones..."
"One should accomplish whatever action is necessary, but one should abandon that which is devoid of substance.

Likewise, even if one of two litigants should somehow accept as decisive a means of proof—whether divine or human—that has been presented by the other party, [the author] states that when a human means is possible, that alone is the deciding factor, not the divine one:
"If one should state a human means and the other should state a divine one..."
"In that case, the king should employ human means of proof and not divine ones.
Thus, the general rule is that when human evidence is in every way unavailable, divine proof is to be used. He himself states an exception to this in certain cases:
"In cases involving assault, verbal abuse, and physical violence..."
In matters arising from force, there shall be either witnesses or divine proof.

And this discretionary option (*vikalpa*) pertains to cases other than those involving secret perpetrators; for in those [latter] cases, because humans are unavailable, such discretion is impossible. For this very reason, it was stated by that same [author]:
"But for secret perpetrators, examination by means of ordeals is appropriate, based on the reasoning, signs, gestures, facial expressions, speech, and eye-movements of men."

The meaning is: "of those who commit secret acts of violence (*gūḍhasāhasika*), whose forms are unperceivable due to the influence of excellent disguises and the like. This renewed commencement of the statement is intended to show that for them, ordeal (*divya*) applies even in the absence of logical evidence and the like, and not merely in the absence of witnesses and so forth. Likewise, he [Bhṛgu] states that even for those who commit the highest acts of violence (*uttamasāhasika*) openly, the examination must be by means of ordeal alone: "And in all cases of the highest violence, one should investigate the true state of affairs through the perspective of ordeal, even when witnesses exist," says Bhṛgu.
Regarding disputes over debt, Nārada states a specific rule:
"In cases where, due to negligence, there is neither a document nor witnesses for the creditor,
and the defendant denies the matter, a threefold procedure has been prescribed for him."
The plaintiff is one who has received the money. The procedure is the means for recovering that money; it too has been shown by him:
"A summons, a timely reminder, a brief application of reasoning, and likewise an oath—by these, one should recover the debt in due order. (118)

"Prompting at the proper time" means that whenever the time for repayment arrives, one should urge the return of the debt three, four, or five times in the presence of neutral witnesses, saying, "Let my property be given back," provided there is no obstruction by another party; this is the first method. In the event of its failure, "a slight application of reasoning" is the second method, such as stating: "In such a place, at such a time, and in connection with such a matter, you borrowed this much amount for the purpose of this specific work"—and so forth. In the event of even that failing, the third method is an oath; this is the meaning. And this point has been demonstrated by that very [author].
Even if urged repeatedly, one should not reject those words;
rather, after three, four, or five times, one should carry out the matter.
But in the case of the refutation of an objection, [the proof] is endowed with fragments of reasoning based on place,
time, the connection of objects, measure, action, and so forth.
Even when arguments are insufficient, one should reach a decision by means of oaths alone—
such as those involving wealth, time, strength, allies, fire, water, or meritorious deeds.
Kātyāyana also says: "A document, witnesses, or even a fraction of circumstantial evidence,
or divine proof (ordeals) has been declared as legal means of action for the subjects, out of a desire for their welfare."
Likewise, he himself says regarding mere disputes:
"In all disputes whatsoever, the lord of men should always reach a definitive conclusion through means of valid cognition, by means of reasoning, or even by divine proof."
"But when all [other means] are absent, one should act with effort, and never otherwise.
Thus Vyāsa states the meaning of the terms *pramāṇa* (means of proof) and *śabda-hetu* (verbal evidence):
"Written documents, witnesses, and possession—these are remembered as the threefold means of proof (*pramāṇa*)."
"The wise know inference to consist of the reason (*hetu*) and the deliberation (*tarka*).

Thus, the intended meaning is that when a matter is not established by a visible means of knowledge (*dṛṣṭapramāṇa*), one must resort to an invisible means of knowledge (*adṛṣṭapramāṇa*), and not otherwise. However, Bṛhaspati states that even when a matter is not established by what is seen, an invisible means of knowledge need not be resorted to: "In the first or in the third [instance], the means of proof is both divine and human."
But on the fourth day, the northern [party] shall present the document of victory along with witnesses.

The intention is that if a plaintiff fails to prove his case by either witnesses or a document of victory (*jayapatra*) in a matter previously decided (*prāṅnyāya*), he is not considered the victor of the prior proceeding. With this very same intention, Vyāsa also states:
"In a matter previously decided, through a document of victory [issued] by the judge and others, the plaintiff obtains whatever truth was presented by him."
The plaintiff is the defendant, because he alone is the one asserting the matter to be proved therein. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:
"In the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a plea of denial (*pratyavaskanda*), the defendant himself must prove [his claim];
however, in the case of a plea of non-liability (*mithyottara*), the plaintiff must prove both the meaning of the reply and the meaning of the original plaint."

In the case of a "false" (mithyā) reply, since there is no admission [of the claim], the status of the subject matter of the plaint as something to be proven is lost; thus the meaning is that the plaintiff must prove the very matter he asserted in his plea. However, in the case of a "causal" (kāraṇa) reply, because the subject matter of the plaint is indeed admitted, its status as something to be proven is not lost, and therefore the proponent of the plea does not need to prove the matter asserted in his plea. Rather, the defendant must prove by means of evidence that very cause which was not admitted by the plaintiff regarding the subject matter of the reply. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "If, having first accepted a [prior] cause, one later asserts another that is more serious..."
[120] One should state that which pertains to the opponent's statement, for by that alone is the point established, and not otherwise.

If the defendant (*pratyarthī*), having first accepted (*prapadya*) what was stated by the plaintiff (*pratijñāvādin*) and acknowledged it, should then state another matter—such as a *kāraṇa* (a legal justification) like "returning" (*pratyarpaṇa*)—which is more significant and capable of subverting the matter of the claim (*pratijñātārtha*) contained in the opposing statement or the subsequent reply, then that alone is indeed what is established by him; for the plaintiff has not accepted it. The meaning is that the plaintiff does not establish the collection of matters claimed which were accepted by the defendant. The word "having accepted" (*prapadya*) is used as an illustration; therefore, even when one says "it is false" regarding what was stated by the plaintiff and then states a *kāraṇa*, it is the *kāraṇa* itself that is established.

"Or, even between a false plea (*mithyā*) and a plea based on a cause (*kāraṇa*), the plea based on a cause is to be accepted as the reply," according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Hārīta. Likewise, he [Hārīta] himself states that when the plea of *satya* (admission) is raised, there is no burden of proof (*kriyā*) for any litigant:
"But when the plea of *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment) or a plea based on a cause is stated, the defendant (*pratyarthin*) shall point out the burden of proof."
If the proponent speaks falsely, however, that [status] would not exist when there is a response.

The intention is that in both the plaint (*bhāṣā*) and the reply (*uttara*), the matter to be proven (*sādhya-artha*) is absent; therefore, when there is a mutual agreement (*saṃpratipatti*), the legal proceeding is designated as "two-legged" (*dvipāt*). And so says Kātyāyana:
"In the case of a false plea (*mithyokti*), it shall be four-legged, and likewise in the case of a counter-plea (*pratyavaskandana*);
in the case of a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), it should be known as such [four-legged], but in cases of mutual agreement, it is two-legged."

Therefore, in the case of *saṃpratipatti* (admission), since there is no indication of an action (*kriyā*) and so forth, the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) concludes at the very end of the defendant’s reply. And thus, one should understand that between *mithyā* (denial) and *kāraṇa* (pleading a defense), the action may be either human (*mānuṣī*) or divine (*daivikī*), whereas in the case of *prāṅnyāya* (judgment on the basis of a prior decree), it is exclusively human; and in the case of *satya* (truthful admission), there is none at all. Bṛhaspati states that even in the cases of *mithyā* and *kāraṇa*, the divine action is not always employed: "In cases of verbal abuse and disputes over land, divine action is prohibited.
The intention is that, therefore, one should not employ it in those instances. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"And in cases of verbal abuse and regarding land, one should not prescribe an ordeal.

Now, it might be argued that by the verse beginning with "when [the matter] has commenced," an ordeal was indeed prescribed for verbal abuse. True, that was stated, but that refers to the subject of grave verbal abuse (*mahāpāruṣya*), whereas this refers to the subject of minor verbal abuse; thus there is no contradiction whatsoever. The phrase "regarding land" (*bhūmau*) is intended as an illustration for immovable property (*sthāvara*). For this very reason, Pitāmaha says: "In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals."
One should establish these [matters] by means of witnesses, a written document, or possession.

In this matter, it should be understood that the determination [of guilt] is made by means of human evidence when such is available, and by royal decree when it is not. Likewise, in some cases, he (Yājñavalkya) himself has stated that divine ordeals are to be prescribed for the purpose of restriction: "In cases of grave curses or accusations, as well as in the misappropriation of deposits, the king should examine the matter through divine ordeals even when witnesses are present."
Kātyāyana also says:
"Where there is equality among witnesses, one should purify [the matter] even by means of ordeals;
or in a dispute involving the loss of life, even when witnesses are available."
"The litigant resorts to divine [proof]; he need not question witnesses therein.
Bṛhaspati also says: "When a doubt arises regarding a written document or a dispute concerning witnesses..."
And when inference is confused, divine means (or scriptural authority) is the purification therein.
[122] Inference, possession, and reasoning such as "holding a torch in hand" are also means of proof. Vyāsa also says:
"If one disregards this document, saying, 'This was not written by me; it is a forgery made by another,' then a decision regarding the matter shall be reached through an ordeal."
The meaning is that one should reach a decision regarding a matter to be adjudicated by means of an ordeal. Kātyāyana also says:
"If there should be a document involving fraud, and it has been brought to the king's attention, then the king, seated upon the seat of justice, shall clear the matter by means of an ordeal."

Likewise, since a document may exist in some cases, possession in others, and witnesses in yet others, that same author [Yājñavalkya] stated the following as a restrictive rule regarding their applicability: "The established custom of guilds, merchant associations, corporations, and the like is declared to be proven by a document; neither ordeal nor witnesses are required for it."
Likewise, in matters concerning doors, paths, works, enjoyment, water-conduits, and the like, possession alone shall be weighty;
neither a written document nor witnesses [are required].
Now, when a dispute arises between a master and his servants regarding what was given or not given,
or concerning the relationship of sale and gift, one who has purchased wealth but does not pay for it [is subject to this].
"In cases of gambling, duels, and when a dispute has arisen,

witnesses are declared to be the means of proof, neither divine ordeal nor written documents. Having stated this, Nārada says that the established rule regarding the means of proof must be maintained by the judges.
The means of valid cognition must be diligently protected by those who know them;
for the means of valid cognition fail when they are unsettled by the doctrines of atomists.

The meaning is as follows: since those who act upon unreliable means of proof (pramāṇa) are ruined, therefore those skilled in investigation should investigate, thinking, "In this matter, what is the appropriate proof for whom? Here, some who consider themselves scholars have argued that the mention of writing and other proofs regarding immovable property is not intended to establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*), but rather to demonstrate their common occurrence; otherwise, they claim, there would be a lack of legal determination if such documents were somehow destroyed. This is incorrect, because even if it were a restrictive rule, a determination could still be reached through logical reasoning or by the word of the king. For this very reason, Pitāmaha said: [123] "In this matter, what is the appropriate proof for whom? This must be investigated by those skilled in close examination. Regarding this, some who fancy themselves scholars have stated that the mention of written documents and the like in the case of immovable property is not for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule of evidence, but rather to show that such means are generally applicable; otherwise, they argue, if the document or other evidence were somehow lost, there would be no way to reach a decision. That is improper, because even if it were intended as a restrictive rule, a decision can still be reached through logical arguments or by the command of the sovereign. It is for this reason that Pitāmaha says:
Where neither a written document exists, nor possession, nor witnesses,
and where there is no application of divine ordeals, the king himself is the authority in that case.
"Those discourses which cannot be determined and whose nature is doubtful—

the king shall be the authority for them, since he is the lord of all. For this very reason, after stating the means of valid cognition regarding what is seen and what is unseen, it was said by Vyāsa:
"In the absence of these, the wise know that the king's command is the final decision.
This means that when there is an impossibility of the means of proof due to their inherent nature or by way of prohibition, the decision is made by the king's command.
Thus ends the section on the Reply (*pratyākalita*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now begins the section on the Plaint (*kriyāpāda*).
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
Having heard the plaintiff's case,
the members of the court shall direct that he who holds the burden of proof establish his entire claim by means of written documents and other evidence.
*Bhāvanā* means action. Nārada also says:
"When the plaintiff's claim has been recorded in its entirety according to the syllables, the defendant shall establish it by means of evidence in the third stage. [124]

The *pūrvavāda* is the *bhāṣā* (the plaint). The *abhilikhita* is that which is written as the means of overcoming the *pūrvapakṣa*; that is to say, the *uttara* (the reply). The third stage is called *pratyākalita*. When that exists, there is *kriyā*, which is the means of proof (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the meaning is this: when the three stages called *bhāṣā*, *uttara*, and *pratyākalita* exist, the plaintiff (*arthin*) should establish his case through action; he should prove his matter by means of evidence. Vyāsa states the meaning of the words *kārya* and *kriyā*: "For it is said that *kārya* is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), and the means of proof (*sādhana*) is called *kriyā*."
Furthermore, that [speech] should be known as twofold: human and likewise divine.
The means of accomplishment is the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*). Bṛhaspati also speaks of the distinction between types of action: "Action is said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine;
each of these is divided into many ways by the sages who know the truth."

Kātyāyana also says: "The divine ordeal is of five kinds; the human is recorded as being of three kinds. The phrase "of five kinds" is not intended as a restrictive definition, because other types of divine ordeals, such as the *taṇḍula* (rice) and *taptamāṣa* (heated bean), are seen in other Smṛtis. The phrase "of three kinds," however, is for the purpose of restriction, since it does not conflict with subsequent Smṛti texts. Therefore, the meaning here is simply that "the [human ordeal] is recorded as being of three kinds. As for what was stated by Nārada:
"A written document and witnesses—these two methods are proclaimed here.
This [statement] is not intended to establish a restrictive rule regarding their number. For if that were the case, it would contradict the following:
"A written document, witnesses, and possession—proof is declared to be threefold."

Thus, since a contradiction with one's own statement would otherwise arise, it should be understood that the phrase "two types of injunctions are proclaimed" was stated in order to show that, by way of their application (*bhukti*), the other two have a wider scope. Thus ends the section on the distinctions between ritual acts (*kriyābhedāḥ*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the description of writing. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states:
"One should know that written documents are of two kinds: secular and royal."
The local document is that which pertains to the countryside. And so says the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"The royal and the local are recorded as being of two kinds.
Regarding these, Vasiṣṭha states that the royal document is of four types, distinguished by the edict (*śāsana*) and so forth.
The royal edict is to be known as the first, and the decree of victory as another;
the proclamation of command and the royal document—thus the royal writ is fourfold.
In that regard, Yājñavalkya spoke in order to define the royal edict:
"Having granted land or having established a fixed endowment (*nibandha*),
the king should cause a document to be prepared for the information of future benevolent monarchs."

*Nibandha* refers to wealth that must be given annually or monthly by those engaged in trade and other occupations to this Brāhmaṇa or to this deity, as established by a formal agreement with a superior. Although the act of giving the wealth is performed by the merchant or trader, the merit belongs solely to the one who established the *nibandha*, because the other party acts solely for his sake. The mention of "land" (*bhūmi*) is intended to include villages, gardens, and so forth; therefore, Bṛhaspati says:
"Having granted land and the like, the king [should record it] on a copper plate or likewise on a cloth."
One should cause a righteous edict to be made, incorporating the place, the lineage, and other such details.
"He should cause it to be made"—the remainder of the sentence is "by the official in charge of peace and war," because he alone is restricted as the agent for its drafting here. And so Vyāsa says:
"But the scribe of peace and war, personally commanded by the king, shall inscribe the royal edict either on a copper plate or on cloth."
"The relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*), conjoined with the action that constitutes the meaning of the compound.

This means: that teaching (*śāsana*) in which there is a relationship between the action and its factors is so described; "conjoined with the action of the meaning of the compound" means endowed with the action of presenting a condensed meaning. Yājñavalkya states the matter to be inscribed upon a copper plate and the like:
"The lord of the earth, having inscribed his own lineage and himself..."
This concludes the description of the measurement of gifts received and the cutting off of the distribution.

The meaning is as follows: having first inscribed the benediction (*āśīrvāda*) that conveys the granting of a boon, which is obtained through established custom for the Lord of Śrī who assumed the form of a boar (*varāha*) after lifting up the circle of the earth; and having thereafter inscribed three ancestors of one's own lineage—namely the great-grandfather, grandfather, and father—in the stated order by way of describing their qualities such as valor; and finally, having inscribed oneself as the fourth, one should cause the measurement of the gift and so forth to be written. "Gift" (*pratigraha*) refers to land and the like, as well as a fixed endowment (*nibandha*). Its "measurement" (*parimāṇa*) is its extent. A "boundary of the grant" (*dānaccheda*) is the limit of the land and other objects being given. Vyāsa also says:
"Marked by the year, the month, and half of that day, bearing the name of the king, and including the caste and so forth of the recipient, as well as his *gotra* and *brahmacarya*.

The meaning of the second half of this verse is that one must also write down the caste, family, *śākhā*, and so forth, which serve to identify the uniqueness of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). He states that other things must likewise be written down:
One should record the place, the lineage succession, the region, and the village reached,
as well as the Brahmin and other venerable persons who have been appointed.
Then, addressing all his household members, officials, envoys, physicians, and high-ranking dignitaries, down to the Mlecchas and Cāṇḍālas, he spoke as follows:

"For the merit of my parents and myself, this gift has been given by me to such-and-such a person, a fellow practitioner of the holy life, for the sake of such-and-such a son. Thus [says] Bṛhaspati as well.
Inviolable, unassailable, and free from all that is subject to becoming;
coextensive with the moon and sun, it follows through the lineage of sons and grandsons.
"One who severs the gift [of land] shall write down the fruit of that act as sixty thousand years in hell for the one who takes it, and heaven for the one who gives and protects it.
The words "for the sake of informing future kings and others" are to be understood as the ellipsis. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
For the sake of informing future kings and vassals, the king should record that the fruit of interrupting such a gift lasts for sixty thousand years.
Likewise, another verse was also to be written, which was recited by him as follows:
"This bridge of dharma is common to all kings; it must be protected by you from time to time.
Rāmabhadra entreats all these future lords of the earth again and again."

Then the king himself should write with his own hand. And so it is said by that same author: "He himself should write the location, the measurement, and his own hand. The meaning is that he should write himself: "This is the opinion of me, the son of so-and-so, the king named so-and-so, regarding what is written herein. And the scribe should likewise write his own name; and so it is said by that same author: [128]
The one who conducts peace and war, as well as the scribe,
being personally commanded by the king, shall write the royal edict.
"But one should write one's own name afterwards, sealed with the royal seal;
such is the royal edict for villages, fields, houses, and so forth.

And this should be delivered to the recipient, because it is useful to him. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "One should give [the document] written on cloth or copper-plate, marked with the royal seal, for the sake of recognition by future kings. The author of the Saṃgraha also says:
It is provided with the king’s own hand-signature, accompanied by the king’s command,
joined with the king’s name, and sealed with the royal seal.

"A royal edict (*śāsana*) shall be written by the secretaries of peace and war (*saṃdhivigrahalekhaka*), its syllables and components complete, and free from errors of sandhi or corrupt words. This means that what is written in the aforementioned manner by the secretaries of peace and war and granted by the king to another person is called a *śāsana*. Furthermore, this *śāsana* is not for the purpose of establishing the gift itself, since that is established merely by acceptance; rather, it is for the purpose of ensuring the stability of what has been given, for it is heard in scripture that when there is stability, the fruit is inexhaustible. Thus it is said: [The remainder of the passage follows: "Whatever gift is given without a *śāsana*, that gift, O King, goes to waste within seven nights. And: "The merit of a gift made with a *śāsana* is eternal, while that of one without a *śāsana* is said to be non-eternal. And: "By means of a *śāsana*, a gift becomes stable and is not lost; therefore, one should cause a *śāsana* to be written for the sake of stability.
