As long as his vigorous fame fills the two worlds,
so long indeed shall this virtuous man occupy the station of the gods.
With this very intention, Yājñavalkya also stated:
"One should cause a firm edict to be made, complete with one's own hand and the date.
"Complete with the date" means endowed with the specific details of the year and so forth, such as the time of the gift. And likewise, Vyāsa says:
"Known by me"— thus it is written, accompanied by the signatures of the donor and the superintendent,
and likewise marked with the seal of the year, month, fortnight, day, and night.

"By this procedure, one should write out the royal edict. And likewise, that same author, in order to define the document of victory (*jayapatra*), says: "Having personally observed or heard the legal cases from the presiding judge..."
Then the king should grant a certificate of victory for the sake of recognition.
When the question arises as to whom one should give [the property], he himself says:
"He by whom movable and immovable property has been brought under his own control according to the legal proofs,
and who is free from doubt regarding shares or curses, shall be the rightful victor."
To him, the king must certainly grant a formal document of victory.
Bṛhaspati also says: "When the king, having completed the preliminary and subsequent proceedings and reached a final decision,
grants a document to the victor, that is called a *jayapatra* (document of victory)."
The phrase "connected with the prior and subsequent proceedings" is intended as an indication of the entire case history; for that very reason, he [the author] himself stated:
"Whatever has occurred in the legal proceeding—the plaint, the reply, and so forth—along with the determination of the evidence, one should write all of it in the document of victory (*jayapatra*)."
Vyāsa also says: "The prior and subsequent stages of the legal procedure, the evidence, its examination,
the oral testimony, and the statements of the Smṛti, as determined according to the members of the court."

"All this should be inscribed in brief upon the *jayapatra* (the document of victory). This refers to the *kriyāpāda* (the section on the act), the *kriyābhimarśanapāda* (the section on the examination of the act), and the *pratyākalitapāda* (the section on the reconsideration). *Nigada* means the testimony of witnesses. *Yathāsabhya* means without transgressing against the members of the court. *Samāsena* means in summary. Kātyāyana also says:
"The statements of the plaintiff and the defendant, the formal plea (*pratijñā*), and likewise the testimony of witnesses."
And how he departed, and how it was determined by himself.
"This should be written according to the syllables, distinguishing each point as before.
This phrase "as before" has been explained by that very [author]:
"One should first record the statements of both the accuser and the accused."
After that, [the property goes] to the court members, the presiding judge, or the families.

"One should cause the opinion of the Smṛti-śāstra to be recorded right there with certainty. The word "opinion" (*mata*) refers to the opinion of the king and others; this is the ellipsis. Furthermore, the recording of the opinion must be done with one's own hand, because recording the opinion by another's hand has already been prescribed previously by the very statement, "just as it was determined by himself. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author: "The plaintiff should be joined with the proven matter, preceded by due honor."
The king should give him a written document bearing his own signature.

"And those members of the assembly who are present there, being experts in the treatises on law (smṛti-śāstra), should likewise cause their own signatures to be placed there, just as in the procedure for written documents. The meaning is that the king should cause those members to place their own signatures on the document of victory (jayapatra), just as in the case of a document concerning the countryside. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says:

[131] When the matter has been settled, the judge and others shall give a certificate of victory (*jayapatra*) to the winning litigant, marked with the hand-signature of the presiding judge and sealed with the royal seal.

Kātyāyana states that the document thus described is called a *paścātkāra* (subsequent decree): "The wise know that a document written according to this rule is a *paścātkāra*. Furthermore, he says that this *paścātkāra* is specifically a form of judicial decision and does not apply in all cases: "And this *paścātkāra* is indeed a particular kind of determination; it is not [applicable] everywhere."
But where an action has been refuted by the proponent himself through a means of valid cognition, there a retrial may take place;
it is not prescribed in all cases.

Action is that which is to be accomplished. By stating "by means of proof alone," one declares that legal procedure consists of four components (*catuṣpāda-vyavahāra*) and not two components (*dvipāda-vyavahāra*). This has been clearly elucidated by Bṛhaspati:
"One should establish the matter to be proven in accordance with victory consisting of four components;
and a document of victory (*jayapatra*) is required, bearing the royal seal."

In a lawsuit between two parties, however, there is indeed a written judgment (*jayapatra*) consisting of the plaint and the reply, because in that case the defendant's subsequent admission (*paścātkāra*) is prohibited as being a false rejoinder. Another type of written judgment was also stated by that same author:
"To others—those other than those who are defeated, those who have withdrawn their plea, and so forth—it is granted;
and that written judgment shall be established by a summary of the proceedings."

The meaning is: "of the other inferior disputants. Two types of *ājñā-prajñāpanā-patra* (orders of command) were shown by Vasiṣṭha: "That by which a task is assigned to neighboring kings, servants, or provincial governors and the like, is called an *ājñā-patra*."
"But when a matter is presented to officiating priests, family priests, teachers, or other venerable and worthy persons, that document for the purpose of making it known is called a *prajñāpanā*.
Thus Bṛhaspati speaks of another royal document known as a *prasādalekhya*.
"That which a king grants to someone by means of a written document, being pleased by their service, valor, or other merits—that indeed is a *prasāda-likhita* (grant by favor).

Therefore, it should be understood that the statement that royal documents are fivefold or fourfold was spoken without strict adherence [to a fixed number]. Furthermore, the *jānapada* (local) document has been defined by Vyāsa:
A local document should be written by a scribe in a well-known place,
containing the royal seal and the year, month, fortnight, and day.
The word "endowed with" (yutam) is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. "Vāsaraḥ" means a day. He states that other things must also be written down:

"One should record the paternal lineage, the names, and the castes of both the creditor and the debtor; as well as the specific types and quantities of the property, and the interest agreed upon by both parties."
The mutual agreement of both parties is also a qualification for the substance [of the debt] and so forth. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"Whatever matter has been settled by the mutual consent of the parties, a document should be executed for it, provided with witnesses, beginning with the name of the creditor."

It must be witnessed by those who are present, experts, knowers of the matter, and impartial; and it should be endowed with as many qualifying attributes as are necessary to establish the specific nature of that which is to be recorded—namely, the time, the creditor, the debtor, the witnesses, and so forth. To this effect, the same author says:
"Marked by the year, the month, its fortnight, the day, the names, the caste, one's own *gotra*, fellow-students, one's own name, and the names of one's father and so on. [133]

The name of one's fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), such as "Bahvṛca" or "Kaṭha" used in connection with a specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*); the name of one's own father; and the names of the fathers of the creditor, the debtor, and the witnesses. By the word "etcetera," local customs, the number of times [the document] has been used, and so forth, are included. For this very reason, Vyāsa says: "An act is marked by the local custom regarding the creation of a pledge (*ādhi*) and its acceptance. An act (*kriyā*) is performed according to local custom; "creation" (*ādhāna*) refers to a pledge (*ādhi*). Nārada also says:
A document, however, should be executed with witnesses, containing an uncorrupted sequence of words and letters,
conforming to the established customs of the region, and complete in all its matters.
Vasiṣṭha also [stated]:
"Having recorded the date, the king, the place of residence,
as well as the donor and the recipient, together with the name of the ancestors."
"Birth, one's own lineage, the branch [of the Veda], the substance, the pledge along with its number, the interest, the hand of the debtor, and two witnesses who understand the matter.
Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya himself states the manner of recording the hand of the debtor:
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall record his own name by his own hand:
"What is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so."

By saying "above," he indicates that the arrangement of his own hand-signature is below the arrangement of the letters previously written. By saying "the debtor," it is intended to include the witnesses as well; and thus that same author states:
"And the witnesses, preceded by the names of their fathers, should write 'I, so-and-so, am a witness here' with their own hands; they should all do so alike. [134]

In the document where witnesses are recorded, they too should each write: "So-and-so, the son of so-and-so, is a witness in this matter. They should be distinguished by an even number, such as two or more; the meaning is that they should not be an odd number, such as three or more. Some, by imagining the elision of the letter *a* (reading it as *na* instead of *na*), have described the rule for the number of witnesses in the opposite way. That [interpretation] is to be accepted only in a region where such a custom exists, and not elsewhere, because the natural sense of the text would otherwise be violated. The use of the plural "witnesses" (*sākṣiṇaḥ*) refers to documents concerning weightier matters.
The creditor and the debtor, as well as the witnesses and the scribe—
by the agreement of these parties, one should cause a document to be made, and not otherwise.

For Hārīta has stated that there must be two witnesses for a mere document (*lekhyamātra*). Thus, because a document executed by another is based upon five persons—namely, the creditor, the debtor, the two witnesses, and the scribe—it is commonly referred to in the world as a "five-based" (*pañcārūḍha*) document. However, it should be understood that when the number of witnesses exceeds this, such usage is figurative. With reference to a mere document, Vyāsa also said: "In the hand of the debtor, [the document] shall bear his signature, preceded by [the names of] the witnesses and their ancestors."

Therefore, the rule that there must be at least two witnesses who are equal [in status] is to be applied in accordance with local custom. However, when a witness or a debtor is illiterate, Nārada says:
"A debtor who is unable to write should have his own statement recorded;
or a witness should have it recorded by another witness in the presence of all the witnesses."

And because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana: "Even one who knows a foreign script may write by himself, since he knows writing; however, he should cause all the castes of the district to sign the document. Following this, Yājñavalkya states after the signing with their own hands by the witnesses:
When this has been requested by both parties, the scribe should then write at the end: "This has been written by [Name], the son of [Name]."
Vyāsa also says: "Requested by both [parties], the scribe shall write his own name at the end, along with his hand-signature, together with the names of such-and-such a person and his son."
"Thus has the rule regarding documents of local custom been stated in detail by Vyāsa.

The word "of the document" (*lekhyasya*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence], meaning "the endless variety of the document. He (Vyāsa) himself states that such a document is of eight kinds:
"The *ciraka*, the one in one's own hand, and likewise that designated as *upagata*..."
The fourth is the deed of dominion, and the fifth is the deed of purchase.

"The sixth is called the document of agreement (*sthitipatra*), the seventh is the document of settlement (*saṃdhipatraka*), and likewise the document of purification (*viśuddhipatraka*); thus, the worldly [documents] are remembered as being eightfold.

Here, the specific number is not intended; for even the document of partition (*vibhāgapatra*) and others are considered worldly. Regarding that, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states the definition of the *ciraka*:
The document known as the *ciraka* was recorded in ancient times by city scribes designated by the plaintiff and the defendant, who were praised according to their respective merits.
It shall be marked with the names of the plaintiff and defendant, as well as those of the witnesses, beginning with their own paternal names,
and signed by the hands of the plaintiff and the witnesses themselves.

"It shall be endowed with clear comprehension and possess the characteristics as stated in the Smṛti. The meaning is "by those who are well-known and praiseworthy. Kātyāyana, however, speaks of the "own hand" (svahasta):
"[A document] written by the debtor's own hand, even if devoid of witnesses..."
A document written by one's own hand is to be understood as valid; it is so declared by the wise.

In this very way, a document written by the debtor and accepted by the creditor is to be known as an *upagata* (acknowledged) deed. Regarding the pledge-deed (*ādhipatra*), Nārada says: "When a creditor, having made a pledge, employs his own wealth [as a loan], the document executed in that regard is called a pledge-deed."
Prajāpati states the specific rule regarding the subsequent mortgage document:
"If the creditor should take another pledge with that same wealth,
he must first have a document for that pledge executed and then deliver it to him."
The father has stated this regarding the deed of sale:

"Whatever document is executed in some place concerning an object purchased, for the purpose of making the purchase public, with the consent of the seller and by the buyer— that is to be known as a deed of sale."
Furthermore, *sthiti-patra* (certificates of custom) and other such documents were described by Kātyāyana:
"The established custom (*sthiti*) of the four classes of scholars, guilds, assemblies, citizens, and so forth—
for whatever document is written for the sake of establishing that [custom], it shall be a *sthiti-patraka*."

"When the curse has been lifted and the expiation has been performed by the people, a certificate of purification (viśuddhipatraka) should be obtained from them, accompanied by witnesses. Thus [says the law]. Bṛhaspati also speaks of the classification of documents:
Secular documents are of seven kinds, arising from shares, gifts, sales, mortgages, agreements, slavery, and debts; royal edicts are of three kinds.

Here too, the specific number is not intended to be restrictive, since more than these types of documents have been shown elsewhere. For this very reason, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used here; otherwise, since the sevenfold nature would already be established by the enumerated items alone, the inclusion of "etcetera" would be purposeless. By this it is understood that the enumeration of documents is not for the sake of limitation. Therefore, there is no contradiction among statements regarding various numbers. He himself explains the document of partition (*bhāgalekhya*) and so forth: "Brothers who have divided [the estate] by their own mutual consent..."
When they draw up a document of partition, that is called a deed of division.
But that document which one should have made after giving land, to remain as long as the moon and sun,
which is neither to be confiscated nor to be taken away— they know that indeed to be a *dānalekhya*.
That document which one causes to be executed after purchasing a house, field, or the like, accompanied by the letters indicating the equivalent price,
is called a *krayalekhya* (a deed of purchase).
When one, having given movable or immovable property as a pledge,
executes a document specifying it as being subject to the acts of custody or enjoyment, that is called a pledge-deed (ādhi-lekhya).
Whatever agreement a village or a district may make with one another,
provided it does not conflict with the king and is for the sake of dharma and material interest, they call that a "contract document" (saṃvitpatra).
Whatever work one who is destitute of clothing and food performs in the wilderness, I shall perform those actions for you; that is called a "slave-deed" (dāsapatra).
"Having taken wealth at interest, one may either do [the work] oneself or cause it to be done;
that is called an *uddhāra-patra* (a deed of release), which the wise term a debt-document (*ṛṇalekhya*).
Thus [it is said]. Kātyāyana also mentions another type of secular document:

"When a boundary dispute has been decided, a boundary-deed (sīmāpatra) is prescribed," so says Yājñavalkya as well: "Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document; or, in case of clearance, one should cause another to be made."
Marīci states the purpose of a written document:
"In regard to immovable property— whether in sale, mortgage, partition, or gift—
one attains legal success and freedom from dispute through a written record."

*Ādhāna* means a pledge (*ādhi*). The first *ca* (and) is for the purpose of including items such as debts and the like. *Avisaṃvāda* (non-contradiction) is the non-alteration of the settled matter even at a later time. And thus, having considered that success is achieved through non-contradiction even in the case of immovable property and the like, the insertion or deletion of those items to be written—such as the royal lineage, the year, and so forth—should be performed, because they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). Therefore, in a document concerning a gift and the like, the creditor, debtor, and so forth need not be written; nor should matters such as acceptance be written in a document concerning a debt and the like. In this same way, what is to be written in other documents should be inferred, since a document has a visible purpose. For this very reason, when a document that has served its purpose becomes unfit for action or is destroyed, another document should be produced. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
If a document is located in another country, is difficult to read, lost, erased, stolen, torn, burnt, or likewise cut, one should have another document executed.

In the case of a document located in another country, situated in a place from which it is entirely impossible to bring back, illegible due to indistinct characters, torn into two, cut, or decayed— Kātyāyana also states:
"That document which is marred by stains, burnt, perforated, or even worn away,
as well as one rubbed out by perspiration— one should have another document executed."
"Vīta" means gone away; "ullikhita" means wiped away. Furthermore, as stated by Nārada:

"When a document has been deposited in another country, is decayed, poorly written, or stolen, there shall be a formal procedure for its production at that time; if it does not exist, one must produce what was seen. [139]

Thus, that [rule] refers specifically to the case of a debtor intent on paying the debt at that very moment; for in that situation, there is no purpose in creating another document. "Fixing a time" means determining a suitable period for the delivery of that document. "Showing what has been seen" means making known to the witnesses—who already know the matters obtainable from the document—that the payment of the wealth must be carried out; this is the meaning. And this [showing] must be done even when tearing up the document is impossible, in order to terminate the witness-status of the witnesses. Furthermore, for the sake of publicizing the repayment, a document of receipt (*pratidattapatra*) should be taken. However, if the money is to be paid at a later time, another document must certainly be made. For this very reason, it was stated by him as well:
"In cases where [a document] is torn, broken, lost, erased, burnt, or poorly written, another document should be executed; this is the traditional rule for documents.
Thus ends the section on the determination of documents in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the examination of documents; regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
Having summoned the legal proceedings, the king should investigate them according to justice.
A document is established by the conduct of writing, and witnesses by the conduct of witness testimony.
The practice of writing consists of clearly articulated syllables, sentences, and so forth. That too has been demonstrated by him [Manu] himself:
"A document that is endowed with correct syllables and sentences, free from doubt, with clear letters, and lacking no sequence or marks, shall attain validity."

Action is that which is to be accomplished. The mark is the seal, and that exists only in royal documents. And so Nārada says: "A document issued by the king, bearing his own hand and marked with his own seal, is declared to be a royal document in all matters, provided it contains witnesses."
Likewise, the same author speaks regarding local custom:
"Writing is said to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another;
it may be without witnesses or with witnesses, and its validity depends on its established usage in the region."

"According to the location" means in accordance with the local customs of that place; "the establishment of those two" means their validity—this is the meaning. Regarding the specific case of one's own handwriting, Yājñavalkya says:
"Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is declared to be valid in all cases, except when it was executed through force or fraud."

By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even without," it is understood that there is also a document written in one's own hand which possesses witnesses. However, a document prepared by another is authoritative only when it has witnesses. And so Pitāmaha says:
"A document written by a scribe with witnesses, authorized by both parties, is declared by the wise to be authoritative in all legal matters."

Kātyāyana also says: A document is said to be that which is consistent with local custom, specifies the increase in years, months, fortnights, and so forth, and bears the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
The mention of "interest" (vṛddhi) is intended as an illustration for "pledge" (ādhi). For this very reason, Nārada says:

"A document that is not contrary to local custom, which possesses the characteristics of a clear pledge and formal procedure, and whose sequence and letters are uncorrupted, is declared to be authoritative."

The definition of a document that possesses the characteristics of a formal legal instrument (*ādhividhi*) is clearly stated: a document that is endowed with the characteristics of uncorrupted sequence, letters, and so forth, is authoritative; the meaning is that even at a later time, it serves to reveal the true nature of the matter. By implication, it is established that what is not of such a kind is not authoritative. Nevertheless, Kātyāyana has stated this for the sake of clarity: "When the letters have lost their proper positions, are out of alignment, are ambiguous, or have deviated from the [prescribed] characteristics, then that document shall be considered forged."
"That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which has been done by a master [without authority], and that which is devoid of a point to be proved— these are defective. Thus says Hārīta as well.
That document which is covered with crow's-foot marks shall be considered fraudulent; likewise, that which is devoid of dots and mātrās, or that which is incorrectly joined or misplaced.
Bṛhaspati also says:
A document that is brilliant [in appearance] though made long ago, or soiled though made recently,
or which contains erased and rewritten syllables, shall be considered forged.

"A document executed by one who is about to die, a child, one who is terrified, one seeking wealth, a woman, one intoxicated, one afflicted by vice, or one made under duress at night or through fraud, is not valid. Thus [says] Nārada as well.
However, that document which was executed through the coercion of women, children, or those intoxicated,
as well as that which was made under fear or fraud, is not authoritative.

Kātyāyana also states: A document executed by one who is intoxicated, one who is apprehensive due to a legal impediment, one who is insane, those who are afflicted, women, children, or those who are not independent, is not valid.

The intended meaning of the statements of Bṛhaspati and others is that what is produced by one who is about to die and so forth does not attain the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to the suspicion that it is untrue. Likewise, even when there is a deficiency in witnesses and the like, it is not valid cognition. And thus Vyāsa says: "Where a witness who is corrupted or of evil conduct is appointed, they call that a forged document; the same applies if the scribe is of such a kind."
Kātyāyana also says: "A document may indeed be rendered invalid due to a defect in the witnesses, or by that of the scribe,
or by a defect of the creditor, or likewise of the debtor."

Regarding this, he [the author] himself states: "Those defects which are concealed must be pointed out by the disputant; however, those which are manifest must be pointed out by the members of the assembly at the proper time through the citation of the scriptures.

For indeed, whatever defects exist in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those that are concealed must be stated by the disputant, whereas those that are manifest must be pointed out by the members of the assembly at the appropriate time by demonstrating the relevant treatises.

"Of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that has been proclaimed as being valid—'at the time' means at the time for the examination of the means of proof. Bṛhaspati states that defects declared after the lapse of time do not invalidate validity:
'Whatever defects of a document or of witnesses are recorded, they must be stated at the time of the trial; once stated later, one may not use them to invalidate [the evidence].'"

The meaning is that one should not raise an objection after what has been stated, namely, after the conclusion of the examination of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*). Kātyāyana describes the method for exposing hidden defects: "The witnesses, the scribe, and the author [of the document] likewise fall into falsehood; thus, defects should be brought forward by the litigants so that the document is rendered invalid. [143]
Alternatively, he [the author] himself states that one must point out the defect by saying, "It was not written by the scribe who signed it," or "It was not seen by the witnesses who signed it":
"When the defendant has stated, 'It was not written by the scribe' and likewise, 'It was not seen by the witnesses,' the document is declared to be forged."
The phrase "by the meaning already stated" is to be understood as the ellipsis. And thus, that same [text] says:

"One should not invalidate a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through a groundless fault; rather, one should invalidate it only through a [genuine] defect. In the case of a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the object to be proven."

Thus, when a defect has been raised by the opponent, the presiding officer of the assembly should examine those defects for the other party. And so it is said: "In that royal court where such a case is being deliberated, he should, after reflecting together with the Brahmins, examine the defects of the written document."
In this regard, he himself has stated that if those defects have not been avoided by the other party, then the document is defective; but if they have been avoided, it is not defective:
"By that [cause] through which the witnesses, the scribe, and the author fall into falsehood, by that the document shall be deemed defective; one should declare its purity when they are pure."
Regarding the document known as *upagata* (admission by the debtor), that same author states that it is not invalidated even without the consent of the debtor:
"A document written by the creditor's own hand, even if devoid of witnesses,
shall not be considered forged unless the maker proves that 'it was done [by me]'."

The meaning is that if the creditor does not prove—that is, establish—that the document was executed with the consent of the debtor, then the document would be considered forged on the grounds of the debtor’s claim, "I do not know [of it]. [144] Furthermore, when he defames the writing by denying his own handwriting, then it must be determined whether it is valid or invalid based on the witnesses recorded therein. And so says that same author: "If the debtor denies his own handwriting on the document, he should be questioned by the witnesses present in the document or according to the opinion of the scribe."
Even when [the matter] has been refuted on the grounds of being unexecuted, he states that this very same certainty applies:
"In disputes concerning what has been done or not done, the decision is by means of documents; witnesses [are mentioned] as an illustration.
The mention of witnesses is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
"Once the document has been refuted, the proponent shall point out those [points] recorded therein"—
since this was stated by that very same [authority], as for what was further stated by Nārada:
"But when there is some doubt regarding a document as to whether it was produced by the actual party or not..."
One should establish that [meaning] through one's own manual action, indicative signs, logical reasoning, and scriptural attainment.
Thus, as for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"The purification of a disputed document may be established by means of a writing in one's own hand and so forth,
through reasoning, acquisition, performance, marks, connection, and the grounds of title."

Thus, this refers to the subject matter of a document executed by one's own hand in the absence of witnesses. This is because, in such a case, there is a lack of clear determinants such as witnesses and the like. For this very reason, Hārīta states: "In case of doubt regarding a debtor’s own handwriting—whether he be living or deceased—the determination of that document is made by other documents written in his own hand."

The phrase "by those written by one's own hand" is intended as an illustration for the previously mentioned actions and so forth. However, where there exists a document written by one's own hand with witnesses (*sasākṣika-svahastakṛta-lekhya*), and where witnesses and other such clear means of determination are present, there the determination should not be made based on similarity to another document, even if that other document is a clear means of determination. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
[145] Direct perception is never sublated by inference;
therefore, in the case of a defective document, the determination should be made through the words of witnesses.

"For a judgment made for the sake of one's own wealth indeed invalidates the document itself. This means that [the debt] is established by the words of the witnesses, and not from the statement of the debtor, because of the possibility of defects in his intention. With this very intent, Nārada also stated: "A written document should be [validated] by another written document; one with witnesses should be established by witnesses."
The meaning is that one should rectify a document whose witnesses and other elements are non-existent by means of another document of a similar nature. As for what he [Kātyāyana] further stated:

"A document is to be understood as superior to witnesses, but witnesses are not superior to a document," that refers to the case of witnesses who have not been recorded in writing. Therefore, a decision regarding a document possessing witnesses and other elements should be made by means of witnesses and other elements recorded in a [corresponding] document; whereas for a document lacking witnesses, it should be determined by means of similarity with another document written in one's own hand, and so forth—this is how it should be understood. When it is asked, "How then is a decision reached regarding a document whose witnesses and others have died? Kātyāyana says:
Then, if the scribe together with the witnesses has met his death, he shall be purified by their own handwriting and other such evidence; of this there is no doubt.

"Of them" refers to those such as deceased witnesses. "By that" means by means of [evidence] such as their own handwriting, which establishes similarity in hand, lineage, caste, and so forth, as found on other documents. Viṣṇu also states:
"Where a debtor, a creditor, a witness, or even a scribe dies, one should validate that document by means of their own handwriting."
Kātyāyana replies regarding the royal decree:
"That which is recorded as a subsequent judgment should be deliberated upon with great care;
if it is indeed consistent with reason, then that written document shall serve as authoritative proof."
Otherwise, one must re-examine the matter from afar if something untrue has been established as true due to a confusion of knowledge.
That [law] would be subject to reversal, even if it were established with great effort by kings.

The meaning is that it is "bound by a subsequent act," which refers to being recorded in a document of victory known as a *paścātkāra*. Likewise: "In the case of an ocean, however, just as all those who have died remain within its waters, so too that written document remains authoritative even when they have passed away."

The phrase "by means of seals and so forth" is the ellipsis for "is the proof. For this very reason, Prajāpati, having cited a seal, stated regarding the royal edict: "A definitive determination must be made with great effort from the sight of the king’s own hand, his seal, and the letters of the scribe in the royal edict."
Kātyāyana also says: "A royal edict that is pure in its seal, pure in its execution, pure in its enjoyment, accompanied by a mark,
and authenticated by the king's own hand, attains validity."

"Pure in its execution" means it is free from the use of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) and other such defects. Regarding even a document written in a local dialect, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that it attains purity through possession in certain cases: "A document by which the property of one who is capable is enjoyed for twenty years in his presence is free from defects."
It is also stated in another Smṛti: "Now,
if possession for twenty years is well-established by means of a document,
that document is proven to be free from defects."
When a boundary dispute has been settled, a formal deed of the boundary (sīmāpatra) is prescribed;
its defects must be scrutinized for a period of twenty years.

A document accompanied by a receipt and recorded as a promissory note is known by the wise to remain valid even after the death of the creditor, provided there has been at least some small enjoyment of the debt.

*Ādhāna* means a pledge (*ādhi*). *Mṛtasākṣi* refers to one whose witnesses have died, and so forth. And thus says Nārada: "Where the witnesses, the creditor, the debtor, and the scribe have all died, that document is invalid, unless there is a pledge serving as a stable basis."

The basis is the repayment. Alternatively, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that there is purification through the recovery of some interest or other wealth obtained by means of the strength of the written document, or by the disclosure of that document before the debtor: "If something has been received, or if a settlement has been made, the document is indeed authoritative even if the witnesses have died."

One merely elaborates upon a legal fiction. That which has been shown at the proper time, as well as that which has been proclaimed and likewise reminded, is established as a written document everywhere, even when the witnesses have died.
Prajāpati also states that purification may sometimes occur through enjoyment: "In a case where one who has mounted a document produced by other means denies it,
one should declare that the enjoyment belongs to him in whose hand the document is found."
The word "as a means of determination" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The mention of "enjoyment" (bhoga) is for the purpose of illustration. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"A document that bears another's name and was executed for some other purpose must, in case of dispute, be examined by means of connections, possession, and causes. [148]

"Caused by another motive" means made for the purpose of deceiving heirs and the like. "Disagreement" (*vipratyaya*) is a conflict of views. "Connection" (*saṃbandha*) is the prior relationship characterized by the giving and receiving of wealth and so forth. "Tradition" (*āgama*) consists of such matters as whether or not there is the possibility of possessing this much wealth. "Reason" (*hetu*) is inference. Likewise, even a document bearing the signature of a wealthy person must be examined when it has been produced through motives such as deception. And so Bṛhaspati says: "Relatives deceive women, children, the afflicted, and those ignorant of writing by having them sign a document marked with their own names; that [document] must be scrutinized through logic and tradition."
Having ascertained the matter, those skilled in place and time who forge documents produce a similar writing; therefore, one should examine such a document with great care.
"One ignorant of writing" means one who is unacquainted with writing. Kātyāyana also says:
"Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears as if it were real though it is unreal, so too do skilled people create the likenesses of what is to be written."
Vyāsa also says: "Some skilled men write a document like a painting;
therefore, it is held that success is not invariably achieved through the power of a document alone."
The intended meaning is that [the matter] must be thoroughly examined by him. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"There are men who, out of greed, might state a case otherwise;
and there are others, evil-minded people, who forge false documents."

"Both of these must be examined by the king himself, especially: a document according to the procedure for documents, and witnesses according to the procedure for witnesses. By "according to the procedure for documents," the meaning is: by the aforementioned collection of causes for validity. Furthermore, that document which does not attain validity through that collection of causes is indeed invalid; having discarded it, he should reach a decision by means of an ordeal (*divya*).

"In a legal proceeding where there is no documentary evidence or witnesses, one should point to divine [ordeals]," according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana. Likewise, Hārīta has also stated with this very same intention:
"This document was not written by me; it is forged and was caused to be made by another."

"Having set aside that document, the determination of the matter shall be by means of divine proof (*divya*). The intended meaning is that where there is no possibility of removing suspicion of forgery regarding a document in any way, the determination of the matter to be proved must be by divine proof. This is because a document written in one's own hand, which was cited merely as an example, is not to be relied upon. Therefore, even when the signatures, lineage, and identifying marks are present, if there is a firm contradiction from the defendant such that suspicion of forgery cannot be removed, the determination must still be made by divine proof. And so says Prajāpati:
"If a document should exist somewhere that bears a name and lineage identical to those [of the parties]..."
If the wealth has not been recovered there, a decision must be made by means of an ordeal.

"Of a similar form" means having a form identical to another document that has not been contested. This refers to a case where the defendant has not denied the debt and is firmly established. Furthermore, as stated by Nārada: "If the debtor does not clearly point out a defect in a defective document, then after twenty years have passed, the document shall become valid."

Thus, this is its meaning: a document whose validity is doubtful due to malice or the passage of a long time should be established as stable by means of an ordeal to prove the matter; for stability cannot be achieved through the mere fact of a long time having elapsed. Furthermore, Kātyāyana states the punishment for one who does not remove the defects of a document:

[150] "In the case of a false statement, the testimony of the witnesses and the document of the scribe must be brought to clarity. He who does not [clarify] what is forged shall be made to pay the highest fine."

The meaning is this: regarding the testimony of witnesses or the document of a scribe, if a litigant makes a false statement as described above and does not purify that falsehood, he shall be punished with the highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*). However, in cases involving immovable property and the like, the same author prescribes a different punishment: "He who fabricates a forged document concerning the sale or mortgage of immovable property, when fully convicted, shall be deprived of his tongue, hands, and feet."
Therefore, Vyāsa states that the person holding another's document must disclose the reason for the arrival of that document:
"When a document executed by one person is seen in the hand of another,
he must necessarily explain the document and the manner in which it came into his possession."

The meaning is: "from the owner of the document. Likewise, regarding the mutual contradiction of documents, he [Yājñavalkya] himself stated this for the purpose of determining the sublated and the sublator: "A document executed by one's own hand is superior to a *jānapada* document; however, a royal edict is held to be more authoritative when it has come before the court for the sake of legal proceedings."

In this context, by the term *jānapada* (local), something other than what is written in one's own hand is meant, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull. By the word *nṛpa* (king) as well, through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), anything royal other than a formal edict (*śāsana*) is intended; thus, that which is made by another is stronger than what is written in one's own hand, that which is royal is stronger than even that, and the edict is stronger than even that. This progressive strength should be understood from the decreasing possibility of forgery in each successive case. Therefore, it should be understood that a document written in one's own hand without witnesses is stronger than a document known as an *upagata* (acknowledgment), and a document written in one's own hand with witnesses is stronger than that. For this very reason, Saṃvarta states that a mere document is stronger than the testimony of witnesses.
Testimony that is false regarding a document is called *kūṭa* (forged/false);
for it is the gateway to unrighteousness, and therefore the king should avoid it.

The meaning is that testimony which contradicts a written document is weaker than it. Bṛhaspati also says: "Where the capacity of the letters to convey meaning is obstructed by the witnesses, there would be a total destruction of legal actions and a state of instability would arise."
Regarding legal actions, specifically those involving written documents, Kātyāyana also states:
"A written document is never invalidated by ordeals or even by witnesses;
for the rule of documentary evidence is always superior, and thus one is not defeated by any other means."
But he [Yājñavalkya] himself says that one is defeated by means of a document:
"The legal action based on a document is always set aside by a counter-document (pratilekhya) associated with it or by one superior to it; it can never be set aside by anything else."
The meaning is: "by another means, such as witnesses and so forth. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"A document is never defeated by witnesses or by an oath;
it suffers defeat through neglect, by being neither produced nor read out."
The phrase "extending over a long period" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus Vyāsa says:

"A document that has not been seen or heard [by witnesses], one where the creditor or debtor is deceased, and one for which no surety has been bound—even if it be of long standing—is not established [as valid]."

"Without a seal or a signature, and lacking a guarantor or a surety; having been held for a long time—that is, for many years—it does not become valid by itself; this is the intended meaning. Kātyāyana also says:
"A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor read aloud, does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still exist."
He himself states the distinction even regarding non-production:
"But when the profit has been received, if the debtor does not produce the document,
nor does the creditor demand it, that shall incur the status of being doubtful."

The remainder [of the meaning] is "the debtor who is nearby and wealthy. And so Bṛhaspati says: "If that which was not requested by a capable person from one who is wealthy and nearby is not cleared because of suspicion, then the document therein shall become weak."
Thus, since there is no distinction made regarding the loss of a document due to non-appearance, the same author states an exception:
"The loss of a document shall not apply in the case of those who are insane, idiotic, or minor; those who have fled out of fear of the king; and those who are timid, fearful, or afflicted."
Saṃvarta, however, states that even documents appearing to be forged may become subjects of legal inquiry after a long period of time:
"That which was executed under force or through fraud, as well as that which was done by one who is intoxicated or insane—
these and many others remain grounds for litigation even after a long time has passed."
The intention is that the rules for purification mentioned in such passages as these are to be applied by those who determine [the validity of documents]. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
"A document which, after taking property, is delivered to another;
or one that is concealed, or one that has been mounted by another, or one held in the house of another."
"Whether the transaction has already taken place or whether some document was previously written,
this same rule is to be understood as the means for determining the validity of a document.
Thus ends the examination of documents in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
[153] Now follows the determination of possession;
regarding this, Nārada says:
Having heard the reply, one should point out the document in the section on legal procedures (kriyāpāda),
or long-standing possession characterized by the marks of neighboring witnesses.

Here, by the word *sādhana* (means of proof), witnesses are intended according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Therefore, the meaning is this: in disputes concerning houses, fields, and so forth, one should point to either a written document or witnesses, or else possession (*bhukti*) should be proclaimed. For this very reason, a distinction regarding witnesses is described by this [author]: "In disputes over houses, fields, and the like, the decision is reached through neighbors;
as well as those who are the heads of city or village communities and the most venerable men."
Whatever those established in legal authority say, that should be accepted as conventional practice.

This is what is meant: in disputes concerning immovable property such as fields and the like, one should point to any one of the human means of proof (*pramāṇa*), and never to divine proof (*divya*). Regarding that, Kātyāyana says that among those [human proofs], written documents and possession are the best:
"Written documents, witnesses, and possession are accepted as the three means of proof;
among these means of proof, for men, possession is traditionally held to be equal to a formal document."

The grammatical connection is "among the means of proof for men. This means "among human means of proof. *Sallekhya* refers to a faultless document. He states that in some cases, possession alone is superior to the other two:
"When there is doubt regarding a road, an exit gate, a watercourse, and so forth, possession alone shall be weightier among the means of proof; this is the settled rule. [154]
Nārada states that even in cases other than those involving public roads and the like, the two [documents and witnesses] do not possess superior weight without the support of possession:
"Even when a document exists and witnesses are living,
that which has not been possessed— especially in the case of immovable property— is unstable."

Yājñavalkya also says: "Even in the case of title (*āgama*), possession has no strength at all where it is even slight. The meaning is: "In the case of title"—that is, in cases such as purchase that must be known through documents or witnesses. By this, it is stated by implication that possession, being merely a supportive factor that removes suspicion of defects in the title, documents, and so forth, is not itself a means of proof (*pramāṇa*). And it has been said by Kātyāyana:
When the object of a document is enjoyed in the presence of the capable owner for ten years, that document is considered free from defect.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"When a village, a field, or a garden is recorded in a single title-deed,
they all become enjoyed even by the enjoyment of only one part."
Furthermore, regarding a document issued by a master who gives land without restriction or opposition, that [document] is indeed fruitless; as he himself says:
"He who, seeing another giving away land, does not object—even though he is the owner recorded in the document—shall not regain it again."
"Even by one who is virtuous" means even by one who is upright. "Land" (*kṣiti*) is used as an illustration for any object to be given. As that same author says:
"If property is delivered in the presence of someone by heirs or others, he does not deserve to obtain it later from another who is already enjoying it. [155]

The meaning is that when there is a document of acquisition by the owner—indicated by the fact that the gift was made in his presence and not prohibited—it becomes an obstacle to its being a proof of ownership. By this, it is stated that a document concerning property, by one desiring to achieve their own purpose through it, must be diligently prohibited by the owner from the gift being made in his presence. This should be understood to apply equally to the non-prohibition of possession in his presence. And thus Vyāsa says:
"If land has been enjoyed here by others for twenty years..."
While the king is present, his success here is not achieved despite his capability.
The phrase "even by a document" is to be understood as the ellipsis. For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
"When a house or field is being enjoyed while the king is present, for him who possesses such enjoyment, the document is not the cause [of ownership] therein."

The meaning is this: since for that possessor (*bhoktṛ*), there must be something being enjoyed (*bhujyamāna*), in that case, a document of indifference (*upekṣā-lekhya*) is neither a cause nor a means of proof; for the capacity of a document to establish [ownership] is obstructed by possession characterized by indifference, which indicates the acquisition of ownership. This statement regarding the uselessness of the document was made for that purpose, and not for the sake of establishing the possessor’s actual ownership, because ownership is not established by mere possession alone. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "The force of possession should not be admitted as a legal ground by the acquirer or his son, in the case of cattle, women, men, and so forth; such is the settled law."* *Note: The term *upabhogabala* refers to the evidentiary weight of possession.*
For this very reason, Vyāsa has provided the illustration of a cow:
"Just as a cow that is desired perishes without a keeper, so too land that is being watched over by others is lost to him [the owner] when it is enjoyed [by another]. [156]
Yājñavalkya also has stated in this way that there is only the loss of the owner who neglects his property, and not the acquisition of ownership by the possessor:
"The loss of land occurs after twenty years for one who sees it being enjoyed by another but does not speak out; for wealth, it occurs after ten years."

In this context, "loss" (hāni) is intended merely as the proof of ownership by means of the written document, and not as the loss of actual ownership (*svatva*) over the land or its fruit; for it has been stated that ownership does not depart through mere neglect. Therefore, in this case, there is no loss for the neglecting party due to the legal determination known as *dharma*, because the proof of ownership remains possible through that [document]. It is not so, however, by virtue of the legal determination known as *vyavahāra* (procedural litigation), since defects in the document have already been mentioned; rather, it is due to the second legal determination known as *vyavahāra* that the possessor is not censured, while the owner is defeated for being unable to provide a defense.
