[Manu 8.131] "One who denies a debt
"If [the owner] is not an idiot and not a minor, and his property is enjoyed [by another], that [claim] is defeated by legal procedure; the enjoyer deserves that wealth.
Thus [it is said]. Bṛhaspati states the meaning of the word "legal procedure" (vyavahāra):

"That legal proceeding which is determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is called [the first]; the second is proclaimed as that which results from the failure to provide a reply due to quibbling with words (*vākchala*). Thus, "determined by means of valid cognition" means determined by human means of knowledge. Even for one who has been defeated either through the practice of quibbling or through the inability to provide a reply, the legal proceeding remains essentially real; for, in the absence of valid cognition, the victory of the defendant is merely precarious.

"A king should conduct legal proceedings by means of the truth, having set aside deception"—since this has also been stated by Yājñavalkya, it should be understood that if the seizure and enjoyment of property by an opponent are not prohibited in this manner, the futility of witnesses is established by the logic of the "stick and the molasses" (daṇḍāpūpanyāya). For this very reason, Nārada says:
"Of him who remains silent and indifferent..."
When the aforementioned time has elapsed, the legal proceeding is not established.
The meaning is that his own legal claim is not established by human means of proof alone. The author of the *Saṃgraha* also says:
"Possession without title is fruitless, even when being enjoyed by others.

Here, by the word *āgama* (title), both written documents and witnesses—which constitute such title—are intended. For this very reason, Marīci states that loss [of the claim] generally occurs even in cases to be proven by witnesses.
A cow used for riding and its ornaments, requested as a gift of affection, should be returned within four or five years; otherwise, one incurs loss.
Regarding this, Manu states the exception:
"Cows, camels, draft horses, and those animals used for taming that are enjoyed through mutual consent are never lost [to the owner]."
A calf is a young ox to be tamed. Regarding borrowed items, Vyāsa states this exception:
"That which has been enjoyed by learned brahmins (*śrotriya*), royal servants, friends, or kinsmen according to the custom of borrowing is not lost through such enjoyment."
The meaning is "that which is an ornament and so forth. He himself also states the reason why it is not lost:
"In the case of a learned brahmin (śrotriya), there would be merit; in the case of a king's servant, there would be fear;
toward friends and kinsmen, there is affection; what has been enjoyed by these is not lost."

The phrase "even after five years" is understood to mean that even beyond that period. By this, it is stated that there is never any loss when neglect is accompanied by a valid reason. Consequently, an exception to the rules regarding loss after ten or twenty years should also be understood to apply in cases of neglect where a valid reason exists. For this very reason, Manu says:
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the wealth of a Vedic scholar do not perish through mere enjoyment."

The ease of establishing [ownership] by means of local marks within the boundaries is a reason for indifference; likewise is timidity toward women; and for the king and the learned brahmin (*śrotriya*), distraction due to visible and invisible duties [respectively]. For the remaining [categories], the reasons for indifference are obvious. Thus, even when reasons for indifference based on the nature of the relationship exist, there is no loss [of ownership]. And so Vyāsa says:

"When property has been enjoyed by paternal kinsmen, relatives, or one's own people, there is no legal proof of ownership established therein; one should consider such enjoyment as occurring elsewhere [in a different context]."

In that regard, because indifference is possible toward the property of kinsmen and others due to their relationship, the meaning is that there would be no establishment [of ownership] through the loss of land and so forth. The grandfather [Yājñavalkya] also says:
"In that case where another person is the enjoyer, possession is powerful;
however, among those who possess property within one's own lineage, the possession of men is not capable of being eternal."

"Powerful" means that which renders futile documents and the like that are adverse to itself; "in one's own lineage" means among one's own maternal and paternal relatives—this is the meaning. And so says Kātyāyana:

"One should not presume possession in the case of women, nor in the property of a deity or a king, nor in the wealth of a minor or a Vedic scholar, nor in the property inherited from the mother or the father, respectively."

Because the gods possess a nature that does not exclude others [from their property], there is no loss when their wealth is enjoyed by another. The mention of a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) is intended as an illustration for anyone who is attached to another [place]. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"A certain person, a student (*brahmacārī*), may observe the vow for thirty-six years;
or a man seeking wealth may dwell in another region for a long time."
[159] Having returned home, the student under vows should then seek out his own property;
possession for fifty years constitutes the seizure of that property.
For students of the Vedas, a period of twelve years for each Veda is prescribed;
for those studying the arts and crafts, it is proclaimed that their study lasts until mastery is achieved.

"That which was enjoyed by their friends and kinsmen while they were unaware [of the seizure], as well as that of those who offended the king, does not lapse with the passage of time. This collection of exceptions is to be understood as applying when there is no legal title for the possessor. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
There shall be no enjoyment of women's property by any means without a written document;
nor [shall there be enjoyment] of the wealth of the king, of a Śrotriya, or of the property of the mentally disabled or minors.
The word "of women" is to be understood as the object, with "property" being the understood subject. "Without a document" means without the authority of a title-deed. Nārada also says:
"The property of women is never lost to kings, even if it is enjoyed for hundreds of years without a legal title."
And "the wealth of kings" means their property; for thus says that same [author]:
"Through direct enjoyment, even two hundred years of ownership [are lost];
even mortgages and the like perish, except in the case of the property of women and kings."

The statement "even mortgages and the like" is an assertion made with confidence (*prauḍhivāda*), because since these also possess the possibility of being neglected due to their enjoyment, they are equivalent to the property of a woman or the property of a king. By stating "without title," he shows that if a title exists, the property indeed becomes worn away by adverse possession. And this has been shown by Hārīta:
"Whatever is enjoyed, seized, hidden, or guarded by force through soldiers or flatterers;
or what is given out of affection or friendship, or lent for hire;"

"Likewise, [the acquisition] of clothing requested for the sake of protection or out of affection— thus, in regard to various kinds of property, this is declared to be the determination of legal title."

[This is] for the purpose of protecting one’s dwelling and for the purpose of protecting one’s house. Furthermore, it should be understood that possession which is adverse—being devoid of the grounds for indifference—even in the absence of a title-deed, renders the written document and witnesses useless if it exceeds the prescribed period. Therefore, in matters concerning houses, fields, and so forth, a written document and witnesses should be cited as evidence only when they are accompanied by favorable possession and are free from adverse acts such as open transfer. As to what kind of possession should be cited, it has been stated in response to this inquiry: "Possession that possesses the characteristics of neighbors, or possession that is long-standing."

The neighbors of the field or other property that constitutes the subject of the dispute are those who live on all sides of it; possession "accompanied by neighbors" is that which is known by them. However, possession "accompanied by characteristics" was shown by Pitāmaha: "Possession is declared to be of five kinds: accompanied by title, of long duration, uninterrupted, undisputed, and in the presence of the opponent."
That [possession] which is accompanied by title is rooted in title. And so says Hārīta:
"A branch does not grow in the air without a root;
title shall be the root, and possession is proclaimed as the branch."

When it is asked, "What, then, is the source of income? Nārada says: "Acquisition through gift, acquisition through purchase, as well as that obtained by valor, that from marriage, and that born from a relative of one who has no offspring—this is the sixfold source of wealth. [161]
"Obtained by birth" means acquired through paternal inheritance and so forth; "obtained by sight" refers to such things as buried treasure. Bṛhaspati also says:

"That which is obtained through learning, by purchase, by marriage, or through valor, as well as that which is accompanied by a wife, and the share of a sapinda who is childless—immovable property is thus declared to be sevenfold."

A pledge (*bandha*) is a source of legal obligation (*ādhi*). We shall explain later that even this may, in certain cases, serve as the basis for ownership. "For a long time" means for no less than thirty years. And thus says the same [author]: "If possession has been uninterrupted for thirty years, beginning from the time of its acquisition, one should not displace it from him."

Possession (*parigraha*) is the act of occupying. Thus, long-term enjoyment is a means of proof supported by title (*āgama*), whereas short-term enjoyment is supported by title; this is how it should be understood. For this very reason, Pitāmaha stated: "There is no possession without title, nor is there title without possession. Because of their mutual connection, their status as valid evidence is established."
The phrase "by the previously stated rule" is to be understood as the ellipsis. With this very intention, Bṛhaspati also says:
"Possession alone shall never attain validity;
it is established by both [possession] and a pure title, and not otherwise."
The meaning is "by means of possession alone, devoid of traditional title. Likewise, there is non-establishment even by means of other such qualifications. Therefore, Vyāsa says:
"Possession is held to have five constituent parts: it must be accompanied by traditional title, long-standing, free from interruption or dispute, and in the presence of the opponent" [162].

By stating that [title] has five constituents (*pañcāṅga*), he shows that even the absence of a single constituent renders the enjoyment itself invalid. And this has been shown by Nārada: "He who asserts mere enjoyment but never cites a legal title (*āgama*) should be known as a thief under the pretext of enjoyment."

The intention is that, therefore, even the source of authority (*āgama*) and other ancillary elements should be proclaimed in the presence of the court members. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "By a plaintiff who has lost the document of title or whose possession has become established, the time, the evidence, and the gift must be proclaimed in the assembly."

The mention of "gift" (*dāna*) is intended as an illustration for "title" (*āgama*). The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including specific qualifications such as continuity (*sāntatya*) and so forth. And thus is the meaning: by one who speaks of the measure of enjoyment (*bhoga*), the measure known as enjoyment and its qualifications—such as title, long duration, and so on—must be proclaimed; and once proclaimed, they must be proven in case of dispute, because there is no certainty through mere proclamation alone. Regarding that, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states that the ascertainment of possession characterized by long duration and other such factors depends upon witnesses:
"In establishing possession, the primary [witnesses] are first those farmers."
The village headmen and the boundary-markers of the fields shall, in turn, reconcile them.

The meaning is that for one who seeks to reconcile [the matter], the qualification of "long duration" and so forth, as well as possession (*bhukti*), must be brought forward. However, for one who brings forward traditional title (*āgama*), he (Yājñavalkya) states that the triad beginning with written documents (*likhita*) constitutes the means of proof:
"In disputes concerning fields, houses, and the like, the evidence consists of written documents, witnesses, and possession;
whereas in cases such as purchase or gift, when a long-standing [title] is denied, traditional title is the proof."

The meaning is as follows: when the doctrine of "lost title" (*utsannasattā*) has been rejected and the opponent has refuted the claim of acquisition through purchase and other means, then for one who asserts acquisition (*āgama*) regarding fields and the like, documentary evidence, witnesses, and possession (*bhukti*) are the valid proofs. Now, one might ask: how can possession be a valid proof regarding acquisition, given that possession is seen even in cases such as theft where there is no basis in acquisition? Do not say so; when possession characterized by long duration and other qualities is observed and no other basis is seen, its very foundation in acquisition is determined, just as the *Manu* and other Smṛtis are understood to have the Veda as their basis. But even so, if possession is initiated during a period capable of being remembered, since the absence of the underlying acquisition is certain through the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), how can the establishment of acquisition occur there solely by the force of possession? True; for this very reason, when possession is initiated at that time, acquisition is determined by means of documents and witnesses alone. However, when initiated during a period capable of being remembered, it is established by its own force as well; thus, it is logical to state three types of evidence regarding acquisition. This very point was also stated by Kātyāyana.
"In the period of memory (smārta-kāla), possession of land is held to require a title;
in the period beyond memory (asmārta), because there is no possibility of tracing the title, it is established by mere succession through three generations."

The meaning is: "due to the absence of non-apprehension of what is otherwise perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhi*), which constitutes a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). This is what is being said: possession (*bhukti*) that has begun within a period of time exceeding one hundred and five years from the past—during which [the owner] would have been capable of remembering—is accepted as proof of ownership only when its basis in a title (*āgama*) is known through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because, when the basis is known by oneself, such possession is subverted by the non-apprehension of what is otherwise perceptible. However, possession that has begun in a period prior to one hundred and five years—that is, in a time beyond the reach of memory—is proof of ownership even without the basis in a title being known through other means of knowledge, provided its own firmness is established. Furthermore, the author of the *Saṃgraha* has provided the explanation for the phrase "come down through three generations" (*tripuruṣāgatā*) in due order.
[164] That possession which has been enjoyed by three ancestors— the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather— who were independent,
is to be known as "possession of three generations," provided it was maintained throughout their lives.

And this has been stated primarily as an illustration of possession (*bhukti*) that begins in a period beyond the reach of memory (*asmārtakāla*); therefore, when possession is based on the authority of tradition (*āgama*), the fact that it has passed through three generations (*tripuruṣāgatatva*) is irrelevant, whereas its commencement in a period beyond the reach of memory is what is relevant. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati has stated that possession possesses the status of "three generations" by virtue of time alone, even in the absence of the passage of three persons:
"If one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are alive, land that has been possessed for thirty years without being obstructed by others [is established]."
That possession is to be known as *pauruṣī* (of one generation); that which is double is *dvipauruṣī*;
that which is triple is *tripauruṣī*; and beyond that, it is *cirantanī* (ancient).

"Thirty years plus five more"—this is the remainder [of the phrase]; for it is stated in another Smṛti: "Possession lasting thirty-five years is called *pauruṣa* (belonging to one man). Thus, the proponent of a title-deed must establish that title by means of a document and witnesses alone, because possession that has its commencement beyond the period of memory (*asmārta-kāla*) is impossible. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
Where the defendant is accused of having taken [the property], then documentary evidence is superior to witnesses;
but in the absence of those, possession alone is weightier than even the sons' [testimony].

"In the absence of that" means in the absence of the person who initiated the possession. With this very intention, Kātyāyana also says: "The initiator, even if his possession is accompanied by documentary evidence, must clear away defects in the document; but his son must clear away defects in the possession, yet he shall not incur defects in the document. [165]
The mention of "son" (*suta*) is intended to include the grandson (*pautra*) as well. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"He by whom the title-deed (*āgama*) was executed, being sued, must produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson [need do so], for in that case possession (*bhukti*) is more weighty."

For one who has established title (*kṛtāgama*), the production of that title must be accomplished by means of documents and witnesses alone; for possession, since its commencement falls within the period of legal memory (*smārta-kāla*), is capable of establishing title as well. Thus, for one who has established title, the title itself must be proven separately from possession. However, it should be understood that in the case of sons and grandsons, even when the possession is not of long standing, the title is proven as an inseparable concomitant of the proof of possession. Therefore, Bṛhaspati stated that in the case of long-standing enjoyment, the title itself is sufficient: "The original acquirer (*āhartṛ*) shall prove both possession and title in court."
His son shall enjoy only the usufruct alone, while his grandson and descendants shall receive nothing at all.

The meaning is this: his son must establish the sole right of enjoyment—extending from the time the first ancestor began to enjoy it until the present dispute, without interruption, and in the presence of persons capable of being opponents. The mention of the "son" (*putra*) is intended to include the grandson (*pautra*) as well; the compound *pautrādiḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* where the qualities of the members do not apply to the whole. Therefore, the case of the grandson should be understood to be exactly like that of the son. For this very reason, another Smṛti states: "He by whom the title-deed (*āgama*) was made shall be punished if he does not produce it."
Neither his son nor the son of that son shall suffer the loss of their enjoyments.

The phrase "even in the case of long-standing possession" is the ellipsis to be supplied. By this, it is stated by implication that in the case of long-standing possession, there is no loss of the right to enjoy the property even if the great-grandson or others have not produced documentary evidence. And it has been stated by Viṣṇu:
"But land which has been enjoyed by three persons in accordance with the law—even in the absence of a document—the fourth person therein shall acquire it."
The meaning is: "even in the absence of a document," that is, even in the absence of evidence such as possession that reveals the mode of acquisition. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"That which has been enjoyed for three successive reigns by other kings, even without documentary proof—that gift to a Brāhmaṇa must never be seized by the king."
"By means of proof" means by means of the proof that reveals the title-deed (*āgama*). Nārada also says:
"That which has been enjoyed for a very long time by three preceding generations without a title-deed cannot be taken away, having come down through the succession of three persons."

The meaning is: even when possession is perceived despite the total absence of a title deed (*āgama*). Śaṅkha also states: "One may acquire that which was possessed by two preceding ancestors even without a title deed. This has the same sense as the previous statement. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the fourth descendant and those following may acquire it. And so Bṛhaspati says:
"Where possession has been exercised for three generations and is continued into the fourth, that possession attains stability; one need not inquire about the title deed anywhere."

The meaning is that one should not inquire anywhere regarding any evidence for the source of possession as previously described; however, one must certainly inquire regarding the evidence for possession characterized by continuity and other such qualities. And so says Nārada:
"The possessor alone, when challenged, should produce proof of his title;
possession itself shall be pure for those who have acquired it through succession from their fathers."

"Place" (pada) means a location, that is to say, a title deed (*āgama*). It is "pure" because it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through its possession of continuity and other such qualities. Regarding those who have obtained [the land], such as the fourth [descendant] and so forth: Bṛhaspati also says:
"When possession has been enjoyed by three generations of men without interruption, no title deed need be produced there; in that case, possession is more weighty."

In those cases beginning with the fourth generation, it is not strictly necessary to establish documentary evidence (*āgama*). This is because, in such instances, possession (*bhukti*) that has descended through three preceding generations and is established as possessing specific qualifications such as continuity (*sāntatya*) and so forth, is more weighty; even without the certainty of documentary evidence, it is itself an independent means of proof (*pramāṇa*). Thus, he [Yājñavalkya] himself says: "In disputes concerning immovable property, possession that has lasted for three generations is to be known as independent; it is the authoritative means for determining the matter to be proven."
"Independent" (svatantrā) means not depending on the certainty of one's own foundational scriptural authority (āgama). Kātyāyana also says:
"Possession (bhukti) is said to be of two kinds: with scriptural authority (sāgamā) and likewise without scriptural authority (anāgamā).
That which has continued for three generations is independent; however, that which is of short duration requires scriptural authority."

"With established title" (*sāgamā*) means that the title is certain. Now, one might object: even an independent possession is indeed one with a certain title, because the certainty of the title arises precisely from the firmness of the possession itself. This is not so; for long-standing possession—that is, possession during a period beyond the reach of memory—lacks the firmness required when there is no manifestation of specific qualifications such as continuity (*sāntatya*). Nor should it be said that the fourth descendant and others must also manifest their own possession, because of the prohibition against manifesting possession during a period beyond the reach of memory in the rule: "But the grandson and his descendants [may claim] something [even after three generations]" (*Bṛhaspati Smṛti*, cited above).

"Enjoyment itself shall be pure when it has been acquired from one's father in due succession" (YDh 2.27). This is because the rule prescribes the bringing forward of possession belonging specifically to the period defined by the Smṛtis. Therefore, independent possession is uncertain without a title (*āgama*). How, then, can it be authoritative regarding ownership? It is said: even in the absence of certainty regarding the title, the authority of such [possession] is accepted. This is because the alternative of its being accompanied by a title is absolutely impossible, and because there is no subverting factor consisting of the certainty that there is no title. Likewise, in cases such as *sāhasa* (heinous crimes), the authority of witnesses is accepted merely on the basis of the absence of certainty regarding their speaking falsely.
"Everyone is a witness in cases of adultery, theft, verbal assault, and violence.
Thus, here too, everything is well-established. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
"One should not, out of greed, disturb a long-standing possession that has been unchallenged."

"Unknown" means by reason of its non-arrival [in memory]. This is what is meant: just as a possession that has been adjudicated according to legal pretext (*chala*) may be overturned even after twenty years of enjoyment if it is subsequently found to be contrary to the facts (*bhūta*), such is not the case for a very long-standing possession. Hārīta also says:
"Even if it was enjoyed through unjust means by a father or a brother, that which has reached the third generation cannot be taken away."
The meaning is that [the possession] has arrived after having passed over the third [generation]. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"Even if it was enjoyed through improper means by the father and the three preceding ancestors, that which has come down through the succession of three persons cannot be taken away."
The meaning is that it is impossible to say that what was enjoyed by one's father along with three preceding ancestors was done unjustly, much less to claim it as stolen. Furthermore, as he stated:
"Possession attains the status of valid evidence when accompanied by pure title;
possession whose title is impure never attains validity. [169]

Thus, this refers to the subject matter of possession inherited through three generations; for if it were merely a matter of possession in general, it would contradict the numerous statements previously cited, and it would also contradict the statement of Yājñavalkya:
"Title is superior to possession, except in the case of that which has come down through a prior succession.
As for what was stated by Bṛhaspati:
A gift to Brahmins (brahmadeya) of such a kind— where possession has lasted for three generations and is accompanied by a formal deed— cannot be taken away.

Thus, that refers to the case of possession by three generations that has not exceeded the period prescribed by the Smṛtis. Furthermore, as stated by Nārada: "But he who enjoys property without title, even for many hundreds of years—the king should punish that sinner with the punishment for a thief."

Thus, this refers to the subject matter of possession (*bhoga*) that is determined by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be without legal title (*anāgama*), because it is stated as an established fact that [such possession] is "without title. And possessions that are determined to be without title have been demonstrated by that very [text]: "What is deposited, what is held as wages, what is seized by force, what is requested, and what is enjoyed out of sight—these six [cases] exist without legal title."

*Anvāhita* is that which has been entrusted to another for the purpose of being given away. *Yācita* is property belonging to another brought [for use], such as ornaments and the like. *Balāvaṣṭabdha* is that which is enjoyed by means of royal favor and so forth. Even if such enjoyment has continued for a long time, it possesses no legal validity. And thus, the same [author] says:
[170] A village, a field, or even a house, which has been enjoyed by one through hereditary succession—unless it was obtained by royal favor—one may not transfer that enjoyment to another.
"From royal favor" means from that which is unjust; this is the ellipsis. And so Saṃvarta says:
"That [gift] which has been made by a king out of anger or greed, or through fraud or injustice—even if given to another because he is pleased—does not attain validity."

The meaning is that land which has been made subject to another’s enjoyment by a king through anger and the like, or which has been given to another out of favor, does not become established for the enjoyer even through long-standing possession. In this way, it should be understood that even possession that contradicts a royal edict (*śāsana*) is not established. And so Bṛhaspati says: "Possession extending over three generations, acquired through a continuous succession, cannot be overturned except by means of a prior edict."
As for that which was stated by Pitāmaha: "A royal edict is more authoritative than a document written by one's own hand;
therefore, possession by three generations is held to be even more authoritative."

Thus, this refers to the subject matter of possession based on an uncertain tradition (*āgama*) that has attained renown through a succession of oral reports; otherwise, it would contradict the statements previously cited. In this way, one should understand that even possession established by ancestors possesses greater evidentiary weight. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"According to the treatise, long-standing possession that is uninterrupted is powerful;
indeed, it should be known as such even if interrupted, provided it was previously established. [171]
The meaning is that an ancient title-deed, established by ancestors, should be known as authoritative even if it has been interrupted. Vyāsa also says:
"Land that was established by the original acquirer through valid proof, and which has passed to his son, must never be seized."

The grammatical connection is: "it must not be recovered from his son. When the possessor has not been proven by the one who brought forth the title, then it must be proven by his son—even if he has established long-standing possession—just as it was for the original possessor. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"The original possessor shall produce the document; his son, however, shall produce only possession.
If the one challenged has died, his son shall produce that [title]."

The meaning is that because possession based on prior application is not firm, and because title (*āgama*) is not established here merely by the removal of that [possession], one must also produce the title. The mention of "document" (*lekhyagrahaṇa*) is intended to illustrate witnesses as well, since they too serve as evidence for establishing the title made by the acquirer. Nārada also says:
"In the case of a litigant who has died while the lawsuit was thus pending, the matter must be settled by his son; he does not lose it simply through [the father's] possession."

The meaning is that the title of ownership must be established in the same manner as it was by the claimant through both written documents and witnesses. The mention of the "son" is intended to include any heir who takes the property. Therefore, Yājñavalkya says:
"If one who is sued should pass away, his heir shall establish his title;
in that case, possession is not a valid ground when it is devoid of a legal title."

One who possesses even a fourth-generation title must necessarily produce that source of title (*āgama*), because in such a case, mere possession (*bhukti*) is not an independent means of proof, since it lacks the quality of being uncontradicted; this is the meaning. And thus, as it was stated by Nārada:
"In the beginning, the cause is the title (*dāna*); in the middle, possession accompanied by a title (*sāgamā*);
but in the case of long-standing, continuous possession, possession alone is the cause."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to a case where the absence of a legal claim has been determined by the person who brought the suit. As for the literal meaning, it has been shown by the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"In the case of one who has established title, possession at the stated time makes the title effective;
for him alone, when accompanied by himself as the third [party], possession is clear when there is manifest title."

"Whatever possession has continued uninterruptedly over time is the proof for the fourth [category]; possession that is devoid of [any] title is considered authoritative by itself. Here, "one who has made a title" (*kṛtāgama*) means the one who created the title. "In the stated time" means in a period consisting of thirty years. "Authoritative" (*prabhu*) means preeminent. "With a clear title" (*sphuṭāgamā*) means with a title determined by proof; such possession that has continued uninterruptedly for a long time, belonging to the fourth [category] and so forth, is the proof when the certainty of the title has been abandoned. It is "authoritative," meaning capable of determining ownership—this is the meaning of the second verse. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Vyāsa:
Having been enjoyed for twenty years by the owner without interruption,
that possession of land belonging to one person becomes doubled when it belongs to two persons.
"Three generations and three times [the period of possession]—no further source of proof need be sought beyond that.

This [rule] is to be understood as applying when there is an absence of living persons from the time of the commencement of possession lasting sixty years, such that it would otherwise result in an equivalence to possession from a very remote antiquity; otherwise, in the era of Smṛti law, it is held that for land, possession must be accompanied by a title (āgama).

Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with such statements as these. Thus, it should be understood that the designation of the period ending at one hundred and five years as the "period of Smṛti" (smārtakāla) is intended in a general sense.
This concludes the determination of possession (*bhukti*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the characteristics of witnesses (*sākṣin*).
In this regard, Manu says:
"I shall fully declare what kind of persons the wealthy should employ as witnesses in legal proceedings, and how truth must be spoken by them."
The meaning is that I shall now declare the characteristics of witnesses and the procedure for their examination. First, he sets forth those characteristics:

"Householders, those with sons, indigenous inhabitants, born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, and those who understand the matter—such persons are fit to give testimony, but not just anyone except in times of emergency."

The *maulās* are established [as witnesses]. Those who know the facts (*arthajñāḥ*) are those who have understood the matter to be proven; for it has been stated by that very same [author]: "Testimony is established through direct perception and through hearing. In the phrase "householders" (*gṛhinaḥ*) and so forth, the masculine gender is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*), because it pertains to the subject to be enjoined (*upādeyagatatvāt*). For this very reason, Nārada says:
Worthy witnesses should be men of noble birth, upright, pure by birth, by action, and by wealth; they should be honest, irreproachable, and possessed of sound intellect.
The meaning is that such persons shall be witnesses in matters such as debts and the like. And so Vyāsa says:
“Those who know the Dharma, who have sons, who are indigenous, of noble birth, speakers of truth, engaged in the performance of Vedic and Smārta rites, and free from hatred and envy.”

"Those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), those who are not dependent on others, wise men, those who do not live abroad, and young men should be made witnesses in matters such as debts by one who knows [the law]. Here, *śrotriya* means those who recite the revealed scriptures (*śruti*). Having ascertained the matter at hand, those skilled in place and time who are forgers produce a document that appears identical; such persons shall not be considered witnesses.
Kātyāyana also says:
"The testimony of those who are from renowned families and of good character, who are free from greed and delusion,
who are trustworthy, pure, and distinguished, is undoubtedly valid."
The plural number in the word *teṣām* (of them) is intended to demonstrate that the testimony of witnesses numbering two or one alone is not determinative. For this very reason, Manu says:

"The case should be established by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and the Brahmins. Here, *bhāvyaḥ* means "to be proven"; *tryavarāḥ* refers to those for whom three is the minimum—that is, a number lower than three is not approved among witnesses. As for what was stated by Bṛhaspati:
There should be nine, seven, five, four, or even three;
or both may be renowned Vedic scholars. One should never consult only one person.
Thus, regarding the phrase "both there," it refers to the subject of written and secret witnesses; for he says immediately thereafter:
"Two written witnesses, as well as three, four, or five secret ones; those who appear by chance, those reminded of their duty, kinsmen, and likewise superior witnesses."

The distinctions between written documents and the other types will be explained below. Furthermore, it has been stated by him: "A witness, a timekeeper, one who is present within the matter, as well as the king and the official, may each alone serve as authoritative evidence."
Thus—the astrologer who reads the hour; the superintendent, the judge—furthermore, as stated by Vyāsa:
"Even a single witness who is virtuous in his conduct, knows the dharma, and has personally experienced the matter shall be authoritative, especially in cases of violence."
Thus it is said; and also by Kātyāyana: "In the case of a deposit, even a single witness may be declared;
even a single messenger sent by the plaintiff becomes a witness."
That by which a matter has been well-considered and renounced should be reflected upon by that very person alone;
he alone is declared to be the sole authority in a dispute regarding that matter.

Thus, all of this refers to witnesses who are agreed upon by both parties. Just as plurality serves to eliminate the suspicion of unreliability, so too does being mutually accepted by both parties. For this very reason, Nārada says: "Alternatively, he who is approved by both of two litigants—even if he is alone—should be questioned as a witness in the assembly. [176]

Thus, it should be understood that the restriction of the number "at least three" applies only to witnesses other than those who are recorded, secret, or mutually agreed upon; for in the case of witnesses who are mutually agreed upon, as well as in the case of recorded or secret witnesses, even a smaller number is prescribed. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states: "In all legal matters, witnesses should be appointed starting from three;
there shall be a prohibition against two or one, except that even a single witness is admissible if he is approved by both parties."
Witnesses are those other than written documents and secret witnesses; the meaning is that they should be appointed starting from three onwards. Regarding the term "witnesses," Nārada continues:
"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and Śūdras who are blameless—these may be witnesses for each respective caste, or alternatively, all may be witnesses for all castes."

The meaning is that, when possible, witnesses should be of the same caste (*savarṇa*) as the litigant. Likewise, even in cases involving castes other than those [of the four], they should be of the same *jāti* as the litigant; for Yājñavalkya records: "They are prescribed according to *jāti*, according to caste, or all may serve for all. The mention of *jāti* is intended to include guilds (*śreṇi*) and the like by implication. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"In guilds, the members of the guild; in their own groups, the group members;
among outsiders, the outsiders; and among women, women shall be witnesses.
Regarding this, the same author states an exception:

But if someone within groups such as guilds should become an object of hatred, he shall not be a witness for them; they are all indeed his haters. [177] The meaning is that those who harbor hatred toward someone among guilds and the like are not witnesses for him. The mention of "guilds and the like" is intended to illustrate castes and other such groups, and the mention of "hatred" is intended to indicate those who possess causes for speaking untruthfully. For this very reason, Manu says:

Trustworthy persons from all castes who are knowledgeable in all matters of dharma and free from greed should be appointed as witnesses in legal proceedings; however, those who are the opposite should be avoided.

"Trustworthy persons" (*āpta*) means those other than deceivers. The meaning is that one should avoid those who are contrary [to the truth] and possessed of causes for speaking untruthfully. He himself states who these are: "One should not appoint as witnesses those who have a financial interest in the case, nor those who are not trustworthy, nor associates, nor enemies; nor those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt."
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor one learned in the Vedas, nor one living in a religious order, nor one who has withdrawn from all social groups.
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an elderly man, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.

"One who is not distressed, not intoxicated, not insane, not afflicted by hunger or thirst, not overcome by fatigue, not tormented by passion, not angry, nor a thief. [Thus it is said. "Those related to the matter" means those related to the subject matter under dispute. Reliable witnesses (*āpta*), however, have been shown by Kātyāyana:
"Furthermore, those who live off his earnings, those who perform services for him, his kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates are not to be witnesses. Thus it is said.

*Saḥāyāḥ* (associates) refers to guarantors (*pratibhū*) and the like. *Vairiṇaḥ* (enemies) are those whose faults have been observed in one of two litigants; they are known elsewhere as false witnesses. *Dūṣitāḥ* (corrupted persons) are those tainted by major sins (*mahāpātaka*) and other such offenses. The *nṛpati* (king) is excluded because he is preoccupied with many affairs. A *kārukaḥ* (artisan) is one who subsists on a craft, such as a goldsmith and so forth. A *kuśīlavaḥ* (actor) is one who enters the stage; both are prohibited because their minds are inclined toward their respective arts. Here, a *śrotriya* is intended as one devoted to the performance of ritual acts, not merely a reciter of the Vedas, for the latter is mentioned [elsewhere] as being eligible to serve as a witness. A *liṅgasthaḥ* (one established in an emblem) refers to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) and an ascetic (*yati*). One who has departed from the communities (*saṅgha*) refers to forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others. Regarding these, such as the *śrotriya* and the rest, even in the absence of a reason for speaking falsely, their exclusion is to be understood solely on the strength of the scriptural injunction. An *ādhyadhīnaḥ* (one dependent on another) is one overwhelmed by mental affliction. A *vaktavyaḥ* (one of ill repute) is one whose body is loathsome due to leprosy and other diseases. A *dasyuḥ* (bandit) is one of cruel conduct. A *vikarmakṛt* (one who performs forbidden acts) is one who performs actions contrary to the scriptures. A *vṛddhaḥ* (old man) is one whose intellect has faltered due to old age. A *śiśuḥ* (child) is one less than sixteen years of age. An *ekaḥ* (single person) is one not authorized by the two disputing parties. An *antyaḥ* (outcaste) is a *caṇḍāla* and the like. A *vikalendriyaḥ* (one with impaired senses) is one who is deaf and so forth. Those who are "afflicted" (*ārtādi*) are self-evident. Their specific distinctions, which were previously stated, should also be applied here. Nārada also mentions those who are to be avoided:
A slave, a deceitful person, one lacking faith, an elder, a woman, a child, a follower of the Cākrīka sect,
one intoxicated, insane, negligent, afflicted, a gambler, and a village priest;
Great travelers, sea-faring merchants, those who have gone forth into homelessness, and the sick;
couples, a single śrotriya, those devoid of proper conduct, eunuchs, and actors.

Atheists, those who have abandoned their wives and the sacred fire, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who eat from the same vessel, companions of enemies, and those related by birth or kinship to such persons.
Actors whose faults have been previously observed, poisoners, snake-charmers, those who administer poison, arsonists, usurers, and those who commit secondary sins such as having a Śūdra child; [179]
Those who have exhausted their rashness, those whose inner resolve has been stilled and shaken off,
those of broken conduct, those who have not returned to proper discipline, the dull-witted, oil-pressers, and followers of Pauṣa.

Those possessed by spirits, those hostile to kings, those who predict rain or the positions of the stars, those who proclaim misfortune, those who sell themselves, and those whose limbs are deficient or whose livelihood is based on prostitution;
One with deformed nails, one with a dark face, one with white leprosy, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a cruel person, and those who oppose guilds or corporations;
A murderer, a painter, a fool, one who has fallen from his caste, a forger, a cheat, one who has abandoned his religious duties, a thief, and a royal officer.
A Brahmin who sells human beings, poison, meat, bones, honey, milk, water, or clarified butter, as well as a twice-born man who is a usurer;
"One who has fallen from his own duty, a member of a guild, a slanderer, a servant of the low, one who disputes with his father, and a creator of dissension—these are non-witnesses. Thus it is said.

A *naikṛtika* is one who is habitually intent on seeking out the vulnerabilities of others. A *cākrika* is a bard (*vaitālika*). A *sāmudravaṇik* is a sea-trader who travels by ship. The term "pair" (*yugma*) refers to those characterized by duality. Regarding the compound *ekasthālī*, there are two analyses: either it refers to a person whose cooking-pot is shared with another, or it refers to one who shares a single dining-plate with one of two litigants; that is to say, it means sharing a meal or cooking together. An *aricara* is one who moves among enemies—that is, one associated with the enemy. As for *sanābhas* (kinsmen), they have been shown by Kātyāyana [in verse 180].
"The daughters of one's mother's sisters, sons of uterine brothers, and maternal uncles—these are declared to be sapindas; one should not employ them as witnesses. Thus it is said.

A *śailūṣa* is an actor. A *viṣajīvī* is one appointed to the activities of collecting and guarding poison. An *āhituṇḍika* is a snake-catcher. A *garada* is a poisoner. An *agnida* is an arsonist who sets fire to houses. A *kīnāśa* is a miser. A *klānta* is one who is exhausted or distressed. A *nirdhūta* is one who has been expelled. An *antāvasāyī* is one born of a reverse-order (*pratiloma*) union. A *bhinnavṛtta* is one of wicked conduct. An *asamāvṛtta* is a lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*). A *jaḍa* is one of dull intellect. A *tailika* is a sesame-pounder, meaning a maker of oil-presses. A *paupika* is a seller of cakes and the like. A *varṣasūcaka* is a predictor of rain, meaning an astrologer (*naimittika*). A *nakṣatrasūcaka* is one whose livelihood is astrology. An *aghaśaṃsī* is one who proclaims the faults of others. A *bhagavṛtti* is one who makes his wife a prostitute for his own livelihood. A *śauṇḍika* is a seller of liquor. A *mūrkha* is a beggar who invokes a deity [for gain]. A *kuhaka* is a hypocrite. A *pratyavasita* is one who has returned from the life of a renunciant (*pravrajyā*). A *sūcaka* is one appointed by the king to report the faults of others. A *bhedakṛt* is a slanderer (*piśuna*). The others are well known. Kātyāyana also mentions several such persons who are not eligible to be witnesses.
Relatives by birth, kinsmen, those with whom one has a marriage alliance, the husband of one's sister, the father, paternal relatives, the paternal uncle, the father-in-law, and likewise teachers;
"Those appointed to positions in cities, villages, and districts, as well as favorites, should not be questioned; those royal servants are not [to be relied upon].
This means that those enumerated starting from the *kulyas* and ending with the royal servants should not be questioned to give testimony; the sense is that they are not to be witnesses.

[181] But surely this elaborate discussion regarding those who are not witnesses is useless; for by the very statement of the definition, it is established by implication that those possessing contrary characteristics are non-witnesses. True, this is so; nevertheless, in cases where witnesses of the prescribed types cannot be obtained at all, the status of any human being whatsoever as a witness is obtained by implication from Manu’s statement, “Not just anyone, except in times of distress. It is for the purpose of prohibiting certain individuals in such cases that the composition of the rules beginning with “not those connected to the matter, nor friends” was made; thus, this elaboration is indeed meaningful. And so, it should be understood that when witnesses endowed with the defined characteristics are unavailable, the status of witness is prescribed for those who merely lack the aforementioned prohibitions. For this very reason, Vyāsa has offered praise even for them.
"Divine [proof] is generally subject to error due to medicinal herbs and spells;
indeed, there is no error among witnesses who are not corrupted by defects.
As for that which was further stated by Manu:
But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants in a private house, in a forest, or during a life-threatening emergency;
"In the absence of a woman, the task may be performed by a child, an elderly person, a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant. [Thus it is said.
"Anubhāvī" means one who is conversant with the matter. As for that which was stated by Nārada:
Even those who have been designated as non-witnesses— such as slaves, deceitful persons, and the like—
may become witnesses when the gravity of the matter requires it.

Thus—[the phrase] "gravity of the matter" refers to the absence of a praiseworthy witness for the matter at hand; all of this concerns cases such as *sāhasa* (heinous crimes) involving stable actions, because in those instances, even praiseworthy persons are weak [in number or status]. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states:

"In the absence of superior or middling witnesses, even those who are disqualified should be considered as witnesses in cases such as *sāhasa*, provided they are bound by the constraints of time and the nature of the matter. [182]
Regarding this, Uśanas states a specific rule:
"A slave, a blind man, a deaf man, a leper, women, children, the elderly, and so forth—
even these are considered competent witnesses in cases of violence, provided they are not personally related to the parties."

"Unconnected" means being devoid of the relationship of friend or enemy; that is, [they are exempt] from acts of violence and the like. However, if they are connected [to the parties], they must certainly be avoided even in cases of violence and the like. For this very reason, Nārada says: "Among them, neither a child, nor one alone, nor a woman, nor a forger, nor a kinsman, nor an enemy shall give testimony otherwise."

The meaning is that even among those such as slaves and rogues, fools and the like—who possess manifest causes for lying—should be excluded. By this, the causes for manifest falsehood are also shown to exist among them:
"A fool speaks falsely through ignorance; a woman, through habitual wickedness;
a forger, through deceit; a kinsman, out of affection; and an enemy, out of a desire for revenge."

The meaning is: "because of being untruthful," that is, because of having an untruthful character. By this, it is shown that the causes for manifest falsehood are precisely such qualities as ignorance, an untruthful character, devotion to unrighteousness (*adharma*), and being possessed of extremely intense passion and hatred; it is not, however, mere childishness (*bālatva*). Thus, even in the case of a single person, it is not oneness (*ekatva*) that is the cause of manifest falsehood, but rather greed (*lubdhatva*); as Manu says: "A single person who is greedy shall not be a witness. Consequently, when defects such as ignorance and an untruthful character are present, even slaves and the like must be rejected; but in their absence, even children and others may be accepted—this is to be understood regarding matters such as acts of violence (*sāhasa*). As for what was further stated by Manu:
In all cases of violence, theft,
and adultery, as well as in verbal and physical assault, witnesses need not be examined.
Thus it is said; and also by Kātyāyana:
"In cases of contradiction, in matters concerning the king's command, in the collection of debts, in violent crimes, and in cases of theft and verbal assault, one should not examine witnesses."

Thus, that [statement] prohibits the examination of the multitude of qualities such as being a householder, but it does not prohibit the examination of defects such as ignorance, because that would contradict the previously cited statement. Furthermore, as stated by Kātyāyana: "In matters of debt and the like, one should examine witnesses in stable legal affairs; however, in cases of violence and urgent matters, examination is prescribed in some instances."

Thus, if in cases such as *sāhasa* (violent crime) there is the possibility of incurring heavier punishments like death in the event of defeat, then for the purpose of establishing the rules of examination therein— given that the examination of defects such as ignorance is universal due to its association with debts and the like— it is impossible for it to be prescribed only in some specific instances. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya, "Every person may be a witness in cases of adultery, theft, assault,
and *sāhasa*," that too should be understood as being intended merely to preclude the requirement of examining [specific] qualifications.
Thus ends the section on the characteristics of witnesses in the Smṛticandrikā [184].
Now, the classification of witnesses.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "The document, the defendant, and the witness—these constitute the two paths.
Prajāpati says:
Witnesses should be known to be of two kinds: one is formal (kṛta) and the other is informal (akṛta).
That which is recorded in writing is to be known as formal; the latter is called informal.

"Recorded in writing" means such as a written document (*likhita*) and so forth; this is the intended meaning. And thus says Nārada: "The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness, the secret witness, and the subsequent witness—witnesses are declared to be of five kinds."
Likewise, the non-contradiction of witnesses has also been shown by that very same [authority]:
"The wise have proclaimed six kinds of non-contradictory witnesses:
the village headman, the judge, the king, and [the witnesses] of the litigants."
"One who is an insider in the affairs [of the parties], one who has been sent by the plaintiff,
and those of noble family in disputes between families— these also shall be witnesses.
Regarding that, Bṛhaspati first states the definition of those [witnesses] who have been appointed:
He by whom one's own [name], that of one's father, the caste,
and the place of residence have been recorded should be known as a witness designated as "written."
He who is summoned and made a witness in matters such as debts, deposits, and transactions,
and who is repeatedly reminded of his duty, is declared to be a "reminded" witness (smārita).
But when a duty is being performed, whoever happens to come of his own accord is said to be our "voluntary" witness here.
But he who is made to hear the debtor's statement while separated by a wall, and who likewise testifies when the matter has been settled, is called a hidden witness (*gūḍhasākṣin*).

"Where a witness, while departing for another direction or being on the verge of death, causes another to hear [the testimony] exactly as he heard it, one should know that person to be the 'subsequent witness' (uttara-sākṣin). Regarding written evidence, Hārīta states a specific rule:
Even after a very long time, that which has been written shall attain success.
One who knows [the ritual] should write it oneself; however, one who is ignorant should have it written by another.
Furthermore, it has been stated by that same [author]:
"In this world, the success of a witness who was summoned is established up to eight years;
likewise, the success of one who appeared voluntarily is established up to five years."
The success of a secret witness is established up to the third year;
however, they say that the success of a subsequent witness is established for up to one year.
Thus, it should be understood that this has been stated as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the same author immediately thereafter says:
"Or rather, no fixed time limit is observed with respect to a witness;
for those learned in the scriptures declare that witnesshood depends upon memory."
"He whose intellect and memory are not impaired,
even after a very long period of time, that witness is fit to give testimony"— thus it is said.
Bṛhaspati has also described those who are disqualified from being witnesses.
Where there has been destruction or theft on all sides of the boundary, the village itself shall be the witness there, even if it was not formally appointed; of this there is no doubt.
But when a legal case has already been decided and a new trial is required, the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, shall act as the witness therein; it cannot be otherwise.
Whatever statement of the plaintiff and the defendant has been heard directly by the king himself,
that alone shall be the witness in the event of a disagreement between the two.
He in whom both [parties] place their trust and who is informed of the matter at hand should be known as a secret bearer of messages, stationed thus in the midst of the business.
But he who, being sent, listens to the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant—
one who is virtuous and approved by both— is declared to be a messenger (*dūtaka*).
"Even in the case of partition and so forth regarding a debt, he who is a kinsman useful to both parties— one who knows the dharma and belongs to the same lineage— is proclaimed to be a *kulya*.
Furthermore, that which was stated by him:

The written witness, the recorded witness, the secret witness, the reminded witness, the kinsman witness, the messenger witness, the incidental witness, the subsequent witness, the witness within the matter itself, the king, the official, and likewise the village headman— the witness is thus declared to be of twelve kinds.
Thus, this was stated by relying on the internal subdivisions of written testimony, consisting of one's own authorship of the document or causing another to write it;
for Nārada has stated, disregarding [other categories], that "eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the treatises by the wise."
Thus ends the section on the types of witnesses in the Smṛticandrikā [187].
Now, the types of non-witnesses.
In this regard, Nārada says:
"Indeed, even one who is not a witness is designated as fivefold by the wise in the treatises:
[a witness] by virtue of his own statement, by fault, by dissension, by self-accusation, and the deceased intermediary."

The meaning is that because there are five types of reasons for being a non-witness, the wise have accordingly specified five kinds of non-witnesses as well. For this very reason, the author of the summary verse states: "On account of having been observed, on account of being prohibited, on account of not having acted, on account of uncertainty, and on account of being deficient in one limb, there may likewise be five kinds of non-witnesses."

"A thief and the like, a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) and the like, one who speaks for himself, one whose testimony is mutually contradictory, and fifthly, one other than those heard from a dying person—this is the 'one who dies in the interval' (*mṛtāntara*). The meaning is: a thief and the like are non-witnesses because of their wickedness; a Vedic scholar and the like because they are prohibited [from testifying]; "one who speaks for himself" because he has not been formally appointed; "one whose testimony is mutually contradictory" because of uncertainty; and "one who dies in the interval" because of being deficient in a single limb. Nārada also says:
Thieves, violent assailants, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise murderers—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; in them, truth is not found.
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those who have renounced the world—these are not witnesses; no further reason for this has been stated here.
One who speaks on his own initiative, without being questioned, having come of his own accord, is called a "needle" in the legal treatises; he is not fit to be a witness.
When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
if their testimony should diverge, they shall be considered non-witnesses due to that disagreement.
"If there were no matter to be communicated, nor anyone to request it, where could he exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness. [188]

*Sūcī* means *sūcaka* (an informer). The meaning of the phrase "the matter" (*yo 'rthaḥ*) is as follows: regarding that matter in which the witness was appointed by the claimant (*arthin*), thinking his own position to be unstable, he must inform [others] and make it known to his son and so forth; if that matter is not made known while the claimant is still alive, and the claimant subsequently dies, then since it is uncertain where, in regard to what matter, and at the time of whose testimony, the son or others of the claimant—who were made witnesses by the claimant—should speak, they are non-witnesses because of the death of the other party (*mṛtāntara*). The mention of the "claimant" (*arthi*) is intended to include the "defendant" (*pratyarthin*) as well. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
Where no plaintiff is found, there a witness is considered as good as dead;
or where the defendant has died, one should likewise determine it to be so.

When the plaintiff or the defendant has died, "one who is other than that witness heard by the dying person" means one who is different from the witness who was heard while the person was at the point of death;

as stated in the Smṛti of Nārada: "When the plaintiff has passed away, one who is other than the witness heard by the dying person. The mention of the "dying person" (mumūrṣu) is intended to include even one who is healthy. For this very reason, there is another Smṛti text:

Even if one has not been informed by a person who is not ill, if a matter connected with dharma is stated, he shall be a witness therein even after death; this applies in the case of six types of transactions, such as deposits and the like.
And thus, as stated in another Smṛti:

"In cases of deposits, goods left for carriage, articles sold, things stolen, gifts, or what has been asked for, as well as debts confessed by one about to die—one should inquire into the testimony from those who survive. [189]

Thus, it should be understood that this is intended to demonstrate that the status of one who has been informed [of the lawsuit] as a witness does not lapse even if the plaintiff dies after being so informed; it is not, however, for the purpose of prescribing the witness-status of another deceased person in any case, because such a thing is impossible.

Just as the witness-status of one who has been informed does not cease, so too in the case of a conflict between witnesses (*sākṣidvaidha*), the witness-status of those belonging to the superior category remains intact. And so says Yājñavalkya: "In a conflict, the testimony of the majority prevails; when the numbers are equal, that of those possessing superior qualities."
But when there is a conflict between those possessing virtues, the testimony of those who are more virtuous should be accepted.
The author of the *Saṃgraha*, however, states its meaning as follows:
"In the case of a conflict among witnesses, there shall be a determination based on the plurality of their virtues or the degree of their excellence;
[only] when there is total equality [of qualities] does [the testimony] possess authoritative validity."
The meaning is that one is not a witness due to uncertainty because of the failure to perceive the distinction between the two sides. As for what was stated by Kātyāyana:
"Among witnesses who have been recorded or designated by the plaintiff, if even one of them speaks otherwise, all are not witnesses because of their disagreement."

Thus, it should be understood that by the word “all” (*sarva*), the status of being non-witnesses is stated for many people who are accompanied by those who speak otherwise, and not for those alone; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such statements as, “In a conflict, the testimony of the majority [prevails]. Likewise, lest their status as non-witnesses arise due to having spoken on their own initiative, he [Yājñavalkya] himself says that the designation of witnesses must not be made by anyone at random: “For one person should not dispute a witness appointed by another. In his absence, however, either a commissioned person or a relative may dispute him. [1.190]

The meaning is that either the plaintiff or his representative should designate the witness, and no one else. Thus, it should be understood that one designated by another is like one not designated at all, and is therefore not a valid witness. On this occasion, Nārada has stated something else as well:
"When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses for both sides, the witnesses shall belong to the one whose case is the *pūrvapakṣa* (the initial claim)."
"In a legal dispute, the witnesses of the defendant should be questioned in that case where the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff due to the nature of the matter."

An illustration of this is as follows: Suppose one person, having acquired a field through a formal gift (*pratigraha*), enjoyed it, and then left for another country with his family after abandoning it; meanwhile, that field was acquired and enjoyed by another person, who also left for another country with his family due to political unrest or similar reasons. Later, when a long time had passed, both of them returned to their own place out of greed for their livelihood and arrived simultaneously at the court of justice (*dharmasthāna*) for a decision regarding the dispute over the field. There, the first party asserts: "This field belongs to me alone, for it was given to me by the king named Jayaticandra during his reign. The other party also asserts: "This field belongs to me alone, for it was given to me by the king named Haricandra, the son of Jayaticandra, when he was consecrated for the sake of the kingdom. Alternatively, the other party's assertion might be: "It is true that it was given to him by Jayaticandra, but Haricandra purchased that field from his hand and gave it to me; therefore, it belongs to me alone. In such a case, there are witnesses for both disputants. Regarding this, it has been stated: "When two parties are in dispute over a matter... The meaning of this is as follows: of the two disputing parties, the witnesses of the one whose claim (*pakṣa*) is based on the presentation of a prior gift as the cause of ownership (*svatvahetu*) should be questioned by the judges (*sabhyas*), not the witnesses of the other party, because the latter’s witnesses are practically non-witnesses (*asākṣiprāya*) since they bear witness to a gift made at a later time. However, when the weakness or irrelevance of the party asserting the prior gift is established by the force of the other party's claim—such as "I purchased it from his hand and gave it to me"—then the witnesses of the one asserting the subsequent claim should be questioned. Those of the one who asserted the prior claim should not be questioned, as it would be useless to do so since what they seek to prove is already established. Rather, they should be treated like non-witnesses and disregarded.

Thus ends the section on the different types of non-witnesses in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the presentation of witnesses. On this matter, Gautama states: "In a case of conflicting testimony, the determination of truth is based upon witnesses. By this, the intention is that immediately after the defendant's plea, if there are witnesses, they must be pointed out by the plaintiff. Furthermore, if those who have been pointed out are found to be defective, they must be refuted. To this effect, Bṛhaspati says:
One may refute witnesses designated by the plaintiff only when actual defects exist;
a plaintiff who refutes those who are without defect deserves a fine equal to the value of the claim.

That is equal to the punishment for a false witness. Those reasons—such as being an object of hatred—which have been stated as grounds for disqualification from being a witness, are the defects of a witness (*sākṣidoṣa*). The meaning is that if these are hidden among the witnesses designated by the plaintiff, they must be exposed by the defendant; however, if they are manifest, they must be pointed out by the members of the court (*sabhyas*) themselves. Thus says Kātyāyana: "Indeed, those defects of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) which are hidden must be stated by the litigant;
but those which are manifest, the members of the court should point out at the proper time by citing the legal treatises."
Indeed, whatever faults there may be in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be stated by the disputant;
however, those that are obscure should be made manifest by the members of the assembly at the proper time through the citation of authoritative scriptures.

"At the time of the means of proof" means at the time when that which has been designated as a means of proof is being determined; that is to say, at the time of the final decision. And so Bṛhaspati says:
"But when a decision has already been commenced by the witnesses and the members of the court, if anyone initiates a lawsuit again, the king shall investigate that case."

The meaning is that the decision has been reached by witnesses who have been designated by the plaintiff and whose statements are manifestly free from defects. The inclusion of the term "when the decision has been reached" (*prakrānte*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that this is the time for raising objections after the decision has already been made. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:

"Whatever defects of the written document there may be, and whatever defects of the witnesses are recorded, they must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have already been stated."
The same author states the punishment for one who, after [the matter] has been spoken,
impeaches [the witnesses]: "But he who, when the matter has been stated, impeaches witnesses who were previously unimpeached,
and does not state the reason for that, shall incur the first amercement."
Likewise, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that one should not defame [the opponent] through false faults or by the absence of qualities such as being a householder:
"One should not invalidate the proof with what is untrue, but rather with a fault;
in the case of a false accusation, there shall be punishment, and one also loses the matter to be proved."

The intention is that one should invalidate [a witness] solely on account of a *doṣa* (defect), and not by the mere absence of *guṇas* (virtues), because the latter does not cause the subversion of the authority of his testimony. For this very reason, it is stated that even one devoid of virtues may serve as a witness in cases such as debts, provided he is not otherwise disqualified. Therefore, it should be understood that in matters such as debts, the status of being a non-witness for those cited as witnesses is not established merely by pointing out the absence of virtues, but rather by pointing out grounds for disqualification such as slavery. In cases of *sāhasa* (violent crimes) and the like, however, it is not by that alone; rather, it must be understood that the status of being a non-witness is established only by pointing out defects such as ignorance or a character for untruthfulness. For this same reason, Vyāsa also stated that the status of being a non-witness is determined solely by the manifestation of a defect.
The defendant must set forth the defects of the witnesses in court;
having written all of them down on the document, those [defects] must be stated as a rebuttal.
"But they [the witnesses] are never eligible as witnesses in the case of a confession;
otherwise, they must be made [witnesses] by means of legal action through the defendant.

Here, "confession" (*pratipatti*) means the admission of a fault. The phrase "by means of legal action" (*kriyayā*) implies that it is by means other than [relying on] witnesses. And so says that very same author:
But if the refutation of the previous witnesses were to be established by other witnesses,
there would be the fault of infinite regress, because further witnesses could likewise be produced for those.

Thus, the respondent should not state a refutation when the fault is already manifest, as that would be redundant; rather, such a refutation must be grasped by the members of the assembly themselves. To this effect, he [Uddyotakara] says: "A refutation of witnesses is to be accepted if it is well-known among the members of the assembly, or even if it is established in the world at large; for it cannot be successfully countered by the mere description of faults."

The ellipsis is "to be accepted by the examiners. And in that case, the refutation is not to be established by the opponent, because the exclusion [of the witness] is already established due to the fault being well-known; this is the meaning. However, regarding a case where an unestablished refutation is alleged, he himself states the penalty for one who fails to prove it: "If the defendant clearly fails to prove the witnesses, he shall be made to pay a fine. Witnesses who have been proven [guilty of a fault] are to be excluded, as they are disqualified by the rules governing witnesses."

The meaning is: "in such a way that it becomes clear," that is, without proving a defect in the witnesses. The intention is that witnesses who have been proven to be defective should be excluded, but they are not to be punished. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that when the witnesses have been excluded, if the plaintiff has no further expectation for other means of proof, then he is defeated and should be punished:

"The defeated one shall be made to pay the fine according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, if the litigant remains free from further expectations regarding the witnesses and the members of the court."

The phrase "without expectation" means that he does not require another means of proof (*pramāṇāntara*). However, when there is an expectation [of further proof], the intention is that, in the absence of human witnesses, the determination of victory must be made even by means of divine proof (*divya*). But when the witnesses are faultless, the determination of victory must be made by them alone. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"When witnesses are challenged, the purification of the witnesses must first be carried out;
once the witnesses have been purified, one should thereafter purify the matter of the case."

The meaning is: "then, from the pure witnesses. By this, it is stated that the determination regarding the dispute over defects in the evidence must be made within the very course of the prior legal proceeding; it is not, however, at a time subsequent to the conclusion of the prior proceeding, as is the case with the determination of a separate legal proceeding. Nor should it be argued that this is improper because it is unsuitable to determine a separate legal proceeding in the midst of another, for the determination of the dispute over defects in the evidence is a supplement to the prior proceeding and must therefore be carried out therein, and because, lacking a separate result, it does not constitute a distinct legal proceeding. And so says that same [author]:
In a legal dispute, if either the documents or the witnesses are found to be tainted,
the case shall not succeed until they have been cleared of suspicion.
Vyāsa also says: "A dispute arising from internal [evidence] and produced by all witnesses does not reach a final decision; as long as that is the case, one should avoid the previous [witnesses]."

"Whether it be the defendant or the plaintiff, in the matter of proving a defect in the witnesses, there shall be no separate lawsuit against the witnesses; rather, it is another stage within the same legal proceeding.
Therefore, it is established that the determination regarding a dispute over defects in the means of proof must be carried out precisely within the context of the original lawsuit.
Thus ends the presentation of witnesses in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the examination of witnesses;
regarding this, Kātyāyana says:

"The king, having summoned the legal procedure (*kriyā*), shall investigate according to the rule: 'A written document by means of the procedure for writing; witnesses by means of the procedure for witnesses. By "by means of the procedure for witnesses" is meant "by means of the collection of characteristics pertaining to witnesses. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
I shall now describe, as enjoined by the scriptures, those witnesses who are to be questioned and those lowest of men who are to be excluded.
