Regarding this, he first states those who are to be questioned:
"Those engaged in the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, free from greed and hatred,
of noble birth, blameless, and endowed with austerity, charity, and compassion— such are the witnesses. Likewise, he also states those who are to be excluded:
A mother’s father, a paternal uncle, a wife’s brother, a maternal uncle,
a brother, a friend, and a son-in-law are not competent witnesses in any legal disputes.
"Those addicted to other men's wives or to drinking, gamblers, those previously discredited, the insane, the afflicted, the violent, and atheists are not witnesses.

This enumeration of who is and who is not a witness is for the purpose of demonstrating the qualified witnesses and non-witnesses mentioned by Manu, Nārada, and others; for this very reason, it was stated that they must be "enjoined by the scriptures. Likewise, he [Manu] himself says that witnesses must also be examined by their voice and other such means.
"Those who have been summoned must be examined by means of their voice, complexion, gestures, and so forth.

In this regard, those who remain free from such changes are witnesses in the true sense; however, those who exhibit such changes should be understood as false witnesses. For this very reason, Manu states:
"When children, the elderly, or the sick speak falsely in their testimonies..."
One should likewise recognize that the speech of those with arrogant minds is unstable.

Viṣṇu also says regarding those who are arrogant and lacking in self-control: "One should recognize a false witness by a natural change in demeanor, a loss of facial color, and incoherent speech. Nārada also states:
"But he who, because of being corrupted by his own faults, appears as if unwell, moves from one place to another, and keeps running after every single person..."
He coughs suddenly and violently, frequently sighs deeply,
scratches the earth with his feet, and shakes his arms and his garment.
The color of his face changes, and likewise his forehead perspires;
his lips become parched, and he looks upward and sideways.
"He who speaks excessively without being asked, as if in great haste—he should be known as a false witness; that sinner one should punish severely. Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.
He goes from one place to another, licks the corners of his mouth,
his forehead perspires, and his face turns pale.
With parched mouth and faltering speech, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips.

"He who undergoes a change from his natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body, both during the legal proceeding and while giving testimony, is proclaimed to be wicked. Thus, it should be understood that if witnesses who are free from signs of wickedness and endowed with the characteristics of a witness present themselves, then the case must be decided by them; however, if they are the opposite, then it must be decided by other means of proof.
Thus ends the examination of witnesses in the Smṛticandrikā [198].
Now follows the procedure for questioning witnesses.
In that regard, Manu says:
"The presiding judge, having consoled all the witnesses within the court in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, shall interrogate them according to this rule."
By this method about to be described, one should interrogate all witnesses; that is to say, one should cause them to be inclined toward speaking the truth. He demonstrates that very method:
"Whatever you two know to have been transacted between yourselves in this matter, declare it all according to the truth, for your status here is that of witnesses."
Testimony is established through seeing in person and through hearing;
in that regard, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from dharma and worldly prosperity.
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
A Brahmin is the foremost among men, just as the sun is among luminous bodies;
truth is the highest of all virtues, like the head is of all limbs.
The witness is honored by truth; dharma increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.

"For the gods do not recognize in this world a man superior to him whose testimony, when he speaks, the wise Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) does not distrust. Here, "brāhmaṇa" means "like a brāhmaṇa. Similarly, in the phrase "or like a head," the word "vā" (or) should be understood as having the sense of comparison. The meaning of the final verse is: "The gods do not know anyone more excellent in this world than that witness whose testimony, when he speaks, the wise Knower of the Field does not distrust. Nārada also says:
Truth alone is the supreme gift; truth alone is the supreme austerity;
truth alone is the supreme dharma for the worlds—such is our sacred tradition.
In brief, O gods, truth is for humans, while falsehood is traditionally held to be otherwise;
he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
"There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood; especially regarding the duty of a witness, one should therefore speak only the truth. Thus says Vyāsa as well.
When those appointed to the role of witnesses stand before them, the deities stationed in the sky and the ancestors look down with apprehension, fearing that the testimony may be false.
"By truthful words they go upwards; by acting otherwise, they go downwards.
Therefore, truth must be spoken by you in the presence of the court.
Thus [says] Manu as well.
A man who speaks falsely when giving testimony is bound by the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred lifetimes, rendered helpless; therefore, a witness should speak the truth.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self;
do not despise yourself, the supreme witness of men.
Evil-doers indeed think, "No one sees us";
yet the gods see them, as do the inner selves within each person.

[200] "The sky, the earth, the waters, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, the wind, night, the twilight, and Dharma—these know the conduct of all embodied beings. Thus it is said. "A hundred births" means up to a hundred lifetimes. Nārada also says:
Kubera, Āditya, Varuṇa, Śakra, Vaivasvata,
and the other guardians of the world constantly behold [him] with their divine eye.

The intention is that, for this reason, even deception is not easily accomplished. As Uśanas also says: "A witness who gives false testimony while speaking fearlessly on earth certainly leads both [parties] and seven generations of their lineages to misfortune."
"Whatever sin has been committed over seven lifetimes that remains in the body,
he who gives false testimony seizes all of it.
Thus says Bṛhaspati as well.
A fraudulent juror, a false witness, and a killer of a Brāhmaṇa are declared to be equal;
a killer of an embryo or a thief of wealth is said to be no greater than these.
Manu also says:
A witness who declares in an assembly of noble men anything other than what was seen or heard goes headlong to hell after death and is deprived of heaven.
Vasiṣṭha also says: "If, however, he should speak a falsehood, it is equivalent to eating impure substances in every respect;
having died, he goes to hell, and immediately thereafter he enters the state of an animal."

The meaning is that one who has consumed impure substances goes to hell after death. Kātyāyana also says: "The servant of Yama, filled with rage, shall lead him—who has his neck bound by the noose of Time and is overwhelmed by the blows of a mallet—to the thorny ground."
"Afflicted by the embrace of thorns from the blow of the forest of sword-leaves (asipatravana), they shall drink the dreadful river filled with pus and blood. Thus [it is said].
With their necks encircled by the noose of Time (kālapāśa), their necks bound by a noose of black iron—Nārada also [says]:
And in the hells, those fierce and powerful servants of Yama will constantly cut out their tongues and sever them with swords.
Having cast him upon a stake like a sacrificial animal, they will throw him— crying out, helpless,
and with his head hanging down— into fires and into lakes.
"Tormented by the crushing of iron machines and the like, and utterly overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, he is likewise cast into the terrible Saṃpratāpana hell. Thus [it is said]. Uśanas also [says]:
With their eyes gouged out by iron vultures and their faces torn apart,
those deluded by sin shall fall into the Andhatāmisra hell.
The Grandfather [Yama] has also said:
"The servants will cast those who have fainted from the biting of their tongues by heated tongs inside their houses into the Mahāraurava and Raurava hells."
Vyāsa also says: "Witnesses who speak falsely are bound by the nooses of Varuṇa;
they certainly remain in hell for sixty thousand years."
"When a full hundred years have passed for them, one bond is released;
when that time has elapsed, one whose bonds are released is born among the animal wombs.
Thus also says Nārada.
Moreover, those who give false testimony, those who seize the wealth of others, and even unrighteous kings shall dwell in hell for an eon.

"And having experienced the torments of hell for a long time, afflicted by suffering, those unworthy ones will come here again into births such as those of vultures, crows, and the like. Thus [says] Vasiṣṭha as well.
He remains a pig for ten years, a donkey for a hundred years,
a dog for twelve years, and a vulture for twenty years.
Likewise, for forty years he is born among worms, insects, and moths; it is traditionally taught that as a human being, he is born as a wild animal for ten years.
"But even if he attains human birth, he shall be mute and blind;
moreover, poverty shall be his lot in birth after birth. Thus says Vyāsa as well.
Thereafter, a human being is born, utterly abandoned by kinsmen;
he may be lame, blind, deaf, mute, afflicted with leprosy, naked, and parched with thirst.
Hungry, he begs at the house of his enemy along with his wife;
having understood the faults of falsehood and having understood the excellent qualities of truth.
"Therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony, for it brings welfare both in this world and the next.
[203] Thus, the exhortation must be performed using these very words, and not with those composed by other persons. For Nārada says:
"By means of ancient declarations of dharma that proclaim the majesty of truth..."
"And he should even greatly terrify him with censures for falsehood.

This means that the witness should be encouraged by Vedic injunctions concerning truthful speech accompanied by praise, and should also be excessively intimidated by prohibitions against falsehood that entail the results of demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Thus ends the section on the procedure for questioning witnesses in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the procedure for questioning witnesses; regarding this, Manu says:
"In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, he should question the twice-born witnesses concerning the truth."
Being himself pure, he should [seat] those who are pure in the forenoon, facing either northward or eastward.
The term "twice-born" (*dvijān*) is intended as an illustration for any witness-persons, since it functions as a qualifying attribute. For this very reason, Nārada says:

"Having summoned the witnesses and bound them strictly with oaths, he should question them individually—whether all together or separately—once they are known to be of good conduct and have understood the matter."
The meaning is that one should question each person individually after making them committed to truth by means of terrifying oaths; and those oaths have been shown by him [Manu]:
"One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all sins. [2.104]

The meaning is that one should cause the Brahmins and others to swear by pointing out the destruction of their desired objects through truth and so forth, and the Śūdra by pointing out the occurrence of the undesirable consequences that will be mentioned hereafter. Regarding the interrogation, however, a distinction has been shown by Manu:
"One should ask a Brāhmaṇa, 'Speak'; one should ask a king, 'Speak the truth.'"

To a Brāhmaṇa, one should say: "If you speak otherwise than this, your truthfulness will perish; therefore, speak after having reflected. To a Kṣatriya, however, the question should be understood as: "If you speak otherwise, your mounts and weapons will become useless; therefore, speak the truth after having reflected. Regarding a Vaiśya, since no specific [curse] is remembered in the question, one should interrogate him at will after binding him by an oath such as: "There shall be separation from cattle, seed, and gold if you speak otherwise. As for a Śūdra, the manner of the interrogatory statement has been elaborated upon by Manu.
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, for those who kill women and children,
for the betrayer of friends, and for the ungrateful— may those same worlds be mine if I speak falsely.
O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—
all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, "I am alone"— this sage, the witness of merit and demerit, is ever-present within your heart.
The god Yama Vaivasvata who resides here within your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the land of the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty,
blind— such shall he be who gives false testimony while seeking alms at the house of his enemy.
With his head hanging downwards in blinding darkness, the sinner shall go to hell if,
when questioned during a legal determination of dharma, he should speak falsely in response to the inquiry.
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception, eats fish along with their bones, like a blind man.
Listen, O gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony, in that very order, according to their count.
One kills five by lying regarding cattle, one kills ten by lying regarding cows;
one kills a hundred by lying regarding horses, and one kills a thousand by lying regarding men.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak a falsehood concerning land.
They say that [the rule] regarding water is like that regarding land, as well as in the enjoyment of women and in sexual intercourse,
and with respect to all aquatic gems and those made of stone.
"Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and as it was seen, straightforwardly."

*Kuru* refers to Kurukṣetra. *Añjasā* means with a pure heart. On this point, some hold that the three verses beginning with "Naked and shaven-headed" (*nagno muṇḍaḥ*) should be extracted and inserted into the section on the rules for interrogation; otherwise, there would be a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). They conclude that in that case, after saying "Do not go to the Kurus," one must say "As many kinsmen as... and so forth. Furthermore, this rule regarding the questioning of a Śūdra applies even to twice-born men who subsist by low occupations when they are not in times of distress, because they cannot be restrained by a minor oath. For this very reason, Manu says:
One should treat cowherds, merchants, as well as artisans,
actors and singers, servants, and usurers— even if they are Brahmins— as one would Śūdras.
Those who have fallen away from their own duties and subsist on the food of others,
yet desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them as one treats Śūdras.

By stating that they "desire the status of the twice-born," [the author] demonstrates that for those of non-twice-born origin, such as the Ambaṣṭhas and others, the procedure for questioning is exactly like that for Śūdras.
Thus ends the section on the Procedure for Questioning Witnesses in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follows the Procedure for the Testimony of Witnesses.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states: "Witnesses must give their testimony while standing within the court, and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in the case of immovable property."

The meaning is "on top of something stationary. And so he [the author] says: "In some cases, it may be stated even without those two; this rule applies to quadrupeds and to bipeds as well as to stationary things."

"In those two aforementioned places" means that in those two cases, testimony must be given even in some instances of disputes concerning killing. And so says that same [author]: "If there is a dispute regarding the killing of living beings, one should cause testimony to be given in the presence of Śiva; in his absence, however, one should cause testimony to be given by means of a mark, and not otherwise."
Regarding the mark, such as a horn and so forth; Vasiṣṭha states the manner of the witness's testimony:
"Facing east, seated on a seat, the witness, bound by his own oaths, shall speak the truth after touching gold, cow dung, and darbha grass."
Bṛhaspati also says:
Having removed his upper garment and the turban, he should raise his right hand;
taking gold, cow dung, and darbha grass, he should speak the truth.

The meaning is that one should raise the right hand and arrange the garment so that it is covered, like a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Regarding the injunction "one should speak the truth," Manu states an exception in certain cases:
"In the case of Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas, if [the truth] would result in their death as previously described, a falsehood must be spoken; for that is superior to the truth."
Bṛhaspati also says: One should protect even a Brahmin who has committed an offense through a single lapse of mindfulness, who is afflicted by calamity,
and who is being beaten by soldiers and others— even by speaking falsehoods.
From the use of the word "api" (even), it is understood that even in this case, some sin arises from speaking untruth. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states the expiation:
"In a case where there would be the execution of those belonging to the [first] castes, a witness may speak untruth;
to purify himself from that, the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī."
Manu also says:
"They should worship Sarasvatī with oblations of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to the goddess of speech,
thereby effecting the supreme expiation for the sin of untruth."

"Or one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras, or with the verse beginning with *ud*, which is dedicated to Varuṇa, or with the three verses addressed to the water-deities. Thus it is said. Viṣṇu also states: "To purify that [sin], a twice-born man should offer oblations into the fire with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras; a Śūdra, however, should give for one day the fodder of ten cows. As for what was stated by Gautama: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if one's livelihood depends upon it," and also what was stated by Vyāsa:
A statement joined with jest does not cause harm, nor one spoken toward women, nor at the time of marriage;
they say that these five falsehoods—spoken when life is at stake, or when all one's wealth is being seized—are not sinful.

Thus, the meaning of these two [verses] is as follows: by such statements as "especially regarding the duty of witnesses," whatever excessive sin has been mentioned does not exist here; however, it certainly exists elsewhere. And so says Gautama: "Those who are not assembled together should not speak when questioned, and they would be guilty of a fault for failing to speak. The commentators have stated that from the word *ca* (and), it is understood that this also applies to speaking falsely. The prohibition against those who are not assembled does not mean that only those who are assembled can serve as witnesses in every case. Therefore, Vasiṣṭha says:
But that which is seen by those assembled together must be reported in that very same way;
however, that which is to be done by each individually must be reported separately.
"But when a matter is discovered at a different time, or where it has been learned by the witnesses individually, one should cause each of them to testify; this is the rule proclaimed for such cases.
Thus ends the section on the procedure for the examination of witnesses in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some statements concerning the testimony of witnesses are recorded;
therein, Kātyāyana says:
"The speech of those [witnesses] should be accepted as it was spoken naturally, provided it is free from defects."
Once the witnesses have been questioned by the king, they should not be questioned again and again.

Whatever they may say by its very nature as that which is to be grasped in worldly convention, and whatever else they might speak regarding the Dharma that is meaningless— [all such speech is to be disregarded].
Nārada also stated what is meaningless:
"When the categories of the matter have been specified and the witness has arrived for testimony,
if he does not speak in accordance with the syllables [of the charge], that is not considered properly declared."

When the witness has arrived at the occasion for giving testimony, "corresponding to the syllables" means corresponding to the letters—that is, the matter asked about. By this, it is stated that what presents a matter not asked about is "meaningless" (*apārtha*). Likewise, that which contains less or more than the matter asked about is "vain" (*vyartha*); and thus, the same author says: "Where witnesses state a matter that is deficient or excessive, that too should be understood as unspoken; this is declared to be the rule for witnesses."

The meaning is: "in cases such as those concerning debts and other disputes that are generally stable. And so Kātyāyana says: "In disputes concerning debts and the like which are generally stable, once a decision has been reached, if the matter is stated to be either less or more than [what was proven], the claim to be established does not succeed."

The meaning is as follows: if the testimony of witnesses produced for the purpose of proving the matter asserted (*pratijñātārtha*) is either deficient or excessive, it is indeed a cause for doubt; it does not, however, constitute valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) regarding the matter asserted, even if a portion of that asserted matter has been proven. Furthermore, it should be understood from this very statement that even the testimony of witnesses produced for the purpose of proving a portion of the matter asserted is likewise invalid if it is deficient or excessive, because it is stated in general terms that "the thing to be proven (*sādhya*) is not established. However, he [the author] states that in cases involving unstable matters (*asthirakarma*), the thing to be proven is indeed established.
Even when the portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by the witnesses, the entire case shall be established;
this applies in cases of adultery, violence, and theft, wherein whatever is to be proven has been fully set forth.
Furthermore, as he has stated:
"In a case where there may be deficiency or excess, one should reject that testimony;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for by not speaking, he deserves punishment."

That refers to the subject matter of a stable transaction. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states that even when there is a discrepancy regarding a portion of the matter thus specified, the testimony of witnesses is fruitless:
"When one disagrees in their testimony regarding place, time, wealth, number, form, caste, appearance, or age, the wise know that [testimony] to be unspoken."
Nārada also says: "In cases where there is disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or caste,
that testimony is also vitiated."

And thus, it should be understood that in matters such as debts and other stable transactions, the testimony of witnesses—which is neither deficient nor excessive and which delivers the matter exactly as asked—is the authoritative proof, and nothing else. For this very reason, Vyāsa states: "If the testimony is declared to be non-deficient with respect to time, form, age, substance, place, caste, and quantity, one should declare the object to be proven as established."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Where the entire meaning of the claim has been recounted by the witnesses, that party shall be the victor; otherwise, however, he shall not obtain the object of his suit."
"It has been answered as being true"—this is the ellipsis. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"He whose claim the witnesses have declared to be true shall be the victor;
for him who speaks otherwise, defeat is certain."

The meaning is that all the witnesses have declared the proposition—the statement of what is to be proven—of either the plaintiff or the defendant to be true. However, regarding a case where some witnesses declare the proposition to be true while others declare it otherwise, Manu says: "In the event of a conflict among witnesses, the king should accept the majority; when they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and when there is a conflict between those of equal virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born."
Nārada also says:
"In the event of a conflict among witnesses, many are considered authoritative;
if there is equality [in number], those who are pure should be accepted; if there is equality even among them, those most possessed of memory should be taken."

"But where, in a dispute, an equality of memory is observed among witnesses, one should set aside the testimony from that [group] because of the subtle nature of the requirements for a witness. The mention of "pure" (śuci) is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those possessing qualities such as being a householder and so forth. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:

In a case of division between two sides, the testimony of the majority should be accepted; likewise, when the numbers are equal, the testimony of those possessing superior qualities; and when there is a division even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who are most virtuous should be adopted.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says: "When doubt arises regarding a written document, a dispute over witnesses,
or when inference is confused, then divine means [of proof] provide purification."
Thus ends the section concerning witnesses in the Smṛticandrikā [212].
Now, some other statements concerning witnesses are also being recorded.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows [the truth],
he is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment."

The meaning is that one who, although knowing the matter in dispute according to the ultimate truth, refuses to accept the role of a witness out of wickedness, is a sinner like a false witness and is subject to punishment. Nārada also says: "He who, having caused his testimony to be heard by others, then denies being a witness, must be severely punished, for he is worse than a false witness."

The meaning is that if a person was previously made to declare, "I am a witness," but at the time of the witnesses' arrival he denies it, saying "I am not a witness," he is to be severely punished. Bṛhaspati also says: "A witness who, being free from illness, does not come when summoned, shall be made to pay both the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed."
Vasiṣṭha also says: "That lowest of men who, though not designated as a witness, nor summoned, nor exhorted,
should speak either falsely or even the truth, he too is to be punished."
Kātyāyana states:
"Whether they fail to speak when not questioned, or likewise fail to speak when questioned, witnesses must be restrained; according to the law, they are to be censured and punished."
"In cases of verbal abuse, fraud, or dispute, they shall be made to pay a fine of three hundred;

in disputes concerning debts and the like, they shall likewise be made to pay the debt as well as the wealth. Here, "wealth" refers to the wealth of the fine. By the pronoun "they" (*te*), those who did not answer the question by name are referred back, because they are the primary subject under discussion. For this very reason, that same author says:
If a witness does not state the testimony, he shall bear the debt and pay an equal fine;
for other disputes, he deserves a fine of three hundred.

"In other cases" means in matters other than debt and the like. And so Manu says: "A man who is free from disease but fails to give testimony regarding debt and other such matters within three fortnights shall incur that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth in every case."

The "agada" (non-ailing) person is one who is healthy; that "debt" refers to the wealth to be proven by evidence such as witnesses. The meaning is that he shall obtain—and thus be made to pay—all of it along with interest. And so says Yājñavalkya: "If a man fails to give testimony regarding a debt, he shall be made by the king to pay the entire amount, including the pledge, on the forty-sixth day."

By the term *daśabandha*, the tenth part is meant; and since that constitutes a fine (*daṇḍa*), it must be taken by the king—so say the commentators. In this case, nothing at all need be paid by the debtor; rather, it is precisely that which is to be paid, because the purport of the preceding statement is that "the witness who does not speak [the truth] shall be made to pay. Nor should what was paid by the non-speaking witness be recovered from the debtor, because it was paid due to his own fault. From the mention of "on the forty-sixth day," it is understood that after that time, even if he does not speak [the truth], he is not to be made to pay. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
The time for summoning a witness should be granted when the correct performance of the act is to be fully understood;
however, where the testimony is doubtful, one should settle the dispute immediately once it becomes clear.
And thus, that which was stated by him:
A king must not allow a delay in the testimony of witnesses;
for from such delay there arises a great fault characterized by the obstruction of Dharma.

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to cases where the witnesses are clear; for in the case of doubtful testimony, a period of time is prescribed [for verification]. Furthermore, regarding a witness who, having been made to hear the words of the question, denies his own status as a witness at the time of the trial—saying "I am not a witness here"—being blinded by passion and hatred, Yājñavalkya states the punishment for him:
"He who, having been made to hear the testimony from others, denies it, being shrouded in darkness, shall be made to pay a fine eightfold; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, one should banish."

The term "from the dispute" (*vivādāt*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows: the penalty for losing the dispute is that he shall be made to pay eight times that amount. Regarding the phrase "he shall banish" (*vivāsayet*), its meaning is either making him naked, destroying his house, or expelling him from his own kingdom; however, in this context, because it occurs in conjunction with the increase of the fine, the meaning should be understood as expulsion from one's own kingdom. Kātyāyana’s Smṛti states that witnesses who give testimony one way and then another way are also to be punished: "And those who, having spoken one way, speak otherwise, being possessed of verbal deception, shall be liable to punishment."

Gautama, however, states from the very outset: "One who speaks otherwise is censurable and liable to punishment. He adds: "In the case of false testimony, one should be made to pay a fine and be punished. Yājñavalkya, for his part, specifies a particular punishment for such witnesses:
"The forgers and the witnesses should each be punished individually;
the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, and a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be banished. [215]

"One who gives false testimony" (*kūṭasākṣī*) means one who acts fraudulently, that is to say, a liar; such persons are to be punished by the king individually. The meaning is that they shall receive double the fine prescribed for defeat in a legal dispute. Although it was stated without distinction that "the Brāhmaṇa is to be banished," where a double fine would result for Kṣatriyas and others due to their small wealth, there the punishment for the Brāhmaṇa is "banishment" in the form of being stripped naked. However, where [a double fine] would result for Kṣatriyas and others due to their great wealth, there the "banishment" for the Brāhmaṇa is in the form of the destruction of his house. Furthermore, where [a double fine] would result for Kṣatriyas and others due to their immense wealth, there the "banishment" for the Brāhmaṇa is to be understood as expulsion from his own kingdom; this is because the gradation of punishments follows the gradation of the offenses. For this very reason, Manu has declared a variety of punishments according to the gradation of the offenses based on the seeds of falsehood.
Out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, or likewise anger,
as well as from ignorance and childishness, a false testimony is given.
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for anyone who gives false testimony in any one of those cases.
For taking [something] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first *sāhasa* fine;
for out of fear, indeed, the middle fine; and for out of friendship, four times the first fine.
From desire, the former [retribution] is tenfold; from anger, however, the latter is threefold.
From ignorance, it is two full hundreds; from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
"The wise have declared these to be the punishments prescribed for false testimony. Thus [it is said].

Greed (*lobha*) is the state of being intent upon material gain. Delusion (*moha*) is the failure to comprehend the meaning of a correct question. Fear (*bhaya*) is the apprehension of encountering what is undesirable. Affection (*maitrī*) is an excess of endearment. Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for objects of pleasure. Anger (*krodha*) is intolerance. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is knowing otherwise at the very time of seeing or hearing something directly. Foolishness (*bāliśya*) is the failure to attain stability of intellect. In this context, it should be understood that for a false statement caused by greed, fear, or affection—where the fault is equal—the highest fine (*uttama-sāhasa*) is prescribed. For a false statement caused by desire, however, because the fault is more numerous than that, two and a half times the highest fine is prescribed. Furthermore, for a false statement caused by anger, because the fault is even more numerous than that, three times the highest fine is prescribed. In the case of delusion, however, because the fault is less than that, the first fine (*prathama-sāhasa*) is prescribed. In the case of ignorance, because the fault is even less than that, two hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* are prescribed. Moreover, in the case of foolishness, because the fault is even less than that, it should be understood that only half of that amount is prescribed. And this variety of punishments is to be known as applying even to a *brāhmaṇa* who gives false testimony, because of the general legal tradition (*smṛti*) which states without qualification: "These they call [the offenses] in perjury" (MDh 8.122).
"A righteous king, having punished the three castes who give false testimony, should banish them; however, he should only exile a Brāhmaṇa. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, regarding the subject of giving false testimony (*kauṭasākṣya*), there is a specific traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) concerning the Brāhmaṇa. What, then, is this distinction? It is not that while exile after punishment applies to the Kṣatriya and others, for the Brāhmaṇa there is only exile; such a distinction would be logical if it were the case that even when false testimony is committed once, Yājñavalkya prescribes only exile for the Brāhmaṇa, because otherwise the consequence would follow that no further punishment is mentioned for repeated offenses. Therefore, the claim made by some—that the word *tu* (but) is intended to exclude the monetary fine for the Brāhmaṇa—is refuted. How, then, is a specific punishment for the Brāhmaṇa stated? It is said: here, by the term *pravāsa*, the cutting of the lips, the tongue, or even execution is meant; whereas by the term *vivāsa*, being made naked and so forth is meant. Thus, even though the phrase "having punished" (*daṇḍayitvā*) is supplied [from the previous verse], the statement of a distinction is appropriate. Due to the internal subdivisions of *pravāsa* and *vivāsa*, the cutting of the lips, the tongue, and so on, as well as being made naked and so on, are to be determined according to the nature of the false testimony and according to the increase in the number of repetitions. When false testimony is committed once without a fixed motive, the punishment prescribed by Yājñavalkya in the verse beginning with "separately, separately" (*pṛthak pṛthak*) should be understood to apply, while in other cases, the Mānava [code] applies. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Viṣṇu—"the confiscation of all property (*sarvasva*) shall be carried out for false witnesses"—some have said this refers to the subject of lying regarding land, or it should be seen as referring to Śūdras and others of non-Aryan birth. The mention of "false witnesses" is intended to include the one who directs them as well. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
Having confiscated the entire property of one who has given false testimony out of greed for a particular matter, the king should thereafter banish him from the realm.

[The defendant] should be deprived of his own country and exiled from his domain, being rendered without a legal standing. Regarding this, Nārada states that he who makes an effort to prove the falsity of the witnesses specified by the other party becomes defeated:
"One should not approach a witness designated by the opponent in secret;
nor should one cause dissension between them through another; by acting in this manner, one is surely defeated."

The intention is that one who acts in such a manner should be punished with the lowest fine. Thus, having punished the false witness and the one who directed him, the legal matter decided based on the false testimony of the witnesses must be reversed. And so Manu says:
"In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; even if it has been decided, it shall be as if undecided."
When it is further questioned in what kind of legal matter perjury occurs, Yājñavalkya states:
"Even when testimony has been given by witnesses,
if others who are more virtuous or twice as numerous should state otherwise, the former witnesses shall be considered false."

The meaning of this is as follows: where a plaintiff has designated many witnesses, both present and absent, and having considered the difficulty of summoning those who are absent, he accepts that the present ones alone are sufficient; and when the case is decided based on their testimony, the plaintiff—considering that defeat to be caused by perjury—brings back the previously designated absent witnesses, who are more qualified or twice as numerous as the present ones, and thereby becomes victorious; in that case, the previously present witnesses would be considered false. Kātyāyana also [states]:
When a matter has indeed been proven by witnesses for a plaintiff,
if the defendant should then prove that matter otherwise;

"And false witnesses may be many or of noble birth. The meaning of this is as follows: when the witnesses pointed out by the plaintiff have testified in favor of the plaintiff's side, and the defendant names witnesses who are superior in number or in qualities, or who testify in a manner contrary to what was previously stated, then the plaintiff's witnesses shall be considered false. Now, one might object: how can there be witnesses for both the plaintiff and the defendant in a single legal proceeding?

"And there shall not be a legal procedure for both disputants in a single lawsuit," because this is prohibited. For this very reason, the statement beginning with "where [the matter] has been proven" is taken as referring once again to the scope of sublation (*bādha*). Thus, there is no contradiction. Regarding the case of one person serving as a witness, Manu says:
"If, within seven days, misfortune should be seen to befall a witness who has given his testimony..."
Disease, fire, the death of a kinsman, and debt—he shall be made to pay the fine as well.

The meaning is that the examination of a single witness must be conducted by demonstrating a divine calamity for a period of up to seven days. Furthermore, this examination should be performed for witnesses such as messengers and the like, but not for those endowed with excellent qualities, nor for the king or the presiding judge, because even in their case, the possibility of falsehood cannot be entirely excluded. For this very reason, Vyāsa states: "Even a divine ordeal may prove inconsistent if administered through the power of gems, mantras, or herbs, or if not according to the prescribed rules; however, a witness endowed with excellent qualities [does not prove inconsistent]."
For this very reason, Bṛhaspati established a distinction between the king and the official regarding the witness and others:
"The witness, the timekeeper, and likewise one who is present in the midst of the proceedings—
each of these alone shall be authoritative, as shall the king and the official."

The *gaṇaka* (astrologer/calculation expert) is one who takes the water-clock (*ghaṭikā*). The other two have been shown by Kātyāyana: "In the case of a deposit, even a single person may be declared a witness;
even a single messenger sent by the plaintiff becomes a witness."
Thus ends the section on witnesses in the Smṛticandrikā, concerning the subject of witnesses.
Now, regarding those cases where there is no reliance on witnesses, Nārada says:
"Other six types of disputes are proclaimed to be those in which there is no reliance on witnesses."
The wise say that their very characteristics constitute their witnesshood.
The meaning is that in disputes such as arson and the like, the very signs—such as having a torch in one's hand—perform the function of witnesses. And so it is said in that same [text]:
"One who sets fire with a torch in hand is to be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer;
and one seized by the hair upon both sides is a simultaneous adulterer."
One who approaches with a spade in hand should be known as a destroyer of the embankment;
likewise, one with an axe in hand is proclaimed a cutter of the forest.

"A man who has committed an assault can be recognized by fresh marks; for in cases of assault, these are matters of conviction even without witnesses. However, in the case of cruelty, there must be an investigation. By "fresh marks" is meant recent wounds and the like. "Matters of conviction even without witnesses" means that through the marks alone, one becomes free from doubt even in the absence of witnesses. "However, in the case of cruelty, there must be an investigation" means that in the case of *daṇḍapāruṣya* (criminal assault), an investigation must be conducted to distinguish between genuine and fabricated marks. And so says that same [author]:
Someone, having made a mark upon themselves, might harm another out of malice;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate by means of logical arguments, reasons, and the connection of facts.
In this context, the meaning is "harshness.
[Objection: But surely these words are meaningless, like saying, "The sky appears like a surface; a firefly is like a fire."
There is no floor in the sky, nor is a firefly a fire.
Therefore, it is proper to examine objects even when they are seen through direct perception;
by declaring objects after having examined them, one is not deprived of dharma.

Thus, since examination by that very method has been prescribed in all cases, such as [the case of] one with a torch in hand, this is correct. There is no fault here, for the examination is restated precisely in that context for the purpose of prescribing the means [of proof]. In this way, a certain dispute regarding theft (*caurya-vivāda*) should also be understood as one not dependent on witnesses. Accordingly, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One who seizes by the hair is an adulterer; one with a torch in hand is an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer; one with stolen goods in hand is a thief. *Loptra* refers to a sign such as a portion of what was stolen; in this case too, an examination must be performed. And so says Nārada:
"Even one who is not a thief incurs the status of a thief, and a thief attains the status of a non-thief;
through legal procedure, Māṇḍavya—who was not a thief—was treated as a thief.
Therefore, the intention is that investigation is essential. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
Where doubt arises regarding a written document, oral testimony,
or inference, there divine ordeal is the means of purification.
Inference is the reasoning based on such [marks] as "having a firebrand in hand" and so forth;
for the wise know inference to be both the logical reason (*hetu*) and deliberation (*tarka*),
according to the traditional teaching of Vyāsa.
Thus ends the section on those who are not witnesses in the *Smṛticandrikā* [222];
now follows the description of ordeals (*divya*).
In that regard, the Grandfather [Brahmā] said: "In whatever lawsuit there is no possibility of witnesses,
and especially in cases of violence (sāhasa), one should cause ordeals (divya) to be administered."
The mention of witnesses is intended as an illustration for all human means of proof (*mānuṣapramāṇa*). For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"Written documents, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the [human] means of proof.
In the absence of any one of these, any one of the divine means of proof (*divya*) is prescribed."
The phrase "the absence of any one of these" is intended to include the absence of *yukti* (logical proof) as well. For this very reason, Nārada states:

"Even when logical proofs are insufficient, one should reach a decision by means of oaths, taking into account the nature of the matter, the time, and the strength [of the parties], through [ordeals such as] fire, water, and good deeds."
The meaning is that [the ordeal] depends upon the object, consisting of the smallness or greatness of the matter sought to be proven. And thus Vyāsa says:
"Oaths such as those of truth, the water-jar, and so forth, are recorded as being in accordance with the value of the object.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states that oaths such as those of truth correspond to the smallness of the object.
Truth, horses, weapons, cattle, seeds, and gold;
the feet of gods and brahmins; and the heads of one's sons and wife.
"These oaths, however, are declared to be always easy to perform even in a minor matter.
The phrase "in a minor matter" is intended to indicate even a minor suffering that one wishes to prove. For this very reason, Nārada has stated generally:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cows, seeds, and gold..."

"The deities and the ancestors, and the meritorious deeds performed"—these oaths have been declared by Manu for a minor cause (*svalpakāraṇe*). Here, "for a minor cause" means for a minor offense. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the meritorious deeds," other oaths well-known in the world are also included. For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should cause [the defendant] to perform sacrifices, works of public utility, and other oaths. As for that which was stated by Nārada:
"For men seeking a legal trial, the divine ordeal is prescribed when the matter at hand is great.
And as for that which was stated by Pitāmaha:
"The lord of the earth should cause the divine ordeals to be administered in cases of grave offenses."
Thus, that refers to the subject matter of ordeals such as the balance and so forth. As Yājñavalkya said:
"The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals here for the sake of purification;
these are employed in cases of grave accusation when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake]."

By the word *agni*, a heated iron ball, a heated bean, and a heated ploughshare are indicated because they are denoted by that term in a general sense. Therefore, it should be understood that the heated bean and the ploughshare are also prescribed for a major accusation (*mahābhiyoga*) when the accuser is placed upon the head (*śīrṣakastha*), based on this very statement. The "head" (*śīrṣaka*) is the penalty resulting from defeat in a lawsuit, so called because it stands at the head (*śiras*) of the legal proceeding; one who stays there is "placed upon the head. This is what is meant: "The balance and other ordeals do not apply merely to every major accusation, but rather only where the accuser accepts—either corporal punishment or a monetary fine—that he shall be punished in such a manner if he loses, provided that such a penalty has been ordained for the false accuser [Nārada 224]. It is for this reason that Nārada says:"

"When the one standing at the head [of the case] is absent, then the ordeal is not administered. The phrase "when the one standing at the head is absent" implies that it refers to the plaintiff (*abhiyoktṛ*). And so Pitāmaha says:
"The plaintiff is designated as the one occupying the position of the head in ordeals."
The divine ordeal should be administered to one who is accused, based on the observation of the flow [of the liquid].
The *divya* is any one of the five [ordeals] beginning with the *dhaṭa*, because Yājñavalkya has specified them with the words "these. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"A king who always administers the five divine ordeals according to the rule and in accordance with dharma rejoices both in this world and after death."
By this it is implied that these ordeals belong to the accusers; and as stated by Kātyāyana:
"One should never subject an accuser to any of the ordeals;
those expert in ordeals must administer the ordeal to the accused."

"Someone" refers to the presiding judge (*sabhāpati*) and others. "Experts in divine ordeals" refers to the chief judges (*prāḍvivāka*) and others. By this, it is implied that this rule does not apply when an ordeal is accepted at the will of either the plaintiff or the defendant. And it has been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"Or, by mutual consent, one party may undergo the ordeal, while the other shall shave his head.
Nārada has also stated:
The plaintiff is assigned to the position of the head in all cases;
however, the other party may act according to his own wish, while the other must maintain the head.

The meaning is that in all cases involving a head (i.e., a person), there is the "divine fivefold" [set of ordeals]. The requirement for the accused to place his head [at stake] is for the purpose of demonstrating firmness in not denying the charge. For this very reason, if he wins, there is the acceptance of the prescribed penalty by one who had previously denied, thinking, "If I am defeated, I shall be punished in this way. Likewise, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that in certain matters no one at all should place their head [at stake]: "When a person standing as a head (i.e., a witness) has appeared as the accuser, the administration of a divine ordeal is appropriate; otherwise, it is by the king's command."
By the king's command—that is, by the king's order—even ordeals such as the balance (dhaṭa) and others may be performed without the head [of the accused]. And so says that very same [author]:
"The king shall cause even headless ordeals to be administered to his servants.
Yājñavalkya, however, states an exception even to the rule regarding the placement of the head, depending on the specific nature of the offense.

One may employ [ordeals] even without the *śīrṣaka* (the formal charge) in cases of treason against the king or mortal sin (*pātaka*). "With the *śīrṣaka*" means by means of the formulation of the charge. Likewise, Viṣṇu states: "In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, even without the formulation of the charge. The ellipsis to be supplied is that the balance (*tulā*) and other ordeals are to be employed. And so says Kātyāyana:
"The king should employ the balance and other ordeals for those who are suspected by the authorities."
And in the performance of the rite for self-purification, one should not imagine a head there.
[226] "For those who are defiled by public scandal and suspected by bandits, balances and the like should be employed; indeed, Bhṛgu says that the head should not be used in such cases.
The meaning is: for those suspected because of their living together with bandits. Furthermore, as he stated:
"One should never, however, employ the *kośa* (divine ordeal) for [cases involving] suspicion regarding the head.

This statement means that when an accusation based on suspicion is brought against one—even in matters such as debt—the *kośa* is not restricted to being without the head, because of the use of the word "never" (*kadācana*). Furthermore, the *kośa* is prescribed by Vyāsa for cases of accusation based on suspicion:
"The balance, fire, poison, and water are the fourfold means of proof."
This fifth treasury, concerning divine matters, is for use when doubts arise.

The phrase "in cases of suspicion" (*śaṅkāsu*) is intended to illustrate [cases involving] trust (*viśvāsa*) and so forth. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "In matters of suspicion, trust, making an agreement, partitioning among heirs, and in being the agent of a series of transactions, one should always cause the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) to be administered."
The Grandfather [Brahmā] also said:
"In matters of confidence, in all instances of suspicion, and likewise in the business of making peace—
in these cases, the treasury must always be surrendered for the sake of purity of mind."
The "treasure" (kośa) is headless; this is the implied meaning. And so it is said in that same [text]:

"One should avoid divine ordeals that are devoid of those residing in the head—those beginning with the balance (dhaṭa) and ending with poison (viṣa). The treasure alone is recorded as being headless."

The phrase "in cases of suspicion, formal accusation, and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In a formal accusation concerning a major matter (*mahātattva*), even the *kośa* ordeal must be avoided if the accuser is not present at the head of the assembly. This is because Yājñavalkya, in the context of the five divine ordeals, stated: "When the accuser is present at the head [of the assembly]. Furthermore, even in cases involving major matters and the like, there is no requirement for the assignment of the head in the set of five divine ordeals—such as the balance scale (*dhaṭa*)—when the court consists of anyone other than the king and the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*). As it is said: "Both the punishment of speech (*vāg-daṇḍa*) and the punishment of censure (*dhig-dama*) are traditionally held to depend upon the Brāhmaṇas; both the punishment of fines (*artha-daṇḍa*) and corporal punishment (*vadha*) are declared to depend upon the king."

This is because the punishment, which occupies the position of the head in a legal proceeding, is mentioned specifically in the context of the royal court of justice (*rājaprāḍvivākasabhā*). Consequently, statements such as "one should avoid ordeals that are devoid of a standing head" must be understood as referring exclusively to the royal court of justice. And thus, that which was stated by Pitāmaha for the purpose of setting aside the rule "the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff in a false case" is as follows:

"The divine ordeal should be administered to one who is accused, according to the evidence of the scriptures"—this too must be understood as referring specifically to the court of the king and the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), and not to any other assembly. Therefore, it should be considered that the administration of a divine ordeal by the members of the court is proper only when done without transgressing the meaning stated in the rule, "The ordeal is [administered] falsely in the case of the plaintiff," and thus it is just like the written testimony and other such means. Furthermore, one should employ these two—the rice-ordeal and the oath—only in cases of suspicion.

Thus, because of the association with rice (*taṇḍula*) in the statement of Pitāmaha, the ordeal of the *kośa* (water-ordeal) should be administered only in cases of suspicion (*śaṅkā*). This is because otherwise there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statement of Yājñavalkya beginning with "when the head is at stake" (*śīrṣakasthe*). The association with rice, however, is for the purpose of indicating that the *kośa* may be employed even in cases of minor accusation (*alpa-abhiyoga*). For this very reason, Nārada says: "One should cause the *kośa* to be administered even in a minor case. And thus, it should be understood that the restriction stated by Yājñavalkya—"these [ordeals] are for major accusations"—applies only to the ordeals beginning with the balance (*tulā*) and ending with poison (*viṣa*). If there were a restriction on the *kośa* as well, it would contradict the aforementioned statement of Nārada. For this same reason, the author of the Saṃgraha says: [228]
"One should cause the ordeals beginning with the *dhaṭa* and ending with poison to be administered in cases involving serious matters.
Furthermore, he stated: "The three beginning with the *kośa*, however, are for minor matters, respectively."

Thus, that [rule] is intended only to state a restrictive rule for minor offenses (*laghu-artha*), and not even for denial (*apahnava*); for since the *kośa*, *taṇḍula*, and *taptamāṣa* are prescribed for the denial of major offenses (*guru-artha*), a restriction to minor offenses alone is impossible. Even regarding minor offenses, rice (*taṇḍula*) is used only when there is suspicion (*śaṅkā*), as stated by Pitāmaha: "Rice and the *kośa*—these two one should employ in cases of suspicion. The *taptamāṣa* also applies to minor offenses only when there is suspicion.

"In cases of suspicion of minor theft and the like, one should prescribe the *taptamāṣaka*," because it has been so stated by that very [author]. Furthermore, the *phāla* (plough-test) should also be administered in some instances for the sake of a lighter penalty; and thus Bṛhaspati says:
"The members of the court should diligently administer the *phāla* to one who is a habitual offender."
And thus,
regarding these [ordeals] in cases of great charges when the accuser is the one standing at the head [of the ordeal],

this rule stated for fire must be understood as referring specifically to the iron ball and fire, and not to the ordeal of the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*) or the ploughshare (*phāla*). For this very reason, Bṛhaspati has provided separate illustrations for the various divine ordeals involving fire.
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation (kośa);
rice is declared the sixth, and the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka) the seventh.

"The eighth is said to be the balance (phāla), and the ninth shall be that born of dharma (dharmaja). All these divine [ordeals] have been prescribed by the Self-Existent One. It should be understood, however, that because the ordeal born of dharma is excluded from cases of great accusation, it is restricted to minor matters. As for that which was stated by Pitāmaha:
The examination of dharma and adharma [is required] for men who have committed murder, those who are pleading, those seeking expiation, and those accused in a doubtful matter.
This is its meaning: in cases of minor charges such as violence, theft, or mortal sins, for those who have been accused, the ordeal shall be one born of dharma.
Thus ends the determination of ordeals in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some statements useful for ascertaining the smallness or greatness of a charge (*abhiyoga*) are recorded;
therein, Manu says:
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are established on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.

The meaning is that, in order to eliminate confusion regarding the purpose of the treatises on legal punishments and divine measurements, the designations based on the dimensions of copper and other materials are now being demonstrated. He shows the subject matter he has promised:
"That minute particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice—this they call the *trasareṇu*, the first among all measures."
Eight *trasareṇu*s should be known as one *likṣā* in measurement;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six *yava*s make a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*); three *yava*s make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇala*s make a *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make a *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute a *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa* or a *paṇa*.
"Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure as being four *suvarṇas*.

The essential meaning of these verses is stated here in reverse order: the terms *niṣka* and *śatamāna* both refer to a single *pala* of silver. Therefore, under the section concerning the nomenclature of silver:
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, and ten *śatamānas* make one *pala*;
four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*.

Thus it was stated by Yājñavalkya. The words *paṇa* and *kārṣāpaṇa* are names for a *karṣa*—a fourth part of a *pala*—of copper. The words *purāṇa* and *dharaṇa* are names for a tenth part of a *pala* of silver. A *māṣa* is the designation for a fortieth part of a *karṣa* of silver; a *dharaṇa* is the designation for ten *palas*. This [designation of *dharaṇa*] should be understood as referring to substances other than silver, because a *dharaṇa* of silver is of a smaller measure. The designation *pala* should be understood as applying to all substances, since no specific exception is recorded. The word *suvarṇa*, however, denotes a *karṣa* of gold, because Amarasiṃha has specified that "a *suvarṇa* and a *viṣṭi* are [terms for] gold. It means a *karṣa* of an *akṣa*, because he himself stated: "Sixteen of those [gold *māṣas*] are an *akṣa*; a *karṣa* is not feminine. A *māṣa* is the designation for a sixteenth part of a *karṣa*. And that should be understood as referring to substances other than silver, because a silver *māṣaka* is a fortieth part of a *karṣa*. The word *kṛṣṇala*, moreover, expresses an eightieth part of a *karṣa*, because it is a fifth part of a *māṣa*. In this same way, the quantity of substances regarding the items *sarṣapa*, *likṣā*, and *trasareṇu* should be inferred by oneself. Regarding the phrase "a middle-sized barley-corn" (*yavo madhyaḥ*), it is stated in the commentary on that [text] that the word "middle" (*madhya*) is for the purpose of completing the verse. Furthermore, the name *padmarajas* (lotus-dust) is also shown in the *Purāṇa* for the *trasareṇu*.
"When there is a conjunction of eight atoms, it is called a *trasareṇu*; that is said to be a *padmarajas*.
Thus says Kātyāyana: "The word *māṣa* refers to the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*."
A māṣa should be known as one-twentieth of a kārṣāpaṇa;
a kākaṇī, however, is one-fourth of a māṣaka and of a paṇa.
"In the region of the Five Rivers, however, this is the conventional designation.
Thus says Bṛhaspati: "The word *suvarṇa* denotes twelve *palas*;
a coin made from a *karṣa* of copper is to be known as a *kāṣika-paṇa*."
She alone is declared to be Caṇḍikā, and those four are the Dhānakās.
"Those twelve *suvarṇas* are indeed what is called a *dīnāra*.
Kātyāyana also says:
"A *kārṣāpaṇa* should be known as an *aṇḍikā*; four of those [make] a *dhānaka*."
"Twelve of those *suvarṇas* are known as a *dīnāra* or a *citraka*.
Regarding the *pala*, however, an option has been shown by Yājñavalkya:
"A *pala* is proclaimed to be four or even five *suvarṇas*. [232]
Nārada states that there is also the *kārṣāpaṇa* from the king's treasury:
"In the southern region, the silver *kārṣāpaṇa* circulates.
Vyāsa, however, states the measure for the golden *niṣka*.

"Eight *palas* of gold and fourteen *suvarṇas*—this is the measure of a *niṣka*, as proclaimed by Vyāsa. Regarding this, even if there is a conflict with local custom (*deśavyavahāra*) in matters concerning divine punishment (*divyadaṇḍa*), another measure stated by Manu must certainly be accepted. Thus says Bṛhaspati:

"The number [of gold pieces] has been declared by Manu to be rooted in a ray of light and a mote of dust; that [scale] ending with the *kārṣāpaṇa* is to be employed in ordeals as well as in legal proceedings.

The mention of "ending with the *kārṣāpaṇa*" is for the purpose of establishing that this rule does not apply in the case of the *niṣka* measure. Therefore, there is no contradiction in some ordeal involving a different amount of *niṣkas* being mentioned further on.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [the section on] matters useful for knowing the gravity or lightness of a legal accusation has been concluded.
Now follows the determination of ordeals according to the amount of wealth;
regarding this, Kātyāyana says:

"Where there is a denial of what has been given, one should determine the measure [of the fine] therein. Here, "denial" (*apahnava*) means concealment. When it is asked how one should determine it, he himself says:
"Having ascertained the value of all the goods, one should calculate the gold [fine]."
At that time, one should employ a divine [image] endowed with the correct proportions of gold.
[233] Having ascertained the amount of gold, poison is prescribed for the loss of one hundred;
indeed, for the loss of eighty, one should offer oneself to the fire.
If the loss amounts to sixty [paṇas], water should be administered; for a loss of forty, indeed, the balance ordeal;
but for a loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of the sacred libation (koṣapāna) is prescribed.
Upon the loss of more than five [measures], one should offer rice-grains equal to half of that amount;
but upon the loss of half of that half, one should touch the heads of one's sons and others.
"But when half of that half has been destroyed, worldly activities are said to occur. Thus [it is stated].

In all these cases, the word *vināśa* (loss/destruction) should be understood as meaning "denial," because the context was introduced with the phrase, "where there is a denial of what has been given. The meaning is: in the case of a loss of twenty or ten [units], or a loss of thirty, or a loss of twenty and so forth; that is, more than five, meaning six and upwards. Upon the loss of half of that half—a handful (*prasṛti*) of gold weighing one and a half [units]—there is an ordeal with rice. But upon the loss of half of that half again—the loss of a handful of gold weighing less than eight parts of a half-unit—there is an ordeal involving the touching of the heads of one's son and wife. Upon the loss of half of that half again—the loss of a handful of gold weighing seven and a half *kṛṣṇalas*—there are worldly oaths such as the recitation of the eightfold formula regarding property. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including other Smṛti terms. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "In all types of matters, one should calculate the value in gold. In that regard, if the value is less than one *kṛṣṇala*, one should cause a Śūdra to swear by touching *dūrvā* grass; if less than two *kṛṣṇalas*, by touching sesame; if less than three *kṛṣṇalas*, by touching silver; if less than four *kṛṣ�ṇalas*, by touching gold; if less than five *kṛṣṇalas*, by touching earth turned up by a plough. When the value is double, the procedure is as prescribed for a Vaiśya; when triple, for a Kṣatriya; when quadruple, for a Brāhmaṇa. The phrase "touching earth turned up by a plough" means touching earth turned up by a ploughshare with the hand. The mention of "less" (*ūna*) is for the purpose of excluding the oath when the value is higher. Regarding the specific details of the oath, Manu says:
[234] One should cause a Brahmin to swear by means of truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by his cattle, seed, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all sins.

The meaning of this is as follows: [the judge] should cause the Brāhmaṇa who is taking the oath to say, "If I were to deny the facts, then my duty of speaking the truth would be fruitless for me. Similarly for the Kṣatriyas and others: in place of the phrase "my duty of speaking the truth would be fruitless for me," it should be "my weapons and missiles would be fruitless" for the Kṣatriya; "cows, seed-corn, and gold would be fruitless" for the Vaiśya; and "all sins would be mine" for the Śūdra—this is the distinction. The scope for touching the foot and so forth is shown in another Smṛti.
For a fine of one *niṣka*, there shall be an oath of truth; for two *niṣkas*, touching the feet; for less than three, the *puṣpa* ordeal; and for more than that, the *kośa* ordeal.

By the word *niṣka* here, that which is stamped with a seal and constitutes a fourth part of a *karṣa* of gold is intended; for in certain regions, the term *niṣka* is used in common parlance even for such a measure. Now, one might object: since there is a rule stating that the *māṣa* and other units mentioned by Manu should be understood in the context of ordeals and the like, it is not appropriate to interpret this as referring to the conventional (commercial) *niṣka*.

Not so; for it has been stated that the rule regarding the taking of a *niṣka* as mentioned by Manu does not apply here. Furthermore, in that case, the value of the *niṣka* mentioned by Manu—which consists of a silver *pala*—is greater than half a *karṣa* of gold. In that regard, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Viṣṇu concerning the injunction for speaking the truth: "In a matter four times [the value], for a Brāhmaṇa. This is because five *kṛṣṇalas*, which constitute four times [the amount], are indeed one-fourth of a *karṣa*. Therefore, it should be understood that the regulation for speaking the truth and so forth is stated based on the *vyāvahārika* (current) *niṣka*. By process of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the giving of merit such as *iṣṭāpūrta* and the like should be understood to apply to wealth that is more than the scope of oaths taken by caste (*jātiśapatha*) but less than the scope of divine ordeals (*dharmaja-divya*). Bṛhaspati, however, states the scope for the *dharmaja* (ordeals):
"When a hundred [kārṣāpaṇas] have been taken and denied, the purification by ordeal (dharmaśodhana) must be administered.

This means that for the lowest class, starting from one hundred kārṣāpaṇas; for the middle class, starting from two hundred; and for the highest class, starting from four hundred, the divine test born of dharma is to be employed.
This number is traditionally held to be doubled for those of the middle and lowest classes respectively.
But for those who possess the four supreme qualities, however.

This is because it is stated by that very [author]: "The value of a *kārṣāpaṇa* is the eightieth part of a *vyāvahārika-niṣka*. A *kṛṣṇala*, however, is the twentieth part of a *vyāvahārika-niṣka*. A *suvarṇa*, moreover, consists of four *vyāvahārika-niṣkas*. Thus, the rule for all ordeals (*divya*) should be understood as being based on the *vyāvahārika-niṣka*: poison is prescribed for those from four hundred *niṣkas* upwards; fire for those from three hundred and twenty *niṣkas* upwards; water for those from two hundred and forty *niṣkas* upwards; the balance (*dhaṭa*) for those from one hundred and sixty *niṣkas* upwards. The ordeal of the sacred libation (*kośa*) is prescribed for major charges (*mahābhiyoga*) starting from one hundred and twenty *niṣkas*. That same *kośa* may also apply starting from eighty *niṣkas*, or forty *niṣkas*, or twenty-four *niṣkas*. Rice (*taṇḍula*) applies starting from six *niṣkas*. For the highest class, the ordeal based on *dharma* (*dharmaja*) applies starting from five *niṣkas*; the *kośa* for minor charges starts from three *niṣkas*; flowers start from slightly less than three *niṣkas*; the *dharmaja* ordeal starts from two and a half *niṣkas*. For the middle class, the ordeal of touching the feet of a deity, a father, or a Brāhmaṇa starts from two *niṣkas*. Touching the heads of one's children or wife starts from one and a half *niṣkas*. For the lowest class, the middle ordeal starts from one and a quarter *niṣkas*; the giving of merit such as sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*) starts from one *niṣka*; worldly oaths (*śapatha*) start from four times a tenth part of a *niṣka*; and caste-based oaths start from a twentieth part of a *niṣka*. Among these, the properties such as the use of *dūrvā* grass and so forth are to be understood according to the words of Viṣṇu. This established rule regarding the *dharmaja* and other ordeals like the balance (*dhaṭa*) is not to be applied in cases involving the theft of wealth. Bṛhaspati has stated a different rule for them in cases of theft of wealth."
When a thousand [palas] have been subtracted, poison is used; at three-quarters less, fire;
at one-third less, water; and when half remains, the balance (dhaṭa) should always be administered.
In a charge involving four hundred [paṇas], the ordeal of the heated gold-piece (taptamāṣaka) must be administered;
for three hundred, rice (taṇḍula) should be given; and for half of that, the ordeal of the sacred water (kośa).
When a hundred [coins] have been taken and denied, the purification by ordeal must be administered;
the members of the court should diligently provide a ploughshare for the testing of the accused's livelihood.

"This number is prescribed for those of low status; for those of middle status, it is remembered as double; however, for those of superior status, it should be calculated as fourfold by the examiners.

Here, since a fixed ordeal such as the *ghaṭa* (water-vessel) is mentioned in the context of a "great accusation" (*mahābhiyoga*) involving the theft of five hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* or more, it should be understood that an accusation concerning a sum starting from that amount is a "great accusation," whereas one concerning a smaller sum of *kārṣāpaṇas* is a "minor accusation" (*alpābhiyoga*). For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states:
Whether it be a debt, a fine, or even a penance,
where the amount is five hundred [paṇas] or more, that is declared to be a heavy case.
"Starting from ten up to one hundred and four, that which is to be done is declared as 'light' by those expert in the *Smṛtis* and *Tantras*.

The phrase "up to one hundred and four" means up to five hundred. The term "debt" (*ṛṇa*) is used here loosely to refer to wealth that is the subject of dispute. The intended meaning is that, regarding the magnitude of a lawsuit concerning property, the amount should be understood according to either the number of the fine, the wealth for penance (*prāyaścitta*), or the wealth for restitution prescribed therein. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:

"One should not employ the ploughshare for less than a thousand [paṇas], nor the poison, nor likewise the balance. This is intended as a prohibition for those of middling status who, due to their conduct and other factors, fall below that level. For those of inferior status, since there is no "great accusation" (*mahābhiyoga*) when there is theft or denial for an amount less than a thousand, the balance and other ordeals are prohibited. Similarly, it should be understood that for those of superior status, the balance and other ordeals are prohibited for amounts less than two thousand, because such cases involve only a "minor accusation" (*alpābhiyoga*). Furthermore, as stated by Pitāmaha:
"One should administer the balance for a thousand, and likewise iron for half a thousand."
In half of that half, however, there is water; and in half of that, poison is said to reside.

Thus, that [rule] refers to a person whose faults have been previously observed. As Viṣṇu says: "In the case of one whose faults have been previously observed, even for a small matter, one should cause him to undergo one or another of the ordeals. And thus, the intended meaning of Pitāmaha’s statement—that for an excellent person whose faults were previously observed, the balance ordeal (*dhaṭa*) is used for a small matter when the sum is four times a thousand—should be understood. Likewise, Yājñavalkya states that in cases of treason against the king and in accusations of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), ordeals are to be administered even for a small matter: "In matters concerning the king and in cases of formal accusation, those who are pure should always administer [the ordeals]."

Viṣṇu also states: "Now, regarding the administration of an ordeal (*samayakriyā*), it may be at one's will in cases of treason against the king and acts of violence. The administration of an ordeal refers to the performance of divine tests such as the balance (*dhaṭa*) and so forth. And thus, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), Bṛhaspati mentions only the balance and other such ordeals here: "These oaths (*śapatha*) have been declared as always easy to perform in matters of small value;
however, in cases of violence and accusations, they say that divine ordeals (*divya*) are the means of purification."

And it should be understood that in cases such as acts of violence, oaths consisting of [invoking] truth and so forth never occur at all. Furthermore, even regarding theft, the determination will be explained according to the value of the stolen property in current currency.

For the highest class of person (*uttama-puruṣa*), the ordeal of poison begins at fifty *niṣkas*; fire begins at thirty-seven and a half *niṣkas*; water begins at thirty-three *niṣkas* plus seven *kṛṣṇalas* less one barleycorn; the balance (*dhaṭa*) begins at twenty-five *niṣkas*; the heated ball (*taptamāṣa*) begins at twenty *niṣkas*; rice grains (*taṇḍula*) begin at fifteen *niṣkas*; the sacred libation (*kośa*) begins at seven and a half *niṣkas*; the divine ordeal arising from Dharma (*dharmaja-divya*) begins at five *niṣkas*; and the ploughshare (*phāla*) begins at four individual cows.
