For a man of middle stature, however, poison is [administered] from twenty-five *niṣkas* onwards; fire from nineteen and a quarter *niṣkas* onwards; water from sixteen *niṣkas* and thirteen *kṛṣṇalas* plus a measure of barley onwards; the balance (*dhaṭa*) from twelve and a half *niṣkas* onwards; the heated ball (*taptamāṣa*) from ten *niṣkas* onwards; rice grains (*taṇḍula*) from seven and a half *niṣkas* onwards; the oath (*kośa*) from three and three-quarter *niṣkas* onwards; the ordeal based on *dharma* from two and a half *niṣkas* onwards; and the ploughshare (*phāla*) from two individual cows onwards.

For a person of inferior status, however, poison is administered from twelve and a half *niṣkas* onwards; fire from ninety and a half *kṛṣṇalas* plus seven and a half *kṛṣṇalas* (i.e., ninety-seven and a half *kṛṣṇalas*) onwards; water from eight *niṣkas* minus one *yava* and plus seven *kṛṣṇalas* (i.e., eight *niṣkas* and six *kṛṣṇalas*) onwards; the balance (*dhaṭa*) from six and a quarter *niṣkas* onwards; the heated ball (*taptamāṣa*) from five *niṣkas* onwards; rice grains (*taṇḍula*) from three and a quarter *niṣkas* onwards; the ordeal of the sacred jar (*kośa*) from one and three-quarter *niṣkas* onwards; the divine ordeal arising from Dharma (*dharmaja*) from one and a quarter *niṣkas* onwards; and the plowshare (*phāla*) from a single cow-unit onwards.

In cases where the faults have been previously observed, even when the property involved is less than the stated limits, those respective ordeals (*divya*) must be administered. The same applies in cases of treason against the king, false accusations, and acts of violence (*sāhasa*). However, since no specific rule regarding oaths such as those involving truth or flowers is seen here, a restriction should be established based on the context of denial (*apahnava*); for this is supported by the specific traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) found in the words of Viṣṇu and other legal codes (*smṛti*) concerning denial.
Thus ends the determination of ordeals according to the amount of wealth in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination according to the caste and other attributes of the litigants;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
In matters such as debts and the like, when there is a mutual dispute,
a surety endowed with wealth and a specific amount should be provided, taking into account the status of the person involved.

The meaning is: "with respect to the person" refers to the litigants' caste and so forth. Regarding that, Nārada states the established rule with respect to caste: "The *dhaṭa* (balance) should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya, water should be given to a Vaiśya, and poison indeed to a Śūdra."
"The treasury of all [ordeals] is declared by the wise to be common. This rule, however, is not absolute. As Kātyāyana says:
"Or, in all cases, every ordeal may be used except for poison, in the case of the best of the twice-born."
Nārada also states the rule regarding the determination [of guilt] based on the capacity of the *liṅga*,

the strength, and the age: "One should always examine eunuchs, the sick, those devoid of truth, men afflicted on all sides, as well as children, the elderly, women, and the blind by means of the balance."

This rule, however, is permanent, because it is designated as "always" (*sadā*). The mention of the balance (*dhaṭa*) is for the purpose of excluding fire, water, and poison, but not for excluding the oath (*kośa*) and the like. As that same author says: "But for women, poison is not prescribed, nor is water;
one should investigate their inner truth by means of the balance, the oath, and so forth."
By mentioning "the ordeal by balance, the ordeal by sacred libation," and so forth, he indicates the prohibition of fire as well; and this has also been explicitly shown by him:
"Women, children, those who are ill, the elderly, and men who are weak, should not be made to undergo immersion [in water] by those learned in the treatises on Dharma."
"Even when they have arrived for an ordeal involving physical danger, one should never submerge them in water;
nor should one cause them to undergo fire, nor purify them by means of poison. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Pitāmaha:
If dharma is indeed regarded, the ordeal shall not be administered to those who observe vows, those with emaciated bodies, children, the elderly, ascetics, or women.

Thus, that [prohibition] refers specifically to fire and water; for if it were a prohibition of the balance, the *kośa*, and so forth as well, it would contradict the previously cited statement. And in this way, it should be understood that for eunuchs and others, there are two types of ordeals, excluding fire, water, and poison. Likewise, not all ordeals apply even to blacksmiths and the like; as Kātyāyana says: "One should not administer fire to metalworkers, nor water to those who subsist on water, nor should one ever give poison to those who know the application of mantras."
"One should not employ a person suffering from skin disease with rice [for the ordeal]. Thus says Pitāmaha:
"One should avoid fire for those with leprosy, and water for those suffering from asthma and cough."
One should always strictly avoid poison for those who have an excess of bile and phlegm.
"Intelligent men should not lend money to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the way of atheism. Thus says Nārada as well.

One should avoid giving a loan from the treasury to those who have committed a great offense, those who are devoid of righteousness, the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, the atheist, and those whose faults have been witnessed.

"In one who has committed a great offense" means one who is already established as being characterized by a prior grave transgression. And thus, it should be understood that for a eunuch, even a storehouse—just like fire and so forth—is to be avoided. Furthermore, as stated by Kātyāyana:
"For those who have killed their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, a child, a woman, or a king;
for those burdened with mortal sins (mahāpātaka); and especially for atheists..."
But for those who bear the marks [of their sect], who are arrogant, who know the rituals of mantra and yoga,
who are born of mixed castes, and who persist in the practice of sin—
In these very cases of accusation and in those that are indeed contemptible, a king devoted to righteousness should never, even with effort, administer an ordeal.

Thus, that [prohibition] is for the purpose of directly forbidding their status as divine agents (*divyakartṛtva*), and not, however, the examination by means of an ordeal (*divya*). For immediately thereafter it was stated by that same [author]: "An ordeal is fit for virtuous men who have been appointed by these [means];
where virtuous men do not wish [to administer it], there the accused should be tested by his own men. [242]
The king ought to administer divine ordeals; this is the implied sense. And so it is said by that same [author]:
"In these cases of dispute, divine ordeals are strictly prohibited;
one should have them performed by one's own kinsmen, and Manu says one must not abandon a person who has been falsely accused."
"He should abandon" means he should purify [the matter] in the manner described; this is the remainder of the sense. Furthermore, it was stated by him:
"In the case of those whose wealth is untouchable, of slaves, of Mlecchas, of evildoers, and of those born of inverse unions, there is no final determination by the king."
One should point to those well-known divine signs when there is doubt regarding them.
Thus, it should be understood that this refers to cases where one's own kinsmen appointed by those [parties] are unavailable.
Thus ends the determination of ordeals based on the caste and other attributes of the litigants in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
now follows the determination of ordeals based on the season.
In this regard, Pitāmaha says: "The balance (dhaṭa) is prescribed for all seasons, but one should avoid it when the wind is blowing;
fire is proclaimed [as the ordeal] for the cold, winter, and rainy seasons."

"In autumn and summer, water; in winter and the cool season, poison. The mention of the balance (dhaṭa) is intended to indicate the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) as well. However, the sacred libation must be administered at all times, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada: "The balance may be used at any time. The commentators have stated that the mention of the sacred libation is intended to include rice and other such ordeals. Therefore, the restriction regarding the seasons applies specifically to fire, water, and poison. For this very reason, the prohibition of those same ordeals during other seasons has been demonstrated by him: "There shall be no success with water in the cold, nor purification by fire in the heat of the season."
"A king should not administer poison during the rainy season, nor should he employ the balance scale in a strong wind. Thus it is said.

"In a *pravāta* [wind] means in a place where there is an excess of wind. Viṣṇu also states: "Fire must not be administered to lepers, the infirm, or blacksmiths; nor should poison be administered during autumn and summer to lepers, those with bilious disorders, or Brāhmaṇas; nor should water be administered during the rainy season to those afflicted by phlegmatic diseases, the timid, those suffering from asthma or cough, or those who live by water; and during the winter and the dewy season, the ordeal of the sacred vessel (*kośa*) must not be administered to atheists, nor when one is afflicted by disease or death. The mention of "winter" (*hemanta*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the month of Puṣya, and not for Mārgaśīrṣa as well, because the latter lacks an excess of cold and thus does not contradict the administration of the water ordeal. Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
"Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these are the common months, not incompatible with divine ordeals. Thus, the meaning is that these months constitute the proper times for all types of ordeals.
Thus ends the determination of ordeals according to the seasons in the Smṛticandrikā; now, regarding the locations for ordeals,
Pitāmaha says:
The balance (dhaṭa) must always be placed facing east, kept steady, in a clean location—either in the place of Indra, in an assembly hall, at the king’s gate, or at a crossroads.

[244] By "place of Indra" is meant a temple of a renowned deity, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada: "An assembly hall is [located] at the king's palace gate, a temple, or a quadrangle. Regarding this matter, Kātyāyana states the following rule:

One should employ [the ordeal] at the gate of the king for those men who have been accused in the place of Indra, those who are great sinners (mahāpātakin), and those who have committed acts of treason against the sovereign.
"For those born of inverse unions (*prātilomya*), the ordeal (*divya*) should be administered at a crossroads;
for other matters, however, the wise declare it should be in the midst of the court.

Since the term "ordeal" is mentioned in general, one should understand that this regulation regarding location applies not only to the balance (*dhaṭa*) but also to other ordeals whose specific locations have not been prescribed. He states that if the prescribed location and so forth are disregarded, the validity of the ordeal is lost: He himself says: [text follows]
Gifts given at an improper place or time, as well as those bestowed while residing abroad,
undoubtedly cause deviation from the true purpose of wealth in this world.

"Vāsaḥ" means a dwelling; "outside of that" refers to a desolate region. By this, it is implied by the sense that divine ordeals must be administered only in the presence of people. And it has been stated by Pitāmaha: "The king, or his appointed official, shall cause the ordeal to be administered in the presence of learned Brāhmaṇas and likewise of the subjects."
The presiding judge is the *prāḍvivāka*.
Thus ends the section on the places for divine ordeals in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the construction of the balance (dhaṭa);
regarding this, Nārada says:
"One should have it made of khadira wood, free from cracks and devoid of white [wood]."
In the absence of that, however, one should use a śiṃśupā tree or a sāla tree, provided they are free of hollows.

"Añjana, the heartwood of the tinduka, nīmiśa, and red sandalwood—one should prepare such kinds of wood for the purpose of the sacrificial post. By saying "such kinds," he indicates that in the absence of those previously mentioned, other trees suitable for sacrifice may also be used; and this has been shown by Pitāmaha.
Having cut down the sacrificial tree according to the rules and preceded by mantras,
and having bowed to the guardians of the world, the wise should prepare the balance.
"But for the cutting of a tree belonging to the Vanaspati class, a *saumya* mantra must indeed be recited.

Regarding this, some have stated that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *saumya* and *vānaspatya* [mantras] because they serve the same purpose. The mention of the "scale" (*tulā*) is intended to indicate its accessories as well; therefore, the cutting of trees may be performed even for the sake of pillars and other such parts. For this very reason, the measurement of the scale along with its accessories was stated by that same author:
"The scale should be made four cubits long, and the two feet should likewise be made so."
The distance between the two hands on the scales should be exactly one and a half [units].

The two feet are pillars for supporting the wooden beam of the scale; that is to say, they are of such a kind as to measure four cubits. And this measurement of the feet should be understood to refer to the portion above the part to be buried. Therefore, together with the buried portion, they become six cubits in length. Thus says Vyāsa:
"Two cubits are prescribed to be buried for each of the two *muṇḍaka* (pillars);
their total measurement, however, is said to be six cubits."

The measurement of the axle, however, is established by implication through the description of the distance between the two wheels; thus, it is not stated separately. Therefore, it should be understood that the axle must be made such that it does not protrude beyond the region of the feet, the pillars, or the top of the structure, being longer than two cubits or two and a half cubits. Furthermore, another Smṛti text shows that a cubit (*hasta*) consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*): "The measure of a finger-breadth is said to be eight horizontal barley-corns or three vertical grains of rice;
twelve finger-breadths make a span (*vitasti*)."

"A cubit (*hasta*) is two spans (*vitasti*). Thus it is said. However, whatever thickness ensures firmness for the balance and other instruments, that thickness should be employed, as no specific rule is recorded. Alternatively, the specific measurement for thickness should be understood from traditional practice (*ācāra*). Regarding the balance, however, other particulars have been shown by Pitāmaha:
"The balance should be made square, sturdy, and likewise straight."
And bracelets should be given with effort at three places.

*Kaṭakāni* refers to iron rings. They are to be placed in three locations: at the two ends and in the middle. The term *kaṭakāni* is intended as an illustration for other materials besides iron; therefore, at the two ends, two iron pins should be provided, curved at the tips like the horns of a crab, for the purpose of supporting the loops of the scale-ropes (*śikya*). In the middle, however, an iron loop should be attached to the wooden beam (*akṣakāṣṭha*) for the purpose of joining the balance. Thus says Nārada: "Square in shape, with its supports consisting of the balance-beam, the crab-claws (*karkaṭaka*), and so forth. (NSm 1.247)

By the word *dhaṭa*, the loop connected to the middle of the balance beam is indicated here. By the word *karkaṭaka*, the two pegs near the end are expressed due to their similarity. Thus, the meaning is this: the balance must be equipped with iron loops and other such components that serve as supports for its stability. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he shows that there must also be a single *karkaṭaka* peg in the middle of the axle. Likewise, the method for installing the pillars and other parts is also shown by him. Both [the ends] situated to the south and north are joined together at a single point.
Having fixed the two ends, one should place the balance on a level spot.

The meaning of this is as follows: on level ground, having joined both ends of two pillar-like feet situated in a north-south orientation to a single axle-wood at one point, one should place the balance-beam between those two connecting axle-woods. When it is asked how the placement there should be performed, he himself says: "Having grasped it by the middle with an iron chain, the knower of dharma should join the well-fastened balance-beam, extending from east to west."
"Extending from east to west" means long from the eastern to the western direction. And the Grandfather (Brahmā) states that its tip must be directed toward the east:
"The balance should always be placed facing east, motionless, in a pure location.
To ensure its immobility, Nārada says:
"Two cubits should be buried for both feet.

By saying "likewise," he indicates that other components of the balance-beam, such as the arches (*toraṇa*), should also be constructed. This has also been shown by Pitāmaha: "The arches should likewise be made on both sides as well."
The two [ears] should always be ten finger-breadths higher than the forehead.
Two downward-facing supports made of clay,
bound with cords and touching the top of the balance-beam, should be attached to the two arches.
One should always have a balance-scale constructed, adorned with flags and banners;
one should also have a spacious, lofty, and bright hall for the balance-scale built.
In that very place where one stationed is not harmed by outcasts or crows from the outside,
one should install the world-protectors and others in all directions.
One should worship them at the three junctions of the day with perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
[the site] should be secured with door-bolts and seeds, and guarded by attendants.
"The king should cause [the balance] to be joined with earth, water, and fire, and thus not empty.

Regarding this, some have stated that the arrangement of the hall and so forth is intended solely for the purpose of supporting the balance (*dhaṭa*), and not for its production; therefore, if there is no desire to support it, these things need not be performed.
Thus ends the procedure for the construction of the balance in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the general procedure common to all ordeals;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
Witnesses may fall into discord out of affection, anger, or greed;
however, no division ever arises regarding a divine ordeal administered according to the prescribed rule.
Therefore, the intention is that the divine ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed rule. And that rule has been shown by Pitāmaha:
"In all legal matters concerning divine ordeals, the judge shall conduct the proceedings, fasting and by the king's command, just as the Adhvaryu priest acts in sacrificial rites."
The meaning is that all rites are both common and uncommon. Among these, the common ones have been shown by him [the author] himself:
"Then, the knower of dharma should invoke the gods according to this rite.
The meaning of "by this" is "by the one about to be described. He demonstrates that very rite:
Then the judge, facing eastward with palms joined in reverence, should say:
"Come, come, O Blessed Dharma! Enter into this divine ordeal, accompanied by the World-Protectors, the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts. Thus.

The meaning of "then" (*tataḥ*) is "immediately after the preparation of the divine [elements]," because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra "in this divine one," and because of the statement by that same author:

"Having invoked Dharma into the balance (*dhaṭa*), one should subsequently assign the limbs. The mention of the "balance" (*dhaṭa*) is intended to indicate all prepared divine elements, since the invocation of Dharma and the assignment of the limbs will be described for all such divine ordeals. The meaning of "one should assign the limbs" has been shown by that same author.
Having first established Indra in the east, likewise Yama, the Lord of the Dead, in the south;
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Kubera in the north.
One should also place the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions:
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, and Varuṇa has the luster of crystal.
Kubera has a golden luster, and Agni likewise has a golden luster;
Niṛti is dark-complexioned, and Vāyu is praised as being smoke-colored.
Īśāna, however, should be red; thus one should meditate on these in sequence. On the right side of Indra, the wise practitioner should invoke the Vasus.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the path of the Ādityas:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, and then Viṣṇu, who, though born last, is not the least.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names;
one should know that the abode of the Rudras is in the western part of Agni.
And Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly renowned Giriśa; Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita.
Bhuvanādhīśvara, Kapālī, Viśāmpati,
Sthāṇu, and the lordly Bhaga— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
One should arrange the station of the Mothers in the midst of the lords of the pretas and the rākṣasas:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by her hosts—[these are located] in the northern part of Nirṛti; they know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be there.
To the northern region of Varuṇa, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located;
there the wind—Gaganasparśana, Anila, and likewise Māruta—resides.

[251] “Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīva, and the eight Maruts are proclaimed [to be worshipped]; the wise man should invoke Durgā on the northern side of the balance. Here too, as before, the mention of the “balance” (dhaṭa) is intended to indicate the divya (ordeals) that have been prepared. In this manner, one should perform the worship of the deities invoked in their respective places. And so says the same authority:
"The wise know that the worship of these deities is performed by their own names.
And regarding that, he [the same author] states the sequence:
"Having offered everything up to the ornaments for Dharma, one should then offer the *arghya* and so forth in due order."
Thereafter, one should prepare the offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the ornaments for the limbs.

The meaning is: [the worship] of the *aṅgīs*, beginning with Indra and ending with Durgā. The preparation of the *arghya* and other offerings for them should be performed according to the method of *padārthānusamaya* (performing each item for all objects in succession), not according to the method of *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performing all items for one object before moving to the next); for if it were otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the simultaneity (*sahatva*) understood from the injunction regarding the ritual performance (*prayoga*). Having offered ornaments to Durgā, one should perform the service of perfumes and so forth for Dharma and for those beginning with Indra and ending with Durgā as before. And thus says the same [author]: "One should arrange the service beginning with perfumes and ending with the offering (*nivedya*).
Then, an oblation (*homa*) must be performed in the four directions with four [offerings]. And thus says the same [author]:
Likewise, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in the four directions by those who have mastered the Vedas,
using clarified butter, sacrificial oblation, and fuel-sticks as the means for the sacrifice.
"Then one should perform the oblation with the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, and ending with 'svāhā'.

This means that having established the worldly fire in the four directions, one officiating priest in each direction should offer fuel-sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*) one hundred and eight times each, using the mantra "tat savitur" (RV 3.62.10) with the Praṇava at both the beginning and end, and ending with the utterance of *svāhā*. Although the number is not explicitly stated here, nevertheless, it is traditionally held that where no number is mentioned, one hundred and eight is intended.
It should be noted that this is established by another Smṛti text. All of this must be performed in the forenoon, because that is the primary time for these rites. Accordingly, Nārada says:
"When a man has fasted for a day and night, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes, the administration of all ordeals is prescribed for the forenoon."
As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"Having summoned one who has bathed with his clothes on and fasted since sunrise,
he shall cause all ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas."

Thus, it should be understood that in this context, by the expression "at sunrise," the forenoon itself is prescribed through a figurative turn of phrase. Furthermore, the forenoon must be taken as being specifically conjoined with a Sunday, due to the force of the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). After the fire-oblation (*homa*), Pitāmaha [states]: "The object for which one is accused, having written that down upon a leaf (*patraka*), together with this mantra, that matter shall be placed upon the head."
The meaning is "by this which is about to be stated. He shows that very mantra:
"The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama;
day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of a man. [253] Thus.
And this procedure is common to all divine ordeals; thus he [the author] himself says:
"One should apply this entire ritual procedure for mantras to all divine ordeals, and the invocation of the gods is likewise proclaimed in the same way."

The meaning is that in all ordeals, the procedure beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head of the person to be purified must be performed. Likewise, at the conclusion of the application of all ordeals, one should give a gratifying sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests and others. And so says that same author:
"One should satisfy the officiating priests, family priests, and teachers with sacrificial fees.
Thus ends the section on the general rules for all ordeals in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the ordeal by the balance.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Having firmly attached two sets of scales to the hooks of the balance..."
One should weigh a man on one side of the scale and a stone on the other.

The meaning is that one should attach two loops for the two scales, which have been fashioned according to the prescribed rule from a pair of jars or crocodile-shaped weights. The mention of "stone" (śilā) is intended as an illustration for clay and other materials. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says:
"Having attached two loops on both sides, one should arrange darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon both loops."
"In the western [scale] one should weigh the makers; in the other, auspicious earth, free from bricks, ash, stones, potsherds, and bones.
Thus, the conjunction of bricks and stones with the earth is precluded, but not their optionality, since they too are prescribed. And so says Nārada: [254]

"One should fill the pan with bricks, stones, and dust. This means [one may use] bricks, stones, or dust. Alternatively, one may fill the pan with beans, according to the statement in another Smṛti: "Or even a heap of beans. Thus, it should be understood that there is an option regarding the use of stone, clay, brick, stone, dust, or beans as weights. For this very reason, Nārada stated:
"One should place a lump of clay and the accused person equally upon the scale."
"One should place the male figure on the northern side and the stone slab on the southern side. Thus it is said.

The phrase "on the northern side" refers to the scale-beam (*tulā*) constructed with an east-west orientation. Although such a construction was not previously prescribed, nevertheless, by virtue of this very statement, it is established by implication that one should sometimes make the two pillar-posts stand facing east and west and fashion the beam with its end pointing north; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. The phrase "one should maintain the scale" implies "anyone among the merchants and so forth. And so Viṣṇu says: "And anyone among merchants, goldsmiths, or brazier-makers should maintain it. This means "that scale. All of them should be appointed by the king for the purpose of inspecting the balance of the scale maintained by any one of them. And so Pitāmaha says:
Examiners shall be appointed who are experts in weights and measures,
as well as merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers.
And those appointed [to oversee the weighing] should observe impartiality. Thus says Nārada:
"Goldsmiths, merchants, skilled workers in bell-metal, and those expert in handling scales—these should inspect that scale. [255]
The Grandfather (Brahmā) said to the examiners:
"The balance-beam must always be made by the examiners equal to the support;
and water must be poured upon the balance-beam by the learned."
"That balance on which water does not float is to be known as even.

Thus, the balance is "even with the suspension" (*avalambasama*) when its connection to the two earthen suspensions hanging from the two arches (*toraṇa*) is level with the upper part of the two rings (*kaṭaka*). And so says Nārada:
"At the first mounting, the standard [of weight] should be determined by experts together."
The characteristic mark placed upon the archway should be equal in measure to the two heads of the scales.

Immediately after the determination of equality, Viṣṇu states: "Having made two men of equal weight and well-marked, one should cause the [defendant] man to descend. "Well-marked" means that those parts of the body to which the sling-ropes were attached during the state of equality should be marked there with white lines. After the descent, Pitāmaha says:
"Having first weighed the man and then having caused him to descend, one should always have the balance made adorned with banners and flags."

Thus, immediately after the preparation, one should perform the common procedure for all ordeals, beginning with the invocation of the deities (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the document upon the head of the person to be examined. And so it is said: "One should apply this entire ritual procedure of mantras to all ordeals;
likewise, one should perform the invocation of the deities in the same manner."
Regarding the specific requirements for the means of propitiating the Dharma therein, Nārada says:
"One should first worship the balance with red perfumes, garlands, curd, cakes, unbroken grains, and so forth; thereafter, one should worship the remaining [deities]. [256]

The *dhaṭa* is the Dharma presided over by the *Dhaṭa*; [one should also invoke] the remaining deities, Indra and the others. After the document has been placed upon the head of the person to be cleared, the Grandfather (Brahmā), the knower of the scriptures, should address the *dhaṭa* with this following ritual formula:
"O *dhaṭa*, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked."
"Because you are the embodiment of Dharma through the letter *dha*, and because you contemplate the crooked man held by the letter *ṭa*,
you are therefore called 'Dhṛta' (the Sustainer). Thus spoke the judge,
who was learned in the scriptures.

"Since it has been stated by that very same authority: 'The judge shall conduct all proceedings regarding divine ordeals,' therefore the person to be purified (the defendant) should also address that balance. And so says Yājñavalkya:
'The accused, having mounted the balance, [shall be weighed] by experts in the measurement of the balance.'"
Having become equal through comparison, it was brought down after being marked with a line.
O Tula, you were created by the gods of old as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak that truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.

"If I am a wrongdoer, O Mother, then lead me downward; if I am pure, lead me upward"—with this mantra he should consecrate the scale before the person to be tested is placed upon it again. This means that the judge should consecrate the scale with the mantra beginning with "Thou, O Scale" and ending with "lead me upward. Thereafter, the judge should place him upon it once more. [257]
And so Nārada says:
"Then, having bound the man with oaths, one should place him upon the balance again;
having placed a leaf upon his head in a windless place free from rain."

"Having taken him under oath" means having bound the weigher (*tulādhāraka*) by means of oaths. And those oaths have been shown by that very [author]: "Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, whatever worlds for a false witness, and whatever worlds for one who holds the scales falsely while weighing—[may I attain those]."
Furthermore, after the re-ascension, Nārada said:
"O best of the twice-born, when that very target has been made the target,
you are designated by the term 'Dharma-paryāya' as the 'Dhaṭa' (the balance)."
You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings;
O God, you alone perceive those things which human beings do not know.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed by you;
therefore, you ought to protect him, who has fallen into doubt, according to dharma.
Among gods, asuras, and humans, you excel in truth;
O Blessed One, you are true to your word through your discernment of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
"The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, and Yama;

day and night, both twilights, and Dharma know the conduct of a man. (258) Thus, having placed the person to be examined upon the scale according to its proper arrangement, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should recite the passage beginning with "Dharma" and ending with "conduct. After the recitation of the mantra, Pitāmaha says:
An astrologer, the best among Brahmins, should perform an examination of the time;
five *vināḍīs* are to be understood as the duration to be examined by those skilled in time.
The king should appoint as witnesses the best of Brahmins, who speak of matters exactly as they have seen them, who are wise, pure, and free from greed.
"The determination of purity and impurity is to be understood from their words.
Thus, the time required to pronounce three hundred long syllables consists of five *vināḍīs*. Accordingly, another *Smṛti* states:
"Ten long syllables constitute one *prāṇa*; six *prāṇas* shall be one *vināḍikā*."

And thus, the Brahmin astrologer should determine a time-measure of five *vināḍīs* by the pronunciation of long syllables. The person to be cleared should then ascend the scale and remain there for that duration. At that time, the appointed witnesses should determine the verdict of purity or impurity based on the signs of victory or defeat; this is the meaning of the previously cited texts to be understood. When it is asked what these signs of victory and defeat are, Nārada says:
"If, when weighed, he increases in weight, he shall be pure, without a doubt; if he remains equal or decreases, the man shall not be pure."
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati):
"One who loses [the case] would not be pure; according to some, however, one who is equal is impure.
One who has committed a small sin should be known as equal, but one who has committed a great sin is defeated. [259]

In that context, the phrase "of some" (*ekeṣām*) is for the sake of showing respect [to their view], but not to indicate that it represents the author's own position, because even one with minor sin is considered impure. Therefore, there is no difference between the declining party and the defeated party; the only distinction lies in the punishment and the penance, since punishment and penance must correspond to the gravity of the offense. As for what was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"If a person accused in a balance ordeal is weighed again and has become lighter, he shall suffer loss;
if he is equal, he should be weighed again; if he is heavier, he shall be the victor."

The meaning of this is as follows: the determination of equality should not be made during the first weighing; rather, when it is weighed again, if it remains exactly equal, then its purity must be ascertained. Likewise, in the event of a break in the scale-pan or similar incidents, the purity or impurity of the person being weighed again must be determined. And so says Kātyāyana: "In the case of a break in the scale-pan, a fracture of the balance, or likewise of the cord, and also when there is doubt regarding purity, one should examine the man once more."
But regarding purity, a doubt was elaborated by Nārada: when the balance,
having become unsteady and wavering due to its two ends, is marked with signs,
and when it has encountered the wind, it moves either upward or downward.

"Or if it is suddenly released, then one should not decide either way. This is the meaning: when the ends of the beam sway sideways; when the water or other substance placed for the purpose of ascertaining balance moves; when the beam, impelled by the wind, oscillates upward and downward; and when the beam is released from the hand of the holder—then one should not determine victory or defeat. Furthermore, as he has stated:
"In the case of the tearing of the garment, the breaking of the beam, or likewise of the *dhaṭa* and the *karkaṭaka*..."
Upon the severing of the rope and the breaking of the axle, one who has fainted shall attain purification.

Thus, that [rule] refers to cases where the breaking of the scale-pan and so forth have no visible cause, since only a divine (accidental) breaking of the scale-pan and such constitutes a ground for purification. Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
"All witnesses declare purity or impurity before the king;
the king, surrounded by virtuous men, having summoned one who is pure, shall honor him."
He should satisfy the officiating priests, the domestic chaplain, and the teachers with sacrificial fees;
thus acting as the instigator, the king shall enjoy delightful pleasures.
"He attains great fame and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Thus ends the procedure for the ordeal of the balance in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follows the procedure for the ordeal of fire.
In that regard, the Grandfather said:
"I shall proclaim the procedure for the fire exactly as it is enjoined in the scriptures;
one should cause eight mandalas to be made in front, and likewise a ninth."

The meaning is that the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*), having fasted and being authorized by the king’s command, should prepare nine mandalas ending toward the east in a place prescribed for the shrines of renowned deities and the like, after performing the purification of the ground through digging and sprinkling with water. And these should be made with cow-dung, because it has been stated by that same [author, Yājñavalkya]: "They should be made with cow-dung and sprinkled with water. The measurement of the space between them is shown by both [Yājñavalkya and Viṣṇu].
"The mandala should be known as sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width, and the interval between them likewise.
This means that both the mandalas and their intervening spaces should each be made with a measurement of sixteen finger-breadths. As for the deities of the mandalas, they have been shown by Pitāmaha:
"The first mandala is of Agni, and the second is traditionally held to be of Varuṇa."
The third has Vasu as its deity, and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth, however, has Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity, and likewise the eighth belongs to Savitṛ.
"The ninth belongs to all the gods"—thus do those who know the divine understand.

It is called *āgneya* because Agni is worshipped therein; for it is impossible for the maṇḍala itself to be *āgneya* either by virtue of being an oblation (*havis*) or by virtue of being a hymn (*sūkta*). In the same way, its *vāruṇa* nature and so forth should also be understood through its status as the locus of worship. Thus, just as the designation "the cup of the Hotṛ" found in the injunction-mantra "Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forth" establishes that the Hotṛ and others are entitled to drink from that cup, it is well known from this very statement that the worship of Agni and the other deities must be performed in their respective maṇḍalas precisely by means of the designations *āgneya* and so on. Therefore, after sprinkling the maṇḍalas, one should perform the worship of the presiding deities of the maṇḍalas. Then, for each maṇḍala, one should scatter *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward.

"Kuśa grasses, as enjoined by the scriptures, should be offered in each and every mandala," because it has been so remembered by that very [author]. Then, having established the worldly fire (laukikāgni) not too far to the south of the first mandala, one should perform the pacification homa;
for the sake of pacification, one should offer ghee into the fire one hundred and eight times.

This is because of the traditional legal authority (*smṛti*). Furthermore, the commentators have stated that the oblation (*homa*) should be performed with this mantra: "Svāhā to Agni Pāvaka. Thereafter, one should heat a lump of iron in that fire. And so Pitāmaha [states]:
"Having made it eight finger-breadths long, symmetrical, and free of sharp edges, one should heat a uniform iron ball weighing fifty *palas* in the fire."

It should be level, neither depressed nor elevated. The repetition of the word "level" (*sama*) is for the purpose of enjoining that one should heat it on all sides. Alternatively, one may heat a ball weighing sixteen *palas*. For the *Smṛti* of Śaṅkha and Likhita states: "Then, having taken with both hands a red-hot iron ball weighing sixteen *palas* enclosed within seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, one should proceed to the boundary. Nārada, however, states that the heating must be performed by a blacksmith:
"An iron-smith who is such by birth, skilled in the work of fire, and whose practice has been witnessed elsewhere—he shall heat the iron in the fire."

By the phrase "and the application has been seen elsewhere," it is shown that just as in the world iron is heated until red-hot and then plunged into water, and this process of heating and plunging is repeated for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the iron, so too should it be done here. In that context, while the third heating is taking place, one should perform the common procedure for all ordeals, beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head of the person to be purified. And thus Pitāmaha says:
"One should apply this entire ritual of mantras to all ordeals."
"And one should likewise perform the invocation of the gods.
Regarding this, he (the same author) states the specific procedure for the means of accomplishing the propitiation of Dharma:
"In that regard, O lord of men, the king should cause the worship of the sacrificial fire to be performed."
"With red sandalwood and incense, and likewise with red flowers.

This refers to the fire-offering for the Fire-god, that is to say, for Dharma who has been invoked into the mass of glowing iron. "Red sandalwood and incense" means *raktacandanadhūpau*; by these two [the offering is made]. This specific rule does not apply to the means of propitiating Indra and the other deities, because of the specification "of the Fire-god. Once the document of the oath has been placed upon the head, Hārīta states what must be done immediately thereafter for the person undergoing purification:
"Then he should stand facing the east, with his fingers and limbs extended."
Wearing wet clothes and remaining pure, he should place a leaf upon his head.
"And the [initial] position must be taken in the first circle;

one should stand in the western circle, facing east, with palms joined in reverence and purified," according to the Smṛti of Pitāmaha. Viṣṇu states what must be done by the person to be tested and by the judge:
"One should first observe his hands as being rubbed with rice," [it is said].

Those two by which rice has been rubbed are "the ones rubbed with rice. By this, it is stated by implication that having performed the rubbing of rice with both hands, the accused should have his fingers extended. The meaning of "one should observe" has been elaborated upon by Nārada:
"One should observe the marks on both of his hands."

The meaning is that one should make *haṃsapada* (swan-foot) marks with the juice of lac or similar substances at the locations of wounds and so forth on both hands of the person to be examined (*śodhya*), in order to indicate that these [marks] were present prior to the application of fire. And thus, that same author says:
"In all hand-wounds, one should indeed make *haṃsapadas*."
Then Yājñavalkya states what must be done:
"Having marked the two hands with crushed grains of rice,
one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread."

Viṣṇu also states: "Then, one should place seven *aśvattha* leaves in the hands of the person facing east with both arms extended; these, together with the two hands, should be bound with a thread. In both [these texts], by the word "then" (*tataḥ*), it is understood that whatever is prescribed in other Smṛtis—such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth—to be performed between the marking of the hands and the placing of the leaves, is not to be done according to this opinion. And thus, as stated by Nārada: "Having thus first performed the marking of the hands for the accused..."
For the sake of pacification, one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire with mantras according to the prescribed rule.
Then, when the gods and the world-protectors have been satisfied,
one should face the sun and recite this mantra:
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
you carry the oblation to the gods, and when offered, you bestow peace.
The hidden sins and good deeds of human beings—you alone know them, O God; those which mortals do not perceive.
"O Fire, I stand here in doubt, accused in a legal proceeding;
therefore, you ought to protect me, who am thus mounted upon uncertainty, according to dharma."
When he, the wise one, had spoken thus while facing the east,
[the disciple] filled his joined palms with seven equal leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.

The meaning is: when the gods—the Vasus, Ādityas, and Rudras—as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas), have been gratified with oblations of ghee and other substances offered under their respective names, by means of the nine mantras beginning with “ākṛṣṇena” which illuminate the planets. All of this should be understood as optional. However, that which was stated as a qualification of the leaves—namely, that they be “even” (samaiḥ)—is mandatory; therefore, in both cases, the leaves must be of equal dimensions. Likewise, a specific rule regarding the binding threads has also been shown by him.
"One should wrap the hands with seven white threads of cotton. Here, "white" means pure white. As for another Smṛti text:
"But [one should hold] heated iron with both hands using seven *arka* leaves."
If he takes it away while it is still hidden, he is pure; he is not burned until the seventh step.
Thus, this refers to the case where the *aśvattha* leaf is unavailable. As Pitāmaha said:
"Fire is born from the *pippala*; the *pippala* is remembered as the king of trees.
Therefore, a wise man should place its leaves in his hands."

Since the *aśvattha* is praised, the meaning is that its leaves alone should be taken whenever possible. The *śamī* leaves and so forth, however, are to be used in conjunction with the previously mentioned leaves. Accordingly, another Smṛti states:
"One should offer seven *pippala* leaves, or else *śamī* leaves, or seven leaves of *dūrvā*; and one should place those unbroken grains (*akṣata*) upon them. [266]

Likewise, one should place flowers, seven *pippala* leaves, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and *sumanas* (flowers), according to the traditional teaching of Pitāmaha. Here, *sumanas* refers to flowers. Then, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should consecrate the fire situated within the heated iron ball with the mantra beginning with "O Agni, you are the gods... and ending with "O Great Fire. And so says Pitāmaha:
After that, once [the vessel] has been heated, the pure person,
knowing the prior ritual procedure, should perform the invocation of Agni and the invocation of the deities.
O Agni, you are the four gods, and you alone are invoked in the sacrifices;
you are the mouth of all the gods, and you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman.
For, residing within the bellies of all beings, you therefore know their good and evil;
since you indeed purify sin, you are called Pāvaka (the Purifier).
"O Purifier, reveal yourself as radiant among the wicked;
or else, O Great Fire, become cool among those of pure intent.

This [verse] is intended to indicate the entire ritual procedure for the deities, beginning with Dharma, starting from the invocation (*āvāhana*) and reception, and ending with the placement of flowers—the purificatory rite performed upon the person to be tested. Viṣṇu, however, states a different mantra for the consecration of the fire within the iron ball.
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
O Agni, you alone know those things which human beings do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."

The efficacy of this mantra for consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is through conjunction (*samuccaya*), and not by way of option (*vikalpa*), because their functions are distinct: [the mantra] reveals the object of prayer as residing within the specific individual to be purified. As it is said: "On the third heating, one should address the person who has been heated while being presided over by the members of the court:
'Listen to this human law (*mānava dharma*) presided over by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).'"
O Agni, you are the supreme purifier and the mouth of all the gods;
residing within the hearts of all beings, you alone know their every action.
Truth and falsehood are both found within your tongue;
this has been declared by the gods and others, and you ought not to act otherwise.
By this [formula], it is declared: "May he speak a falsehood;
and in every way, just as it is false, so do I maintain the fire."
This man sustains you by means of this truth;
O Consumer of Oblations, become cool toward him who speaks the truth.
Burn the hands of the sinner for the sin of speaking falsehood.

Thus, as for the consecration of the fire (*agny-abhimantraṇa*) mentioned by Nārada, it is treated as an option (*vikalpyate*) with the consecration of the fire mentioned by Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha, because they serve the same purpose. When the consecration of the fire mentioned by Nārada is performed, he [Viṣṇu] states that the following must be done immediately after the consecration: "Having caused the defendant to hear the meaning of this matter as it stands in the document, and having placed [the document] upon his head, the ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed procedure."

The meaning is that after having caused [the defendant] to hear the meaning of the previously mentioned mantra for consecration and the meaning of the mantra written on the leaf placed upon his head, one should place that leaf in its proper position and then give him the iron ball. However, when the consecration of the fire as prescribed by Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha is performed, Pitāmaha states what must be done once that has been completed:
"Then, taking hold of it, the king devoted to dharma, or one appointed by him, should place it in the hands of the [defendant] using tongs."

The grammatical connection is: "having taken up that iron ball with tongs. The judge is appointed [for this task]. Yājñavalkya states what must be done for the person undergoing purification on both sides prior to the casting [of the ball]:
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, speak the truth to me regarding my merits and sins."
When he has spoken thus, one should place a lump of iron weighing fifty palas and heated to the color of fire equally upon both his hands.

The meaning is: of that person to be tested who has spoken thus and performed the aforementioned consecration of the fire. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states what must be done by the person to be tested once the iron ball has been placed [on the ground]:

"Taking it up, he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles. The meaning of this has been explained by Viṣṇu: "Taking it up, he should walk neither too quickly nor too slowly, placing his footstep upon the circles. This means on the second circle and so forth, ending with the eighth. And likewise Nārada says:
Taking it up with both hands as impelled by the judge,
he should then stand still for one step and walk seven steps in a straight line to the others.
Unperturbed and free from anger, he should proceed slowly toward the fire;
he must not let go of that [bowstring] before reaching the ground that was designated.
"One should not step over the maṇḍala, nor should one place a foot before it.

Having reached the eighth maṇḍala, the person should then dismiss the fire. This means that there is one [maṇḍala] at the beginning; the others are the second and so forth. And the dismissal of the fire should be performed at the ninth maṇḍala.

"Having gone to the eighth circle, the wise man should deposit [the ball] in the ninth," according to the Smṛti of Pitāmaha. Regarding what must be done by the examiner immediately after the deposit, Narada says:
"One should perform the examination of the hand of that very person from whom the ball was released."
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "for the sake of thoroughly knowing purity and impurity. Regarding that, he himself states the characteristics that indicate impurity:
"One should recognize [the presence of a corpse] by means of signs previously observed, even elsewhere than there;
where there is a mandala appearing red, or anything else produced by fire."
"He should be known as impure, established in untruthful dharma.

This means that one should recognize him as impure if a boil or similar lesion is found anywhere in the middle of his two palms; however, he whose [palms] show no such thing should be known as pure. And thus Viṣṇu says:
"One should designate him as impure who has a burn on his hands anywhere."
But that man who has not been burned in every way—he shall be pure.
But when there is doubt as to whether [the hands] have been burnt or not burnt, Nārada says:
"If no distinction can be made by means of knowledge, then both hands are considered burnt;
in that case, one should cause the rice grains to be offered with great care seven times. [270]

"If he is rubbed [clean] but not burned, he is declared pure by the members of the court; he who is pure shall be released with honor, but he who is burned shall be punished according to the law. Thus says Pitāmaha as well.
"And having removed [the powder], one should subsequently rub [the hands] with either rice or barley;
when no change occurs at the end of the day, one should designate that person as pure.

The meaning is: when both hands remain unchanged, one should designate that person as pure. Some read, "When the two hands are without change"; according to that view, purity is to be determined by the rubbing immediately following the removal. Now, regarding the reading, "At the end of the day, one should designate him as pure":

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Yājñavalkya: "Having released the fire and having crushed the grains, one who is not burnt shall attain purification. Do not speak thus; for just as in the case of the rule, "Having placed the enclosing-sticks [around the fire], he offers the oblation," the use of the suffix *ktvā* is appropriate even in the absence of immediate sequence. Furthermore, he [Yājñavalkya] stated:
"If the rice-ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, one should offer it again."

Thus, this refers to a case where doubt does not depart even when the rice has been crushed; that is, a case where there is doubt as to whether the non-burning or burning is due to truth or falsehood, or rather due to causes such as visible intervention. In the rule, "If the ball falls in between," one must understand the remainder of the phrase to be "and the burnt [ball] is not perceived. For if the burnt ball were perceived, there would be no occasion for a second taking because of the certainty of impurity. Therefore, Nārada says: "But he who causes it to fall in between, and the burnt [ball] is not discerned..."
One should again cause that fire to be carried away; this rule has been firmly established.

"And burnt" means that he is not perceived as being burnt while inside the palms of both hands; this is the remainder [of the sense]. In other cases, even if burning is perceived, one should nevertheless cause him to pay the fine. And so says Kātyāyana: "If the accused slips away and is burnt elsewhere than at the designated spot, the gods consider him unburnt; one should cause him to pay again."
"Furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) means "again. On this point, Nārada says:
"By this procedure, the fire-rite should always be performed;
except during the summer, it is prescribed for other cool seasons."
Thus ends the section on the rules regarding fire in the *Smṛticandrikā*.

Now, since the performance of the rules concerning water has fallen into disuse, their procedure will not be described; instead, the procedure for the *kośa* (the ordeal by sacred libation) is stated.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having worshipped the fierce gods, one should take the water from their ablutions. Thus it is said.

The *ugras* are fierce deities such as Rudra, Durga, Aditya, and others. The meaning is that the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), having fasted and worshipped one of those deities with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having bathed the deity, should lead the water from that bath to the place of the ordeal. Having placed the man there, he should perform the common procedure for all ordeals—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the document on the head of the person undergoing purification—and then, having made the person facing east, have him drink three handfuls (*prasṛti*) of the previously deposited water. The commentators have stated that at that very time, a circle of three handfuls should be drawn with cow-dung. Having turned the person toward the sun and caused them to hear the oath, he should have them drink. And so says Yājñavalkya: [272] *... (text of Yājñavalkya)* ...* (The remainder of the passage is omitted as per instructions.)
"Having caused [the accused] to hear [the oath], one should afterwards have him drink three handfuls of water. When it is asked what he should be made to hear, Nārada states:
"And having caused him to hear the sin, one should have him drink three handfuls."
That sin, which is the evil act, has been shown by him through the very description of its consequences:
"If any man, being defiled, should drink from the royal treasury of his own will,
that deceitful and wicked-minded man shall be ruined."
He who, out of his own will, drinks from the treasury and then breaks his word,
is born poor, diseased, and foolish for seven lifetimes.
"For he who, by force, gives his treasury while desiring his own welfare shall meet with ruin, and that task of his will not succeed. Thus it is said.

In this context, the proponent must have the final verse recited by implication. The defendant, having heard it recited, should drink while declaring, "This was not done intentionally. Thus Viṣṇu states: "Having worshipped fierce deities, one should face those deities and drink three handfuls of water from their bathing-rites, declaring: 'This was not done intentionally. Accordingly, Pitāmaha has stated the following rule regarding the performance of the *kośa* ordeal, which applies when water from the bathing-rites of any fierce deity whatsoever is brought forth:
"One should cause the defendant to drink the water belonging to whichever deity he is devoted to."
But in the case of equality among the gods, one should cause [the victim] to drink from the vessel of Āditya.
[273] “One should cause thieves and those who live by weapons to drink the water of Durgā; however, one should not cause a Brāhmaṇa to drink that water which belongs to Bhāskara.
Thus he [the same author] states the rule regarding the location for the ritual bathing:
"One should bathe the trident of Durgā, the discus of Āditya, and likewise the weapons of the other gods as well. Thus [it is said]. After drinking three handfuls, Kātyāyana states:
Now, regarding the failure of the ordeal by divine means: after three weeks, the judge, being satisfied, shall cause the accused to pay that sum and also a fine.

The failure of fate (*daivavisaṃvāda*) is the manifestation of divine diseases (*daivikavyādhi*). And those divine diseases have been shown by him [the Lord] himself: consumption, dysentery, eruptive boils, pain in the palate and bones, eye disease, throat disease, and likewise insanity, O Prajāpati.
"Headaches and the breaking of the arms—these are the divine diseases of men.
Thus [it is said]. Other causes of defeat have also been shown by Viṣṇu:
"If one should see [an omen] within fourteen days, or even within twenty-one days..."
Illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or even royal punishment—
"One should know that [the document] to be impure; likewise, it is pure in the opposite case. Thus [it is said].
Nārada has also stated that loss of the object and other such factors constitute defeat:
"If, within seven days, or again within fourteen days..."
Illness, fire, the death of kinsmen, loss of property, and the depletion of wealth.

"Whose [claim] is personal (*pratyātmika*), one should know that person to be defeated. Here, "personal" does not mean employed by a collective group. In this context, "wealth" (*artha*) is intended to mean a son and so forth; otherwise, the word "wealth" (*dhana*) would be redundant. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"If, within seven days or fourteen days, no distress arises for the [creditor]," [he is defeated].
He shall be purified of [the sins regarding] sons, wives, and wealth; of this there is no doubt.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) has also stated the interval for execution:
"Whether after three nights, seven nights, or even fourteen days,
that man who is seen to have caused a portentous change in the cooking [of the food] shall be punished."

The meaning is: "of that person who is to be purified. Not only does one become a doer of evil when the one to be purified falls into a state of corruption, but also when one's own people fall into a state of corruption; thus he says: "If that [corruption] should happen to that one person alone, and not to all people—if it be disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman—that indeed is his [the corruptor's] manifestation."

If that abnormality, such as disease and so forth, were to occur to only one person who has drunk from the vessel, then it would not necessarily mean he is the wrongdoer; rather, the meaning is that it applies even when it occurs to anyone at all among his entire circle of people. Manu has also stated another criterion for innocence:
"He who does not quickly meet with misfortune should be known as pure by means of oaths."

“Affliction” (*ārti*) refers to disease and so forth, as previously mentioned. “Swiftly” (*kṣipram*) means quickly, that is, within one night at most. This time limit applies to cases involving oaths of truth and the like used to resolve minor matters, because the cultivation of purity for such a short duration is appropriate precisely in those instances, and because it was stated in reference to oaths of truth and the like. However, limits of three nights and so forth apply to the *kośa* ordeal, since they were stated with reference to the *kośa*. Even among those, the three-night limit pertains to substances other than rice used in the *taṇḍula* ordeal. The limit of two weeks, however, pertains to cases of serious accusation (*mahābhiyoga*). As for the limit of three weeks:
"In the case of death within twenty days, however, the drinking of the ordeal-substance (doṣapāna) is prescribed.

This should be understood as referring to the subject matter of the treasury (kośa) as established [in the texts], because of its appropriateness (*aucityāt*). In every case, even if a deformity (*vaikṛta*) is observed after the deadline, the sinner is not to be cleared by the ordeal, due to the force of the deadline itself; for a disease or similar condition occurring at a later time arises from a subsequent cause. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"If, after two weeks have passed, a very great deformity should occur..."
He should not be prosecuted by a wise man because of the lapse of the prescribed time.

The phrase "after two weeks" is intended as an illustration of the previously mentioned time limits; for the reason stated—"due to the transgression of the fixed time"—applies equally even to other time limits.
Thus concludes the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the ordeal by rice (*taṇḍula*); regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
I shall explain the procedure for rice grains as enjoined by their defining characteristics;
it is a settled rule that rice grains are to be administered in cases of theft, and not in any other case.

The meaning is: in other cases, such as those involving adultery with women (*strīsaṃgrahaṇa*) and so forth, as well as in disputes over property (*dhanavivāda*). However, in disputes over property, rice must be administered even outside of cases of theft, because Kātyāyana stated: "Rice is for half of that amount" (2.276). Nor should it be argued that this statement refers exclusively to the subject of theft, for that would contradict the introductory phrase: "Where there is a denial of what was given. Therefore, it should be understood that the mention of theft is intended merely to illustrate disputes over property. In this matter, the procedure lasts for two days. Regarding what must be done on the preceding day, he (Kātyāyana) himself says:
One who is pure, having placed white śāli rice grains— of whatever variety—
in an earthen vessel, should wash them before the Sun.
"One should let them remain there very night mixed with the water used for the Sun's bath, having first performed the invocation and other rites according to the rule.

This means that the judge, having purified himself, should prepare rice grains at night not too far from the Sun; having performed the common procedure for all ordeals beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the oblation (*homa*); and having sprinkled the rice grains as they were placed with the water from the Sun's bath, he should leave them exactly as they are until dawn. Furthermore, what is to be done at dawn has also been shown by him [in the following verse].
"At dawn, [the rice] should be given three times to the litigant facing east.

This means that the rice consecrated during the night should be given three times for consumption to the person undergoing purification. He also shows what must be performed by the one being purified, using the guise of a restatement:
"The one facing east, having fasted, having bathed, with a leaf placed upon his head..."
"Having eaten the rice grains, one should spit them out onto a leaf in three portions.

This means that everything from facing eastward until the act of spitting must be performed by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) and also by the person undergoing purification. Furthermore, the specific type of leaf is shown by that same author:
"It must be of *bhūrja* bark alone and not of anything else; however, in its absence, it may be of *pippala*."
And Bṛhaspati states that these morning duties, such as eating and so forth, must be performed during a solar eclipse:
"During a solar eclipse, one who is fasting and pure should eat rice grains.
Likewise, he has also shown the causes for purity and impurity.
"There shall be purification if [the semen] is spat out white; however, if it is mixed with blood, one incurs fault.
The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that one incurs fault not only when it is mixed with blood, but also under other circumstances. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says:
"He in whose [semen] blood is seen, and whose jaw and palate fail..."
And he whose body trembles should be declared impure.
Thus ends the procedure for the rice-ornament (*taṇḍulavidhi*) in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follows the procedure for the heated gold-piece (*taptamāṣavidhi*).
Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
I shall now describe the auspicious procedure for extracting the heated ball of gold (taptamāṣa).
One should have a vessel made of iron or copper sixteen finger-breadths in size.
"A mandala made of clay, dug four finger-breadths deep.

By "mandala" is meant circular or round. Having filled such a vessel with ghee and oil—or indeed with cow's ghee alone—and having established a worldly fire in a pure location, one should heat it therein. And so he says: "One should fill it with ghee and oil, specifically twenty *palas* of it."
Having taken cow's ghee, one who is pure should heat it over the fire.

Some here, relying on the use of the word "vā" (or), desire a combination (*samuccaya*) of ghee, oil, and cow-derived ghee; that is incorrect. For, just as in the case of rice and barley, an option (*vikalpa*) is understood solely by the force of the independent scriptural statement (*nirapekṣa-śruti*). Therefore, having placed twenty *palas* of either ghee and oil, or cow-derived ghee, into the vessel, one should heat it. While the heating is taking place in either of the two cases, one should perform the common procedure for all ordeals, beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head of the person undergoing the ordeal (*śodhya*). Beyond that, there is a difference in method between the two cases; regarding that, he [the author] states the distinction first in the case of heating ghee and oil:
Then, one should cast that gold māṣaka into the well-heated [liquid];
thereafter, one should extract the heated māṣaka using the thumb and finger.
"He whose fingertips do not tremble, nor does a blister arise, becomes pure through the Dharma, his fingers and limbs free from distortion. Thus it is said.

A *māṣaka* is a measure equal to one-sixteenth of a *karṣa*. The mention of "gold" here is for the purpose of excluding silver weighing two *kṛṣṇalas*, because that is difficult to perceive due to its smallness. Therefore, the meaning is that one should place a *māṣaka* of either gold or copper [into the liquid]. Regarding that [liquid], whether clarified butter or oil, the phrase "by the joining of the thumb and finger" means by the combination of the index, thumb, and middle fingers. Even in the case of heating cow's clarified butter, he (the author) states the specific rule regarding the procedure common to all ordeals:
"One should use a well-purified [vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, or iron."
One should cast into it a ring that has been washed once with water.
In that place rich with whirling ripples and waves, which is beyond the reach of the touch of a fingernail,
one should examine it with a moist leaf, making a "curu" sound accompanied by a resonance.
Then, one should consecrate that [clarified butter] once with this mantra:
"O clarified butter, you are the supreme purifier and nectar in sacrificial rites."
O Fire, burn more fiercely; become cold as snow during the summer heat.
Then, [the king] approached, having fasted, bathed, and being still wearing his wet clothes.
One should cause that seal to be placed within clarified butter;
then, experts shall examine its index finger.
"He whose eruptions do not appear is pure; otherwise, he is impure.
In this context, the extraction of the ring is performed with the index finger itself, because that finger is prescribed for the procedure of examination.
Thus ends the procedure for the *taptamāṣa* ordeal in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the *phāla* (ploughshare) ordeal; regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
An iron plowshare, weighing twelve palas and forged,
is described as being eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide.

Having placed such [hot] iron balls into divine vessels established in that manner, and having performed the common procedure for all ordeals—beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head of the person to be purified—one should cause it to be well-heated. Regarding what must be done once it is well-heated, he himself says:
"The thief shall lick that fire-colored [ball] once with his tongue;
if he is not burned, he shall go as pure, but otherwise he is defeated."
The mention of "theft" is for the purpose of indicating the person under investigation.
Thus ends the section on the rules for the Phālguna month in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the rule for the Dharmaja fire.
In that regard, the Grandfather said:
"Now I shall fully explain the examination of dharma and adharma.
One should have dharma made of silver, and adharma of lead or tin."
One should draw Dharma and Adharma, white and black respectively, either on birch bark or on cloth;
having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow, one should worship them with perfumes and garlands.
Dharma is represented by a white flower, while Adharma holds a black flower;
having prepared them in this manner and smeared them, one should place them within the two funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Two balls should be made from either cow dung or clay on all sides;
they should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel and remain unobserved.
In a purified and smeared place, in the presence of gods and Brahmins,
he should then invoke the gods and the guardians of the world as before.
First, having performed the invocation of the Dharma, one should write the written pledge:
"If I am free from sin, may the Dharma come into my hand."
Then the accused should immediately accept one [of the two vessels];
if he accepts the vessel containing dharma, he shall be purified, but if he accepts the one containing adharma, he is defeated.

"Thus has the examination of dharma and adharma been briefly explained. Regarding the phrase "made of lead and iron" (*sīsakāyasam*), they describe it as being fashioned from iron mixed with lead, or simply made of iron. "He should place those two within the two lumps" means he should position them inside the two lumps. The two lumps must be made of equal measure; having made them equal, they should be placed in a new pot, unobserved.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati: "If I am freed from sin, may Dharma come into my hand"—the person to be purified should utter this mantra, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra, namely the word "I. Everything else has its meaning evident.
Thus ends the procedure for determining the truth through divine means in the *Smṛticandrikā*; and the section on judicial proceedings (*kriyāpāda*) is also complete.
Now, regarding the ritual duties such as the final determination (nirṇaya), the author of the compendium states:
"The rite established according to one's own school of thought in the manner already described..."
Having investigated the matter, the king and the members of the court shall determine victory and defeat.
Whoever accomplishes the objective by means of any one of the aforementioned methods,
achieving a result equal to the words and syllables [of the opponent's claim], is proclaimed the victor.
"He who, having failed to prove his case, proves a contrary matter for himself,
is defeated, provided that a fault in the cause is perceived.
On this point, Vyāsa says:
The king should punish those who have been defeated, yet he should confer honors upon the victor;
even those who have not been defeated in debate should be punished if they oppose the Vedas and the Shastras.

And worship should be performed with perfumes, garlands, garments, and so forth, because it was stated by that very same [author]: "Worship proceeds for the Victor with perfumes, garlands, robes, and the like. After the commencement of worship, Kātyāyana says:
The king should first honorably join the plaintiff with his case,
and then give him a written document bearing his own signature.
Nārada also says: "Whatever property has been deposited in the middle, whether movable or immovable,
that shall later be made over with interest to the victor, together with the document."
A *patra* is a document of victory (*jayapatra*). And so Bṛhaspati says:
"When the king grants a written document to the victor, containing the evidence of the plaint and the reply and concluding with the decision, that is called a document of victory."

Whatever is to be stated regarding the document of victory has been explained entirely in the section on the rules for writing [the document]; that should be understood here as well. Regarding the rule, "He should be joined with the proven matter," Yājñavalkya states a specific exception in a certain case: "If he denies a written document and is proved on even one part, he must be made by the king to pay the entire debt; however, what was not previously declared [in court] shall not be accepted."

The meaning of this is as follows: when various items such as gold coins, clothing, and ornaments that were written down at the time of the plaint are denied by the defendant, who says, "This is false," and he is "partially proven"—that is, when he has been made to admit by the plaintiff through proof of even one part that "this is true"—then the king shall cause him to pay the entire claimed object to the claimant. However, what was not so written in the plaint, but is asserted later by the plaintiff, should not be accepted by the king as something for which payment must be made. This is what is being said. [283]

"A king should conduct legal proceedings by means of the truth, having cast aside deception (*chala*).
