It is argued that in such a case, the king should not heed [the defendant's plea], because his wicked intent is established therein. Nor should it be said that because he follows deception, the king should never heed even a confession of guilt. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"He who, having made a total denial, should later agree even to a small portion of the matter..."
But Bṛhaspati says that the person accused should be made to pay the entire amount.

The mention of Bṛhaspati is for the sake of showing respect. Nārada also states that what is owed by one who has been formally accused must be respected as a debt to be paid, in order to demonstrate that the entire claim must be satisfied: "When a person accused of multiple matters denies all of them, yet a single part is proven, he must pay what he was accused of."

[Objection: But surely, if the statements of the ancient authorities express the meaning previously stated [as being solely spiritual], they would not serve the purpose of determining legal procedure (*dharmanirṇaya*), because those statements, following the logic of equivocation (*chala*), declare the determination of worldly transactions (*vyavahāranirṇaya*). [Reply: True. Nevertheless, there is no fault, because in the matter previously discussed, the determination of legal procedure overrides the determination of spiritual duty (*dharmabādha*). For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "When a decision is made by relying solely on the [spiritual] scripture, that should be known as a worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); by that, even spiritual duty (*dharma*) is lost."
The meaning is: "in the case of the aforementioned [claims], such as those concerning ownership" (*viṣyādi*). As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
"Even when there is a lawsuit involving multiple matters, the creditor recovers from the witnesses only as much wealth as he can prove;
only that much proven wealth does he obtain."

Thus, this [rule] refers to cases where there is an absolute absence of firmness in the corrupt intention (*duṣṭāśayatva*). This is because, unlike in the earlier statements, there is no mention here of the opponent’s malice characterized by a total denial [of the claim]. Some say that this statement concerns debts owed to a father and others by a son and others, arguing that the three possible defenses—such as "I do not recognize that very thing"—are applicable therein. That is not correct; for even in a dispute over a debt incurred by oneself, the three defenses are possible through forgetfulness and the like. Furthermore, in a dispute over a debt incurred by a father and others, if a son or other heir says "this is false," he would be a defendant who denies the claim, yet it would follow that he must pay only what has been proven. If it is argued that the defense "this is false" is impossible for a son or other heir, do not say so; for it is possible for such a person, whether conscious or unconscious at the time of contracting the debt, to offer that defense based on the testimony of their mother or others. If you argue that when a son or other heir offers the defense "I do not recognize it," the rule regarding paying only what is proven applies, then let that rule be conceived as referring to the three defenses beginning with "I do not recognize it," rather than specifically to the case of a son or other heir. Or else, [if you maintain the latter view, consider the following:]...

If it is argued that, because of the legal tradition stating, "A debt must be paid by sons and grandsons when [the debtor] denies it and it is established by witnesses," this refers to the case of sons and others who have been declared [guilty],

and not to the case of sons and others who say, "I do not recognize [the debt]," since the tradition specifies, "when [the debtor] denies it and it is established by witnesses," then that argument is false.

Others, however, establish the matter differently: they claim that the statement regarding the recovery of all items refers to a case of denial accompanied by a defiant assertion, such as, "If the plaintiff fails to prove even one item among those claimed, then I shall pay all these items. They maintain that the statement regarding the recovery of only what has been proven refers to a case devoid of such defiance. This too is incorrect, because the remainder of the text states, "He does not deny even one written item," which implies the former case. Furthermore, it is not logical to assume that this sentence refers to a case of defiant denial in order to establish the example of *chala* (quibble), since the text explicitly mentions the conclusion of the legal proceeding by taking up the *chala* consisting of a total denial. The fact that the sentence serves as an example of *chala* is established by that alone. Moreover, since the recovery of everything in the aforementioned case occurs solely through the force of the initial plea (*bhāṣā*), the subsequent statement beginning with "denies" would be a mere restatement; thus, both statements would have the same meaning. Nor...

It is reasonable to maintain that this [interpretation] is adopted precisely to avoid the contradiction with the statement of Kātyāyana, "Even when multiple claims are brought forward, the creditor shall recover only as much as he can prove," and so forth; for that contradiction has been resolved by the direct path. Enough, then, of this extensive introduction and refutation of alternative views.
As for the method of compelling payment, it has been shown by Kātyāyana:
The king, however, should cause the Brahmin to pay the debt to the owner by means of conciliation alone;
but others who are wicked, he should cause to pay by afflicting them according to the customs of the country.
"Or even by means of trickery, one should cause the heir or a friend to pay.
Thus [it is said]. Nārada states that not only should the king cause the debt to be paid to the creditor, but he himself should also take a fine:
"But if a debtor who possesses wealth refuses to pay out of malice..."
The king should cause [the offender] to be made to pay, having taken a twentieth part as his share.

The meaning is that one should take from the debtor as much wealth as constitutes the twentieth part of the amount to be recovered. This also applies to the case of a debtor who acknowledges the debt. However, regarding a debtor who denies it, Viṣṇu says: "If the creditor approaches the king, the debtor, once proven, shall pay to the king a fine equal to a tenth part of the wealth; and the creditor, having obtained his due, shall pay a twentieth part. That the creditor pays this is by way of a fee for the service of recovering the payment, not by way of a fine, because he is without fault. But when the debtor approaches the king, then Manu says:
If one should report to the king that a creditor is recovering his debt by his own will,
he shall be made to pay to the king a fourth part of the debt, and the creditor's debt itself shall be paid by him.

If a debtor who is dear to the king, with the intention of having him imprisoned by the king’s command, should inform the king—of his own accord and will—that a creditor is attempting to recover the debt when the creditor has not yet proceeded to demand the lent money, thinking "he will harass me," then that [debtor] shall be made by the king to pay the debt along with a fine equal to one-fourth of that amount; this is the meaning. Furthermore, as for what was stated by him:
"He who denies a certain amount of wealth, or he who falsely obstructs it for a certain amount—both of them, being ignorant of dharma, shall be made by the king to pay double that amount" (MDh 8.59).

Thus, this refers to the case of a debtor who has become insolvent (*udvṛtta-adhamarṇa*) and a creditor; for it is stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that [verse] by Medhātithi: "because of the mention of one ignorant of *dharma*. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya—"If he denies [the debt], and is proven [guilty], he shall pay the money to the creditor and an equal amount to the king"—that is to be understood as applying to a case where an insolvent debtor lacks sufficient wealth to pay the aforementioned fine. Otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid contradicting the previously cited statements of Viṣṇu and Manu. Furthermore, for one who makes a false accusation, even if he lacks sufficient wealth, there is no fine equal to that [debt]. As he himself says:
"One who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim.

This means that from the "accusation"—that is, from the wealth claimed—he shall pay double the wealth to the king. However, in the absence of such wealth, one should understand that the secondary alternative (anukalpa) prescribed in [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.287], "He may discharge his debt through labor," and so forth, applies. As for what was stated by Nārada:
"One should not bring a false accusation; there is a fault for the one who makes a false accusation."
Whatever disciplinary rule has been proclaimed therein shall apply to the accuser.

Thus, this [rule] refers to cases where no specific punishment has been prescribed, because it is a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*). Therefore, it should be understood that the same punishment which Viṣṇu has declared for one of bad conduct who denies a claim applies to one of good conduct who makes a false accusation. Likewise:
"But when a litigant himself admits what was denied, that admission is to be known as his [confession], and half of the fine is ordained for him."
It should be understood that the penalty prescribed by Vyāsa applies equally to one who, having made a false accusation, admits its falsity of his own accord. Furthermore, as stated by Manu:
"But one who denies a claim when it has been proven by evidence, shall be compelled to pay the debt to the creditor and a small portion of the fine according to his capacity" (MDh 8.51).

Thus, it has been stated in the commentary on that [verse] (Medhātithi on MDh 8.52) that this refers to a debtor of good conduct who is unable to pay a fine equal to one-tenth of the amount. By using the phrase "on account of a reason," he shows that in a two-limbed lawsuit (*dvipādavyavahāra*), there is only the imposition of the payment of the debt, not the imposition of a fine, because in such cases there is an absence of denial or false accusation. In the same way, even in a four-limbed lawsuit (*catuṣpādavyavahāra*), the absence of a fine should be understood to apply when there is no false accusation or denial due to an accusation based on suspicion, ignorance, a rejoinder, and so forth. As for the other Smṛti text:
In the first case, however, there shall be a quarter of the punishment; in the second, half;
in the third, less by a quarter; and in the fourth case, he shall suffer the full punishment.

Thus, it has been explained at length by Viśvarūpācārya that such [a statement] is not authoritative because it is contradicted [by other sources]. Therefore, the punishment occasioned by denial and false accusation should be understood as applying only to the fourfold judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) where the grounds for the claim exist. In that regard, specific punishments have been shown concerning the judicial procedure regarding the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*). However, specific punishments for judicial procedures concerning deposits (*nikṣepa*) and so forth will be stated under their respective sections. Furthermore, as stated by Kātyāyana: "One who is pure should be made to pay half a hundred; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment."
Thus, that [rule] refers to a pure person whose innocence has been determined by means of divine ordeals; for he himself states immediately thereafter:
"In the case of poison, water, fire, the balance, the holy water-vessel, rice-grains, and the ordeal of the heated gold-piece, one shall prescribe punishment in due order."

"One thousand, six hundred, five hundred, and likewise four, three, two, and one; one should thus prescribe a reduction among those who are lesser. This fine based on divine ordeal is to be combined with either the fine for denial or the fine for a false accusation, because of the conjunction of the causes. However, the *paṇa* is to be combined with the fine prescribed in the scriptures; so says Yājñavalkya.
If a dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay the fine,
his own stake, and the money to the creditor.
Nārada also says: "In a dispute involving a counter-stake, whichever of the two parties loses, he shall be made to pay the stake he himself undertook, as well as a fine for his defeat. [289]
On this point, Kātyāyana states:
"Thus, seated upon the seat of justice and remaining impartial toward both litigants, the adjudication of cases should be observed by him together with Brāhmaṇas, and not otherwise."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"The king must diligently investigate matters that are doubtful;
in doing so, three parties are benefited, while the loss falls upon one."

"The victor obtains wealth and honor; the defeated receives discipline and restraint. The king, the giver, the self-controlled, and the members of the assembly shall all obtain merit. Thus [says Manu]. Nārada also says:
Seeing thus at all times, the king, composed in mind while conducting legal affairs,
spreads his radiant glory here and attains the same world as Śakra.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"A king who thus carries out the administration of justice as ordained by the scriptures,
having spread his fame throughout the world, shall become a counselor to Mahendra."
"By resolving legal cases through witnesses, written documents, and inference,
a king who spreads his fame in this world attains the realm of the Sun.
Thus says Manu as well.
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives his purpose through righteousness,
the subjects follow him just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
"But that lord of men who, out of delusion, should perform his duties unrighteously—
his enemies will soon bring that evil-souled man under their control.
Thus ends the section on the determination of duties and so forth in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some other statements concerning punishment are also written here;
regarding this, Nārada says:
"Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporeal and monetary."
Physical punishment, such as beating and so forth, is declared to extend up to the point of death.
"But the monetary fine begins with a *kākaṇī* and likewise ends with one's entire property.
Regarding this, he [the author] states that while the varieties of corporal punishment can be enumerated, the same cannot be said for the varieties of monetary fines:
"Corporal punishment is declared to be tenfold, whereas monetary punishment is manifold."

The phrase "tenfold" (*daśadhā*) is not intended to establish a fixed numerical limit, because various types of corporal punishment will be described hereafter. For instance, Manu has shown that corporal punishment is ninefold:
"Manu, the son of the Self-existent, declared ten locations for punishment:
the genitals, the stomach, the tongue, the two hands, and the feet as the fifth."
"The eyes, the nose, the two ears, as well as wealth and the body. Thus it is said.

The *upastha* (genital organ) is the organ of men and women; its restraint consists in abstaining from approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyā*). In the case of theft, however, it is the restraint of the stomach by means of abstaining from food and so forth. In verbal abuse, it is the tongue. In physical assault, it is the hands. In cases such as kicking with the feet, it is the feet. In cases such as looking at what should be concealed, it is the eyes. In cases such as smelling the scent or applying ointments to the breasts of another's wife, it is the nose. In cases such as overhearing the king’s secret counsel, it is the ears. In cases such as giving bribes, it is the restraint of wealth by means of obstructing expenditures and so forth. In cases such as the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), it is the body. Furthermore, this restraint of the *upastha* and other organs is to be applied in cases where no specific punishment for the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras has been explicitly mentioned regarding acts such as approaching those who should not be approached or theft.
"Those [punishments] should apply to the three castes; an unharmed Brāhmaṇa may depart. (MDh 8.124).

Because this is stated generally regarding Kṣatriyas and the others, the meaning is that an "unharmed Brāhmaṇa" is one who has not been punished in the aforementioned places of punishment. By using the word "may depart," he shows that the exemption from punishment in those ten places applies only to one who, having been banished, goes to another country, and not to every Brāhmaṇa indiscriminately. For this very reason, he has also stated as a supplementary rule to the ordinance of banishment:
"One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is situated in the midst of all possible crimes."
"He should banish him from the kingdom, with all his property and unhurt.
But for one who is not to be banished, the punishment is exactly as it is for a Kṣatriya and the others. And thus says that same [author]: "For all four castes who do not perform penance..."
He shall prescribe lawful corporal punishment accompanied by a fine.

As for what was stated by Gautama—"There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa"—that is intended as a prohibition against forms of execution consisting of the breaking of limbs, and not even against forms of restraint consisting of the suppression of limbs. For were that the case, it would contradict the previously cited statements. It is for this very reason that Bṛhaspati has specified:
"Even one endowed with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) does not deserve death for being a Brāhmaṇa. Hārīta also says the same.
"But the wise do not speak of a division of limbs for a Brahmin," so it is said.

Thus, it should be understood that for a Brāhmaṇa, corporal punishment consists solely of the mutilation of a limb and not of execution or similar penalties. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "In these cases, however, for a Brāhmaṇa there shall be the blinding of the eyes. "Blinding" means that the eyes should be affected by means of binding or other such methods, but not by the extraction of the eyeballs, because the breaking of limbs is prohibited. As for what Śaṅkha stated—"For all three castes, there may be the seizure of property, execution, and imprisonment; for a Brāhmaṇa, there shall be exile and branding"—that refers to a Brāhmaṇa who is indigent. Accordingly, Gautama, speaking with reference to a Brāhmaṇa, says: "Exclusion from duties, public proclamation of the crime, exile, and branding [are the punishments] when he has no means of livelihood. "When he has no means of livelihood" means when he is destitute. This refers to the category of the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). However, regarding the denial of debts and similar matters, Manu says:
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who is unable to pay a fine shall attain freedom from debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa shall attain it gradually, step by step.

But regarding the inability to perform labor, Kātyāyana says: "Having ascertained that [the debtor] is unable to pay the debt, one may compel him to perform work under one's own control; if he is incapable even of that, he should be cast into prison, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa."
Manu also says:
"The king shall inflict punishment upon women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, the helpless, and the sick by means of whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like. [293]

Thus, five types of corporal punishment (*śārīradaṇḍa*) are to be understood as consisting of: binding, branding, forced labor, imprisonment, and flogging. Therefore, the statement that “corporal punishment is tenfold” should be regarded as being for the purpose of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), not for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Furthermore, the statement that “punishment is traditionally held to be twofold” is likewise merely illustrative, since other varieties are also recorded in the legal tradition (*smṛti*). For instance: “Punishment of the head is shaving; his banishment from the city; branding the forehead with the mark of his crime; and being made to travel on a donkey.”

The meaning is "of that Brahmin," because the Brahmin is the subject under discussion. Furthermore, Yājñavalkya states that shaving the head is the punishment in place of execution: "For a Brahmin, execution consists of shaving the head, banishment from the city, as well as branding the mark of his crime on the forehead, and being made to travel on a donkey."

And thus, in the case of a Kṣatriya and others, there is indeed death and not tonsure; for in that regard, [tonsure] is not recorded as a substitute. For this very reason, Manu says: "Tonsure is prescribed as the penultimate punishment for a Brāhmaṇa, but for the other castes, the punishment may be one ending in death."

The word "highest fine" (uttamasāhasa) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. And so says Nārada: "Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, and the amputation of that limb—this is declared to be the punishment for the highest fine."

"This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction, except for the execution of a Brāhmaṇa; a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death. In this context, the phrase "except for execution" is intended to include even the amputation of limbs.
But the wise do not speak of a distinction in limbs for a Brahmin;
rather, a Brahmin is always honored through austerity and sacrifice.
Thus it is from the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Hārīta. Manu, however, states the reason for abandoning the punishment of death:
"There is no sin greater than the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, nor does any unrighteousness exist anywhere;
therefore, the king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind."
Therefore, Bṛhaspati declares that even a Brahmin who is guilty of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) is not to be executed:
"Even one joined with a mortal sin, a Brahmin does not deserve death.
When it is asked what he does deserve instead, it was stated immediately thereafter by that same author:

"The king shall cause him to be branded with the mark of expulsion and shaved," so it is said. Here, "expulsion" refers to [banishment] from the country, not merely from the city. Regarding this, Bodhāyana states: "Having branded the forehead with heated iron, there is expulsion from the realm. The word "shall do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. As for the specific marks for branding, Nārada has shown them:
"In the case of violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; in the case of drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag."
For theft, however, the mark of a dog's foot should be made; for killing a Brahmin, the mark of a headless man.
This branding, moreover, should not be performed on Kṣatriyas and others. As Uśanas says:
"In the case of the four offenses of a Brahmin, branding is prescribed."
In the case of violating the teacher's bed, drinking liquor, theft, or harming a Brāhmaṇa.
"But for the other castes, one should not perform branding there.
[295] When it is asked, "What then is the punishment in that case?", Bṛhaspati says: "And those who are guilty of great offenses, one should punish with the death penalty."
But when great offenders cannot be restrained even by the punishment of death, then Manu said:
"But when one is unable to restrain these [offenders] even by execution,
then one should employ all four of these [measures] against them."
When it is asked what those four are, Yājñavalkya says:
"The punishment of speech, the punishment of reproach, the punishment of wealth, and likewise the punishment of death;
these should be applied either collectively or individually according to the nature of the offense."

The punishment of speech (*vāgdaṇḍa*) consists of harsh words and curses. The punishment of reproach (*dhigdaṇḍa*) is the censure "fie! Manu states the sequence for the application of all these: "One should first employ the punishment of speech, immediately after that the punishment of reproach, thirdly the punishment of fines, and after that the punishment of corporal chastisement."

Bṛhaspati has stated the arrangement for the application of these punishments when they are used individually: "For a minor offense, there shall be the punishment of speech; for the first degree of violence, the punishment of reproach;
for the middle degree, the punishment of fines; and for acts of treason against the king, imprisonment."
"Exile or even execution should be carried out by one who desires his own welfare,
against a single perpetrator of a great sin, whether [the offenses] are committed individually or collectively.
Thus, the legal determination has also been shown by that same author with respect to the person.
One should employ verbal punishment against friends and others, saying, "Shame on you, you wretched ones!
But other men who are litigious and guilty should be punished with a fine.
By the use of the word "etcetera," respectable persons are included;
one should punish teachers, domestic priests, and those worthy of honor with the punishment of speech alone.
Other litigants, however, one should punish with reproach, fines, and physical force.

For it has been stated by that very [author]: "Furthermore, Śaṅkha has said: 'The mother and father, the *snātaka* and the domestic priest, wandering mendicants and forest-dwellers, and those who possess [exemplary] birth, conduct, Vedic learning, character, purity, and behavior—these are not to be punished. And also by Kātyāyana:
'In the case of offenses committed against the teacher, the father, the mother, and likewise kinsmen—for these, no punishment whatsoever is ordained.'"

Thus, this is for the purpose of prohibiting corporal punishment and fines, but not punishment in general. As Manu says: "Father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, or domestic priest—none of these are exempt from punishment by the king when they have deviated from their own duty."
Bṛhaspati also says: "Priests, domestic chaplains, ministers, sons, kinsmen, and relatives who have deviated from dharma should be punished; those who injure the king should be banished."

As for that which was stated by Gautama: "One who is exempt from the six [penalties] is not to be killed by the king, nor bound, nor fined, nor banished, nor censured, nor excluded"—this refers to the person described as follows: "He is one of great learning (*bahuśruta*); he knows the *Loka*, the *Veda*, and the *Vedāṅgas*; he is skilled in *Vākovākya*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*; he relies on those [scriptures], lives according to them; he is consecrated by the forty sacraments (*saṃskāras*); he is devoted to the three [or six] duties; and he is well-trained in the conventional rules of conduct. Thus, this concerns the subject of one who is "greatly learned," and therefore there is no contradiction with the earlier statement. Kātyāyana also mentions one who is not to be punished.
But where an improper act has been committed during a life-threatening emergency, there shall be no punishment at all; this is the righteous law remembered by Bhṛgu.
Nārada, however, states that the punishment shall be half of that prescribed: "But for one who, having committed an improper act of violence, seeks reconciliation,
or who confesses it himself in the assembly, half of the fine is ordained."
Vyāsa also says:
"If one who is afflicted by disease, or anyone else who is suffering,
should say, 'I shall not do this again,' the fine for him is half."

Regarding this, Gautama states another view: "Or there may be acquittal by the declaration of those who know the Veda and the established legal conventions. Acquittal (*anujñāna*) means releasing [the offender] without imposing a fine. Likewise, he says that one should impose upon the offender a punishment greater or less than that prescribed, provided it is capable of causing pain: "They say that punishment is for the sake of subduing; therefore, one should subdue the unsubdued. The meaning is that one should inflict such a degree of pain as will bring about the cessation of the criminal tendency. And so Manu says: "Having fully understood the motive, as well as the place and time in their true nature..."
Having considered both the essential nature of the offense and the degree of transgression, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength, as well as the age,
the occupation, and the wealth, one should inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment."
Regarding this, Manu states the following example:
"If an ordinary person should be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*, the fine for the king in that case shall be one thousand; such is the established rule."

The commoner is poor; the king is established in sovereignty; and so too is Kātyāyana. "By whatever fault a punishment for a Śūdra is prescribed according to dharma, that same fault, if committed by a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, shall be doubled, doubled."
A Śūdra who has entered the life of a renunciant and is devoted to the recitation of prayers and burnt offerings,
if he commits a sin, should be punished with death or else fined double the usual amount.
Bṛhaspati also says:
A man deserving of death shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
one deserving of the amputation of a limb shall pay half of that, and one deserving of the *saṃdaṃśa* punishment shall pay half of that again.
Beating, binding, and likewise humiliating—
this indeed is the punishment for a slave, but not a monetary fine, says Bṛhaspati.
Nārada also says:
"The punishment beginning with a *kākaṇī* is traditionally held to culminate in a *māṣa*;
that which is declared to begin with half a *māṣa* culminates in a *kārṣāpaṇa*."
One [fine] begins with a minimum of one *kārṣāpaṇa* and increases by four *kārṣāpaṇas*;
another begins with a minimum of two and increases up to eight; and yet another begins with a minimum of three and increases up to twelve.

[299] "But all those *kārṣāpaṇas* which have been mentioned shall each be fourfold. Thus the meanings of the words *kākaṇī* and so forth have been shown in the section on ordeals (*divya*). On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"Whatever punishment has been specifically prescribed for a particular offense..."
There should be the seizure of the coins, or else their value [should be paid] to the king.
Where a punishment is being applied, it may consist of one *māṣa* or two *māṣas* per foot;
however, where no specific amount is prescribed, it should be understood that a *māṣaka* is to be calculated.

"Where a fine is stated in *māṣakas*, one should specify there [the weight] in silver; and where it is stated in *kṛṣṇalas*, that indeed shall be the determination of the stated fine. This means [fines stated in] *paṇas* or *kārṣāpaṇas*. Two hundred and fifty paṇas is declared the first amercement;
five hundred is to be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest.
This definition is to be applied in the case of a first offense. However, regarding repeated offenses, Yājñavalkya says:
"A fine of one thousand and eighty *paṇas* is the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*);
half of that is declared the middle amercement (*madhyama*), and half of that is remembered as the lowest amercement (*adhama*). [300]

Therefore, wherever a punishment is declared by such terms as "the highest amercement" (*uttamasāhasa*) and so forth, there these specific numbers of *kārṣāpaṇas* or their equivalent value in *niṣkas* and the like must be understood. He himself states that a punishment administered in the manner described is the cause of joy for all the world: "When applied according to the scriptures, it brings joy to the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, it would provoke its wrath."
Thus, he [the same author] speaks of the censure of punishment contrary to the śāstras and the praise of that which is correct:
"Unrighteous punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world;
but righteous punishment brings a king heaven, fame, and victory."

Nārada says that those who are punished with such punishment become cleansed of their sins: "But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds."
Kātyāyana also says:
"Purification has been declared by those who know the true principles of the scriptures to be medical treatment;
it is traditionally held to be of two kinds: expiation (prāyaścitta) and punishment (daṇḍa)."
Thus ends the section on punishments in the Smṛticandrikā; now follows the legal procedure (*nyāya*),
regarding which Nārada says:
A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, within the house, or with enemies—
even if already completed— must be performed again.

The meaning is that a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) determined in secret by women or by enemies must be reconsidered, because ignorance or partiality may have occurred. Likewise, a decision reached through force or under the influence of passion, hatred, and other such conditions should be overturned and a new legal proceeding initiated. And so says Yājñavalkya: "[301] One should set aside legal proceedings concluded through force or fraud. The intention is that thereafter one should initiate another legal proceeding. Furthermore, he states that the same should be done even in the case of a deficiency on the part of the litigants.
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, distressed by calamity, a child, or terrified,
as well as one that has been conducted without doubt [of its validity], is not upheld.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), transactions such as those involving interest and the like are included. For this very reason, Manu states: "A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, or under the control of others; or by a child, or by an elderly person;
or one entered into by someone unrelated [to the parties]—such a transaction is not valid."
"Unconnected" means devoid of a relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant. Nārada also says:
"A lawsuit that is opposed to the city or the kingdom, and one which has been rejected by the king, is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible."
Hārīta also says:
"But he who is shunned by the king, or who himself causes opposition among the citizens,
or likewise among the entire kingdom and its subjects..."
Furthermore, those which were previously contested by many people in a city or village, and all those that are inadmissible— these are declared to be invalid legal proceedings.

The intended meaning to be understood is that even when a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) has been thus decided (*tīrita*) or adjudicated (*anuśiṣṭa*), one must desist from it and another legal proceeding must be undertaken. Kātyāyana states the distinction between what is decided (*tīrita*) and what is adjudicated (*anuśiṣṭa*):

[302] "That matter which is determined by the members of the court (*sabhyas*) themselves as being 'unreal' or 'real' is called *tīrita*; however, that which is declared on the basis of the testimony of witnesses is proclaimed as *anuśiṣṭa*."
The meaning is that he has been adjudicated, having been determined by the testimony of witnesses. Furthermore, as stated by Manu:
"Whatever may have been decided or adjudicated anywhere, one should know that to be settled according to dharma; one should not reverse it again."

Thus, it should be understood that this is merely a general rule (*utsarga*) concerning the absence of grounds for overturning [a decision] based on such factors as being committed by a woman. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states an exception (*apavāda*) to it: "Even when a matter has been determined by the family and others, if the king does not remain satisfied, he should investigate what was done and rectify any wrongful act."

The meaning is that even when a case has been decided by judges appointed for the purpose, if the litigant considers the conclusion of the legal proceeding to have been unjust, then the matter must be retried. Once it is established that a decision was wrongly made, Nārada states the punishment for those who judged the prior trial:
"In a wrongly decided lawsuit, the members of the court shall incur punishment;
for indeed, no one ever remains on the path of justice without the threat of punishment."

And this punishment applies only to the members of the court when the victor did not instigate the *durdarśana* (the wrongful judgment); it should be understood that if he was the instigator, then he too is subject to punishment there. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"Having deliberated together with many Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the scriptures, one should first punish the culpable members of the court along with the victor."

Yājñavalkya states that even the punishment of the victor must be carried out according to the very procedure prescribed in the section on the punishment of court members: "But having reviewed cases that were wrongly decided, the king shall punish the court members along with the victor with a fine double the amount of the dispute."

The meaning is: "due to the fault of both the winner and the members of the court. However, when the defect of the legal proceeding arises from the fault of the witnesses, then the witnesses alone are to be punished according to the rules stated in the section on the punishment of witnesses; neither the winner nor the members of the court are to be punished. On the other hand, when the fault lies with both the winner and the witnesses, then they alone are to be punished, not the members of the court—this is the intended meaning. Thus, a retrial (punar-nyāya) should be conducted only when there is mere dissatisfaction, provided that the original decision was a semblance of justice (*nyāyābhāsa*). Nārada states that if the case has been properly adjudicated and the judgment delivered, yet one considers it to have been done contrary to the law: *tīritaṃ cānuśiṣṭaṃ ca yo manyeta vidharmataḥ |* [He who thinks that what has been decided and adjudicated was done unjustly...]
Having imposed a double fine, he should restore that property once again.

The meaning is that one who disputes on the grounds of *vidharmitā*—that is, on the grounds of contradiction with the *dharmaśāstra*—is one who, despite a correct decision having been reached, still maintains his position out of arrogance. Since a reversal of the conclusion of a legal proceeding is otherwise impossible, Yājñavalkya states that even after a subsequent trial, one who was previously defeated in a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya-parājita*) shall be punished with the same fine he had already accepted: "He who, though defeated according to justice, thinks 'I am not defeated'—having defeated him again when he returns, the king shall cause him to pay double the fine."

Thus, a retrial (*punar-nyāya*) involving punishment must take place specifically in a higher court (*uttara-sabhā*) presided over by the king, because the authority to inflict punishment belongs to the king alone. However, in a higher court that is devoid of the king, a retrial must be conducted without punishment, since the portion pertaining to punishment is the exclusive duty of the king. Furthermore, the higher court must be superior to the previous court; otherwise, doubt would not be removed. The relative superiority among the members of the court has been demonstrated in the section concerning the determination of judges. If there is a suspicion that a case seen in the king’s court was wrongly decided, a retrial should take place in the court of another eminent king; and so it is stated in another Smṛti text.
Whatever has been done by another king that is devoid of justice and performed through ignorance— even that which was established unjustly— he should bring back into accordance with justice.
Furthermore, as it has been stated by the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati):
"One seen in a village may go to the city; one seen in the city may go before the king;
but once seen by the king—whether rightly or wrongly—the case is not reopened."

Thus, that [rule] refers to a case where one has obtained another court superior to the previous one. However, even if a superior court exists, there is no retrial for one who has been defeated by his own statement; so says Nārada:
"There is a retrial upon the exposure of defects in witnesses or assessors;
but for those defeated by their own words, no rule for a second trial is declared."

The meaning is that there shall be a renewed examination of the lawsuit for those who have been defeated by a verdict based on the testimony of witnesses or by a decision rendered by the members of the court (*sabhyas*), provided that the previous decision is found to be flawed. The mention of the *sabhyas* is intended to include the ministers (*amātyas*) and others as well. For this very reason, Manu states: "If a minister or a judge should decide a case improperly, the king himself should decide it and fine him one thousand [paṇas]."
Thus concludes the section on "Re-examination" in the *Smṛticandrikā* [305].
Now begins the section on "Rescission of what has been Done."
In this regard, Manu says:
"A fraudulent mortgage or sale, a fraudulent gift or acceptance—
whenever one perceives fraud, he shall annul all such transactions."

*Yoga* is a connection, such as being in one's possession through borrowing and so forth, even in the absence of a cause that would make another’s property one’s own. *Adhamana* is the act of pledging; thus, "pledging by means of *yoga*" (*yogādhamana*). The analysis of compounds is similar for "sold by means of *yoga*" (*yogavikrīta*) and other such cases. Manu also says: "That which is given by force, enjoyed by force, and whatever is caused to be written by force—Manu has declared all transactions performed by force to be void."
Kātyāyana also says: "Whatever has been given or whatever has been done by one who is insane, intoxicated, or likewise in another state of mind— that shall have no legal validity."
Nārada also says: "Whatever act a child performs, or likewise one who is not independent,
those learned in the scriptures declare that it is as good as not done."
By that [definition], both the *bāla* (child) and the *asvatantra* (dependent) are defined.

One should know that the infant (*śiśu*) is similar to those still in the womb up until the eighth year; from the eighth year until the sixteenth year, one is called a *bāla*, and from then on, one is termed *paugaṇḍa*.
"One who knows legal procedure from others is independent when without a father.

By this, it is implied that one who has a father is not independent. And it has been stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "Those who have a father are not independent. The mention of the "father" is intended to indicate the mother as well; for this very reason, Nārada says:
"One shall not be independent while both parents are alive, even if he is advanced in age."
The phrase "while the mother and father live" is to be understood as the remainder [of the context];
even between those two, the father is superior because the primacy of the seed is observed. In his absence, the mother; and in her absence, the elder brother.

Because this was stated by that very same author immediately thereafter, it is implied by this that even one who has an elder brother is not independent. He [the same author] states that it is not only those who have elders on the father’s or mother’s side who are dependent: "Women, sons, slaves, and those who are dependents are not independent. "Dependents" (parigraha) refers to those who live off others. Hārīta states that women lack independence in specific matters: [The text continues: "In the performance of religious rites, in the management of property, and in the administration of punishment, women are not independent. In matters concerning the household, in the preparation of food, and in the care of the family, they are dependent upon the men. Thus, he says: "In matters concerning the household, in the preparation of food, and in the care of the family, they are dependent upon the men. Furthermore, Manu says: "A woman does not incur sin by acting according to her own will in these matters: in the husband's family during her youth, in her own family when widowed, and while remaining under the protection of her sons in old age. And again: "She must never act independently in any matter; she should remain subject to the will of her father, husband, or son. And Yājñavalkya says: "Women are not independent in any matter whatsoever. Therefore, it is established that women are dependent in all matters, except for those specifically mentioned where they possess authority. Thus, the meaning is that they are dependent in all other respects. Furthermore, Manu says: "The father protects [her] in childhood, the husband protects [her] in youth, and the sons protect [her] in old age; a woman is never fit for independence. And again: "The father incurs blame by neglecting [her] before marriage; the husband by neglecting [her] while she is with him; and the sons by neglecting [her] when she has passed away.
