Whether for the sake of giving, or for the sake of wealth, or especially for the sake of dharma;
whether in taking or in spending, a woman does not deserve independence.
Nārada speaks of others who are also not independent:
"All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent.
The pupil is declared to be dependent, while independence resides in the teacher."

In this context, it is shown that an independent determination and an action performed by one who is not independent must be set aside by that very person [who has authority]. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "The master shall annul an act performed by one who is not independent;
no one else may dispute it, except in cases involving what was done out of fear or by one who is insane."

The intention is that since the authority to rescind transactions entered into by those who are frightened, insane, and so forth, rests solely with the king, it is not entirely improper for a great dispute to arise between one who has rescinded such a transaction and the owner of the person who was frightened, insane, etc. Regarding this, Nārada states an exception in some cases to a rescission made by one who is not independent: "These very [transactions] are valid if the master approves;
or, in the absence of the husband, the son [may rescind]; or the wife [may rescind] in the absence of both husband and son."
Likewise, a deed performed by a slave is declared to be as if not done, except by the master’s command;
for a slave has no authority over himself.

"And that which has been done by a son against the will of the father is said to be as if not done at all; a slave and a son are equal in this regard. The meaning is that the annulment of what was done by one who is not independent must be carried out in cases where there is an absence of consent from the independent party. Kātyāyana also says:
The gifting, mortgaging, or selling of fields, houses, or slaves does not achieve validity if performed by one who is not independent; such acts are not recognized as valid.
He himself states that those who have been described [as experts] attain authority:
"All of these are authorities in the buying and selling of commodities,
provided they are approved even as they carry out their transactions."

Thus, he [the author] says that even those who are not independent— such as brothers and others— may be authoritative when appointed by an independent person to perform transactions such as the purchase of fields and so forth:
"In the same way, a brother, a brother’s son, or a son may be [authoritative] regarding fields and other property,
provided they have been authorized for the performance of the transaction by a departing superior."
"Entrusted" (nisṛṣṭa) means "appointed. And so Bṛhaspati says:

"He who is appointed by his master over the protection of income and expenditure, as well as in lending at interest, agriculture, and trade, is known as one to whom the matter has been entrusted (nisṛṣṭārtha)."

"Whatever has been done by him [the agent] is authoritative, including all gain, loss, expenditure, and income, whether in his own country or abroad; the master shall not contradict that. Thus Kātyāyana also stated that the master is not entitled to reverse a transaction performed by one who has been fully authorized.
But he who has been authorized with full power regarding a particular matter is indeed the master in that matter;
his employer cannot undo the business transacted by him.

Thus, even in the absence of consent or formal authorization, Manu states that a dependent person who has acted for the sake of maintaining the family may not have his act altered by an independent person, provided it was done for the purpose of supporting the household: "Whether in his own country or abroad, even one who is dependent may conduct legal business for the sake of the family; one should not set aside such an act on account of its nature."

The same should be understood regarding matters intended for the remediation of calamities. And so says Nārada: "They declare that transactions entered into by women are invalid when not in a state of distress. The mention of "women" is intended to indicate those who lack independence. Thus, the implied meaning to be understood is that even transactions entered into by those lacking independence are valid when in a state of distress. To demonstrate an exception to this rule, he [Nārada] himself says:
"Especially [forbidden are] the gift, mortgage, or sale of a house or field.

This means that the gift, mortgage, or sale of a house or field, even if made during a time of distress, is not valid if performed by one who lacks independence. Thus it is explained in its commentary. Likewise, Nārada states that a transaction performed even by an independent person is not valid if he acts in a manner equivalent to one lacking independence:
"For even an independent person, if he has fallen from his natural state, whatever transaction he may perform..."
They say that even this is uncreated, due to the reason of its independence.
And by that very [authority], independent [persons] have been defined:
"In this world, there are three who are independent— the king, the teacher,
and likewise the householder in his own home for each and every member of the social classes."
"But independence is declared for the eldest; seniority is determined by qualities and age.

By using the word *gṛhī* (the householder), he shows that the wife has no independence. Therefore, although the lack of independence of one who is under her mother's authority (*mātṛmataḥ*) has been stated, nevertheless, the mother’s own independence must be understood. For this very reason, it is stated that an act performed by a woman whose husband is deceased is accomplished only through the consent of her son and others. The meaning of the phrase "having returned to her natural state" (*prakṛtiṃ gataḥ*) is also shown by that same [text]:
"Those overcome by lust or anger, those afflicted by distress, and those tormented by fear or calamity..."
And those who are overwhelmed by passion and hatred should be known as having fallen into a state contrary to their true nature.

And thus, an action performed by one who is independent and established in his natural state is valid, but not one performed by one who is not established in his natural state or is dependent; as that same [author] says:
"In a family, he who is the eldest, the most excellent, and established in his natural state—what is done by him is truly done; an act performed by one who is not independent is never [valid]."
Even an act such as the sale of a son, though performed by one who is independent and acting in his natural capacity, is not valid; for in that matter, he lacks independence. Thus Kātyāyana says:
"A father has authority over his son and wife in matters of instruction;
however, he has no authority over his son in matters of sale or gift. [310]

Therefore, the intention is that even an act such as the sale of a son, though performed by one who is independent and of sound mind, must be annulled. We shall explain in the section titled *Dattāpradānika* (Non-delivery of Gifts) that this refers specifically to the case of an only son. Likewise, in cases such as a sale where multiple transactions have been made by the same agent for the same object, a subsequent sale and so forth is not valid due to the absence of ownership; thus Yājñavalkya says: "In all disputes concerning property, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a prior gift or purchase, the former is stronger."
The intention is that, for this reason, the subsequent ritual action must be brought to an end.
Thus ends the section on the reversal of what has been done in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some statements concerning the property of minors and others are recorded;
therein, Manu says:
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor heir until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed beyond childhood.

"An inheritance with a minor heir" refers to property whose owner is a minor; this concerns cases where no trustworthy person is available. To clarify that the mention of a "minor" is intended to indicate anyone incapable of protecting their own wealth, that same author [Yājñavalkya] says: "The same rule shall apply to women who are barren, those without sons, those whose families have perished, to women devoted to their husbands, widows, and those who are afflicted by illness."

A *vaśā* is a barren woman; an *aputrā* is one who has no son; a *niṣkulā* is one deprived of her own kin. He himself states the punishment for those who seize the property of such women as the *vaśā*: "But if their own kinsmen should seize that property while they are still living, the righteous lord of the earth shall punish them with the penalty for theft."

Gautama states that even if a person is capable of protecting property, if the owner has not taken possession of it due to ignorance of its location or other reasons, but another person takes possession of it and reports it to the king, who then makes it public among the masses, the king must protect it: "Having found property that has been lost and is without an owner, they should report it to the king; after making it public for one year, it shall be protected by the king. As for what was stated by Manu:
"The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in deposit for three years."

Thus, that [period] refers to the possibility of the owner being located in an extremely distant place. Furthermore, the king must carry out the depositing [of lost property] in a manner that does not mix it with his own wealth; and so says that very same [author]: "Lost property that has been found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials.
Any thieves who should seize it there, the king shall have them executed by an elephant."

"Lost and found" (*praṇaṣṭādhigatam*) refers to property that has been lost by its owner and subsequently recovered by another. Regarding the restitution of such lost and found property, Yājñavalkya states:
"The king shall restore to the owner the wealth that was lost and found.
Thus, the owner should take possession of that wealth after establishing his ownership. And so says Manu:
He who says, "This is mine," shall be questioned according to the rule;
after verifying the form, number, and other details, the owner deserves that property.

The meaning is this: if someone should say, "This is mine," he may be entitled to take that property provided that—when questioned by the king's officers for the sake of verifying his ownership—he describes the lost item exactly as it was in terms of its location, time, color, shape, number, and size. However, the intention is that if there is a discrepancy, he is not entitled to take it because he lacks ownership; on the contrary, since he has engaged in the misappropriation of another's property, he deserves punishment. Thus says that very same [author]:
One who reports the place and time of the lost object according to the facts,
as well as its color, form, and size, deserves a fine equal to that [value].

In reality, one who does not recognize [the object] and thus acts in contradiction [to the truth] is treated as if it were "lost and then found. Yājñavalkya states that what has been lost and then found may be reclaimed by the owner only within one year:
"If an article that was lost or stolen has been recovered by customs officials or local guardians, the owner may take it back before a year has passed; after that, the king shall take it."
Regarding the case of a master residing in an extremely distant land, Manu says:
"The owner may recover [the property] within three years; beyond that, the king shall take it.
Now, one might object that the statement "the king shall take it" contradicts the scriptural injunctions prohibiting the seizure of another's property.

True; for this very reason, since its place of deposit was separate, the meaning should be understood as follows: the king shall take his own share from the place where the wealth is located. Thus, even if the owner arrives after the time limit has expired, the lost-and-found property must indeed be returned to him once it has been identified by its appearance, number, and so forth. However, the king may take a certain portion of that property as a penalty for the offense of exceeding the time limit. And so says that same [author]: "Then the king, remembering the duty of the virtuous, may take a sixth part, a tenth, or even a twelfth part from the lost-and-found property."

The word *atha* (then) expresses the immediate sequence following the arrival of the owner after the stipulated time limit has passed. It should be understood that the established rule is as follows: if the arrival is extremely delayed, the sixth part [of the property] belongs [to the king]; if it is very delayed, the tenth part; but if there is no delay, the twelfth part. As for what was stated by Gautama—"After the lapse [of the time], the fourth part belongs to the finder, and the remainder to the king"—that should be understood to apply to a case where the death of the owner who has exceeded the time limit is certain. From this very statement, it is understood that while the owner is still alive, the finder receives a fourth part as the king's share. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:

"One should give one *paṇa* for a single-hoofed animal, four or five for a human, eight for a buffalo, two each for cows, and a quarter *paṇa* each for goats and sheep. Regarding this, some commentators have stated that this specific rule concerning single-hoofed animals and others sets aside the injunction for taking a sixth part and so forth as prescribed by Manu. Others, however, have said that the word "that" (*tat*) was used to specify what should be given to the finder in the case of single-hoofed animals and the like. With reference to the seizure of lost property, found treasure, and stolen goods, Manu states the following distinction:
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king shall take a sixth part, or indeed a twelfth part, from him.
"But one who speaks falsely shall be fined one-eighth part of the wealth," so it is said.

The meaning is that he should establish, by means of truth and proofs such as the description of the form, the number, and so forth, that "this is mine, because it was deposited by me or by my agents. Regarding the owner's lack of qualities, the rule is that he should take a sixth part; however, if he possesses qualities, he should take a twelfth part—this distinction is to be understood here. Likewise, if the owner of the treasure-trove is a learned Brāhmaṇa, he need not give anything at all to the king; thus says the same author:
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the master of all.

"Deposited previously" means deposited by one's father or others. The mention of "the learned" (*vidvat*) is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who perform the six duties (*ṣaṭkarmin*). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states: "If a Brāhmaṇa engaged in the six duties should discover [a treasure], he may take all of it. This means [engaged] in the six duties such as sacrificing and so forth. Furthermore, as stated by Manu: "For the king is the lord of the earth; therefore, he receives half of ancient treasures and of minerals found in the ground, because of his duty to protect them."

Thus, that [rule] refers to a treasure discovered by a Brāhmaṇa possessing the aforementioned characteristics, whose owner is no longer remembered, because of the mention of "ancient [treasures]. As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Whatever property is found whose owner is unknown, the king shall take it after giving a sixth part to the finder," that refers to a case where the finder lacks the aforementioned characteristics. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"When a treasure is obtained by another, the king shall receive a sixth part;
if he takes it without reporting it but is subsequently discovered, he must pay that [sixth part] and also a fine."

The meaning of the first half-verse is that the king shall take a sixth part from the discovered treasure to give to someone other than a Brāhmaṇa who is accomplished in the six sciences and the six ritual acts (ṣaṭkarma). The meaning of the second half-verse is that the king shall seize the entire treasure from one who deceives him regarding the discovery, as well as a fine according to his capacity. Regarding the case where the king himself is the discoverer, Manu says:
"Wherever the king may see an ancient treasure deposited in the earth, having given half of it to the twice-born (Brāhmaṇas), he shall place the remainder in the treasury. [315]

Upon discovering his own hidden treasure, however, he should deposit it all in the treasury, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "The discovery of a treasure is the property of the king. Regarding wealth stolen by thieves, he has stated: "Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he should restore it to its proper place, or he should give it from the treasury. The second alternative applies to cases where one is unable to implement the first option. As Vyāsa says: "If wealth has been stolen by thieves and one is unable to recover it, then that must indeed be given from his own treasury by the king who is powerless [to retrieve it]."
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, regarding matters concerning the property of minors and others:
having obtained this True Moonlight (Saccandrikā) produced by the divine Śrī Keśavāditya, who is the embodiment of the tranquil king of twice-borns,
may people perform all legal proceedings with ease.

Thus ends the section on judicial procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*, composed by Devaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya, a performer of Soma sacrifices and son of Śrī Keśavādityabaṭṭopādhyāya, who was proficient in all branches of knowledge.
First Chapter [317] Second Chapter
Having entered the snare of the speech of many sages, with Bṛhaspati as their chief, the teacher Devaṇa compiles this collection of words.

In this regard, the collection of rules common to all titles of law (*vyavahārapada*) concerning the application of wealth has been explained previously. Now, the collection of rules specific to each individual title is being set forth. Furthermore, the nature of the eighteen titles and their various subdivisions were shown in the second section. Here, following the order of enumeration of the titles, the rule for the title known as "Recovery of Debt" (*ṛṇādāna*) is stated first. Even therein, the duties regarding the giving of wealth are stated at the outset. Regarding that, Bṛhaspati says to the creditor:
Having received a pledge or a bond that is complete,
or one accompanied by a surety, whether it be recorded in writing or witnessed, the creditor shall always repay the debt.
"Complete" means fully sufficient, including the principal amount along with the interest. Now, when it is asked what a pledge (*ādhi*) is and how many kinds there are, it is as follows:
A pledge (*ādhi*) is declared to be a bond (*bandha*), and it is said to be of four kinds:
movable and immovable, as well as that which is to be guarded (*gopya*) and that which is to be enjoyed (*bhogya*).
"Whether it be casual or for a limited period, whether recorded in writing or witnessed by witnesses. [318] Thus it is said.

Although eight types of pledge (*ādhi*) have been shown here, it is stated that "the fourfold [pledge] has been declared" in order to indicate that the detailed explanation is intended primarily for the specific rules regarding the various distinctions of the *gopya* (to be kept secret), *bhogya* (to be used), *yādṛcchika* (voluntary), and *sāvadhi* (with a time limit) types, and not for the others. A *yādṛcchika* pledge is one made without a specific temporal limit, such as: "As long as I do not repay your debt, this remains a pledge. A *sāvadhi* pledge is one made with a time limit, such as: "Having given the loan at the time of the Festival of Lights, this pledge shall be released by me; otherwise, it shall remain yours. If it is thus said here that a pledge is indeed a "bond" (*bandha*), then why was it described as a "bond" (*bandham vā*) in the previous statement? It is replied: the intended meaning of the word "bond" in that context has been demonstrated by Nārada.

"A deposit placed in the hand of a friend is known as a *bandha* (pledge) of trust. This means that when a debtor places the money of the creditor with a mutual friend for the sake of the creditor's confidence, it is designated as a *bandha*. A *lagnaka* is a surety (*pratibhū*). He should be taken as someone other than the owner and so forth, because it is difficult to recover the debt from an owner and the like. For this very reason, Kātyāyana has shown a prohibition against them:
"Neither the owner, nor an enemy, nor one appointed by the owner [should be a surety]."
He has been suppressed, punished, and indeed rendered doubtful; he is nowhere to be found.
Neither an heir, nor a friend, nor those who reside permanently [with him],
nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants [are liable for the debt].

"One who is incapable of paying the debt to the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king should not be accepted as a surety for the transaction, provided he is unknown. (319) "Accused" (*abhiśasta*) means one who is under suspicion. "Those residing permanently" (*atyantavāsinaḥ*) refers to lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*). "Equivalent to that" (*tatsamam*) means equal to the property that has become the subject of the dispute. The phrase "not an heir" (*naiva rikthī*) refers to the case of those who have not yet divided the inheritance. As Yājñavalkya says:

"Indeed, it is recorded in the Smṛti that among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, standing as a surety, contracting debt, or acting as a witness is not permitted so long as they remain undivided. Thus says Nārada as well.
Brothers who have divided their inheritance may act as witnesses, stand surety, give gifts, or receive them from one another; those who have not divided may not do so.

The phrase "recorded in writing and accompanied by witnesses," found in the first verse, should be understood as a qualification of the debt. Regarding that, the author of the *Saṃgraha* explains the very method—in its broadest outline—by which the recording of the debt in writing must be performed: "A document known as a *ciraka* is written by ancient city scribes, designated by the plaintiff and the defendant, and who are appropriately acquainted with one another."
It should be marked with the names of one's own ancestors and so forth, as well as the names of the plaintiff, the defendant, and the witnesses,
written in the same hand as that of the plaintiff and the witnesses.
"Endowed with clear comprehension, according to the characteristics stated in the Smṛti.

[The word] *saṃstutaiḥ* means "by those who are well-known and praiseworthy. Here, the prefix *prati-* is connected with the word *ākānta-*. The details of this should be seen in the section on documents (*lekhyaprakaraṇa*), specifically in the description of the document known as the *jānapada*. However, Vyaṣa has stated only a mere indication of the manner in which witnesses (*sākṣin*) are required:
"Those who know the Dharma, who have sons, who are indigenous (*maula*), of noble birth, and speakers of truth..."
[320] Engaged in the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis, they were free from hatred and envy.

"Those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), those who are not dependent on others, wise men, those who do not live abroad, and young men should be made witnesses in matters such as debts by one who understands [the law].

A detailed exposition of this should be sought in the section on witnesses and elsewhere. Thus, according to the rule stated, a creditor should always lend money; that is to say, he should engage in the lending of capital for the sake of interest. The various distinctions regarding the amount of interest, however, will be explained later in the section on interest.

"Or they may pay the interest agreed upon by themselves; this applies to all [debtors] in all castes"—by such statements as these, those [rules] are to be understood here. Thus, for one who engages in the lending of wealth bound by numerous restrictive rules, the result is indeed visible (*dṛṣṭa*), because these traditional law codes (*smṛtis*) have as their sole purpose visible worldly ends. For this very reason, Hārīta stated that the purpose is indeed visible by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"Lending money without a pledge (*ādhi*) or a guarantor (*lagnaka*), or without a bond (*bandhaka*)."
However, that which lacks both witnesses and documentary evidence does not succeed when there is a dispute.
Nārada also says:
"In this matter, there are two causes of confidence:
the surety and the pledge; and two means of proof that bring about clarity: the written document and witnesses."

*Visrambhaḥ* means trust; *vyaktiḥ* means manifestation. In this way, even the practice of lending without collateral (*abandhaka*) would be obtained, since even in such a practice, it is possible for the lent wealth to be recovered in some manner. For this very reason, a rule regarding interest will be stated even in the case of lending without collateral:
"In a secured loan, the share is one-eighth; in a loan with a pledge, the share is one-sixth;
in a loan without collateral, a two-hundredth part per month is declared as the profit. [321]
By such statements [the rule is established]. Kātyāyana declares the prohibition against lending to those who lack independence:
"One should never lend anything withdrawn [from one's store] to women, slaves, or children;
the lender does not recover that wealth, even if he should give property to them."

The intention is that women and others lack independence. "Uddhṛta" means taken for the purpose of lending. Thus ends the section on the rules for lending money and matters concerning pledges by a faultless creditor in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some statements concerning pledges (*ādhi*) are recorded. Regarding this, Hārīta says:

"One should maintain the pledge exactly as it was deposited. The meaning is that after the pledge has been taken, the creditor must protect it with diligence until its return, so that no loss, depreciation, alteration, deterioration, or transformation into another object occurs. He further states that even while the pledge is being thus protected, if loss or other damage should occur due to the force of fate or similar causes, there is no fault on the part of the creditor.
"But in the case of damage caused by fate or the king, there is never any fault on the part of the creditor.

Here, "damage by fate" refers to fire, the ravages of a region, and so forth. "Damage by the king" refers to injury caused by the king through his arbitrary conduct, even when [the debtor] is without fault. On this point, Kātyāyana states:
"Whatever has been mortgaged as a pledge that is destroyed by fate or by the king..."
In that case, the debtor must pay the debt to the creditors along with interest.
Vyāsa also states another alternative:
"But in the event of damage caused by fate or the king, the creditor is never at fault."
Upon the loss of that [pledge], however, the debtor shall be made to pay the debt or provide another pledge at that time.

The same should be understood to apply even when the pledge has become worthless. And so says Nārada: "If, even while being guarded, a pledge should in the course of time become worthless, another pledge must be provided, or else the debt must be paid to the creditor."

"Insufficiency" (*asāratā*) refers to the inadequacy of the principal amount together with its interest. Some say that "insufficiency" consists in the inadequacy of the principal amount even when accompanied by the interest accrued over one year; however, this must be considered, for the objection arises as to what the reason is for relying on such a specific qualification. Alternatively, another pledge (*ādhi*) already established previously may be made sufficient. This is because the mention of "another" has the sole purpose of indicating that it must be made sufficient. For Hārīta states that even when [the pledge] is insufficient, something should be given in some cases in order to make it sufficient.
If the borrower has received property exceeding the value of the pledge,
he shall give that excess to the creditor, saying, "I will give you the surplus."

By the debtor, who is the borrower; "additional" means that which completes the amount. Although two alternatives have been stated regarding loss caused by divine calamities and the like, nevertheless, when it is clear that the creditor is free from fault, these two alternatives should be understood to apply even in cases of loss caused by thieves, kinsmen, and so forth. This is because the mention of "divine calamities and the like" was made with the intent of referring to any cause that excludes the fault of the creditor. For this very reason, it is said:
"But in the case of injury caused by divine or royal power, there is never any fault on the part of the creditor. [323]

Thus it has been stated by Vyāsa and Hārīta. For this very reason, Kātyāyana declares that the alternative of providing another pledge is permissible only when the debtor is free from fault: "If [the property] does not perish or become damaged through the fault of the creditor, he (the debtor) shall be made to provide another pledge; the creditor shall be released from the debt."

If the pledge is lost through an act of negligence by someone other than the creditor, the debtor is not released from the debt; therefore, the meaning is that the debtor must be compelled by the king to provide another pledge to the creditor. As for the other Smṛti text: "When a field has been swept away by a flood or confiscated by the king, another pledge should be provided, or the money should be paid to the creditor."

Thus, that [text] also concerns the two-fold rule regarding the faultlessness of the creditor; otherwise, the two-fold [rule] in the case of loss by fire and so forth would not have been stated by him. Thus ends the section on pledges by a faultless creditor in the Smṛticandrikā; now follow the sections on pledges by a faulty creditor.
On this point, Hārīta says:
One should maintain a pledge exactly as it was established;
otherwise, by violating it, one loses either the profit or the principal.

In whatever manner—whether as a pledge to be kept (*gopya*) or as one to be used (*bhogya*)—it was established by the debtor, in that very same way the creditor shall protect the pledge: keeping it as a pledge to be kept, and using it as one to be used. Otherwise, if a pledge to be kept is used as one to be used, or a pledge to be used is kept as one to be kept, then due to the violation of the agreement, either the interest (*lābha*) is lost or the principal substance (*mūla-dravya*) is lost; this is the meaning. Yājñavalkya also states the loss of interest: "There is no interest on the use of a pledge to be kept. The word "by force" (*balāt*) is to be understood as the ellipsis for "use. Likewise, Manu says:
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.

The meaning is this: since the person who, having overstepped the depositor who forbids enjoyment, uses a pledge for protection (*gopyādhi*), commits an extreme offense, there shall be a loss of all interest even through a small amount of enjoyment. However, the destruction of the entire principal is not considered an option in this case, because that would constitute an excessive forfeiture. Therefore, the statement of Hārīta, "or the principal," which sets forth an alternative involving the destruction of the entire principal, should be understood as referring to cases of great enjoyment committed by force. As for one who, having deceived the depositor, uses a pledge for protection, Manu states that the interest-bearing wealth itself is destroyed portionally according to the extent of that enjoyment.
If a prudent person enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner, he must relinquish the interest on the debt; that enjoyment constitutes its compensation.

The mention of "half" (*ardha*) is intended as an illustration of the amount sufficient for expiation (*niṣkṛti*), determined according to the enjoyment of what was not permitted. Otherwise, since it would be impossible to provide expiation for one with great wealth merely by relinquishing half the interest, there would be a contradiction with the remainder of the sentence: "the expiation for that enjoyment. If, in order to avoid this contradiction, it is argued that this statement refers only to cases of small-scale enjoyment, then in the case of large-scale enjoyment that was not permitted, the loss of profit (*lābhahāni*) would not be stated by this [text]. Nor can it be said that even though it is not stated here, the loss of profit is stated in that case by the Yājñavalkya-smṛti rule, "In the case of the enjoyment of a pledge to be kept (*gopyādhi*), there is no interest," because that rule concerns small-scale enjoyment effected by force. Therefore, it is logical that the mention of "half" is indeed an illustration. However, in the case of a pledge to be used (*bhogyādhi*), if it is maintained as something to be kept (*gopyatvena pālita*), there is only the loss of the profit; for the position that the principal (*mūla*) is lost does not apply merely due to the transgression of the agreement. Nor should it be said that because there is no interest (*vṛddhi*) in a pledge to be used, the position regarding the loss of profit also does not apply, because enjoyment itself constitutes profit. Nor can it be said that in that case, if there is no enjoyment, the profit will take the form of interest, for Manu says: [325] *Manu* states: "Interest on money-lending shall be at the rate of five per cent per month, unless there be a special agreement; or else, two per cent, three per cent, or four per cent [per month], according to the order of the castes. "But one shall never obtain interest on a loan secured by a pledge that provides a benefit [to the creditor] through negligence. Thus it is said.

"In the case of a pledge with benefit" (*sopakāra*) means in the case of a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*). "Interest on negligence" (*kausīdī vṛddhi*) is that which is ordained by such scriptural injunctions as, "He may take the eightieth part [as interest]. This is what is meant: when money lent for the sole purpose of using the pledge fails to yield that use due to the debtor's own fault, there is only a loss of profit; however, the interest agreed upon does not thereby become established. But if the failure to yield use is due to the fault of the pledgor or others, it should be understood that the creditor must accept only the use from the debtor who is currently enjoying it, and not the interest. If this is so, and there is never any interest in the case of a pledge for use, how then is it that Yājñavalkya [states]: [The text continues with the citation of Yājñavalkya.]
No interest shall accrue on a pledge that is used by the creditor, nor on one that is improved, nor on one that is lost.

Thus, even in the case of a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*), when the debtor has rendered it incapable of fulfilling its purpose through neglect, the creditor effects a prohibition of interest; for since there is no prior acquisition [of interest], a prohibition would otherwise be illogical. It is replied: where the pledgor, in times of distress, agrees both to the enjoyment of the pledge and to the payment of interest, the interest that would otherwise be acquired is prohibited by the rule, "But [interest is] forbidden in the case of a beneficial pledge that is lost. Nor should it be argued that there is no agreement at all to combine both interest and enjoyment, because such a combination is precluded by the words of Manu, "But never [in the case of a pledge]. This is because Manu’s statement is intended to dispel the doubt that interest might still accrue in the case of a pledge for use if it is not used. Therefore, it is established that in every case of a pledge, if it is maintained otherwise than agreed, there is a loss of profit, but this does not apply to the mere preservation [of the object]. By this, the view of Śambhu—that in the case of a pledge for custody (*gopya*) there is a loss of profit, whereas in the case of a pledge for use (*bhogya*) there is a loss of the principal due to the absence of profit—is refuted. Kātyāyana also states that in certain cases of maintaining it otherwise, there is an option between the loss of profit and the loss of the principal amount itself.

If one should compel a person to perform work against their will and without their consent, that person shall be made to enjoy the fruit of the labor; the employer shall not receive interest on the loan.

The fruit of the labor shall be [the value of] slavery and so forth as a pledge, or wages in the case of a pledge consisting of a cart and the like; however, it is not the fruit of the labor performed—such as threshing and so on—by the slave or others, because that would be disproportionate to the offense. Here too, it should be understood that this applies "according to the nature of the work. The remainder of the sentence, "he should be made to pay to the owner of the pledge by the king," is to be supplied. The term "unwillingly" (*akāmam*) refers to the case of a pledge where there is no intention for slavery and so forth, since such a thing is impossible otherwise. Likewise, regarding a horse or other animal used as a pledge, he states that when a transgression occurs during its labor, there is a fine, but there is no forfeiture of the principal capital.
But he who, while another is performing work as a pledge, should oppress or threaten him with words, with a staff, or by physical acts,
shall incur the first amercement.

If [the debtor] does not act [to repay], there is no punishment even for one who inflicts pain or threats, because the text specifies "one who is doing so. In some cases, loss may occur through either punishment or the removal of the pledge; thus, that same author says: "If one should forcibly cause a person who is unwilling to enter upon a pledge that has not been surrendered, he shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine, and the pledgor shall forfeit the pledge."

The essential meaning is that if one enjoys a pledge (*bhogyādhi*) without permission or without it being formally deposited—even if it is of small value—the enjoyer shall be punished and the entire principal shall be lost. However, if enjoyment occurs through fraud, the loss of the principal is proportional to the enjoyment; otherwise, the act of taking it by force would be rendered meaningless. Regarding one who causes damage, such as depreciation, to the pledge, Yājñavalkya says: "If it is destroyed, it must be restored. This means that if the pledge has been destroyed or altered due to the creditor's negligence, the creditor must restore it to its former state and give it back to the debtor. Furthermore, the creditor may recover the debt along with interest from the debtor, because the pledge was handed over in its unaltered state. If, however, he hands over a pledge that has already been altered, then he recovers only the principal, as his right to interest is forfeited. Thus says Nārada:
"In the same way, there is a formal courtesy regarding his gain and loss; likewise, for a wealthy man, when a pledge has undergone a change due to negligence. Thus [it is said].

In this context, the first half [of the verse] has the same meaning as the statement of Hārīta beginning with “*bandhaṃ yathā sthāpitam*. The meaning of the second half, however, is as follows: just as there is a loss of profit in the case of a reversal [of the pledge], so too, if the object has undergone a change (*vikṛti*), one should hand it back only if it is indeed changed. And this alternative applies when there exists sufficient profit to restore the changed pledge to its former state; otherwise, the previous rule alone applies. The phrase “through negligence” (*pramādāt*) is intended to indicate a fault on the part of the creditor. Therefore, even if the pledge has undergone a change due to a fault other than [excessive] enjoyment, it should be restored as before, or else there is a loss of profit. However, it should be understood that in the case of a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), both consequences apply if it has undergone a change through enjoyment. By the very expression “having undergone a change,” diminution, transformation into another substance, lack of essence, and so forth are also included, because they are equal in being a deviation from the pledge’s original nature. Thus, this same procedure should be known to apply there as well. But regarding the loss of essence through enjoyment, Bṛhaspati says that the principal amount itself is lost.
"But when the pledge has been consumed and reached a state of worthlessness, a loss of the principal arises.

This means according to its lack of value. However, when the pledge is destroyed due to the fault of the creditor, then the creditor, having provided a pledge by way of its value, may take the debt along with the interest. Regarding this, Vyāsa says: "If a pledge consisting of gold or other valuables should be lost through the fault of the debtor..."
Having cleared the debt along with the interest, the creditor shall cause the debtor to pay its principal value.

This [rule] also concerns the case where the pledge is of greater value than the debt together with the interest. However, regarding the loss of a pledge that is sufficient to cover the debt, Nārada says: "If it is destroyed, there shall be a loss of the principal. But regarding the loss of a pledge that is sufficient to cover the debt together with the interest, Hārīta also says that there shall be a loss of the debt together with the interest: "Whether the pledge deposited with the creditor is equal to or double the amount of the debt, if the pledge is lost, the wealth is lost for the creditor, as is the pledge itself."

The wealth [to be paid] shall be equal or double [the value of the pledge]. In this case, the creditor suffers the loss of the pledge because he has not obtained the profit from the intermediate period. This is what is meant: the creditor shall suffer a loss of wealth equal to the destroyed pledge. However, regarding the loss of a high-value pledge when the debt with its interest remains, Bṛhaspati states that the value of the pledge remaining after the debt with interest is deducted must be given to the pledgor: "Where a high-value [pledge] is lost, one should satisfy the debtor therein.
One should not suspect from the statement "and one should not satisfy" that an amount of wealth sufficient to satisfy him must be given; for Manu says:

"One should satisfy him with its value; otherwise, he would be a thief of the pledge. This means that one should satisfy the debtor with the value of the remaining portion of the pledge after the interest and principal have been cleared. If the creditor does not satisfy the debtor with its value, then the surety for the return of the pledge must satisfy the debtor with its value. And so says Hārīta:
"If the consumer is devoid of wealth, but the surety is wealthy..."
Its price alone should be paid; one ought not to pay interest upon it.

The intention is that, just as with property given in friendship (*prītidatta*), interest cannot be stipulated for property pledged as security (*ādhīkṛta*). A "devourer" (*khādaka*) is one who consumes the pledge; that is to say, a destroyer of the pledge. A "surety" (*lagnaka*) is a guarantor (*pratibhū*). "Value" refers to the value of the consumed pledge. If, in this case, the debtor forcibly takes interest, then he becomes liable for a fine corresponding to the offense along with the interest taken; thus says the same author:
"He who recovers from a surety double or even triple [the debt], that property shall go to the king, and the recoverer deserves punishment."

The mention of the debtor (*lagnaka*) is intended as an illustration for the creditor (*dhanika*) as well, because the principle regarding the impossibility of recovering interest applies equally to the creditor. Thus, the creditor who acts unjustly is also subject to punishment. And so says Katyayana: "If a creditor enjoys a pledge from a debtor on the basis of a fraudulent document, the king, having caused him to pay a fine, shall cause that pledge-document to be destroyed."
In this case as well, the loss of interest should be inferred for the purpose of compensating the debtor for the enjoyment of the property.
Thus ends the section on defective mortgagors and pledges in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning the destruction of ownership (*svatvadhvaṃsa*) and related matters regarding mortgages;
therein, Yājñavalkya says:
"A pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, if it is not redeemed. Thus [it is said].

If a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*) is not released when the principal has doubled, then it is lost; the meaning is that it shall no longer belong to the debtor. However, regarding a pledge for which a specific time has been fixed—whether it be for custody or for use—if it is not released at the agreed-upon time, its loss occurs as previously stated; Yājñavalkya himself says: "A pledge fixed by time is lost at that time. A pledge is said to be "fixed by time" when it is stipulated thus: "If I do not pay this debt within such a period, then the pledge itself shall belong to you so that you may be freed from the debt. Regarding the creditor’s acquisition of ownership in this case, Vyāsa says:
When gold has doubled and the fixed period has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for two weeks.
By this, it is implicitly stated that even the loss of the pledge does not occur before the fourteenth day; and this has been stated explicitly immediately thereafter:
"Therefore, having paid the money in the interim, the debtor shall recover the pledge."

Therefore, the meaning is "within fourteen days. Now, one might ask: why does the debtor not recover the pledge even after giving the money back beyond fourteen days, since there is no cause for the destruction of his ownership? If you argue that the doubling of the debt and the passing of the fixed time limit are what destroy that ownership, we say no; for it is only through acts such as gifting (*dāna*) or selling (*vikraya*) that ownership is destroyed. If you argue that the doubling of the debt and so forth are included under the term "and others" (*ādi*), we say no; for the term "and others" includes only those things well-known in the world as causes for the destruction of ownership. If you claim that doubling the debt is likewise such a cause, we say no—for there is no such common worldly recognition regarding doubling the debt. The answer is this: it is true that doubling the debt and the like have no such recognition. However, there *is* such recognition for the exchange of goods (*dravyavinimaya*). This is because the sale of sesame seeds is prohibited, yet we see that even when a sale is not performed, ownership of the sesame seeds ceases through exchange. Consequently, in the case of a pledge with a fixed time, at the very moment the loan is taken, there is a mutual agreement between the creditor and the debtor that if I do not pay within this much time, then the pledge itself shall serve to discharge your debt. Since this exchange of wealth is known to have occurred, it is logical that ownership is destroyed at the fixed time limit. Yājñavalkya expressed this very cause of loss with the words "one made by time" (*kālakṛtaḥ*). In the case of doubling the debt, however, there is no such rule of mutual agreement between creditor and debtor at the time of taking the loan, such as: "If I do not release the pledge even when the debt has doubled, then the pledge itself shall serve to discharge your debt. Nevertheless, where such an agreement has been made, it is precisely there that ownership is destroyed upon doubling, because the cause exists; and the statement "the pledge shall be lost" refers specifically to that case. Thus, even in the absence of purchase or acceptance, the creditor acquires ownership of the pledge through exchange alone—just as the person exchanging sesame seeds acquires ownership of rice and the like. Therefore, the statement "the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge" is rightly said. The waiting for fourteen days was mentioned only to ensure the firmness of the exchange, because, like the sale of goods, only a firm exchange serves as the cause for the destruction of ownership and so forth. And thus, the statement "therefore, having given the money within [that time]" is also quite logical. As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
When the full term has elapsed and peace is attained, the debtor becomes the master and the owner of the property;
however, if ten days have not yet passed, the debtor deserves to be released.

Thus, this refers to items such as clothing used for the purpose of interest (*vṛddhi*), according to the maxim of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), as in the case of the statement, "Let curd be given to the Brahmins. The pacification of profit (*lābha-śānti*) regarding clothing and other items is also to be understood in accordance with the injunctions concerning the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth. And so, since ownership (*svatva*) accrues to the pledgee after fourteen days, the user's disposal of gold as he pleases is not contradictory; however, it should be understood that for the user of clothing and other such items, this applies only after ten days. As for what was further stated by him:
A pledge consisting of a deposit, once the value has doubled, or when the stipulated time has expired according to the rule,
may immediately be enjoyed by the creditor after notifying the debtor's family.

Thus, that [statement] refers only to the prohibition of enjoyment by the mortgagee prior to the acquisition of ownership; it does not mean that there can never be any disposal at will regarding the mortgage, because of the statement immediately following it. Therefore, there is no mutual contradiction between the two statements of Bṛhaspati, nor between the statements of Vyāsa and Bṛhaspati. As for what was stated by Manu: "There is neither alienation nor sale of a mortgage due to the lapse of time."

Thus, this is its meaning: "obstruction by time" means that even when the debt has doubled due to long-term retention, there is no release. Therefore, from such obstruction by time alone—meaning when, at the time of taking the loan, there was no agreement regarding an exchange—the pledge cannot be surrendered; nor can it be transferred to another as a pledge, given away, or sold. Rather, it remains with its interest ceased until it is released by the pledgor. However, when the debtor's death or similar event occurs before the release of the pledge—which remains in that same state while the principal plus interest is still outstanding—Bṛhaspati says what should be done in that case: [He states: "If the debtor dies while the money is still outstanding and the pledge remains in that condition, the heirs shall pay the debt from their own property, provided they possess wealth. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 10.83) This implies that if the debtor dies while the interest has ceased and the pledge remains as it was, the heirs must discharge the debt from their own assets if they have the means. If they lack wealth, they are not liable. This rule applies specifically to cases where the interest has ceased, as indicated by the phrase *śāntalābhe* ("when the interest has ceased"). If the interest has not ceased, the heirs are liable for the full amount, including the accrued interest, according to the principle that the obligation follows the person. Thus, Bṛhaspati’s statement is intended to exclude liability in cases where the interest has ceased. Furthermore, the mention of "death" (*maraṇa*) here is illustrative; it includes other incapacitating conditions such as insanity, exile, or being afflicted by a disease. Therefore, the meaning is that the heirs are liable for the debt if the debtor is deceased or incapacitated, provided the interest has ceased and the pledge remains unreleased. If the interest has not ceased, the heirs are liable for the entire sum. This is the settled conclusion. If the debtor is neither dead nor incapacitated, the creditor may simply wait for the time of release, or he may take recourse to legal action. Thus ends the section on pledges. Now follows the section on deposits. Regarding that, Nārada says: [He states: "A deposit (*nikṣepa*) is defined as an object placed in the hand of another with the thought, 'Let this be kept by you. (Nārada Smṛti 4.1) The term "in the hand" (*pāṇau*) indicates that the object is delivered directly into the other's possession. The phrase "with the thought, 'Let this be kept by you'" indicates that the object is entrusted for safekeeping. The word "deposit" (*nikṣepa*) refers to the act of placing the object down (*nikṣepaṇa*). The object so placed is also called a "deposit" by metaphorical extension. It is of two kinds: one made with a relative (*viśvasta-nikṣepa*) and one made with a non-relative (*aviśvasta-nikṣepa*). Among these, a deposit made with a relative is one where the object is entrusted to a trusted friend, kinsman, or neighbor. A deposit made with a non-relative is one where the object is entrusted to a stranger. The deposit made with a relative is further divided into two types: one where the nature of the object is disclosed and one where it is not. The deposit made with a non-relative is likewise of two types: one where the nature is disclosed and one where it is not. Among these, the deposit made with a relative where the nature is disclosed is one where the object is entrusted after stating, "This is gold," or "This is silver. The deposit made with a relative where the nature is not disclosed is one where the object is entrusted without specifying, "This is gold," or "This is silver. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is disclosed is one where the object is entrusted to a stranger after stating, "This is gold," or "This is silver. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is not disclosed is one where the object is entrusted to a stranger without specifying, "This is gold," or "This is silver. Among these, the deposit made with a relative where the nature is disclosed is of two types: one where the object is sealed and one where it is not. The deposit made with a relative where the nature is not disclosed is likewise of two types: one where the object is sealed and one where it is not. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is disclosed is of two types: one where the object is sealed and one where it is not. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is not disclosed is likewise of two types: one where the object is sealed and one where it is not. Among these, the deposit made with a relative where the object is sealed is one where the object is entrusted after sealing it with a seal. The deposit made with a relative where the object is not sealed is one where the object is entrusted without sealing it. The deposit made with a relative where the nature is not disclosed and the object is sealed is one where the object is entrusted after sealing it, but without disclosing its nature. The deposit made with a relative where the nature is not disclosed and the object is not sealed is one where the object is entrusted without sealing it and without disclosing its nature. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is disclosed and the object is sealed is one where the object is entrusted to a stranger after sealing it and disclosing its nature. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is disclosed and the object is not sealed is one where the object is entrusted to a stranger after disclosing its nature but without sealing it. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is not disclosed and the object is sealed is one where the object is entrusted to a stranger after sealing it but without disclosing its nature. The deposit made with a non-relative where the nature is not disclosed and the object is not sealed is one where the object is entrusted to a stranger without disclosing its nature and without sealing it. Among these, the deposit made with a relative where the object is sealed is of two types: one where the object is returned in the same state and one where it is returned in a different state. The deposit made with a relative where the object is not sealed is likewise of two types: one where the object is returned in the same state and one where it is returned in a different state. The deposit made with a relative where the nature is not disclosed and the object is sealed is of two types: one where the object is returned in the same state and one where it is returned in a different state.
