When gold has doubled [in interest], and the debtor has died or disappeared,
the creditor may take his property and sell it in the presence of witnesses.
"Or he should guard it for ten days in the assembly of people after its price has been paid;
thereafter, he may take another [item] corresponding to the debt, but he should avoid taking anything else. Thus it is said.

The remainder [of the rule] applies prior to the pledging of collateral once the gold has doubled in value. Regarding "lost," this refers to when it has been unknown for a long time where it has gone. The mention of the "debtor" (*adhamarṇa*) is intended to include by implication anyone authorized to pay the debt, such as a son. "Property" (*dravya*) refers to the property that was pledged. "Proportionate to the debt" means sufficient to cover the doubled amount of the wealth. By stating that one should avoid any other [pledge], he shows that even when the gold has doubled, the creditor has no ownership over the pledge. Therefore, this statement should be understood as applying to pledges that have not undergone exchange, just like the preceding statement. The phrase "when the gold has doubled" is stated by way of illustration; consequently, this rule should be inferred to apply to clothing and other items even when their profit has ceased. For this very reason, Kātyāyana stated it generally: *na tvevādhau sopakāre kausīdīṃ vṛddhim āpnuyāt | na cādheḥ kālasaṃrodhān nisargo 'sti na vikrayaḥ ||* "But one shall not obtain interest on a beneficial pledge; nor is there transfer or sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time."* *Note: *Kusīda* (interest) here refers to the profit derived from using the pledge.*
But where the depositor is not present, the creditor shall report the pledge to the king; thereafter, it is the established rule that it may be sold publicly.
"Having taken [the debt] along with interest, he should then hand over the remainder to the king. Thus it is said.

The mention of the "mortgagor" (*ādhātṛ*) here also serves, as before, as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). The phrase "he should hand it over to the king" refers to a situation where there is an absence of close relatives such as kinsmen; for when they exist, it is only logical that the handover should take place to them. If the pledge is taken back by the very same person to whom the remainder was handed over, after he has paid the money along with interest, then it is not a sale, because the purpose has been accomplished. For this very reason, the alternative of "waiting" (*tiṣṭhet vā*) has also been stated. However, in other cases, even making it a mortgage (*ādhīkaraṇa*) in this matter is not contradictory, according to the logic of the "stick and the sweetmeat" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*). But in other instances, one should mortgage only the principal and not the amount including interest. As Prajāpati said: [334]
If the creditor should cause another person to become a pledgee by means of that very same wealth,
he must first execute a written document for that pledge and deliver it to him.

Thus, the meaning is that the creditor should transfer the pledge to another creditor with exactly the same amount of wealth as that which was lent to the original debtor-owner, but not with more. This rule regarding the *anvādhi* (sub-pledge) should be understood to apply to a sub-pledge made before the doubling of the debt (*dvaiguṇya*) has occurred. The procedure described above—ending with the handing over to relatives and so forth—applies only to the case of a pledge of high value, because the handing over of the remainder and other such measures are possible only in that case. However, when the value is equal [to the debt], he should sell it in the presence of witnesses and take everything himself. Even when the value is small, he should likewise sell it, take the proceeds, and somehow recover the remaining debt from the person authorized to receive the loan; this is to be inferred from the very words of the aforementioned texts. But when the pledgor, having taken a loan for a small-value asset or for a religious merit (*sukṛta*), delays the repayment of the debt even after the doubling of the principal has occurred—thinking that the interest-bearing wealth will no longer increase and that, while he remains, the creditor cannot effect a new pledge or a sale of the pledge—the king should compel him to pay it. Thus says Yājñavalkya: [He who] takes a loan for a small-value asset or for a religious merit, and when the doubling [of the principal] has occurred, does not repay the debt, shall be compelled by the king to pay it. *YDh* 2.58. 2.61. 2.62. 2.63. 2.64. 2.65. 2.66. 2.67. 2.68. 2.69. 2.70. 2.71. 2.72. 2.73. 2.74. 2.75. 2.76. 2.77. 2.78. 2.79. 2.80. 2.81. 2.82. 2.83. 2.84. 2.85. 2.86. 2.87. 2.88. 2.89. 2.90. 2.91. 2.92. 2.93. 2.94. 2.95. 2.96. 2.97. 2.98. 2.99. 2.100. 2.101. 2.102. 2.103. 2.104. 2.105. 2.106. 2.107. 2.108. 2.109. 2.110. 2.111. 2.112. 2.113. 2.114. 2.115. 2.116. 2.117. 2.118. 2.119. 2.120. 2.121. 2.122. 2.123. 2.124. 2.125. 2.126. 2.127. 2.128. 2.129. 2.130. 2.131. 2.132. 2.133. 2.134. 2.135. 2.136. 2.137. 2.138. 2.139. 2.140. 2.141. 2.142. 2.143. 2.144. 2.145. 2.146. 2.147. 2.148. 2.149. 2.150. 2.151. 2.152. 2.153. 2.154. 2.155. 2.156. 2.157. 2.158. 2.159. 2.160. 2.161. 2.162. 2.163. 2.164. 2.165. 2.166. 2.167. 2.168. 2.169. 2.170. 2.171. 2.172. 2.173. 2.174. 2.175. 2.176. 2.177. 2.178. 2.179. 2.180. 2.181. 2.182. 2.183. 2.184. 2.185. 2.186. 2.187. 2.188. 2.189. 2.190. 2.191. 2.192. 2.193. 2.194. 2.195. 2.196. 2.197. 2.198. 2.199. 2.200. 2.201. 2.202. 2.203. 2.204. 2.205. 2.206. 2.207. 2.208. 2.209. 2.210. 2.211. 2.212. 2.213. 2.214. 2.215. 2.216. 2.217. 2.218. 2.219. 2.220. 2.221. 2.222. 2.223. 2.224. 2.225. 2.226. 2.227. 2.228. 2.229. 2.230. 2.231. 2.232. 2.233. 2.234. 2.235. 2.236. 2.237. 2.238. 2.239. 2.240. 2.241. 2.242. 2.243. 2.244. 2.245. 2.246. 2.247. 2.248. 2.249. 2.250. 2.251. 2.252. 2.253. 2.254. 2.255. 2.256. 2.257. 2.258. 2.259. 2.260. 2.261. 2.262. 2.263. 2.264. 2.265. 2.266. 2.267. 2.268. 2.269. 2.270. 2.271. 2.272. 2.273. 2.274. 2.275. 2.276. 2.277. 2.278. 2.279. 2.280. 2.281. 2.282. 2.283. 2.284. 2.285. 2.286. 2.287. 2.288. 2.289. 2.290. 2.291. 2.292. 2.293. 2.294. 2.295. 2.296. 2.297. 2.298. 2.299. 2.300. 2.301. 2.302. 2.303. 2.304. 2.305. 2.306. 2.307. 2
"One should cause the debtor to pay the money, along with interest, for that which was made by way of a pledge of character."

This text has two meanings. First, one meaning is as follows: a pledge (*bandhaka*) consisting of a clear intention, a debtor, a ring, or some other object of little value was given; this is a "pledge of character" (*caritrabandhaka*). Regarding the debt incurred by that pledge, if the debtor does not pay it to the creditor with interest, the king shall compel him to pay after the doubling of the principal. The other meaning is: *caritra* refers to merit such as *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable works); that itself is the pledge or mortgage (*ādhi*). "Incurred by that," and so forth, is the same as before. The intention here is that in the case of such a pledge, there is no discharge of the debt for the debtor who fails to repay the money. Even in the case of a pledge where the time is fixed or where the fruit is to be enjoyed (*phalabhogya*), the debtor’s discharge of the debt occurs only through the payment of the money and not otherwise; for even if there is no interest due to the enjoyment of the fruit, the principal is not lost. Nor should it be argued that the loss of the principal occurs through the pledge itself, since he himself says: "That which is to be enjoyed for its fruit is not destroyed. The intention is that if the principal is not paid, the thought "the pledge shall remain yours" is rejected because the destruction of the pledge is impossible immediately after the taking of the money due to the agreement of exchange, and because no other cause for its destruction exists.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, following the sections concerning the destruction of ownership and other matters relating to mortgage (*ādhi*),
there now follow the sections concerning the establishment of a mortgage;
therein, Nārada says:
A pledge is declared to be of two kinds: movable and immovable;
the fulfillment of both occurs through its use, and not otherwise.

*Siddhiḥ* means the establishment of the status of a pledge (*ādhitva*). Otherwise—that is, in the absence of enjoyment—by the mere acceptance by the creditor of what was designated by the debtor; so much is meant. In the case of a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), since there is no enjoyment, the establishment of the status of a pledge is to be understood from activities such as its deposit within a storehouse or similar acts that stand in place of enjoyment. Likewise, the declaration before witnesses and intermediaries in the presence of the debtor, "This house or other property belongs to us as a pledge," should be understood as the proof of the pledge in the absence of enjoyment and the like due to distance or other reasons. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states the probative nature of these aforementioned factors by way of their contrapositive: [336]
If one does not enjoy his own pledge, nor take it back, nor surrender it,
then the debtor who has died and whose witness is deceased renders that document useless.

The pledge itself; the written document is the "pledge-deed" (*ādhilekhya*). It is implied by the context that the purpose [of this document] is also the purification of a doubtful document through proof. In this very way, a writing that records the specific details of the person to whom the pledge is made is also a means of establishing the pledge. And so says Kātyāyana:
"When a field or even a village is marked by boundary signs, and the village and other such things are recorded in writing, then one attains success."
And villages and so forth serve as qualifiers for the field and the pledge (ādhi); this is the sense. By the word "pledge" (ādhi), places and other such things are included.
Thus ends the section on the establishment of pledges (*ādhisiddhi*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning the resolution of disputes regarding pledges and the like;
therein, Viṣṇu says:
When two men dispute over a pledge deposited with two different parties,
victory belongs to the one whose possession has been established without force.

The intention is that [the ownership] arises from the very enjoyment of that [property], which establishes the pledge. However, Bṛhaspati says regarding the case where both [creditors] are equally possessed of enjoyment:
"When a single field has been mortgaged to two [creditors] at the same time, whichever one enjoys it first shall obtain its establishment [of ownership]."

"Given" means that which has been pointed out by the debtor. The mention of "land" is intended as an illustration for any pledge (ādhi) that is to be enjoyed. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha stated without distinction:
"When documents are produced at the same time regarding the act of pledging, whichever has been enjoyed first, its pledge is the stronger."

The meaning is this: although documents produced at the same time are equal in terms of their formal existence (*sadbhāva*), since possession (*bhoga*) is the primary cause for establishing ownership of the object enjoyed, it is logical that its strength is based on its priority. Regarding a specific case of possession, he [the author] says the same:
"If both [creditors] arrive on the same day desiring to enjoy [the pledge], the decision is that the pledge must be enjoyed by them equally after dividing it."

The meaning is: "by him" [referring] to those two. Even in the case of a pledge (*gopyādhi*), victory belongs to the one who performed its delivery and so forth, because the establishment of that very pledge has already taken place for him. Kātyāyana states this even when the establishment of the pledge is equal for both: "If one should make a single pledge for two [creditors], what rule should apply?
Of those two, the one made first is to be accepted; the maker of the latter shall be liable to the punishment of a thief."

Because it is the commencement of taking a loan, the act of pledging (*ādhikriyā*) is called *pratipad*. That which was previously established through prior acquisition and so forth is termed "prior. Regarding specific types of pledges, Viṣṇu states the specific penalty: "He who, without releasing it from one person, gives land exceeding the measure of a *gocarma* that has been pledged by another to a third party, shall be put to death; if it is less than that, he shall be fined sixteen *suvarṇas*. Bṛhaspati also speaks regarding simultaneity in acquisition and so forth:
"In the case of two [pledges] presented at the same time, the result shall be equal for both."

The ellipsis is "in order to perform the taking of possession (*upādāna*) and so forth" regarding the two parties who have appeared. Regarding mortgages (*ādhi*) and the like which are established solely by witness-declarations, Kātyāyana states that when there is a conflict, that which is established by a document (*lekhyasiddha*) is to be accepted among them: "When a mortgage, sale, or gift is performed by both document and witnesses, but the document contradicts the single act [performed], then that document is subversive [of the claim]. [338]

A document is that which is written, produced by writing, or established by writing; it is authoritative in cases of seizure. Although there is no difference in their being established by writing, he (Kātyāyana) himself states the relative strength and weakness [of such documents]:
"That which is not specified and that which is specified, and that which is written in one place and that which is written with particular detail—the latter is superior," so said Kātyāyana.

The meaning is that what is recorded with specific details regarding the subject matter and so forth in one place is "specified writing" (*nirdiṣṭalekhita*); it is superior to "unspecified writing" (*anirdiṣṭalekhita*). What is entered into a document is "inscribed" (*vilekhita*). He explains the meaning of the terms "unspecified" and "specified" himself:
"If one should pledge existing property whose nature has not been specified—[property] which is as if it were empty space—that [pledge] shall certainly not be considered 'specified'."
"Whatever he may possess at that time, one should point out that which has been assigned. Thus it is said.

The word *pra* is for the purpose of completing the meter. "Of unspecified nature" (*anādiṣṭasvarūpaka*) means of unascertained nature. "Become like space" (*ākāśabhūta*) means as good as non-existent. "It would not be specified" (*ādiṣṭaṃ naiva tad bhavet*) means it would not be pointed out; that is to say, it would remain unspecified. "Specified" (*ādiṣṭa*) means pointed out. And thus the meaning is this: at the time of making a pledge (*ādhi*), whatever wealth exists and whose nature is ascertained, that wealth, being specified as a pledge, is called "pointed out. However, wealth that is the opposite of that, when being conceived as a pledge, is called "unspecified. Even though there is equality in its existence at the time of making the pledge, he [the author] says the same thing.
But if one should deposit all one's property, having first or afterwards marked it with a name, how could that which is marked be more authoritative? [339]

The meaning of this is as follows: Suppose someone, having previously taken a loan from another person by pledging their entire property without specifying particulars, later—upon the creditor’s agreement—gives back only a specific portion, such as a field, marked with boundary signs (ghaṭṭa) and the like, for the sake of that very same previously contracted debt. In that case, the marked [pledge] is more powerful. This is because the prior pledge was relinquished by the creditor himself, who was obstructed by the act of creating a subsequent pledge or other transaction. The term "marked" (*cihnitam*) is intended to indicate any other conflicting transaction. Therefore, it should be understood that when a creditor, having first taken a pledge and paid the debt, subsequently—ascertaining the debtor's honesty—performs a new transaction by another means, saying, "From now on, let the debt remain with you even without the pledge," then the pledgeless transaction alone is to be regarded as more powerful. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"In all disputes concerning property, the subsequent transaction is stronger.

The intention is that it thus serves as a sublater (*bādhikā*) of the prior transaction. Another example is as follows: when a debt bearing interest at the rate of one-eighth has been subsequently made to bear interest at half that rate due to friendship or other reasons, the transaction involving the one-eighth interest is sublated by the transaction involving the half-interest. It should be understood that the previously mentioned [cases], such as those involving marked items and so forth, are also examples of this very point. He himself states an exception to the rule regarding the strength of the subsequent transaction in certain cases:
"In the case of a pledge (*ādhi*), a gift (*pratigraha*), or a purchase (*krīta*), the prior [transaction] is indeed more powerful.
The intention is that because the prior act has already been completed through the removal of the obstacle to ownership (*svāmitva-pratibandha-apagama*). With this very intention, Vasiṣṭha also says:
"But if one sells again that which was previously pledged..."

Which of these two would be stronger? The prior one is more powerful. Even though ownership is not extinguished by the act of pledging, it is nonetheless obstructed. Consequently, a sale made by one whose ownership is thus obstructed is weak and must be set aside, as it is as invalid as if it were made by another; thus, there is no flaw in this reasoning. He says the same regarding the simultaneity of pledges and so forth: "Where on a single day a gift, a pledge, and a sale are all performed..."
When there is doubt regarding these three, how should one reflect upon them?

"All three shall divide that lawful wealth according to their respective shares; both [the original owner and the buyer] shall share it by a third part each, in accordance with the transaction. This means that when a doubt arises as to how it should be in a case where a gift or other transfer has been made by all three, one should reflect upon this for the sake of a definitive decision. "Both" refers to the owner of the wealth and the purchaser. "In accordance with the transaction" means in accordance with the wealth that was given. The word *kriyā* (transaction) is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Bṛhaspati also says:
If the sale, the ownership, and the acceptance [of the price] were all performed on a single day,
and the matter is thus doubtful for all three parties, how should the investigation proceed in that case?
"In this matter, they should divide the three [shares] according to their respective portions;
both [the father and mother] shall take two shares in accordance with the purpose, while the recipient shall take one-third.

The ellipsis here is that "both shall take two shares in accordance with the purpose. Similarly, in the preceding statement, the specific distinction regarding the phrase "in accordance with the action" (kriyānusāreṇa) should be understood. The ellipsis is that "the recipient is connected with one-third. However, if the reading is *pratigraha* (instead of *pratigrahī*), the distinction should be grasped as follows: it results in the same construction as the preceding statement.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, the topics concerning the removal of disputes [341]; now,
the topics concerning the transfer of ownership.

Regarding this, Vyāsa states: "The debtor shall redeem a pledge for a secret deposit after [the debt] has doubled. This means that when the interest on the lent wealth has ceased once it has reached twice the principal. The phrase "shall redeem" implies by paying back the principal along with the interest. And this should be understood to apply to cases where there is no loss of the pledge due to its reaching the state of doubling and so forth; however, in cases where the pledge is subject to loss based on those same conditions, one must redeem it even before such loss occurs. Thus it has been stated by that very author:
Therefore, having paid the money in the interim, the debtor shall obtain the pledge. Thus it is said.

In this context, "wealth" (dhana) is intended to mean the principal together with interest (*savṛddhika-mūla*). Therefore, the meaning of "intermediate time" (*antarā-kāla*) is the period within the stated time limit for waiting upon the debtor. And the period for waiting upon the debtor begins from the cessation of profit and lasts for fourteen days (*dvisaptadina*). It should be understood that by this very statement, the recovery of the pledge (*bandha-āpti*) even when the wealth together with interest is paid back within the aforementioned intermediate period is declared through the logic of the "stick and the rice-cake" (*daṇḍāpūpa-nyāya*). However, regarding a pledge for the enjoyment of fruits (*phala-bhogyādhi*), the same author states that the debtor shall recover it by paying only the principal at the end of the period of fruit-enjoyment.

"Having given the substance together with its equivalent value, [the debtor] shall deliver what is to be enjoyed as the fruit for the prior period. The phrase "the debtor shall obtain the pledge," which is recited in the first half-verse, is supplied here by ellipsis. *Sāmakam* means exactly equal; that is to say, the mere principal. Because of the mention of "that which is to be enjoyed as the fruit," there is no fixed time limit for pledges such as clothing and so forth that are to be used in their own form. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says to the creditor: "When the debtor, having paid the money made into principal, should demand the pledge..."

At that very time it must be released; otherwise, the creditor incurs guilt. This applies in the same way to a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*). However, in the case of a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), it must be released at the very moment the debtor requests it after having paid the principal together with interest. This is because the mention of "the principal" refers to the wealth to be given by the debtor. "Guilt" here means the guilt of theft. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"The pledge must be released when [the debtor] has presented himself; otherwise, he becomes a thief."

"Of one who has approached" means of one who has presented himself for the purpose of pledging [the property] preceded by the payment of wealth. "A thief shall be punished like a thief" is the meaning. When there is an intervention by the creditor—whether due to place or time—for one who has approached, the pledge must be released by the creditor's family. This also follows from the sense of what that same author stated:
"When the [original] user is present, one may obtain the pledge after depositing the wealth with the family."

The "instigator" (*prayojaka*) is the one who employs the capital. The phrase "he shall obtain it at that very time" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Alternatively, even if the debtor has deposited the wealth with the family of the creditor, he shall obtain the pledge or its value—calculated at the time of clearing the debt and free of interest—only after the creditor's arrival. He [Yājñavalkya] states this very point through the force of his words: "Or, having been appraised at that time, it shall remain there free of interest."

The word "should remain" (*tiṣṭhet*) is understood as referring to the pledge (*ādhi*). In that context, the meaning is "in the family of the creditor. Bṛhaspati states that even when the money-lender possesses the wealth and the interest has ceased, in certain cases the debtor may recover the pledge only after a long time: "When land or other property has been enjoyed [by the creditor] such that the profit arising therefrom has entered into the principal and interest, then the debtor shall recover the pledge."

When a field or other property pledged as collateral has been enjoyed by the creditor after the cessation of interest, if the wealth produced from that enjoyment exceeds the expenses incurred for the sake of the field—being equal to the principal plus interest—and at whatever time this amount has entered the hands of the creditor, at that very time the debtor recovers the pledge; such is the meaning. When it is asked in what case the recovery of the pledge occurs in this manner, he himself says:
"When the debtor, having made an agreement, should deliver the field to the creditor..."
It has been decided by you that this must be enjoyed for the sake of attaining peace.
"When the principal together with interest has been entered [into the pledge], you must deliver it to me.

Having thus stipulated "this by you" and so forth, when one provides a field or other property as a pledge (*ādhi*) at the time of taking a loan, the meaning is that the acquisition of the pledge occurs according to the previously stated rule. In this very way, the acquisition of the pledge occurs through this same stipulation after the cessation of the debt, once the pledge has been delivered; thus says Yājñavalkya:
"But when the debt has become doubled in the pledge, then indeed..."
The pledge shall be released when the money produced from it has doubled and been paid in.

"In the beginning," the word "given" (*datta*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "That immovable property which was given solely for the purpose of introducing the received wealth, one shall return upon the introduction of that received wealth. By such a technical definition, worldly people refer to this as a *kṣayādhi* (a pledge subject to loss). However, regarding the formulation of such a definition, it should be understood that even if an amount exceeding the principal by a great margin has been introduced, there is never a recovery of the pledge without the payment of interest (*sodaka*). Likewise, in certain other cases as well, Bṛhaspati states that there is no recovery of the pledge without the payment of interest.
Where a house or field has been pledged and its enjoyment has reached full maturity,
there the debtor shall not suffer seizure of the property, nor shall the creditor recover the debt.
"When [the period] is complete, the ownership of that [property] is proclaimed to belong to both;
even when it is incomplete, the two may act [regarding it] with each other's consent."

Since its purpose cannot be understood without knowledge of the subject matter, the subject matter is first stated: A pledge (*ādhi*) is given after an agreement has been made that "this pledge is to be enjoyed until the profit ceases, for the sake of obtaining only the increase (*vṛddhi*). At the time of taking the loan, or at the time when the profit ceases, it was not mentioned during the time of making the agreement that "let this be for the sake of the full increase even if the increase produced from this pledge during this period is insufficient. Alternatively, in that case, the portion beginning with "from this pledge" and ending with "let it be" was indeed stated; thus, the subject matter is twofold. The purpose (*artha*) is also stated: The "purpose produced from the pledge" refers here to what remains after the expenses for production have been deducted, as indicated by the word "excess" (*prakarpa*). When that [excess], though insufficient for the full increase, has entered into the creditor, the debtor, having paid only the principal, shall not lose the pledge even after the expiration of the agreed-upon time. And the creditor, at that time, shall not obtain—that is, shall not take—the mere principal of the debt; rather, when the excess is complete and sufficient for the full increase, the pledge belongs to the creditor, and the debtor's ownership [ends]. Therefore, the remainder is that at that very time, having paid the full amount (*sāmaka*), one should release the pledge. Even when the excess is incomplete—insufficient for the full increase—they both may establish ownership by mutual consent, because at the time of making the agreement it was established that "even if insufficient for the increase, let it be for the sake of the full increase"; such is the case for the creditor and the debtor. And the fruit of establishing ownership is that, upon the expiration of the agreed-upon time, even in the absence of the entry of an excess sufficient for the full increase, the debtor releases the pledge simply by paying the full amount. By saying "by mutual consent," he shows that in the absence of such consent, the creditor's ownership persists even regarding the remainder of the increase. Likewise, he says the same even when the excess sufficient for the full increase enters during only a portion of the agreed-upon time.
"If that [debt] were increased, then the creditor would not possess wealth, and the debtor would not incur bondage, without mutual consent. Thus it is said.

In both statements, the remainder "the lapse of the stipulated time" (*paribhāṣitakālātyaya*) should be understood [as applying]. And thus the meaning is this: if that pledge (*bandhaka*), having reached its maximum value—that is, being endowed with the maximum increase sufficient for the whole—should exist at some point within the stipulated time, then upon the lapse of that stipulated time, the creditor (*dhanin*) does not become the owner of the wealth, and the debtor (*ṛṇin*) does not lose the pledge; rather, once the maximum increase sufficient for the whole has been reached, the creditor becomes the owner of the principal wealth, and the debtor, having paid the principal, recovers the pledge. By saying "without mutual agreement," he shows this: whether or not there is an entry into a maximum value exceeding the whole sufficient increase at some point within the stipulated time, in every case, when the debtor says, "Let the pledge be used for the sake of interest until the stipulated time," and the creditor says "yes," then even if there is an entry into a maximum value exceeding the interest, only upon the lapse of the stipulated time does the debtor recover the pledge by paying the full amount (*sāmaka*), and not during the middle of the stipulated time. By this very explanation, [the following is shown].
As long as that [debt] remains outstanding, the creditor shall not receive his share of the property;
likewise, the debtor shall not be subjected to confinement without the mutual consent of both parties.
Thus the statement of Vyāsa is also explained.
Thus ends the section on pledges (ādhi) in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, the types of sureties (*pratibhū*):
next, some statements concerning the subjects of suretyship are recorded. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"In [the case of] appearance, in [the case of] confidence, in [the case of] payment, and likewise in the delivery of the debtor's property."
In the treatises, four types of sureties have been observed by the wise.

*Pratya-ya* means trust. *Dāna* is the handing over of wealth for the purpose of discharging a debt. The "handing over of the debtor's property" refers to the surrender of that property belonging to the debtor, such as household goods and utensils. The manner of acceptance for the four types of sureties has also been shown by that same author: "One says, 'I shall produce him [the debtor]'; another spoke thus: 'I am the payer'; and yet another says, 'I shall hand over this property.'"

One, acting as a *darśana-pratibhū* (surety for appearance), says while assuming the responsibility: "I shall produce him when he has set out to flee. Another, acting as a *pratyaya-pratibhū* (surety for confidence), says: "This man is honest and not a deceiver; give him money on my guarantee. A *dāna-pratibhū* (surety for payment) says: "Whenever he does not pay the wealth that was taken, including interest, I myself will pay that wealth. Another, acting as an *ṛṇidravyārpaṇa-pratibhū* (surety for the delivery of the debtor's property), says: "When he does not pay the wealth that was taken, I will deliver his wealth [to you]. This is the meaning of the fourfold statement. Hārīta also [says]:
In matters of safety, trust, giving, attendance, and seeing profit—
in these five instances, a wise person should indeed accept a guarantor.

"Security" (*abhaya*) means not causing harm. Here, "standing near" (*upasthāna*) is intended to mean the delivery of the pledged object, not mere sight, because that [sight] has already been mentioned by its own specific term. Furthermore, it would be inconsistent with the phrase "in the five cases. Vyāsa also says:
"When a document has not been made, or when there is a second [document], upon seeing proof of the gift;
likewise, when the pledge has been taken and delivered, or when the debtor's property has been handed over."

The word "sureties should be taken" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. In the case of a document not being produced—that is, when there is no sight of the document—or in the case of an ordeal not being performed, this is the connection [of the rule]. This is what is meant: where, for the sake of deciding a dispute, a means of proof—whether visible or invisible—will come into existence after a lapse of time, even in such a case a surety should be taken for the purpose of that proof. The evidences of delivery have already been explained. "The presentation of the pledged property" refers to the re-delivery of the pledge taken from the debtor with the creditor's permission, either because he is a petitioner or for the purpose of showing it to a purchaser. Kātyāyana also [says]:

In matters concerning gifts, attendance, or verbal agreements, one should certainly cause a guarantor to be appointed for the sake of establishing trust; likewise, in the opposite case, one should act as appropriate.

"Upasthāna" means appearance [in court]. "Vāda" means dispute. In that regard, immediately after the defendant has been brought forward, the members of the assembly (sabhyas) should take a surety (*lagnaka*) for the purpose of recovering the money or other property proven to be due. When there is suspicion of theft or similar offenses regarding a slave or the like, a surety must be taken for the sake of assurance. Taking a surety for an oath should be done when there is a delay in taking the oath. Thus, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that in other cases as well, where the reverse occurs, one should cause a surety to be taken according to the possibility within the scope of legal procedure. Consequently, it should be understood that in the case of prior mortgages, sales, or gifts, when there is a suspicion of fraudulent heirs, the surety known as the "keeper of the pledge" (*ādhipāla*) for a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), the one known as the "causer of enjoyment" (*bhuñjāpaka*) for a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*), and the one known as the "restorer" (*pratyarpaka*) even in the case of high-value items, are all included by this very rule.
Thus ends the section on the various types of masters in the *Smṛticandrikā* [348].
Now follow the specific rules regarding sureties.
Now, Kātyāyana says:
"He who is a surety for appearance shall produce [the debtor] at the place and time [specified].

The meaning is this: whoever was the surety for appearance for another must produce that person at whatever place and time the creditor has need of seeing him. He further states that if he has produced him, he is released from his suretyship.
"If he should produce him there, he must be released; he shall be the surety.
But regarding one who does not produce him there, Manu says:
"Whatever man stands here as a surety for the production of another..."
If he does not produce it, he shall pay that debt from his own property.

In this context, "debt" is intended to include interest, since it is recorded in the legal tradition that even a debt to be paid by the son of a surety must include interest. However, when the person for whom the surety stands is not known—having gone somewhere and being untraceable—Bṛhaspati says:
"The creditor should grant time for the search of the lost person to the surety, [giving him] a fortnight, a month, or even one and a half months, according to the distance of the country."
One should not grant more than one and a half months [for the search], because the statement is intended to be restrictive. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"However, for the purpose of searching for what is lost, a period of up to three fortnights should be granted;
if he should produce him there, the surety must be released."
"If, when the appointed time has passed, the surety does not produce him at all, he shall be made to pay that debt;

this same rule is prescribed for the case of his death. (349) "Param" means the ultimate limit. "Pratīte" means when the time has been agreed upon or determined, that is to say, fixed for the purpose of searching. "Tamartham" refers to whatever may be obtained from the person who was to be produced. "Evamvidhiḥ" refers to the rule that "he shall be made to pay that debt. If the surety did not produce the person due to no cause—whether by fate or by the king—then the previously mentioned rule applies; thus says that very same [author].
But a surety for appearance who does not produce the defendant at the proper place and time shall pay the debt,
except in cases caused by fate or the king.

*Nibandha* refers to the object to be delivered. *Āvahet* means he should cause it to reach the creditor. *Daivakṛta* (calamity caused by fate) includes long-term illness, the death of a kinsman, and so forth; *rājakṛta* (calamity caused by the king) includes seizure, imprisonment, and the like. Regarding certain other types of sureties, Nārada states the following rule: "When debtors fail to act, or when the security (*pratyaya*) is lost, the surety shall pay that debt, as shall one who fails to produce [the debtor]."

The phrase "when debtors do not repay" refers to the case of a surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*). The phrase "and when confidence is lost" refers to the case of a surety for trust (*pratyaya-pratibhū*). The phrase "not producing [the collateral]" refers to the case of a surety for the delivery of the pledge (*ādhi*) held by the debtor, which he fails to produce in some manner. "When debtors do not repay" means when they fail to pay the debt due to deceit or because of poverty and so forth. "When confidence is lost" means when trust has been violated. "Not producing" means not somehow bringing back to the creditor's side the pledge that was with the debtor and placing it again near the creditor. Pitāmaha also says the same.
But a pledge made with a guarantor (*ādhipālaka*) is characterized by a fixed time limit.
If that [pledge] has not been delivered to the creditor, then its delivery must be effected by those [guarantors].

(350) The meaning is as follows: if, due to his own fault or other reasons, the debtor does not deliver the pledge within a short time, then those guarantors who have undertaken the obligation to deliver the pledge—stating, "We shall deliver the pledge"—must effect its delivery when it has not been delivered by the debtor. The plural number in the word *taiḥ* ("by those") is intended to indicate the number one and so forth; for this very reason, Hārīta says:
When a pledge has been made for the sake of confidence but is not accepted by the creditor,
it must then be delivered by him, or else the debt must be paid to the creditor.

The meaning is: "by that security" (*ādhipālena*). When it is impossible to recover [the debt], then indeed the second alternative applies. Regarding one who has pledged a high-value object as collateral for a debtor, he says the same concerning the guarantor for the return of that pledge:
"If the consumer is destitute of wealth and the pledge-holder is wealthy, the value of that [pledge] must be paid; he ought not to pay interest."

The *khādaka* is one who consumes the pledge; that is to say, a creditor who destroys a pledge of high value. The *mūlya* is the price of the pledge of high value. Even a surety for appearance (*pratyaya-pratibhū*) is not liable to pay interest here; even for the *khādaka*, only the price itself is to be paid, based on the statement: "He should satisfy him with the price. In this manner, the rules regarding the goods to be paid by the remaining types of sureties are to be observed in other *Smṛtis*. When neither a written document (*lekhyam*) nor an ordeal (*divya-darśanam*) has been executed, these rules should be inferred from other *Smṛtis* prescribing the method of recovery, such as "the sureties shall be made to pay the debt," or they should be formulated through the application of similar principles. For instance: a surety for the delivery of the debtor's property (*ṛṇidravyārpaṇa-pratibhū*) should deliver the property when the debtor fails to do so. A surety for safety (*abhaya-pratibhū*) should provide a remedy when danger arises. A surety for proof (*pramāṇa-pratibhū*) should pay the disputed sum when he fails to produce evidence. A surety for litigation (*vivāda-pratibhū*) should pay both the proven sum and the fine when the plaintiff fails to prosecute. Furthermore, if a slave or other property pledged is lost and cannot be recovered, a surety for confidence (*viśvāsa-pratibhū*) should pay its value; such rules are to be formulated in their respective contexts.
Thus ends the section on the specific rules regarding sureties in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the rules concerning the sons and other descendants of sureties;
therein, Yājñavalkya says:

Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stood as sureties for payment (*dāna*) must pay it.

A *prātyayika* is one who stands as a guarantee for trustworthiness (*pratyaya-pratibhū*). When such a person has died, as well as when a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) has died, their sons shall not pay the paternal debt incurred on account of that suretyship. However, if a guarantor for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*) has died, his sons shall pay the aforementioned debt; this is the meaning. But when the aforementioned living guarantors do not pay the debt, and the sons of the deceased guarantor for payment likewise do not pay, then they must be made to pay; thus that same author states the king’s duty. "But first, in the event of failure, the sons of the other [guarantor] must also be made to pay."

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is shown that even a surety for payment (*dānapratibhūḥ*) must be made to pay in the event of a breach of contract during his lifetime. This has been explicitly stated by Bṛhaspati himself:

"But the first two must be made to pay the wealth reported at that time if the transaction fails; however, in the case of a breach of contract, the latter two must pay, as well as their sons in their absence. [352]

The first two are sureties for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*). In the event of their falsehood—meaning when the statements of these sureties, such as "I shall produce him" or "He is a righteous man," prove to be untrue—the latter two are the sureties for delivery of the debt and the property (*dāna-ṛṇidravyārpaṇa-pratibhū*). In the event of a disagreement due to fraud or other causes, and the debt is not repaid by the debtor; the meaning is that [the liability] arises when the latter two [sureties] are absent, whether due to departure or death. This is what is meant: where a surety has promised, "I will give you the debt or some other wealth and so forth," there the surety must be made to pay; in his absence, his son may be made to pay. But in other cases, it is the surety alone who is liable. And thus, since those who are sureties for proof (*pramāṇa-pratibhū*) do not make such a promise, only the sureties for proof are to be made to pay, not their sons. However, because a surety for litigation (*vivāda-pratibhū*) has promised, "I will pay the wealth won in the dispute and the fine," he must be made to pay like a surety for delivery, provided he exists; otherwise, it should be understood that his son is liable. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:

When there has been no denial of the debt and no examination of documents or ordeals has been conducted, the sureties should be made to pay the debt; however, one should not cause their sons to pay it.
"In that case, the two sons of the surety for payment shall be made to pay the debt. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that when the guarantee has failed and the condition is proven false, the surety for the condition (*pratyaya-pratibhū*) shall be made to pay. In this same manner, having considered the manner in which other types of sureties—such as those for safety (*abhaya*), for the delivery of a hostage (*bandha-upasthāpana*), and so forth—have either accepted or refused their obligation, the rules for compelling payment should be inferred accordingly, whether they follow the model of the surety for the condition or the surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*). As for what Manu stated after declaring, "Suretyship and a loan at interest," and so on, that "the son is not liable to pay," that refers specifically to the case of the surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*), since he says immediately thereafter: [Manu 8.160]... [text omitted] ...[Manu 8.161]. Thus, the liability of the sons of other types of sureties must be determined by examining the specific nature of the agreement entered into. In the case of a surety for appearance, however, the sons are not liable even if the father was insolvent at the time of death; this is because the purpose of such a surety is merely to produce the debtor. Therefore, the sons are not liable for the debt of a surety for appearance, nor for one who stood as surety for a non-existent person, nor for one who stood as surety for a minor, nor for one who stood as surety for a woman. "But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply.

(353) The meaning is that the rule previously stated in the preceding verse—"a son is not liable to give a surety for appearance"—is to be understood as applying to the subject of a surety for appearance (*darśanaprātibhāvya*). Regarding that matter, Kātyāyana states an exception in certain cases: "But he who, having taken a pledge, stands as a surety for appearance..."
Having investigated the matter there, the son of that person should also be made to pay the debt by the plaintiff.

The meaning is as follows: having received money from a debtor for the sake of his own confidence, one who stands as a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) remains; "remains" (*saṃsthitaḥ*) means, in effect, that he has died. When his son is requested by the creditor—the claimant—after it has been determined that the guarantee was based on the retention of the debtor's wealth, he must be made to pay the debt incurred through that guarantee. Although this exception appears to concern only the son of a guarantor for appearance, rather than the son of a guarantor for proof (*pramāṇa-pratibhū*), nevertheless, in the case of making the son of a guarantor pay, what is intended here as the cause is the guarantee preceded by the receipt of money from the deceased father as a debtor; it is not merely the status of being the son of a guarantor for appearance. Therefore, it should be understood that based on this very statement, the exception is intended to apply elsewhere as well whenever the specific cause exists. It is precisely to illuminate this intended cause that Manu has presented the exception in the form of a question and answer.
Furthermore, when the debtor is not the one who received the loan, but the guarantor—
who was known for his character— is deceased, by what means should the creditor seek to recover the debt?
"But if the surety has been assigned funds and possesses sufficient wealth, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one for whom funds have been assigned."

Here, the meanings of the words are first stated: *adātari* means "when the surety has not paid"; *darśayitari* means "when he has produced the debtor"; *dātā* means "the one who pays"; *dhanaprayoktā* means "the one who employs the wealth. *Vijñātaprakṛtau* means "one whose nature is known," that is, one whose disposition is generally understood such that he becomes a surety after taking something from someone; *ṛṇaṃ prātibhāvyāgatam* means "a debt incurred through suretyship"; *parīpsel* means "he would wish to obtain. The meaning of the sentence, however, is this: when the surety who has not paid and whose nature was known has died, why would the creditor wish to obtain the debt from his son later, by what reason not opposed to the scriptures, given the rule: "his sons shall not pay the debt"? The commentary on the following verse is also explained in this way: *nirādiṣṭadhanaḥ* means "one to whom wealth has been assigned," i.e., handed over as security. *Alaṃdhanaḥ* means "one who possesses sufficient wealth," i.e., one who has taken enough wealth as security. By the word *nirādiṣṭa* used in its entirety, the son of the surety for appearance (*darśanapratibhūḥ*) who had his wealth assigned is indicated. *Sthitiḥ* means "the established limit of the scriptures. The meaning of the sentence, however, is this: if the surety for appearance, having had his wealth assigned and possessing sufficient wealth, should die, the rule is that the one to whom the wealth was assigned (i.e., the son) should pay that debt from his own wealth. By this very reason—namely, the state of having had wealth assigned—the answer "he would wish to obtain it" is stated by implication. Setting aside the recourse to ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) as a characteristic of this statement, another meaning is stated: if the surety to whom wealth was assigned possesses sufficient wealth, he himself, being assigned [that wealth], should pay from his own wealth. One who has had wealth assigned is not released simply by producing the debtor like one who has not had wealth assigned; rather, he should pay like a surety for payment (*dānapratibhūḥ*). This is the intended meaning. And this alternative interpretation was stated by Devasvāmin. Regarding the specific case of what must be paid by the son of a surety, Vyāsa says: [The verse of Vyāsa follows here.]
A grandson shall pay his grandfather’s debt, and a son shall pay a debt incurred by way of surety;
the two grandsons [of the debtor] need not be made to pay—this is the settled rule.
The son is the son of the surety (*pratibhūsuta*). "Equally" means merely the principal amount. The two sons are the sons of the grandson and the son of the surety. As for what was stated by Manu:

"When the surety for payment has died, one should cause even the heirs (*dāyāda*) to pay," in that context the word *dāyāda* is restricted to the sons alone; otherwise, if it were used to denote all *sapiṇḍas*, it would result in a contradiction with the previously cited statement: "But the two sons are not to be made to pay—this is the settled rule."

Furthermore, this would contradict the statement of Bṛhaspati: "That which was undertaken as a guarantee (prātibhāvya) need never be paid by grandsons. Regarding the case where there are multiple sureties for the debt to be paid, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"If there be many sureties, they should pay the money according to their respective shares."
When these [debts] rest under a single liability, the creditor may act according to his pleasure.

Those who have resorted to the "single shadow" (*ekacchāyāśrita*) are those who, by virtue of a similarity consisting in being liable for the payment of the entire debt, have each individually taken recourse to the shadow of a single debtor. The meaning is that among them, whichever one the creditor demands from, he shall pay the whole amount. However, if there is a specific agreement between the creditor and the debtors, then even in this case they shall pay according to their respective shares, following the principle that "it should be equal, as nothing [specific] has been heard. Regarding the son of a surety who has resorted to the single shadow, Kātyāyana states the distinction: "If the father who resorted to the single shadow has gone abroad, the son shall pay the whole;
if the father is dead, Bṛhaspati says he shall pay the father’s share, not the other debts."
The meaning is that "all" refers even to the debt of another, and not merely the father's share; however, it should not be explained as "all including interest," for it is said:
"Even by a son, the entire paternal debt must be paid together with him. [356]

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati: "The debt consisting solely of the principal that has come down from a father by way of suretyship—this should always be given when there is the creditor's wish in the form: 'The son of one who is away should give to me. However, in the absence of the creditor's wish, it should be understood that "the son of one who is away should give the father’s share without interest. Regarding the debt of another—that portion of the debt belonging to someone other than the father, such as a paternal uncle, who is under the same roof—the son is not required to pay upon the death of the father even if the creditor so desires; rather, Bṛhaspati declares that he must pay only the father’s share without interest. As for the case of a surety's misconduct, Pitāmaha says:
He who, having become a surety for someone, departs in a false manner,
shall be made by the king to pay the creditor's wealth and a fine equal to that amount.
"If a surety should engage in a dispute with the plaintiff on behalf of the debtor,
he shall then be punished with a fine of twice the amount involved in the dispute;
'sopasarga' means one who causes trouble."
Thus ends the section on the rules concerning the sons of sureties and others in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follow the rules for the recovery of what has been paid by a surety or others;
regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
Whatever was given for whose sake and by whom, when one has been requested as a surety in a dispute,
that surety shall obtain it once he has been proven by the witnesses.

The meaning is this: when a person has caused another to act as a surety (*prātibhāvya*), and that surety—having been requested by creditors and others, and having been determined by witnesses and the like to have "delivered the object for the sake of another"—gives his own gold, cattle, grain, clothing, and so forth to those creditors, he shall recover from the one who caused him to act as surety an amount equal to that very object. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya: "In a case where a surety is made to pay money to the creditor openly, the debtors must repay double that amount to him."
Thus, this refers to the case of a surety who has been oppressed by the creditor (*dhanika*). And so says Nārada:
"Whatever amount a surety may pay when oppressed by the creditor, the debtor shall cause that amount to be paid back to the surety doubled."
This also refers to the case of a delay in repayment. And so Kātyāyana says:
"But he who, being pressured by the debtor for whom he stands as surety, gives the surety-money, shall be entitled to receive that amount doubled after three fortnights have passed."

"Secured by a surety" means made to act as a guarantor. Furthermore, the meaning is also understood that one ought to receive the same amount [of interest] before three fortnights have passed. Although a person generally becomes a surety out of affection, and there is neither interest nor doubling of the principal on what is given out of affection, it ought to be lawful at this time; nevertheless, everything shall be so by the force of the scriptural statement, for it should be understood that there is no burden too great for a word of command. Thus, the aforementioned rule regarding the doubling of the profit applies to gold. But in the case of cattle and the like:
"Offspring [is the interest] on female animals and livestock, grain is tripled,
clothing is declared to be fourfold, and liquids are recorded as being eightfold"—
thus Yājñavalkya records this as an exception to the rule of doubling [the principal].

"The fivefold interest is prescribed for vegetables; for seeds and sugarcane, it is recorded as sixfold"—this was stated by the authors of the *bhāṣya* as an illustrative example (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the fivefold interest and so forth should be applied to vegetables and the like. Thus, the various types of lending with interest mentioned above apply to cases where the loan is given at the debtor's own request; otherwise, however, only an amount equal to what was lent should be returned. And so says Ucathya:
"That wealth which has been returned by a surety when the debtor was not present..."
That debt shall not be doubled and paid by the debtor to the guarantor.

This refers to cases involving debtors and others where the place and time for questioning are appropriate; therefore, even if the debtor has not been questioned elsewhere, this prohibition does not apply, but rather there is simply equality with one who has been questioned. Regarding the common procedure for the liability of the surety (*lagnaka*) and the co-debtor (*upakṣayin*), Nārada states in this very context—following the discussion on the rules for the liability of the surety and the co-debtor:
"Whatever is lost or stolen through the fault of anyone, that must be borne by him, as well as whatever was destroyed through negligence."
Thus ends the section on sureties in the *Smṛticandrikā*, concerning the procedures for counter-claims against those provided by a surety and so forth.
Now, some statements regarding interest (*vṛddhi*) are recorded;
therein, Bṛhaspati says:
"Vṛddhi is declared to be fourfold, proclaimed as fivefold by others, and described as sixfold in this [work]. Understand them according to their true nature.
[359] When it is asked how there is a sixfold nature "in this," that is, in our own Dharmaśāstra, he himself says:
The bodily [interest], the periodic, and furthermore the compound interest;
likewise the stipulated, the interest on a pledge, as well as the profit from enjoyment.
When it is further asked what the nature of bodily interest and the others is, he says the same thing:
"Bodily interest is connected with labor; monthly interest is taken month by month;
compound interest is the growth upon growth; and stipulated interest is that which is agreed upon by the debtor."
"That which is collected daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (interest on the crest).
Satisfaction from the house, [income] from the assembly hall, and the gain from enjoyment from the field are proclaimed [as other forms].

The meaning of *kāyikā* is that where the physical labor itself—such as milking or driving [animals] of cows, camels, and so forth, once they have been pledged—is calculated as the interest. And thus Vyāsa says:
"Engaged in the acts of milking and carrying, it is declared to be bodily (*kāyikā*). Thus:
interest that is receivable monthly, obtainable every month, is *kālikā*; that interest which flows month by month is called *kālikā*.

Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Nārada: *Cakravṛddhi* is interest that accrues again every month as principal upon the original principal. *Kāritā* is interest agreed upon by the desire of the debtor; for it is stated in another legal text (*smṛti*) that "interest made by desire shall be *kāritā*. Therefore, this *kāritā* should be understood as having the reflexive suffix (*ṇic*) in its own sense, as per Vedic usage. However, interest caused by the instigation of another is strictly prohibited. And so says Kātyāyana: "But that interest which is stipulated by the debtor to be excessive, yet is always paid because it was agreed upon during a time of distress—that indeed is *kāritā*."
[360] "In no way should interest that has been stipulated otherwise be paid.

This means that interest called *kāritā*—which is more than what is stated in the scriptures and is devised by the debtor himself for the purpose of enticing the money-lender—may be paid; however, interest of a different kind, even if stipulated by the creditor, must not be paid. That which is obtained daily is designated as *śikhāvṛddhi* (top-knot interest) because of its resemblance to a top-knot (*śikhā*). When it is asked what this resemblance of the interest to a top-knot is, Bṛhaspati himself says:
"Like a top-knot, it grows constantly, but it ceases upon the cutting off of the head."
When the root is given, this is likewise remembered as the "crest-increase" (śikhāvṛddhi).

The phrase "is taken daily" is intended as an illustration for the taking of interest characterized by a specific number of days that has been agreed upon. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "But where a debtor pays interest exclusively at every [stipulated] time, that is remembered as *śikhāvṛddhi* (crested interest)."

The meaning of the passage beginning with "satisfaction from the house" (*gṛhāt toṣa*) is as follows: satisfaction derived from the vicinity of a house based on its habitation; and the fruit consisting of grain and so forth produced from a field, which is a specific type of interest known as the gain of enjoyment (*bhogalābha*). The mention of "house" and "field" is intended to include by implication any pledge consisting of immovable property that serves as an object of enjoyment. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "But when the entire pledge is used for enjoyment, and interest has been fixed [at zero], such a transaction is called 'pledge-enjoyment' (*ādhibhoga*)."
The meaning is that it pertains to all stationary things without exception.
Thus ends the section on the varieties of interest in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the rules regarding the measurement of interest.
On this point, Manu says:
"A moneylender may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month."

The meaning is that when a hundred *niṣkas* are lent, the moneylender (*vārdhuṣika*)—the one who lends the wealth for the sake of interest—may take an increase of three-quarters of a *niṣka* per month. This refers to cases involving collateral (*sabandhaka*); "with collateral, the monthly interest shall be one-eightieth part."

Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Yājñavalkya: the meaning is that when a loan is made preceded by the taking of a pledge (ādhi), the interest for each month shall be the eightieth part of the principal amount lent. As for what was stated by Manu as an alternative—"or he may take two per cent"—that is stated as a restricted option (vyavasthitavikalpa). For Vyāsa says: "In a secured loan (sabaṃdha), the share is one-eightieth; with a pledge (salagnaka), the share is one-sixtieth; in an unsecured loan (nirādhāna), a profit of two per cent per month is declared."

The meaning is that of the two types of transactions involving a guarantor (*ādhi*) and a surety (*pratibhū*), sixty and eighty percent respectively shall be taken each month; however, in a transaction free from these [guarantors], fifty percent shall be taken each month. "Two per hundred" means that two is given as interest on this hundred; by this turn of phrase, the fifty-percent share is stated. This rule of "two per hundred" applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa debtor; for a debtor who is a Kṣatriya or others, the rule is otherwise. And so says Manu: "Two, three, four, five, or even six percent on a hundred."
One may take interest for a month according to the sequence of the social classes (varṇas).

[362] This refers to the case of lending without a pledge or a surety, because it prescribes three hundred per cent and so forth in place of two hundred per cent for other classes. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"According to the order of the classes, [the interest shall be] two, three, four, or five percent; otherwise [it shall be different]."

Otherwise, the meaning is that there is an absence of both a pledge (*bandha*) and a fixed time for repayment (*kalagnaka*). Likewise, regarding a specific type of debtor, he himself stated another measure for the interest per month in place of the two-percent rate and so forth:
"Those traveling through forests [should pay] ten percent, while those traveling by sea [should pay] twenty percent."

Those who travel by difficult roads after taking money at interest shall pay ten percent every month; however, those who travel by sea shall also pay twenty percent—this is the meaning. Thus, he (Yājñavalkya) states that there is an option regarding the amount of interest agreed upon by the debtor, alongside the scriptural measures of interest such as the eightieth part: "Or they may all pay the interest agreed upon by themselves, among all classes."

The meaning is that all [debtor] classes, beginning with Brāhmaṇas, should pay the interest agreed upon by themselves to all creditor classes. And this option applies only to interest that has been stipulated (*kāritā*); in other cases, however, there is a rule regarding the restriction of the amount according to the scriptures—this is his own established position. Regarding property such as cattle employed for the sake of interest, he says that their offspring alone constitutes the interest: "But the offspring of cattle and women [is the interest]" (YDh 2.39). Here, "women" refers to female slaves. In the absence of offspring, the profit on the employed cattle and so forth consists in their nourishment or non-destruction.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, the rules regarding the measurement of interest [363].
Now,
the regulations concerning interest not stipulated by contract.
In this regard, Viṣṇu states: "He who,
having previously taken a loan on equal terms with the agreement 'I shall repay it tomorrow,' does not pay it later out of greed, shall incur interest at the rate of one per cent per day."

"Equal" means "without interest," that is to say, without increase. This is what is meant: even a debt accepted as being without interest, having been taken on the condition of a specific deadline for repayment, nevertheless begins to increase from the time immediately following that deadline. Regarding the case where items such as jewelry are handed over for the purpose of enjoyment and so forth, Nārada says: "No interest shall ever accrue on things given out of affection unless it was agreed upon.
Even if not agreed upon, [the interest] increases after half a year."

"Unstipulated" means not formally agreed upon; the implication is that it refers to gifts given out of affection (*prītidatta*) that are devoid of any specification regarding a request for repayment or a fixed date for return. The meaning of the phrase "even though unstipulated" and so forth is as follows: however, if a date for return has been specified, then even a gift of affection increases [in interest] after six months have elapsed from that date. Regarding the matter of failing to pay the price of goods received, Kātyāyana states:
"If one, having taken merchandise, should depart for another region without paying the price, that wealth shall incur interest after the lapse of three seasons."

This refers to interest that has not been specifically requested. What is the measure of interest in this case? It is said: since a measure dependent on the debtor’s acceptance is impossible here, and because any other measure conceived by human intellect would be outside the scope of the scriptures and thus improper, only the measure declared in the scriptures should be accepted; and that was shown in the preceding section with the words “the eightieth part,” and so forth. For this very reason, Viṣṇu stated: “One should pay interest even if it was not agreed upon, once a year has elapsed, as prescribed. The phrase “as prescribed” implies “as prescribed in the Dharmaśāstra. One should not argue that the meaning of the expression “as prescribed” cannot be that one should pay it exactly as it was stated by the defendant, the mediator, or the plaintiff; for Manu says: [364] *...* (Manu 8.152) ...and so on. Therefore, the meaning is that one should pay according to what is established by the authoritative legal treatises. Thus, the rule is settled. Furthermore, since the word *vṛddhi* (interest) is mentioned, it follows that the rule applies to all types of interest, including compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*), periodic interest (*kālavṛddhi*), and interest paid through labor (*kāritā-vṛddhi*). This is because the term *vṛddhi* is used generically for all forms of interest. As Yājñavalkya says: “Interest is of four kinds: stipulated, periodic, compound, and that paid through labor. Therefore, the rule regarding the maximum limit applies to all these types of interest. Consequently, the rule concerning the maximum limit of interest is established. "A rate higher than the established [legal] rate is not valid;
they call that the path of usury, for it deserves a fine of five percent."

The phrase "they call it the path of usury" censures interest exceeding what is prescribed by the scriptures. For the worldly custom regarding the taking of interest—which follows the interest rates established by the scriptures—is considered "fixed. Therefore, any interest higher than that does not hold for a creditor and the like if it is not fixed; the meaning is that such excess is outside the scope of the Dharmaśāstras. For this very reason, the censure—"they call it the path of usury, not the path of dharma"—is justified. The specific scope of the rule "it deserves five per hundred" will be stated later. As for what is said in the Vaiṣṇava text regarding "exceeding one year," that refers to the case of borrowed goods. And so says Kātyāyana:

"He who, having taken a borrowed item, departs for another region without returning it, shall have that property accrue interest after one year has passed. This means "having taken a borrowed item from which the principal has been settled. However, in the absence of such departure, the same author states the interest on the borrowed item starting from the time of its request: *Yācitakam upabhuñjāno dadyād vṛddhim atandritaḥ | anivedyopabhuñjāno dadyād vṛddhim ca sodayām ||* "Enjoying a borrowed item, one should diligently pay the interest; but enjoying it without reporting [the use], one should pay both the interest and the principal with interest. *Niyatāniyatā vṛddhir deyā sarvatra dharmiṇā | gṛhītuḥ sādhutāṃ vīkṣya kālaṃ caiva kulocitam ||* "The creditor should provide interest, whether fixed or unfixed, in all cases, having considered the borrower's integrity, the time, and the family custom. *Adattā yācitā vṛddhir aśuśrūṣā ca vai punaḥ | yācyamānasya mūrkhasya bhaved dāpyas tu tatsamam ||* "If interest promised [in advance] is not paid, or if there is a refusal to serve, then for the foolish person who is being asked [for the debt], he should be made to pay an amount equal to that [interest]. *Vṛddhiṃ caivāgrahītā yā vārddhuṣyaṃ vṛddhireva ca | caturguṇā bhavet kāle dviguṇā mūlyataḥ smṛtā ||* "The interest that is not taken, as well as the usury and the interest itself, shall become fourfold in time; however, it is traditionally held to be double the principal [if the time limit is exceeded]. *Gṛhītamūlyā yā vṛddhir vārddhuṣyaṃ vṛddhireva ca | dviguṇā sā bhavet kāle dviguṇā mūlyataḥ smṛtā ||* "The interest on what has been taken, as well as the usury and the interest itself, shall become double in time; it is traditionally held to be double the principal. *Vṛddhiṃ caivāgrahītā yā vārddhuṣyaṃ vṛddhireva ca | caturguṇā bhavet kāle dviguṇā mūlyataḥ smṛtā ||* "The interest that is not taken, as well as the usury and the interest itself, shall become fourfold in time; however, it is traditionally held to be double the principal. *Gṛhītamūlyā yā vṛddhir vārddhuṣyaṃ vṛddhireva ca | dviguṇā sā bhavet kāle dviguṇā mūlyataḥ smṛtā ||* "The interest on what has been taken, as well as the usury and the interest itself, shall become double in time; it is traditionally held to be double the principal. *Gṛhītamūlyā yā vṛddhir vārddhuṣyaṃ vṛddhireva ca | dviguṇā sā bhavet kāle dviguṇā mūlyataḥ smṛtā ||* "The interest on what has been taken, as well as the usury and the interest itself, shall become double in time; it is traditionally held to be double the principal. *Gṛhītamūlyā yā vṛddhir vārddhuṣyaṃ vṛddhireva ca | dviguṇā sā bhavet kāle dviguṇā mūlyataḥ smṛtā ||* "The interest on what has been taken, as well as the usury and the interest itself, shall become double in time;
