it is traditionally held to be double the principal. *Gṛhītamūlyā yā vṛ

"But even one who, while residing in his own country, does not pay what has been requested at any time—that person, though unwilling, shall be made to pay interest from that point, calculated as if it were an uncaused debt.

[365] The phrase "does not pay what has been requested" is to be connected with the subject under discussion. "From that point" means starting from the time of the request. Furthermore, regarding a gift of affection (*prītidatta*) or a loan for use (*pratimācita*), another rule was indeed commenced by that same author to specifically regulate the particular rate of interest starting from the time of the request.
A gift given out of affection shall not increase so long as it has not been asked for;
if it is not returned when requested, it increases by five percent per month.
Regarding deposits and other such matters, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that even what is not given increases [in interest] when requested:
"A deposit, the remainder of interest, as well as purchases and sales—
if these are not returned when requested, they increase by five percent per hundred."

By the term "buying and selling," the price of merchandise is indicated. As for that which was stated generally in the previously cited Mānava verse—"he deserves five per cent"—that should be understood as referring to subjects such as loans requested or gifts given out of affection. Thus ends the section on the rules regarding interest not stipulated in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now follows the exceptions to interest not stipulated.
In this regard, Nārada says: "The price of goods, wages, a deposit, a fine, and whatever is stipulated as a wager in gambling—
these increase [with interest] unless they are intended not to do so."

The "value of merchandise" (*paṇyamūlya*) refers to the price of goods such as clothing and the like. "Vain gifts" (*vṛthādāna*) refers to what has been promised to dancers and similar performers. "The stake of a gambler" (*ākṣikapaṇa*) refers to the gambling materials. The meaning is that when these aforementioned items exist, there is no interest on what has not yet been paid. In this context, interest on the value of merchandise applies only in the absence of a request for repayment while traveling abroad. However, for a deposit (*nyāsa*), there is no interest at all in the absence of a request for repayment, as it remains exactly as it was placed. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement made in the preceding section. Saṃvarta also says: "There is no interest on women's property, on profits, or on a deposit, as long as it remains in its original state."
In cases of uncertainty and regarding suretyship, it is not valid unless it is made by oneself.

There is no interest on what has been received. By stating "as it stands," he shows that interest accrues when there is a change in the nature of the deposit, such as its transformation into another form. When the wealth is doubtful—that is, when it remains in a state where it is improper for someone to give it due to uncertainty—and even in the case of a surety (*prātibhāvya*), such as the delivery of the debtor's property directly to the surety, there is no interest even after the demand for repayment. By saying "if it were not self-made," he shows that even in the case of a woman's property (*strīdhana*) and the like, if interest was stipulated, it must indeed be paid. Kātyāyana also [states this].
Interest shall never accrue on the price of leather, grain, liquor, gambling wagers, merchandise, and the bride-price,
nor on amounts received as surety.

By saying "always" (*sarvadā*), he shows that even after a formal request for repayment, there is no interest on what remains unpaid. Regarding the price of merchandise, the absence of contradiction with other statements should be understood as before. Although it may appear that "always" qualifies the entire preceding section, nevertheless, for the sake of consistency, it should be regarded as qualifying the price of merchandise. Vyāsa also says: "When those wishing to pay have already enjoyed a pledge or have received a loan secured by a surety, the interest on what has been admitted does not increase; likewise, the fine and the promised toll [do not increase]."

The mention of "enjoyed collateral" (*bhuktabandha*) is for the purpose of ensuring that interest does not accrue on a pledge or deposit that has been used, just as interest does not accrue on the enjoyment of a deposit. This point has been clarified by Gautama: "A pledge that is being used does not increase in value; this includes clothes, ornaments, and so forth. Furthermore, the phrase "those wishing to give back what was not taken" is mentioned alongside the exceptions regarding uncontracted interest (*akṛtavṛddhi*), because the discussion of the absence of interest follows from the exception to contracted interest. Its meaning has been clarified by Yājñavalkya: "He who does not accept his own wealth when it is being offered..."
But that which is established by one remaining neutral increases no further than that.

The ellipsis implies that he does not take [the object] due to reasons such as being incapable of protecting it or being greedy for its increase. In the absence of establishing a neutral mediator, even if something has been deposited and is requested, it continues to grow as before, because it is impossible for an effort to return it to have been made.
Thus ends the section on exceptions to the non-payment of interest in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the prohibitions regarding the taking of interest;
therein, Manu says:

One should not collect interest exceeding that of a year, nor that which is not sanctioned; likewise, one should not collect compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, or bodily interest.

Regarding the meaning of the first quarter-verse here, some say as follows: since the taking of interest is prescribed until the doubling [of the principal], there is no fault in taking interest even after a year; therefore, if one desires prosperity, one should not discharge—that is, should not take—that interest which accrues beyond a year. This is indeed the meaning that should be accepted, as there is no contradiction. Others, however, having supplied the words "such that by the magnitude of the interest the doubling [of the principal] would occur," say that one should not take interest exceeding a year. These are dull-witted, because this would result in the same meaning as already established by the rule: "Interest on a loan does not exceed doubling" (MDh 8.152), and because it is illogical to prohibit a magnitude of interest that would cause doubling in merely a year. Still others explain it thus: regarding the interest previously mentioned—where one might take five percent per month from a debtor—that interest, when taken from a debtor such as a Brāhmaṇa due to some form of agreement, should be taken for only a year and not beyond that. This meaning may also be accepted, as it lacks many of the faults found in the previous interpretation. As for the phrase "nor should he discharge what is not seen," its meaning is this: one should not take interest that is not seen in the Dharmaśāstras—such as six percent per month—which is merely imagined by one's own intellect.
But surely,
according to the nature of what has been done, nothing more or anything additional is established.

This statement would have its meaning already established by the preceding [verse] if it were explained in this manner. Some say: "Let it be a redundant restatement (*anuvāda*), since there is no other way [to account for it]. Others consider it to be a repetition of what has already been said for the sake of reinforcement (*dārḍhya*). But in reality, even though the prohibition is made by this [verse], because there is no agreement regarding interest when interest has not been previously established, it follows that only the interest prescribed by the scriptures is valid, and not some other interest obtained merely through agreement; thus, the purpose of that statement is to convey this, and so its meaning is indeed not already established. The two words "na vinirharet" (he shall not take) are connected by syntactic attraction (*anuṣaṅga*) with the words of the second half-verse. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: he shall not take that fourfold interest which is divided into *cakravṛddhi* and so forth. This is what is being said: interest such as *cakravṛddhi* and the like should not be accepted according to their own inherent nature.

But surely, even interest calculated as an eightieth part and so forth, when taken month by month, becomes *kālikā* (periodic); and that, being accepted by its own natural course (*svarasataḥ*), as well as interest agreed upon (*kāritā*) that is not excessive in amount, must likewise be accepted by its own natural course. Likewise, bodily interest (*kāyikā*) that is free from excessive oppression [is acceptable]. Therefore, how can there be a prohibition of these? It is said:
By whom was it stated that there is a prohibition of those?
Of which ones, then, is there a prohibition?
It is said:

Just as the interest prescribed by the statement of Vasiṣṭha—"But twenty [coins] for every five māṣas; thus the law is not violated"—is prohibited by another statement of Manu, namely, "the interest ordained by Vasiṣṭha," so too the periodical interest (kālikā) prescribed by Gautama—"Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five māṣas per month for every twenty [coins]"—is here prohibited. However, bodily interest (kāyikā) that causes excessive oppression is also prohibited by him; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.

But surely, how can that which was spoken by Gautama—the *kālikā* [interest]—which was ordained by him as being consistent with *dharma*, be prohibited? Just as that which was ordained by Vasiṣṭha was prohibited even though it was stated to be "consistent with *dharma*" in the words, "In this way, *dharma* is not lost," so too is it here prohibited. This is because it is unrighteous (*adharman*) due to its excessive amount. And its unrighteousness was stated by Manu when he said, "[Interest] which increases wealth.
How then is there a description by both Vasiṣṭha and Gautama of it as being consistent with *dharma*?

We say that [the rule] regarding five hundred [paṇas] refers specifically to the case of a Śūdra debtor. And thus, since it would be unjust (*adharmya*) if it applied to debtors other than Śūdras, it should be understood that Manu prohibited what might otherwise have been accepted there by some means. However, some explain the words of Gautama and others in this way in order to establish its justice even among the three higher castes:
"A māṣa is declared to be the twentieth part of a paṇa."

The *māṣa* mentioned in the *Smṛti* as being the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa* is what is understood here in the phrase “pañcamāṣikī” (five-māṣa interest). This being the case, the five-māṣa interest applied to twenty *kārṣāpaṇas* is only slightly more than the eighty-part interest; therefore, the argument that such interest is unrighteous (*adharmya*) is untenable. Regarding the two interpretations, even in the first, although both explanations are possible for Vasiṣṭha’s statement, the contradiction with Manu’s statement beginning with “vasiṣṭhavihitām” is unavoidable, because the phrase “one should abandon that which increases wealth when it is righteous” would otherwise be inconsistent. In Gautama’s statement, however, the contradiction with its own explanatory supplement—“thus, in sixteen months, it becomes double”—is difficult to resolve. For instance, according to the interpretation of the first commentators, four *kārṣāpaṇas* result from sixteen months; according to the second commentators, five *suvarṇas* result. Therefore, both interpretations are incoherent. In my view, however, there is no contradiction with the explanatory supplement, because when five well-known *māṣas* are charged as interest on twenty *vyāvahārika-niṣkas*, doubling is established in sixteen months. But there is a contradiction regarding its righteousness (*dharmyatva*), and that has been refuted by us; thus, there is no room for the objection. Precisely because this is a prohibition stating that “it should not be accepted according to its natural course,” and not that it should never be accepted at all, the same author states that if compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) is somehow admitted, it may fail to be recovered in some cases due to the fault of the creditor.
One who has ascended to the increase of the wheel, being established according to place and time,
will not obtain that fruit if he transgresses the requirements of place and time.

Regarding the phrase *atikrāman deśakālau* ("transgressing place and time"): if one transgresses the stipulated place or time and is not present there, then, due to his own fault, he shall not obtain that fruit; the meaning is that he does not receive that interest (*vṛddhi*). Because of the prohibition regarding the fruit, it is understood that he shall receive the principal, and because of the aforementioned prohibition, it follows that he may receive some other form of interest. Furthermore, there are other prohibitions against taking interest, such as "for a Brāhmaṇa, there is no usury," which were stated by Nārada and others. However, since those have already been demonstrated within the section on conduct in times of distress (*āpad-vṛtti*) in the midst of this daily discourse (*āhnika*), we have not presented them here.
Thus ends the section on the prohibition of taking interest in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the determination of the limit for the cessation of interest;
regarding this, Nārada says:
This rule for increasing interest is remembered as being universally applicable to debts;
however, there may be another local custom where the debt remains fixed.
A Vaiśya may indeed overcome adversity at his will through the practice of usury.

By these and other such statements, the rule that causes debtors' debts to increase is remembered as being desired everywhere, even regarding land. Where the debt remains increasing until it reaches double and so forth, there the established local custom differs from the established customs of other regions; this is the meaning. When it is asked how it differs, he himself says: "In one place it is double, in another triple, and likewise in another fourfold;
in yet another place, an eightfold amount is to be paid—thus it is settled in each region."

The debt to be paid increases; in some regions it becomes twofold, in some threefold, and in some fourfold—this is the meaning of how far it increases. Thus, the classification of the types of debt is established based on the difference in the goods lent. And so says Bṛhaspati: "Interest on gold is declared to be twofold, threefold on clothes and base metals, and fourfold on grain, as well as on wool, beasts of burden, and woolen cloth."
It is taught that for potherbs, the increase is fivefold; for seeds and sugarcane, it is recorded as sixfold;
and for salt, fats, and liquors, an eightfold increase is considered.
"It is said that when molasses and honey are administered, they take a long time [to produce their effect]."

Base metals (*kupya*) consist of tin and lead. *Śada* is the produce of a field; and according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), this refers to flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth, excluding grain. *Vāhya* refers to draft animals such as oxen, horses, and the like. *Lava* refers to wool, such as that of sheep, or hair, such as that of the yak (*camarī*). *Sneha* refers to substances like beeswax and the like. The two words "when lent" (*prayukte*) and "for a long time" (*cirakālike*) are connected with the word "gold and so forth" (*hiraṇyādipadena*) ending in the locative singular. For *śada*, *vāhya*, and *lava*, the phrase "for a long time" (*cirakālikeṣu*) is to be supplied. Similarly, for salt, oils, and liquor, the same supply is required. To illustrate the long period that constitutes the cause for doubling [the principal], the same author states that money lent at an interest rate of one-eighthth part becomes doubled when six years and eight months have elapsed.
The interest shall increase by one-eightieth part until the principal has doubled;
this occurs after seven years less one-third, without a doubt.

When interest is collected monthly at the rate of one-eightieth part of the profit, then for diamonds and the like, as well as for gold, the interest is likewise only double [the principal]. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "For diamonds, pearls, corals, gold, and silver, a double interest is prescribed when it has been stipulated according to the time."

The term *śukti* (oyster shell) is used figuratively for the pearl because it is produced from the *vajrasāha* (the oyster). However, Kātyāyana has stated it using its direct denotative word in the phrase "of gems, pearls, and corals"; this too is a reason for determining the figurative usage here. Regarding base metals such as copper and the like, the interest is exactly threefold. And so says that same author: "For copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin, and lead, the interest remains threefold after a long period of time."
As with seeds, even in the case of cotton, the increase is sixfold. And so Vyāsa says:
"In the case of vegetables, cotton seeds, and sugarcane, a sixfold increase is proclaimed.
As with oily substances, the increase of liquids is also eightfold. And so he [Vyāsa] says:
"They say that at the proper time, liquors, oils, juices, and fermented spirits possess eight qualities. Thus also says Kātyāyana:
"And of all oils, as well as of all liquors and clarified butters..."
The increase for molasses and salt should be known as eightfold.

In the case of sugar and other substances measured by weight (tulā), the interest likewise does not exceed eightfold, as in the case of molasses. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "Ghee measured by weight [incurs] eightfold [interest]. As for what he further stated: "Grain [incurs interest up to] threefold; liquids are explained by [the rule for] grain; and so too are flowers, roots, and fruits," that refers to a region where threefold interest is established as the limit, or it concerns a debtor who is impoverished. However, as for what Manu stated: "In the case of grain, fodder, wool, and beasts of burden, [the interest] does not exceed fivefold."

Thus, this refers to the case of a debtor who has fulfilled his obligation at the time of returning the loan. However, as for items such as blankets which are not mentioned in the Dharmaśāstras—such as the rule that "interest on gold is double"—their interest is indeed double, because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "For those not mentioned, it is double. The meaning is that when the interest remains fixed upon the debtor due to non-payment over a long period, the doubling of the principal does not exceed that limit in these cases, but not otherwise. In the absence of such long-term standing, however, the lent amount continues to increase; this is understood from the contrast in the rule "until the repayment," even though the limit is one hundredfold. Furthermore, Manu states that even during long-term standing, the limit of doubling is exceeded only in the case of interest that has been specifically stipulated, and not otherwise.
Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double the principal.

The term *kusīda* refers to that small amount which is given with the thought, "I shall take more. Because it is mentioned in connection with doubling (*dvaiguṇya*), gold is intended here. Its interest (*vṛddhi*) is established once; that is to say, it has not been transferred to another person, nor has it been cleared by being made principal; the meaning is that it does not exceed twofoldness together with the principal. Here too, it is understood through contrast that if it is transferred to another person or if the interest is made principal again, there is indeed doubling. When the debtor himself makes the debt, along with its interest, payable to another person, or when he clears the principal, or when the creditor, having made a pledge (*ādhi*) with another creditor, takes his own wealth back, then from that day until the limit of doubling or until repayment, it should be understood that it continues to grow. Thus, even in cases of threefoldness and so forth, interest established once does not exceed [the limit]; however, in the case of clothes and the like, it does exceed it, because the underlying principle is the same. It should be understood that in the case of threefoldness and so forth, the cessation of interest occurs only after a long duration, whereas otherwise it continues to grow.
Thus concludes the determination of the limit for the cessation of interest in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the exception to the cessation of interest;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
The growth of grass, wood, bricks, thread, yeast, leather, bone, armor, weapons, flowers, and fruits does not cease.

*Kiṇva* is a specific type of root that serves as the raw material for the substance *surā*. *Carman* is a shield used to ward off arrows and the like. *Varman* is armor. *Hetis* is a weapon. Regarding flowers and fruits, the non-cessation of interest is to be understood as applying to cases where the debtor is extremely wealthy at the time of repayment; otherwise, it would result in a contradiction with the statements in the preceding section which establish rates such as triple the principal. Viṣṇu also states: "Interest on *kiṇva*, cotton, thread, leather, armor, weapons, bricks, and charcoal is inexhaustible. However, regarding cotton, the lack of contradiction with the statement in the preceding section prescribing a sixfold rate should be understood as before. Vasiṣṭha also says:
The increase of ivory, hides, bones, horns, as well as those made of clay,
and likewise of flowers, roots, and fruits, is inexhaustible.
The meaning is that interest is inexhaustible; even when there is no repayment of the principal, it continues to increase a hundredfold. Bṛhaspati also says:
"The creditor may collect compound interest (*śikhāvṛddhi*), bodily labor (*kāyikā*), and likewise the profit from use (*bhogalābha*), as long as the principal has not been cleared."

The nature of *śikhāvṛddhi* and other types has been shown in the section defining the various kinds of interest (*vṛddhibheda*). "Not cleared" means that it has not been repaid by the debtor. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"But the pledge is enjoyed only so long as it is not returned.

This exception to the cessation of interest mentioned above is to be understood to apply to interest that has accrued over a long period and to interest that was stipulated once; for in those cases, there is the attainment of the general rule regarding the cessation of interest.
Thus ends the section on exceptions regarding the cessation of interest in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
and the chapter on debts and the giving of wealth by a debtor is concluded.
Now follows the procedure for the repayment of debt. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"A debt contracted for a short period must be paid when requested."
When the period has expired, there is the acquisition of peace; and in the absence of the father, [the property] belongs to the sons.

"For a short time, not for a long time" means for a limited duration. "Made [to be] returned on occasions such as the Festival of Lights" means made with a specific deadline. "With interest ceased" means when the growth of interest has stopped. This is what is meant: a debt for a short period must be paid immediately after being requested; however, one made with a deadline must be paid once that deadline is reached. As for a debt where interest has ceased, it must be paid immediately after the cessation of interest. Furthermore, in the absence of the debtor, his sons must likewise pay it in this same manner. And this rule regarding repayment immediately after the request and so forth does not exclude repayment prior to that, because a debt ought to be discharged quickly whenever possible. Regarding one who does not discharge a debt, the loss of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is shown in the *Purāṇa*.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still burdened by debts,
both his ascetic merit and his fire-sacrifices shall all belong to the creditor.
The meaning is that, for this reason, the debt must necessarily be discharged. With this very intention, Kātyāyana has also stated:
"He who, having taken a loan or other such advances, does not repay them to the owner, is born as his slave, servant, wife, or beast in the debtor's house."

A loan for use (*uddhāra*) and the like exist as something that must be returned, whereas a gift of affection (*prītidatta*) and the like do not. The distinction between a slave and a servant will be explained later. As for that which was stated by Nārada:
"If one does not pay a debt when requested—whether it be a loan or a pledge—that property increases until it reaches a hundred million."
Then, when a full hundred million [lives] have passed, encircled by that karma,
he shall become a horse, a donkey, a bull, or a slave in birth after birth.

Thus, in this context, the mention of "being asked for" (*yācyamāna*) is intended to demonstrate the excessive suffering that arises when a debt or similar obligation is not repaid upon request; it should not be understood as asserting that suffering occurs only when the one who is asked fails to repay, and not otherwise. Regarding what must be done by the debtor after repaying a debt recorded in a document, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having paid the debt, he should tear up the document, or else have another [document] made for the sake of his own purification."

The meaning of the second quarter [of the verse] is that one should receive a receipt from the creditor for the purpose of declaring freedom from debt. It is stated in the commentary on that [verse] that this alternative applies when the document of debt cannot be returned due to its being kept elsewhere, its loss, or similar reasons. When even this is somehow impossible, another alternative has been stated by Nārada:
"When the debt is cleared, he should give back the document; in its absence, a verbal acknowledgment.
In this way, there shall be mutual clearance between the creditor and the debtor."

The term *pratiśravaḥ* (promise) is used here in the sense of "having been repaid. To establish the testimony, one must inform learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) and others. Yājñavalkya says regarding the debtor who has witnesses:
"Whether it be with witnesses or otherwise, that [debt] must be paid back in the presence of witnesses."

The meaning is that a debt must be repaid in the presence of witnesses, specifically in the presence of the same witnesses as before. If the original witnesses are somehow unavailable, the debt may be repaid in the presence of other witnesses, since the general statement "in the presence of witnesses" is intended to support both alternatives. However, the new witnesses should be superior in number and quality to ensure they are capable of overriding the testimony of the previous witnesses.
Thus ends the section on the procedure for the repayment of debts in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the matters concerning insolvent debtors;
regarding this, Manu says:
He who, being unable to pay the debt, wishes to have a new transaction made, shall,
after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond.

Although the word *kriyā* (action) here denotes proof in general, because it refers specifically to the means of proof regarding a debt, it is restricted to documents and witnesses. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when a debtor, due to a lack of funds at the time of repayment, is unable to pay the principal along with interest, and wishes to perform again an act such as a document in order to secure the creditor’s consent and avoid the burden of the debt's long duration, he should pay the accrued interest and renew the instrument; that is, he should execute a new document or other act marked with the current year and so forth. However, when he is unable even to pay the interest already earned, the same author says:
Without showing the gold back there, one may exchange it;
one ought to give back as much interest as has accrued. [379]

The meaning of this is as follows: without having shown the gold and without paying the interest that has been earned, one may, right there at the very same time when the prior document was executed, cause a reversal; that is, one should treat the earned interest as the principal. However, that interest need not be equal to the interest on the lent capital; rather, it should be applied only in an extremely small amount. Even regarding the interest, by one who is able to pay only a portion, having paid that possible portion, the other portion which is impossible to pay should subsequently be applied in the same manner at the time of the prior document, because the logic is identical. But regarding one who is unable to pay the principal along with the interest at the time of repayment, Yājñavalkya says:
"The debtor, having paid the money, should write on the back of the document: 'Paid.

This means that even over time, as long as the entire debt has not been discharged, one should act in this manner and finally effect the tearing [of the document]. Alternatively, having paid a small amount according to his capacity, he should obtain from the creditor a document known as an *upagata* (acknowledgment of payment); and that must necessarily be granted by the creditor, or the creditor should provide the *upagata* marked with his own hand.

This is because he himself immediately thereafter stated it as an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*). Its meaning is that the creditor should give a receipt (*praveśapatra*) to the debtor, stating, "He has given this much to me. We shall explain another interpretation of this further below. And this alternative view applies when the previous one is not possible; thus Viṣṇu says: "In the case of partial payment and when the document is not present, the creditor should provide his own writing. The word "to the debtor" (*ṛṇikāya*) is to be supplied as the object. Likewise, Nārada says: "Having received [the debt], the creditor should give a receipt to the debtor upon the full repayment. [380]

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having taken the interest (*udaya*) earned by the debtor, the creditor shall give to the debtor what has been received. By using the word "interest" (*udaya*) to denote what has been earned, [the text implies]: "But a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay slowly, according to his earnings."

He shows that this same rule should be understood even regarding the subject matter already mentioned. Therefore, the alternative of writing on the back of the leaf (patrapṛṣṭha) should also be understood as applying to this very subject, since it has been considered by him. Thus, by the force of the rule for taking a loan in parts, one should understand that in this case alone there is a taking in parts, whereas elsewhere the entire debt is taken. Consequently, where there is a rule for taking in parts, there only does the cessation of interest apply to the portion paid; but elsewhere, as long as the whole is not paid, even what is being given in part must be rejected, or else interest must indeed be taken on the portion paid, because in that case the non-payment of the whole is equivalent to a mere deposit (*nikṣepa*). Nor should a small amount being given in a case of total depletion be rejected for fear of breaking the interest, because one who is depleted must be pursued and because of the injunction that he may be made to pay gradually. Even in the case of total depletion, the release of the pledge (*ādhi*) occurs only once immediately after the full repayment of the debt, and not repeatedly according to the portions paid, because even a high-value pledge remains pledged until the debt is fully discharged, as in the case of saying, "This pledge remains until I have paid you the debt. Nor should it be said that the debtor is not destitute simply because he holds ownership over the pledged wealth, for by having his ownership restricted, he is effectively like one who possesses nothing. Regarding the use of the pledge, there is no cessation of use according to the portion paid, following the logic of interest. For the acceptance of an eightieth part or similar interest per coin was established according to the wealth being held; therefore, it is logical that interest ceases for the portion returned while that wealth is still held. But the use of the pledge follows the status of the pledge as something to be used, not the wealth being held, since we see that even in the case of a small loan, if a high-value item is pledged, the entirety of it remains usable. Nor should it be argued that its usability is seen as such only due to the agreement, for we see it so even when it is not stated, "This entire thing is to be used by you," and because it remains as a pledge to be used until its release. And it has been stated that release occurs only once after the full repayment of the debt. Therefore, even in the case of total depletion, there is no cessation of use based on the portion of the pledge corresponding to the portion paid. Just as when a cow or similar animal is pledged with bodily interest (*kāyika-vṛddhi*) and a *niṣka* is taken by the debtor, the creditor takes the milk from all four teats even when only a portion of the *niṣka* has been returned; he does not, however, hand over one, two, or three teats to the debtor according to the portion paid. Likewise, when a horse is pledged, the creditor himself mounts the horse and travels the entire path; so it is here as well—enough of this excessive elaboration.

Regarding one who, out of wickedness, does not give what has been brought for him even when requested, the same author states his loss: "But he who, being asked, does not give, shall incur the loss of the remainder. Here, "remainder" refers to the portion that remains to be given. This should be understood to apply when the remainder is small; however, if it is not small, because the loss would be greater, he would not incur that [specific] loss, but rather the loss resulting from the failure to pay interest on the portion already received. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
A debt should be taken from a righteous person and others; however, if one does not record it in writing, nor pay what has been acknowledged, that debt shall accrue interest for him.
[382] For the purpose of explaining the meaning of this, the subject matter and the intended purport are first determined.
Or the creditor shall give back what has been brought forward, marked with his own hand.

The statement of Yājñavalkya has two meanings. One meaning is that the creditor should write upon the back of the debt-document (ṛṇalekhya), with his own hand as a mark, a note of admission (*upagata*) stating, "I have received this much wealth from him. The other meaning has been shown previously. By this statement, the loss of the creditor who fails to perform either of these two acts is declared. As for the literal sense: if a creditor, having recovered an incomplete debt from a debtor through legal pressure (*dharmopadhi*), force, or means such as confinement in prison, does not write upon the debt-document, "I have received this much," nor provide a receipt (*praveśapatra*), then from the day [the debt was recovered] until he makes the entry or gives the document, the money received from the debtor shall accrue interest—that is, it continues to increase for the debtor. When the question arises as to what kind of interest, Nārada [provides the answer].
Or if he does not write it down, even when urged by the debtor,
then that debt shall increase for the creditor in exactly the same way as it would for the debtor.

The meaning is that just as that debt-asset, being held over the debtor, increases for the creditor, so too does it increase for the debtor when held over the creditor. Thus ends the section concerning insolvent debtors in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now follow the means of recovering a debt from a debtor who is averse to returning it.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"A debtor who has admitted the debt should be made to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods.

The meaning is that one who has "admitted" (pratipanna)—that is, who has acknowledged the existence of the debt—should be made to pay, or rather, should be induced toward repayment by the creditor. And so says Manu: [383]
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth,
by those very means he should cause the debtor to pay, having brought him under control.
When it is asked, "What are those means?", Bṛhaspati states:
"By means of religious duty (*dharma*), fraud (*upadhi*), force (*balātkāra*), and by the confinement of the house.
By the phrase "by the confinement of the house," the very means known as *ācarita* (customary practice) is taught. He himself explains *dharma* and the others.

A debtor should generally be made to pay through the mediation of friends and relatives, by means of conciliatory speech, or by following [the creditor's] compliance; this is declared to be the righteous method.
When a creditor, having brought back wealth requested under a pretext from a debtor,
or having recovered a deposit and the like, causes [the debtor] to pay, that case is one involving fraud (sopadhi).
When a debtor is brought to his own home and compelled to pay through methods such as beating and the like, that is declared to be "force" (balātkāra).

"Having bound his wife, sons, and cattle, and having subjected her to the ordeal of being seated upon a red-hot iron image—if the debtor is made to pay his own debt, that is called *ācarita* (customary practice). Thus it is said.

By means of messages sent by friends and relatives, or by the commands of respectable persons; by being encouraged with affectionate words; by following or pursuing her; by frequent entreaties; or by artifice, such as bringing ornaments under the pretext of a festival or similar occasion; "borrowed" (*yācitaka*) refers to what has been requested; "lent for use" (*anvāhita*) refers to what was entrusted to another to be given back; by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), anything else brought about in some manner is included. One's own property (*artha*) means one's own wealth; it is "made to be returned" (*dāpyate*), meaning she is induced to give it back. The rest is clear in meaning. Furthermore, the means beginning with *dharma* (virtue) should not be employed at will, but rather should be applied as appropriate. And so says Katyayana:
One should cause a king, a master, or a Brahmin to pay by means of conciliation alone;
however, one may cause an heir or a friend to pay even by means of deception.
Bhṛgu said: "Merchants, farmers, and artisans shall be made to pay according to local custom; having oppressed the wicked, one should make them pay.

By the word "peacefully" (*sāntvena*), the means known as "righteousness" (*dharma*) is intended. By the word "having oppressed" (*saṃpīḍya*), the two means known as "force" (*bala*) and "customary practice" (*ācarita*) are included. When it is asked what this "local custom" (*deśācāra*) is, he himself says:
But the debtor, being restrained, should be kept in public view in an assembly of people until he pays what is due,
according to the established customs of the region.

In a place where a creditor detains [the debtor] himself and holds him, he should be held in that very manner. However, in a case where a merciless person seeking wages detains and holds [the debtor] from the presence of the debtor himself, there he should be held through the mediation of that other person; such is the meaning of the phrase "according to the established local custom. Thus, the act of detention itself is called "local custom" because it conforms to local practice. He states that even for one who has been detained, a slight favor should be shown regarding his necessary obligations.
If a person carrying [the corpse] should feel the urge to void excrement or urine,
he should be followed from behind, or one should release it while it is securely bound.

"Secured" means bound by chains or other such means. The second alternative applies to the case of a debtor who is indigent, while the first alternative applies to cases other than that; this distinction should be understood according to what is appropriate. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states another rule regarding both types of cases: "He [the debtor] should be released day after day once a surety has been provided;
however, at the time of meals and during the night, he remains under restraint because of the surety."

That person being held—such as a merchant or the like—must be released at the time of his necessary business once he has provided a guarantor for his appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*). The meaning is that the guarantor stands as a guarantee against flight. However, when no guarantor can be found, or when one who has been found does not provide him, then, regarding the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) in this most inferior case, he states another alternative: "He who cannot find a guarantor for his appearance, nor provide one, shall be confined in prison or placed under custody after informing the guards. (NSm 1.23)

"In a prison" means in a place for moving about, that is to say, in a common jail. "Should be placed" means he should be sent there. The first alternative concerns one who does not pay even when a surety has been obtained, because of his extreme wickedness. The second alternative concerns one for whom no surety can be found, because of the absence of such extreme wickedness. Regarding the case of one who is neither of these two types [i.e., one who is not excessively wicked], he (Yājñavalkya) states another pair of alternatives in place of these two:
"A nobleman, one who is trustworthy, or one who is pure, should not be confined in prison;
he should be released unbound, or if bound, only under oath."

*Prātyayikaḥ* means trustworthy because he will not flee; *anibaddhaḥ* means one who is not bound by a guard. Thus, in place of the phrase "having informed the guards and sent him away," it is understood that this is one alternative (*pakṣa*). The other alternative, however, by process of elimination, should be seen as occupying the place of the alternative stated as: "He should be confined in a prison" (*sa cārake niroddhavyaḥ*). Although the method called local custom (*deśācāra*) has been described as pertaining to merchants and the like, nevertheless, since the alternative of favoring those worthy of it—such as the noble classes (*ārya*) and others—is being established, it should be understood that even for Brahmins and others who are to be dealt with through the method called *dharma*, the method of local custom must be employed together with the alternative of favorable treatment. One who employs the methods of *dharma* and so forth in the manner described above should not be prevented by the king, because an act of humiliation (*dharṣaṇa*) performed according to the path of traditional law (*smṛti*) and custom is not to be obstructed. For this very reason, Manu says:
A creditor who recovers his own property from a debtor shall not be prosecuted by the king for recovering his own wealth.

He must not be prosecuted, nor should anything be said against him. And so Viṣṇu states: "One who recovers a loan lent in any manner whatsoever shall not be censured by the king. The phrase "in any manner whatsoever" implies that it must be done without contradicting the path of the Smṛtis and established custom; for one who recovers it in contradiction to those, the king must certainly restrain him because of his wickedness. As for what was stated by that same author: "If the debtor, while being pursued for recovery, approaches the king, he should be fined an amount equal to that [debt],"—here too, the phrase "without contradicting the path of the Smṛtis and established custom" should be understood as an ellipsis, otherwise the imposition of a fine would be unjustified. "Equal to that" means equal to the debt being recovered. He is not only to be fined, but also made to pay the debt. And so says Yājñavalkya.
One who is proving his case before having approached the king should not be censured by the king;
but one who, while being tried, goes to the king [himself], shall be punished and made to pay that debt.
The general statement "he is to be punished" is intended so that even a very small fine may be imposed in cases where the offense is minor; for this very reason, a small fine was shown by Manu:
"He who, at his own pleasure, reports to the king a creditor who is recovering his debt, shall be made to pay to the king a fourth part of the debt, and the debt itself to the creditor. [387]

"By *chanda* means by one's own will; that is to say, without even informing the king. On this point, Bṛhaspati says: "This is the rule for one who has admitted [the debt]; however, if he denies it in court, he is made to pay after establishing [his liability] by means of a document or witnesses."

This aforementioned group of legal means applies to a debtor who admits the existence of the debt. However, as for one who denies it—one who is in disagreement regarding its existence and attempts to evade it—he must have the debt established by evidence in an assembly and then be made to discharge it; this is the meaning. And thus, what was stated by Manu is consistent: "One should recover a lent object by means of moral suasion, by legal process, by artifice, by social pressure, and fifthly, by force."

In this context, it should be understood that "by means of legal procedure" (*vyavahāreṇa*) refers to cases involving denial (*vyapalāpin*), while the other [term] refers to cases of mutual agreement (*saṃpratipanna*). For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states the prohibition of means other than legal procedure in the case of non-agreement:
"One who asserts a legal action (*kriyāvādī*) in a doubtful matter should by no means be obstructed.
But he who obstructs one who should not be obstructed becomes liable to punishment according to the law."

The phrase "it must not be obstructed" is intended to demonstrate the prohibition of *chala* (equivocation) and other such fallacies. He himself explains the meaning of the terms "one who asserts action" (*kriyāvādī*) and "one with ambiguous words":
"Whatever is to be given according to justice, that I give.
Where a debtor speaks in this manner, he is called one who asserts action.
"Where there may be a dispute between two parties regarding the acquisition of form, number, and so forth,

or even concerning what is to be given or not given— that matter is declared to be doubtful. Regarding a doubtful matter, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that for one who acts contrary to the established dharma, there shall be loss of the object and a fine.
But he who proceeds with regard to a doubtful matter without having informed the king should be forcibly punished, and that legal matter shall not be established.
"By force" means by compulsion. Kātyāyana also says:
"But where a creditor causes suffering to a debtor who speaks rightly, he shall lose that amount of wealth and incur a fine equal to it."

The intention is that even when the debtor acts contrary to his obligations, one must apply oneself to the very means called "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*) in order to bring about the cessation of that misconduct. And since that means—extending from the formal claim (*pratijñā*) to the penalty (*daṇḍa*)—has been explained in the first chapter, we shall now conclude.
Thus ends the section on the means of recovering a debt from a debtor who is averse to returning it, within the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow other statements concerning debtors who are difficult to compel.
In this regard, Yama says:
"But a debtor who possesses wealth yet does not pay due to wickedness should be made to pay by the king, having seized him, after [the debt] has doubled."

The meaning is: "then from the wicked debtor. The term "twofold" is intended to indicate the principal amount together with interest (*savrddhika*). One should recover the debt from the wicked creditor by means of force, deception, or other such methods. And so says Bṛhaspati:
[389] "When the deadline has expired, the creditor shall recover the debt along with the agreed-upon profit (*śāntalābha*)."

"Securing" (*udgrāhaṇa*) means recovering [the debt] by means such as force. When the fixed period has expired, for one who has contracted a debt with a time limit, "securing" must be carried out after the cessation of the profit [accruing from the use of the property]; likewise, for one who has made a peace-treaty regarding the profit without a time limit, "securing" must be carried out due to the fear that it will be difficult to recover. Otherwise, it would be improper. Regarding the debtor, however, he [Yājñavalkya] states another alternative for the purpose of repayment: "Or the debtor may cause a document to be executed according to the arrangement of compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
Compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) is interest upon interest. He also states a specific rule regarding the principal: [He] says the same regarding the principal: [text follows].
When interest at double the rate is stipulated,
then the profit from the use of the property shall constitute the principal with interest for the men involved.

By this very statement, it is understood that either a pledge capable of yielding enjoyment proportionate to double the value of the object, or compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*), takes its place. Because of the mention of "doubling," it is understood that the previously mentioned alternative of executing a new document applies only when the profit has ceased, and not at the completion of the stipulated period or other such occasions. Therefore, in that case, the debtor must execute a new document according to the actual agreement, rather than by the rule of compound interest and the like; for the doubling of the amount and so forth [apply only to the latter]. Regarding the three alternatives mentioned earlier, the arrangement depends on the creditor's wish. As for the debtor who, due to poverty, simply does not pay, Nārada says that he too should be made to pay little by little.
Now, if he should become devoid of means due to the lapse of time,
he shall be made to pay the debt according to his capacity, from time to time, as it arises.
The word "brāhmaṇa" is to be supplied as the subject of "should be made to pay. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"One of low caste who is impoverished should be made to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
but a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income."

The ellipsis implies that he should make him work even by force; having bound him when there is no possibility of providing him with wealth, he should make him perform labor under his own control, according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana. However, one who is incapable of performing labor should be kept in a prison.

"One who is unable [to pay] should be cast into prison, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa," because it has been stated by that very same [author]. The result of this imprisonment is that, upon the emergence of the capacity [to pay], a debt is somehow recovered. Furthermore, as it was stated by that same author: "One should compel farmers—whether they be Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who are making an effort, to pay."

Thus, the phrase "according to the [order of] arising" refers to the scope of those who are capable of paying the debt. As for the statement, "having caused one who is incapable of paying the debt to be seized by his wife," this refers in every respect to the scope of those who are entirely incapable of paying the debt; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. However, when it is required to consider how one who is difficult to compel because of the simultaneous presence of multiple creditors (*aneka-ṛṇa-samavāya*) should be made to pay, Yājñavalkya states: "The debtor shall be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they received the loans.
But having paid to the Brāhmaṇa first, he shall pay to the king immediately thereafter."

The meaning is "of the king who is a Kṣatriya. The meaning of the statement has been explained by Kātyāyana: "But when there is a concurrence of multiple debts, whichever was contracted first must be paid first; however, for the king, it shall be after [the debt owed to] a Śrotriya."

In this context, a *śrotriya* is one who possesses merely the Brāhmaṇa caste, and not one who possesses learning and Vedic study; for the term *śrotriya* is used here with reference to a higher caste in relation to the royal (Kṣatriya) caste. When there is a conflict between the order of the creditor and the order of the caste, the order of caste must be followed, because the Brāhmaṇa is to be favored due to his venerability. Likewise, when a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, or a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, present themselves simultaneously, the debt should be paid according to the order of the castes (*varṇakrama*), because each preceding one is more excellent and thus more worthy of favor. When the discharge of debts is carried out in this manner and a debtor becomes impoverished before the debt has been fully discharged, his only recourse is to follow the path prescribed in the verse beginning with "one of low caste who is impoverished. However, when multiple debts contracted on the same day coincide, the aforementioned order of payment does not apply; rather, if the debtor has abundant wealth, the payment must be made simultaneously. But if his wealth is meager, he should be made to pay the portions simultaneously after dividing them according to those respective debts. Thus says Kātyāyana:
Where a debt is recorded on a single day, one may discharge it equally at any time;
however, for the receipt, the characteristics, and the profit, it shall be according to the sequence.

One should treat the seizure (*ādhi*), the lending of wealth (*ādhidhana*), its protection—that is, its preservation—and the profit, which is the gain in the form of enjoyment, all equally. Otherwise, in the case of a difference in days, the repayment of the debt shall follow the order of writing or the order of the castes (*varṇa*). Regarding pledges and the like, however, one should refer to what has been stated in the section on the summary of legal pronouncements concerning the removal of disputes over pledges. He himself states an exception to the rule beginning with "In that case, one should repay the debt equally": "Whichever person should prove that whatever commodity was acquired by means of another's property..."
That property must be returned by the debtor alone; it cannot be otherwise.

Whatever merchandise was taken by the debtor for the purpose of trade from the creditor's wealth, and whatever wealth has been acquired through the sale of that merchandise—even if there is a combination of other debts—that must be given by the debtor specifically to that creditor for the purpose of clearing the debt; it means it must not be given otherwise than in the manner previously described.
Thus ends the section concerning debtors who are difficult to recover from in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
and with this, the major section summarizing the rules for the recovery of lent capital is concluded.
Now follows the determination of those to whom a debt must be repaid.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
A debt contracted for a short period must be paid upon request;
once the term has expired, it must be paid with interest at the rate of one śānta, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons.

"It must be paid by the debtor"—this is the remainder [of the sentence], because when possible, the debt must be discharged by the debtor himself. And "in the absence of the father, by the sons"—the meaning of this is as follows: in the absence of the father who is in a state of being burdened by debt, upon his death, the debt incurred by the father must necessarily be paid to the creditor by the sons. Nārada states the reason why the discharge of the father's debt is mandatory:
"Fathers desire sons for their own sake, thinking:
'He will liberate me from both the creditor and the debtor.'"
Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive with effort to liberate his father from debt, so that he may not fall into hell by abandoning his own welfare.

The meaning is: "by whatever means among those such as approaching a wife, adopting a daughter, or taking a son. "The highest debt" refers to that which is declared by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), beginning with: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born burdened with three debts. "The lowest debt" is that which has been taken from another's hand according to the rules of usury. Alternatively, by the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the terms "creditor" (*uttamarṇa*) and "debtor" (*adhamarṇa*), it should be understood that only the debt contracted through the practice of usury is intended. As Kātyāyana says: "By sons who have been born, fathers are released from the lowest debt only through giving."
"Since liberation [comes] from that, therefore fathers desire sons. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is: "by means of giving," that is, by repaying the debt, having renounced one's own interest in the form of enjoyment and so forth; for it is impossible to renounce one's own interest in the form of *dharma*. As for the sense of the sentence: since they desire this, therefore the father must necessarily be released from the debt. Nor should it be said that because of the expression "by those who are born" (*jātaiḥ*), the obligation to release the debt belongs to one merely at birth; for [the requirement] to "renounce one's own interest" and so forth is not possible during the state of infancy. Therefore, the meaning of the word "born" (*jāta*) should be understood as depending on the supply of the word "having become" (*jāta*) in the sense of being capable of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). For this very reason: [The verse continues: "Therefore, one should perform sacrifices, procreate offspring, and practice charity. (Gautama Dharmasūtra 8.1) This is stated to exclude the possibility that the duty of performing sacrifices and so forth might apply even to one who has not yet reached the age of discretion. Furthermore, the phrase "one should procreate offspring" implies that the son must be procreated with the intent that he will perform the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*); otherwise, the purpose would not be fulfilled. Thus, the meaning of the word "procreate" (*prajayeta*) is that one should procreate a son who is capable of performing the rites. Otherwise, the injunction would be useless, for the mere act of procreation does not accomplish the intended goal. Therefore, the meaning of the word "born" (*jāta*) in the previous passage is to be understood as referring to one who has attained the capacity for worldly activity. Consequently, the following statement is made: "One who, having been born, does not perform sacrifice, nor procreate offspring, nor practice charity, steals the wealth of the ancestors and falls headlong into hell. (Manu Smṛti 3.160) In this context, the word "born" (*jāta*) is used in the sense of "having become capable of worldly activity. This is because the term "born" is employed elsewhere in the same sense, as in the passage: "By the mere fact of being born, a Brahmin is freed from his debts to the seers" (Manu Smṛti 6.35). Since the word "born" is used there in the sense of "becoming capable of worldly activity," it follows that here too the word "born" is used in that same sense. Therefore, the meaning is that one should perform sacrifices and so forth after having become capable of worldly activity. It is not the case that the duty to perform sacrifices and so forth applies to one who has not yet reached the age of discretion.
