Therefore, the meaning is that one should perform sacrifices and so forth after having become capable of worldly activity. It is
If one has not attained legal capacity, even if independent, he is liable for debt in this world.

Thus it was stated by that very [author]. One who has attained legal capacity (*vyavahāra*) is sixteen years of age; this is because at that stage, there is the full maturation of the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. However, one becomes independent (*svatantra*) even during childhood due to the death of the father. Therefore, it is said here: "even though independent. And thus, even when the father has passed away, [the debt] must not be paid by those who have not attained legal capacity, since there is no fault in non-payment. But at the time of awakening [to responsibility], it must be paid with all one's power, because there is a fault in non-payment. Regarding this, Katyayana says: "But when the father has passed away, [the debt] is never [to be paid] by those who have not attained legal capacity."
[394] But it must be given at the proper time according to the prescribed rule; otherwise, they shall dwell in hell.

In the phrase "in some cases," the word "should be paid" is to be supplied. "By rule" means by the rule set forth in the section on the repayment of debts. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that even while the father is still alive, if he is unable to repay the debt incurred by the father, the sons must pay it: "Even while the father is present, if he is afflicted by disease or likewise residing abroad, the debt incurred by the father must be paid by the sons after twenty years."

The phrase "starting from twenty years" implies that this refers to the commencement of his absence. The debt must be paid by the sons only when the place where he has gone is unknown; otherwise, since the father himself could have settled the matter through means such as sending him away, the sons would not be liable. However, in the case of one afflicted by disease, the debt is to be paid only after a determination has been reached regarding his actual condition, age, number, and so forth. Thus says Bṛhaspati:

"Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven [as due], provided he is blind from birth, an outcast, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, or similar diseases."

In the case of no disagreement, however, the gift must be made immediately after the request, as stated in the passage beginning, "it should be given to one who asks," because there is no recollection of any other time. By the word "etc. in the phrase "consumption, leprosy, etc.," only those diseases that are difficult to cure and resemble consumption or leprosy are included, but not fevers and the like. Furthermore, even if they are sons born blind and so forth, nothing should be given by them when the father has passed away, is abroad, or is afflicted by disease and thus incapable, because they are unworthy of a share of the paternal estate; this is because those suffering from consumption and similar ailments are excessively tormented. And so says Kātyāyana:
One should cause the son to pay the debt if he is free from affliction, capable of wealth, and fit for the burden; otherwise, one should not cause the son to pay. [395]

"Worthy of wealth" (*draviṇārhaḥ*) means worthy of a share in the paternal estate. "Bearing the yoke" (*dhuryaḥ*) means one who carries the burden for his father. By using the word "worthy," he shows that even if the son does not take the paternal property, if he is capable, he must be made to pay [the debt]. One afflicted by diseases difficult to cure and the like, as well as those unworthy of the paternal estate such as the blind and so forth, and those not bearing the yoke—meaning those lacking the authority to discharge debts contracted by the father—it has been stated [in the verse] "one should not make the son pay otherwise. And this phrase "and bearing the yoke" refers to the case of multiple sons existing in a relationship of primary and secondary status; thus says Nārada:
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, or whoever may have undertaken that burden.

The phrase "according to their respective shares" refers to the case of divided sons, in accordance with the scriptures prescribing the distribution of unequal shares. However, those who are undivided and share equally shall give an equal portion of the wealth. Those who are undivided but exist in a state of mutual subordination shall give by way of collective enterprise (*saṃbhūya-samutthāna*). Among undivided sons existing in a relationship of subordinate and principal, only the one who is the principal shall give the whole, because the subordinate has no independent authority. Furthermore, where there are sons both divided and undivided from the father, that debt which was contracted by the father after the division need not be paid by them; for while the undivided sons remain, the divided ones have lost their entitlement to the paternal estate through the act of partition, and thus they do not inherit the paternal property once the father has died. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
While the debt to the ancestors remains unpaid, a son shall not take the inheritance;
that wealth must be given to the creditor, for he who takes it after [the father] has died shall be made to pay it back.

The meaning is that even while taking possession of that property when the father has died, the son must be made to pay [the debt]. However, in the case of a conflict between a debt incurred by the father and one incurred by himself, the debt incurred by the father must be paid first; for Bṛhaspati records: "First the debt contracted by the father, and afterwards his own. Furthermore, the father's debt must be paid just like one's own:
"A debt contracted by the father must be paid by the sons as if it were their own, provided it is proven."

This is because it was stated by that very same [author]: "Like one's own" means that just as one's own debt is to be paid with interest, so too [is the father’s]. Regarding the phrase "we do not know," where a denial is made by the sons, the meaning of the word *vibhāvita* (established) is: if it is established by evidence, it must be paid; if not, it need not be paid. He himself states that in every case, certain paternal debts should not be paid by the sons:
"A debt for spirituous liquor, a gift made in vain, a promise made out of lust or anger, a suretyship, and the remainder of a fine or tax—these the sons shall not be compelled to pay."
"Saura" refers to that given for the purpose of procuring liquor; "ākṣika" means that which is caused by defeat at gambling. "Vṛthādāna" (fruitless giving) is described in another Smṛti:
"What is given to a rogue, a bard, a wrestler, a quack physician, a gambler, a cheat, a flatterer, an elephant-driver, or a thief, becomes fruitless."
Kātyāyana has stated that there is a promise made out of lust and a promise made out of anger:
"Whatever has been promised, whether recorded in writing or given orally, to a woman who previously belonged to another— know that among men, this is a promise made out of lust."

"For that which is spoken to cause satisfaction after having produced injury or destroyed property out of anger, one should know that to be debt created by anger. *Muktaka* means without a written document (*lekha*). "To a woman previously belonging to another" means to the wife of another. Regarding the passage beginning with "where... injury," this is the meaning: having committed injury or the destruction of wealth against another out of anger, and having promised, "I shall give wealth for his satisfaction," that debt is born of anger. By "suretyship" (*prātibhāvya*), what is intended here is that which is to be paid by a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*). And so says Manu:
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous debt, what is due from gambling, what is due from liquor, or the remainder of fines and taxes.
"But regarding surety for appearance, there shall be the rule previously enjoined.

The "rule previously enjoined" refers to the rule stating, "A son is not liable to provide surety. However, that a son must pay the surety-debt, and in what manner it must be paid—all of this has been demonstrated in the very section on sureties (*pratibhū*). The meaning of the two terms "fine-remainder" (*daṇḍaśeṣa*) and "toll-remainder" (*śulkaśeṣa*) has been clarified by Uśanas:
"Whether it be a fine, or the remainder of a fine, or a toll, or the remainder of a toll."
But a son must not give that which is not legally available for transaction.
The meaning is that it is conventional, pertaining to the solar year.

Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, regarding the determination of those who must repay a debt, the rules concerning sons have been presented; now, some statements concerning grandsons (*pautra*) are recorded therein.
On this point, Kātyāyana says:
Bhṛgu says that a debt seen by the father which descended from the grandfather,
being faultless and not discharged by the sons, must be paid by the grandsons.

Seen by the father means that it was understood by the father without doubt as having been made by his own father. Inherited from the grandfather means obtained through the succession of ancestors due to the absence of preceding generations. Faultless means free from defects that would render it non-transferable. Not withheld by sons means not set aside by sons on account of incurable diseases or other such conditions. And thus says the same author: "But that which belongs to the grandfather and was not given away by the sons while they were living in a state of illness—it is of this kind that the grandfather's property, being equal, should be given by the citizens."
"Equal" means without interest, that is to say, the principal alone. However, when the sons discharge only a portion [of the debt], they must pay the remaining unpaid share;

for it has been stated by that same author: "That debt which remains after what was given, or the remainder of the debt, is what must be paid regarding the grandfather's debt. He further states that what is not of this nature is not to be paid.

"A debt that is defective or repudiated by the father should never be paid. Here, "defective" means tainted by faults such as being incurred for the purpose of drinking liquor and the like. "Repudiated by the father" means rejected or denied by him; however, a debt established by evidence—even if not seen or denied by the father—must be paid. "A debt should be paid by sons and grandsons; when it is denied, it must be proven by witnesses."

Thus it was stated by Yājñavalkya. The inclusion of the word *sadā* (always) is for the purpose of indicating that which is not to be given (*adeya*); therefore, other things also mentioned as not to be given to sons—such as the *śulka* (bride-price) and so forth—should be understood to apply to grandsons as well. Furthermore, it has been shown in the section on sureties (*prātibhū-prakaraṇa*) that no kind of suretyship whatsoever is to be paid by grandsons. Grandsons, too, must pay only when they have attained legal capacity (*prāpta-vyavahāra*), because those who have not attained legal capacity lack the authority [to pay], according to the principle already stated regarding sons. Regarding the case of one who has gone abroad (*proṣita*), the time for repayment is the same for grandsons as it is for sons; and thus Viṣṇu says: "When the debtor is dead, has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), or has gone abroad, the wealth must be paid by his sons and grandsons after twenty years. Beyond this, it need not be paid by those who do not desire it. The term *pravrajite* means one who has taken up the life of a wandering ascetic (*saṃnyasta*). "After twenty years" means during an absence lasting twenty years, or an exile lasting twenty years, committed by the debtor. The phrase "beyond this, not by those who do not desire it" means that after twenty years, no delay should be made even by those who do not wish to repay the debt. Alternatively, the meaning is this: beyond these [three generations], namely the sons and grandsons, those born after them—such as great-grandsons (*prapautra*) and so forth—need not pay if they do not desire it. This is what is meant: only sons and grandsons, excluding those such as those born blind from birth, possess an unconditional right to inherit (*riktha-arhatva*); others, such as great-grandsons and so forth, do not. In the absence of inheriting property, great-grandsons and the like must certainly not pay, just as sons and grandsons [do not pay beyond their limit]. For this very reason, Nārada says: [The text continues with further citations and commentary.]
That debt which was cleared by sons, having been received in succession without obstruction, the grandsons must pay; that debt of the grandfather ceases with the fourth generation.
Kātyāyana also says:
"Even in the absence of a son, the debt must be paid by the grandson with effort;
it need not be paid by the fourth descendant, for from him that obligation ceases."

Thus, it should be understood that the lack of entitlement to discharge the debt incurred by a great-grandfather and others applies only to one who has not received the inheritance from the fourth descendant onwards, and not to one who has received the inheritance. Even before the father has paid his own debt, the grandson must pay the great-grandfather’s debt when there is a concurrence of the three debts incurred by himself, his father, and his grandfather;
in such a case, the great-grandfather’s debt must always be paid first.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati: "Of those two," meaning by those two, namely the father and one's own [self]. In this way, the son’s obligation to pay the debt arises from his entitlement to the inheritance, provided there is no other primary grandson (dhuryapautra) or the primary paternal uncle (pitṛvya). However, if a primary grandson exists, the non-primary grandson has no authority, because he lacks such status. When grandsons and others who are equal sharers are divided, the discharge of the debt occurs according to their respective shares; but when they are undivided, it occurs through joint effort (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*), and so forth—this should also be understood here. For the statements concerning grandsons are intended merely to demonstrate specific exceptions; since it is understood that apart from the specified exceptions, the rule is the same as for sons. Furthermore, the authority of grandsons who have received the inheritance lies in the discharge of the debt along with interest, because the rule "the grandfather’s debt should be paid in full" applies to cases where the inheritance has not been received.
"The debt of the grandfather must always be paid first by those two"—
this statement establishes a specific rule regarding the sequence [of payment], because of the use of the word "always," even for grandsons who have not received the paternal estate.

Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, regarding the determination of those who must repay a debt, [the section on] the grandson has been concluded; now follow the matters concerning the heirs to the estate (*rikthagrāha*) and others.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
A debtor shall be made to pay the debt, as shall one who has taken a woman [as a wife];
likewise, a son whose property is not dependent on others shall pay for his father who is heirless.

Here, first the meaning of the words is stated. One who takes possession of the property according to the order of inheritance is the *rikthagrāha* (heir). One who, out of passion or other motives, takes another’s wife as his own wife is the *yoṣidgrāha* (one who takes a woman); this does not refer to a paramour (*jāra*) appointed to procreate a son, because those two lack the status of a "taker" since they merely engage in sexual enjoyment. One who, being unfit for inheritance due to disability such as lameness, does not possess property dependent on his parents, is one whose property is not dependent on others (*ananyāśritadravya*). Those who are *rikthagrāhas* are further designated by the term *rikthin* (heirs). Now the meaning of the quarters (*pāda*) is stated. Regarding the first and last quarters, the meaning is this: whether there exists a son unfit for inheritance or not, the *rikthagrāhī* shall pay the debt. And thus says Viṣṇu: "Whether he has sons or is sonless, the *rikthagrāhī* shall pay the wealth. This is what is meant: just as when there exist sons or grandsons who are entitled to a share of the inheritance, no one other than them bears the debt, so it is here. Just as the *rikthagrāhī* pays the debt whether a son characterized by lameness or similar disabilities exists or not, in the same way, when there is an absence of a *rikthagrāhī*—whether a son characterized by lameness or similar disabilities exists or not—the *yoṣidgrāha* shall pay the debt; such is the meaning of the second quarter. And thus says Viṣṇu himself: "The woman-taker (*strīgrāhī*) of one who has no wealth (*vidhana*). The phrase "whether he has sons or is sonless" carries over from the previous context. By saying "of one who has no wealth," he indicates one who is devoid of a wealth-seizer (*dhanahārin*). However, Bṛhaspati has stated this clearly.

"And likewise, in the absence of the one who takes the wealth, there shall be the one who takes the wife. The meaning is that just as the one who takes the wealth is liable for the debt, so too, in the absence of the one who takes the wealth, the one who takes the wife shall be liable. The meaning of the third quarter [of the verse] is that in the absence of both the one who takes the wealth and the one who takes the wife, the son who is otherwise ineligible for inheritance shall pay the debt. And thus it has been stated by Nārada: "Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the sons, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt."

Having said this, it was stated: "The son [is the heir] when the wife and the wealth-holder are absent. The term "heir to the debt" (*ṛṇabhāk*) is understood to follow. The meaning is that in the absence of both the one who takes the wife and the one who takes the wealth, the son who is otherwise ineligible for inheritance becomes the heir to the debt. However, that which was stated by the same author immediately thereafter—"The taker of the wife [is the heir] when the wealth and the son are absent"—appears somewhat inconsistent. This is because it contradicts the meaning previously established by another statement, namely that "in the absence of the taker of wealth and the son, the taker of the wife is the heir to the debt," and because it contradicts his own prior assertion that a son's liability for the debt occurs only in the absence of the taker of the wife. True, there is a contradiction; nevertheless, it is removed by a difference in scope (*viṣayabheda*). For instance, by the statement of Viṣṇu, "the taker of the wife of one who has no wealth," two alternatives are presented: either the taker of the wife shall pay the debt for one who has a son but lacks a taker of wealth, or for one who has no son and lacks a taker of wealth. Of these, the second alternative is expressed by the rule "the taker of the wife [is the heir] when the wealth and the son are absent," since it is identical in meaning to the second alternative. The meaning previously established by the other statement refers only to the first alternative. Therefore, there is no contradiction between this [second rule] and the first, just as there is none with the second alternative, because they are optional alternatives (*vikalpita*). By the rule "the son [is the heir] when the wife and the wealth-holder are absent," it is stated that the son—who is ineligible for inheritance—shall pay the debt for one who has a son but lacks a taker of wife or wealth, as this has the same meaning as the statement "the son whose property is not dependent on others. Thus, there is no contradiction with what was previously established or with his own prior statements; therefore, what was stated by Nārada is correct. As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:

Where a son is seen to be overwhelmed by calamity, or where a minor is seen [in charge], the one who takes the property shall be made to pay; in his absence, the one who takes the wife shall be made to pay.

Thus, this is intended to demonstrate that in that particular state, a son who is entitled to an inheritance lacks the right [to pay the debt]; it is not, however, intended to establish an alternative sequence—namely, that a son who is not entitled to an inheritance becomes liable for the debt only when in a state of calamity or affliction and so forth, whereas otherwise, the son who is not entitled to an inheritance comes first and the creditor (the one who takes the wealth) comes after, because such a sequence is not mentioned here, and because it would be inconsistent to grant the status of a non-inheriting son at the outset. Furthermore, as he himself has stated:
"The one who takes the wealth should pay first; the son immediately after him."
A woman is like a crocodile when there is no son, or a son who is utterly destitute.

Thus, with respect to the "taking of the woman," it is entirely consistent that this refers to the son who possesses very great wealth, for the purpose of establishing his immediate succession to the inheritance. Nor should one suspect that the taking of the woman is itself a scriptural duty for the one who pays the debt incurred by her former husband, on the grounds that the scriptural injunction regarding the authority to give her away would otherwise be inexplicable; for since the taking of the woman occurs through natural inclination (*rāga*), there is no inconsistency in the scripture. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:
"In cases where the husband of a remarried woman (*punarbhū*) or an unchaste woman (*svairiṇī*) shall pay the debt to the bearer [of the debt]..."
Therefore, that appropriation would not be prescribed by that treatise.
Furthermore, "taking them up" (tad-upādāna) refers to the gathering of women who have been previously married and are now independent. These have been defined by Nārada:
"Other women who have had previous husbands are said to be sevenfold in sequence;
among them, the *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) is of three kinds, while the *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman) is of four kinds."
A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage,
is declared the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) by virtue of the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
When a woman, having disregarded the laws of the country, is given by her elders to another man out of impulsive passion,
she is proclaimed as the second [type of wife].
[404] When there are no brothers-in-law, a woman who is given by her kinsmen to a sapinda of the same caste is proclaimed as the third [kind of marriage].
If a woman, whether she has borne children or not,
out of desire resorts to another man while her husband is still alive, she is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, resorts to another man and then returns again to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type].
But when her husband has died, she who, having obtained [a protector] such as a brother-in-law and so forth,
rejects them and approaches another out of lust, is proclaimed as the third [type].
"She who has come from another land, purchased with wealth, and overcome by hunger and thirst, having approached you saying 'I am yours'—she is proclaimed as the fourth. Thus it is said.

"One whose passion has arisen" means one who has lost her virginity, that is to say, one who is mature. "To another" means to a brother-in-law (*devara*); the word "another" is used here with the intention of referring to a brother-in-law, as this intention is understood from the subsequent statement, "when there are no brothers-in-law. The phrase "she should resort to" implies "for the sake of sexual pleasure"; likewise, the ellipsis must be supplied for the phrase "having thus resorted to" as well. "She should go again to the husband's house" implies "for the purpose of residing. And thus, it should be understood that he who approaches a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) other than the first [type] is merely a "designated man" (*niyuktamātra*) and not a "husband" (*yoṣidgrāha*); therefore, he is not entitled to the payment of debts incurred by the husband of that *punarbhū*. Similarly, he who approaches a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman) other than the fourth [type] is also merely a "lover" (*jāramātra*) and not a "husband"; therefore, he is not entitled to the payment of debts incurred by the husband of that *svairiṇī*.
