The last among women who have lived as they pleased and the first among those who have remarried—
whosoever inherits from them shall pay the debt contracted by their husband.

The word "as the husband" (*patitvena*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* stated: "But he who is the husband of a remarried woman (*punarbhū*) or an unchaste woman (*svairiṇī*) shall pay the debt of the [former] husband. As for that which was stated by Nārada:
For when a man dies without wealth and without a son, he who takes his wife incurs the debt of the deceased; she is declared to be his property as well.

Thus, if the phrase "he approaches a woman" (*striyam upaiti*) were taken according to its literal meaning, there would be a contradiction with what was stated previously—that even a man who has taken a wife by appointment (*niyuktā*) or a paramour (*jāra*) shares in the debt. On the other hand, if it is intended to mean "he takes a wife," there would be redundancy. This constitutes a dilemma. It is replied: this statement is commenced for the purpose of establishing that even one who merely enjoys a woman is liable for the debt, provided he is otherwise devoid of one who takes the wealth or a son who takes the wealth. Therefore, there is no dilemma whatsoever. Furthermore, it has been said by that same author: "But if a woman who possesses wealth, or one who has offspring, should resort to another..."

"He shall pay her debt to her husband, or he may release her in that same manner. This is its meaning: if a woman who possesses wealth and has young children should seek refuge with a maternal uncle or another relative for the sake of protection, that maternal uncle or other relative acting as her protector must cause her to pay the debt incurred by her husband. However, if she is unwilling to pay, then he may abandon her along with her wealth and her children. And so says Kātyāyana:
"A woman with young children or excessive wealth who has sought refuge with another protector..."
One who has resorted [to another] should repay that debt; this is recorded as the rule for one whose son is a minor.
The meaning is that one should give or cause [another] to give.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, within the determination of those who must repay a debt, are the matters concerning the heirs to the estate and so forth; now follow the matters concerning the family.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
Whatever has been borrowed by a paternal uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil,
or a dependent for the sake of the family, the householder is liable to repay it.

By the term "pupil" (*śiṣya*), the resident student (*antevāsī*) is also included, because the intention is to refer to any student in general. By the word "householder" (*gṛhin*), there is no reference to a mere house-dweller, but rather to one who maintains a family (*kuṭumbin*), as that alone is intended here. And so says Nārada:
"What has been borrowed for the sake of a family by a pupil, a resident student, a slave, a wife, a servant, or a laborer, that must be repaid by the head of the family."

A *śiṣya* is one who seeks the knowledge of the Vedas; an *antevāsī*, however, is one who seeks the knowledge of crafts. "On account of the family" means for the sake of the family, a debt incurred even without the consent of the head of the household when he is absent due to travel or other reasons. The meaning is that the head of the family must pay such a debt even in the absence of any calamity or misfortune befalling the debtor, because the maintenance of the family is his own duty. Kātyāyana also states this very point: "Even without the consent of one who has gone abroad, a debt contracted for the sake of the family must be paid by the slave, the wife, the mother, the pupil, or the son—so says Bhṛgu."
He (Yājñavalkya) himself states that even a debt contracted by a woman or a mother for the sake of the family must be paid:
"A debt contracted by a wife must be paid by the husband, and one contracted by a mother by the son;
likewise, that which was contracted for the sake of the husband [must be paid] when he has gone abroad after having made a declaration."
Nārada also says:
"But a woman who, having sons, abandons her son and resorts to another man—her entire debt shall be borne by him; however, for a woman who is destitute, the son alone shall bear it."

[The word] *anya* refers to another person, such as a maternal uncle or the like. However, even if a debt was contracted for the sake of anyone at all with their permission, it must always be paid by the head of the household alone, according to the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "That which was promised, or that which was done for the sake of the family, must be paid by whomever [the promise was made]. The meaning of the term *pratipanna* (promised) has been elaborated upon by Kātyāyana:
"That which was undertaken by a son, or that which was described [as such], that which was done without being authorized, and that which was heard [of] but not urged [for payment], must be paid."
The word "done" implies that it was done without hardship. However, what was done as a *kṛcchra* (hardship) must be paid back even if it was not formally acknowledged.
And so says Nārada:
"Whether by the father's command or for the sake of maintaining the family..."
Or whatever debt has been incurred in times of distress, that the father shall repay to the son.

In this and the preceding case, the mention of "son" is intended to indicate the family in general, and the mention of "father" here is intended to indicate the master of the household. Thus says Kātyāyana: "But that which is borrowed for the sake of the family when one is incapable, or when one is ill, or on account of a calamity, should be known as being contracted in times of distress."

"Whatever was done for the marriage of a daughter and whatever was done for funeral rites—all this must be given to the master by the family," [it is said]. "Incapacity" means one who is unable to maintain the family; the meaning is "by the female head of the household. "For the marriage of a daughter" means on account of the marriage of a daughter. "Whatever was done" means by whomsoever it was performed. "To the master" means by the master, that is, the head of the family. Just as in the *Nāradīya* [Smṛti], the words "son" and "father" are used as illustrative examples (*upalakṣaṇa*), so too here.
A debt contracted by a son must be cleared by the father if it was approved by him;
otherwise, he may pay it out of affection for his son, but he is not otherwise obliged to pay it.

This should also be understood from the statement of Bārhaspatya: "That which is to be purified (śodhya) is that which is to be discharged. The inclusion of the term "consented" (*anumodita*) is intended as an illustration for what has been promised (*pratiśruta*), because of the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana: "That which is to be given, whether it has been promised or whether it has been consented to. A gift made out of affection refers to a debt other than the various types of debts to be paid previously specified. This applies equally to debts contracted by a wife, since the mention of a "son" was made merely as an example of affection. And thus, as stated by Kātyāyana [409]:

"By law, a debt incurred by a son need not be paid by the father"—this should be understood as referring to debts other than those of the various kinds of debts previously mentioned. By saying "by law," he indicates that it may be paid out of affection. Furthermore, as stated by Nārada:
"A debt incurred by a wife should never, under any circumstances, be brought upon the husband."
Thus, that [rule] also refers to subjects other than the aforementioned debts. To demonstrate that its scope is of such a nature, the same author stated immediately thereafter:
"For the maintenance of a family is difficult to overcome for a man, except for what is incurred in times of distress.

The meaning is that even a debt contracted by a wife during a time of distress, if it was contracted for the sake of the family, must be discharged by the husband. He himself states that the previously mentioned prohibition applies to women other than those of washermen and similar castes.
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and liquor-sellers;
their livelihood depends upon them, and their families rely on them.

"Of them" refers to washermen and the like. "Livelihood dependent on them" means a mode of subsistence that is reliant upon women; the intention is that even if such debts were incurred for the sake of the family during non-emergency times, they must be paid by the husbands. The mention of washermen and others is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those whose livelihoods depend on women, such as oil-pressers, actors, and so forth. Yājñavalkya also, demonstrating through the statement of a reason that this is illustrative, stated the very same point as being within the purview of Nārada's intention: "The wives of cowherds, vintners, actors, washermen, hunters..."
The husband shall pay their debts, since their livelihood depends upon him.

A *śailūṣa* is an actor. And thus, regarding what was stated by Viṣṇu—"Neither a wife nor husband nor sons [have authority] over what is done by a woman"—it should be understood that this refers to matters other than those already mentioned as being subject to disposal. Manu, however, states that even an action performed by a dependent servant or others for the sake of the family must be accepted by the head of the household:
"But whatever legal transaction an dependent may carry out for the sake of the family, whether in his own country or abroad, one should not annul it on account of justice."
But rather, he should accept it—this is the ellipsis.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, within the determination of those who must repay a debt, are the matters concerning the family; now follow the matters concerning the members of the family.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
Whatever debt may have been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided,
the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad.

The meaning is this: a debt incurred for family expenses by brothers and others who are undivided in property and of equal status need not be paid at all times by them; rather, it must be paid when the head of the household (kuṭumbin), who is authorized to incur such debts, has died or is away on a journey. Even in that case, in the absence of some members, he who remains shall pay it, according to the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "He who remains among those undivided [brothers] who contracted the debt shall pay it. In both the preceding and the present context, the plural number in the word *avibhaktaiḥ* ("by the undivided") is not intended to be restrictive. Thus says Nārada:

Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle or a brother, or whatever has been contracted by a mother for the sake of the household, all the heirs shall pay it. (411) The words "when the debtor is deceased or absent" are to be supplied as the remainder. For while that person—the principal—is present, these others—the subordinate members—lack the authority to discharge the debt. Therefore, Manu says:
If the borrower has perished and expenses were incurred for his family,
it is ordained that his kinsmen— even if they are divided— must pay that debt.

If the debtor—such as a paternal uncle or other relative—is lost, gone abroad, or deceased, then the debt incurred for the expenses of his family must be paid by the heirs, whether they are divided or not; this is the meaning of the phrase "by themselves. Thus has the commentator (Vṛttikāra) explained it. Considering that in this interpretation the mention of "undivided" (in the subsequent verse) would be redundant, the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) stated the meaning of the text to be that the debt must be paid from their own respective wealth by the paternal uncles and others whose property was divided. He then demonstrated the meaning of another text: that those who are undivided should pay from the common property itself, and after paying, the remaining portion should be divided, but not without having paid. When those whose wealth is divided pay the debt, they should give a share proportionate to their inheritance, according to the Smṛti of Viṣṇu: "And those who are divided [should pay] a share proportionate to their inheritance."
Thus ends the section concerning members of the family who are liable for the repayment of debt in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning women who are dependent on others;
regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
A debt contracted in this manner—whether jointly with a husband or a son, or by oneself alone—must be paid; otherwise, that which was contracted by a woman [alone] need not be paid.

Otherwise, that which was contracted solely by the husband or by the son need not be paid even in the absence of the wife, nor does she have to pay for what was contracted by both of them together; however, a debt contracted jointly with the husband or the son must be paid in their absence. But a debt contracted by herself alone must be paid even in their absence—this is the meaning. By saying "of this kind," he indicates that there is another type of debt also to be paid by the wife. When asked what that is, Yājñavalkya says: "A debt admitted by the wife must be paid. "Admitted" means accepted, in the sense of: "I shall pay the debt incurred by the husband or the son."
A woman shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband, nor likewise one contracted by her son, except in the case of a voluntary undertaking... [or in the event of distress].

Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Nārada, it should be understood that Yājñavalkya’s statement is intended as a restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyā*)—to the effect that even a debt acknowledged by a woman need not be paid if it was contracted by anyone other than her husband or son; for it cannot be taken as an injunction (*vidhi*), since its meaning is already clear. On the other hand, Kātyāyana states that in certain circumstances, even an unacknowledged debt contracted by the husband must be paid by the wife: "If a wife has been told by her husband who intends to die, 'You must pay this debt,' she shall be made to pay it even if she did not acknowledge it, provided that wealth has been received by the woman."

In this context, it is understood by implication that if a woman who has not taken refuge [with another] does not rely on her husband’s wealth, the debt is not to be paid. As for what was stated by Nārada: "A childless widow, or one authorized by him, or he who would take his inheritance, shall pay the debt; for from whom the inheritance comes, from him the debt follows."

Thus, that statement was made with reference to a widow who possesses the wealth of her dependent husband; therefore, it is not in contradiction with what was stated previously. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu—"not [a debt] contracted by the husband or son of a woman"—that indicates a general prohibition and remains applicable to cases other than the scope of the specific injunction mentioned above; thus, there is no contradiction. Since the determinations regarding what may and may not be paid are difficult to treat individually, they have been dealt with by us within the context of determining the person to whom payment is to be made, and so they should be understood accordingly.
Thus ends the section on the determination of the person who must repay [a debt] concerning women dependent on others in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
and now follows the section concerning the repayment of debts by a deceased creditor (*uttamarṇa*).

Regarding this, Nārada says: "If there is no one belonging to the same lineage (sānvaya) to whom the inheritance of a Brāhmaṇa should be given, he should offer it to his kinsmen (sakulyas); in their absence, to his relatives (bandhus)."

The mention of the "brāhmaṇa" is intended as an illustration for any creditor (*uttamarṇa*). Thus, the meaning is this: the debt that is to be paid by a creditor must, in his absence, be paid by his descendant—such as a son—or by one who has taken possession of his property, acting as the restitutor of the debt. In the absence of a creditor who has descendants, it must be paid among his *sakulyas* (agnates), without bypassing those who are more closely related. In the absence of *sakulyas*, it must be paid among kinsmen such as maternal uncles and others, again without bypassing those who are more closely related. When even those previously mentioned are absent, he [the author] says the following:
But when there are no agnates, nor kinsmen or relatives, then one should give [the property] to the twice-born; if they too are absent, one should cast it into the water.
Prajāpati also says:
"In the absence of relatives, however, it should be given to Brahmins or cast into water;
wealth cast into water or likewise into fire shall serve the deceased in the next world. [414]

The meaning of the second half [of the verse] is that by discharging one's debts, wealth offered into water and so forth becomes beneficial for the next world. Regarding the phrase "and in the fire," the word *hutam* (offered) is to be supplied as an ellipsis; one should not, however, connect it with the word *kṣiptam* (thrown). As Gobhila says: "When the debts are unknown, one should offer oblations from the middle leaf of a *golaka* with the mantra, 'Whatever debt... Furthermore, Agni is the deity here based on the wording of the mantra. This oblation is for the purpose of discharging the debt, as indicated by the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "May I become free from debt. *Golaka* refers to the *palāśa* tree. And so says the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
But as for the property held by a debtor, if it should at some point come into the possession of a Brāhmaṇa,
this applies when there is no one among the heirs— beginning with the son and ending with the Brāhmaṇa— to inherit it.
"One should offer an oblation with the middle leaf of the *palāśa* tree;
then one should cast [the debt] into water with the verse beginning 'yat kusīdam' (whatever debt...), for that wealth [is thus returned] to the waters.

This means that in some cases, this applies when there is an absence of all things from the creditor down to the pledge. The phrase "yat kusīdam" is connected only with what precedes it, because the root text (*mūla-smṛti*) does not record a mantra for casting into water. This same rule is to be understood as applying to deposited property and the like when the owner of the deposit or other such property has passed away, because the underlying cause is the same; so it was stated by Devasvāmin.

Thus ends the section on the repayment of debts by a deceased debtor in the *Smṛticandrikā*, composed by Yājñika Devaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya Somayājī, son of Śrī Keśavādityabhaṭṭopādhyāya, who was a master of all branches of knowledge; herein concludes the detailed exposition of the legal category (*pada*) known as the Non-payment of Debt (*ṛṇādāna*).

Now, the rule for the second category of witnesses— which is of many kinds according to distinctions such as *nikṣepa* (deposits) and *upanidhi* (open deposits)— is stated by Manu: "In one born of a noble family, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, and truthful..."
A wise person should deposit a trust with one who has a large following, who is wealthy, and who is trustworthy.
Regarding the phrase "in a great faction, possessed of kinsmen," when it is asked what constitutes a deposit (*nikṣepa*), Vyāsa states:
"When one's own property is placed in the hand of another due to leaving one's place, fear of the king, or deception by heirs, that he calls a deposit."

The meaning is that the term *nikṣepa* (deposit) applies to that which is handed over for safekeeping into the hands of another person possessing qualities such as being born of a noble family (*kūlaja*), namely one's own property—such as clothing, gold coins (*niṣka*), and so forth—and which is delivered specifically in the presence of the recipient. Furthermore, that delivery must be performed by counting the items in the presence of the recipient, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada: "They know a deposit to be that which has been counted. Bṛhaspati states the procedure for establishing a *upanidhi* (sealed deposit):
[one should record] the location, the house, the householder, his caste, and his various qualities.
Having tested truthfulness, purity, and one's kinsmen, one should establish a treasure there.
"Nidhi" means "upanidhi. Its essential nature has also been stated by that same [author]:
"That which is given unannounced, kept apart, uncounted, not shown, and marked with a seal—that is known as *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit)."

That which is placed inside a casket or similar container and deposited is *vyavahita*; regarding its delivery, there is no restriction as to whether it is done in the presence or absence of the recipient, because it is generally stated simply as "given. However, that same author describes the manner of depositing a *nyāsa* by way of defining its essential nature:
"Because of fear of the king, thieves, or enemies, and for the sake of deceiving heirs, wealth is deposited in another's house; that is proclaimed to be a *nyāsa*."

"Property" refers to items such as oxen, bronze vessels, and so forth. By using the word "house," it is shown that a deposit (*nyāsa*) is one which has been established by saying, "It must be handed over when the owner of the house—who is currently away at another place—returns," and not one that was handed over in his presence.
Thus ends the section on the procedure for depositing items such as trusts in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the protection of deposits and the like; regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
A loan is declared to be of two kinds: that given in the presence of witnesses and that given in private.
It must be protected like a son; it perishes through neglect.
And that same [author] stated the fruit for one who protects:
"Whatever merit may accrue to one who gives gold, base metals, garments, and so forth,
that same merit shall belong to one who protects a deposit as well as one who has come for refuge."
Base metals refer to tin, lead, and so forth. The fault incurred by one who consumes [the deposit] and others has also been shown by that same author:
"Just as there is fault for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or friend, so too is there fault for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit."
"One should not accept property placed in deposit; its loss, however, brings dishonor.

Here, the mention of "accepting a deposit" (*nyāsagrahaṇa*) in all three ancient citations is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it should be understood that the rewards mentioned in the scriptural texts apply equally to the triad of deposits, pledges, and so forth.

Thus concludes the section on the rules for preserving deposits and the like in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, some statements concerning the recipient who has become a member of the court (*sabhyabhūtagrahītṛ*) are written here. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
If it should meet with destruction due to an act of God or the king,
there is no fault in that case, provided the deposit is returned along with the goods belonging to the recipient.

The word "of the receiver" (*grahītuḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The intended meaning is "due to the absence of negligence and so forth. The phrase "together with the substance belonging to the receiver" is stated as a means of determining the absence of negligence and other such factors. It should be understood that even in the case of something merely deposited, if the absence of negligence and so forth is established by some other cause, no fault exists on the part of the receiver. The mention of "divine or royal seizure" (*daivarājagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating the causes for which the receiver must provide redress. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "Where a deposit has been destroyed not by royal or divine force, but by [ordinary] means, that loss is said to belong to the giver along with the goods, and not to the receiver."
"With the vessel" means "with the object. And so says Nārada:
"That which is lost together with the object of the borrower is lost to the lender;
the same applies if it is caused by fate or the king, provided it was not brought about by his own dishonesty. [418]

The meaning of the final quarter-verse, "if [the object] has not been destroyed along with the purpose for which it was taken," is as follows: by the speaker stating that "it is lost to the giver," he implies through this turn of phrase that the taker should not be made to pay the value of the lost property. And Yājñavalkya has stated: "But that which has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves, he shall not be made to pay. The meaning of the term *daivika* (by fate) has been clearly explained by Manu: "By fire, water, kings, thieves, or even by the negligence of the keeper, if the deposit is lost, the taker shall not be made to pay.
(MDh 8.196) Thus, the meaning of the term *daivika* is explicitly stated by Manu.
If he does not give what has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire,
it is because he does not take anything back from that [debt].
The meaning is that he should not take even a small portion of that wealth. Regarding the receiver of a deposit as well, it was stated by that same author:
"He shall not receive anything from the sea if he does not recover [the deposit] from him" (MDh 8.188).

The same should be understood regarding the recipient of the deposit (*nyāsagrahītṛ*) in the absence of negligence (*upekṣā*) and so forth, since there is no lack of propriety [in his case]. It should be considered that the separate mention of the *upanidhi* in another statement—"he shall not recover from the ocean"—is intended for those who delight in detailed elaboration (*prapañca*). Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that in some cases, even if the property is lost through any cause whatsoever, the recipient need not be made to pay by way of its value: "But where the depositor, having known the loss of the goods, deposits them [with someone], the recipient is not at all made to pay, even if they are destroyed by every possible means."
Thus ends the section concerning judges who have become actual members of the court in the *Smṛticandrikā* [419].
Now follows the section concerning those who appear as judges but are not actual members.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
Whatever has been deposited with someone, that person should protect it with great care;
any destruction other than that caused by fate or the king is declared to be his responsibility.

The meaning is that whatever has been deposited with someone must be protected by him with diligence; for any destruction or loss other than that caused by fate or the king is declared to be the fault of that receiver. It is not merely ill-repute [that follows], but rather, when destruction or loss occurs due to his own negligence, there is a great loss of wealth as well; thus he [Yājñavalkya] says: "Whatever may be destroyed or stolen through his fault, he shall be made to pay that property along with interest, except in the case of destruction caused by fate or the king."
In this context, "defect" (doṣa) is intended to mean negligence and the like. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"If the depositary should destroy the deposit through neglect or by treating it as his own, or if he does not return it when asked for, he shall be made to pay it back along with interest."

In the event of loss, he should be made to pay by way of its value; however, if there is no loss, he must pay the item itself. Regarding the amount of interest, that which was stated generally in the section on non-payment of interest should be applied in the case of loss.
But in the case of non-payment, if he does not pay when requested, the debt increases by five percent per month.

Thus, it should be understood that this is stated specifically in that very context. By stating "through neglect with distinction," he shows that if there is destruction through neglect *together with* one's own property, the rule regarding interest (*sodaka*) does not apply. Therefore, only the principal is to be paid, as prescribed by another Smṛti: "In that case, one who has neglected [the deposit] shall be made to pay the equivalent. Likewise, Kātyāyana says:
"[420] If, immediately after being requested, [the deposit] is destroyed—whether by fate or by the king—the borrower shall be made to repay it... and so forth.

The word "merely the principal" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. For, when the offense consists merely in a delay in returning [the deposit], it is improper to compel payment with interest. Furthermore, that same amount must be paid to the king; and thus says Nārada: "But he who, being asked to give, does not deliver the deposit, shall be fined by the king and, in case of loss, shall be made to pay an equivalent amount."

In the phrase "it is lost," the words "by fate or by the king" are to be supplied as an ellipsis. Furthermore, regarding one who incurs expenditure from the deposited wealth, or uses it for personal enjoyment, or employs it for investment for the sake of profit—concerning that case as well, the same author says: "If he should recover the wealth there without the consent of the depositor, he shall be punished for that and shall restore it along with interest."
He should be punished according to the value of the object proven [to have been misappropriated]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"If he makes use of it at his own will, he should be punished and made to pay that [value] along with interest.

Here, "making use" (*ājīvan*) means living off it; "at his own will" means without the consent of the depositor. By the word "that" (*tat*), the deposit (*upanidhi*) is referred to here, as it is the subject under discussion. Bṛhaspati also says:
Whoever should accomplish his own business by means of property deposited with another shall be punished by the king and shall be made to pay that [property] along with interest.

The phrase "he should recover" implies "without the owner's permission. However, that there is no fault for one who recovers it with the owner's permission is understood by implication from the ancient legal texts themselves. Kātyāyana also states:
"Whatever property belonging to another—such as a deposit and the like—is consumed, neglected, or destroyed through negligence, the person responsible must restore that very thing. [421]
Regarding this, Vyāsa states the specific rule:
"If [the deposit] is consumed, [the bailee] shall be made to pay it with interest; if it is neglected, he shall be made to pay the same amount;
if the property is destroyed through negligence, he shall be made to pay something less."

Some have stated that the phrase "slightly less" (*kiṃcin nyūnam*) should be understood to mean "reduced by one-quarter" (*pādāṃśahīnam*). He should be made to pay what was stolen, just as if he had eaten it; for Viṣṇu records: "The thief of a deposit must be made to pay the money to the creditor along with the interest. In this case, he must also be made to pay a fine: "The king shall cause the thief of a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value, and likewise especially for the thief of an open deposit (*upanidhi*)."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Manu; and regarding denial [of a deposit], Vyāsa states that one should cause the debtor to pay only the principal amount once it has been proven:
"But the man who denies a deposit, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen, shall be made to restore it after having it established through witnesses or by ordeal."
Bṛhaspati, however, has also stated that one may impose a fine:
"In a case where a person, having received a deposit, denies it, the judge should establish the truth through witnesses or by means of an oath;
he should then cause the deposit to be returned and likewise impose a fine equal to its value."
Thus ends the section concerning the semblance of a court member and the witnesses in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the matters concerning the duties of the debtor, the creditor, and others.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati speaks to the debtor:

Whatever has been deposited by whomsoever, in whatever manner, and according to what procedure, that must be returned to him exactly as it was; it must not be given to the next-of-kin (*pratyanantara*). Here, the "next-of-kin" is said to be anyone other than the depositor who holds ownership over the deposited property. Regarding the depositor, Manu says:
Whatever object a person deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the receipt.

*Ādāya* means giving; that is to say, depositing. *Graha* means taking. This is what is meant: that which was deposited in the presence of witnesses must be received in the presence of witnesses; that which was deposited in secret must be received in secret. When the question arises as to when it should be received, Kātyāyana states:
"A deposit (*upanidhi*) should be received at the proper time; one should avoid receiving it when the time has passed.
One who returns it after the time has passed shall be fined and made to pay double [the value]."

The meaning is that when the time has passed during which the deposit was placed in another's hand out of fear, it should be returned; even when that period of fear has elapsed, it must be surrendered of its own accord without being asked, because of the traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati: "One should return it once requested. If it is given by oneself without being asked while that fear still persists, such a gift is deficient in timing and is merely due to malice; therefore, punishment for one who gives [it back] in this manner is appropriate. Regarding the punishment for the depositor's malice, Manu says: "Whatever deposit was made by whomsoever, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses..."
He should be known as being exactly that much; by speaking falsely, he deserves punishment.

The family acts as witnesses. This is what is meant: one who speaks in contradiction to the testimony of witnesses in a matter that has witnesses is to be punished. But regarding a matter without witnesses, Bṛhaspati says: "In a case where a disagreement arises concerning a treasure deposited in secret, it is recorded in the Smṛti that divine proof (divyam) is the means of determination for both parties."

Regarding the deposit (*nidhi*) and the counter-deposit (*upanidhi*): the meaning is that [the decision] belongs to one of the two among both. Both are mentioned so that this very position—namely, "either one may act according to his own inclination"—may apply. Manu says to the king:
"He should investigate the one who misappropriates a deposit and the one who is not the depositor by all means, as well as by Vedic oaths."

"He who does not restore a deposit, and he who demands what was never deposited—both of these are to be censured like thieves and should be made to pay a fine equal to that [value]. Regarding "to be censured like thieves," this means they are to be punished with the punishment for theft. And it is stated in the *Manu-vṛtti* that the punishment for theft is the first *sāhasa*. He (Manu) says the same thing concerning the judge (*prādvivāka*):
If, however, he does not pay them that gold according to the rule, he should be made to pay it by seizing both [his wife and children]; such is the established principle of Dharma.

"In the case of lost wealth as well as that deposited out of friendship, the king shall make a decision without harming the holder of the deposit. [This refers to] those plaintiffs; that gold, or the gold equivalent to its value, must be made to be paid to the plaintiffs. In both cases, having seized and punished them with double the amount, he should do so "without harming," meaning without striking them.
Thus ends the section on the duties of the borrower, the depositary, and others in the *Smṛticandrikā* [424].
Now follows the exception to the prohibition against returning a deposit to another person.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"If one should himself deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased,
he must not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the relatives of the depositor."

The explanation given for the term *pratyantaram* in the preceding section should also be understood here. By this statement, it is declared through a particular turn of phrase that, upon the death of the depositary (*sthāpaka*), the delivery must be made to the next-of-kin (*pratyantaram*) by the claimant (*grāhaka*). Even an unsolicited delivery is mentioned here as an ornament rather than a defect, because it serves to prevent a lapse of good faith; thus it is said: "But he who should give it himself. Furthermore, even to a next-of-kin, the object must not be delivered at an improper time without being asked, as that would result in a lapse of good faith. When there are many next-of-kin, the delivery should not be made to just one, but should be made in the presence of all the next-of-kin; for if that is done, the depositor cannot be prosecuted by the relatives who have become the next-of-kin. However, when he does not give it himself, then the same author says regarding the next-of-kin: [the following verse].
One should seek that object with sincerity and with affection;
having examined his conduct, one should accomplish the matter through conciliation alone.

Investigation (*anveṣaṇa*) consists of determining that a deposit or similar object exists with this person. This must be done by oneself, without artifice (*acchalenaiva*), according to the facts (*bhūtānusāreṇaiva*), and not according to deceit. Recovery (*parisādhana*) is the taking back from the holder. Regarding a holder of good character, it should be done through conciliation (*sāma*) alone—that is, with pleasant and respectful speech—and not by instilling fear or other such means. However, having investigated the conduct of a holder of bad character, one may seek recovery through deceit; indeed, it is understood from this very statement that one should recover it by means such as instilling fear or through deceit and so forth, as mentioned in the section on the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*). Just as the employment of deceit and the like is improper toward one of good character, even purification by oath (*śapatha*) is inappropriate. As for the case where the holder has died, whatever property such as a deposit (*upanidhi*) subsequently came under his control, that must be returned to the depositor or his successor; since this is so obvious, it was overlooked by the authors of the *Smṛtis*, and the reason for its non-mention must be inferred. If he does not return it himself, just as the holder would have done, then the depositor or the successor should investigate according to the previously stated method. One who admits the claim should be recovered in the manner previously described. This too was not explicitly stated by the authors of the *Smṛtis* because it can be understood through logical inference (*ūha*).

Thus ends the exception to the prohibition against returning [a deposit] to a neighbor in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, some statements concerning the subjects of borrowed and entrusted items are recorded;
therein, Yājñavalkya says:
"This rule applies to borrowed items, things deposited for safekeeping, pledges, trusts, and so forth."

*Yācita* refers to ornaments or other items belonging to another that have been borrowed for occasions such as festivals and brought into one’s own presence. *Anvāhita* refers to another's property held by oneself which has been placed there by someone else who was present nearby. Although the specific nature of *nyāsa* (a deposit) and *nikṣepa* (an open deposit) has been shown in the section on the rules for establishing deposits and so forth, and although the rules for establishing them are taught in other *smṛtis*, they are not taught in this particular *smṛti*; therefore, it is appropriate that these rules be extended (*atideśa*) here from those taught for *upanidhi*. Bṛhaspati and others likewise extended these rules to *anvāhita* and similar items where no specific rules had been taught.

[426] "The same rule applies to what has been deposited, what has been borrowed, what has been placed in trust for craftsmanship, and what is given as a pledge; likewise in the case of one who has sought refuge. Regarding "placed in trust for craftsmanship," the meaning is gold and other materials placed in the hands of a goldsmith or similar artisan for the purpose of making bracelets and the like. By this, it should be understood that the rule is extended such that if an unrequested deposit for craftsmanship is destroyed by fate or other causes, the goldsmith or others are not to be made liable for its loss. On this point, Kātyāyana states an exception:
If the deposit is being processed by the artisan over a fixed number of days,
the artisan shall continue to hold it beyond that period and must return it even if it has been destroyed by fate.

Where clothes and the like that are already worn out—or even new ones—are entrusted to a washerman or similar artisan for the purpose of cleaning and so forth, and their destruction occurs either due to defects such as wear caused by the artisan’s handling or merely through the impact [of washing], they say that in such cases the obligation to pay the value along with interest, as stated in the verse beginning with “yasya doṣeṇa,” applies by extension (*atideśa*). In reality, however, there is no fault on the part of the artisan regarding worn-out items, because the impact was for the purpose of cleaning. This is not the case with new items; thus, the artisan is at fault in the latter instance. Therefore, for worn-out items, nothing need be paid; but for new items, only the value must be paid, because since the impact was for the sake of cleaning, the greater portion of the damage is not considered a fault, as the defect is minimal. Having all this in mind, he (the author of the *Smṛti*) says:
If destruction occurs due to a fault in the installation, that loss shall not be made to pay by the artisan;
however, if it is destroyed due to a fault in the craftsmanship, he shall make him pay for the purpose of restoring what was entrusted.

In the phrase "due to a defect in craftsmanship," the word "destruction" (*vināśa*) is to be supplied. Where thread and so forth, placed with a weaver or similar artisan for the purpose of making cloth, are lost during the stage of being a fragmentary cloth, or where they are not accepted by the owner when offered by the weaver at the stage of completion, and thus perish—in that case too, he (Yājñavalkya) says: "And if even a small amount of work is lost by the laborer, it shall be [paid]; but if he intends to give the full amount and it perishes because he does not accept it, that loss shall be his."

The meaning is this: if a work such as weaving a garment is defective or ruined due to even a slight deficiency in the fringe or other parts, it is considered ruined for the hired artisan himself; he must perform the weaving and other tasks again, even without receiving further wages. If the owner does not provide the yarn and other materials again, then even in the absence of further weaving and so forth, the artisan shall not receive the wages already paid. The meaning of the second half of the verse is that if the owner, intending to give a sufficient or complete garment and the like, does not accept what is being given by the hired worker, that sufficient amount shall be lost [to the owner]. Thus, it should be understood that here it is stated by way of a particular phrasing that the hired worker is not made to pay for what was ruined. Having thus stated the specific rule regarding the deposit of an artisan, the same author speaks also regarding the subject of borrowed items: [The text continues with the following verse: *Yācitam avadhau dattam adeyam avadheḥ param | naṣṭaṃ deyaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ ca daivike nopaśāmyati ||* "An item borrowed and returned within the stipulated time need not be returned after the time limit has passed. It must be returned if it is lost, and if it is destroyed, [the borrower is liable]; however, in the case of destruction caused by an act of God (daivika), the liability ceases. [And further: *Avadhis tu kṛto yatra sāmakālaṃ prayojanam | tasmin prāpte na dātavyaṃ gṛhītur viparītataḥ ||* "But where a time limit has been set for the purpose, once that time has arrived, it need not be returned; otherwise, it must be returned to the owner. [And: *Vināśo yadi daivena mūlyam eva pradāpyate | saṃyuktaḥ pāradāryena naṣṭaṃ sarvaṃ pradāpyate ||* "If the loss is caused by an act of God, only the value is to be paid. But if it is connected with adultery, the entire [value] of what was lost must be paid. [And: *Naṣṭaṃ deyaṃ tv adhigataṃ svasya dadyād amūlyataḥ | mūlyād dhi hīnaṃ yad bhagnaṃ bhagnam eva pradāpayet ||* "What is lost must be restored; but if it is found, one should give it back to oneself without payment. If it is broken for less than its value, one should cause only the broken portion to be restored. [And: *Yācitaṃ kālacopasthite na dadyād yadi kaścana | sa tasyaiva bhaved doṣo na dātus tu kathaṃcana ||* "If someone does not return a borrowed item when the appointed time arrives, the fault belongs to him alone, and never to the giver. [And: *Yācitakam avijñātaṃ gamayitvānyathā punaḥ | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed item is used without permission and then returned otherwise, or if it is lost, the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam anāhūya yadi kaścid vināśayet | dātā tasya bhaved doṣī na ced asau pradarśayet ||* "If someone destroys a borrowed item without having been summoned [for its return], the giver shall be at fault, provided he does not produce [the item]. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ yo na dadyād yathākṛtam | sa tasmād dviguṇaṃ dāpyo vinayaṃ tāvad eva ca ||* "He who does not return a borrowed utensil as it was received shall be made to pay double its value, and a fine of the same amount. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost. [And: *Yācitakam upaskaraṃ paribhogakṣamaṃ vinā | naṣṭaṃ vā yadi naṣṭaṃ syāddātā taddhanam arhati ||* "If a borrowed utensil, fit for use, is lost or destroyed without [fault], the giver deserves to pay the value of that which is lost."
If, having been requested for the purpose of that specific work or for a fixed period of time,
the object is only half-finished and not yet delivered, he shall not be compelled to pay.
The underlying intent is now stated:
if one who is being petitioned does not give, he shall be compelled to pay that [debt] along with interest.

Thus, this rule, which by extension applies to borrowed items, is here restricted in certain cases. The meaning of this prohibitory statement is as follows: if a task is to be accomplished over a long period, and during the course of that task one is asked for the loan, or if one is asked for a fixed duration such as "let it be given for up to a year," then if he does not return the borrowed item when asked for it again—either during the course of the task or within the fixed period—he shall not be made to pay it with interest (*sodarya*). He need only return the mere borrowed item once the task is finished or the fixed period has expired. If even then he does not return it, and subsequently its loss or theft occurs through fate or other causes, he must pay its value; so says the same author.
If a transaction is concluded when the time has arrived, one shall not pay even when requested;
however, if that [property] is lost or stolen, the taker shall recover its value.
Now,
if after the loan has been requested, it is lost— whether through an act of fate or by the king—
the borrower shall be made to repay it.

The instruction to cause the payment of the mere value, as taught in such Smṛti texts, was already obtained here by way of extension (atideśa); why then is it taught again here? It is said in reply: since a fine would also have been obtained from another Smṛti text in this same manner, it is stated here specifically to exclude that. He himself says: "Even at a time when [the term] has not yet arrived, if it is in the midst of business, one should cause the borrower to pay the loan. Now, if there is a failure of the business, that loss shall belong to the owner alone;
however, if the time has not yet arrived, he must pay it even if only half the work has been done.

The failure of the purpose of the borrowed object occurs if it is not returned; the meaning is that if he is asked for it again even in the interim, he must be made to give back the loan. If he does not give it back in the interim, then he must be made to pay it with interest (*sodaya*), because even that which is extended by analogy is to be accepted unless there is an instruction prohibiting it. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the following in order to preclude the employment of means such as conciliation (*sāma*)—even though the duties toward the depositor and the king are obtained through analogy regarding the borrowed object:
"He who, having taken a loan, does not return it when asked for it, shall be seized by force and compelled to pay; and he who does not pay shall be fined. [429]

Having restrained him by force and compelled him to observe fasts and other penances, the *sthāpaka* (the one who deposited the object) should make him pay; that is to say, he should be made to give by inducing a disposition toward charity. Even so, if he still does not give, the meaning is that he must be made to pay and punished by the king. Bṛhaspati states that even though the rule—“When the *sthāpaka* has died, one should give to the immediate neighbor for the sake of avoiding suspicion of internal corruption”—is applicable here as well because it falls within the category of rules extended to borrowed items, it is not necessarily mandatory: “One who returns a borrowed item with the owner’s permission does not commit an offense.”
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "even after the request."
Thus concludes the section concerning borrowed and pledged items in the *Smṛticandrikā*,
and the exposition of the rules for the title known as "Deposits" (*nikṣepa*) is finished.
Now, the rule for the title known as "Joint Undertaking" (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*) is stated.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
One should carry out business together with those who are of noble birth, skillful, untiring, wise, knowledgeable in coinage, experts in income and expenditure, pure, and brave.

The meaning is that [the group] consists of those whose nature is trade, agriculture, crafts, ritual sacrifice, music, or theft. Among these, the activity of trade should be undertaken collectively by those who understand coinage and know income and expenditure; the activity of agriculture, however, by those who know income and expenditure; the activity of crafts and the activity of music by the wise; the activity of ritual sacrifice by those of noble birth, who are wise, intelligent, and pure; the activity of theft by the brave; and all six types of activities beginning with trade should be understood as being performed by those who are skillful and not indolent. The mention of "skillful" and "not indolent" is intended to exclude those who are overly dependent on fortune or afflicted by disease. Furthermore, the mention of "those who understand coinage" is intended to exclude the wealthy. Therefore, while he prohibits the unskillful and the indolent, he thereby also excludes those of meager fortune and the like.

"Those who are powerless, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support—wise men should not engage in activities such as trade with these. Here, "support" (*āśraya*) refers to capital. And so says Nārada:

For those who, through skillful means, perform actions in combination for the sake of the fruit, the contribution serves as the basis; from that, [the results] arise according to their respective portions.

It is the basis, the foundation. "Deposit" means the depositing of the principal capital. The meaning is that from that deposit of principal capital, they shall arise as sharers of profit. Loss and so forth are also exactly like this; thus he himself says:
"In whatever proportion a share—whether equal, greater, or less—belongs to someone, in that same proportion shall their loss, expenditure, and increase be."
The meaning is that loss, expense, and profit are to be understood according to the proportion of the invested shares. Bṛhaspati also says:
"For those who engage in business with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth, their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to whether their shares are equal, less, or more."
Just as with profit, so too with expenditure and work; thus he himself says:
"The share—whether equal, deficient, or excessive—by which one is assigned shall likewise incur expenditure, perform work, and indeed receive profit. [431]
Yājñavalkya also says:
"When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership,
the gain or loss shall be according to the capital invested, or as determined by their agreement."

The meaning is that profit and loss are to be understood according to the *samavāya*—that is, through the connection with the capital goods—in accordance with the specific portion of the goods involved as they exist within the combined stock. "By agreement" (*saṃvidā*) means by convention; the point is that profit and loss are to be understood as determined in accordance with the individual persons. Vyāsa, however, states the duty of those working in partnership:
"Whether in the presence or absence [of others], not deceiving one another, they should carry out buying and selling in accordance with the various commodities."
"Those who do not protect their goods shall pay the toll on the road;
otherwise, those standing outside the toll station shall be made to pay double. Thus also says Nārada.
Established in their own duties without deviation, they should carry out the inspection of goods, the collection of fees, expenditures, receipts, weights, and quality.
Alternatively, with the permission of all, a single person may perform the work for everyone. And so says Bṛhaspati:
If one person, approved by many, should give wealth in secret,
or cause a legal document to be executed, it shall be considered as having been done by all.
The means of proof includes documents and so forth. He (Yājñavalkya) also states regarding disputes among those who act in partnership:
"In a doubtful matter or in a case of fraud, those very persons are declared to be both examiners and witnesses for one another, provided they are not possessed by mutual enmity. [432]
But when they are joined by malice, then he [Yājñavalkya] says the same:
"Whosoever among them is known to be a deceiver in buying or selling, he shall be cleared by oaths; this rule applies in every legal dispute as well."

"He is to be cleared by the members"—this is the ellipsis. "In every lawsuit," meaning even in a dispute other than one involving fraud. When it is established that he is a fraud, what should be done? To this question, Yājñavalkya says: "They should expel the dishonest one, deprived of his profit. "Dishonest" means a fraudulent person; "deprived of his profit" means having him stripped of his gain; they should expel him. The others, who are the co-partners, remain outside—this is the meaning. Regarding those among the co-partners who are incapable, he [Yājñavalkya] himself says: "One who is unable should have it done by another. The ellipsis is "work corresponding to his own share. Bṛhaspati, however, speaks regarding all [co-partners].
When a loss or diminution occurs therein caused by fate or the king,
it is declared that this shall be apportioned among all [the partners] according to their respective shares.

The phrase "by all those acting in concert" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "For loss alone" means for diminution; that is to say, a loss other than that which results from an increase in value. The mention of "divine or royal seizure" is intended to indicate causes other than individual faults. Regarding loss resulting from an individual fault, he (the same author) says: "But if one who has not been specifically assigned [a share] should, through negligence, cause destruction while being restrained, he alone must pay it; it shall be the responsibility of all the partners. [433]

The meaning of the first quarter [of the verse] is as follows: one who, acting by his own intellect alone, destroys a composite substance (*samavāyidravya*) that has not been specified or authorized for such destruction; or one who, even when being restrained by the constituent parts (*samavāyin*), proceeds to destroy it. Here, "negligence" (*pramāda*) refers to a deficiency in wisdom, mentioned as an indicator for individual faults. Therefore, it should be understood that everything arising from desire, anger, greed, and so forth, which serves as a cause for destruction, is included here. The remainder of the statement beginning with "But he who... is easy to understand. Regarding protection as well, the same author says:
"But he who, out of fear of gods or kings, protects [the property] to the best of his ability..."
Having given them a tenth part of that, you should take what remains from those others at the end.
They should give him a tenth part of that; these are the partners. "He should protect the property of the partners"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. And so says Kātyāyana:
"Whoever recovers property from thieves, water, or fire, a tenth share should be given to him; this rule applies in all legal disputes."

"Samāharet" means he should recover [the debt] according to his own capacity; "pratyāharet" has the same meaning. This rule is to be understood as applying even to the protection of non-composite (asamavāyin) property; this is the meaning of the final quarter-verse. Regarding one who, after having given [money] to debtors and others, does not recover the composite (samavāyin) property along with the partners through repeated requests and so forth—Bṛhaspati states that such a person suffers a loss of profit: "That which is given by those who are united [in partnership] must be requested in that very same manner;
whoever does not request it is deprived of his profit."

The mention of "begging" is for the purpose of illustrating the duties that must be performed according to one's share. Therefore, from this very statement, it should be understood that even when other duties are not performed, there is a loss of profit in accordance with the non-performance.
Thus ends the section on the rules for merchants acting in partnership in the *Smṛticandrikā* [434].
Now follow the rules for farmers acting in partnership.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"A wise man should engage in agriculture together with those who are equal in terms of external laborers, seeds, and other such implements for the cultivation of the field."

"Draft animals" refers to oxen used for pulling plows and the like; "farmers" refers to men hired for the purpose of cultivation. By the word "and so forth," the inclusion of wealth intended for agriculture is intended. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states those to be avoided among draft animals:
"A wise farmer should not take as a draft animal one that is emaciated, excessively old, small, diseased, prone to running away, one-eyed, or lame."
"One-eyed" means having only one eye; "lame" means having defective feet. He [the author] himself stated that such fields are to be avoided:
"One should carefully avoid a field that is on a mountain, near a city, or by a royal road, as well as one that is saline or infested with rats."

"On a mountain" means on a mountain peak. "In the vicinity of a city" means near a city; the phrase "and near a royal road" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This is what is meant: one should avoid a field that is close to mountains and the like, even if it is not [otherwise] close, provided it is saline or infested with rats. Whatever regarding the distribution of profits and so forth was shown in the previous section concerning the joint undertaking of commerce, agriculture, and other activities—that too should be applied here. He states that a single person suffers loss due to another defect, in addition to the individual defects already shown previously: [435]
If the loss of a field occurs due to the failure of external seeds, it must be made good by that very person for the benefit of all those who live by agriculture.

The phrase "of those acting in combination" is the ellipsis to be supplied. It should be understood that the mention of "external seeds" is intended as an illustration for all the implements of agriculture.
Thus ends the section on the rules for farmers working in partnership in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the rules for artisans working in partnership.
To define the nature of an artisan, Bṛhaspati says:
The wise have declared that a craftsman is one who knows the various arts and is skilled in working with gold, base metals, thread, wood, stone, and leather.

*Kupya* refers to base metals other than gold and silver, such as tin, lead, and so forth; Amarasiṃha has stated, defining gold and silver, that "whatever is other than those two is *kupya*. He [the same author] states the division of the artisans' profit:
"Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively, they shall receive wages (*nirveśa*) according to their respective shares in accordance with the work performed."
"Nirveśa" means wages. Kātyāyana also states:
"Instructors, experts, craftsmen, and teachers are artisans;
they shall receive one, two, three, or four shares respectively, in ascending order."

Bṛhaspati states the principal share for those who construct palaces and other structures made of wood and similar materials: "For those working together to build a palace, a temple, or even leather goods and utensils, the leader deserves two shares."
Furthermore, that entire collection of dharmas such as the performance of ritual actions, which was shown in the preceding section due to its unfailing nature, should also be understood here.
Thus ends the section on the rules for artisans working in partnership in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the rules for priests working in partnership;
regarding this, Manu says:
Just as the officiating priests, having assembled at a sacrificial session (sattra) by invitation,
perform their duties according to their respective roles and receive their sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), so should they act.

Here, the word *satra* is employed with the intention of denoting sacrifice in general, and not with the intention of denoting the specific sacrifice named *satra*, because in that [specific] case, the sacrificers themselves are the performers (*kartṛ*), making the presence of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) impossible. Therefore, by this statement, the acquisition of activity (*vyāpāra*) is declared for the Soma-sacrifice and others. To explain the division of the gains in that very context, the same author says:
"By men here who, acting together, perform their respective duties, the allotment of the shares of the performance must be made through this application of ritual action."

The phrase "his own rites" refers to those other than the *yājamāna* (the sacrificer’s duties); this is the remainder of the sense. Furthermore, the apportionment of shares (*aṃśaprakalpanā*) applies only to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed merely as being connected to the ritual in general—such as "its sacrificial fee is one hundred and twelve"—and not to that which is prescribed in connection with specific officiants, such as "a chariot for the *adhvaryu*, the best of the *nivid*-verses and a horse for the *hotṛ*, a horse for the *brahmā* at the fire-laying, and a cart for the *subrahmaṇyā* at the purchase of the *soma*" [437], because that would result in a contradiction with the sacred scripture (*śruti*). For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the establishment of the fires;
the Hotṛ the horse that chooses the *nivid*, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of Soma].

The meaning is that he alone who is specified by name as a particular officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) shall receive the portion ordained for him. Regarding the fees ordained by specifying the subsidiary acts—such as the rule "one should give a boon when the *pūrṇāhuti* has been offered"—he alone says:
"Those subsidiary fees (*pratyaṅgadakṣiṇā*) which may be prescribed for a particular rite, he alone shall take them, or all [the priests] together may divide them."

The meaning is that whoever is the performer of a particular rite should receive the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed for that rite. Thus, in the case of the *pūrṇāhuti*, the Adhvaryu priest should take the boon (*vara*), because he is the performer therein. The alternative view, "or all [the priests] may share it," refers to the sacrificial fees for the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) performed by multiple performers; therefore, the fees for the chants (*stotra-dakṣiṇā*) should be shared only by the *chandoga* singers who perform those chants. Regarding the method of apportioning shares among the principal sacrificial fees (*pradhāna-dakṣiṇā*), the same author states: "The primary priests are the half-sharers (*ardhin*); others are half-sharers with half of that amount."
Those entitled to a third share receive a third part, while those entitled to a quarter receive a fourth part.

The *mukhyās* (principal ones) are the first group, beginning with Brahmā and the others. The *apare* (others) are the second group among the *gaṇins* (group members), beginning with Pratiprasthātṛ and the others. The *tṛtīyinas* are the third group among the *gaṇins*, beginning with Pratihartṛ and the others. The *pādinas* are to be understood as the fourth group among the *gaṇins*, beginning with Grāvastut and the others. Consequently, this is the meaning: among all the officiating priests (*ṛtvijas*), the *ardhinas*—those entitled to half—are the principal ones; they possess half of the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Here, the word "half" refers to a portion slightly less than half of the fee. The other *gaṇins* are the second group; they are *ardhinas* in the sense that they possess half of that half (i.e., one-quarter). The *tṛtīyinas* are the third group; they are sharers of a third part of that slightly less-than-half portion. The *pādinas*, however, are sharers of a fourth part of that slightly less-than-half portion. Thus, in the case of a hundred cows as the sacrificial fee, it should be understood that the four principal priests receive forty-eight cows; the next four receive twenty-four cows; the next four receive sixteen cows; and the next four receive twelve cows. The internal distribution among the four principal priests is equal. Likewise, the internal distribution among those following them is also equal. Accordingly, the *Kātyāyana-sūtra* states: "Twelve each for the first group, six each for the second group, four each for the third group, and three each for the others. Since no unequal distribution is mentioned in the context of animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) and the like, the distribution should be understood as being equal. Manu says that the share should be given according to the specific portion of the ritual performance performed by each individual.
If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should neglect his own duty,
a share proportionate to that work must be given to him by the other performers together.

The meaning is "by the performers acting in concert. Alternatively, the meaning is that it should be given "together with the performers" by the sacrificer at the time of giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Or else, the meaning is that it should be given "together with the performers" who have relinquished their respective shares in the ritual. This is what is being said: the group of those acting in concert, or the sacrificer, should present at the time of the sacrificial fee to both the performer of one part of his own work and the performer of another part, according to the work performed by each. He himself states an exception to this in certain cases: *Yājñavalkya Smṛti* 1.205–206: "Among those performing a sacrifice together, the distribution of the sacrificial fee should be made according to the work performed. However, in the *Soma* sacrifice, the distribution is equal for all, except for the *Brahman*, the *Hotṛ*, and the *Udgātṛ*. *Śaṅkha*: "The sacrificial fee should be distributed among the officiating priests according to the work performed, or equally, except for the *Brahman*, the *Hotṛ*, and the *Udgātṛ*. *Gautama Dharmasūtra* 8.17–18: "The sacrificial fee is to be divided according to the work performed. Or, it may be divided equally, except for the *Brahman*, the *Hotṛ*, and the *Udgātṛ*. *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 10.2.1–2: "In a *Sattra* (sacrificial session), the sacrificial fee is equal for all. In other sacrifices, it is according to the work performed. Thus, while the general rule is that the fee is distributed according to the labor, specific exceptions—such as the equality of shares in a *Sattra* or the preferential treatment of certain priests—are established by these authorities.
And when the sacrificial fees have been given, he should contemplate his own ritual action;
he shall obtain the entire share and may have it performed by another.

It must be performed by another person who is either a member of one's own group (*svagaṇa*) or someone closely associated with them; for if it were performed by just anyone else, there would be a contradiction of the specific designations (*samākhyā*) such as "the office of the Adhvaryu" and so forth. This same principle should be understood to apply even when a priest (*ṛtvij*) has died. Therefore, Nārada says: "In the event of the misfortune of the priests, another shall likewise complete that ritual work; he shall receive the portion of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) that was assigned from it."

The meaning of the word "other" (anya) here should be understood as it was previously explained. As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati: "When someone among those engaged in a ritual action passes away, the rite must be performed by his kinsman or by all the collaborators together."

And as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha—"If a priest should die once the *savana* has commenced, his kinsman or his pupil should complete his duties; but if there is no relative, one should choose another priest"—all of that must be understood as referring to a sacrifice performed by priests who belong to a group devoid of intermediate sub-groups (*avāntaragaṇa*). To resolve the dispute regarding to whom the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belongs when the sacrificer appoints another priest while the original priest is still alive, he [Śaṅkha] himself says: "If, after one priest has been chosen, one should choose another later, the fee belongs to the one previously invited; the one invited later shall receive something small."
Thus concludes the section on the rules for officiating priests acting in concert, in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the rules for performers such as dancers and others, as well as for thieves and others, who act in concert.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"This very rule has been declared by the virtuous as the law for dancers:
one who knows the rhythm (tāla) receives half, while the singers receive equal shares."

This is the rule stated for the chief artisan; this is the meaning: "The leader deserves two shares"—thus, this rule consisting of receiving two shares, which was stated for the chief among artisans working together on a palace or similar structure, has been cited by the wise as the same rule for the leader among dancers and others working together on a performance or similar task. One who knows the rhythmic timing (*tāla*) receives one and a half shares—that is, a share increased by half. Regarding thieves as well, that same author says: "But whatever has been brought from a foreign land by thieves at the command of their master..."
Having given a sixth part to the king, they should enjoy [the remainder] according to their respective shares.
The principal hero shall take four shares; a brave warrior shall obtain three shares;
one who is capable shall take two shares; and the rest shall receive equal shares from what remains.

"From a foreign land" means from an enemy country; this refers to property brought from a territory of a particularly powerful enemy. However, regarding property brought from the territory of a weak enemy, Kātyāyana has stated: "Whatever wealth may have been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves under the king's command, they shall divide it after setting aside one-tenth for the king; otherwise, [the rule is] different."

But the leader of the thieves shall take four shares from that; the brave one, three shares; the capable one, two; and the rest, only one each. "Capable" means powerful.
