If among those who have fled, someone should capture [the property],
they shall carry it off according to their respective shares for the purpose of redeeming it from him.

Anticipating the objection that "since those who act in combination will divide profit and loss according to their respective shares based on their agreement alone, rules regarding division are redundant," the same author says:
"For merchants, farmers, thieves, and likewise for artisans—
for all of these who do not determine their own shares, this is the settled rule."

The meaning is that, in cases such as trade and the like, when there is no fixed agreement regarding profit and loss, a share is not determined for each individual among those who engage in the activity.

Thus concludes the section on the rules for performers such as dancers and thieves who act in concert, within the *Smṛticandrikā*. Here ends the detailed exposition of the legal procedure concerning the title known as "Joint Undertaking."
Now, the legal procedure concerning the title known as "Non-delivery of what was Given" is stated;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Thus has been fully declared the settlement for those who have engaged in a joint undertaking."
The [karmic result] of what is not to be taken, what is to be given, what has been given, and what has not been given is now described.
The meaning is that the nature of what is not to be given (*adeya*) and so forth is now being explained. In that regard, he first states the nature and divisions of what is not to be given:

"Common property, sons, wife, pledged assets, one's entire wealth, a deposit, what has been requested, and likewise what has been promised to another—this is remembered as the eightfold [list of] things not to be given. [402]

"Common property" (*sāmānyam*) here refers to that which belongs to many owners, such as a public road (*rathyā*); it does not refer to gold or other assets belonging to an undivided family (*avibhakta-kuṭumba*), because such items will be mentioned later as being fit for gift. Although a road or similar property, by virtue of having multiple owners, is comparable to family wealth, it nevertheless cannot be given away because its ownership is shared by independent individuals. For instance, no single owner can give such property away without the consent of the other owners; and in the case of a road with many independent owners, obtaining such consent is virtually impossible. In contrast, regarding family wealth, consent is easily obtained from a few independent owners—this is the distinction. Now, one might ask: since sons, wives, and all one's possessions (*sarvasva*) belong to the father and others, and are thus fit for gifting, why are they considered non-transferable? It is said: just as beans (*māṣa*), though belonging to the sacrificer, are deemed unfit for sacrifice due to the prohibitive Vedic revelation, "Beans are indeed unfit for sacrifice," so too sons, wives, and all possessions, though belonging to oneself, are non-transferable by force of Smṛti texts prohibiting their gift, such as: "Except for wife and son, [one may give]; but not one's entire estate while there is progeny. Regarding pledges (*ādhi*), deposits (*nyāsa*), and borrowed goods (*yācitaka*), their non-transferability should be understood as resulting from the absence of ownership. "Promised to another" means verbally given to someone else. Although ownership does not depart through a verbal promise (*vāgdāna*), nevertheless, by force of the prohibitive Smṛti—"Not one's entire estate while there is progeny, nor what has been promised to another"—it should be understood that even a promised gift is non-transferable, just like the entire estate. Furthermore, the non-transferability of the entire estate applies only to that which is connected to undivided family property, because the prohibition of giving specifically concerns that. Therefore, the entire estate may be given by one who lacks his own progeny, or by one to whom the inheritance has been assigned for his own offspring. Nārada has likewise stated the non-transferability of such items as entrusted property (*anvāhita*) and the rest.

That which has been deposited as collateral, that which has been borrowed, and so forth, as well as property held in common, a deposit, one's wife and children, and one's entire estate when there is offspring; [these should not be divided].
"For even when a person is beset by dire calamities, the teachers declare that there are things which must not be given, namely that which has been promised to another.

*Anvāhita* refers to what has been entrusted to someone else for the purpose of being given away. Like such an entrusted object, a woman’s property (*strīdhana*) is also not to be given away, because [the husband] lacks ownership over it. For this very reason, Dakṣa says:
Common property, what has been requested, a deposit, a pledge, one's wife, and her wealth; likewise, a loan for use, a sealed deposit, and one's entire estate when there is a male heir.
"Even in times of distress, nine things must not be given away by the wise;

he who gives them is a foolish soul and that man becomes liable to penance. Here, "foolish soul" refers to one who acts with the notion that ordinary objects, which do not actually fulfill the purpose of a gift, are such fulfilling objects. He "becomes liable to penance" because by giving away his son, wife, and so forth, he has transgressed a prohibition. Furthermore, in this case, the recipient is also indeed unrighteous, because he has acted improperly. For this very reason, Nārada states that punishment applies to both parties.
He who takes what is not given out of delusion, and he who gives what should not be given—
both of these are to be punished by a king who knows the Dharma.

The term "taking what is not given" (*adattagrahaṇa*) is intended as an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that which should not be taken (*adeya*). Therefore, it should be understood that by this statement, a punishment is prescribed for both the receiver of what should not be taken and the receiver of what has not been given. Furthermore, it is understood from the mention of taking what is not given and what should not be taken that the king must also effect the restitution of what has been seized; for since there is no accomplishment of a gift through what is not given or what should not be taken, ownership in another does not arise.
Thus ends the section on things that should not be given in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
now follow the matters concerning what may be given.
On this point, Nārada says:
Whatever wealth remains in excess after providing for the maintenance of one's family should be given away;
by giving it while neglecting others [to whom it is due], one incurs sin.

"Having harmed another" means having obstructed the family members who are to be maintained. Here, "obstruction" (uparodha) is intended to mean the deprivation of food and clothing due to poverty, rather than the lack of means for luxuries such as betel-leaf and the like. As Bṛhaspati says: "That which remains after providing for the family's food and clothing should be given. Here, "food" (bhakta) refers to eating; "clothing" (vasana) refers to covering; and the word "that which" (yat) in the verse refers to wealth, grain, and other such assets. Regarding property such as gardens and the like, he [Bṛhaspati] himself says:

From among the seven types of fields— those belonging to a monastery, those acquired by purchase, those inherited from one's father, or those obtained by oneself— that specific field which is set aside should be given as intended.

The meaning is that the *Smṛti* scriptures intend to convey that whatever exceeds the seven items beginning with the garden—that is, whatever is surplus—should be given away. As for what was stated by Kātyāyana:
"Except for one's entire property and house, whatever wealth remains after providing for the maintenance of the family, that is one's own [disposable] wealth to be given..."

Thus, that [rule] refers to houses numbering no more than seven. "One's own" (*svakam*) means one's property, that is to say, wealth fit for disposal according to one's will. How, then, can there be the giving away of a son? Anticipating the objection that in that case there is no relationship characterized by ownership (*svasvāmi-lakṣaṇa*), but rather only a relationship characterized by the produced and the producer (*janya-janaka-lakṣaṇa*), Vasiṣṭha says: "A person is born from semen and blood, having parents as his cause; in the giving away, selling, or abandoning of him, the mother and father have authority. Thinking that even a son possesses the fitness for disposal according to one's will because he was acquired by the parents through the mere act of procreation, he says they "have authority. Therefore, the intention is that even a son becomes an object to be given. As for another Smṛti text:
A father has authority over his son and his wife regarding instruction, as well as in their sale or gift; however, he has no such authority over his son in matters of sale or gift.

Thus, as for the two statements—one by Yājñavalkya stating, "It may be given without detriment to one's own family, except in the case of a wife or a son," and the other [implied], both refer to a situation where there is no other son. For in that case, if the son were given away, it would result in the extinction of the lineage. Therefore Vasiṣṭha says: "One should neither give nor receive a single son, for he is for the continuation of the ancestors. Even among those with many sons, only one who is capable of enduring separation from his mother and father should be given.

"Wives and sons should not be led into sale or gift against their will," according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana. The meaning is that just as wives should not be subjected to sale or gift by a husband, so too sons should not be led away from their mother and father against their will when they do not desire separation from them. This rule—"they should not be led away against their will"—applies to circumstances other than times of distress (anāpad).
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [one's possessions] may be performed;
otherwise they would not be utilized—such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
This is because it was stated immediately thereafter by that same author with reference to those very persons: "But as for what was said by Nārada:
'A deposit, a son, a wife, and one's entire property—even when a person is living in the midst of dire calamities, provided there is a male descendant...'"
The teachers say that these [objects] are not to be taken...

Thus, that [rule] also refers to the case of an only son, for otherwise it would be difficult to avoid contradiction with the statements previously cited. Now, one might object: even if the mother possesses authority, the giving away of a son is improper because she lacks independence. True; however, it is indeed proper when done with the permission of an independent person. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "A woman shall not give or receive a son except with the permission of her husband. Furthermore, some things may be given only when permitted by the husband, some only when permitted by the primary brother, and some, even if self-acquired, may be given only when permitted by the master in the case of a slave. And so says Bṛhaspati:
That which is received as a dowry, inherited in due order, or acquired through valor,
as well as that which is given with the permission of the wife, kinsmen, or the owner, shall attain validity.

The meaning is as follows: that which is *saudāyika*—obtained at marriage—may be given only with the consent of the wife by whom it was obtained at her wedding; however, that which has come down through the lineage of a grandfather or others may be given only with the consent of kinsmen whose wealth is undivided; and what is obtained by a servant in battle may be given only with the consent of the master. That which is permitted by the wife or kinsmen must be given along with its remainder;
but in the case of property obtained at marriage or inherited through lineage, there is no such requirement for giving away everything.

This is because it was stated by that very same author: "But what is self-acquired may be given even without the consent of those who share undivided property," for he declared, "that which is acquired by oneself. And thus, even immovable property acquired by oneself may be given away—even if it exceeds seven [plots]—without the consent of kinsmen. Furthermore, as he stated: "Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights regarding immovable property; for one alone is not empowered in any act of giving, mortgaging, or selling."

Thus, this refers to the case of undivided immovable property. It should be explained that even those who are divided [have no power] if they are equal [in status], let alone those who are undivided; otherwise, the act of division would be purposeless. And so, as it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Even a single person may perform the giving, mortgaging, or selling of immovable property in times of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of dharma."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers both to immovable property that has come down in succession (kramāyāta) and to immovable property exceeding seven [ancestors], because the particle *api* connects with both [conditions], like the eye of a crow. When it is connected with the latter, the meaning is as follows: even regarding immovable property, even in the absence of a multiplicity of such properties, one person may perform acts such as giving (*dāna*). Since a pledge (*ādhi*) is also a form of giving—because ownership is understood through that form and because of the scriptural statement, "the pledge is [secured] by the practice of binding"—it is understood that it must be given. And thus, the fact that a pledge is not to be given, which was stated in the previous section [verse 448], should be understood to apply to it in its capacity as a pledge, but not in its capacity as something other than a pledge. In connection with the mention of what may be given, Yājñavalkya has shown a specific manner of acceptance for the recipient of what is to be given.
"The acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property. Thus it is said.

*Prakāśaḥ* means manifest, that is to say, in the presence of witnesses. A specific procedure for the acceptance of a son has been shown by Vasiṣṭha: "One intending to accept a son shall summon his kinsmen, inform the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras in the middle of the house, he should accept one who is not a distant kinsman (*adūrebāndhava*) and who is not too closely related (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*). The term *adūrebāndhava* refers to a relative such as a maternal uncle who is nearby; *asaṃnikṛṣṭa* means one distinct from those who are very closely related, such as a brother’s son, and so forth—one should accept only such a person. Having stated this incidental matter, Yājñavalkya has also stated what pertains to the main subject at hand.
"What has been promised as a gift must be given, and once given, it must not be taken back again.

The meaning is this: that which has been promised with the words "I shall give this to you" must necessarily be given to him, and once given, it must under no circumstances be taken back. Regarding the fault of one who does not give what was promised, or who takes back what has been given, Hārīta says:
"By failing to give what was promised, and by seizing what has been given..."
One goes to various hells and is born in the animal realm.
But a promised gift does not depart like a debt without being given; thus he himself said:
"That which is promised by word alone, but not fulfilled through action, remains joined with the nature of a debt both in this world and in the next. [449]

The meaning is that wealth which is connected with *dharma*—or promised verbally for the sake of fulfilling the religious duties of the recipient—but is not subsequently delivered, does not depart [from the debtor] like a debt, both in this world and the next. By the expression "like a debt," it is implied by the sense that the one who fails to deliver it must be compelled to pay and shall be punished. And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"He who, having voluntarily promised a gift to a Brāhmaṇa, does not give it, shall be compelled to pay like a debt and shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine."

The phrase "to a Brāhmaṇa" implies one who is not devoid of the practice of the prescribed duties (*pravṛtadharma*); for the Smṛti of Gautama states: "Even after having given a promise, one should not give [the gift] to one who is joined with unrighteousness (*adharma*)."
Thus ends the section on things to be given in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections on things already given;
regarding this, Nārada says:

Those who know the rules of giving recognize as a gift that which is given for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return favor, or for the sake of a bride-price or as a mark of favor.

The price of merchandise refers to the value of goods purchased. Wages (*bhṛti*), however, have been demonstrated by Kātyāyana: "Where a gift is determined for the purpose of obtaining an unknown service, that which is obtained through the performance of that service is proclaimed as wages."

The meaning is that what is given for the purpose of accomplishing a task with a specific motive is called *bhṛti* (wages). By the word "out of satisfaction" (*tuṣṭyā*), what is given to bards and the like is indicated; by "out of affection" (*snehāt*), what is given to daughters and others is indicated. "In return for a service" (*pratyupakārataḥ*) means what is obtained from one who has rendered a service for the sake of a reciprocal favor. To demonstrate this, Kātyāyana says:
"What is obtained according to this rule—for protection from fear, for defense, or for the accomplishment of a task—one should know as being received 'in return for a service. (NSm 1.38)

"For protection from fear" means for guarding against danger. "For the sake of protection" means for the purpose of safeguarding the property of children and others. "From the accomplishment of tasks" means from the performance of marriage and other such rites. "Obtained by this method" means, in short, obtained through the aforementioned instruments characterized by protection from fear and so forth. "Marriage-fee" (*strīśulka*) refers to what is given to the girl's relatives for the purpose of a wedding. "For the sake of favor" means given by the force of the rule that one must perform service for the benefit of others. Regarding this, Nārada says that what is given as a favor to a worthy recipient becomes fruitful: "To one's mother and father, to a teacher, to a friend, to a humble person, and to a benefactor..."
But that which is given to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished becomes fruitful.

"To one who has been helpful" means to one intent on helping others. "Fruitful" means endowed with an excellence of results; this is the meaning. "Those who know giving" understand that which is given—namely, these seven types of gifts beginning with the price for goods—to be truly given; the meaning is that they know it to be non-returnable. Bṛhaspati also says:
"Wages paid out of satisfaction, the price for goods, the bride-price for a wife, and what is given to a benefactor out of faith, favor, or affection—they know these to be the eight kinds of gifts."
Kātyāyana states that if one's entire property is offered to a benefactor, it does not constitute a valid gift: "Even if it has been said,
'I shall give my entire property to him who rescues me from this life-threatening danger,' it would not be so [considered a gift]."
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, the sections concerning what has been given [451]; now,
the sections concerning what has not been given.
But what is taken without it being given may be so through the force of fear, anger, or grief;
likewise, through bribery, jesting, exchange, or by means of deception.

That which is performed by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent" and "this is my deed."
"When one says 'this is a worthy recipient' regarding an unworthy recipient, or when an act is joined with unrighteousness,
that which is given through ignorance is likewise declared to be as if not given."

The following is what is meant: that which is given by one terrified by fear, such as from being taken captive; that which is given by one tormented by anger, in order to spend wealth upon those who are objects of his wrath and whose property has not been divided, giving it to others; that which is given by one tormented by the force of grief, with the thought "what is the use of this wealth remaining?", giving it for the time being; that which is given as a bribe to royal officials and the like; that which is given in jest; that which is given publicly in the presence of people for the purpose of deceiving another, while intending to receive it secretly through a reversal or a trick; that which is given by one who has not attained legal majority; that which is given by a fool to someone other than the person intended in his mind; that which is given by one who is not independent, such as a slave; that which is given by one afflicted by illness, whose natural state is impaired by disease; that which is given by one intoxicated, whose intellect is deranged by consuming *dhuttūra* (datura) and the like; that which is given by one who is insane, whose intellect is deranged by an excess of bile (*pitta*) and so forth; that which is given as a form of hospitality to a non-laborer for the sake of making him work; that which is given to one who does not return a favor out of a desire to receive a favor in return; that which is given to an unworthy person merely by saying he is worthy; and that which is given to one who misuses wealth merely by saying he uses it well—this sixteen-fold variety is called "not given" because it is subject to being reclaimed again. What has been given by those who are dependent on lust or anger, who are distressed, weak, insane, or deluded, and what is given through error or in jest— that one may take back.
But as for a bribe that has been promised for the sake of accomplishing a task,
even when that matter has been successfully accomplished, it must by no means be given.
"Furthermore, if she has already been given away previously, he should be compelled to give her back by force;
and Gārgya and the followers of Mānava state that the fine shall be eleven times [the value].
By this same [author], the nature of a bribe (*utkoca*) has also been shown.
Because of proclaiming thieves, violent criminals, the depraved, and adulterers;
because of seeing one whose livelihood has been ruined; and likewise, because of promoting untruth.
"Whatever has been obtained by these [mediators], however small, is called a bribe (*utkoca*).
In that case, the giver shall not be punished, but the mediator alone shall bear the guilt. Thus it is said.

This is what is meant: if one takes any wealth from a thief or similar person by instilling fear, saying, "If you do not give it to me, then I shall report what you have done"; or if one takes anything from a fugitive by instilling fear, saying, "If you do not give it to me, then I shall show you to the police (vāraka)"; or if one takes anything from a servant or similar person by speaking agreeably before the master, saying, "If you give it to me, then I shall speak the truth," implying that otherwise I shall speak falsely—this is all called *utkoca* (bribery). That must be made over to the giver by the king, and both the one who caused the bribery and the receiver are to be punished. Bṛhaspati, however, says it is to be recovered.
If a gift is given with the desire for personal gain, to one who is unworthy while suspecting him to be worthy,
or for a purpose connected with unrighteousness, the owner shall recover it.
Manu also says:
"If wealth that was given by someone for the sake of dharma to another who requested it should later not be used for that purpose, it must be taken back by him."

The meaning is this: if one who has been solicited to perform a duty such as a sacrifice does not perform that duty with the wealth given to him, then the wealth given must be reclaimed. Furthermore, if the solicitor should wish to establish that such wealth is not subject to forfeiture, he must be made by the king to pay back that wealth, such as gold and so forth. And thus says that same author: "If, however, he should recover that [wealth] out of pride or through force, he shall be made by the king to pay one *suvarṇa*; that shall be the expiation for his theft."
Bṛhaspati also points out certain things that have not been given:

"By those who are angry, fallen from their status, intoxicated, afflicted by pain, children, insane, or overcome by fear; by those who are drunk, very old, driven away, deluded, or overwhelmed by the force of grief."

"Likewise, that which was given in jest by them is declared to be as if not given. [This refers to] what was given by one who is intoxicated or possessed by an evil spirit. "Nirdhūta" means shaken off; "avadhūta" means the same. "Narmadattam" means given in jest. The status of being "not given" regarding what is given by one in distress applies only to matters other than religious duties (*dharmakārya*);
for what is given or announced for the sake of a religious duty by one who is either healthy or in distress is valid.

"But if he dies without having given it, his son shall be made to pay; there is no doubt in this matter" (Kātyāyana Smṛti 454). Likewise, the following rule, common to all titles of dispute, was stated by Manu: "That which is fraudulently mortgaged or sold, and that which is fraudulently given or received..."
Or wherever one perceives any underlying motive, one should completely turn back from all of that.

*Yoga* means a means (*upāya*). And thus is the meaning: when those specific conditions (*upādhi*) under which the acts of lending, giving, and receiving were performed have ceased, all of them must be rescinded. On this point, Nārada says: "He who, out of delusion, accepts what was not given, and he who gives what should not be given—both of these are to be punished by a king who knows the Dharma."

Here, the person who has become the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is specified. However, for a person who has become the agent (*kartṛ*), the non-delivery or non-payment of what was not to be given, or its subsequent recovery, does not entail punishment, because such an act follows the path of traditional law and custom (*smṛti-ācāra*). Nor does it entail sin (*pratyavāya*), since Manu describes it as "righteous" (*dharmyā*) when he states: "This is declared to be the righteous way of properly returning what has been given."
Thus concludes the section concerning what has not been given in the *Smṛticandrikā*;

the exposition of the rules for the legal category known as "Non-delivery of What Was Given" (*dattāpradānika*) is finished. Now, the rule for the legal category known as "Failure to Serve After Having Agreed" (*abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*) is stated.
In this regard, Nārada says:

"The pupil, the resident student, and the hired servant—these three, along with the fourth, the laborer for extra work, are to be known as 'workers' (karmakarāḥ); but slaves (dāsāḥ) are those born in the house."
"The wise say that their commonality is dependence;
however, the distinction is said to be based on genus, action, and likewise on their mode of subsistence. [455]

These four types—disciples and the rest—are to be understood as attendants (*śuśrūṣaka*) who perform work. However, the fifteen kinds of household-born attendants are to be understood as slaves (*dāsa*). The wise, such as Manu and others, declare that the common characteristic of these workers and slaves is their lack of independence (*asvatantratva*). The meaning is that the specific distinctions among disciples, students (*antevāsin*), and slaves are stated to be based on birth (*jāti*), action (*karman*), and livelihood (*vṛtti*). Among these, the distinction based on birth for disciples—consisting in being one of the three higher castes—is to be determined from scriptures such as, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring. But the distinction among them based on action has been stated by Bṛhaspati.
The triple Vidyā is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
for the sake of that, one should perform service to the teacher as enjoined by the scriptures.
The word "disciple" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. And so says Nārada:
"Until the acquisition of knowledge, the disciple, being self-restrained, should serve the guru.
In this same way, service should also be performed toward the wife of the guru and others.

"His conduct toward the wife of his guru and likewise toward the son of his guru is as follows"—thus it was stated by that very [author]. The specific details regarding the disciples' conduct concerning the giving of alms and so forth have been described in the *Saṃskārakāṇḍa*; therefore, for fear of redundancy, they are not mentioned here. Having stated some particulars of their conduct, he says the same author:
"But one who has returned home, having presented the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) to the guru..."
She should return to her own home; this is declared to be the conduct of a female disciple.

"Should return to his own home" means he should go toward his own residence. When it is asked what the distinction among pupils (*antevāsins*) is based on birth or occupation, Bṛhaspati states: "Skill (*vijñāna*) is said to be craft, such as the refinement of gold and base metals, as well as dance and so forth; for the sake of acquiring these, one should perform service in the teacher's house."

The knowledge concerning the manufacture of bracelets, anklets, and so forth, as well as the performance of dance, song, and so forth—and by the word "and" (ca), also the construction of pillars, pots, and so forth—is called *śilpavijñāna* (artisanal knowledge). For the sake of attaining that, a pupil should perform work, such as making bracelets, anklets, and the like, in the house of the teacher; this is the meaning. By this, the distinction among pupils based on caste—such as goldsmiths and others—and based on their specific tasks, such as making bracelets and anklets, is shown. Nārada, however, states what must be done by pupils at the time of beginning the practice of their craft:
Desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his relatives,
he should dwell in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time.

"Having made a firm determination near [the teacher] regarding the duration—meaning, having firmly determined the limit of time stated by the teacher that 'one must remain in my presence for this much time'"—he (the same author) states what must also be done by the teacher:
"The teacher, having provided food in his own home, should instruct him;
he should not cause him to perform other work, and he should treat him like a son."

"Other work" refers to labor distinct from one's own craft. Thus, it should be understood that a pupil must perform service to the teacher merely by offering the fruits of his work, such as bracelets and the like. By stating "one who has been given seed-grain in his own house," the author indicates the specific distinction regarding the livelihood of pupils. Regarding a teacher who does not act in this manner, Kātyāyana declares the punishment:
"But he who does not cause [the pupil] to learn the craft, yet causes him to perform other tasks, shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; from him the pupil withdraws."
Regarding even the wickedness of a disciple, Nārada says:
"If one should abandon a teacher who is instructing him and is himself free from fault,
he should be forced to stay [with him], or he may deserve corporal punishment or imprisonment."

"He should be made to dwell by the side of the teacher"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, "killing" (*vadha*) means beating, not the severing of life, because the offense is minor. He states the duty of one who has completed his studies: "Even though he is trained, the resident pupil (*antevāsī*) should complete the full period;
whatever work he performs there, its fruit belongs to the teacher alone."

The *kṛta* period is defined as the time limit for remaining in the presence of the teacher. During that remainder of the period, even when the daily practice has ceased, the student must necessarily perform the ritual acts for the sake of the teacher’s material gain. Even during this remainder of the period, his meal is to be taken only at the teacher’s house. Thus says Yājñavalkya: "Even after completing his craft, the resident pupil (*antevāsī*) shall dwell in the teacher’s house for the full duration; he shall receive his food from the teacher and offer him the fruits of his labor."
Regarding the duties of the apprentice after the acquisition of knowledge, service, and completion have been accomplished, Nārada says:
"Having mastered the craft at the proper time, the apprentice, having circumambulated the teacher from left to right and honored him according to his ability, should take leave of him. [458]

For hired laborers (*bhṛtaka*), however, there is no distinction based on caste or occupation as there is for apprentices (*antevāsin*); rather, the distinction is based on the wages, the work performed, and the duration of time. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"He who enjoys the wife of another should be known as a 'hireling of a woman' (*vanitābhṛta*);
he must perform that work for her master just like any other man hired for wages."
One is said to be a bearer of many purposes, while another is a bearer of a portion; furthermore, the states of being inferior, middling, or superior have been declared for all of them indeed.
Likewise, it is carried for a day, half a month, six months, three months, and a year.

"He shall perform the work as promised and receive the stipulated wage"—this refers to the master of the female slave. The various types of wages for one who is hired should be understood according to the relative degree of the smallness or greatness of the payment. That gradation is to be inferred in accordance with the capacity of the laborer;
"the wage based on their work shall be proportionate to the capacity of the laborer."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada, he himself states the division for the share-taker:
"Share-takers who live by agriculture or cattle-rearing are said to be of two kinds;
from the grain produced and likewise from the milk, he shall receive his share—of this there is no doubt."

"The distinction between inferior, middling, and superior, produced by their actions and based on tasks such as guarding and so forth," he himself has said: "Among them, the one skilled in weaponry is the best; the plowman is middling; the burden-carrier is declared the lowest, as is the one who performs domestic chores. [459]

A *sīravāhaka* is a ploughman. Just as one who carries a burden is declared to be of the lowest rank, so too is one who performs all domestic tasks such as cooking declared to be of the lowest rank; this is the meaning. As for the distinction among servants based on time, which is determined by the brevity or length of the period [of service], that has already been explained [in the section] beginning with "for a day, a month," etc., and should be understood accordingly. Nārada, however, states the nature of the *adhikarmakṛt*: "He who is appointed over all [servants] and likewise over the household is to be known as an *adhikarmakṛt*, and he is remembered as a *kauṭumbaka*."

Among all types of laborers (*bhṛtaka*), the *adhikṛta* is one who is placed above others; that is to say, a supervisor (*adhiṣṭhāyaka*). Some read the term as *arthādhikṛta*; in that case, the meaning is: one appointed as a guardian over matters such as fields, gold, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "above the family" (*kuṭumbasyopari*), the word *kṛta* must be supplied. Being placed above the family means being appointed as the manager of income and expenditure. Having thus defined the student (*śiṣya*), resident pupil (*antevāsin*), laborer (*bhṛtaka*), and overseer (*adhikarmakara*), the same author states that these are performers of auspicious works (*śubhakarmakara*).
"For these four are declared to be performers of auspicious deeds. And auspicious action is to be understood as that which is other than contemptible action; thus he himself said:
"The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps..."
Touching the secret parts of the body, receiving the remnants of food, and the taking up or discarding of feces and urine.
"Service by means of one's own limbs at the will of the master, and finally [the removal of waste];
this should be understood as inauspicious action, whereas that which follows it is auspicious.

Here, *avaskara* refers to a heap of dust that has been swept away. The word "cleansing" (*śodhana*) is connected individually with each of the four [locations], beginning with the door of the house. *Ujjhana* means abandonment. "Finally" (*antataḥ*) refers to the surrender of one's own hands and so forth at the master's wish for the purpose of smearing and sweeping once the voiding of urine and excrement has ceased.
Thus ends the section concerning laborers in the Smṛticandrikā; now follows the definition of slaves.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"But the remaining fifteen are slaves who perform the lowest tasks.

Here, "the remaining" refers to those left over from the categories of students (*śiṣya*), resident pupils (*antevāsin*), hired laborers (*bhṛtaka*), and overseers (*adhikarmakṛt*). "Those who perform the lowest tasks" means they are engaged in inauspicious work such as cleaning the house, the door, and unclean places. By this, the distinction among slaves based on their labor has been stated. Regarding the number "fifteen" (*tripañcaka*), Kātyāyana explains the distinction between slaves and laborers by demonstrating the etymology of the word "slave":
"Bhṛgu says that slavery arises from the giving away of one's own independent self, just like [the gift of] a wife."

The meaning is that the teacher Bhṛgu considers that just as one becomes a means (*dvāratva*) by giving up one's own body for the sake of the master’s enjoyment, so too does one become a slave (*dāsatva*) by giving oneself up for the sake of another who is independent. By this, it should be understood that a distinction is also stated: those who serve having attained absolute dependence on another are slaves (*dāsas*), while those who serve having attained mere dependence on another are laborers (*karmakaras*). Absolute dependence on another, however, belongs to those who have resorted to service for another by obstructing their own pursuit of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). Such slavery is to be known as existing only among the other three castes, excluding the Brāhmaṇa, because he himself has declared: "A Brāhmaṇa never [enters] into servitude" (MDh 8.411). By this, the difference in the caste of slaves is stated. Even among those other than Brāhmaṇas, servitude occurs only in the direct order of castes (*ānulomyena*).
Servitude follows the direct order of the castes and not the inverse order;
for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who abandon their own wives, [the same applies].

The meaning is: for those who renounce their independence and devote themselves entirely to the interests of others. The phrase "in the inverse order" (pratilomataḥ) is to be understood as applying to ascetics other than those who have abandoned their own duties;
servitude is not ordained for the castes in the inverse order.
Except in the case of those who abandon their own duties, servitude is considered equal to marriage.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Nārada: "Just as a woman of lower caste or even one of the same caste may become the wife of a man of higher caste, but never a woman of higher caste may become the wife of a man of lower caste, so too may a slave [be taken]"; this is the meaning. Because of the statement "slavery is like marriage," it might appear that for a Brāhmaṇa, slavery toward one of his own caste is permitted in times of distress; therefore, with the intent to prohibit that, Kātyāyana says: "Even toward one of equal caste, a Brāhmaṇa must never be made to perform servitude.
Furthermore, he stated the same thing again as if it were being repeated.
For the royal splendor of a king is destroyed by the servitude of a Brahmin;
however, the duties of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra may at times apply to one of the same caste.
"Bṛhaspati says that one should not cause a Brāhmaṇa to perform the duties of a slave."

Here there are three statements. Regarding them, the meaning of the first statement, when read in reverse order, is that if one causes a Brāhmaṇa to be made a slave, a loss of luster (*tejohāni*) arises for the one who causes it to be done. The meaning of the second statement is that slavery, however, is not a characteristic of the mixed castes (*saṃkara-jāti*). The meaning of the third statement is that one should by no means cause a Brāhmaṇa to perform the duties of a slave—even a person of the same caste (*savarṇa*)—just as one would not enslave him. Thus, there is nothing at all that seems redundant. He himself says that even while performing such work for the benefit of a specific person according to his own will, a Brāhmaṇa should not perform an inauspicious act.

Even toward one endowed with virtue and Vedic study, a superior twice-born man should not intentionally perform any action that falls short of his status; nor should he perform anything unwholesome even in that case.

The meaning of the first half-verse is as follows: since one must perform service for the benefit of others, another person may—whether out of desire or even without wages—perform work that is inferior to that [standard], namely work distinct from middling or superior labor, for the sake of another's welfare, acting of his own accord. Regarding this, Manu says to the master:
"A Brāhmaṇa should support a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood out of compassion, and have them perform their own duties."

In the phrase *vṛttikarśitau* (“those emaciated by lack of livelihood”), the accusative case is employed—just like the second case in the *pāśa* mantra—to express merely the status of being an object (*karmatva*). Thus, the meaning is as follows: “The master should support the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya who are emaciated by lack of livelihood and have become slaves, making them perform tasks without cruelty. By saying “emaciated by lack of livelihood,” he shows that the acceptance of slavery by the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya must be done out of necessity alone, and not when such a necessity does not exist. By saying “the master” (*svāmī*), he indicates that one should not make them perform the duties of a kinsman or a father. By using the general term “tasks” (*karmāṇi*), he suggests that there is no fixed rule that they must only be made to perform menial labor. By stating “he should support those emaciated by lack of livelihood,” he also makes known that, according to the requirements of the situation, the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya should be made to perform servitude, and not merely be subjected to the master’s authority. For this very reason, the same author, having restated the offense of one who employs them merely through his authority—which stems from ignorance of the enjoined meaning—prescribes a punishment for him.
If a Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, should compel initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will through his superior power,
he shall be made to pay six hundred [paṇas] by the king.

"Prābhavya" means the state of being a master (*prabhava*); therefore, "on account of prābhavya" means precisely on account of mastery. By using the term "the twice-born," he shows that this punishment does not apply to a Śūdra. For this very reason, the same author states: "But one may compel a Śūdra to perform servitude, whether he has been purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for servitude."

Viṣṇu, however, states the punishment for one who causes a person of higher caste to perform servitude in reverse order: "He who employs a person of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement."
Thus ends the section on the definition of slaves in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some other statements concerning the subject of slaves are recorded;
therein, Nārada says:
One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir,
one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who has been placed there by the master;
[464] Released from great debt, won in battle as a prize,
approached saying "I am yours," and made one who has completed his period of wandering life.
"One should know the slave by inheritance, as well as the one acquired through a mare;
the seller of oneself—these are recorded in the treatise as the fifteen kinds of slaves. Thus it is said.

"Born in the house" means born of a female slave belonging to one's own household. "Purchased" means acquired from another owner for a price. "Obtained" means acquired from that same person through gift or other means. "Inherited" means acquired by virtue of being an heir to the estate. "Supported during a famine" means one who was nourished during a time of scarcity. "Entrusted" means one who has been made a pledge (ādhi) with the creditor of the master. "Released from debt" means one who has entered into servitude as a reciprocal favor for the clearing of a debt. "Captured in battle" means seized after being defeated in combat. "Won at stake" means one won in gambling or similar activities where servitude was the wager. "Approached saying 'I am yours'" means one who has voluntarily accepted servitude, saying, "I am your slave. "One who has fallen from renunciation" means one who has lapsed from the state of a wandering ascetic (saṃnyāsin). "Contracted" means one who has agreed, "I shall be your slave for this much time. "Slave for food" (*bhaktadāsa*): *bhakta* here means food; one who has agreed, "As long as I provide you with food, I am your slave. "Brought by a mare" (*vaḍavāhṛta*): having married a mare—a female domestic slave—one enters into servitude for the sake of obtaining her master's consent. "Seller of oneself" means one who himself has sold his own self for the sake of wealth or other purposes. Such are the fifteen types of slaves recorded in the *Dharmaśāstra*. Regarding this, he [the author of the *Manusmṛti*] states that the release from servitude for the first four—those born in the house, purchased, obtained, and inherited—occurs only through the favor of the master, and not otherwise.
In that regard, the first group of four is not released from slavery except through the favor of the master; their servitude is hereditary.
Thus, he says the same regarding another who has sold himself: his slavery is not released by anyone other than the favor of the master.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
he is the most contemptible among them, and he is not released even from slavery.

The phrase "except by the favor of the master" (*prasādāt svāminaḥ*) is understood to apply here as well. Consequently, the meaning is this: even one who has sold himself for a price is not released from servitude to anyone other than through the favor of the master, just like those born in the house and the others. Thus, it should be understood that by means of this phrasing, it is shown that those born in the house and the others—making five including the one who sells himself—are released from servitude through the master's favor, just like those who were not supported during a time of distress and so forth. He states the same point: that even by saving the life of the master, all those born in the house and those not supported during a time of distress are released from servitude.
Whosoever among these masters might liberate one from the danger of death,
that person shall be released from slavery and receive a share equal to that of a son.

The meaning is: "among these fifteen kinds of slaves. Furthermore, this release from slavery—whether through the favor of the master or by protection of one's life—applies to all cases except that of one who has fallen away from the religious order (*pravrajyāvasita*). For Yājñavalkya records: "One who has fallen away from the religious order is a slave to the king for life. This means he is a slave only to the sovereign (*pārthiva*), not to anyone else. Therefore, Nārada says:

But a man who has fallen from the religious life shall become the slave of the king alone; there is no release for him, nor is there purification for him in any way whatsoever. [466] The term "man" (nara) is intended here to mean one other than a Brahmin, because slavery is prohibited for a Brahmin. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:

"Where the three twice-born castes have resorted to renunciation, the king shall cause the Brāhmaṇa to be banished and the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya to enter into servitude," says Bhṛgu. The ellipsis "the king shall cause [him] to be banished" is to be supplied. And so too Nārada:
But having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, he who does not abide by his own duty,
the king should brand with the mark of a dog's foot and quickly banish.

Even for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who refuses to perform menial service with a heated iron foot resembling a dog's foot, banishment shall be carried out according to the prescribed rule, because it is stated in general terms that "one who does not abide by his own duty" [is subject to this]. However, as he himself has stated:
"These two are outcastes by their actions in this world and are to be shunned from afar:
one who has returned from renunciation and one who has entered renunciation in vain."

This refers to slaves other than royal slaves (*rājadāsa*), because it is illogical to exclude the royal slave [from this rule]. And thus, it should be understood that the liberation of slaves—excluding those who have fallen from the religious life (*pravrajyāvasita*)—from their masters occurs through the master’s favor or by saving his life. However, regarding the nine types of slaves beginning with those hired during times of distress (*anākālabhṛta*), excluding those who have fallen from the religious life and those who sold themselves, he [the same author] states that the slavery of each of these nine is removed even by the gift of a single pair of cattle (*goyuga*) and so forth: "One hired during times of distress is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle;
one pledged as collateral is also released by giving wealth, provided the master rescues him."
A debtor is released from slavery by paying back the debt along with the interest;
likewise one who has entered [into servitude] saying "I am yours," or one captured in battle, or one won at a wager.
They may be released through the granting of a substitute for each head by means of an equivalent act;
even one who has acted [culpably] is released once the appointed time has passed.
"By the lifting up of the food, the slave for food is immediately released;
by the restraint of the mare, one who has been taken as a slave by a mare is released. Thus it is said.

This is what is meant: a slave who has been made so by being supported during a famine is released by the surrender of two cows. An *āhitadāsa* (a slave pledged for a debt), however, is released from the slavery of the creditor once the debt held by the creditor has been repaid. A *ṛṇadāsa* (a slave for a debt) is released by giving to the person who discharged his own debt that same amount of money with interest. As for the three specific types of slaves beginning with those who have submitted saying "I am yours," they are released by the gift of another slave capable of performing all the tasks required by their master. A *kṛtadāsa* (a slave by contract) is released upon the expiration of the period of time stipulated as the limit of his servitude. One who has entered into slavery out of a desire for a female slave is released by renouncing her enjoyment. Yājñavalkya, however, speaks of the dismissal of those who are merely semblances of slaves.
"One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves, or even one who has been sold, is released.

This means that if someone, though not a slave, has been made a slave by some master through force, or if he has been abducted by thieves and sold into slavery, or has been placed there or given away, and remains in the state of slavery under that master, he must be released by that master immediately, even without a cause for release. If the master does not release him due to greed or other such motives, then he must be caused to be released by the king. And so says Nārada:
Those who have been robbed, sold, or forcibly enslaved as slaves must be released by the king; servitude is not permitted among them.
But he who, having previously been the slave of one, enters into servitude under another, is to be released by that other; thus he himself has stated in a figurative manner:
"He who, being dependent, offers himself up saying 'I am yours,' shall not obtain his desire; the former master may take him back."

"Dependent" means one who is not independent due to being the slave of another; "at will" refers to servitude under a new master, because she was desired by the previous master as a slave. Thus, everything that has been stated regarding a male slave should be understood to apply to a female slave as well, as appropriate. Regarding a female slave's master, Kātyāyana states a specific rule: "If a man has sexual intercourse with his own female slave and she subsequently gives birth, considering the seed [of the father], she should not be treated as a slave, provided she is accompanied by her offspring."

The meaning is this: having taken account of the pregnancy conceived by her own master, the master’s female slave, together with her offspring, shall be made free from slavery—by means of the procedure for releasing one from servitude—for the purpose of removing the state of slavery resulting from the pregnancy she conceived and so forth, and she is to be treated as no longer a slave. When it is asked, "What, then, is the procedure for releasing one from slavery?", Nārada says:
"He who, with a joyful mind, desires to make his own slave a non-slave, should take [a jar] from the slave's shoulder and break that jar along with its water."
He should sprinkle water mixed with unbroken rice grains and flowers upon his head;
then, having said "Thou art no slave," he should release him while facing eastward, repeating this three times.
Since this is the case regarding such a renunciation, that very same [author] states that the unfitness caused by servitude departs:
"From that time forward, he should be treated as a master protected by favor;
his food may be eaten and he may receive gifts from him, being esteemed by the virtuous."

The meaning is that when he has been protected by the master’s favor—consisting of the removal of his most grievous condition—and restored to his own true nature, such that he becomes fit for conversation and other social interactions, only then [does this apply]. This rule applies equally to one who wishes to make a female slave (dāsī) no longer a slave; for in the word *dāsam*, the gender and number of the qualifying attribute of the subject are not intended to be significant. Protected and maintained by the master’s permission, he becomes one whose food may be eaten, one who may accept gifts, and one who is esteemed by the virtuous. For this very reason, it is said: "Whatever wealth a slave may possess, the master is declared to be its lord."

Thus, although Kātyāyana has recorded the master’s authority over the property of a male slave, it should be understood that his authority over the property of a female slave is likewise recorded. And so he himself states that even a woman married by a slave falls into the status of a slave:
"But a woman who was married by a slave, though not herself a slave, shall also attain the status of a slave;
because her husband is her master, and since the master is dependent upon the owner."
Thus ends the exposition of the rules concerning the subject of slaves in the *Smṛticandrikā*, within the section known as "Service after Agreement.
Now, the rule for the section titled "Non-payment of Wages" is stated; therein Manu says:
"Henceforth, I shall declare the non-payment of wages."

Wages are the price for labor; their non-payment is the failure to deliver them to the servant, or the returning of what has already been delivered. Regarding that delivery, Nārada states a specific rule: "The master of the work shall pay wages to the servant in due order—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end—according to what was determined."

The meaning is that one should give the wages—whatever amount has been determined by measure, thinking "I shall give this much"—by dividing it into three parts at the beginning, middle, and end of the work. This should be understood to apply when there is no specific technical rule (paribhāṣā) stating that "this must be given all at once at the start" and so forth. Regarding the absence of a specific rule stating "I shall give this much," that same author says: "But when the wages are not fixed, the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall receive a tenth part of the profit, the cattle, and the crops, respectively."

"Ten parts" means the tenth part. They shall receive "the strength of the cow," that is, milk and so forth produced by the cattle such as cows being protected; the phrase "in due order" is to be understood as the ellipsis. However, Yājñavalkya says this when the master of the work becomes an obstacle to the receipt of the aforementioned share: "But he who causes [work] to be done without having fixed the wages must be made to pay a tenth part of the profit from trade, cattle, and crops by the king."

This rule regarding the taking of a tenth part of the grain as rent should be understood to apply to the case of a cultivator who works land that requires little effort. However, regarding the case of a cultivator who works land requiring great effort, Bṛhaspati says: "The plowman may take a third or a fifth part. This is an alternative based on specific circumstances. When it is asked how this distinction is determined, he himself says:
From the ploughshare of one who is supported by food, let them take a fifth part;
but from one who is not so supported, they should take a third part of the grain once it has grown.

A farmer who is supported by food and clothing shall take a fifth part of the crop grown in the field ploughed with his own plow; however, one who is not supported by those two shall take a third part—this is the meaning. Alternatively, in cases where there is no prior agreement stating "I shall give this much," the rule stated by Manu should be observed:
"Those skilled in sea-voyages, who perceive the requirements of place, time, and profit, shall determine the wages which would have been fixed had they not already been settled."

Even when it has been stipulated, "I shall give this much," Yājñavalkya states that in some cases a wage may be given that is less than that—being merely conceived by the master's own judgment—and in other cases even more than that may be given: "If one exceeds [the agreement regarding] place and time, or effects a profit otherwise, in that case the will of the master shall prevail; if more [work] has been performed, more must be given."

If a servant, acting independently without the master’s command, exceeds the place or time that brings about the accomplishment of the fruit of his work—such as trade—or makes the profit small by incurring excessive expenditure, the master may, according to his own discretion, give him a portion from the middle of the previously stipulated wages. However, for one who, acting independently, produces great profit, something more than the stipulated value should be given by the master as a reward; this is the meaning. He (the same author) states the method of paying the stipulated wages when a task is to be accomplished by many people: [The text continues with the specific rules regarding the distribution of wages among multiple workers.]
Whatever amount of work one performs, that much indeed is his wages;
if the task is impossible for both, [the wage is forfeit], but if it is possible, one should perform it according to what was heard [in the agreement].

The meaning is as follows: when a well has been constructed and a wage has been promised to its builders in the form of "I shall give this much," if it is commenced by two or more workers and remains incomplete due to obstacles, then something must be given to each worker in accordance with the work performed by each. However, if it is completed without obstacles, only as much as was agreed upon should be given.
Thus ends the section on the payment of wages in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follow the matters concerning servants.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
Whatever has been entrusted to them as an instrument for their work must be protected with a sense of trustworthiness, and never by means of deceit.

The meaning is this: the implements of work, such as plows and the like, which have been placed in the hands of the servants for the sake of the labor of agriculture and so forth by these masters of the work, must always be protected by them without any deceit. Bṛhaspati also says:
"A hired servant must not practice even the slightest deceit toward his master; he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a legal dispute arises. [473]

Consequently, due to such deceitful conduct, a dispute arises with the employer; in that case, the defeated laborer suffers a loss of wages in accordance with his deceit—this is the meaning. Regarding the failure to perform work, he (Yājñavalkya) says: "When a hired laborer who has received wages does not perform the work, if he is capable, he shall be made to pay a fine and twice the amount of those wages."

One should pay a fine to the king according to the offender's capacity; the meaning is that one should pay the wages already received to the owner at double the rate. Regarding this very matter, Yājñavalkya says concerning the non-payment of wages: "If [the wages] were not received, he should be made to pay an equal amount. The meaning is that one should pay to the owner exactly as much as the wage for which the service was undertaken, but not a fine to the king. Alternatively, having paid the agreed-upon fee, the master should compel the servant to work by force, as Nārada says:

"Having promised to perform work, one who fails to do so after having been given wages by force [should be punished]. Here, "having promised" (*pratiśrutya*) is intended as an illustration for "having commenced. As Kātyāyana says:
"But having undertaken the commencement of work, if one does not complete it even though it is finished..."
He must be compelled by force; if he does not comply, he deserves punishment.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "two hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. As Vṛddha-Manu says:
"He who, having promised, does not perform [the task], should be made to do it even by force;
if he still does not perform that work, he shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. Thus it is said.

As for that which was stated by Manu: "A hired servant who, though not ill, does not perform his work as prescribed out of arrogance, shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* and his wages shall not be paid. [474]

Thus, because the punishment is slight, this refers to a case of partial non-performance (*bhāgāsiddhi*); since giving [wages] is prohibited, even what has been paid should be recovered, as it is effectively unpaid. However, in the case of a minor degree of non-performance, he (Yājñavalkya) states that the aforementioned rule applies, with the exception of the fine: "Whether afflicted by illness or in good health, if one does not cause the work to be done, his wages must not be given, even for work that is only slightly incomplete."

By stating that "one who is healthy should not cause [the work] to be done," he shows that even for one who is unwell, there is no restriction on being the agent himself. However, if someone who is afflicted fails to have the work performed at the time of his affliction due to a lack of wealth or other means, but performs it himself after the affliction has passed—then, because the duration of his affliction was long, even though there was a delay in time, there is no fault on the part of the servant; thus, he undoubtedly receives his wages. On this point, the same author says: "But if one who is afflicted should perform [the work] after becoming healthy, starting from the beginning exactly as agreed, he shall indeed receive his wages, even after a very long period of time."
Regarding one who, having promised work for a specific period, abandons that work before the promised time has elapsed, Nārada says:
"By abandoning the work before the time is complete, he shall suffer the loss of his wages.

Regarding this, Viṣṇu also prescribes a fine: "And he shall pay a hundred paṇas to the king. In this very context, Nārada states that if a servant abandons the work due to a fault of the master, such as the commission of gross violence (*mahāpāruṣya*), he receives wages calculated according to the amount of time actually worked.
"One who flees due to a fault of the master shall receive whatever has been done [for him].

Regarding one who destroys the master’s property, such as oxen and the like, through his own fault such as negligence, Viṣṇu says: "If it is destroyed by his fault, that [value] must be given to the master, except in cases of injury caused by the king or fate. The meaning is that the appropriate value of what was lost must be paid. Regarding this, Vṛddhamanu states a distinction based on the specific nature of the fault:
"What is destroyed through negligence must be made to pay an equal amount; what is destroyed by intentional malice, twice as much."

If [the animal] is lost through negligence (*pramāda*) or lost through lack of care (*anavadhāna*), he should pay an amount equal [to its value]. If it is lost through malice (*droha*), meaning lost by means of a severe blow or the like, he should be made to pay twice—that is, he should give double the value. He (Nārada) himself states that if there is no fault on the part of the servant, and it was lost for some other reason, then it need not be paid: "But he should not be made to pay what has been stolen by thieves, or burnt, or carried away by water. "Carried away" (*ūḍha*) means taken away. Regarding one who, as a driver, destroys the draft-animal through his own fault such as lack of intelligence, Nārada says:
If a loss of goods should occur due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever is lost therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king.

Having placed merchandise such as betel nuts and the like in bags and other containers, it should be transported; [if] misfortune occurs, he shall incur a penalty for the damage and so forth. In this regard also, the specific rule stated by Vṛddha-Manu should be observed: "If [the goods] are destroyed through negligence, he must pay [their value]; if destroyed through malice, twice as much. Regarding the carrier who, by his own fault, causes an obstruction to the journey, Kātyāyana says:
"A carrier who causes an obstruction shall be made to pay double wages; this is the traditional rule.

Here, "carrier" is merely an illustration and not intended as a definitive restriction; therefore, it should be understood that this same rule applies even to a servant such as a soldier who causes an obstruction during a journey. For this very reason, Nārada states:
"But one who creates an obstruction at the time of departure shall be made to pay double wages."

Thus it has been stated in general terms. Here, "obstructing the work" is intended to mean the non-performance of the task that has been undertaken, and not such acts as confinement and the like. Furthermore, Yājñavalkya says regarding a case where the non-performance of the undertaken task does not cause an obstruction to the progress [of the work] due to the obtaining of other assistants: "If he abandons [the work] when it has commenced, he shall be made to pay a seventh part [of the wages]; if on the way, a fourth part; if at the halfway point, the entire wages. Thus it is said.

When the act of setting out has commenced, one who abandons the work he has undertaken shall be made to pay a seventh part of the wages; if he abandons it when the distance to be traveled is more than half-way, he shall pay a fourth part of the wages; and if he abandons it at the halfway point, he shall pay the full wages—this is the meaning.
Thus ends the section concerning servants in the Smṛticandrikā; now follow the matters concerning masters.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
If a servant, being commissioned by his master,
performs an inauspicious act for that purpose, the master incurs the guilt therein.

Inauspicious work (*aśubha-karma*) refers to such acts as plowing fields by improper means, including the transgression of boundaries. This is stated in order to declare that when a servant performs inauspicious work with the master's consent, the punishment falls upon the master. Kātyāyana also says:

"He who abandons on the road a companion who is exhausted or afflicted by disease shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise for one who fails to provide protection in a village for three days. [477]
Even Bṛhaspati [has said]:
"If a master does not pay wages to a servant who has performed his work,
he should be compelled by the king to pay them, as well as a proportional fine."

Regarding the hired servant (*bhṛta*): Viṣṇu also states, "If the master should abandon the hired servant before the term is complete, he must pay him the full value of his wages, as well as one hundred *paṇas* to the king, except in the case of a fault on the part of the servant. Here, the genitive case in *tasya* is used in the sense of the dative, because of Pāṇini’s rule, *śeṣe*, which continues [from the previous sūtra], stating, "*bahulaṃ chandasi*" (the genitive is frequently used in the sense of the dative in Vedic literature). In this context, "fault" (*doṣa*) refers to theft and the like, and not to such matters as eating excessively. Yājñavalkya also says: "Abandoning [the servant] while the work has begun, [the master incurs a fine of] a seventh part; a fourth part if he abandons him on the way."
The person who abandons [a traveler] must be made to pay the entire fare for the remaining half of the journey.

When the act of setting out has commenced, if one causes a servant who is performing work on a path where the portion to be traveled is still great, or on a "path of goods" (*arthapatha*), to abandon the journey, he is considered here the "causer of abandonment. He too, by abandoning the servant in the aforementioned places, must be made to pay a seventh part [of the wages] to the servant; this is the meaning. Regarding the payment of a fourth part on the road, that refers to the case of the owner of goods not yet sold. However, regarding the case of the owner of goods already sold, Vṛddhamanu says:
"If a merchant, having sold those goods on the road, should abandon the servant..."
Then, if he too should be entitled to a share, he shall receive half of the wages.

The phrase "excessive portion of the distance to be traveled" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the case where the goods are obstructed by the seizure of customs officers and others, or the case where the owner of the goods has had them stolen by the king and so forth, Kātyāyana says:
"But when those goods are seized or stolen on the road, the carrier shall receive wages proportional to the distance he has already traveled. [478]

The master shall pay the wages not previously given according to the distance traveled; however, for wages already paid, he may take back a portion. This is the meaning. Regarding the carrier of goods using a vehicle or the like that was hired for a fee, Nārada says: "But one who hires a vehicle and its driver and does not use it, or abandons it on the way, shall be made to pay a fourth part of the wages; if he abandons it halfway, he shall pay the full amount."

A "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to carts and the like; a "conveyance" (*vāhana*) refers to horses and the like. Having hired these by means of a contract for a specific purpose, such as reaching a destination, even if one does not take them for the sake of assistance, they must nevertheless be made to pay a fourth part of the wages—that is, a fourth part of the price. This is the meaning. Furthermore, because there is a rule regarding the payment of the full amount if [the vehicle] is abandoned halfway, it should be inferred that if one abandons vehicles hired for hire on a shorter distance, they are to be made to pay according to the calculation of a third or a half part. As for one who hires a cart or similar vehicle, takes it away without providing any service, and goes to another country without paying the hire, Vṛddhamanu says concerning him:
He who, having hired a cart and taken it elsewhere,
does not pay the hire, shall be made to pay the hire even for that which he did not mount.

This refers to the price for hiring based on the specific purpose of the task. The meaning is that even for a vehicle such as a cart that has not yet been used—that is, one for which no service has been rendered—the user must pay the hire fee. Kātyāyana, however, states that once the work has been performed, the hire fee does not cease until the vehicle or other item is returned, even if it is returned immediately after the task is finished:

"One who, having taken elephants, horses, cows, donkeys, camels, and so forth by means of a hire fee, does not return them after having accomplished his purpose, shall be made to pay the hire fee. [479]
The same author states that this applies to houses and other such things as well:
"He who takes a house, a cow-pen, a shop, or the like on lease and does not return it to the owner shall be made to pay the rent for as long as he retains it."

Here, by the word "water" (*vāri*), the vessel that contains it, such as a water-jar (*maṇika*) and so forth, is indicated. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one who has completed his task should not [be held liable for its loss]. Regarding the case of the total destruction of the water-jar or other vessels, Nārada says:
"One should bring back the vessels used for carrying the *stoma* [offerings] when they are full at the appointed time.
If a vessel is broken or lost, the liability shall fall upon the receiver, except in the event of an inundation."

"Stoma" means a rental fee (*bhāṭaka*). Goods taken for the purpose of transporting liquid substances are "stoma-carriers. The meaning is that when the period of full rental has expired, one should deliver them to their owner. Having established this, it is stated: "it shall belong to the taker," and so forth. This is its meaning: "collision" (*saṃplava*) is the impact with another substance, either partially or entirely; in such a case, what is broken—even if only slightly—or what has been restored as before, or what has acquired a similar form, must be returned to the owner of the goods. But in cases other than collision, such [damaged] goods shall belong to the taker of the rental—that is to say, they become his property and need not be made good by the giver of the rental. Regarding the location of the house and the giver of the rental, he (the same author) says:

"Whoever, having built a house on another's land, should dwell there after paying the *stoma* (fee), must depart taking with him that house, including the grass, wood, bricks, and so forth. Thus it is said.
He [the same author] also says regarding the non-payment of the *stoma*: [480]
But having stayed on another's land without a formal agreement and without a boundary marker,
one should by no means take grass, wood, or other such things while departing.
"Whatever grass, wood, or bricks have been placed there, he, upon departing, must report all of that to the owner of the land. Thus it is said.

"To the owner, to the owner" means he should inform him, that is, cause him to know. By the use of the word "uncertain," [the author] shows that this refers to a case where no convention has been established regarding whether grass, wood, and so forth may be taken or not. However, in a case where a convention has been established, it must be exactly as that convention dictates. The statement, "Having taken that, he should go out," should be understood—lest it contradict established custom—to refer to matters other than the taking of the root [or essential property]. Śambhu, however, provided an explanation for "having taken that" as meaning "having taken the house, that is to say, having taken the household utensils"; this should be disregarded as it contradicts [the rule concerning] "grass, wood, bricks, and so forth. Vyāsa also speaks of the connection specifically with the property of the dwelling.
However, for one who constructs a house with affection over a long period of time, the wood departs from him when he leaves, provided the ritual fee has been given; it is not otherwise.

For one who builds a temple or similar structure on another's land, when he departs—that is, when he leaves having abandoned that site—the wood and other materials that stood in the form of the temple belong only to the giver of the lease, provided a lease was given; otherwise, they belong to the owner of the land. This is the meaning.
Thus ends the section concerning owners in the *Smṛticandrikā* [481].
Now follow the sections concerning courtesans and their clients.
In this regard, Nārada says:
Having received the nuptial fee (*śulka*), a courtesan who does not wish [to have intercourse] shall pay double;
likewise, the giver of the fee who does not wish [to have intercourse] shall suffer the loss of the fee.
An exception to the rule "she who does not wish [to go] shall bear double [the fine]" is shown in another Smṛti:
"One who is ill, one who is in a state of agitation, one who is distracted, one devoted to royal duties,
or one who, having been invited, does not come— such a woman is declared to be a 'mare' (vaḍavā) beyond reproach."

In matters that are absolutely necessary, she who has become agitated is described by the term *saṃbhramā* with respect to the client (*viṭa*) who enjoys her; in that same context, she who is distressed is described by the term *vyagrā*.
