A "mare" (*vaḍavā*) is a female slave; her mention here is for the purpose of illustrating the courtesan (*paṇyastrī*), because the prohibition against speaking of [sexual acts] based on their connection to diseases and so forth applies equally elsewhere as well. Regarding the enjoyer, however, Nārada says:
"If a man, having enjoyed a woman, does not pay the fee (*śulka*) accordingly, yet engages in intercourse out of order (*akrameṇa*), [or] strikes her with teeth, nails, and so forth..."
"He who approaches a woman in an improper place, or even by many means, shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine.
Thus [it is stated]. Furthermore, regarding the offense of a courtesan, the punishment and other matters are shown in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.

If a courtesan, having received her fee, goes elsewhere out of greed, the king should cause her to pay a fine; he should likewise cause the other man to pay the fee. [482] Nārada speaks of those who decide disputes, excluding the presiding judges:
Those libertines who reside in her house and for whom the courtesan is the primary concern are known to provide a decision in cases of doubt regarding matters arising from her.
Thus ends the exposition of the rules concerning courtesans and their clients in the *Smṛticandrikā*, within the section titled "Non-payment of Wages. Now,
according to the intention of Nārada, the rules for the section known as "Disputes between Owner and Herdsman," which constitutes a supplement to the preceding section, are stated.

However, according to the opinion of Manu, because this section was stated independently immediately after the sections on rescission of purchase and sale, it ought to be discussed right after that in accordance with the order of the enumeration. Furthermore, we follow the order of the enumeration in the *Nāradasmṛti*; thus, its presentation here is faultless. And the promise to explain [this topic] was made by Manu for the purpose of demonstrating his independence:
"I shall now duly declare, according to the principles of Dharma, the legal dispute arising from transgressions between owners and herdsmen regarding cattle."

The meaning is: "dispute" refers to the procedure for resolving a dispute. The phrase "regarding cattle" is stated for the purpose of restricting the scope of the proposition (*pratijñā*). By this, the procedure concerning the determination of wages and so forth in cases of transgression between the owner and the herdsman regarding cattle is what is proposed as the subject matter to be expounded in this section; however, the procedure regarding warding off, punishment, beating, and so forth in cases of transgression by owners and herdsmen regarding crops and the like is not. Therefore, it should be understood that the rules on warding off and such are merely incidental here. Consequently, only those statements which expound the rules on the determination of wages and so forth, as proposed by us in this section, are now recorded. Regarding this, Nārada says:
From a hundred cows, a young heifer shall be the cowherd’s fee; from two hundred, the milk is his wage.
This is to be paid annually to the cowherd, along with the milk collected on the eighth day.

Every year, a cow that has passed the stage of being a heifer (*vatsatarī*) is the wage to be given to the herdsman. This is to be given based on the number of cows being tended; however, if there are more than one hundred, a cow with its calf takes the place of the heifer, and on the eighth day, the entire milk-yield (*saṃdoha*) is due. *Saṃdoha* means the milking of all [the cows]. As Bṛhaspati says:
"Likewise, one who is supported by a cow shall receive all its milk on the eighth day."

By this, the claim made by Śambhu—that there is a state of maintenance (*bhṛti*) between the cow and the herd independently of one another—should be understood as refuted. Following this line of reasoning, the specific amount of maintenance for cows numbering less than or more than one hundred or two hundred, as well as for other animals such as buffaloes, must be determined. This [rule] applies to cases where no specific maintenance has been previously agreed upon; however, regarding cases where such an agreement exists but its specific extent is not defined, Manu says:
"A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the permission of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten... and so forth.

The phrase "he should milk" implies "for the sake of his own maintenance. This is what is meant: from among ten cows that yield milk, the servant who is paid with milk should take for himself the best and most excellent one and consume its milk. This wage is intended for the purpose of maintaining those ten milch-cows. Following this principle, wages for maintaining a number of cows less than or greater than ten, as well as for maintaining buffaloes and other animals, should be calculated accordingly. For animals that do not yield milk, however, the wage should be calculated based on the value of their milk. Regarding the case of a herdsman who is not paid with milk but with another substance, he (the same author) states: "That [wage] shall be the maintenance for a herdsman who is not paid with milk. Nārada, however, describes the duties of both the owner and the herdsman.
He should cause the cow to be brought to the cowherd every day at the end of the night;
and those cows, having been entrusted [to him], the cowherd should bring back at evening.
The mention of "cows" (*gograhaṇa*) is intended to indicate cattle in general. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"In the same manner as the cattle were entrusted, the cowherd should return them in the evening.

The meaning is that however many were delivered in the morning, that many must be returned in the evening. Accordingly, Bṛhaspati says: "He should return everything in the evening. Regarding the non-return of all the cattle, however, Yājñavalkya says:
A keeper who has received wages must make good those [animals] that have perished through negligence;

"keeper" here means one for whom wages have been paid. The mention of "negligence" is intended to indicate the fault of the keeper. Therefore, in cases such as death caused by no fault of the keeper, he should not be made to pay; however, this does not apply when there is merely an absence of negligence. For this very reason, Manu says:
"But if they are stolen by thieves after a public proclamation, the keeper is not liable to pay."
If she reports [the matter] to her husband regarding both the place and the time, [she is blameless].

The meaning is that he has made a sound with horns, drums, flutes, and so forth, for the purpose of driving the cattle after having proclaimed them. The "place" intended is where the owner is stationed; the "time" intended is also one not excessively delayed from the time of collection. When, by his own fault, he has passed over such a place or time and reports it at another place or at another time, then it is understood that because he is at fault, he ought to pay in accordance with that. Vyāsa, however, intending to state that the keeper is not liable to pay because he is faultless, declares the keeper's faultlessness in certain cases.
In the event of an attack by predators, a raid upon a village, or the upheaval of a kingdom,
whatever may be lost or stolen there, the herdsman is not at fault.

The phrase "even in the absence of human effort" is to be understood as the ellipsis. But in other cases, if human effort is not exerted, he certainly becomes guilty of sin. For this very reason, Manu says:
"But the keeper alone shall restore what is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by dogs, or dead on uneven ground, provided it was deficient in human effort."

"Lost" means its location is unknown. "Destroyed by worms" means ruined by insects. "Killed by a dog" means killed by a dog. "Killed in a dangerous place" means dead in a ravine, a hole, or similar terrain. As for human effort, it was demonstrated by Nārada:
"One should protect [the property] from the fear of worms, thieves, tigers, ravines, and pits;
one should strive according to one's ability, cry out for help, or inform the owner."
"Should strive" means he should exert himself to remove the calamity. Reporting to the owner applies to the case of an incompetent keeper. As that same author says:
"If a calamity should befall the cattle, the cowherd should strive to remedy it to the best of his ability;
if he is incapable, he should quickly come and report it to the owner."

He himself states that one who fails to exercise human effort and thus allows the cattle to perish by the aforementioned causes of destruction must, in due order, deliver both the animal and a fine to the owner: "Without making an effort, without raising an outcry, or without informing the owner, the cowherd must bear the loss and pay a fine to the king. [486]
Yājñavalkya states the authoritative rule regarding the law of cattle:
"In the event of destruction due to the fault of the keeper,
a fine of twelve and a half paṇas is ordained for the keeper, as well as the restitution of the property to the owner."

"Thirteen and a half paṇas" means thirteen and a half kārṣāpaṇas; the meaning is that this fine is to be imposed upon the herdsman. This is because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "He shall give the lost property—the value of the lost animal—to the owner. To demonstrate the fault of the herdsman, that same [author] has pointed out a certain fault of the herdsman: "If cattle are harmed by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman does not come to their aid, it is the fault of the herdsman. "Does not come to their aid" means he does not arrive to prevent the harm. Furthermore, "harm" (*upaghāta*) here is intended to mean fatal injury, and not a mere slight affliction. As Manu says:
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman.

The meaning is: "that individual belonging to the species of goats or sheep. The mention of the wolf is for the purpose of illustrating such a predatory animal. This rule applies to cases where the animals are situated in accessible places. However, regarding cases where they are situated in inaccessible places, the same author states that the keeper is free from blame even if he has performed all possible human effort: "If, among those [animals] being grazed together in the forest, a wolf should approach and kill one, the keeper is not at fault in that case. [487]

Regarding those animals confined by a herdsman in a forest or an inaccessible wilderness, after Nārada has stated three statements of equivalent meaning to the two verses spoken by Manu, he extends the application of the meaning of his own three statements to herdsman-keepers of animals other than goats and sheep. By this, the dispute concerning all herdsmen is fully illustrated.
Likewise, that same author states the means for establishing the innocence of the herdsman:

"And there shall be purification [of the owner] upon the death [of the animal], because of the sight of its tail-hair, horns, and so forth. This means that even when animals have died in the forest due to the force of time, the herdsman must show the tail-hair, horns, and other parts belonging to the animal in order to remove any suspicion of theft. The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been elaborated by Manu:
"The two ears, the hide, the tail-hairs, the bladder, the sinew, and the gallstone..."
In the case of animals, one should give [the meat] to the owners; if they have died, one should show the limbs.
Thus concludes the exposition of the section titled "The Master and the Herdsman" in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, those statements which resolve disputes concerning the transgression of animals and the like, being relevant to the context, are set down;
therein, Kātyāyana says:
Bṛhaspati states that for those who enter fields, groves, pastures, houses, or cattle-pens, there shall be either seizure or corporal punishment.

An *ārāma* is a grove or garden. By the word *vivīta*, a region belonging to another that is rich in grass and wood is meant. "Cattle-pens and the like" refers to cowsheds and so forth. The meaning is that Bṛhaspati declares that for the purpose of warding them off, one may seize by the ears or other limbs, or beat, the cattle of others who have entered fields and such places. The distinction—that seizing applies to calves and the like, while beating applies to large bulls and the like—should be determined according to what is appropriate. Furthermore, even beating should not be done beyond what is necessary for warding them off; as he himself says:
In cases where an owner disputes the beating of animals— whether they be of low, high, or middle quality—
the king shall determine the appropriate punishment.

Where the owner disputes an excessive beating that deviates from the path of traditional custom (*smṛti*) and conduct (*ācāra*), the determination of punishment shall be made in accordance with the excessiveness of that beating. He (Yājñavalkya) also states another means for warding off cattle:
"One should erect a large enclosure even before the crops have grown;
for wild animals, having once tasted their sweet flavor, are difficult to turn away in this world."
That this refers to a field situated near a forest is understood from the mention of wild animals. Regarding a field adjacent to a road, however, Nārada says:
"A fence should be made around a field on the road such that a camel cannot look over it;
neither a beast, nor a horse, nor even a pig should be able to leap over or break through it."

"Fencing" (*vṛti*) means enclosing by means of thorny branches; that is to say, a surrounding enclosure along the perimeter. The mention of "on a path" (*pathi*) is intended to indicate any place that is congested. He states another qualifying condition regarding the inclusion of a path for movement:
"On a path at the edge of a village pasture (*vivīta*), there is indeed no fault for a short duration" (YDh 2.160).

However, from the counter-argument that "one deserves punishment for long-term grazing," it is understood [that there is no fault] because a fault is possible on the part of the keeper. And thus, following the word "fault" (*doṣa*), Gautama states: "On a path or in an unenclosed field, [the fault lies] with both the keeper and the owner of the field. The remainder [of the meaning] is that there is damage to the crop by the cattle over a long period of time. The "owner of the field" (*kṣetrika*) is the cultivator; the fault of the one who does not provide a fence consists in the destruction of the king’s share, and the intention is that he too is to be punished according to the nature of the fault. But the fault belongs to the owner of the cattle together with the keeper; in its absence, it should be understood as belonging to the keeper alone, since the fault of the owner is based on the transgression of the servant. And thus, where no fault exists on the part of the keeper, there, due to the absence of fault even for the owner of the cattle together with the keeper, it should be considered that the value of the destroyed grain and so forth must be paid to the owner of the field and to the owner [of the cattle]. Furthermore, it need not be paid even by the owner of the cattle who is without a keeper, because even when the cattle stray, he—like the keeper—is not at fault, as his transgression is unavoidable. For this very reason, his exemption from punishment in this matter should be understood to be like that of the keeper. For this same reason, he should not be made to pay the fine (*śada*) to the owner of the field either. And because a fault is recorded [in such cases], so says Uśanas:
"The ancestors do not eat the food of that man who demands back grain destroyed by cattle, nor do the dwellers of heaven eat it.
And thus it was said by Manu:

"But in all cases, a fee (śada) must be given to the owner of the field; this is the settled rule. This should be understood as referring to cases other than those involving innocence. The inclusion of the word "in all cases" is for the purpose that the owner of the field may receive the fee even when the animal is without a keeper. "Fee" means the fruit of the field; this is the settled rule, meaning this is the certainty. However, he himself says that the penalty (daṇḍa), on the other hand, applies to cases other than those involving innocence.

"But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one *paṇa* and a quarter. This means that the owner of the animal or the keeper deserves [the fine]. The designation "animal" is used by way of metonymy to refer to its owner or keeper, for the purpose of prescribing a fine of one *paṇa* and a quarter for each individual animal when there are many animals. Therefore, a fence must indeed be constructed even around fields situated near villages and the like. Regarding this, Manu says: "One should fill every opening through which dogs, pigs, and other such creatures might pass, making it free of gaps with thorns and the like. Thus, he states that one should repair any breach made by dogs and so forth, ensuring the enclosure is once again without holes.

Thus, even when measures have been taken to prevent cattle from entering, if they nevertheless trespass and destroy the crops, the same author states: "If the field is enclosed by a fence along the road or on the outskirts of a village, the keeper is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, he should drive away the unattended animal."

"In a village-bound field" refers to a field situated near a village, a grove, or the like. The qualifying term "enclosed" (*parivṛta*) is to be understood here as well. Thus, the meaning is this: an animal with its keeper that, having broken through the enclosure, destroys more than a mouthful of grain, is liable to a fine of one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*; that is to say, the keeper of that animal is to be fined one hundred. Furthermore, the owner of a field should ward off an animal without a keeper using a staff or other means. In this matter, the owner of the animal with its keeper must provide the field-owner with the value of the grain destroyed; we shall state the source for this point later. This penalty applies specifically when there is a failure to ward off the animal—even to the best of one's ability—as it breaks through the enclosure. On this point, Nārada says: [491]
If cattle or other animals, having broken through the enclosure, should cause damage to the crops,
the keeper shall be punished therefor, unless he was able to prevent it.
Regarding even the unavoidable destruction of crops due to the absence of a fence, that same author says:
"If a field located on the outskirts of a village, at the edge of a pasture, or by a great road is unfenced,
there is no fault on the part of the keeper if it is destroyed."

By saying "on a great path," he shows that there is no transgression for those traveling on a road that cannot be avoided. By implication here, the absence of punishment is also stated; however, it is stated explicitly in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "If cattle should damage unenclosed grain, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the guardians of the cattle."
The phrase "in the case of those who did not wish [to enter]" is to be understood as the ellipsis for "in the case of warding off. As Yājñavalkya said:
"There is no fault in [entering] a field at the edge of a path, a village, or a pasture, provided it is unintentional;
if it is done intentionally, one deserves punishment like that of a thief."

The word *anta* here signifies proximity, and it is connected to each member of the series beginning with *pathin*. Regarding this matter of legal liability for damage, Gautama states: "In the case of injury to livestock, the fault lies with the owner; but when the animal is under the charge of a herdsman, the fault lies with him. This means that "injury to livestock" refers to the damage to crops caused by the animals. When the livestock is without a herdsman, the fault belongs to the owner alone; however, when the animal is under the charge of a herdsman, the fault lies with both. In that case, if the fault lies with the owner alone, he must pay the compensation (*śada*) and the fine (*daṇḍa*). But if the fault lies with both, it should be understood that while the owner pays the compensation, the herdsman receives only the fine, and not the compensation as well. As for what was stated by Nārada:

"If a cow that has been lost due to the fault of the keeper should destroy a field, there is no fault on the part of the owner; the keeper alone deserves the punishment. [492] In this case, it is stated that the owner lacks the fault that would incur punishment, but it does not mean he lacks the fault that would incur the obligation to pay the fine; thus, there is no contradiction. "Lost" means its location is unknown. As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
One should drive away cattle from standing crops; if the fault has been committed, liability shall be shared between both parties.
The owner shall be made to pay a fine of ten [paṇas], while the keeper deserves corporal punishment.
Thus, the analysis of the compound *śadadamam* is "that which consists of both *śada* (decay) and *dama* (damage). Furthermore, Yājñavalkya stated:
"The cowherd is to be fined, but the owner of the cattle deserves the previously mentioned punishment.

Here, "cowherd" (*gopa*) means the keeper of the animals, and "owner of the cattle" (*gomī*) means the master of the animals. Both of these [rules] concern the destruction of a fully grown plant, because in that case there is no further regrowth and the offense is greater, and because the owner also deserves punishment. For this very reason, Nārada says:
But when there is destruction of standing crops along with their roots, the owner of those crops shall receive compensation;
the herdsman may be released from corporal punishment, but he must impose the fine upon the owner.

The owner of that [land] is the owner of the crop. Here, the term *śada* is employed by those who follow the *Śadakalpaka* tradition to signify total destruction. The *Śadakalpakas* should be understood as those who deal with the lands situated on all sides of the damaged field. Furthermore, if a man demands compensation for grain eaten by cattle, the grain that was sown in that [field] should be given to him with the consent of the neighbors.

Because it has been stated by that very same author: "In this context, 'killing' (vadha) means striking with a whip or similar instruments; the 'fine' (daṇḍa) here should be understood as that which was previously mentioned by Yājñavalkya. What, then, is that? It is said:
'A buffalo that causes damage to crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that; and a goat or sheep, half of that.'"

"For those who sit down after having eaten [the crops], the fine is double that which was stated; for those [animals] standing in a pasture (vivīta), it is equal to them; and for donkeys, camels, and buffaloes, it is equal to a cow. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is as follows: the owner of a buffalo other than a young female (bāletarā) that causes damage to another's standing crop shall be fined eight *māṣas* for each such buffalo. The owner of a cow possessing the two aforementioned qualifications shall be fined four *māṣas*. Likewise, the owners of goats and sheep of the same description shall each be fined two *māṣas*. If these same animals are left unconfined from the time they begin grazing on the crop until they go to sleep, their owners shall be fined double the aforementioned amount, as previously stated. Even when there is damage to grass and other vegetation situated in a pasture (*vivīta*), the owner of the animal shall be fined in the same manner as for damage to a crop-field. The owner of a donkey or a camel shall be fined like the owner of a buffalo. It should be understood that although the term "owner of a buffalo" (*mahiṣīsvāmī*) and so forth would have been the appropriate expressive words (*vācakapada*) to state the fine, the use of the non-expressive terms "buffalo" (*mahiṣī*) and so forth is intended to indicate that the fine applies to each individual animal. In this context, for the purpose of inflicting punishment according to the offense, a copper *māṣa* is to be taken, and not a gold or silver one. Furthermore, a copper *māṣa* constitutes the sixteenth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. As for those [who hold] that the fine must be proportionate to the offense...
"A māṣa is declared to be the twentieth part of a paṇa"—
thus the *māṣa* mentioned by Nārada is accepted; their number, rooted in *raśmi*, *rajas*, and *mūla*, has been set forth by Manu.
One who is short by even a kārṣāpaṇa should likewise be subjected to the ordeal in matters of legal dispute.

Thus, the contradiction with the statement of Bārhaspatya is unavoidable, because Manu has accepted the *māṣa* as defined by him. However, there is no contradiction whatsoever if one accepts the copper *māṣa* mentioned by Manu; therefore, enough with this consideration of the arguments put forward by the opposing side. As for what was stated by Manu, "He deserves a *paṇa* and a quarter," that refers to a case of intentional transgression regarding livestock. The statement of Yājñavalkya, however, refers to an unintentional case; thus, there is no contradiction between the two. As for what was stated by Viṣṇu, "If a buffalo should destroy the crops, the keeper shall be fined eight *māṣas*; if it is unattended, the owner [shall be fined]," that refers to the destruction of rootless crops, since it is appropriate that the fine for either party be proportionate to a minor offense. As for what was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita, "A buffalo [is fined] ten," that intends the *māṣas* mentioned by Nārada; in that case, the resulting fine will effectively consist of eight copper *māṣas*, and thus there is no contradiction with the statement of Yājñavalkya, "Eight *māṣas*," nor with the statement of Bārhaspatya, "The number [of *māṣas*] is equal to the number of rays," and so forth. And that [statement of Bārhaspatya], "Sixteen for a donkey or camel, four for a goat or sheep," refers to cases where a donkey or similar animal remains after having eaten. As for what was stated by Kātyāyana...
"One should cause a quarter-pana to be paid for a cow, and likewise two quarters for a buffalo"—
and that which was stated by Nārada:
"Cows should be fined one quarter, but buffaloes twice as much."

Thus, since this is effectively equivalent to the position of accepting copper *māṣas*, it is indeed not contradictory. However, there is a contradiction only with respect to the position of accepting the *māṣas* mentioned by Nārada. For this very reason, that position is not ours; thus, everything remains consistent. As for another Smṛti text: "Two quarters of a *paṇa* for a cow, and likewise two double-quantities for a large bull; similarly, two quarters each for goats, sheep, and calves—this is proclaimed as the fine. [495]

Thus, that [penalty] refers to the case where [the animal] has eaten and then sat down, because by a shift in phrasing it specifically denotes the punishment for that particular situation. Furthermore, as stated by Nārada:
"One should cause a cow to pay a fine of one māṣa, and likewise a buffalo two māṣas;
similarly, the fine for goats, sheep, and calves shall be half a māṣa."
Thus, in this context, the designation of a silver *māṣa* by the word *māṣa* should be understood as referring to those who have eaten and sat down together with the calves.
For those staying [overnight], it is declared to be double; for those staying with the calves, it is fourfold.

Thus, by virtue of this traditional authority (*smṛti*), this statement will have the same meaning [as the previous one], because in the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*) sixteen copper *māṣas* are equal in value to a single silver *māṣa*. Alternatively, let there be a designation of the copper *māṣa* alone even here; nevertheless, since the subject matter concerns eating for only a moment (*muhūrta*), there is no contradiction. And likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state, under the recurring phrase "one shall incur a fine": "A cow grazing at night [incurs a fine of] five *māṣas*, three [at] day, and one *māṣa* for a *muhūrta*; but there is no fine for grazing while eating. This refers to the case of one who grazes out of sight.

"However, for those who are caught in the act, the punishment of a thief is prescribed by the wise"—so says the Smṛti of Nārada. Regarding the statement "there is no punishment for a mouthful," this is its meaning: if a buffalo or other animal somehow eats even a single mouthful of another's crops and so forth, there is not even the slightest punishment for either the keeper or the owner. But in the case of an animal that is ill, even if much of the crop is destroyed, there is likewise no punishment; thus Nārada expresses the absence of fault by way of stating the lack of punishment:
"Whether seized by royal possession (or an epidemic), or struck by lightning or a thunderbolt... [496]
Then, either bitten by a serpent or fallen from a tree to the ground, [he died].

"Even if [a beast] is struck by a tiger or afflicted by diseases, there is no fault on the part of the keeper, nor is there any fault on the part of the owners. The remainder of the sense is that this applies because sick animals cannot be restrained. He states the same author [Yājñavalkya] that even in the case of transgression by certain animals that *can* be restrained, there is no punishment:

A cow that has recently calved, for up to ten days; a large bull; and horses and elephants—these must be restrained with great effort [from entering a field], yet their owner shall not be subject to punishment.

The owner of a cow that has recently calved and cannot be restrained for ten days is not subject to punishment. Likewise, the owner of a large bull is not subject to punishment because it must always be kept unconfined for the purpose of impregnating all the cows. The reason why the owners of horses and elephants are exempt from punishment was shown by Uśanas:
"Horses and elephants are traditionally considered exempt from punishment, as they are beneficial to the protector of the subjects.

Thus, since royal animals possess the aforementioned characteristics, they are indeed exempt from punishment. The mention of the "owner" (*svāmin*) is intended to include the keeper (*pāla*) as well, as Manu says:
Manu has declared that a cow that has recently calved within ten days, bulls, and animals dedicated to the gods— whether they have no owners or have owners— are not to be punished.
Bulls and great oxen, or those released according to the ritual for the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*),
as well as one-eyed or humpbacked animals, and bulls marked with specific signs, are exempt from punishment.

This is because it has been stated by Uśanas: "A *kāṇa* is one-eyed; a *kūṭa* is one-horned; a *kṛtalakṣaṇa* is one marked with a brand made of heated iron. Since such an animal has no owner, even though there is no punishment for the owner, if a herdsman is appointed at some point to protect the crops, he does not incur the penalty for damage, because they are difficult to restrain. To express this, it was said, "and a bull that is branded. Similarly, to express the same point, the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] says, "as well as the animals dedicated to the gods" (*devapaśūṃs tathā*). For "animals dedicated to the gods" are those given for the purpose of bathing the images of deities with milk and so forth; since there is no actual relationship of ownership in their case, the mention of "animals dedicated to the gods" is solely for the purpose of exempting the herdsman from punishment, just like the branded bull. Regarding a cow that has recently calved, Uśanas has shown that there is an exemption from both penalties in the case of specific types of cattle.

Furthermore, a cow that has recently calved, a stray cow, and one that has strayed from its herd are exempt from punishment. A "recently calved" cow is one that has just given birth. A "stray cow" is one that has not yet become accustomed to its place. A cow that has "strayed from its herd" is one that has departed due to excessive beating and is returning to its own flock. Thus, by this very [text], the absence of punishment regarding cattle in general is shown for specific times: "Cows are exempt from punishment during a festival, and likewise at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony."
On this point Vyāsa says:
"O tiger among men, that which is eaten by twice-born ones who have been oppressed and whose kinsmen are impoverished, as well as by cows, is superior even to the horse sacrifice."
On this point, Manu says:
"A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions involving owners of cattle, the animals themselves, and the herdsmen."
Thus ends the section concerning the transgression regarding animals and the like in the *Smṛticandrikā* [498].
Now follow the sections concerning sale by one who is not the owner (*asvāmivikraya*).

Having thus explained the section on disputes between owners and herdsmen—which forms a supplement to the section on the non-payment of wages—and having discussed the matters pertaining to the transgression of animals and the like connected thereto, the rule for the section known as "Sale by One Not the Owner," which follows in the order of enumeration, is now stated.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"The owner shall recover property sold by one who is not the owner."

The meaning is that if one's own property is seen in the possession of someone by whom it was sold by a non-owner, the owner may take it back from that person. This refers to property sold without the consent of the owner, because Manu has specified this particular case: "He who, being a non-owner and not authorized by the owner, sells what belongs to another... The meaning of the phrase "what belongs to another" has been elaborated upon by Bṛhaspati.
One who sells a deposit, a thing sent for delivery, a pledge, a borrowed item,
a requested loan, or a security— whether secretly or otherwise— is declared to be a non-owner.

"Stolen" means taken away. The other words occurring in the first half of the verse have been explained in various ways. "In secret" (*upāṃśu*) means not publicly. This elaboration is for the purpose of illustrating those things commonly known as the property of others. The mention of "in secret" is intended to indicate the general rule; therefore, one who sells even lost or found property belonging to another, or one who sells even openly a deposit or the like, is likewise a non-owner. When it is asked what the purpose of defining "sale by a non-owner" is, Nārada [states]:
"Any purchase or sale that is made by one who is not the owner is always to be understood as invalid in legal proceedings. Thus also says Kātyāyana.

"One should nullify a sale by one who is not the owner, as well as a gift and a pledge. Thus, it should be understood that this is established by the *daṇḍāpūpa* (stick-and-cake) maxim: before a sale or similar transaction has taken place, if one's own property—which was lost, stolen, or carried away—is found in the hands of someone other than the owner, the true owner may take it back from that non-owner. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"He who recovers property that was stolen or lost from the hand of another... [the implication is that he may do so provided the transfer was not yet finalized].
"Without reporting it to the king, he shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*.

In this context, the reason for the fine is not the acquisition from another's hand—since that is justifiable—but rather the failure to report it, because such non-reporting is unjustified as it results in the concealment of a thief. However, when the owner is unable to recover [the property] from the hand of another, the same author says:
"Having recovered what was lost or stolen, one should cause the man who took it to be apprehended."
Or, if there is a lapse regarding place or time, one should take it and offer it oneself.

The meaning is as follows: having discovered one's own property that has been lost or stolen, and having seen it in the hand of the finder or the thief, one should cause the finder or the thief to be apprehended by royal officers and others through means such as conciliation (*sāma*). If there is a delay due to the passage of time or distance—such as when traveling to another region to bring the person back or when time is spent waiting—one may apprehend him oneself upon suspicion of flight and hand him over to the royal officers or the king. Thereafter, the royal officers and others, having caused the owner to receive that wealth through means such as conciliation and having punished the offender, should release him; this is to be understood here from the force of the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) of the rules regarding apprehension and handing over. However, when he sees the purchased item in the hand of the purchaser only after the sale has already taken place, he says the same thing: "One should recover one's own property sold by another. The meaning is that the owner should take back his own property—which was sold by someone other than the owner without the owner's consent—from the purchaser. Viṣṇu also states: "If one purchases another's property openly and unknowingly, there is no fault in that case; the owner shall recover the property. "Unknowingly" means without knowing the seller's lack of ownership. "In that case" refers to the purchase of another's property. "No fault" means the purchaser incurs no guilt for that act. The fault certainly remains with the seller; therefore, in this instance, only the seller is to be punished like a thief, and not the purchaser. But where one knowingly purchases another's property out of greed and the like, having learned of the seller's lack of ownership through secret dealings, low prices, or similar means, then the purchaser also incurs the guilt of a thief and is to be punished like a thief. And so he (Viṣṇu) says: "If one sells secretly or for a low price, then the purchaser is to be treated like a thief. Bṛhaspati also shows that depending on whether the purchase is made knowingly or unknowingly, the purchaser becomes either a thief or is without fault, respectively.
But if it was purchased for a price and previously reported to the king, no fault exists therein; one becomes a thief only through fraudulent sale.

"At a price" means at a non-deficient price. "Previously announced to the king" means it has been made public even before the purchase. He explains the term *upavikraya* (fraudulent sale) himself: "That which is purchased inside a house, outside a village, at night, from an unknown person, or for a deficient price—this should be known as fraudulent sale. [501]

"From an *asat* person" means from a *caṇḍāla* or similar individual. The inclusion of the term *asat* is intended to indicate by implication those specific sellers such as slaves who lack ownership (*asvāmitva*). For this very reason, Nārada states: "Purchasing in secret from a slave without the owner's consent, or from an *asat* person, at a low price and at an improper time, one becomes a partaker in that fault."

"From one who is not the owner" means from one who has given permission without being the owner—that is, from one devoid of the owner's consent. The mention of a "slave" (*dāsa*) is intended as an illustration for those who are not independent. "He partakes in that fault" means he partakes in the fault of a thief; for it has been stated by that same author: "Theft belongs to the buyer because of a secret purchase. Likewise, it should be understood that in the statement of Yājñavalkya, "the fault of the buyer [lies] in what is not publicly declared," the fault of theft itself is what is expressed. And so it was said by that same author: "One who buys secretly from a low person, at a low price, or at an improper time, is a thief."

By employing the word "taskara" (thief), it is indicated that the fault of theft itself is what is expressed by the word "doṣa" (fault). The meaning of "hīnāt" is: from one who lacks the means for acquiring the goods to be purchased.
Thus ends the section concerning sales by one who is not the owner when [the status] is undisputed in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning sales by one who is not the owner when [the status] is disputed;
regarding this, Kātyāyana says:

"The claimant shall first establish his own property through his kinsmen. Here, the "claimant" (*abhiyoktā*) is the owner who has lost his wealth, for it is only one whose wealth has been lost who is the claimant in this context. The meaning is that when he sees the wealth in the hand of another, he should prove it to be his own (*svakam*)—that is, his property (*svakīyam*)—by means of his kinsmen acting as witnesses, in such a manner that it becomes established as his. When it is asked how the owner who has lost his wealth can prove his own ownership, Yājñavalkya states: "The lost [property] must be proven by title (*āgama*) and possession (*upabhoga*)."... [as above].
The traditional scripture (āgama), however, states:
"That which is obtained through gift, purchase, valour, marriage,
or born from a relative when one has no offspring— such is the sixfold acquisition of wealth."

This should be understood as having been established in the section on possession (*bhukti*) by such statements as these. The meaning is that the ownership of lost property is to be proven by means of title (*āgama*) accompanied by possession, which is well-known among one's kinsmen. And so says Kātyāyana: "But the owner of the lost property should establish that wealth as his own through his kinsmen. Here, "that wealth" refers to the lost wealth; "his own" means belonging to himself; "should establish" means he should prove it. He [Kātyāyana] further states that even the recognition of one's own wealth as being one's own must be proven by the absence of gifts and other such transactions: ... [The remainder of the passage follows]. ... Thus, the meaning is that the proof of ownership of one's own wealth is to be accomplished by demonstrating the absence of acts such as gifting. He [Kātyāyana] says the same: ... [The remainder of the passage follows]. ... Therefore, the point is that the status of one's own wealth as being one's own must be established through the absence of [unlawful] transfers such as giving away. He [Kātyāyana] says the same: ... He [Kātyāyana] says the same:
"Having established that [the property] was not given, abandoned, or sold, one recovers one's own wealth.

This means that having established through proof that the object was not given (*adatta*), abandoned (*tyakta*), or sold (*vikrīta*)—that is, the opposite of "given, abandoned, or sold"—the original owner (*nāṣṭika*) recovers his own wealth from the purchaser and others. Regarding the purchaser, Bṛhaspati says:
"But when the former owner arrives and investigates that property..."
In that case, the root source must be shown; from that, the buyer shall attain purification.
The "root" (mūla) refers to the seller. "Purification" (śuddhi) means the cessation of being subject to legal accusation. Regarding this, Vyāsa states after the production of the root:
"When the root has been established, the purchaser can by no means be accused;
rather, at that time, the dispute shall be between the owner of the lost property and the seller."

[This applies] to the owner of the lost property, the one who has suffered a loss. If, in that legal proceeding, the defendant asserts, "I also purchased this from another seller," then in that case as well, this very same sequence—beginning with the production of the original source (the prior seller)—must be followed. However, if he produces someone who is shown to be ineffective as a source because he is either a finder of lost goods or a thief, then Bṛhaspati says: "Where the seller, when produced, is defeated in the legal proceeding, he shall pay the purchase price and a fine to the king, and the value of the property to the owner."

The meaning is that he should give the price to the purchaser, a fine to the king, and the wealth to the owner. Nārada also says: "In a sale without ownership, the seller should give his own property to the owner, the price paid by the purchaser, and likewise a fine to the king; such is the rule."

But when the original seller is situated in another country, Kātyāyana says: "A period for the production of the original must be granted according to the number of *yojanas*. This means that the time depends on the distance between the locations. However, when it is impossible to produce the original even after a lapse of time, he says the same thing: "Or he should make the purchase public. This means he should make the previously made purchase known to the world through the testimony of witnesses. And so says the same author: [504]
One should conduct the sale openly with trustworthy and knowledgeable persons of one's own;
no other procedure, whether divine or human, is prescribed for that case.
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that once the purchase has been made public, the buyer is not to be punished by the king:
"When the purchase has been cleared, the king should say to him: 'He owes you nothing at all. Manu also says:
Now, if the original owner cannot produce the root evidence, but the sale was public and cleared [of suspicion], he shall not be punished by the king; the claimant shall recover his property.

The meaning is that the owner (nāṣṭika) recovers the wealth cleared by the sale from the purchaser, and the purchaser, being exempt from punishment, is released from royal restraint. By the statement, "But if the source [of the goods] cannot be produced," it is indicated that, when possible, the option of producing the source must be adopted. And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"But one whose source cannot be recovered shall clear the sale itself.
The meaning is that only when the source cannot be recovered shall he clear the sale. In that regard:
When a litigant, having first presented the root of the transaction, subsequently speaks of the purchase, he must produce that very root; the purchase itself serves no purpose.
"He should speak openly" means he should declare the purchase. When he neither produces the original source nor makes the purchase public, then that same author says:
"Failing to produce the source, or failing to clear up the purchase, [he must pay] to the creditor according to the claim; or, failing to clear up the purchase..."
When even the claimant of loss cannot prove that the lost property belongs to him, then the same author says:
"If the claimant of loss does not establish the property as his own through his kinsmen,
he deserves punishment like a thief in order to prevent the recurrence of such instances."

This would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) and an over-extension of the rule (*atiprasaṅga*). Yājñavalkya also states: "A lost item may be recovered through legal title (*āgama*) or through possession (*upabhoga*); otherwise, if it is not proven [to belong to the claimant], the king shall impose a fine of five times its value."

Where a fine equal to one-fifth of the wealth that is the subject of dispute is prescribed, that is called *pañcabandha*. This refers to cases of minor offenses. However, regarding cases of major offenses, Vyāsa says: "If the plaintiff fails to prove the claimed property through witnesses, he shall be made to pay a fine double [the value], and the purchaser deserves to forfeit that property."

The purchaser’s acquisition of the property occurs even within the scope of the fivefold penalty. Furthermore, it should be understood that when the original owner establishes his own ownership and demonstrates its continuity, the purchaser’s acquisition of the purchased property occurs only in that instance and not otherwise. Thus, as stated by Manu: "He who receives any wealth through sale in the presence of the family members obtains that wealth lawfully, for it is purified by purchase."
Thus, as Marīci has stated:
"That which is situated on a merchant's street and is recognized by the king's officers,
or that which is seized during the day— the purchaser of such is pure and recovers his wealth."

Thus, this refers to the case where the lost property has not been recovered. If it is argued that even in a case where the lost property *is* recovered, the buyer should obtain the wealth by virtue of the authority of the statements of Manu and Marīci regarding an open purchase (*prakāśakraya*), we say no; for it cannot be established—even by a hundred statements—that what was sold by one who is not the owner can legally belong to the buyer. Furthermore, if the buyer were to always obtain the wealth in an open purchase, the contradiction with the previously cited statement, "But if the source [of the goods] cannot be produced," etc., would be unavoidable. Therefore, it must be understood that even in an open purchase, the buyer obtains the wealth only when there is no recovery of the lost property. As for the claim made by Śambhu—that in order to avoid the aforementioned fault, the statements of Manu and Marīci merely express the buyer's *fitness* for the wealth, but do not state that the wealth actually becomes his—it is incorrect, because there is no utility in speaking of mere fitness alone. Bṛhaspati, however, speaks as follows when even the purchase itself cannot be proven by witnesses: [The text continues with Bṛhaspati’s verse.]
But in a case where there is no evidence,
the king himself should make the decision based on his own judgment regarding the person, considering whether they are equal, inferior, or superior.

The meaning is this: in a dispute where there is an absence of evidence for the claimant (*nāṣṭika*) to establish his ownership, and an absence of evidence for the purchaser to establish a public sale, the King himself should issue a decision—dividing the disputed property into equal, lesser, or greater shares according to the integrity and other qualities of the claimant and the purchaser—saying, "This much is yours. Now, one might object: a dispute devoid of evidence is impossible anywhere, because even if human means of proof (*mānuṣa-pramāṇa*) are absent, it is absolutely impossible to say that divine means of proof (*divya*) are absent. Not so; for in a dispute concerning sale by one who is not the owner (*asvāmivikraya*), the absence of divine proof is indeed understood.
"The plaintiff shall first provide his own wealth through his kinsmen;
afterwards, for the sake of his own purification, the purchaser shall provide the purchase price through his own relatives.
Since such statements, which restrict the number of witnesses, are intended to indicate the absence of other means of proof, and furthermore:
One should perform the purchase openly with virtuous kinsmen and one's own people;
no other procedure, whether divine or human, is prescribed for that occasion.

Thus, because of the prohibition of evidence other than witnesses, the absence of divine ordeals (*divya*) is clearly established. And so, regarding what was stated by Kātyāyana—"In a lawsuit lacking documentary evidence or witnesses, one should prescribe a divine ordeal"—that must be understood as referring to a situation where there is no traditional rule (*smṛti*) prohibiting divine ordeals. By this, the following view is refuted, which Śambhu stated concerning both the recovery of the original object and the disclosure of its purchase: "If [the defendant] is unable to do either, yet does not admit to theft, then an ordeal should be administered in accordance with the value of the property."

"Where there is no written document and no witness, one should point to divine [means of proof] in a legal proceeding," because it has been stated thus by Kātyāyana. He shows the same point through a change of phrasing, indicating that even in a case supported by evidence, a fine equal to the amount may sometimes be imposed:
"That which is situated on a merchant's street and is known by the king’s officers..."
If the basis [of the transaction] is unknown, then the purchaser, the seller, or whoever has died therein [is held liable].

"The owner, having paid half the price, shall take back his own property. This means from a seller whose residence is unknown and whose location is unknown. To justify the manner of acquisition as stated by himself, it was said by that same author: "In that case, half of both [the price and the property] shall be recovered through legal proceedings. (YDh 2.173) [508]

The meaning is that, through the legal proceedings between the buyer and the owner, half of one's own wealth has been taken away or lost due to one's own misconduct. When it is asked what this "misconduct of one's own" is, he himself stated:
"Purchase without proper investigation is a fault, as is failure to provide protection;
these two are declared by the wise to be causes of the loss of property."

"Purchase from one whose status is unknown" (*avijñātakraya*) means a purchase made from someone whose standing is not recognized. Alternatively, it refers to a purchase made from one who is not known to be the true owner in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). That itself is the fault or transgression (*apacāra*) of the purchaser. "Non-protection" (*aparipālana*) means neglect; that alone is the transgression of the owner who has lost the property. The meaning is that these two—consisting of purchasing from an unknown source and failing to protect—are declared to be the causes of loss of property for both the purchaser and the owner. Marīci also says: "Because the place of deposit was unknown, where the original source cannot be found."
In that case, the loss should be considered equal for both the buyer and the owner.

Because it is an entry into what is not understood and because it is a station of what is not understood, the seller is the root [of the offense]. This statement is combined here so that the rule regarding the *bārhapatya* fire—stating that even if the purpose is not different, it is for another purpose due to incompleteness—does not apply.

Thus ends the section on sales by one who is not the owner in the Smṛticandrikā. Now, as an incidental topic, some statements of Nārada concerning those who enjoy property belonging to another that has not been surrendered by the owner are set forth.
One should eat only what has been specifically designated, whether it be a woman, an animal, or even the earth itself;
however, he who eats what has not been offered must cause the enjoyment [of that food] to be given away.
But one who enjoys by his own power alone any property not specified— such as clothing, land, cattle, and so forth— is liable to punishment like a thief.
One who consumes an ox, a milch cow, a boat, or likewise a slave without prior authorization,
shall pay a fine of four paṇas.
A female slave, a boat, and likewise a draft animal are not to be used as collateral;
however, one who uses such property must clear the debt by means of merchandise alone.
On the day [of the sale], he gave a maidservant for two paṇas, a milch cow for eight paṇas,
a bull for thirteen, a horse for sixteen, and land for sixteen as well.
He who enjoys by force a boat, a horse, a cow, or the plough of a farmer, shall be made to pay eight times its value for each day.
The sage Jaimini declared that the fine for a mortar is half a paṇa, for a pestle two paṇas, and for a winnowing basket half a paṇa.

Thus ends the exposition of the rules concerning the one who enjoys property belonging to another that has not been surrendered by the owner, in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, the rules concerning the legal proceeding known as "Non-delivery after Sale" (*vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*) are stated.
In this regard, Nārada says: "He who, having sold a commodity for its price, does not deliver it to the buyer,
shall be compelled to pay the value of immovable property along with its loss, and movable property along with the fruit of its use."

If a seller who has accepted the price for a commodity does not deliver it to the buyer upon the latter’s request because remorse has arisen, then if that commodity is immovable (sthāvara), he must be made to pay it along with its depreciation (kṣaya); but if it is movable (jaṅgama), he must pay it along with the fruit of its use (kriyāphala). By the word "depreciation" (kṣaya), the loss of enjoyment (gatabhoga) is meant, since it has perished through being connected to the buyer. The "fruit of use," however, refers to the milk and so forth from a commodity such as a cow, because it is the result of the action of milking and so on. This should be understood to apply when the value has increased by the time of delivery relative to the time of purchase; for if the value has decreased, the rule is stated otherwise. And thus says the same author:
"If the price should fall, he shall deliver the merchandise with its profit.

Here, "with its profit" (*sodayam*) means that whatever amount—exceeding the original cost—is obtained at the time of delivery due to a decrease in the market price since the time of purchase; that is what he must "deliver," meaning he must cause the buyer to receive it, or in other words, he must give it to the buyer. However, regarding the case where the price is the same both at the time of purchase and at the time of delivery, Yājñavalkya says:
"He who, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer..."
"He shall be made to pay that [debt] together with interest...

Thus, because there is no mention of the decrease or increase of the price (*argha*), this statement is understood to apply to a case where the price remains constant. The meaning of the phrase "together with interest" (*sodayam*) and so forth is as follows: whatever interest accrues on the merchandise that is not being delivered, as well as the deposit, the remainder of the interest, and indeed the purchase and sale itself.
If what was requested is not given, the debt increases by five percent.

Thus, it is calculated according to the measure stated in the section on non-increased interest (*akṛtavṛddhi*); the merchandise, together with that [interest], is to be made to be paid. This interpretation was made because, when the price is equal, an increase consisting of the accumulation of the merchandise is impossible. Regarding this, Nārada says: "This rule applies to stationary [merchants]. Those who purchase goods in order to take them to another country to sell them are the others; the meaning is that this rule—stated in such passages as "he shall be made to pay the immovable [property] along with its loss"—concerns them. When it is asked how the rule applies to non-stationary [merchants], he himself says: "The profit of the direction for those traveling in various directions. The meaning is that whatever profit is gained by one selling that merchandise in whichever other direction it was purchased for sale, the [debt] must be paid together with that profit. Viṣṇu, however, also prescribes a fine for the seller: "He who, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, shall be made to pay that [price] with interest by the king and shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. "Having received the price" means the price of whichever merchandise has been received by the seller; "to him, the buyer," is the sense. Regarding him who does not deliver the merchandise whose price has been received even in the absence of a rescission of sale, and him who, due to a rescission of purchase, does not accept the merchandise whose price has not been paid, Kātyāyana says:
He who, having purchased and received an article that is not defective, neither accepts it nor returns it,
shall recover his own property by paying one-tenth of its value as a fine.
"If the time for the performance of the purposeful act has not arrived, one should certainly not cause it to be performed;
such is the law within ten days, but beyond that, there is no [legal] recourse."

"Unspoiled by water and so forth" is the ellipsis. "The time for functional utility" refers to the time for milking, carrying, and so on, regarding goods such as those intended for milking or transport. If that time has not yet arrived, even if one has already taken possession or failed to return the item, one shall not be made to pay a tenth part of the price; rather, [512] one may acquire the property for oneself without having given back the original value. This stated rule is to be understood as applying prior to ten days and after the time of functional utility. Beyond ten days, however, no rescission (anuśaya) should be made, because the period for rescission has elapsed—this is the intended meaning. The aforementioned rule applies when there is an absence of a real cause for rescission. And thus, having cited the buyer, he himself has stated:

If a man, having purchased a commodity such as a milch cow or the like, should abandon it while still possessing a lingering regret (*anuśaya*), he must pay a tenth part of the price at the proper time, provided the item is indeed not defective. "At the proper time" means at the time for rescission; in reality, even if he abandons the commodity with the thought that it is defective when it is actually not defective, he should not [simply] take it back—this is the meaning. The manner of returning a purchased commodity in this matter has also been shown by that same author: "A buyer may rescind a purchase within ten days; after that, he is liable for the loss. A seller may rescind a sale within three days; after that, he is liable for the loss. In this context, the method for returning a purchased commodity is also demonstrated by him alone: "If a person, having purchased a cow, a horse, a slave, a goat, a sheep, or any other such article, should abandon it within ten days because of a change of mind, he shall not be liable for the loss. If the item is truly defective, the rescission is absolute; however, if the defect is merely imagined, the rescission is subject to the payment of a tenth part of the price. If a buyer, having purchased [an article] and while departing, develops a regret once it has come into his hand,
the wise man should abandon that purchase by paying one-sixth of its value.

Aparādityamati holds that this statement refers to a case where a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) exists after the time [of the transaction]; however, that is incorrect, because it has been stated that "the latent tendency is not from another," and because it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Manu also spoke for the sake of avoiding infinite regress:
"If, after buying or selling anything here, one should have a latent regret (*anuśaya*), he may return or take back that object within ten days."
"But after ten days, one shall neither give nor cause to be given;

both he who takes and he who gives are to be fined six hundred by the king. This giving and taking refers to a case where there exists a valid ground for rescission (*anuśaya*); for no mention is made of the giving of a tenth part of the price. He (the same author) states that even in cases of rescission other than buying and selling, the rules regarding rescission in buying and selling should be applied by analogy.
In whatever matter one may have a subsequent regret after it has been performed,
he should be established on the path of righteousness by means of this procedure.

Nārada states by way of a legal formulation that if a seller, having sold a commodity, does not deliver it and the sold commodity remains in his own possession, then in the event of its destruction due to fate or other causes, the seller must give a commodity of equal value to the buyer:
"If the commodity is destroyed, burnt, or stolen,
that loss belongs to the seller alone who, having sold it, does not deliver it."
Yājñavalkya also states:
"If a defect in the merchandise arises due to injury caused by the king or fate,
the loss belongs solely to the seller who does not deliver what was requested."

By the statement "of one who has been asked," it is shown that there is no loss for a seller who has not been asked but refuses to deliver. And thus, passages such as "he shall be made to pay the immovable property along with its loss" should also be understood as referring to the case of what was requested. For it is only in that context [of a request] that the imposition of a penalty exceeding the price is appropriate. Therefore, even at a later time, in the case of what was not requested, only the merchandise itself is to be delivered. Just as when a defect in the merchandise arises, the loss falls upon the seller alone who, having been asked, does not deliver it, so too the loss falls upon the buyer alone who does not accept the merchandise being offered; thus says Nārada.
If a buyer does not accept a commodity being offered for sale, or if he has already purchased it, the fault of the seller who fails to deliver shall belong to him alone. [514]

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Whatever fault belongs to the seller who does not deliver [the goods], that same fault shall belong to him [who refuses to accept them]. The purpose of stating the fault of the buyer is that the price of the merchandise need not be returned by the seller to the buyer. By using the term "being given" (*dīyamānam*), he indicates that there is no loss of price for one who does not accept what is being offered when it is not being requested. Where the seller has not requested [the goods back] and the buyer is not one who refuses what is being given, yet a defect in the merchandise arises, in that case an equal loss should be assigned to both; for after the sale, due to the laxity in both the delivery and the acceptance, the culpability of both is equal. Furthermore, where the buyer, having developed regret, does not accept the goods while they are being delivered by the seller, regarding that too, the same author says:
If a buyer does not accept a commodity being offered,
or if a seller sells it elsewhere after having already sold it, neither the buyer nor the seller shall be held at fault.
The phrase "the buyer has developed regret" (*anuśaya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Yājñavalkya also states:

"Even that which has been sold may be returned if the previous buyer does not accept it"—the ellipsis here being "does not accept it due to regret. It follows by implication that if he does accept it, it cannot be returned. He [Yājñavalkya] further declares that the punishment for one who sells and for one who sells a defective commodity while concealing its defects is the same.
If it is seen being sold in the hand of another, or if it is perceived as being defective,
the fine for selling it shall be double its value.
Nārada, however, explaining the meaning of this by means of two verses,
states a further distinction: "But he who, having shown a faultless [article], delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its value, and a fine of the same amount."

"Likewise, he who, having sold it into the hand of one person, delivers it to another, shall also be made to pay double that amount as a fine; the penalty for the offense is exactly that much. This refers to cases where the act is intentional, because both the punishment and the property to be paid are exceedingly large. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati, having cited the case of a defective item, stated:
If a discerning person sells merchandise knowing it to be defective,
he should be made to pay double that amount, as well as an equal fine as a penalty.

But in the case of an act not preceded by conscious intent, there is simply a reversal of the sale. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that in some other cases as well, the transaction may be reversed: "What has been sold by one who is intoxicated, insane, or out of fear, or by one who is not independent or deluded, must be relinquished; it shall belong to him again."
On this point, Nārada says:
"This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
if it is not delivered, except in accordance with an agreement, there is no transgression on the part of the seller."
This is the meaning of the second half [of the verse]:
"When the price for a commodity has not been paid, and a purchase has been made by word alone, it must not be rescinded... [and so forth].

Thus, in the absence of such a convention (*samaya*), there is no fault whatsoever whether the transaction proceeds or is withdrawn. However, where something has been given by the buyer into the hand of the seller for the purpose of avoiding a mere verbal purchase, if the purchase fails due to a defect in the seller, the buyer shall give that person double the amount of wealth he gave. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"One should cause the wealth given as a token of truth (*satyaṃkāra*) to be returned twofold."

That which is placed in the hand of the seller in order to make the purchase binding is called "satyaṃkāra" (a formal pledge). Regarding the failure of a purchase due to a defect in the buyer, Vyāsa says:

"If one who has given a satyaṃkāra does not appear at the appointed time, that merchandise shall be considered relinquished; likewise, it belongs to him who refuses to accept the goods being offered."

"Released" (nisṛṣṭa) means "abandoned" (utsṛṣṭa); this is the meaning. Here, the abandonment of the wager is intended to extend up to the abandonment of the object used as a stake; otherwise, since the act of making a verbal purchase would be identical [for both parties], the seller would not be the one who receives the stake. In this case as well, the statement that "even what has been sold may be resold" should be kept in mind.
Thus concludes the exposition of the section titled "Non-delivery after Sale" in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, the rule for the section titled "Repentance after Purchase" is stated;
regarding this, Nārada says:

"The buyer should examine the commodity himself beforehand for its merits and defects. This means that so as to prevent regret after the purchase, the buyer himself should examine the commodity prior to the sale in order to ascertain whether it is of excellent quality or defective. Bṛhaspati also states:
"He should examine the commodity himself and show it to others."

The phrase "of others" implies those who are experts in the qualities and defects of merchandise. Thus, examination at that very moment applies specifically to commodities such as leather and the like. As Vyāsa says:
"For leather, wood, bricks, thread, grain, wine, liquids, and crops, as well as for wealth, base metals, and gold, the examination must be immediate."

Although the word *vasu* denotes wealth in general, it nevertheless refers here to objects other than hides and the like, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). *Kupya*, however, should be understood as base metals such as tin, lead, and so forth, distinct from gold and silver. Thus, Amarasiṃha, having introduced the topic of gold and silver, stated: "That which is other than those two is *kupya*. In this way, items such as hides and the like should be examined with extreme care; for once they have been purchased after examination, they cannot be abandoned even if defects are subsequently discovered. Accordingly, Bṛhaspati says: "Having accepted what has been examined and highly approved, one should not reject it again."
"Highly esteemed" means purchased; this is the understood sense. And so says Nārada:
"What has been purchased after inspection and found to be highly esteemed shall not again belong to the seller.
The understood sense is "even upon the discovery of defects. He states the exception to this very same rule:
One should examine what is to be milked after three days, but what is to be carried by beasts of burden after five days;
however, for pearls, diamonds, and corals, the examination period shall be seven days.
For bipeds, however, it is half a month for males, but double that for females;
for all seeds, it is ten days, and for metals and clothes, one day.
"Therefore, if any defect in the merchandise should arise before that time, it must be returned by the seller, and the buyer shall recover the price. Thus [it is said].

"From three days" means starting from the day of purchase; this is the ellipsis. In the same way, the ellipsis should be understood for "five days" and so forth. Since the rule is seen here stating that "the seller must return [the item]" and so on, it is understood that the examination regarding "milkable within three days" and so forth pertains to purchased items such as milch cattle. "Of bipeds" means of male slaves; "twice that in a month" means up to that point. "Of a female" means of female slaves. "Within this time" means within the interval of three days and so forth. By the word "is produced," the establishment [of the defect] through knowledge is stated, not the physical completion of the object. It has been said that examination is the cause of establishment through knowledge. Both establishment and non-establishment through knowledge have been clarified by Kātyāyana.
But that which was purchased without being recognized, and later discovered to be defective, must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.

"Unknown" means not fully understood due to laxity in examination; that is to say, at whatever time the period for examining a particular object has been prescribed, it must be examined during that time. Otherwise, even if the object is later found to be defective after the lapse of that time, it need not be returned to the owner once purchased; likewise, even if it is later found to be devoid of its qualities, it need not be returned to the owner once purchased, because the mention of "defective" is intended to refer to those things that serve as grounds for rescission (*anuśaya*). However, Nārada states what must be known prior to the purchase in order to prevent the arising of such rescission.
"One should know the decrease, the increase, and likewise the arrival of commodities.

This means that from this point forward, one should determine whether there will be a decline or an increase in commodities such as horses based on factors such as place and time. Furthermore, for the purpose of ascertaining [the merchant's] noble lineage and so forth, one should know his origin, such as his birthplace; this is the meaning. Regarding one who does not know these things, Yājñavalkya says:
"If a merchant does not know the decrease and the increase of commodities..."
Having purchased [an item], one should not harbor regret; by doing so, one becomes subject to a fine of one-sixth.

[519] *Anuśaya* means remorse. That [remorse] should not be made in vain after purchasing [something] by a merchant who was unaware of its depreciation and so forth, because it results in folly. "A merchant skilled in merchandise should not harbor regret after having purchased."

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of violating the prohibition thus stated. For this very reason, the final quarter of the verse—stating that "he who makes a complaint shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth of the price"—is appropriately explained as prescribing the punishment. Objection: Even by one who knows [the law], no complaint should be made, since a prohibition exists. Reply: True; however, it is done by virtue of an exception (*apavāda*). And that exception was shown by Nārada through implication (*arthāt*) regarding the return of what has been returned after a complaint:
"If, having purchased a commodity for its price, the buyer considers it a bad purchase..."
That [article] must be returned by the seller to the buyer on that very same day, provided it is undamaged.
"On the second day, the buyer, by failing to pay it, shall incur a fine of one-thirtieth of the price;
on the third day, that fine shall be double; after that, it belongs to the buyer alone."

The connection is as follows: he who, knowing that the loss and so forth have occurred, considers the purchase to be "badly made" (*duṣkrīta*), by him the bad purchase must be returned. "Unimpaired" means unaltered; if it is altered, then for the purpose of rectifying the alteration, it must be returned on the very day of purchase along with the goods provided by a neutral person. "Twofold" refers to a fifteen-part share. "Beyond that" means beyond the third day. The meaning is that the buyer alone, having purchased it, shall not exercise regret even if he knows of the loss and so forth. Even if regret is expressed due to an ill omen, if the buyer is an expert in omens, then what was stated by Yājñavalkya should be observed. But when he is not an expert in omens, then what was stated by Nārada should be applied, because the logic is the same and because it is stated generally that "he considers it a bad purchase. Even due to an ill omen, the buyer indeed considers it a bad purchase. However, where one purchases a commodity for a small price despite knowing it has many defects, there one does not consider it a bad purchase, and thus the sale is not reversed.
