But a garment that has been worn, which is discolored and soiled—
even if it was purchased with defects— it shall not be returned to the seller.

If an item is purchased after agreeing to a rescission period (*parāvartya-samaya*), and it subsequently turns out to be defective, that defect does not belong to the seller, because the agreement is more powerful even when the purchase was made poorly. Thus, regarding the rescission of a purchase based on specific scriptural injunctions mentioned above, the method for rescinding a purchase—which we have already demonstrated in the previous section in connection with the rescission of a sale—should also be applied here. However, Manu states that certain types of goods are unfit for sale in order to prevent the arising of rescission after purchase:
"An item whose form has been mixed with another is not fit for sale."
It is neither blameworthy, nor deficient, nor distant, nor concealed.
The word "standing at a distance" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus concludes the exposition of the section titled "Repentance after Purchase" in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the procedure for the section titled "Removal of Agreements" is stated;
regarding that, Bṛhaspati first declares the matter relevant to it:

Having summoned Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, well-versed in the scriptures (*śrotriya*), and maintainers of the sacred fire (*agnihotrin*), he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
(521) "There" means in that capital city, in a place prepared as a fit dwelling for the Aryans. And so says Yājñavalkya:

"Having established a residence in the city and settled the Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide for their livelihood"— this is the meaning of that [verse], as explained by the author himself: "He should grant them house-sites with taxes that cannot be confiscated."
And having caused it to be inscribed on his own edict, the king declared those who were to be liberated.

"Having taxes that cannot be confiscated" means having taxes that cannot be seized; that is to say, they are not subject to the king's share (rājabhāga) which is otherwise seizable. This is what is meant: he should grant houses and lands with the condition that they shall have no taxes to be collected by future kings and that the taxes already granted by himself shall remain as they are. The procedure for drafting his own edict should be understood from the section on written documents (*lekhyaprakaraṇa*). In this manner, the king should request the community of noble men (*āryavṛnda*), who possess such established livelihoods and are devoted to the performance of their own duties, [to continue]. And so says Yājñavalkya: "He should address those possessing the threefold knowledge and their livelihoods, saying: 'Let your own duty be protected.'"
In the affairs of the citizens and the three higher castes, they should also perform duties such as officiating as priests (*ārvtijya*). Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"They shall perform the daily rites, the occasional rites, as well as rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*);
they shall likewise carry out the business of the citizens and provide a decision in matters of doubt."
Thus, the specific effect of a specific collective has been stated. He himself also states the function of all collectives:
"The convention and the making of agreements for villages, guilds, and assemblies must be carried out in times of distress, and likewise in matters of dharma. [522]

In the phrase "and of the *gaṇas*," the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*), guilds (*naigama*), and so forth. Thus, the meaning is as follows: during times of minor disturbances or for religious works such as the restoration of ruins, whatever conventional agreement (*samayakriyā*) must be made by those designated by the terms "village" and so on—such that without it, the disturbance would be difficult to avert and the religious work difficult to accomplish—that conventional agreement should be enacted by many men joined together, endowed with whatever specific attributes (*upādhi*) they may possess. In times of fear from flatterers and thieves, affliction is known to be common to all;
therefore, its pacification must be performed by everyone together, not by anyone alone.

*Cāṭa* means a wolf; *upaśamana* refers to the act of pacifying, that is to say, a convention (*samaya*). To define the nature of such a convention, two or three examples of conventions are shown: first, in the event of a calamity such as drought, a certain amount of wealth must be given for each field or each house for the sake of performing propitiatory rites such as the *grahayajña*; this is one convention. Likewise, in the event of a threat from thieves, one skilled man with a weapon in hand must come together from each house; this is another. Similarly, in the event of a threat from the king, one prominent person from each house must come for an audience with the king; this is yet another. However, regarding religious duties (*dharmakārya*), the convention has been defined by that very [authority] himself.
The construction of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, tanks, and gardens,
as well as the refinement of the destitute and the poor, and the performance of sacrificial rites.
We must each contribute our share toward the construction of a dwelling and its cessation;
that which is recorded here on this document is a righteous formal agreement.
"But it must be protected by all... [523]. Thus.

An assembly hall (*sabhā*) is a pavilion serving as a public shelter. A water-station (*prapā*) is a place for distributing drinking water. A grove (*ārāma*) is a pleasure garden. Restoration (*saṃskṛti*) refers to the repair of ruins. Sacraments (*saṃskāra*) include rites such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), as well as funeral rites such as cremation. The act of sacrifice (*yajanakriyā*) refers to the giving of gifts to one who performs Soma sacrifices and the like. Seeking refuge (*kulāyana*) means the arrival of a herd of cattle afflicted by the hardships of famine and so forth; the measures that must be taken when such a situation arises are what is expressed here by the word "that" (*tat*). Suppression (*nirodha*) means confinement; it refers to the maintenance of those seeking refuge until the end of the famine or other calamity. By us—those possessing the specific conditions that serve as the grounds for applying terms such as "village" and the like—either through wealth collected by means of houses, fields, men, and so forth, or through wealth held in the capacity of a mediator (*madhyaka*). [The phrase] "by all" implies "by the members of the community. Thus, a formal agreement (*samayakriyā*) made in this manner, as well as one established by tradition, is not to be observed by the members of the community alone, but by the king as well. And so says Nārada:
The king should likewise protect the established conventions among heretics, guilds, castes, corporations, assemblies, and communities, both within the fort and in the countryside.

Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*) are all those who bear religious marks (*liṅgin*) other than those prescribed by the Vedas; among them, there are conventions (*samayas*) such as the practice of maintaining monasteries (*maṭha*) and so forth. Merchants (*naigamas*) include caravan leaders, traders, and the like; among them, many conventions exist, such as the rule that those who wear disguises or act as messengers must be punished. Guilds (*śreṇis*) consist of those who subsist on a single craft, such as weavers and others; within these, there are conventions such as "this may be sold only by this particular guild. Associations (*pūgas*) consist of elephant-riders, horsemen, and so forth. The terms *vrāta* and *gaṇa* have been explained by Kātyāyana. [524]
"Multitudes bearing various weapons are declared to be those who have assembled;
indeed, a collection of families is proclaimed to be a *gaṇa*. Thus it is said.

In that regard, there are conventions (*samaya*) such as: "In a *pūga* or a *vrāta*, one must not depart from the battle after having abandoned one another. Regarding a *gaṇa*, there is a convention such as: "The piercing of the ears must be performed on the fifth day or in the fifth year. In the phrase "in a *gaṇa* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) indicates the *brahmapurī* (the city of Brahmins) and those places occupied by the *mahājana*; there exists a convention such as: "One who has come for the sake of a teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) and the like is to be honored. Regarding a fortress (*durga*), there is a convention such as: "When someone takes grain and other goods intending to go elsewhere, they must not be sold. Regarding a district (*janapada*), there are various kinds of conventions, such as: "In some places, a ten-percent premium (*daśabandha*) is to be taken from the hand of the seller; in others, from the hand of the buyer. In the phrase "in the district likewise" (*janapade tathā*), the word "likewise" (*tathā*) is intended to indicate villages, cowherd settlements (*ghoṣa*), cities, and so forth, which were not explicitly mentioned. In that context, there is a village convention such as: "One must not stand in a place where cattle graze. There is a cowherd settlement convention such as: "There is no punishment for the sexual misconduct of men or women among the *ābhīra*s. In a city, however, there are conventions such as: "Those who capture criminals and the like are to be executed, while the wealthy and others are to be protected according to their means even without the payment of a fee. The meaning is that the king should act in such a way that this collection of conventions does not fall into ruin nor is it transgressed. Bṛhaspati [says] concerning the persons belonging to corporate bodies:
Having first established mutual trust— either by means of a sealed deposit, a written document, or through neutral mediators— they should thereafter carry out their business affairs.

"By means of a written deed" refers to a formal agreement (*samayapatra*), which implies the presence of mediators and sureties. "Matters" refers to the affairs of the corporation. Kātyāyana also states:
"But whatever is the law (*dharma*) of those belonging to a corporation, by that law they should always perform all their actions, remaining established in their own duties."

The meaning is that members of a community should carry out collective affairs without transgressing their own conventional duties (*sāmāyika-nija-dharma*). Yājñavalkya also states: "That which is established by convention, provided it does not conflict with one's own duty, as well as that which is enacted by the king—such dharma must also be preserved with effort."

One's own duty (*nijadharma*) refers to the duties pertaining to one’s caste, stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so forth. A conventional duty (*sāmayika-dharma*) is a duty established by convention. Furthermore, regarding a conventional duty that contradicts one's own duty—for example: "At the time of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), everyone must come to the royal palace, abandoning their own respective occupations; he who does not go shall be punished with the first amercement"—it follows by implication that such a duty is not to be observed. The meaning of the final quarter-verse is that even a duty enacted by the king's command which does not conflict with one's own duty—such as "Horses and other [animals] of our enemy's territory must be dispatched"—must likewise be followed by the community. Kātyāyana also [says]:
The royal decree has issued in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, its practice must first be carried out by the king's command.

"Dharma" refers to the path of dharma consisting of the Śruti and Smṛti and so forth; "established" (nirgatam) means finalized. "Royal edict" (rājaśāsanam) is the dharma ordained by the king. It is precisely that which is prescribed without contradicting the paths of the Śruti and Smṛti. As for any dharma created by royal command that contradicts the paths of the Śruti and Smṛti—such as, "One must not perform mortgages, sales, or gifts of houses, fields, and the like given by us"—the particle "eva" (precisely) makes it understood that the practice of such a thing must not be performed. How is there a contradiction with the paths of the Śruti and Smṛti here? It is said: the principle that one should employ, as one pleases, wealth acquired through the rules for the acquisition of property is itself a path of the Śruti and Smṛti; since a contradiction with that exists in the case [of the forbidden edict], enough with this insistence on providing a counter-example. Furthermore, as he himself stated:
That man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king is blameworthy;
being a sinner, he should be punished for violating the royal decree.

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to matters of dharma established by the king in accordance with the paths of the Śruti and Smṛti. Bṛhaspati states that two, three, or five persons should be appointed as deliberators on affairs, for it is impossible for an unlimited number of members with diverse opinions to determine the correctness or incorrectness of a matter with unanimity:
"Two, three, or five should be appointed who speak for the welfare of the collective;
their word must be carried out by the village, guild, corporation, and so forth."
Those who are to be rejected and those who are to be accepted among those deliberating on affairs have been shown by him [the author] himself:
"Those who are hostile, addicted to vices, modest, lazy, or cowardly;
the greedy, the very old, and children—these should not be appointed as deliberators of affairs."

"Those who are pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, capable, tranquil, of noble birth, and proficient in all tasks—such great men should be appointed. Here, "modest" means those characterized by a sense of shame. "Considerers of affairs" refers to those who deliberate upon what will accomplish or obstruct the collective business of the group. Yājñavalkya, however, states that even those who do not consider the specific affairs [of the group], provided they speak for the welfare of the assembly, their word must be acted upon by all members of the group.
"The words of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out by all. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, he [the same author] states that whoever is antagonistic toward those who speak for the welfare [of the group] shall be punished by the community with the first *sāhasa* fine:
"Whoever there should be contrary [to them], he shall be made to pay the first fine."
Kātyāyana also states:
"He who destroys what is consistent with reason, he who provides no opportunity for the speaker,
and he who speaks what is unreasonable— such a person shall be made to pay the first amercement."
Bṛhaspati:
But he who destroys common property, or reviles those learned in the three Vedas,
or obstructs the performance of a treaty, shall be banished from that city.

The meaning is that one should cause the destruction of common property, such as staffs and the like, by means of assisting those who are to be punished and so forth. "Kṣipet" means he should expel. "Tataḥ" means from the city, that is, from the place where the corporation resides. Regarding the expulsion for ignorance (*avidyākṣepa*), however, the punishment will be stated in the section on verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*). For a member of the corporation alone who reveals secrets and the like, the punishment is indeed exile. And thus says that same [author]: "One who inflicts pain on others, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, a perpetrator of violence, and one who hates the guilds, the corporations, or the king—these shall be swiftly expelled from there."

An *aruntuda* is one who exposes a vital point (*marmodghāṭaka*). A *sūcaka* is a slanderer (*piśuna*). A *bhedakṛt* is one who creates dissension among a group by instilling doubt; "from that," meaning from his position within the group; "he shall be expelled" (*nirvāsyate*), with the understanding that this is done by the group. Nor should it be argued that because the group lacks the authority to inflict punishment, the phrase "by the group" is inappropriate; for he [Yājñavalkya] himself says:
"The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies, as well as those residing in cities and fortresses, shall impose verbal censure, fines, or expulsion upon those who commit evil deeds."

[528] "Whatever punishment or favor toward men has been performed by them according to the law, that must also be approved by the king; for they are traditionally considered as having been delegated with full authority. "Restriction of speech" (*vāgdama*) refers to threats such as "you are most wicked. "Censure" (*dhig-dama*) is the reproach "shame on you! "Exclusion" (*parityāga*) means branding with a mark or banishment. This is intended to include monetary fines and other penalties as well, since the term "punishment and favor" (*nigrahānugraha*) is stated again in general terms. They are "delegated with authority" (*nisṛṣṭārthāḥ*), meaning their actions have been authorized. He states the same regarding what occurs even when they act unjustly:

"If those who have become possessed by hatred should cause harm to one person, they must be restrained and punished by the king once he has learned of it, according to the circumstances. By "according to the circumstances" (*anubandhataḥ*), the meaning is that they are to be punished in accordance with the specific details of the case. Nārada also speaks of those to be punished:
But those who would divide the separate groups must be disciplined especially;
for if they are neglected, they will bring about terrible danger, like a disease.

In this context, the term "group" (*gaṇa*) refers to any collection in general, and not specifically to a collection in the form of a *kula* (clan). Therefore, those who cause division even among heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and others are to be disciplined especially by the king. Because of the use of the word "especially," they may also be disciplined with corporal punishment. Regarding how the king should behave toward all such groups, including heretics and the like, that same [author] has also said: "What is their duty, what is their work, what is their rule of service, and what is their means of livelihood—the king should approve of each of these accordingly."

"Dharma" refers to the wearing of matted hair and so forth. "Karma" refers to the vow of wandering for alms after they have been left overnight and so forth. "The rule of attendance" is the gathering together in a pavilion or similar place upon hearing the sound of a drum or other signal for the sake of collective business. "Pratyupādāna" is the adoption of the dress of an ascetic and so forth for the sake of livelihood. This is the meaning regarding these heretics and others. He (Yājñavalkya) states another royal duty as well: "He shall turn them away from whatever is contrary to the king, whatever is despised by the subjects, and whatever causes harm to wealth."
An example of the contrary case is as follows:
"If a Śūdra performs the administration of justice for a king, his kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish. Thus it is said.

And thus, one should understand that cases such as when a Śūdra like Sārthaka acts as a judge in a dispute between members of the three higher castes or citizens—performing the discernment of dharma and so forth—are examples of what is meant by the phrase, "that which is contrary to the king. By nature, that is, by its very essence, [such conduct] is contemptible and disregarded; for example: the chewing of betel and similar acts among heretics (pāṣaṇḍas) and others. Furthermore, whatever causes the obstruction of wealth, such as the obstruction of flavors and so forth, the king should cause that to cease on their account. He states that other things as well must be prevented: "Forming secret conspiracies, bearing weapons against those who do no harm," and so on.
And the king should prevent their mutual injury.

"Mutual association" refers to performing intermediate *stoma* rites individually prior to the formal installation (*upasthāna*). "Harm" refers to those born of low families and the like. "Mutual affliction" refers to the seizing of each other's wealth and so forth by relying on royal authority. He (the author) states that other such things are also to be prohibited:

"That which is a defective cause, even if it has been established previously or is currently being undertaken—even if it has already begun—a king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be stopped. [530]

The meaning is that the king shall abolish even those practices—such as the prostitution of widows and others—which are caused by defects like greed, which contradict the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, which have been devised by heretics and the like, and which, though long-established, persist; he should likewise act regarding the members of guilds (*samūhin*), performing whatever cannot be accomplished by the guild itself, such as restraining the arrogance of its leaders. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "When a conflict arises between the leaders and the guilds, then the king shall investigate the matter and establish them upon their own path."

But regarding one who is a leader and cannot even be restrained by the king from his own path, Yājñavalkya has stated: "However, he who misappropriates the property of a guild or violates an agreement, the king shall confiscate all his possessions and banish him from the realm."

The word "king" is to be understood as the subject, because he alone possesses the capacity for such application of punishment. When the collective body (*samūha*) also possesses some degree of capacity, then—by virtue of the context—it should be understood that the *gaṇa* itself is the agent of the application of punishment. Kātyāyana has also stated:
"The perpetrator of violence, the one who causes dissension, and the destroyer of the *gaṇa*'s property—all these must be executed by kings after being publicly proclaimed; thus said Bhṛgu."

Some read "nṛpe bhṛguḥ"; in that case, the meaning is as follows: having made public the king's severity and so forth, they are to be destroyed by the community. Regarding one who is primarily incapable of being established in his proper path through an oath, it was stated by Manu: "That man who, having made a compact by means of truth among villages, districts, or assemblies, should break it out of greed—he the king should banish from the realm."
[531] Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the agreement to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one śatamāna of silver.
"In this manner, a righteous lord of the earth shall administer the rule of punishment for those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is: "by means of an oath of truth. The terms *suvarṇa*, *niṣka*, and *māna* have been explained previously in the section on ordeals (*divya*). In that context, there are three monetary fines (*arthadaṇḍa*) which are to be determined according to the wealth of those who are to be punished. However, banishment (*nirvāsana*) is to be determined in cases of persistent transgression. From the mention of the "righteous king" (*dhārmika*), it is understood that there is also a possibility of indifference toward the application of punishment for the unrighteous. And when the righteous king is indifferent regarding the application of punishment, then the village elders and others themselves shall carry out the disciplinary measures, because it has been stated: "For they are considered to be delegated with full authority (*nisṛṣṭārtha*). But for subordinates who violate the established convention, the punishment should be devised according to their audacity. Even for them, if through their capability they become equal to the principal officers, that which was stated by Bṛhaspati applies.

"...he who, being capable, should act in contradiction [to the agreement], his punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city. Here, "capable" (*samartha*) means one who is able to observe the agreement, that is to say, one who is equal to the principal [party]. "Should act in contradiction" (*visaṃvadet*) means he should transgress the agreement. He [the author] mentions others who are also subject to punishment: He himself says: [text follows]
Those who, having come together and formed a single mind, steal what belongs to the king,
as well as merchants who flee, shall be made to pay eightfold.

The phrase "those who seize what is due to the king" (*rājabhāvyaṃ haranti ye*) is to be supplied as the fourth quarter of the verse. [532] If a person, having received from the king what was granted for the purpose of honoring a corporation or for the sake of the corporation's business, does not personally deliver it to the corporation upon arriving at its side, then he must be made to pay eleven times the amount given by the king. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the corporation with gifts, honor, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business is accomplished."
"Whatever one who has been dispatched for the business of the community may obtain, that he shall hand over;

if he does not hand it over himself, he should be made to pay eleven times [the amount]. The phrase "whatever he may obtain" implies by way of his being honored by the community; for what is obtained on account of one's own service, study, or similar activities cannot logically be subject to a rule of handing it over to the collective, as it belongs to the individual. And what is handed over by one dispatched for the community's business, all members of the community shall take by dividing it equally among themselves.

"Whatever may be obtained from that shall be shared equally among all," according to the traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati. Thus, taking possession after such a distribution refers to the case of non-trivial property; however, trivial property that has been acquired should be given to the indigent and others by the group as a whole. As he himself says:
"Whether it be for six months or for one month, it should be divided according to their respective shares."
Or it should be given to the destitute, the elderly, the distressed, women, children, the sick, and the diseased.
"In cases such as those involving heirs and so forth, the eternal law (*dharma*) is likewise.

The intended meaning is this: if what has been obtained is insufficient for the maintenance of one person for six months, or insufficient for the maintenance of a family for even one month, it must be given to the destitute and others. Furthermore, as stated by that same author:
"Whatever they have acquired or protected, or whatever debt has been incurred for the sake of the community..."
Or, whatever is obtained through the favor of the king belongs equally to all.

Thus, this is its meaning: whatever additional land, groves, and so forth was acquired through legal process in a court of law by those dispatched for the sake of the community's business—whether in disputes over boundaries and the like—or whatever was protected from being seized by others; likewise, whatever debt was contracted for the purpose of the community's needs, or whatever was obtained through royal favor generated by the community's favorable conduct—all this is to be understood as equal among all members of the association. Regarding the rule that "a debt contracted for the sake of the *gaṇa* is equal for all," Kātyāyana states an exception in certain cases:
Whatever debt may have been incurred for the sake of the community, or whatever has been consumed,
or whatever has been expended for one's own personal use, that must be paid back by those very individuals themselves.

The meaning is that the debt must be repaid by those very individuals who were dispatched for the collective business. Even if they fail to provide the stipulated provisions for the journey (*pātheya*), the debt incurred by them need not be paid by the group; this is because of the use of the restrictive particle *eva*. Rather, only the provisions for the journey must be given. Regarding those, however, who have gained entry into the group by winning over the assembly, and those who have been excluded from it due to disturbances within the group and the like, he says the same: "Those among the members of a guild or a group who have attained the status of being insiders—whether they be creditors or debtors—they shall all share equally in the prior wealth and debts."

"In the same way, regarding the enjoyment of wealth, the giving of gifts, and the performance of religious duties, one who remains within the group shall share in the portion; however, one who has departed does not share in the portion."
Thus concludes the exposition of the section titled "Removal of Impediments" (*samayānapākarma*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the procedure for the section titled "Disputes concerning Fields" (*kṣetrajavivāda*) is stated.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"At the time of settling [a village], the determination of the boundary must be made;
marked by both manifest and secret signs, it removes all doubt."

The time of settlement (*niveśakāla*) is the time of entering a village or similar place. A "binding" (*nibandha*) of the boundary means a demarcation; that is to say, a "determiner" (*viniścaya*). A determiner is a large ball made of stone or other materials by which the binding of the boundary is fixed. Thus, "the binding of the boundary and the determiner" (*sīmābandhaviniścaya*) means a large ball that serves as the demarcator of the boundary. This is what is meant: at the time of settling a village or similar place, a large ball that demarcates its boundary—endowed with both visible and hidden marks—should be placed at the junction of the boundaries. The visible and hidden marks have also been shown by that same [author].
Reservoirs, wells, and ponds; shrines, groves, and temples; high ground, low ground, river currents, reeds, thickets, mountains, and so forth.
One should always cause these signs of demarcation to be made at the boundary:
dried cow dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, stones, and potsherds.
"Having thrown sand, bricks, cow-hair, cotton, bones, and ashes into jars, one should cause these to be deposited at the boundaries.

Here, *vāpī* means a pond; *caitya* is a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*) constructed with bricks and the like; *sthala* is an elevated region of ground; *nimna* is a depression; *parighāḥ* are ditches; *śarāḥ* are a species of grass; *gulmāḥ* are shrubs devoid of bulbous roots, such as the *karavīra*; and *nagāḥ* are trees. These, however, have been specified by Manu: [535]
He should establish boundary trees such as the nyagrodha, aśvattha, kiṃśuka, śalmali,
sāla, tāla, and other milky-exuding trees.

*Nyagrodha* is the *vaṭa* (banyan) tree. *Kiṃśuka* is the *palāśa* tree. In the phrase "mountains and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes bamboo, creepers, anthills, roads, ancient embankments, and other items mentioned in other *smṛtis*. *Karīṣa* is dried cow dung. "Bones" refers to those of animals and the like. *Tuṣas* are the husks of rice and other grains. *Aṅgāras* are the cooled remnants of burnt wood. *Śarkaras* are hard earth resembling stones. *Kapālikās* are fragments of baked clay pots. *Kārpāsāsthīni* are cotton seeds. One should cause them to be placed [there] by first placing jars within the pits and then covering them with earth. Thus says Manu:
And he should cause other boundary markers to be concealed,
having observed that in this world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries.

"Concealed" means covered; "others" refers to those different from the manifest signs, and these have already been mentioned below. Among them, with the exception of cotton seeds, all [other signs] are also enumerated by Manu. The mention of the signs is intended to serve as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); thus, Manu has no objection to the mention of cotton seeds. For this very reason, after stating the secret signs (*upāṃśuliṅga*), Manu stated: "And whatever other such [signs] the earth might not consume over time, those he should cause to be made inconspicuous at the joints and on the boundary."

These include oyster shells, conch shells, red ochre, the heartwood of khadira, and so forth. Among those boundary markers described above, a boundary possessing tree-marks is called *dhvajinī* (the bannered). One possessing water-marks is called *matsyinī* (the fish-marked). One possessing hidden marks such as husks or charcoal is called *naidhānī* (the deposited). And thus Vyāsa says:
"Where trees grow tall along the boundary of two villages, rising high in the shape of banners, that is proclaimed as *dhvajinī*."
Where there is a river flowing freely, abounding in water, filled with fish and turtles,
and ever-flowing— that is considered the Matsinī boundary.

"The boundary should be marked by husks, charcoal, potsherds, jars, and likewise by sanctuaries; that is called the *naidhānī* [boundary]. Thus, "elevated" means uneven or irregular; "raised" means high. Boundary markers, whether established through effort or existing naturally, must be made known to those of declining age by those in the prime of their youth. And so says Bṛhaspati:
Then, with great care, one should show it to children of the *paugaṇḍa* stage;
and likewise, when they have grown old, those children should show it to them in the same manner.

"In this way, when there is a continuous tradition of knowledge, no confusion regarding the boundary arises. Thus, "paugaṇḍabālāḥ" refers to children who have attained some degree of awakening. Those *paugaṇḍabālāḥ*, having in time reached old age, should diligently point out to the infants—who have attained some degree of awakening—the boundary markers made known by their own kinsmen. The meaning is that an uninterrupted succession of knowers must be maintained even after the lapse of a very long period of time, for the purpose of preventing confusion regarding the boundary.
Thus ends the determination of boundary marks in the *Smṛticandrikā* [537]. Now begins the decision regarding disputes over boundaries.
Regarding this, Manu states:
"By these marks, the king should determine the boundary between two disputing parties.

The meaning is that he should lead—that is, decide—the boundary by means of these previously established boundary marks shown by the plaintiff. Now, if there is a lack of confidence in the plaintiff, then he should decide based solely on the testimony of witnesses. To this effect, the same author says:
If there were doubt even upon seeing the indicative marks,
then the testimony of witnesses alone would be the means for determining a boundary dispute.

The meaning is that testimony concerning boundary marks (*liṅga*) or concerning boundaries (*sīmā*) shall be the cause for deciding a dispute over boundaries. In this regard, witnesses who possess knowledge concerning boundary marks should be understood as possessing the very characteristics stated in the section on witnesses [in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*]. However, Bṛhaspati has shown here an additional requirement for the characteristics of witnesses concerning boundaries: "Those who know the title-deed (*āgama*), the evidence (*pramāṇa*), the possession (*bhoga*), the time (*kāla*), the name (*nāma*), and the description of the plot of land (*bhūbhāgalakṣaṇa*), they are the witnesses in this matter."

*Āgama* refers to the means of acquisition, such as purchase and so forth, which establishes ownership. *Pramāṇa* refers to the measurement determined by means such as a measuring rod. However, when there is an absence of witnesses of the aforementioned kind, one should decide the case by means of marks pointed out by the neighbors. Manu has stated this very point in another formulation:
"In the absence of witnesses, however, four inhabitants living on the borders of the village shall, being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king."

Kātyāyana also states: "In their absence, the neighbors. This refers to those two types of witnesses. When it is asked who the neighbors are, he says: "[538] 'The neighbors, however, are the contiguous ones' (saṃsaktakas). The meaning is that for a village or other settlement whose boundaries are disputed, the owners of the lands immediately adjacent in the four directions are the contiguous ones; they alone are to be known as the neighbors. When such declared neighbors are found to possess manifest defects such as passion or hatred, he further states: "When the neighbors are corrupted in the pursuit of their own interests, [the decision should be made] because of the gravity of the matter."
In cases involving those associated with that [sin], an extraction [of the penalty] must be performed; there is no doubt about this.

Regarding "those adjacent to them" (*tatsaṃsakteṣu*), which refers to those adjacent to the neighbors: "removal" (*uddhāra*) means the removal of the boundary, that is to say, the determination of the boundary. This is what is meant: the owners of villages and so forth situated in each respective direction, being immediately contiguous to the villages and so forth belonging to the neighbors situated in the four directions, are "those adjacent to them" (*tatsaṃsaktāḥ*); by means of the boundary marks indicated by them, one should determine the boundary of the village and so forth. When even they are found to have manifest defects, he says the same thing: "But when there is a defect in those adjacent to the neighbors, then those adjacent to them are proclaimed [as witnesses]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.153).

"Those attached to them" (*tatsaṃsaktāḥ*) refers to those who are attached to those who are themselves attached to the villages and so forth. This is what is meant: those who enjoy the villages and so forth situated in each respective direction, being immediately adjacent to the villages and so forth situated in the four directions that are "attached" (*saṃsakta*) or "closely attached" (*sakta*), are the "those attached to those who are attached" (*saṃsaktasaktasaṃsaktāḥ*); by means of the boundary marks indicated by them, one should determine the boundary of the village and so forth. But when even they possess manifest defects, then he says the same author: "But having set aside the corrupt neighbors, one should have the boundary determined together with others such as the *maula* (original inhabitants) and so forth; thus do those who know the Dharma understand. [539]

Even those who are *saṃsakta*, *sakta*, and *saṃsakta* are situated at the boundary (*sāmanta-koṭi-niviṣṭa*); therefore, their designation by the term "neighboring" (*sāmanta*) is not improper. Consequently, this is the meaning: having set aside the wicked *saṃsakta-sakta-saṃsakta* [witnesses], one should appoint as boundary-settlers (*sīmānta-pratinirṇāyaka*) others than the witnesses, the neighbors, and the boundary-limits—namely, those who are familiar with the boundary marks, who are original inhabitants (*maula*), elders (*vṛddha*), and those who have been previously appointed (*uddhṛta*). When it is asked, "Who then are these others besides the witnesses, neighbors, and boundary-limits?", Nārada says: "Those who are heads of city or village corporations (*gaṇin*), and those men who are the oldest."
The phrase "those who know the boundary marks" is the ellipsis to be supplied. However, the *maula*, *vṛddha*, and *uddhṛta* [witnesses] have been shown by Kātyāyana:
"Those who were former neighbors there but later went to another region are proclaimed as *maula* by the seers because they are the root-source of that [boundary]."
Those endowed with human virtues who have witnessed a task being accomplished—
whether they be old or even not old— are proclaimed as "the aged" (vṛddha).

"Because they rescue [beings] from that [state] by means of eavesdropping, enjoyment, performing tasks, and giving explanations, they are therefore known as 'Uddhṛtas' (the Rescuers). Thus it is said.

The phrase "endowed with human qualities" (*nṛguṇānvitaiḥ puruṣaguṇānvitaiḥ*) indicates by way of an alternative statement that seniority of age (*vayovṛddhatvam*) is not the sole criterion. The essential meaning of the third verse is that those who possess knowledge of the matter through traditional lineage (*pāramparyeṇa*) are the ones to be selected. Thus, it should be understood that when there are corrupt individuals—those directly involved, their associates, or those associated with them—the determination of the boundary must be carried out based on boundary markers pointed out by the guilds of city-dwellers and villagers, as well as elders in age, accompanied by former neighbors and others. He states the specific rule regarding neighbors whose faults are concealed: [He says: "When neighbors have concealed faults... [and so forth].
The neighboring kings are considered to possess one unit of excellence when they have previously failed in their efforts;
those further away are known to possess two units, while others beyond them are regarded as possessing three units.

The meaning is: when the opponent has stated an undesirable point and has brought forth a concealed fault. The subsequent ones—those connected to them (*tatsaṃsakta*) and so forth—are to be known as the inner circles of neighbors (*sāmantaka-koṭi*), and they are double [in number]. Beyond those neighbors and their circles, others such as the citizens (*nāgara*) and so forth, together with the hereditary elders (*maula-vṛddha-uddhṛta*), are considered triple. In this same way, when a concealed fault is brought forth even regarding those connected to them and so on, the doubling and so forth of the subsequent groups should be inferred. However, in the absence of everyone from the witnesses (*sākṣin*) up to the hereditary elders, Manu says: "In the absence of neighbors who are hereditary witnesses of the boundary..."
One should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests.

In the absence of neighbors and others—such as benefactors, original founders, and witnesses to the boundary—one should interrogate these following persons, even if they are not members of the assembly; the meaning is that one should ask them about the boundary markers. He shows who they are: "Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who frequent the forest" (MDh 8.260).

The mention of hunters (*vyādha*) and others in the accusative case is for the purpose of connecting them with the word *anuyuñjīta* (should question) found in the preceding verse. Fishermen (*kaivarta*) are those who subsist by digging tanks and similar works. "Others" refers to forest-dwellers (*vanagocara*) who subsist on wood and other forest products. However, Nārada—intending to show that in the absence of these, there are farmers in the vicinity of the boundary, and in their absence, forest-dwellers—first indicates the boundary-farmers before the forest-dwellers:
"And those who live by agriculture outside the village boundaries."
Cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others who dwell in the forest. (NSm 11.3)

In this manner, even among neighbors and others down to the boundary-setters, if superior persons are unavailable, the interrogation of inferior ones is to be inferred. Interrogation (*anuyojana*) consists of making those [neighbors] intent on speaking the truth by means of the words of Manu and others which set forth the merit and demerit arising from truth and falsehood, and then putting them questions regarding the matter at hand. Those words are to be understood as they are stated in the section on the procedure for interrogating witnesses. Only after being sworn by the oaths prescribed in the section on the procedure for questioning witnesses should the neighbors and others deliver their verdict. And so says Bṛhaspati:
Bound by their respective oaths, they shall declare the determination of the boundary and point out the marks; that is established as the authoritative proof.

The meaning is: by transgressing the rules stated in such passages as, "One should cause a Brahmin to swear by his own [sacred] oaths, and a Kṣatriya by [swearing on] his vehicle and weapons," and so forth. By Manu also:
The witnesses to the boundary should be questioned in the presence of the village families and of those two litigants regarding the marks of the boundary.
Having said this, it was further stated:
"The king shall establish according to dharma that very mark which those questioned declare as the boundary-mark at the junctions of the two villages. [542] Thus.

The meaning of the first verse is that the boundary markers, as well as the witnesses and others, should be questioned in the presence of a group of villagers and the two litigants. The meaning of the second verse, however, is very clear: those who are witnesses specifically to the boundary must be questioned regarding the boundary alone; and it should be understood that one should cause [the decision] to be known in such a way that they, when questioned, declare the boundary. But when the witnesses to the boundary markers are somehow unable to point out the characteristics and merely speak of the boundary itself, then he says the following with regard to them:
Bearing the earth upon their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and bound by oaths sworn on their own good deeds, they shall lead them back in a proper manner.

The meaning is that as many boundary-mark witnesses as there may be, all wearing garlands of red flowers and red garments, carrying clods of earth upon their heads, and indicating the limits of the boundary by walking along the path following the boundary, shall correctly and properly determine that boundary. However, Yājñavalkya says regarding the neighbors and others:
"Neighbors from the entire village—four, eight, or even ten—wearing red garlands and garments, and carrying earth, shall lead [the way] to the boundary."

From the word "or" (*vā*), it is understood that those who are closely associated with them (*tatsaṃsaktaka*) and others likewise should lead the boundary when the display of signs is impossible; this is because, among those who can display the signs, the term serves as an alternative. The specific mention of "four," etc., as being "of the entire village" (*samagrāmāḥ*), "equal in number" (*samasaṅkhyātāḥ*), and "having attained the state of a collective" (*samudāyabhāvam āpannāḥ*), is for the purpose of excluding other equal numbers. Regarding the phrase "of the entire village," the inclusion of the word "entire" (*samagra*) is for the purpose of precluding an unequal number. To exclude even the extreme case of a single number therein, Nārada says: [543]
A man, even if he is trustworthy, should not determine a boundary alone;
because of the gravity of this matter, this procedure is established among many.
Regarding this prohibition, Bṛhaspati states an exception in certain cases:
"Even a single virtuous person, approved by both parties, may [give evidence] even without witnesses or identifying marks,
provided he wears red garlands and garments and carries earth upon his head."
A man, committed to truth and observing a fast, should point out the boundary. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that there is an absence of both the knowers and the marks [of the boundary] without the signs of the knowers. This is what is intended: in the absence of the knowers of the boundary—ranging from witnesses to those familiar with the interior of the forest—and in the absence of manifest or secret marks, any man endowed with the aforementioned qualifications who knows the boundary should, while wandering along the edge of the boundary according to the prescribed rule, point it out. Although it may appear from the statements of Manu and others that a decision is reached immediately after the wandering, nevertheless, it should be understood that the decision is reached at the end of one and a half months starting from the day of the wandering, and not before that. As Kātyāyana says:

"In the case of crossing a boundary, traveling a *krośa*, or likewise touching with the foot, [ordeals] are prescribed for three fortnights, one fortnight, and seven days, respectively—[namely] the divine and the royal. This is the remainder [of the sense]. Even when there is an absence of a person possessing the aforementioned characteristics or of a means of proof, there is still no decision by means of an ordeal (*divya*).

Because of various statements such as, "In cases of verbal abuse and disputes over land, one should avoid ordeals," ordeals are prohibited in disputes concerning land (*bhūvivāda*). Furthermore, a boundary dispute (*sīmāvivāda*) is indeed a dispute over land. As Kātyāyana says:
"Excess, deficiency, a portion, and even existence or non-existence... [544]
"Enjoyment, possession, and boundary—these six are the grounds for a dispute over land.
When the question arises as to how a decision is reached in such a case, Nārada states:
"But when there are no witnesses to the boundary and no defining marks..."
Then the king himself may, as he desires, establish the boundary between the two.

"According to desire" means "according to wish. Regarding this term "according to desire," Manu states an exception: "When a boundary is impossible to determine, the king himself, being a knower of dharma, may enter [the land] for the benefit of some; such is the established rule."

It is "unbearable" (aviṣahyā) because it is devoid of both a knower and one who makes known. This is what is meant: where a plot of land is of extreme benefit to one person who has no other space (niravakāśa), such as for a village or field, but is not so for another who does have space (sāvakāśa), then for the sake of that great benefit, one should cause that land to be entered [into the possession] of the one with no other space, as a subordinate part of his village and so forth. Thus, by the method described, the determination of boundaries is not always easy to perform immediately after a formal complaint, as is the case with the determination of debts and the like; for during the rainy season and other times, when boundary markers such as embankments are obscured by crops and the like, it is difficult to ascertain them. Therefore, the determination should be made when there is an absence of crops or other obscuring factors for the boundary markers such as embankments. And so says Manu: [Manu 8.257: "When the boundary marks are destroyed, or when they cannot be found, the king himself shall determine the boundary between the two villages."
When a dispute has arisen regarding a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.

The meaning is that when a dispute has arisen between two village headmen concerning a boundary, one should determine the boundary under litigation during the month of Jyeṣṭha or another month, provided that boundary markers such as embankments and the like are clearly visible. The mention of "village" (grāma) is intended to include fields and other such properties by way of illustration. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati began his discourse with: "Learn the rules regarding disputes over boundaries of villages, fields, houses, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "houses and so forth," cities and districts are included, since disputes over boundaries also exist there. For this same reason, Kātyāyana states:
In matters concerning neighboring lands, the decision regarding fields and other properties should be made by the neighbors;
likewise, this applies to village boundaries, as well as to cities and districts.

Thus it has been stated. "The determination of fields and so forth" means the determination of the boundaries between fields and houses. Furthermore, in the case of villages, fields, houses, and the like, a mutual determination by the neighbors of one another should not be carried out, because the village neighbors are unfamiliar with the boundaries of fields and houses, and likewise, the field neighbors are unfamiliar with the boundaries of villages and houses. For this very reason, that same author says: "A village is declared the neighbor of a village; a field is proclaimed the neighbor of a field; a house is specified as the neighbor of a house. One should examine these neighbors."

In this context, by the word "village" (*grāma*) and so forth, ending in the nominative case, the one who enjoys (the inhabitants of) the village and so forth is indicated through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Consequently, the meaning is as follows: the people who enjoy the villages and so forth situated on all sides—in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions—of the village and so forth that is the subject of the dispute, are its "neighboring lords" (*sāmanta*); from them, the judge—the king or whoever else—is to examine and determine the boundary markers of the village and so forth that is the subject of the dispute. In this manner, it should be understood that the rule—that for cities and districts as well, one should examine [the boundaries] from their respective neighboring lords—is indicated in this statement by way of illustration. In exactly the same way, in disputes concerning the boundaries of fields, gardens, groves, temples, wells, tanks, water-courses, and places where water flows from rain, the judge shall decide based on witnesses, those neighboring lords, and others. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"This rule has been proclaimed for every stationary legal dispute.
Thus ends the determination of boundary disputes in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some statements concerning the offenses of witnesses and others regarding boundaries are recorded as follows:
In that regard, Kātyāyana states:
"But if, among many who have been summoned, they all do not reach a decision because of fear or greed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine."

The meaning is as follows: when all those who have been proclaimed as witnesses to a boundary have assembled for the purpose of giving testimony, if they do not give testimony due to fear or other such reasons, then they shall each be made to pay the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). Although the word "each" (*pratyekam*) is not explicitly stated, it is understood here because each one individually serves as a witness. However, when they all, out of fear or other motives, create doubt by speaking with discordant opinions, he says that they should likewise be made to pay:
"If there should be a disagreement once [the boundary] has been proclaimed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine."

But when they should speak falsely, Viṣṇu says: "The confiscation of all property should be carried out against false witnesses. Although this is stated in general terms, it should be understood as referring to matters concerning land and the like, due to the severity of the punishment. Regarding the false testimony of neighbors, however, Nārada says:
"If neighbors should speak falsely in a boundary dispute, they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement."

"They might speak falsely" in their testimony means that they might speak while deceiving [others] regarding the boundary markers. Regarding the statement made out of ignorance, Kātyāyana says: "Neighbors are not released from liability for the decision simply by claiming ignorance.
Having punished them for stating their ignorance, one should investigate the boundary once again."

The phrase "in the case of an ignorant statement" is intended as an indication of the absence of a definitive decision; therefore, even when a distinction is stated, since there is still no definitive decision, one should investigate the boundary once again. When the question arises as to who is the decisive authority therein, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In case of conflict with neighbors, the evidence of documents is authoritative; in case of conflict with documents, the evidence of the elders and guilds of the village or city is authoritative; in case of conflict with the elders and guilds of the village or city, possession for ten years is authoritative, except in the event of a royal upheaval. The remainder of the sentence is that the evidence of documents is the decisive authority. In this manner, the remainder should be understood in subsequent cases as well. However, regarding the false testimony of those starting from the "intimately connected" (saṃsakta) up to the "forest-dwellers" (vanagocara), Nārada says:
If the remaining persons appointed to the land-work should speak falsely,
each of those lowest-ranking individuals shall be punished with the first amercement.

"But others, such as the elders of the *gaṇa* and so forth, are to be punished individually; if they persist in falsehood, they are to be fined with the first *sāhasa*. The "remainder" (*śeṣāḥ*) refers to those other than the neighbors (*sāmantāḥ*), namely their immediate associates (*tatsaṃsaktāḥ*). Those inferior to them are the associates of the associates (*saṃsaktasaṃsaktāḥ*). In the phrase "the elders of the *gaṇa* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the village headmen, city elders, those who have extracted the boundary markers, the boundary-drawers, and the forest-keepers. Manu, however, states the punishment for those who persist in falsehood while traversing the boundary: [Manu 8.263–264] "They shall be punished with the first *sāhasa* fine if they lie regarding the boundary. But if they have deviated from the truth, they shall all be punished with the highest *sāhasa*. [Manu 8.265] "If a man, having been summoned to mark the boundary, denies what he saw, he shall be fined five hundred *paṇas* and shall lose his claim to the land. [Manu 8.266] "The king himself shall establish the boundary between two disputing parties by means of witnesses, or by means of the marks of possession (*upalakṣaṇaiḥ*). [Manu 8.267] "The witnesses to the boundary are those who have traversed it, as well as the neighbors, the inhabitants of the vicinity, and those who know the ancient state of things. [Manu 8.268] "The boundary-markers are: trees such as the *nyagrodha*, the *aśvattha*, the *śirīṣa*, the *śamī*, the *pippala*, the *bhallātaka*, and the *veṇu*; as well as thickets, reeds, and creepers. [Manu 8.269] "Clods of earth, charred potsherds, bones, cow-tails, chaff, ashes, bricks, pebbles, and shells—these are the boundary-markers to be established. [Manu 8.270] "Springs, ponds, wells, groves, temples, large trees, and mounds—these are the boundary-markers that endure for all time. [Manu 8.271] "By these signs, or even by the flow of water, the king shall determine the boundary between two villages when it has become uncertain. [Manu 8.272] "If there are no boundary-marks at all, or if the marks have been destroyed, the king himself shall determine the boundary by means of oaths and by means of the testimony of witnesses. [Manu 8.273] "Those who bear false witness concerning a boundary shall each be punished with the highest *sāhasa* fine, and those who cause the destruction of a boundary shall be punished with the middle *sāhasa*. [Manu 8.274] "A field, a house, a pond, a garden, or a pasture—wherever a boundary is not fixed, the king shall determine it by means of possession. [Manu 8.275] "Between two fields, a house, or a pond, the king shall determine the boundary by means of possession, even if it has lasted for a hundred years. [Manu 8.276] "Even if a field has been possessed for a hundred years by another person, provided it was done with force and without title, the owner may recover it. [Manu 8.277] "But a field, a house, or a pond that has been enjoyed without protest by neighbors for twenty years shall not be recovered. [Manu 8.278] "In the case of a house or a shop, the enjoyment of others for ten years is declared to be without protest, whether in a city or a village. [Manu 8.279] "Neither the king nor a Brahmin shall ever take possession of a house or a field by force; if he takes it, he incurs the sin of stealing land. [Manu 8.280] "If a man, having sold a field or the like, does not deliver it to the purchaser, he shall be fined five hundred *paṇas* and shall forfeit the sale-price. [Manu 8.281] "If a man, having purchased a field or the like, does not accept it because of some defect, he shall be fined five hundred *paṇas* and shall forfeit the purchase-price. [Manu 8.282] "If a man, having given a daughter in marriage according to the *brāhma* rite, later abandons her, he shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* and shall be liable for the bride-price. [Manu 8.283] "If a man, having promised a girl to one man, gives her to another, he shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* and shall be liable for the bride-price. [Manu 8.284] "If a man, having promised a girl to one man, gives her to another, he shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* and shall be liable for the bride-price. [Manu 8.285] "If a man, having promised a girl to one man, gives her to another, he shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* and shall be liable for the bride-price. [Manu 8.286] "If a man, having promised a girl to one man, gives her to another, he shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* and shall be liable for the bride-price. [Manu 8.287] "If a man, having promised a girl to one man, gives her to another, he shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* and shall be liable for the bride-price. [Manu 8.288] "If a man, having promised a girl to one man, gives her to another, he shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* and shall be liable for the bride-price.
