Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].

Leading [the boundary] without deviating from the path described by the verse beginning with "Taking the earth with their heads," those who traverse the boundary as witnesses to the truth—possessing the experience of the true boundary—are purified; they are not bound by sin. Conversely, those who lead it wrongly, traversing by overstepping the previous boundary, must be made to pay two hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the "leading wrongly" should be understood to occur if, starting from the moment immediately following the traversal, any calamity caused by fate or the king is observed within the interval of one and a half months.
Thus ends the section on offenses regarding boundary witnesses and others in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning land acquired due to rivers and other causes;
therein, Bṛhaspati says:
When land has been brought from another village and given to someone else by a great river or by the king, how should the legal decision be made in that case?
Land granted by a king or left by a river belongs to him alone;
otherwise, men would not obtain any property resulting from royal or divine causes.
"The decline, rise, and life of men are under the power of fate (daiva) and the king;

therefore, in all matters, one should not subvert what has been done by them. "What is done by them" means what is done by fate and the king. Although the word *daiva* denotes fortune (*bhāgya*), it is nevertheless said that "what is done by a river is done by fate," because fortune alone is the fundamental cause. And so says that very same [author]:
Wherever a river is established as the boundary between two villages,
it effects the giving and taking [of land] among men according to their fortune or misfortune.

"In one place the river causes a collapse of the bank, while in another it establishes a firm foundation on the ground; the former owner shall not displace that [foundation] which the river has created. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "the river creates [it] on the bank. The meaning is: the former owner shall not displace that established position on the land created by the river for one who has acquired the land through the power of the river. This refers to a case where no crops have been sown on the bank. Regarding the case where crops have been sown on the bank, the same author says:
When a field with standing crops is overstepped and the ground becomes divided by the flow of a river's current, the former owner shall regain it.

Regarding that land containing crops: the meaning is that even after the cutting [of the harvest], the former owner retains possession for as long as the fruit of the sown crop has not yet been obtained. However, once the fruit has been obtained, the situation is exactly the same as in the case of the previous statement. Concerning land granted by a king, he himself states that in some cases the former owner may be dispossessed, while in other cases he shall not be dispossessed:
"That which was made by a king out of anger or greed, or through fraud and injustice, or granted by him out of favoritism to another—that does not attain validity."
"Even if land has been enjoyed by someone without documentary evidence,

if it was taken away from him and given to one superior in merit, one must not displace that person from it. The phrase "enjoying land without documentary evidence" means enjoying land for which there is no proof of ownership, such as a written deed or the like.
Thus ends the section on lands acquired by force of rivers and the like in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the rules concerning houses and other structures;
regarding these, Bṛhaspati says:
From the time of its construction, whatever— such as a house, a courtyard, or a shop— was used by whomsoever, to what extent, and in what manner, that shall not be altered for him.

The meaning is that from the time of entering the village onwards, no neighbor or other person shall displace a house or similar structure belonging to an owner, exactly as it was used—complete with its specific pasture lands and so forth, and situated in its particular direction with its doors and such. By stating "from the time of settlement," he indicates that if a property has been used since a different time and there is a dispute, it may be displaced. Likewise, he states that even a window or similar feature established at the time of settlement must not be moved by anyone, even if it causes inconvenience to a neighbor.
One should not disturb the windows, the drainage channels, as well as the turrets and the altars, nor the chariot-paths established in the four courtyards.

A *vātāyana* is a window. A *praṇālī* is a water-outlet made of wood or other materials. A *niryūha* is a turret on a house. A *vedikā* is a square, wooden-framed resting place. A *catuḥśāla* is a collection of four halls; this is stated as an illustration for a house made of grass. Therefore, there are channels for the falling and flowing of rainwater. Here too, by implication, the shifting of those situated in the middle is mentioned as before. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states that windows and the like should not be made because they cause displeasure to others.
"After the time of settling [the house], these should never be employed," it is said;
the remainder of the sense is "because they cause harm to others. And so says that same [author]:
"One should not construct a water-spout or a drain in the houses of others."

A "window" (gavākṣa) is a sight-thrower. "In the houses of others" means facing toward the houses of others; the intention is that by doing so, harm comes to others. With this very intention, Bṛhaspati also said:
"A place for excrement, a heap of firewood, a pit, or the pouring of leftover water should never be made too close to another's wall."
The place for excrement is the latrine. "Atyārāt" means without leaving a space of two *aratnis*. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"One should construct the enclosure for feces, urine, and water, as well as the placement of the fire and the pits, leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the neighbor's wall."
Bṛhaspati, however, stated that carts and the like, which are causes of congestion, should not be kept for long on a thoroughfare:
"That by which people and even cattle pass to and fro without obstruction is called a thoroughfare; it must not be blocked by anyone. [552]
In this same way, one should not cause an obstruction even at crossroads and similar locations. For this very reason, Nārada states:
"One should not obstruct a crossroad, a place for deities, or a royal highway.
Here, "place for deities" refers to temples and the like. Kātyāyana describes the nature of crossroads and royal highways:
That which all people always traverse is a crossroads;
that royal road which is unobstructed at all times is so called.

The meaning is that a *rājamārga* (royal road) is a path where walking is prohibited by royal authorities at all times. Regarding a field that has a road either adjacent to it or within it, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "On a road-field, there is the relinquishment of the path"; the word "should be done" (*kārya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Bṛhaspati states the punishment for one who creates an obstruction on such a road and so forth: "He who, out of desire, creates a mixture [of refuse] there, a pit, or even plants trees, or he who voids excrement, his fine shall be one *māṣaka*."

*Melting* (*saṃkaraḥ*) means *intermixture*, which is to say *obstruction*. The mention of "trees" is intended as an illustration for crops and so forth. Although it may appear here that a *māṣa* consisting of five *kṛṣṇalas* is also to be accepted, nevertheless, in order to correspond to the nature of the offense, one-twentieth of a *kārṣāpaṇa* should be taken, because even there the term *māṣa* is used conventionally. Manu states that there is an increased penalty for one who voids excrement on the royal highway: "But he who, when not in distress, should void impurity on the royal highway, shall pay two *kārṣāpaṇas* and must quickly clean away the impurity. [MDh 8.241]

It should be understood that Manu’s statement regarding the severity of punishment here is intended because of the gravity of the offense due to the excellence of the path [of the victim]. However, in times of distress (*āpad*), there is no monetary fine, but rather a verbal reprimand; as he himself says:
"One who has fallen into distress, as well as the elderly, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a verbal reprimand, and that [offense] must be expiated—this is the settled rule."
Because the one who defiles a tank or similar place commits an extreme offense, Kātyāyana states that the punishment must also be extremely severe:
"He who destroys tanks, gardens, or sacred bathing places with impure matter shall,
after having the impurity cleared away, be fined the first *sāhasa*."
The same author states that this very same punishment applies even to one who defiles a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) by washing his filthy clothes there and so forth:
"He who should defile established sacred bathing places— those meritorious and purifying sites founded by great souls— shall incur the first amercement."
Regarding other offenses, Yājñavalkya states the punishments:
"In the case of breaking a boundary mark, as well as in the case of transgressing a boundary line,
and in the seizure of a field, the punishments are the lowest, the highest, and the middle."

The meaning is that for one who destroys boundary markers, the punishment is the first *sāhasa* fine; and for the seizure of a field, the punishment for the seizer is the middle *sāhasa* fine. As for what was stated by Viṣṇu: "Having punished the breaker of boundaries with the highest *sāhasa* fine, he shall have the boundary re-established," there the term "breaker of boundaries" (*sīmābhettāram*) should be understood to mean "a cultivator who has transgressed the boundary. "Re-establishing the boundary" (*punaḥ sīmāṃ kārayet*) means precisely the non-performance of cultivation and so forth on the boundary site again; thus, the meaning of "he shall have the boundary re-established" is that the king should strive to ensure that this occurs. The mention of the highest *sāhasa* fine refers to cases of partial transgression of the boundary. However, regarding the transgression of the entire boundary, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In cases of boundary transgressions, eight thousand [paṇas]. The word "fine" (*daṇḍa*) is to be supplied. Because of the greater severity of the punishment, it is logical that this statement refers to the transgression of the entire boundary. Regarding the transgression of a small portion of the boundary, Vṛddha-Manu says:
Furthermore, those who out of arrogance transgress the boundary established between the two villages shall be punished with a fine of two hundred [paṇas].

It is logical that this [penalty] pertains to minor transgressions because the punishment is light. As for the first *sāhasa* (fine) mentioned by Yājñavalkya in the case of destroying boundary markers, that refers to the destruction of boundary markers of houses, since the punishment is light. However, regarding the destruction of boundary markers of fields, Śaṅkha and Likhita state that the punishment must be more severe due to the greater gravity of the offense: "In the case of breaking the boundary of a field, however, [the fine is] eight hundred. The word "fine" (*daṇḍa*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the same way, a higher penalty should be inferred for the destruction of boundary markers of villages and so forth. It should also be inferred that after having punished according to the stated rule, one should have the boundary markers of the houses and other structures re-established. As for the middle *sāhasa* mentioned by Yājñavalkya in the case of seizing a field, that refers to seizure by force; for the middle *sāhasa*, consisting of five hundred and forty *kārṣāpaṇas*, is a heavy punishment. But when seizure is committed through intimidation or ignorance, Manu says:

One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field through intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if done through ignorance, the fine is two hundred. As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita—"In the case of seizing water for a field, eight hundred"—the word "fine" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This should be understood to apply to the forcible seizure of fields such as those for rice that are provided with water. In this manner, an increase in the fine should be inferred in consideration of the greater quantity of the fields and other property being seized. Kātyāyana states the matter necessary for avoiding the application of fines for the seizure of fruits and flowers from trees and so forth growing on boundaries:
But for trees grown within the boundary line between two fields,
one should declare that their fruits and flowers belong in common to the owners of both fields.

"Common" means shared. Regarding "among the owners of the fields," this refers to the owners of two fields that share trees and boundaries. If one owner of a field were to take the entire fruit, then he would incur the punishment for the misappropriation of the value of that produce. However, regarding those trees and such whose root regions are in one field while their branches extend over another field, the same author says: "But when branches grown in one field rest upon another, one should know him to be the owner in whose fields they are supported."
"Dependent" means relying upon; that is to say, born [therein].
Thus ends the section concerning houses and related matters in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the matters concerning embankments and the like;
regarding these, Nārada says:

A dam should be known to be of two kinds: that which is to be dug out and likewise that which is to be built up. For the directing of water, it is to be dug out; for the turning back [of water], it should be built up.

A *khanya* is a dam constructed by digging for the purpose of draining excess water from a field; a *bandhya* is that where the flow of water is bound by earth and other materials for the purpose of retaining water that has arrived—this is the meaning. To show that a *khanya* should not be made with excessive depth and a *bandhya* should not be made with excessive height, he (the same author) expresses the censure of both waterless and excessive water:
"Without water there is no crop, and when there is excessive water there is destruction. Whatever fault exists in excessive water, that very same fault occurs in the absence of water."

Therefore, the intention is that the excavation should be carried out in such a way that there is no depletion of all the water, and the embankment should be constructed in such a way that the water does not remain in excessive quantity. Regarding even the obstruction caused by the construction of a dam, he [the author] says the same: "But a dam in the middle of another's field is not forbidden, provided it has great benefit and little harm; for when there is a loss, an increase is desired."

The meaning of this is as follows: A dike being constructed by another on one's own field possesses great virtues, such as providing the necessary water-retention even for that very field; it should not be prohibited by the owner of the field because its defects are minor, consisting merely in the destruction of a small portion of the field, since the abundance of the harvest is desired even at the cost of a slight loss of land. By the use of the word "if" (*cet*), he indicates that in some cases where the opposite is true, it may indeed be prohibited. Yājñavalkya also says: "A dike that causes only slight damage and brings about prosperity should not be prohibited; likewise, a well that takes up a small amount of land but provides abundant water [should not be obstructed]."

The phrase "is not to be prohibited" (na niṣedhyaḥ) is understood as being connected with the word "well" (kūpa) as well. "Of small field" means situated on a small field. Thus, the meaning is this: a well that yields abundant water, even if it takes up a small amount of another's land, is not to be prohibited by the owner of that land; however, the opposite case here too is certainly subject to prohibition. Furthermore, as he stated: "He who constructs a water-channel on a field without informing the owner shall have the enjoyment of the produce belong to the owner; in the absence of the owner, to the king."

Thus, the purport here is that, provided it is possible, one should construct a dam or similar structure on another's field only after obtaining permission from the owner of that field, or in his absence, from the king; it does not concern the determination of who shall enjoy the fruits produced in another's field due to such a dam when no notification has been made, for that would result in the vacuity of the statement. Indeed, merely by the construction of a dam or the like, another person does not acquire the status of an enjoyer of the fruits produced in another's field, such that a statement intended to prevent that would be meaningful. Some, however, say that this statement is for the purpose of determining the enjoyer of the visible and invisible fruits arising from the construction of the dam and so forth. Whatever is logical in this regard should be accepted. The same should be understood regarding the restoration of what is dilapidated without having first given notice. And so says Nārada:
But whoever should construct a bridge without first asking the owner regarding what has already been commenced or built, he shall not partake in the fruit thereof.
But when the master has died, or even when a descendant of his is a human being,
one should then consult the king and proceed with the construction of the embankment.

"Otherwise, one would incur the affliction [of the sin] due to the act of deliberate consideration (*avamarśana*), just as the arrows of a hunter perish for him who shoots again at what has already been pierced. Here, *avamarśana* means "deliberate consideration" or "demonstration. It refers to that hunter. Kātyāyana also says: [558]
But he who performs a restoration of a house, garden, or tank without the consent of the owner does not obtain ownership of that restoration.

"If the expenditure has occurred and the owner has arrived, [the artisan] shall not recover it unless he has reported it to the king; however, if he has reported it and was subsequently commissioned [by the owner], he recovers that expenditure pertaining to him.
Thus, having reported it to the king, the artisan who performs the consecration recovers the expenditure incurred for the consecration when he is commissioned by the owner.
Thus ends the section concerning embankments and the like in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follow the sections concerning the cultivator of a field.

Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states: "Having taken [the field], he should plow it at the proper time. This means that in the case of a field or similar property, the farmer, having taken the field from the owner of the field with the agreement, "I shall do this," should plow it with plows and so forth, or by means of oxen and the like, during the summer season and other appropriate times. The mention of "plowing" (*vāhana*) is intended as an illustration for the entire range of activities ending with the collection of the resulting fruit. For this very reason, he says that a farmer who performs only the mere act of plowing—being at fault for performing only a portion of the required work—must be made to pay the value of the field's produce to the owner of the field by the king: "Not performing the sowing, the guarding, and the gathering, he must be made to pay the owner. "Sowing" (*vāpa*) is the scattering of seeds; "guarding" (*gopana*) is the protection of the crops and so forth; "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) is the collection of the fruit. The meaning of this statement has been explained by Yājñavalkya.
If one neither cultivates nor causes to be cultivated a field that has already been ploughed,
he shall be compelled to pay the value of the crop harvested and have the field cultivated by another.

*Phālāhatam* means that which is struck by the ploughshare, split open, or tilled—that is to say, [land] which does not possess the softness and other qualities suitable for sowing seeds. *Akṛṣṭaśadam* refers to the grass and other produce obtained from a field that remains untilled. Regarding another [type of offender], namely one who, having taken a field, performs the tilling only when half the time for preparing the field has elapsed, Bṛhaspati states that he should be made to pay a fine corresponding to the fault of the lapse of time: "But he [who tills] in the middle [of the period] shall pay a fine. The word "shall be made to pay" (*dāpya*) is understood to follow here. Furthermore, regarding one who, having taken a field, does nothing at all nor causes anything to be done until the end of the period for its preparation, he (Bṛhaspati) says the same concerning him as well.
If anyone, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated,
he shall be made by the king to pay the rent to the owner and a fine equal to that amount.

*Śada* is the crop yield; *tatsama* means equal to that which is to be taken by the owner. When it is asked how much is to be taken by the owner, he himself says: "In land long-fallowed, one-tenth; likewise in land being cultivated, one-eighth; but in land prepared by oneself, it shall be one-sixth, as determined according to the circumstances."

If a field that has long been neglected—meaning one that has not been cultivated for a long time—is taken over with the intention, "I shall cultivate this," but then left unattended, the person who took possession must be made to pay a tenth part of the yield as its value once the fruit is obtained, provided it had not been left unattended [previously]. However, if a field that has not long been neglected is taken over and left unattended while being cultivated, he must be made to pay an eighth part. But if a field that was already prepared is taken over and left unattended, he must be made to pay a sixth part; such is the meaning. Regarding a field that remains fallow due to the owner's incapacity or other reasons, which a cultivator takes and works without the owner’s prohibition, Nārada says: [560]
If some person should cultivate a field when the owners are incapable, deceased, or lost, he may enjoy the fruit thereof without being hindered.

"Incapable" means lacking the capacity for cultivation. "Gone to the world of the departed" (pretāḥ) means deceased. "Lost" means unknown for a long time as to where they have gone. "Landowners" (kṣetrikāḥ) means the owners of the field. This is what is meant: even if it is another's field, in the case of land that has become fallow, the cultivator enjoys the fruit [of his labor], but he is never subject to a fine for the produce. In this context, the same author further states regarding the owner of the field who has returned: "But when a field is being cultivated, if the landowner should return, he shall recover his own field after paying for all the improvements made to the fallow land."

The expenditure for clearing fallow land (*khilopacāra*) is for the purpose of breaking up the fallow; the determination of its amount depends on the degree of hardness of the field that has become fallow. Regarding that degree of variation, he [the author] himself says: "In one year, a field becomes half-fallow; in three years, it becomes fallow; but a field neglected for five years becomes equal to a forest."

A field neglected for one year becomes half-waste (*ardhakhila*), meaning it is somewhat difficult to cultivate; if neglected for three years, however, it becomes waste (*khila*) and would be difficult to cultivate. Furthermore, if neglected for five years, it would become like a wilderness (*aṭavīsama*), meaning it would be extremely difficult to cultivate—this is the sense. When the owner is unable to bear the expense for the purpose of breaking up the waste, Kātyāyana says:
"If, due to inability, he does not pay the expenses incurred for the sake of breaking up the waste, the cultivator shall receive the produce minus one-eighth of that [expense]."
"He shall enjoy it for eight years; thereafter, however, it belongs to the owner. [561] Thus it is said.

If the owner, being unable to repay the expenses incurred for the purpose of reclaiming fallow land (*khila*), does not pay those expenses to the cultivator, then the cultivator, having paid one-eighth of the field's yield to the owner for eight years, may take the remainder; after that period, he must hand over the field to the owner—this is the meaning. It should be understood that all that has been stated in the passage beginning with "when the field is being cultivated" and ending with "but after [eight years] to the owner," applies to the case of a deceased owner’s field even when his son or other heirs arrive; however, in the case of a field lost due to incapacity, it should be understood to apply upon the arrival of the original owners or their sons and other descendants.
Thus ends the exposition of the rules concerning the subject of the field-son (*kṣetraja*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now,
the rules for the section known as "Relations between Women and Men" (*strīpuṃsaṃbandha*) are stated.
In this regard, Manu says:
"I shall declare the eternal duties of a man and a woman who abide in the path of righteousness, both in their union and in their separation."

On the path of dharma, that is, on the way prescribed by the scriptures; in union, meaning in each other's presence; and in separation, meaning through distance of place or time—these being eternal, meaning constant, which is to say, necessarily to be performed. This is what is meant: I shall describe those duties which must necessarily be performed by a husband and wife who are not unrestrained, for the sake of achieving mutual harmony, both in each other’s presence and in their absence. When asked what those duties are, he himself says:
Women must be kept under dependence by their own men day and night; even when they are attached to sensual objects, they should indeed be established under one's own control.
"By their own men," meaning by husbands and other male relatives; "in regard to the object," meaning in regard to objects such as cold and so forth that cause destruction. Nārada also says:
"Even women born of noble families perish through independence;
therefore, Prajāpati ordained their lack of independence."

The implication is that others should also arrange matters such that their own wives lack independence. Protection must also be exercised to prevent improper attachments. Thus says Hārīta: "With the loss of the wife comes the loss of the family; with the loss of the family, the loss of the lineage; with the loss of the lineage, the loss of the gods and ancestors; with the loss of the gods and ancestors, the loss of sacrifice; with the loss of sacrifice, the loss of Dharma; with the loss of Dharma, the loss of the self; with the loss of the self, the loss of everything. Therefore, one should protect this wife, who is virtuous and well-guarded. Manu also says: "Women must be protected especially from even the slightest opportunities for misconduct."
For if they are not protected, they will bring grief to both families.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes,
husbands— even those who are weak— strive to protect their wives.

"By protecting his wife with diligence, he protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. The meaning is that women, if unprotected, would bring about grief—indeed, cause it—to both families, namely the husband's and the father's families. By this, it is shown that they must be protected even by the elders of both families; thus, the description of the distress [caused by their lack of protection] is presented. And their protection has been demonstrated by Bṛhaspati:
A woman must be guarded against even the slightest opportunities for transgression by her own kinsmen;
she should be protected day and night by her sisters and other female elders.

Thinking that women, like men, will protect themselves by their own nature, [the author] says the following in order to demonstrate that a man should not be indifferent toward the protection of women: "They do not wait for beauty; they have no regard for age.
Whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man."
Due to their proclivity for sexual promiscuity, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection,
these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world.
Manu did not attribute to women the desire for beds and seats, ornaments, lust, anger, harmful intent, malice, or bad conduct.
"Having thus understood their nature, which was produced by the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should apply the utmost effort toward their protection.
Thus has the disposition toward malice been explained by Dakṣa.
Like leeches, all women— even when constantly sustained with ornaments, clothing, and food— indeed draw a man down.
That poor leech takes only blood;
but the other [the woman] takes wealth, property, flesh, virility, strength, and happiness.
"In childhood she is full of apprehension, but in youth she becomes averse;
in old age, however, a woman regards her husband as mere straw. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that even when adorned with ornaments, she constantly draws a man down and makes him a perpetual object of contempt; this refers to the "other woman" (the wife). In the phrase beginning with "wealth," the verb "she takes" (*ādatta*) is to be supplied after each word. This is the intention of Dakṣa, who speaks thus with great emphasis regarding her treacherous nature: even when one observes many kinds of wickedness in a wife, what is surprising about it, given its basis in the very nature of her species? Thus, casting aside agitation, one should apply effort toward her protection. Furthermore, a man must strive for his wife's maintenance during her youth; and so says Manu: [Manu 9.25] "A man should exert himself to maintain his wife and children according to his ability, even by performing work not forbidden by the scriptures. [Manu 9.7] "But a wife who is ill-behaved, wasteful, or hostile should be confined in a single room and deprived of ornaments and finery. [Manu 9.8] "She who, being commanded, does not act contrary to her husband's will, who is devoted to the service of her elders, and who is pure and industrious, attains the world of Brahmā. [Manu 9.10] "One should never abandon a wife, even if she is devoid of virtue, lacking good character, or wasteful; for by abandoning her, one abandons the sacred fire, domestic rites, and progeny. [Manu 9.11] "A wife is half the body of a man, his companion in religious duties, and the vessel of his offspring; she is the root of dharma, artha, and kama. [Manu 9.26] "A man should always support his wife, however ill-behaved she may be, for even a wife who is wicked is fit to be maintained, just as a firebrand is fit to be used for kindling another fire. [Manu 9.27] "A man whose wife is well-maintained gains this world; and through her, he also attains the world of heaven. [Manu 9.28] "But a man whose wife is not supported, or who is abandoned by her, is excluded from both worlds—this is the settled rule. [Manu 9.29] "A wife who is patient, virtuous, and skilled in household management, who is not wasteful and is devoted to her husband, brings happiness in both worlds. [Manu 9.30] "One should not despise a wife on account of her lineage, her youth, or her lack of beauty; for a wife who is respected brings prosperity to the family. [Manu 9.31] "But a wife who is despised, whether by nature or through some fault, brings misfortune to the family and destroys all undertakings. [Manu 9.32] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, incurs sin and is reborn as a woman. [Manu 9.33] "A man who, out of anger, strikes a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born in the womb of an animal. [Manu 9.34] "A man who, out of anger, reviles a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a eunuch. [Manu 9.35] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a hermaphrodite. [Manu 9.36] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of low caste. [Manu 9.37] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of impure conduct. [Manu 9.38] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of evil reputation. [Manu 9.39] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of no means. [Manu 9.40] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of little intelligence. [Manu 9.41] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of weak memory. [Manu 9.42] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of dull senses. [Manu 9.43] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of defective limbs. [Manu 9.44] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of deformed appearance. [Manu 9.45] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of ill-fated fortune. [Manu 9.46] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of short life. [Manu 9.47] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant sorrow. [Manu 9.48] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of perpetual fear. [Manu 9.49] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant anxiety. [Manu 9.50] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant distress. [Manu 9.51] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant lamentation. [Manu 9.52] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant weeping. [Manu 9.53] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant trembling. [Manu 9.54] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant perspiration. [Manu 9.55] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant itching. [Manu 9.56] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant pain. [Manu 9.57] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant fever. [Manu 9.58] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant cough. [Manu 9.59] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant asthma. [Manu 9.60] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant consumption. [Manu 9.61] "A man who, out of anger, abandons a wife who is obedient, virtuous, and the mother of sons, shall be born as a person of constant epilepsy. [Manu 9.62] "A man who, out
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth;
the sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.

However, for a woman who is destitute of both husband and son, the protection of both kinds must be performed by someone belonging to the husband's side who is closely related. Thus says Nārada: "When the husband has died, the husband's kin are the masters of the childless woman;
they are the lords over her employment, her personal protection, and her maintenance."

Viniyoga is the application to a task. He (Yājñavalkya) says the same even regarding the absence of the husband's side: "When the husband's family is exhausted, devoid of men, and without support, and when his sapindas are no longer present, the father's side is the authority over the woman. [565]
The phrase "in matters such as the assignment [of property]" is to be understood as the ellipsis. He says the same regarding the absence of even the paternal side:
"But at the end of both sides [of the family], the king is recorded as the husband of a woman;
he shall provide for her maintenance and restrain her if she deviates from her husband."
The supporter is the one who provides maintenance.
Thus ends the section on the rules for the protection of women in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the method of protecting women; regarding this, Manu says:
No one is able to protect women by force;
however, they can be protected through the application of these means.

"By force," "by assault," and "by confinement"—this is the meaning. Although protection from physical infidelity may be possible through confinement, Manu, considering that protection from mental infidelity is impossible, stated:

"No one is able to guard a woman by force," and so forth. Nor should it be argued: "Let there be no protection against mental infidelity, since there is no possibility of offspring belonging to another caste, and thus no destruction of the purity of progeny. For he (Manu) himself says:
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind; therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard women with great effort. [566]

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is that whatever kind of man a woman mentally desires during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), she gives birth to a son of similar character. Thus, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In whichever [man] women fix their affection during their menses, they give birth to a son of his character. Therefore, the remainder [of the sense] is that one should guard women even against mental infidelity. And so, by the second half beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), Manu has shown this very injunction. Furthermore, the means for guarding them have also been shown by Manu.
He should employ her in the collection and expenditure of wealth, as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.

Regarding "acquisition" (*saṃgraha*), it refers to the management of wealth brought in by oneself; regarding "expenditure" (*vyaya*), it refers to the expenditure prescribed by oneself; regarding "purity" (*śauca*), it refers to the sweeping, smearing, and other acts that effect the cleaning of the house and so forth; regarding "duty" (*dharma*), it refers to worldly activities conducive to the *agnihotra* and other rites; and regarding "the supervision of household utensils" (*pārīṇahyasyekṣaṇe*), it refers to the oversight of domestic implements such as cooking pots and the like. What is meant is this: one should act in such a way that the wife remains free from any opportunity for thinking about another man due to being preoccupied with blameless and necessary tasks. Bṛhaspati has also stated these very same means.

Women should be employed in income and expenditure, the preparation of food, the protection of household utensils, cleanliness, and the performance of fire-rituals; this is declared to be the purification for women.

The meaning is that this purity of women, arising from the aforementioned means, is recorded as being virtuous (*sādhvī*). And so it is recorded by Manu: "Those who protect themselves by their own selves are well-protected" (MDh 9.12). By the phrase "by their own selves," the meaning is: with a mind not attached to the accumulation of wealth and the like. He states that women protected by trusted men are not truly protected: [Manu 9.14] "But those who, having been guarded by their own selves, are further guarded by trustworthy men—those women reach the highest world, even if they have no offspring. Thus, the sense is that the aforementioned method is the primary cause for the purification of women. Therefore, it is said: "Women are purified by their menstrual flow (*ṛtu*)," and so forth. This is the conclusion. This is the meaning. "Women confined at home by trustworthy men [are unprotected].

The grammatical construction is: "confined at home by trustworthy men. "Unprotected" means lacking proper protection. That they lack proper protection has already been stated previously. To show that the prevention of drinking and so forth is also a method of protecting women, he (the same author) says:
"Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, and wandering about..."

"Sleeping, dwelling in another's house—these are the six vices of women. The implication is that these must be prohibited in women by the husband and others who are attentive to them. "Drinking" refers to liquor and the like. "Separation from the husband" means remaining in another country after having abandoned the husband. "Wandering" means undertaking pilgrimages and such activities without the husband. "Sleeping" means sleeping anywhere at all. "Dwelling in another's house" means residing in the home of another person. To show that even the husband’s excellence is a method for protecting women, he (the same author) says:
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule,
such qualities she acquires, just as a river does from the ocean.

To demonstrate that the knowledge of the non-deviation and deviation [of conduct] regarding auspicious and inauspicious fruits is also a method for protecting women, he [Manu] states their respective results:
"She who does not transgress her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the worlds of her husband and is called 'virtuous' by the righteous. (MDh 5.165)
"But through infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs censure in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. Thus it is said. To show also the manner in which protection takes the form of maintenance, that same author says:
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support that virtuous woman.

"Given by the gods" (*devadattā*) means she has come under the power of the gods; a husband obtains such a wife at a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage), but he does not obtain her through his own desire or by his own action. Since there is no personal agency in that case, the meaning is that he should always support—that is, nourish—that virtuous and beautiful woman who has come under the power of the gods. Nor should it be argued that, because this applies to a wife obtained through human agency, her maintenance is not mandatory. By the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpa-nyāya*), the injunction "he should always support her" is understood to apply there as well. For instance, when it is stated that even a girl chosen by a suitor must necessarily be maintained, it is understood that one who is chosen by a suitor must be maintained all the more so. Furthermore, one should not argue that because the term "virtuous" (*sādhvīm*) implies "faithful to her husband," the sense "one should not maintain an unchaste woman" is implied, and thus the maintenance of an unchaste woman is not mandatory. This is because even she must necessarily be maintained. In that regard, an unchaste woman whose infidelity is not excessive should be maintained like a virtuous wife; however, she is simply excluded from social intercourse due to the performance of the ultimate penance (*aprāyaścitta*). Even an excessively unchaste woman must necessarily be maintained until her purification is achieved, provided she possesses the specific qualification for performing penance known as "remorse" (*paścāttāpa*), though she should be supported with poor food and the like. Thus says Nārada: [Insert Nārada's verse here] (Note: The final sentence refers to a verse from Nārada’s *Dharmaśāstra*, which is not provided in the source text.)
In the event of infidelity, the woman shall undergo shaving of the head, sleeping on the ground,
eating wretched food, wearing poor clothing, and performing labor in the refuse heap every day.

When extreme infidelity has occurred on the part of a woman, he should enforce shaving of the head and sleeping on the ground; he should provide her with coarse food and poor clothing for her maintenance, and the meaning is that he should also make her perform labor such as cleaning filth. Thus, the alternative interpretation given for the word *sādhvīm* (virtuous) in the commentary on Manu—"or rather, he should maintain a *sādhvī*, a devoted wife, but not an unfaithful one"—is to be rejected. Hārīta also states that the maintenance of even an extremely unfaithful wife is mandatory:
"There is no abandonment of a wife, even if she is unfaithful."
One should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and purify the ragged garment as well as the bed upon which one lies.
*Piṇḍa* means mere food sufficient only to ward off hunger; that is, coarse food. *Adhaḥśayyā* refers to one whose bed is on the ground—that woman who sleeps on the ground. Yājñavalkya also says:
"One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, wearing soiled clothes, subsisting on mere food, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground."

"Deprived of authority" means one whose right to perform rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti has ceased; "overpowered" means one who is no longer authorized [to act]. The ellipsis is "he should cause her to dwell in a part of his own house";
[the rule is: "The husband shall confine a woman who has grievously offended in a single room."

This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu. "Vipraduṣṭām" means one who is extremely corrupted through physical infidelity. Likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should cause an excessively unfaithful woman—who acts according to her own will (*kāmacāriṇī*), is impure, wears dirty clothes, subsists on mere alms, has been deprived of her rights, sleeps on the ground, and is confined—to dwell [under these conditions]. "Kāmacāriṇīm" means one who behaves out of desire for another man. She is explained in this way precisely because one who acts according to her own will must be abandoned. Yama declares her abandonability as follows: [570]

"And that woman who goes according to her own will—her abandonment is ordained. Thus, she who goes with one for whom there is an absence of penance that would restore him to social intercourse—that woman is "one who acts according to her own will. However, a woman who is excessively unfaithful is not to be abandoned, because it is possible for her to become fit for social intercourse through penance. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"Soma gave women purity, and Gandharva gave them a pleasant voice..."
Fire possesses the quality of purifying everything, and women are indeed pure; therefore [this is so].

Thus, "being fit for all sacrifices" means being worthy of all sacrificial rites. This is merely a statement of praise; therefore, it does not contradict what was stated regarding the extreme corruption and loss of eligibility of an unfaithful wife. Furthermore, as Manu has said:
"For the sake of procreation, women are highly blessed, worthy of honor, and the lights of the home;
in the house, there is no difference whatsoever between women and the goddesses of fortune."

Thus, "worthy of worship" means they have become objects of veneration. This refers specifically to women who have not been corrupted. Therefore, the statement that an unfaithful wife is an object of contempt is not contradictory [to this]. Furthermore, he says that even for the sake of auspiciousness, women who have not been corrupted should be honored by their fathers and others: "These [wives] should be honored and adorned by fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, by those desiring abundant prosperity. (MDh 3.56)
The *devaras* are the brothers-in-law of the husband. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Women are to be honored by their husband, brother, father, kinsmen, mother-in-law, father-in-law, brothers-in-law, and relatives, with ornaments, clothing, and food. [571]
In this context, worship by persons other than the husband should be understood as pertaining to the occasion of a festival. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"The wife is to be honored by her husband with garments, ornaments, and food;
but on a festival day, she is also to be honored by kinsmen such as her father, brothers, and fathers-in-law."
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, there all ritual acts become fruitless."

"Where women grieve, that family quickly perishes; but where they do not grieve, there it prospers forever. (The word "grieve" implies [they grieve] due to the absence of maintenance and honor; "where" means in which family). However, one who is about to depart on a journey must make financial provisions for her maintenance until his return. Otherwise, even if she remains on the path of virtue, she may lose her fortitude due to a lack of support and, for the sake of subsistence, fall into misconduct. Thus, he [the author] says:
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's livelihood;
for a woman, even one of firm character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of means.

Regarding a wife who persists in her hatred, [the same author] says that one may take back the clothes, ornaments, and so forth given for her worship before she ceased her hatred, and after a year has passed, one should not have intercourse with her even during her fertile season:
"A husband should wait for a year for a wife who hates him;
but after a year, having taken these [gifts] from her, he need not live with her."

"He should wait" means he should expect the continuation of her hostility. The phrase "after one year has passed" is to be understood as the condition for the continuation of that hostility. "Inheritance" refers to what was given for the purpose of honoring her; however, what was assigned for her maintenance is not to be taken back, because she must be supported even if she is full of hostility. He states an exception to the aforementioned rule in the same text:
"There is no abandonment of one who is insane, an outcast, impotent, seedless, or diseased, even if she is hostile, nor is there a forfeiture of her inheritance."

"Klība" means lacking energy; "abīja" means lacking virility. This is what is meant: even if there is a persistence of hatred caused by visible or invisible defects, because there is an absence of improper conduct, there is no abandonment of approaching her during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) and so forth. Yājñavalkya, however, states that for a superseded wife (*adhivinā*), maintenance alone is obligatory, not honor and the like: "A superseded wife must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue.
The remainder [of the meaning] is that she must be maintained exactly as before.
Thus ends the section on the methods of protecting women in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some statements concerning supersession (*adhivedana*) are recorded;
therein, Manu says:
A wife who drinks liquor, behaves unseemly, is hostile,
is afflicted by disease, is violent, or is constantly wasteful of wealth may be superseded [by another wife].

The term *madyapā* (liquor-drinker) here refers to one who lacks conjugal fidelity (*pātivratya*) to the extent that she is merely fit for supersession (*adhivedana*), and not a *surāpī* (wine-drinker) who is fit for abandonment due to the commission of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). *Asabhyavṛttā* means one devoted to misconduct or of evil conduct. *Pratikūlā* means one who constantly acts contrary to what is desired. *Vyādhitā* means one afflicted by a chronic disease. *Hiṃsrā* means excessively cruel. *Arthaghnī* means one who habitually squanders wealth through her own independence. The phrase "she should be superseded" (*adhivettavyā*) is to be supplied with each of these five. *Adhivedana* is the marrying of another wife over and above the previously established one. The word *ca* in the phrase *arthaghnī ca* serves to include other unstated cases. When asked what those included by the word *ca* are, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One may supersede a wife who is deceitful (*dhūrtā*), noseless (*vaināsikī*), a mother of daughters, barren, abusive, ill-natured, hostile to men, or uncooperative. *Dhūrtā* means a deceiver. *Vaināsikī* means one whose nose is missing. *Strījananī* means one who gives birth only to female offspring. What is meant is this: one may marry another wife beyond her when success in religious duties or in obtaining a son is no longer possible with her. However, regarding the failure or incompleteness of the fulfillment of sexual desire, Devala says that one should marry another wife after satisfying her with wealth.
He who, having left one wife for the sake of desire, wishes to obtain another,
being capable of satisfying the first with wealth, may marry the other.
In some cases, having obtained permission from his previous wife, he may marry another; thus Manu says:
"But she who is diseased, yet is well-disposed and endowed with good character—she may be superseded after being informed [of the new marriage], but she must never be treated with contempt."

A woman who is ill is one suffering from a chronic disease; one who is "beneficial" is one who desires her husband's prosperity. Regarding when supersession (*adhivedana*) should take place—whether by a delay of time or even without such delay—he himself states: "A barren woman should be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth; one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately. (NS 3.28–29)

The phrase "when the eighth year has passed" is understood as the ellipsis [for the first case]. This is because of the traditional teaching of Hārīta: "A childless wife [should be superseded] in the ninth year. In the same way, the ellipsis should be understood for the eleventh year as well:
"The husband should wait eight years for a woman who gives birth too late;
ten years for one who is barren or blameworthy; and twelve years for one who bears daughters."

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Devala: "Atiprasavā" means one whose childbirth has been delayed; that is to say, one who suffers miscarriages with every conception. "Vandyā" (venerable) refers to one who is childless. "Nindyā" (blameworthy) refers to one who drinks liquor, is of vulgar conduct, and so forth. The phrase "ten [cows] for the barren woman" (*daśa vandhyām*) refers specifically to a beloved barren woman. On this point, Manu says:
"But a wife who has been superseded (*adhivinnā*), if she should go out from the house in anger, must be immediately confined or abandoned in the presence of the family."

She whose marriage took place subsequently is called *adhivinnā*. "In the presence of the family" means in the presence of the family of the father and others of the *adhivinnā*. Even though she has been abandoned in the presence of that family, her maintenance must be provided by the husband himself by virtue of his proximity, because it has been stated:
"The father protects [the daughter] in childhood; the husband protects her in youth."

"And she who has been taken in marriage must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue"—because this has been stated. Furthermore, regarding a woman who was married by stealth (*adhyūḍhā*) and, out of anger caused by her husband’s failure to provide proper treatment, has departed from his house and sought refuge with no one other than her own kin: she should be brought back into her husband's home by her kinsmen acting as her protectors. However, if she is without kinsmen, she should herself reflect and return to her husband's house; thus says Nārada: "She who was married by stealth due to a fault of ignorance, and having departed, has not sought refuge elsewhere..."
She who has no kinsmen should be appointed by her relatives; she who has no kinsmen should take refuge with him herself.

Yājñavalkya, however, states that a husband must give to women who have been superseded (adhivinnā) an amount caused by the act of supersession: "He should give an equal amount as a compensation for supersession (ādhivedanika) to the woman who has been superseded;
if no woman's property (strīdhana) has been given to her, half of that [compensation] is prescribed."

To a woman who has been superseded (*adhivinnā*)—that is, one who is destitute of *strīdhana* (woman’s property)—the husband must give wealth equivalent to what was spent for the purpose of her supersession, or as much as was given to her at the time she was subsequently married; this is the wealth caused by the occasion of supersession. However, half of that amount is declared to be the portion to be given to a woman who possesses *strīdhana*. This is the meaning.
Thus ends the section concerning supersession in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follow the matters concerning women who are not to be abandoned.
On this point, Devala says:
For a man who, out of delusion, abandons his own wife, who fails to release others from injustice,
and who forsakes the lineage of dharma, no atonement is prescribed.

The meaning is this: for one who, out of delusion or other such causes, abandons his own wife even without the reasons for abandonment prescribed in the scriptures—that unjust liberator of his own wife—there is no atonement for the abandoner, whether it concerns the Vedic and Smārta duties enjoined together with her, or the progeny being produced in her. Even in this world, he must be punished by the king like a thief. Accordingly, Viṣṇu states, following the rule "he should be punished like a thief": "and likewise one who abandons a faultless wife. This means that even one who abandons a wife free from the defects that constitute grounds for abandonment is to be punished like a thief. Furthermore, if he abandons a virtuous wife, he must be subdued with a heavy punishment and reinstated in that very same wife. Thus says Nārada:
If a man abandons a wife who is compliant, not foul-mouthed, capable, virtuous,
and a mother of children, he shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine.
But when it is impossible to establish her in that state even by means of severe punishment, then Yājñavalkya says:

"One who abandons a wife who obeys his commands, is skillful, bears him heroic sons, and speaks kindly, shall be made to pay a third part of his estate; if he is without property, he must provide maintenance for the woman."

If a man abandons a virtuous wife through stubborn persistence, the king shall cause him to give one-third of her property to the wife he is abandoning; if he possesses little wealth, the meaning is that he shall be made to give enough wealth for her mere maintenance.
Thus ends the section on women who must not be abandoned in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follow the sections concerning women who should be abandoned.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
Dharma belongs to a man and woman who abandon each other or act treacherously toward one another; however, for a married woman, there is no legal action except through judicial investigation. [577]

The meaning is that there would be no fault and no violation of dharma if a man and a woman of low caste, who have not undergone the sacrament of marriage, should mutually repudiate one another due to mutual incompatibility. However, for a woman who has been "married" (*ūḍhā*), meaning consecrated by the marriage rite, there is no repudiation except on the ground of unchastity (*vyabhicāra*). By this, it is stated by implication that if unchastity exists, there is indeed repudiation even of a married woman; and that refers specifically to the case of a woman who is wanton, for it is ordained that she who is a woman of independent will shall be repudiated.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama, abandonment (tyāga) should be performed here as a substitute for killing. And so says that same [author]: "Vivasvat declared that for a woman who acts of her own will with another man, there is abandonment; neither killing nor disfigurement, for the killing of women is their dismissal."

The meaning is that even when committing a great offense against women, one should perform their dismissal rather than their execution. "Deformation" (*vaikṛtya*) refers to the mutilation of limbs such as the ears and nose; the meaning is that even this should never be done by the husband, because he himself has stated:
"One should neither commit the killing of a woman nor the mutilation of her limbs. In this very same way, a woman who has gone to a pupil must also be abandoned. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
However, four [wives] must be abandoned: one who has gone to a disciple, one who has gone to a teacher, one who especially kills her husband, and one who has approached a degraded man.

The "pupil" (śiṣya) is the pupil of one's husband; the "teacher" (guru) is the father; the "outcast" (juṅgita) is one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*) or one born of an inverse (*pratiloma*) union. However, a woman who kills her husband must be abandoned by her kinsmen. For one abandoned by her kinsmen, even the giving of coarse food and such should not be performed, because it is stated that this applies "especially. The statement that there are "four" is not intended to indicate the absence of women to be abandoned beyond those four; for if that were the case, there would be a contradiction with what precedes and follows, since the term "one approached by an outcast" (*juṅgitopagata*) already includes both "one approached by a fallen man" (*patitopagata*) and "one approached by one born of an inverse union. How then is the number "four" stated? It is explained as follows: having treated "one approached by a fallen man" and "one approached by one born of an inverse union" as identical under the meaning of the term "one approached by an outcast," they are consolidated into the number "four. Precisely because the mention of "four" does not indicate the absence of other women to be abandoned, Yājñavalkya mentions other women who must be abandoned.

"...abandonment is ordained in the case of [a pregnancy] in the womb, as well as in the killing of the fetus or the husband, and likewise in the case of a great sin. It should be understood that abandonment is ordained specifically in that situation where, upon the occurrence of a pregnancy by a Śūdra in the wives of twice-born men, they lack the status of being fit for social intercourse due to the need for penance. And so it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"The women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not. Thus it is said.

Hārīta also says: "One should avoid a woman who causes abortion, one who has sexual relations with a man of lower caste, a disciple, or a teacher, one addicted to drinking, and one who sells wealth or grain. In this context as well, it should be understood that the rule of exclusion applies only to those cases where, according to the scriptures, there is no purification through penance for having intercourse with a man of lower caste, for addiction to drinking, or for the sale of wealth and grain. Exclusion (*visarjana*) means the abandonment of social interaction. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of sexual intercourse [with such women], she is excluded from visiting sacred sites and from religious duties. [579]

“Vyavāya” means sexual enjoyment. Here, by the term “visiting sacred sites” (*tīrthagamana*), the Smārta rites are indicated; by the word “dharma,” the Śrauta rites; and by the word “and” (*ca*), worldly acts such as touching and so forth. Thus, the meaning is this: a woman who is excluded from sexual enjoyment and from contact, conversation, and the like, is sent away. By this turn of phrase, it is stated that “sending away” (*visarjana*) consists of the absolute abandonment of sexual enjoyment and the rest. Even for a woman who has thus desisted from sexual enjoyment and the like, poor food and the like must be provided. As Manu says: “[She should live] near the house, or in another house.”
In this very same manner, one should act toward women who have fallen [from virtue];
however, clothing and food should be given to them, and they should dwell near the house.

Devala, however, states that among those women who must be abandoned due to disease and so forth, only sexual intercourse is to be relinquished, not their joint rights to religious duties and the like: "One may abandon at sacred fords a wife who is diseased, who has borne a daughter, who is barren, who is insane, or whose menses have ceased— provided she is not otherwise at fault— but never from her participation in religious rites."

The meaning is "having crossed over" from sexual enjoyment. And so Nārada says: "One should not, out of desire, take pleasure in a barren woman, one who gives birth only to daughters, one who is censurable, or one who is always hostile; by doing this, one incurs no fault."

"Blameworthy" means by reason of giving birth to children who are prone to die; this is the implied sense. "Always hostile" means constantly acting contrary to one's desires; the meaning is: by engaging in sexual intercourse with her against one's will. By stating "he incurs no fault," Bodhāyana shows here that the prohibitive injunction is not absolute: "In the ninth year, one may abandon a wife who bears no offspring; in the twelfth, one who bears only daughters; in the fifteenth, one whose children have died; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately."

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "he should abandon her because of her [inappropriate] enjoyment. However, one should abandon even a woman who speaks unpleasantly upon account of living together. And so says Nārada: "A wife who is constantly inclined toward what is harmful, likewise one who speaks unpleasantly, and she who eats before her husband—such a woman he should expel from the house."
Other women who must be expelled from the home have also been shown by him:
one who has squandered her husband’s wealth or his entire property, one who causes an abortion, and likewise a woman who desires the death of her husband— one should expel such a woman from the home.

She whose entire property has been lost along with her woman’s wealth (strīdhana) is described as such. A woman who causes an abortion is one who has brought about a miscarriage through the use of medicinal herbs and other means. "Desiring the death of her husband" implies by means of administering poison and so forth; this is the understood sense. Baudhāyana also has shown those women who are to be banished: "A wife who, through opposition to her husband, causes her menses to flow [unnaturally], she, having been proclaimed as a killer of the embryo (bhrūṇaghnī) in the midst of the village, shall be led out from the house."
"Wise men quickly abandon a woman who is disobedient, unchaste, harmful, and a speaker of unpleasant words. Here, "bandhakī" means an unchaste woman.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, the matters concerning women who must be abandoned [581] have been concluded.
In this way, the duties of the man have been stated regarding both union and separation. Now, the duties of both husband and wife are stated specifically regarding union. On this point, Manu says:
In that family where the husband is content with his wife and likewise the wife with her husband,
prosperity is indeed certain and constant.

In the same way, the phrase "the wife is contented with her husband" (*bhartṛvad eva bhāryā bhartrā saṃtuṣṭā*) must be supplied by modifying the text, because the masculine gender as it stands cannot be construed here. The implicit meaning is that in whatever family this mutual contentment exists constantly, prosperity—characterized by the birth of good sons, characterized by affection among the wife’s circle of kinsmen, and characterized by mutual fidelity and so forth—necessarily occurs. Thus, the author himself explains the intended meaning of the word "prosperity" (*kalyāṇa*) both by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
For if a woman is not pleasing, she will not delight the man;
and from a lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed.
When a woman is pleasing, the entire family is pleased;
when she is not pleasing, the entire family is not pleased at all.
"Let there be mutual fidelity until the end of life.

Here, "procreation for a man" means the begetting of a son; "that family" refers to the wife's family. He [the same author] states another duty of husband and wife: "Likewise, having performed the prescribed rites, the woman and the man should always strive [to maintain this]."
So that they might not transgress against one another when separated;
"they might not transgress" means in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma—this is the remainder of the sense. As Dakṣa also said:
"For even in heaven, this mutual affection is indeed difficult to find."
Whether one is attached or detached from it—what indeed could be more painful than that?

This mutual affection between husband and wife is difficult to find even in heaven. If, however, the disposition of either one of them should become attached or detached, what indeed could be more painful than that? There is nothing; the meaning is that this alone is the supreme misery. Therefore, the implication is that the man and woman should strive so that mutual affection may prevail. Yājñavalkya also says: "Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish."

The remainder [of the sense] is that the woman and man should strive so that they may be mutually compatible. The "threefold aggregate" (*trivarga*) consists of dharma, artha, and kāma. And thus Dakṣa says: "There is nothing superior to the householder's stage of life if the wife is submissive;
through her, one enjoys the fruit of the threefold aggregate, which is dharma, artha, and kāma."

The meaning is that by means of such a wife who is submissive (*vaśavartinī*), the householder enjoys the fruit known as the three aims of life—dharma, artha, and kāma. The term "obedient" (*vaśānugeti*) is intended to indicate other virtues as well. And so it has been said by that same author: "Dwelling at home is for the sake of happiness, and that happiness is rooted in the wife;
she is a true wife who is disciplined, knows her husband's mind, and is submissive."
"Compliant, not foul-mouthed, skillful, virtuous, and bearing offspring"—thus [is she described].

A wife (*patnī*) is a spouse endowed with the qualification for performing sacrifices; one who lacks these qualities is merely a woman (*strī*), not a wife. That such a woman is also a wife when possessed of the previously mentioned qualities of modesty and so forth, he himself has stated:
"Endowed with these very qualities, she is indeed a wife and a woman, without a doubt. (583)

In the phrase "by these alone," the particle *eva* serves here to exclude non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), and not to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), because connection with other virtues is also desired. Regarding this, he himself said: "She who is always pure-minded, discerning in her conduct and status, and who acts for the pleasure of her husband—she is a wife; any other is old age."

The meaning is that the other [wife] is devoid of virtues and causes affliction. The use of terms such as *patnī* (wife) and so forth applies only to one who possesses qualities such as discipline; the entire duty to be performed by a wife and the like occurs only in her and not in another—this is for the sake of praise. Just as in the Vedic text, “Cattle are cows and horses,” the use of the word *paśu* (cattle) applies only to cows and horses, and the entire function to be performed by cattle occurs only in them and not in goats and the like—this is for the sake of praise; likewise here as well, everything is faultless. Furthermore, he himself says that a well-trained wife, having met with brothers and others who possess external and internal purity, [should perform her duties].
A wife is traditionally considered equal to one's teacher, pure brother, friend, and servant;
he for whom these are disciplined possesses honor in all the worlds.

*Mitradāsa* means *anukūladāsa* (a submissive servant). These are the aforementioned secondary qualities (*upasarjana*). Vyāsa, however, states that a woman endowed with the duties of women and the previously mentioned virtues belongs only to someone of meritorious deeds: "A woman who rises early, is skillful, sleeps on a lower bed, is not foul-mouthed, and is submissive belongs indeed to one of meritorious deeds."

Dakṣa states that a woman possessing the characteristics previously described obtains a happiness comparable to heaven: "For one who has a compliant wife, there is heaven; of this there is no doubt. He further describes the specific suffering of one who possesses two contrary wives: [584] For one who has two contrary wives, there is constant strife, like that between two vipers. One of them will always be angry, while the other will be ever-cheerful. One will be emaciated from fasting, while the other will be fat from eating. One will sleep on the ground, while the other will sleep on a bed. One will be clad in rags, while the other will wear fine garments. One will eat food fit for dogs, while the other will eat the finest delicacies. One will be like a servant, while the other will be like a queen.
