"For one with two wives, there is undoubtedly a miserable existence, strife, discord, mutual injury through vulnerabilities, and hostility from a refractory spouse. Thus it is said.

*Duḥkhāsikā* means living in misery. *Kali* means quarrel. *Bheda* means discord. *Chidrapīḍā* means suffering caused by the pursuit of one's vulnerabilities. "Mutually" (*parasparam*) means between the two wives; this is the meaning. How, then, is there a description of specific sufferings such as quarrels arising from an unfavorable wife or from having two wives? It is said: with the intention that a quarrel and so forth arising between the two wives reaches the husband as well, it was stated, "of one who has an unfavorable wife or two wives."
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [are concluded] the duties of husband and wife; now follow the duties of women.
Regarding this, Manu says:
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman,
a woman must not perform any action independently, even within her own home.
In childhood she should remain under the control of her father, in youth under the control of her husband;
when her husband has died, she should not enjoy independence, even under the protection of her son.

[585] "A woman should not desire separation from her father, brother, or even her sons; for by the ruin of these, she brings reproach upon both families. Here, "both families" refers to the family of her father and the family of her husband. And that she herself becomes reproachable is understood through the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*): she who brings reproach even upon the family does so all the more against herself. And it has been said by Bṛhaspati:
A woman should not live in another's house separated from her husband, father, or sons;
especially by associating with the wicked, she certainly incurs reproach.
Yājñavalkya has also said:

"She should not be deprived [of her property] by her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles; she should not exist without her husband, otherwise she would become an object of reproach."
Vyāsa, however, spoke for the purpose of prohibiting conduct such as that of a courtesan:
"Constantly sitting at the doorway, likewise peering out of the window,
idle chatter, and laughter— these are the vices of women of good family."
The word "constantly" (*nityam*) is to be construed with "observing" (*avekṣaṇa*) and so forth. Bṛhaspati, however, spoke for the purpose of prohibiting conduct such as that of Svairiṇī:
"Drinking, wandering about, sleeping during the day, idleness, and corrupting women."

Inaction (*akriyā*) means non-performance; that is to say, remaining in a state of inactivity. Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated the following for the purpose of prohibiting improper conduct, similar to the rules for courtesans: "A woman should not go outside without being told; she should not wear perfumes, garlands, ornaments, or discolored garments except on festive occasions; she should not converse with a stranger, except with merchants, renunciants (*pravrajita*), or the elderly; she should not expose her navel, but should wear her garment down to the ankles; she should not expose her breasts; she should not laugh uncovered, nor in the presence of a large crowd. The term "discolored" (*vikṛta*) is connected both with what precedes and what follows. A "renunciant" (*pravrajita*) is one belonging to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśramī*). "Uncovered" (*anapāvṛta*) means unhidden; this is an adverbial modifier. The prohibition is repeated specifically to forbid laughing even when covered in the vicinity of a large crowd. They also demonstrate the prohibition against staying in the same place as women such as courtesans: "One should not stand together with courtesans, deceitful women, those of deceptive character, those of fraudulent nature, or those who are ruined [by adultery]. For through association, one's character becomes corrupted. "Fraudulent nature" (*kuhakaśīlā*) means having a dishonest disposition. "Ruined" (*viplutā*) means corrupted by paramours and the like. It is understood from the statement of the reason that this prohibition against standing together applies to cases where it is done repeatedly; for the character of a virtuous wife is not corrupted by standing in one place only once. In this way, one should avoid contact with another's bed and so forth, which causes the destruction of bodily purity. Thus says Hārīta: "One should not even mentally resolve upon the beds, seats, clothes, or ornaments of others until they have been purified again. Likewise, one should avoid using a single vessel, liquor, meat, and so forth, as well as food-leavings and flower-offerings (*nirmālya*), except in the case of one's teacher, husband, or son. "Until they have been purified again" (*ā punaḥ-saṃskārāt*) means until the purification process of washing has been performed. The mention of "single vessel" is intended to include eating with another person. The mention of "liquor and meat" is intended to include all things unfit to be drunk or eaten. For this very reason, he states that what has been touched by a woman whose body is excessively defiled by drinking *surā* liquor becomes impure.
Whether at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, if even a woman who drinks liquor should touch the sacrificial site,
or one who is menstruating, or an unchaste woman, she goes there in this world to the Rākṣasas.

For this very reason, the phrase "liquor, meat, and so forth" was employed, with the inclusion of "and so forth. Regarding the terms *ucchiṣṭa* (remnants) and *nirmālya* (offering remains), they form the compound *ucchiṣṭanirmālye*. By stating, "the father is the guru, except in the case of the son of the guru or the husband," he shows that there is no fault even in consuming the remnants or offering remains of the guru and others. The avoidance of what is unfit to be drunk and so forth must certainly be practiced, because it is a cause of defects for the embryo; for that which is produced from a defective cause cannot possibly be non-defective. Whatever is consumed by the mother—whether defective or non-defective—is a cause for the embryo. Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should avoid liquor, garlic, onions, leeks, *kalañja*, meat, and other such things that are unfit to be eaten, for the embryo arises from what the mother has eaten and drunk. The internal distinctions among garlic and the others are defined in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*; thus, their inclusion as three distinct items is purposeful. However, liquor (*surā*) is especially to be avoided by a woman, as it brings about defects even for the husband. And so says Hārīta.
Half of the body of that man whose wife drinks liquor falls away;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no atonement is prescribed.
Yama also says:
"That Brahmin whose wife drinks wine (vāruṇī) in his presence shall be excluded like a Śūdra from all the duties of the twice-born."

By stating "in the presence of," he indicates that the rule of exclusion applies only when the husband is an associate in the act. Consequently, it should be understood that no such fault attaches to one who abandons a wife for drinking liquor. Yājñavalkya also states the result of the sin arising from drinking that liquor in order to show that liquor is especially forbidden for a Brāhmaṇī woman: "That Brāhmaṇī who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband; even in this very world, she is reborn as a bitch, a vulture, or a sow. [588]

The intention is that, for this reason, liquor should be avoided with great effort. Viṣṇu, however, states other duties: "Now, the duties of women: in some respects, they consist of sharing the same conduct and behavior, keeping household utensils well-maintained, not being loose-fisted, remaining well-guarded, having no delight in root-rites (*mūlakriyā*), and being devoted to auspicious customs. "Keeping household utensils well-maintained" means keeping items such as seats and so forth in the home refined by washing and other means. "Not being loose-fisted" means turning away from improper expenditure. "Root-rite" (*mūlakriyā*) refers to the practice of *mūlakarma*, which is to say, the subjugation of the husband through mantras, tantras, and the like.
Thus ends the section on the duties of women in the Smṛticandrikā; now follow the specific tasks of women, regarding which Bṛhaspati says:
Rising before [their elders], eating and serving food and condiments after them,
and occupying a lower seat or bed— this is declared to be the duty of women.

Rising before her husband means rising prior to his own rising. Likewise, in the rule regarding sitting on a lower seat and so forth, "inferiority" (jaghanya) refers to being lower than the husband's seat and so forth. Regarding those worthy of honor, she should first perform activities such as providing food and the like. Devala also says: "Service to the husband, performing religious duties together with him, honoring those whom he honors, and hating those whom he hates. Śaṅkha and Likhita also say: "She should perform the great daily duties: the smearing of the cooking vessels the day after they have been used, the thorough sweeping and smearing of the house and its door, the offering of oblations (*bali*) made with curds, unbroken rice, *dūrvā* sprouts, and flowers, and the salutation of her parents-in-law. The phrase "the smearing of the cooking vessels the day after they have been used" implies that it was done on the previous day. Ṛśyaśṛṅga also says: [589]
A householder should always wear ornaments and should constantly adorn his braided hair with a garland of flowers after he has bathed.
"One should go to her in secret beforehand, before the women have awakened;

one should perform the worship of the deities with incense, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth. Thus it is said. A householder is devoted to the worship of the household deities. "Having bathed" means having been purified by bathing. "One should go in secret" means one should go into private from the presence of the husband. Kātyāyana also says:
And, never separated from her husband, she should serve the sacred fire with humility,
out of devotion to her lord and with the desire for conjugal bliss and freedom from widowhood.

"Agni" refers to the *gārhapatya* fire or that known as the *aupāsana*. "Possessed of good fortune" means desiring non-widowhood; by this it is stated that good fortune and non-widowhood are the fruits of tending the sacred fire. From the specific qualifications mentioned at the beginning and end of the verse, it is understood that the husband must also be constantly served by a modest wife. Manu says that the husband is not only to be served, but is also not to be transgressed against even in times of misfortune:
"To whomsoever her father or her brother may give her with the father's consent..."

"One should serve him while he is alive and must not disregard him even if he is in a wretched state"—this is the meaning of the word *ca* (and) in the phrase "nor should one hate him. Likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not hate one's husband; one should not be afflicted with *aṣṭhīlā*, nor should one be an outcast (*patita*), deformed in limb, or diseased; for the husband is the deity of women. The term *aṣṭhīvalaḥ syāt* means "one should suffer from the disease known as *aṣṭhīlā*. Regarding an outcast husband, however, Yājñavalkya says that he must be waited for by his wife until his removal from the status of an outcast, for the sake of service. [590]

"For one defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must indeed be awaited until purification. The implied meaning to be understood here is that while the husband is in a state of being an outcast (patita), he is not to be served. However, a husband who is ill-behaved and so forth is not to be waited for until the cessation of his ill-behavior and other such faults. As Manu says:
"Whether he be devoid of character, or act according to his lusts, or be destitute of virtues..."
A husband must always be served like a god by a virtuous wife.

One who acts according to desire moves according to his own will. He is to be served like a god; the meaning is that just as a god is to be served because he brings about the attainment of happiness in this world and the next, so too is the husband. And thus it is said: "The husband, who has performed the consecration with mantras both out of season and during the fertile period, bestows constant happiness upon his wife in this world and in the world beyond."

One who performs the sacraments of mantras—that is, one who performs the sacraments such as marriage and so forth, including those rites initiated by mantras. However, Yājñavalkya, for the purpose of demonstrating that another duty must be performed in accordance with the duty consisting of service to the husband, says: "The word of the husband must be carried out by women; this is the supreme duty of a woman. "Supreme" means excellent. Thus, it is effectively established that the performance of a subordinate act is in accordance with a superior one. Manu also says this very thing by implication.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by serving her husband, she is glorified in heaven.
Śaṅkha also says:
"Neither by a vow, nor by fasting, nor by various religious duties does a woman attain heaven; she attains it through the honoring of her husband."
Viṣṇu, however, stated in order to establish that a fast or vow must not be observed without performing service to her husband:
"A woman who observes a fast or vow while her husband is living takes away the life of her husband and goes to hell."

As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The undertaking of vows, fasts, observances, sacrifices, and so forth with the husband’s permission is the duty of a woman," that refers to the performance of vows and the like accomplished without violating the service due to the husband. As for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi: "Women are the deities of the home; for them there is no impurity, no vow, and no fasting; through service to the husband alone they attain the supreme goal," that should be understood as intended merely to praise the excellence of service to the husband, and not as a prohibition against [undergoing] purification and other such rites. Manu states the fruit for her who acts in this manner:
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech,
and body attains preeminent fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband, well-conducted, and having conquered her senses,
she attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death."
Kātyāyana also says:
"By the mere service of her husband, a woman attains all desires;
returning from heaven to this world, she becomes a treasure-house of happiness. [592]
The meaning is that she, having returned here from the presence of heaven, shall become a treasure-house of happiness. This is also Lakṣmī’s speech directed toward the earth:
"Among women who are always well-adorned, devoted to their husbands, sweet-spoken, open-handed, endowed with auspiciousness, careful with household goods, and fond of making offerings..."

"O Earth, I always abide among those women who keep their homes clean, who have conquered their senses, who are free from strife, who are free from greed, who regard righteousness, and who are endowed with compassion and joy. [Thus it is said. "Free from strife" means devoid of quarrels. Hārīta, however, speaks of the fault of one who is not devoted to her husband.
She who is unvirtuous and lives having abandoned her husband according to her own will does not obtain happiness; she is destined for hell.
Thus ends the section on the duties of women in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the duties of a woman whose husband is away on a journey;
regarding this, Manu says:
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live remaining firm in her observances;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for her, she should live by means of blameless crafts.

When her husband has gone abroad, the wife, having calculated the expenses for subsistence and remaining subject to the rules to be described, shall live upon the funds set aside for those expenses until his return. [593] If those funds are exhausted or if none were provided, she shall live by means of blameless crafts such as weaving—meaning she should avoid entering the houses of others and being associated with improper men, which would lead to scandal. In response to the question, "What then are the rules to be described?", Viṣṇu states: "While the husband is away, she should not perform personal adornment, she should not go to the houses of others, and she should not stand at the doorway or near the windows. "Not performing personal adornment" (*pratikarmākriyā*) means the non-performance of decoration. Likewise, Hārīta says: "She should not adorn herself while he is away, nor should she loosen her braid. Śaṅkha and Likhita also state the rules: "For virtuous women whose husbands are away and who are not independent, there should be no undertaking of swings, dancing, excursions, viewing spectacles, body-unguents, garden visits, carriage rides, sleeping uncovered, superior drinking and eating, ball-games, incense, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, tooth-cleaning, collyrium, looking in mirrors, or elaborate dressing. The connection of the sentence is: "There should be no undertaking of everything from swings to dressing for virtuous women whose husbands are away and who are not independent. When her husband is away on a journey, she should not engage in personal adornment, nor witness dances, songs, social gatherings, or festivals, nor should she indulge in meat or liquor.

Śaṅkha and Likhita have laid down a rule for those who protect women whose husbands are away from improper associations: "When the husband is away, a Brāhmaṇa woman shall protect her character; for others, it is the mother and father, or a close relative, or a member of the royal family. Here, "all" refers to women of the Kṣatriya and other castes; "others" refers to Brāhmaṇa women. "Anantara" means a close relative.
Thus ends the section on the duties of a woman whose husband is away in the *Smṛticandrikā* [594].
Now follow the duties of a woman whose husband is deceased.

Regarding this, Hārīta says concerning the wife of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*): "If the maintainer of the fires should die, she should take the embers of the *aupāsana* fire and dwell kindling it at each of the three daily libations with the *sarparājñī* verses. In the case of the *ardhādhāna* (half-maintenance) rite, the deceased maintainer of the fires is cremated with the *tretāgni* fires; however, the *aupāsana* fire is maintained for the sake of the husband's funeral rites. The term *avakṣāṇa* refers to the fuel remaining as embers. Thus, the meaning is this: having taken the *aupāsana* fire in the form of embers, she should dwell in the house of her father-in-law or others, kindling it at each libation with the four verses beginning with "The earth by its abundance," and so forth. In exactly the same way, the wife of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) should dwell. However, there is this distinction: she should either re-establish the *aupāsana* fire according to the procedure prescribed in her own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, or she should take up a common (*laukika*) fire. And thus he [Hārīta] himself says: "If he has not maintained the fires, she should establish another, or take up a fire from the people (*janāgni*). The phrase "if he has not maintained the fires and should die" is supplied from the context. Having "taken up" [the fire], the remainder is that she should perform the kindling as before. It is stated that since the disposal of the previously existing *aupāsana* fire has occurred during the cremation rite of one who did not maintain the fires, she should establish another for the purpose of re-establishing it. But how, then, is there the service of the fire for a woman whose husband has died under the *sarvādhāna* (full-maintenance) system? Furthermore, what was said regarding the wife of one who did not maintain the fires should be inferred here as well; for by the force of the scriptural statement itself, a non-worldly (*alaukika*) fire is produced for the woman whose husband has died. It is replied: having taken up a fire produced by friction (*nirmathita*), she should perform the kindling as before. This is because Āpastamba, in the rule for the *pitṛmedha* (funeral sacrifice), prescribes the use of a fire produced by friction for the wife in this alternative: "With a fire produced by friction, [he performs the rite] for the wife. Having thus described the kindling of specific fires for specific types of women, he [Hārīta] also states the general duty for any woman whose husband has died: "Resorting to the house of her husband, father, or kinsmen, with her speech, hands, feet, and senses restrained, virtuous in conduct, mourning her husband day and night, emaciated by vows and fasts, she conquers the world of her husband at the end of her life and does not again suffer separation from her husband. The fruit is also stated in another *Smṛti*.
But that woman who is devoted to her husband and remains steadfast when her lord has died,
having abandoned all sins, shall attain the world of her husband.
Bṛhaspati also said: "One who is devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy,
and constantly intent on the gift of Dharma, shall go to heaven even if she is childless."

As for that which is stated in the Śruti, "There is no world for one who has no son," that refers to the case of one who, although the entitlement to procreate a son through the path of dharma has arisen, does not produce a son out of indifference, thinking "What is the use of a son? It is to show that this alone is the scope of this Śruti passage that Manu has also provided an illustration: "Many thousands of Brahmins, remaining celibate from their youth, have gone to heaven without establishing a lineage."

"When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains established in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those lifelong celibates. This refers to the lineage of Aja Śoka, for many thousands of Brahmins who remained celibate from their youth went to heaven without producing a lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth. He himself states the fault for that woman who does not remain established in celibacy for the sake of producing a son:
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the world of her husband.
As for that which was stated by Yama:
"Neither in the Veda nor in the Śāstra is renunciation prescribed for a woman;
for her own duty is procreation from a man of her own caste—this is the settled rule."

Thus—in the *śāstra*, that is, the *Dharmaśāstra*—the term *pravrajyā* means *brahmacarya*. Although the practice of *brahmacarya* for women is enjoined in the *Śruti* and other texts, nevertheless, this injunction regarding *brahmacarya* is made as a censure—being virtually non-existent—for the purpose of praising the *dharma* characterized by the procreation of sons from a husband of the same caste; thus there is no contradiction. This should be understood as having been stated as the *dharma* of other ages (*yuga*) than the Kali age. And so it has been explained by us in the section on sacraments (*saṃskārakāṇḍa*), in the context of the appointment of widows (*niyojana*). Therefore, in the Kali age, the established rule of *brahmacarya* alone is the *dharma*; however, it should be understood that in other ages, even that which is prescribed by Yama constitutes *dharma*. Even in those cases, abiding in *brahmacarya* is the highest *dharma*, because it brings about the attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). And so says Kātyāyana:
That virtuous woman who, upon the death of her husband,
remains established in celibacy and conducts herself like Arundhatī, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

As for that other rule stated by Viṣṇu: "Upon the death of her husband, she may observe celibacy or ascend after him (*tadanvārohaṇa*)"; *tadanvārohaṇa* means ascending after the husband, namely, ascending the funeral fire. And so says Aṅgiras: "The woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the blazing fire, being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world."
— This other duty, moreover, is inferior even to the duty of celibacy, because its fruit is low.
Thus ends the section on the duties of a woman whose husband has died in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the rule for the legal title known as the partition of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) is stated; regarding this, Manu says:
This duty of women and men, connected with pleasure, has been declared to you, as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress; now learn the law concerning inheritance.

The meaning is: "Understand the dharma concerning the substance known as inheritance (dāya) as it is being declared by me. When the question arises, "What, then, is the substance called inheritance? it has been stated by the author of the Nighaṇṭu:
"The wise call that property of a father which is to be divided 'inheritance' (dāya)."

The meaning is that the elders use the word *dāya* (inheritance/property) for wealth that has come down through a father or other ancestors who are eligible for partition. For this very reason, Dhāreśvara stated exactly thus: "By the word *dāya*, only wealth that has come down through a father or through a mother is denoted. The word *ca* (and) is intended to indicate that wealth coming down through other relatives is also denoted by the word *dāya*. The word *eva* (only/exclusively), however, is for the purpose of making known that [the property] does not yet possess the nature of established ownership (*svatva*). But that is incorrect, because it is precisely wealth that possesses the nature of established ownership which comes down to sons and grandsons through the father. And thus, it should be understood that the author of the *Nighaṇṭu* stated that the word *dāya*, when referring to wealth belonging to another, applies to that which is eligible for partition. Furthermore, the *dharma* concerning the subject of *dāya* intended here is characterized by partition, because that alone was mentioned previously at the occasion of the enumeration of the topics [in the verse]: "The duties of husband and wife, and partition. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* [states...].
That wealth which has come down through the father and that which has come down through the mother is designated by the term *dāya*; its partition is now being described.

The meaning of the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*) is as follows: after the exposition of everything included under the heading "Duties of Women and Men," Manu now declares the division of that substance which, having come down through the father, was referred to by the word *dāya* (inheritance) within the compound *dāyadharma*. When the question arises as to how this is stated, Manu says:
"Upon the death of both the father and the mother, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal estate equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive."

The author of the summary (saṃgrahakāra) states its intended meaning as follows: "At whatever time, by whatever method, and by whomsoever it is performed; and for what kind of heir, and in accordance with the scriptures, it is demonstrated."

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding whatever inheritance—whether paternal, maternal, or otherwise—at whatever time, by whatever method (such as equal or unequal distribution), and by whom (such as fathers, brothers, sisters, etc. the partition is to be made—all of this is demonstrated by [the verse] beginning with "ūrdhvaṃ pituś ca," without transgressing the scriptures of Vṛddha-Manu and others. By the phrase "ūrdhvaṃ pituś ca" (after the father), the time for the partition of the father's wealth is stated. By the phrase "mātuś ca" (and after the mother), the time for the partition of the mother's wealth is stated. Therefore, even while the mother is living, the partition of the father's wealth must be performed; likewise, even while the father is living, the partition of the mother's wealth must certainly be performed after her death. This is because there is no utility in waiting for the period after both have passed for the partition of either one's wealth. And so says the author of the Saṃgraha:
The division of the paternal estate shall take place even while the mother is living;
for she possesses no independent ownership in the absence of her husband.
"Likewise, even when the father is alive, there is a division of the mother's property among the children;
for, as long as sons exist, the husband is not the master of the woman's wealth."

Since a wife has no ownership over her husband’s property by virtue of independence even when the husband dies, and since—even when children exist—the husband (bhartṛ) is not the owner of the woman’s property (strīdhana) or the wife’s property (bhāryādhanam) upon the wife’s death; therefore, the meaning is that while either of these two is still living, a division of the other’s property is appropriate. By this, it is implied that while the father is living, a division of his property must not be made by the sons and others, and while the mother is living, a division of her property must not be made. And this is stated by the final quarter-verse of Manu: “They have no power over them while both are living. “No power” (anīśāḥ) means they are not independent. Likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “Sons should not divide the inheritance while the father is living, even if it were acquired by them later; for sons are indeed unfit [to do so], because of their lack of independence in matters of wealth and religious duty (arthadharma). Even though ownership over the father’s wealth was acquired immediately after their own birth, nevertheless, while the father is living, they should not divide the father’s wealth. This is because, due to their lack of independence in wealth and duty, the sons are unfit to perform a partition. Lack of independence regarding wealth means a lack of independence in the taking and giving of wealth; likewise, Hārīta says: “While the father is living, sons have no independence in the taking, giving, or spending of wealth. “Taking of wealth” (arthadānam) means the enjoyment of wealth. “Giving” (visargaḥ) means expenditure. “Restraining” (ākṣepaḥ) refers to the restraint used for the purpose of punishing servants and attendants for their offenses. Lack of independence means the inability to engage in the taking of wealth and so forth according to one’s own will without the father’s permission. Independence regarding duty (dharmāsvātantryam) is similarly the inability to engage separately in sacrifices, works of public utility (iṣṭāpūrta), and so on. Thus, it should be understood that a son must perform his own rites, such as the Agnihotra, only when permitted by the father, and not without permission. As for what was stated by Devala:
When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father’s property;
for as long as the father remains free from defect, they would have no ownership over it.

Thus, it should be understood that the statement regarding the absence of ownership (*asvāmya*) there is intended to demonstrate a lack of independence (*asvātantrya*). For even while a faultless father remains, the sons' ownership over the paternal wealth is established by worldly consensus (*lokasiddha*) from the very moment of birth. Now, one might object: "The ownership of sons is not established by worldly consensus; it is something extraordinary (*alaukika*). To say this would indeed be a futile attempt to subvert the natural force of the statement, "for [otherwise] there would be a lack of ownership. Nor should it be argued that this is merely a formal proposition (*pratijñāmātra*) that ownership is extraordinary, because the author of the *Saṃgraha* states the underlying logic (*nyāya*): "Whatever is in someone's hand, he alone is its owner; no other."
What is there that those who, through theft, place the property of one person into the hands of another, do not possess?
Therefore, ownership arises solely from scriptural authority, and not even from actual experience.

Because it is impossible to determine that he alone is the owner of whatever wealth is seen in someone's possession, since even the property belonging to another might be seen in someone else's possession through theft or other means, thereby resulting in that person being considered the owner. Therefore, the meaning is that ownership is to be understood solely through the scriptures (*śāstra*), and not through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, if he who sees something in someone's possession were that person's sole owner, then one could not say, "This was stolen by him," because ownership would belong only to the one in whose presence it was seen. Moreover, if ownership were cognizable through other means of knowledge, then the acquisition of wealth prescribed in various distinct ways according to the respective castes—without overstepping them—in the *Dharmaśāstra* composed by Gautama, such as "the Brāhmaṇa’s [wealth] is what is received as a gift, the Kṣatriya’s is what is conquered, and the Vaiśya and Śūdra’s is what is earned through labor," would be rendered useless, as other means of knowledge alone would be the determinants. He himself states this refutation: [The text continues with the following verse: "One should not speak of the ownership of what has been seen in the presence of another; for if it were so, the rule regarding the specific modes of acquisition for each caste would be meaningless. Thus, the point is established that ownership is a matter accessible only to scriptural authority.
It is not proper for him to speak otherwise regarding what has been taken away by this person;
for the acquisition of wealth has been prescribed in the treatise separately for each [caste] according to its specific description.
"By receiving gifts, trade, service, and so forth, respectively. Thus [it is said].

It should be understood that by the passage beginning with "asya" and ending with "vaktum," the first subverting argument (*bādhaka*) is stated here; by the remainder, which requires the ellipsis "would be useless" (*vyarthaḥ syāt*), the second is intended. And thus, ownership (*svatva*) also, like proprietorship (*svāmya*), is to be known as cognizable solely through the scriptures (*śāstraikasamadhigamya*). For, since ownership and proprietorship share an identical status regarding their acquisition and preservation (*tulyayogakṣema*), even when one of them is established as being cognizable solely through the scriptures, both are thereby established. Therefore, he [the author] now says the same thing in order to establish that both are cognizable solely through the scriptures, taking ownership as the subject.
Nor is it called "one's own" in that same way, for it is not employed according to one's own will;
rather, the employment of everything is regulated by the scripture alone. [602]

The meaning of this is as follows: we do not say that something is one's own simply because it is perceived as being in close proximity; rather, that object which is employed by someone according to their will is called "one's own. Consequently, there is no fault such as over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), for it must be stated that in the case of stolen property and the like—which cannot be employed according to one's will—the conventional usage of "one's own" does not apply. This is because, even regarding wealth that is not the subject of such conventional usage, its employment in supporting teachers, servants, and so forth is regulated solely by the scriptures; thus, nothing at all can be employed according to one's mere will. All of this has been explained in detail by the venerable Dhāreśvara Sūri. Therefore:
"For they would lack ownership while their faultless father remains"—
since ownership is thus established by the *Dharmaśāstra*, it is proper to interpret the statement from Śaṅkha, "even if it should be acquired by them later," in a different sense.

To this it is replied: We do not say that one's own property (*svam*) is to be employed according to one’s whim; rather, we say that one's own property is *worthy* of being employed according to one’s whim. [Objection: But since the scriptures enjoin the maintenance of teachers, dependents, and so forth, just as it is difficult to define [property] as "to be employed according to one’s whim" because its employment is restricted by rule, so too is it difficult to define it as "worthy of being employed according to one’s whim," precisely because such arbitrary employment is absent. [Reply: Not so. Even in the absence of employment according to one’s whim, it is defined in this way: "that which has been acquired by someone is worthy of being employed according to one’s whim by that person. And thus it was defined by Bhavanātha himself in the *Nayaviveka* with the passage: "And that is worthy of him which has been acquired by him. The meaning of this is: whatever object has been acquired by a particular person, that object is "worthy of him"—that is, worthy of being employed according to his whim. The sense of the word "and" (*ca*) is that, in this view, defining the worthiness of being employed according to one’s whim is as feasible as defining ownership itself. [Objection: But in that case, would the property acquired through theft by a thief be "worthy of being employed according to one’s whim"? Anticipating this, he says: "Acquisition is established in the world as birth and so forth. The meaning is that acquisition of wealth—consisting of birth, purchase, partition, acceptance of gifts, discovery, and so on—is established in the world from time immemorial (*anidampurama*), but theft and the like are not. The sense of the word "and" (*ca*) here is also that it is easy to avoid such over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Anticipating the objection—"Surely this acquisition (*ārjana*) is established in the world as not being for the first time; what then is the restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) that it is not so?"—the same author says: "Therefore, the *Smṛti* (legal/philosophical tradition) is intended to establish the basis for those things situated within the scope of worldly cognition as not being for the first time, like the *Smṛtis* on grammar and other sciences. The meaning is as follows: Since acquisition, which is established in the world as not being for the first time, alone brings about ownership (*svatva*), therefore that very acquisition must necessarily be known for the sake of establishing worldly and Vedic transactions. For this reason, in order to establish in his own work those acquisitions situated within the scope of worldly cognition as not being for the first time, the *Dharma-smṛti* composed by Gautama and others was formulated—just like the *Smṛti* on grammar intended to establish correct words—beginning with: "Ownership arises from inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding; for a Brāhmaṇa, what is received is additional; for a Kṣatriya, what is conquered; for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, what is earned through labor (*nirviṣṭa*). "Inheritance" (*riktha*) means the acquisition of inheritance; that is to say, the birth of a son or other heirs which brings about ownership over the wealth of a father or others. And thus, Gautama himself stated that the cause for obtaining paternal wealth is: "By birth alone, one obtains ownership of property, so says the Teacher. "By birth alone" means by the very production of the body in the mother's womb. "Partition" (*saṃvibhāga*) is the division of the wealth of a father or others that effects a specific ownership. "Seizure" (*parigraha*) is the taking possession of water, grass, wood, and so forth found in forests and such places, which has not been claimed by another. "Finding" (*adhigama*) is the discovery of a treasure-trove and the like. When these causes exist, the son or other heir, the purchaser, the co-partner, the seizer, and the finder become, respectively, the owner of the paternal wealth, the purchased item, the partitioned share, the seized object, and the found treasure.

And thus, that which is obtained and accepted as the specific, individual acquisition of a Brāhmaṇa; likewise, that which is won by a Kṣatriya as acquired through victory; likewise, that which is earned by a Vaiśya as wages for plowing and so forth; and also for a Śūdra, that which is earned as wages for service to the twice-born and so forth—this is the meaning of Gautama’s Smṛti regarding the basis of acquisition, namely, "specifically acquired. Consequently, everything stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha* beginning with "that which remains in whose hand," and that which was elaborated by Dhāreśvara Sūri, should be understood as refuted. And therefore:
For it would follow that these [sons] would lack ownership while their faultless father remains;
thus, by the plain meaning of these statements, the resolution of the contradiction with the statement of Śaṅkha is indeed appropriate—enough with this excessive elaboration.

The subject at hand is now stated: By the inclusion of the term *nirdoṣa* ("faultless"), it is shown that even while the father is alive, if he possesses faults, the sons do not remain under his subjection. This indicates that when the father is alive but possesses defects such as incapacity (*akṣamatva*) and the like, the eldest son has independence regarding the acquisition and distribution of wealth, whereas for the younger brothers, dependence on the eldest must be understood. For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "When the father is incapable, the eldest, or the next [in seniority] who understands the business, shall conduct the family's legal affairs with his permission. "With his permission" means with the permission of the eldest, because at that time he alone possesses independence. The mention of "the next" (*anantara*) is intended to include the younger brothers, since it is specifically one who understands the business who is intended here. Furthermore, the mention of "incapable" (*aśakta*) is intended to include those who are distressed (*dīna*) and so forth. For this reason, Hārīta says: "At will, the eldest may attend to the family's affairs when [the father] is distressed, away from home, or afflicted by illness. In the phrase "when distressed" (*dīne*) and so on, the two words "while the father is living" (*jīvati pitari*) are to be supplied; this is because they are heard in the preceding sentence and are required here as well. By using the word "at will" (*kāmaṃ*), he shows that at that time the father’s subjection has ceased. Since the father’s subjection has ceased, the sons' fitness to act as the dividers of the paternal estate arises; thus, the division of the paternal estate at that time should occur solely according to the wish of the sons. For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The division of the inheritance occurs against the will of the father when he is aged, mentally deranged, or long-ailing. "Against the will of the father" means when the father is devoid of the desire for division. "Aged" means excessively old. "Mentally deranged" means one whose mind is not in its natural state. What is meant is this: when the father has become dependent due to old age and so forth, the division of his wealth occurs by the wish of the sons alone, even without his consent. The mention of "long-ailing" is intended to include those who are long-wrathful and so on. For this very reason, Nārada says: [End of excerpt]
A father who is diseased, incapacitated, whose mind is attached to sensual pleasures,
or who acts contrary to the scriptures, is not the master with respect to the partition [of the estate].

Rather, the implication is that the son himself has the authority. Otherwise, one who acts contrary to the scriptures and follows a path deviating from the tradition of Smṛti and custom—even while a faultless father remains—[the author] states in a certain context that the division of property is to be performed by the sons alone:
"After this, the sons shall divide the father's wealth equally, once the mother’s menses have ceased and the sisters have been given away in marriage."
"And even when the father has ceased his dalliance and his desire has subsided," so it is said.

The first statement, beginning with "ata ūrdhvam" and ending with "samam," indicates the time for the partition of the estate during the father's lifetime; nevertheless, it is recited here for the purpose of completing the subsequent sentence. The meaning of the second statement is that when there is a certainty regarding the absence of the parents' means for procreating offspring, and when a marriage has been performed for a daughter, and the father’s desire for wealth has departed, the sons alone shall divide that wealth. Regarding this point, Bodhāyana states that the father also acts as an agent by way of his consent: "The division of the inheritance is [effected] with the father's consent. When it is asked, "Where then does the division have the father as its agent? Nārada [provides the answer].
"Or the father himself, having reached old age, may divide the sons.

By stating "having reached old age," he shows that this rule pertains specifically to a father who possesses unimpeded independence. Although the word "or" (*eva*) establishes that the agency belongs to the father, the inclusion of the word "himself" (*svayam*) excludes even the sons' role as mere consent-givers in this matter. The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative to living together, and not an alternative with other agents such as the father; for here, the alternative is simply between [living] together and [the father dividing them]. Thus says Vyāsa:

"Co-residence of brothers while their parents are alive is ordained. Thus, even after the father's death, co-residence among brothers certainly exists for the purpose of increasing wealth. To this effect, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "They may, if they wish, live together in one place; being united, they shall attain prosperity. The sense is that this is because there is no expenditure when living separately. Regarding partition, however, Gautama says: "But upon partition, there is an increase in dharma. When it is asked how this is so, Nārada [explains]: * *bhrātṝṇāṃ jīvatoḥ pitroḥ sahavāso vidhīyate* || * *iti | pitur ūrdhvam api bhrātṝṇām anyonyam arthopacayārthaṃ sahavāso 'sty eva | tathā ca śaṅkhalikhitau: "kāmaṃ sahavaseyur ekataḥ saṃhatā vṛddhim āpadyeran" iti | pṛthak pṛthak vyayābhāvād iti bhāvaḥ | vibhāge tu dharmavṛddhim āpadyerann ity āha gautamaḥ: "vibhāge tu dharmavṛddhiḥ" iti | katham ity apekṣite nāradaḥ |* [The text provided above is the translation of the Sanskrit passage. But if those who were reunited should divide again, then there would be a loss of dharma for them. Therefore, partition alone is better—this is the opinion of Nārada. * *vibhaktā bhrātaraḥ parasparam asaṃsṛṣṭāḥ svadhana-vyavahāreṣu svatantrāḥ syuḥ |* * *saṃsṛṣṭās tu yadi punar vibhajante tadā teṣāṃ dharmahāniḥ syāt |* * *tasmād vibhāga eva śreyān iti nārada-matam |* "Brothers who have been partitioned, not reunited with one another, shall be independent in the transactions of their own property. But if those who were reunited should divide again, then there would be a loss of dharma for them. Therefore, partition alone is better—this is the opinion of Nārada. * *vibhakt
For brothers who have not divided their property, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties also become separate for each.
Dharma is that which arises from the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born. And so Bṛhaspati says:
"For those living together in a single household, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one;
for those who are divided, that same worship shall be performed in each individual house."

But surely, even the *dharma* produced by the *agnihotra* and other rites increases for those who have divided their property, but not for those who have not divided it; for since there is no ownership (*svatva*) among those who have not divided, it is impossible for them to acquire the *dharma* produced by the *agnihotra* and other rites belonging to themselves. Therefore, the *dharma* resulting from the *agnihotra* and other rites must be stated as the reason for the superiority of the position of division. And this has been stated in exactly that way by the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "The paternal wealth is made [into] the property of the sons through division.
Since ownership exists [only then], they proceed [in their duties]; therefore, separate action is consistent with *dharma*."

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "they proceed to perform their own duties, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice. To this it is replied: the claim that sons acquire ownership through the partition of paternal property is incorrect, because it has already been established that ownership is acquired by birth alone. Consequently, since ownership exists even for those who have not divided the estate, the merit (*dharma*) arising from the performance of their own duties, such as the *agnihotra*, is certainly attained; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever between the position of partition and the position of non-partition. Therefore, it is in the manner previously described that the increase of merit under the system of partition was stated by Gautama and others—this is the general direction of the argument.

Thus ends the demonstration of the time and the agents of partition in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the method of partition while the father is alive. Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "When the father is alive, the partition of inheritance is permitted—either openly or privately—in accordance with dharma. The meaning is that the method of partition which is permitted while he is alive should be performed either "openly," such that it takes place in the presence of kinsmen and others, or "privately," in secret; and it must be done "in accordance with dharma," by a manner not departing from righteousness. Kātyāyana describes that very method as follows: [608]
When the fathers and brothers take the entire collection of property in equal shares, that division is declared to be righteous.

The meaning is as follows: whatever property is of middling quality, if the father and the others take all of that with equal shares, that division is said to be "not departing from dharma" (*dharmād anapeta*) because it is understood through the scriptures. To state another method of division according to dharma by granting a larger share to the eldest brother, Bodhāyana says: "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons; the share is equal for all, because there is no distinction. The meaning is that since the Brāhmaṇa passage stating "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons" refers to a division made while the father is alive and does not specify any particular distinction, the principle "it should be equal, as nothing is heard to the contrary" (*samaṃ syād aśrutatvāt*) implies that by the force of this very scripture, an equal share for all father and sons is understood. However, he himself states that the superiority of the eldest is established by another Vedic text: "The eldest should set aside one excellent object of wealth; therefore, they satisfy the eldest son with wealth. By saying "one object of wealth," he shows that the singular number in the scriptural phrase "with wealth" (*dhanena*) is intended to be significant. "They satisfy" (*niravasāyayanti*) means they please him. Likewise, Āpastamba says: "Having satisfied the eldest with one object of wealth, he should divide the inheritance among his sons equally while he is still living. The meaning is that while living, the father, having pleased the eldest—the first-born son—with one excellent object of wealth extracted from the middle property, should divide the remainder equally among himself and the sons, beginning with the eldest. Thus, because he was born first, the extraction (*uddhāra*) is for his sake alone; and it should be understood that this is another method stated, wherein the extraction consists of one single best object of wealth, and the remainder is divided with equality. Therefore, between the two positions stated by Kātyāyana and Bodhāyana, the father should adopt whichever position he wishes to follow. Since the father is the sole authority in a division made by himself, his own desire is the cause for adopting a specific position. All of this has been stated concisely by Yājñavalkya.
If the father should make a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will;
either by giving the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers.

Here, the two positions previously established are stated in the latter half [of the verse] by reversing the order mentioned earlier. It should be understood that the first half states that, in adopting either of those two positions, the father’s will alone is the cause, and not the will of the sons as well. Thus, whichever position has been adopted by the father according to his own will must be acquiesced in by the sons, even if it is disregarded by them. And so says that very same [author]: "For those who have been divided unequally, the distribution made by the father is declared to be in accordance with dharma."

The meaning is this: since those other than the eldest who were divided with smaller shares lack the superior portion while it exists [in the eldest], and since the eldest who was divided with a larger share was accepted by them according to the father’s wish—if that division was preceded by an *uddhāra* (preferential share)—then that too, being rooted in the scriptures, was previously declared to be righteous; therefore, it must be acquiesced in by them as well. Nārada also states this very point:
"But for those who have been divided by the father himself with equal, lesser, or greater amounts of wealth, that alone shall be righteous, for the father is the master of all."

The eldest son should not harbor resentment if, in the manner of dividing the wealth arranged by his father, he was not given one additional or superior share. Likewise, the younger brothers should not harbor resentment if the division of wealth made by the father consisted of unequal portions, thinking, "The father gave us less and more to the eldest," because what is obtained here by the father's will alone is lawful (*dharmya*). When it is asked why that alone is lawful, it is stated: "For the father is the master of all. The meaning is that since the father alone is the master of every kind of partition performed by him, those who transgress the lawful partition are subject to punishment. As Bṛhaspati says: [He who transgresses the lawful partition is to be punished.]
If shares have been assigned by the father that are unequal—either less or more—they must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, those sons would be subject to correction.

The phrase “by the father” implies “in accordance with the manner prescribed by the scriptures,” because any division devised in a different manner is unrighteous (*adharmya*) and thus must be rejected. Indeed, even regarding wealth acquired by oneself, a division made according to one’s own whim—where one son receives a thousand *niṣkas* while another receives only a single *kapardika*—cannot be considered righteous. This is because the established rule of ownership (*svatva-vyavasthā*) pertains only to that division which has not occurred for the first time. Nor should it be argued that an unequal division based on mere whim is indeed a precedent, since the Smṛti states, “He may divide his sons according to his wish. This is because that Smṛti does not actually enjoin such a division. For instance, although this Smṛti is inherently improper, Aparārka attempted to establish its purpose as teaching such a division through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). However, that argument is refuted once the existence of the correct meaning previously explained is established. Thus, it is proven that an unequal division made by a father out of mere whim—even regarding self-acquired wealth—is not to be upheld by the sons if there is cause for regret. Furthermore, what Aparārka stated—that the phrase “with the best portion” is intended to illustrate the *uddhāra* (preferential share), and that by this all the various methods of preferential shares mentioned in the scriptures of Manu and others, such as “the twentieth part is the preferential share for the eldest,” are implied here”—is also refuted. This is because it is more logical that the passage refers specifically to the particular types of preferential shares mentioned in the context of division during the father's lifetime, such as: “The eldest may set aside a single excellent object of wealth. Bṛhaspati, however, mentions another method involving an increase in the father’s own share.
"But in the division [of property] during one's lifetime, the father shall take two shares for himself"; the words "the father dividing" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. And so says Nārada:
"The father, dividing [the estate], shall receive two shares for himself."

By saying "dividing," he shows that the two shares for himself apply to a division made by the father while living, and not to a division made by the son while the father is still alive. Regarding the specific rule for taking two shares for oneself even in a division made by the father, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "If he should have only one son, he should take two shares for himself. Here, the word "he" refers back to the father under discussion. "Should have only one son" means that the time for obtaining other sons has passed, i.e., he is advanced in age. For this very reason, even when many sons exist, Hārīta states the inequality of shares between the father and sons regarding the father’s taking a larger portion when he is advanced in age: "Or, dividing while still living, he may retire to the forest or enter the stage of the aged; or, having divided with a small portion, he may live taking the greater part for himself. If he should suffer depletion, he should again take from them; and if they are depleted, he should divide [with them] again. The meaning is as follows: having divided the sons with a small share—namely, a share equal to half of his own—the father should take a double, larger share for himself and live at home. Living thus, if he should somehow suffer depletion—that is, become impoverished due to lack of food and so on—he should then take from those sons sufficient wealth to maintain his own family from the property accumulated through the shares previously given to them. Alternatively, if the sons themselves are depleted due to lack of food and so on, then he should divide with them again as before. "May retire to the forest" means he may become a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). "The stage of the aged" refers to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). By using the term "stage of the aged," he indicates that this refers to one who is advanced in years. Thus, because the father seeks support from his sons in the latter part of life, it is appropriate for the father to be the subject of the Vedic text: "Just as a father, being distressed, approaches his son, such indeed is that. And because the son takes a small share, it is appropriate for the son to be the subject of the Vedic text: "Just as a son, being distressed, approaches his father, such indeed is that. With this intention, the meaning of the two Vedic passages—"if he should suffer depletion... and so on, and "just as the father... just as the son..."—should be understood as having been stated by the phrases "he should again take from them" and "if they are depleted, he should divide [again]. For this very reason, in order to show that his own Smṛti rules are rooted in such Vedic texts, he cites two Vedic passages of similar meaning by way of quotation: "Moreover, in this regard, they cite the Vedic text concerning the depletion and replenishment of the *graha* cups: 'The *Āgrayaṇa* cup is the father, and the other cups are the sons. If the *Āgrayaṇa* should spill or be depleted, one should take [the liquid] from the other cups; if the other cups should spill... [Thus] the two [passages] are explained. "Concerning the depletion and replenishment of the *graha*" means that which restores the exhaustion of the Soma cups. *Āgrayaṇa* is a specific Soma cup. "The others" are the cups other than the *Āgrayaṇa*, such as the Aindravāyava and others. "Upa vā dasyet" means "or should be depleted," i.e., should dry up. The particle "iti" here serves to indicate the remaining portion of the Vedic text. "Are explained" means that the explanation of the Vedic passage shown by the quotation has been provided by us through the two sentences: "if he should suffer depletion... and "if they are depleted, he should divide [again]. In this case as well, according to the father's wish, the option of an equal division among all should also be performed in some instances.
When the fathers and brothers take possession of the entire collection of property in equal shares, that division is declared to be righteous.

Thus, since Kātyāyana, by describing the division among those still living, declares the principle of equal division to be universally applicable, Yājñavalkya states regarding this matter that if the father, by his own will, should establish the system of equal shares, then: "If he should make the shares equal, the wives must be made sharers of equal portions,
provided they have not been given strīdhana (woman’s property) by their husband or by their father-in-law."

Alternatively, if even in old age the father should, by his own will, adopt the position of equal division with himself, then each wife should receive a share equal to his own; this is the meaning. In this way, the apprehension of contradiction with the statement of Hārīta—"No division exists between husband and wife"—is resolved, and thus everything is faultless. He [Hārīta] further states that where a son, due to his capacity to earn wealth, does not wish to take his own share from the paternal estate, then a separation should be made after giving him as much as he accepts.
"For one who is capable but makes no effort, there is a separate rite consisting of giving something [else]."

Furthermore, when a partition is made by sons while the father is still living, it must be carried out according to the method of equal shares stated by Kātyāyana as "the entire collection of property," because there is no other scriptural authority establishing a different rule for a partition made by sons during the father's lifetime; and because the rule of equal division declared by Nārada—beginning with "when the mother’s menses have ceased"—and applied in the preceding section on the occasion of a partition made by sons while the father lives, has already been demonstrated. Thus: "The sons shall divide the father’s wealth equally" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114). Following this, the rule of equal division stated by Nārada—"when the mother’s menses have ceased," etc.—has been shown in the previous context regarding the occasion of a partition made by sons while the father is alive.
Thus ends the section on partition during the lifetime [of the parents] in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follows the method of equal partition in the case of partition after death.

In that context, following the word "when the father has died," Hārīta states: "The division of the inheritance shall be equal. This means that when the father has died, the division of the inheritance performed by the brothers must be made with equal shares. Paiṭhīnasi also says: "When the paternal inheritance is being divided, the division among the brothers is equal. "Dāyādya" means the wealth of inheritance. Nor should it be argued that because of the plural number in the word "of the brothers," there can be no division between two brothers; for that [plural] is intended merely to indicate the transfer of ownership of the common property. For this very reason, Devala prohibits the division of inheritance for one who is the sole owner of the common property.

"One alone shall be the possessor of the same class (savarṇa); in this case, the inheritance is not divided. This statement—that "the inheritance is not divided"—is made in order to show that, in certain regions, the inheritance is not divided even when there are several brothers of both the same and different classes. And it has been stated by Manu: "The son of a Śūdra woman from Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya fathers does not share in the inheritance."

This is what is meant: even though there may be several brothers who are both Śūdras and non-Śūdras, the son of a Śūdra woman who has not been married is unworthy of inheritance; thus, only the non-Śūdra shall take everything. Likewise, because of the association with a person of the same caste (*savarṇa*) who is ineligible for partition, even if there are many, only one shall take [the estate]. And so says the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "The eldest shall take the whole when his younger brothers are ineligible; or the middlemost, or the youngest, when the elder brother is ineligible."
However, even in the case of several brothers who are of the same caste as the person entitled to inherit, the inheritance is not divided. Regarding this, Manu says:
"The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father."

Nor should it be said that this statement is intended for the purpose of training in the practice of living together; for a separate statement was already formulated by that very same author for that purpose, namely: "In this manner they may live together. This is true; nevertheless, the extension (*atideśa*) stating "they may live together" is for the purpose of training in the practice of living together among brothers who are bold. However, in the case of younger brothers who are not bold, the instruction "the eldest alone should take [the property]" is given to show that they must live together in this manner until those younger brothers attain such boldness. Thus, by this change of phrasing, the division of inheritance among several brothers who have a common wife is not prohibited by this statement, and so there is no contradiction. As for that which was stated by Nārada:
The eldest brother should support all his brothers who desire it, just as a father does; or a younger brother, if he is capable. In a family, the maintenance of order depends upon one's capacity.

Thus, that [statement] refers to the case of younger brothers who are entirely incapable. As for what was stated by Gautama—"Or everything belongs to the eldest; he should support the others like a father"—it should not be said that this has the same meaning as the *Mānava* (Manu’s) text. For, by the use of the word "or" (*vā*), it is understood that the purpose is to establish the younger brothers' entitlement to inherit as a contingent possibility in cases where the elder brothers are capable. True—it does not have the same meaning as the *Mānava*. However, it is not to be respected because it contradicts direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Thus says Āpastamba: "Some say the eldest alone is the heir; that is contradicted by the scriptures, for it is heard without distinction in the Veda that 'Manu divided his inheritance among his sons. The meaning is: some teachers further maintain that among the brothers, the eldest alone is the sharer of the paternal wealth; that opinion contradicts direct Vedic revelation, since in the *Taittirīyaka Brāhmaṇa* it is heard without distinction that "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons. His own view was stated immediately thereafter by him: "For all those who are endowed with righteousness are sharers. The word "sons" is to be supplied. Likewise, Bṛhaspati:
"All sons who inherit their father's estate shall receive equal shares. This means they are equal sharers both in the estate and in the debt. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"After the death of the parents, the sons shall divide the estate and the debt equally."
In this context, "debt" refers specifically to that which is paternal, because there is a rule that one who is not the father's heir must discharge such a debt at that very time. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"A debt contracted for the sake of the family by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a mother must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition."
Nārada, however, states that at the time of partition, even the paternal debt must be paid:
"Whatever remains after the paternal debt has been paid from the father's inheritance—that is to be divided by the brothers; otherwise, the father would remain a debtor. [617]

Based on the Gautama-Brāhmaṇa passage, "From the paternal inheritance, there are nine śrāddhas; they should perform the nine śrāddhas together," the division [of the estate] after the father's death occurs immediately following the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

This is also because of the statement of the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "And thus, if the paternal wealth is greater than the wealth required for the purpose of clearing debts such as the *navaśrāddha* and those owed to the ancestors, then that which was stated by Nārada must be followed; otherwise, that which was stated by Yājñavalkya must be understood to apply. Kātyāyana states that even certain paternal debts need not be cleared from the paternal wealth at the time of partition, but rather must simply be divided:

"A debt contracted for religious purposes (*dharmārtha*), one given out of affection (*prītidatta*), or one that is formally assigned (*niyojita*)—such a debt, when it is visible [and can be paid], should be divided; however, there is no obligation to pay it from the paternal wealth [if it exceeds the available assets]."

The meaning is that one must divide these three kinds of visible and known debts: that which was intended for religious purposes (*dharma*), that which was promised by a father out of affection through speech, and that which was designated by the father himself as something to be discharged by the sons. Furthermore, regarding a son who, being capable of acquiring wealth through his own labor, does not desire the wealth inherited through his father—in order to avoid disputes arising from his share due to his offspring—it is said that he must necessarily be divided [from the estate] by the other sons after giving him some money from the divisible property for the sake of seed-capital (*mūladhana*).
But he among brothers who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire wealth,
shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.

Regarding a brother who is distinguished by his greater labor, Nārada states that the other brothers must increase his share with grain and other goods beyond the equal portion, according to the maxim: "From the abundance of work comes the abundance of fruit. He says: "But he who, being engaged in the affairs of the family, performs that work, must be supported by his brothers with food, clothing, and transport."
Thus ends the section on the method of equal division in the *Smṛticandrikā* regarding partition during the lifetime [of the father].
Now follows the method of unequal division;
therein, Bṛhaspati says:
All sons who inherit their father's estate are entitled to equal shares;
however, among them, one who is devoted to learning and virtuous conduct deserves to receive more.

The meaning is this: those sons who are inheritors of the father’s estate and are distinct from those such as the outcastes (patita), and who are similar [to their father] by virtue of the presence or absence of learning (*vidyā*) and so forth, shall all indeed receive equal shares. However, among those who are dissimilar by virtue of the presence or absence of learning and so forth, he alone who is endowed with learning and the like deserves to obtain additional wealth either through a preferential share (*uddhāra*) or through an unequal division. Even in that case, there is a gradation in the amount of wealth obtained and its excellence according to the degree of proficiency in performing ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhātṛtva*), but not according to the degree of mere scholarship; thus says Kātyāyana.

"In whatever manner the wealth obtained through partition may be applied toward the purpose of sacrifice, in that same manner the learned should ensure the honor of the shares. The phrase "when there is an abundance of material" is to be understood as the ellipsis. For this very reason, Manu says: [619]
"There is no deduction for those who have performed their own duties well among the ten shares;
rather, something small should be given to the elder as an honorarium that increases his dignity. Thus it is said.

The *uddhāra* (preferential share) is that portion which is set aside from the mass of property to be divided for the purpose of honoring the eldest brother and others. [This applies] when there are ten or some [number] of brothers who possess sufficient wealth for their livelihood; that is to say, when all the brothers have attained the status of performers (*kartṛtva*) of their respective duties—those actions to be performed according to their own entitlements—and even though there is an abundance of wealth, because they are equal in their devotion to duty (*karmaniṣṭhatva*), there is no preferential share nor a gift intended to increase their honor. Rather, the meaning is that when there are those possessing very little wealth who are dissimilar [to the others] due to learning and so forth, even if no preferential share is given because they possess only enough for their livelihood, something such as a mere garment should be given to the elder brother for the sake of respect. Thus, it should be understood that a preferential share exists in the partition of those brothers who possess abundant wealth and among whom there is a gradation in learning and other qualities. Manu also states the manner of this preferential share:
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the property;
half of that shall be the share of the middlemost, while the youngest shall receive a fourth.

The meaning is as follows: for the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*), that is, the first-born, who is superior by virtue of learning and other qualities, the twentieth part of the mass of divisible property is the *uddhāra* (preferential share), as well as one excellent item from that very same mass. Then, "half" means the fortieth part of that same mass, along with one middling item; this is the preferential share for the middle son by virtue of birth and learning. "A fourth" means the eightieth part of that same mass, along with one inferior item; this shall be the preferential share for the youngest son by virtue of birth and learning. He [Manu] himself states the method of dividing the remainder of the mass that is not thus distinguished: [620]

"In this manner, once the preferential shares (*uddhāra*) have been set aside, one should allot equal shares. This means that what remains after the preferential shares have been taken out should be divided equally. Alternatively, regarding that same subject matter, he states that there may indeed be an unequal division and no preferential share at all: "But when no preferential share has been set aside, this following shall be the allotment of shares for them: [he continues: "The eldest shall take two shares; the middlemost, one and a half; and the youngest, one share. To those who are younger than the youngest, the distribution is equal. Thus, the meaning is that when no preferential share is taken, the eldest takes two shares, the middlemost one and a half, and the youngest one share; and among those younger than the youngest, the distribution is equal. Furthermore, the same author says: "If the preferential share is not taken, the eldest shall take one share more than the others; the middlemost, half a share more; and the youngest, one share less than the middlemost. The meaning is that when no preferential share is taken, the eldest takes one share more than the others, the middlemost takes half a share more than the others, and the youngest takes one share less than the middlemost. Moreover, the same author says: "When the preferential share is taken, the eldest shall take two shares; the middlemost, one and a half; and the youngest, one share. The meaning is that when the preferential share is taken, the eldest takes two shares, the middlemost one and a half, and the youngest one share.
