The particle *eva* in the phrase "by herself alone" (*svayam eva*) is for the purpose of excluding her own children; for the exclusion of the husband is already established by the statement "the husband does not deserve [it]. Since the exclusion of the husband implies, by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*), the exclusion of even more remote relatives such as brothers, the latter need not be mentioned separately. "In vain" (*vṛthā*) means without cause or distress (*āpad*). "Relinquishment" (*mokṣa*) means giving away. This refers to the relinquishment or enjoyment of property without the wife's permission and without force, because it is stated that giving with interest and without punishment is permissible. By stating "the husband does not deserve [it]" and adding the word "in non-distress" (*anāpadī*), he shows that in times of distress, the husband alone deserves to enjoy the *strīdhana*, and no one else. For this very reason:
Or, in order to remove the suffering of a son, he is entitled to enjoy the woman's property.

In this immediately preceding statement, "he is entitled to enjoy," the word "husband" (*pati*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The mention of "son" (*putra*) is intended to indicate one's own family members in general. "Distress" (*ārti*) here refers to that which is difficult to dispel, caused by the failure to obtain wealth. "In its removal" means in its avoidance. Because of the word "or" (*vā*), it is stated that in other cases as well, when there is a great crisis difficult to avoid due to the failure to obtain wealth, the husband is entitled to enjoy or even to relinquish the wife’s property, even without her permission. Now, an objection may be raised: how can he be entitled to relinquish or enjoy another person's property without the consent of that owner? It is replied: even in the absence of the owner's consent, in the aforementioned circumstances—specifically regarding the wife's property where the ownership belongs to a dependent person—it is established by this very text that there is entitlement to relinquishment and enjoyment for the purpose of removing distress, even though such property is otherwise unfit for arbitrary disposal. Thus, there is no fault. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is imprisonment,
a husband is not required to give back the woman’s property that he has taken.

In matters of religious duty—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—or in certain rites for pacification such as sacrifices to the planets (*grahayajña*); or in cases of obstruction that cannot be averted without the payment of wealth, such as a creditor’s legal restraint (*dhanikāsedha*); or when the wife’s property has been taken, the implication being "due to the absence of any other recourse"; or when the husband is poor, the implication being "due to the lack of wealth sufficient for restitution"—for where it is possible, restitution is necessary here. For this very reason, Kātyāyana stated that restitution is required only in certain instances.
Having learned that [the debtor] is diseased, in distress, or oppressed by creditors,
he may, out of affection, give what has been relinquished by him according to his own will.

"Having known [her to be] a woman"—this is the ellipsis. "Granted" means authorized. Although this statement appears to concern husbands and others because it follows the three preceding statements beginning with "Neither husband nor son," nevertheless: "But if he has two wives and does not favor her again, even if she was granted out of affection, he must be compelled by force to give her back."
Where a woman is deprived of food, clothing, and shelter, there she may take for herself what belongs to her husband... [and so forth].

Thus, by reflecting on the subsequent statements, it should be understood that [the right to use] refers exclusively to the husband. Furthermore, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that a woman who is exceedingly wicked does not even deserve to employ her own wealth: "A woman who is intent on doing harm, who is devoid of moral restraint, who destroys wealth, and who is devoted to adultery—such a woman does not deserve her *strīdhana* (woman’s property)."

The ellipsis is "to employ at their own will. However, property belonging to a woman (*strīdhana*) that was promised by the husband must be given even if not yet received; for it has been stated by that same author: "A woman's property, like a debt, must be given by her sons if it was promised by the husband. The mention of "sons" is also an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of grandsons, because of the expression "like a debt. By this also, it is understood that sons and others have no ownership over a woman's property. Consequently, there is no partition during the lifetime [of the parents] regarding a woman's property, since she alone is the owner. For this very reason, Manu says:
If their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still alive,
the righteous lord of the earth shall punish them with the penalty prescribed for thieves.

"Whatever ornament may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide that; those who divide it fall downwards. The word "worn" (dhṛtaḥ) implies "worn continuously" (sātatyena). When [an ornament] is worn continuously and without any indication of being for the sake of yoga (ascetic practice), it is determined to be the woman's property (*strīdhana*). Since the first half-verse is intended to state what constitutes certain *strīdhana*, it is understood that the word "continuously" must be supplied as a remainder. The "heirs" (*dāyādāḥ*) are the daughters and others.
Thus concludes the section on the management of a woman’s property in the *Smṛticandrikā* [660].
Now follows the division of wealth acquired through a woman.
Regarding that, Manu first states the manner of its acquisition:
"The property given as a subsequent gift (anvādheya), and that which was given by the husband out of affection—
when she has passed away while her husband is still living, that wealth shall belong to her offspring."
Anvādheya is that which a woman receives from her husband’s family or her father’s family after marriage;
whatever is received by a woman from her husband’s family subsequent to the wedding,
as well as what is received from her father’s family, is indeed anvādheya.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Kātyāyana. By the phrase "after marriage," the meaning of the prefix *anu-* in the term *anvādheya* is explained. By the word "obtained" (*labdha*), the meaning of the term *ādheya* situated therein should be understood. The sense is that both kinds of woman’s property (*strīdhana*)—that which is *anvādheya* and that which is given by the husband himself out of affection—shall belong to the offspring, whether male or female, who exists at the very moment immediately following the death of the owner of the wealth. This is what is meant: the woman’s property belonging to one who has offspring does not go to the husband upon his death, but rather to the offspring who possess it. And thus it is understood from this: when wealth comes into the possession of someone after the death of the owner, the very act of being alive at the moment immediately following the death of the owner is the cause for the acquisition of ownership (*svatva*) for the person established in the Dharmaśāstras as the rightful heir. Therefore, in every case where wealth comes into possession only after the death of the owner—as in the case of the estate of one who died childless and so forth—it is this very thing that must be postulated as the cause for the heir’s acquisition of ownership. Because the term "offspring" (*prajā*) is used in a general sense here, it should be understood that the entitlement of both male and female offspring to inherit the two aforementioned types of property occurs simultaneously. The acquisition of ownership is likewise simultaneous; it should not be thought that first the sisters, and in their absence the brothers, acquire it. Furthermore, the partition in this case should be understood as being performed by both the brothers and the sisters. And thus, as it has been stated: [The remainder of the passage follows.]
When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance.

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the two types of inheritance previously mentioned, such as the *anvādheya* (gifts received after marriage) and so forth. Regarding this very subject, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule:
"The woman's property shall belong to her offspring, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof;
provided she is unmarried, but if she is married, she does not receive her mother's property."

"Of the offspring" means of the sons' offspring. The word "ca" (and) is used in both expressions to indicate mutual conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*); therefore, it should be understood here that those joined in mutual conjunction are the ones who perform the partition. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"Sisters, together with their kinsmen, shall divide [the inheritance] if they are married."

"By kinsmen" means by uterine brothers; the qualification "having a husband" is for the purpose of excluding widows, but not for the purpose of excluding unmarried daughters, as that would contradict the previously cited texts. Manu speaks of those sisters who, together with their uterine brothers, are entitled to a share: "Of those [sisters] who have no sons, something should be given out of affection from the estate of the maternal grandmother, according to what is appropriate."

The meaning is: "according to what is appropriate," that is, with regard to their practice of virtue, poverty, and so forth. Now, one might ask: since daughters and granddaughters have no ownership over the maternal grandfather's wealth when brothers and sisters are present, why is anything given to them? It is said in reply: Just as in the case of paternal wealth, although daughters lack the right to inheritance, a fourth share is given to them by their brothers on the basis of a scriptural injunction; likewise, here, even though they lack ownership, something is given by the brothers and sisters due to the force of the injunction. However, this is the distinction: in that case, although they are not entitled to the inheritance, ownership exists by virtue of birth; therefore, considering the declaration of the fault—"they would become outcasts if they were unwilling to give"—it must necessarily be given. Here, however, considering that ownership does not exist at all, it is given out of affection based on the author’s own statement; thus, if there is affection, it should be given, but if not, it need not be given. Furthermore, he states that some other portion of the mother's estate belongs to the unmarried daughters alone, and not to all daughters who have sons living together with them.
"But that which may be the mother's *yautaka* (separate property), that indeed is the portion of the unmarried daughter.

Thus, *yautaka* is the wealth bestowed by anyone upon the bride and groom at their wedding or similar occasions when they are seated together in close proximity; it is considered the *yautaka* to be given to the couple once they are joined.

This is because it is stated by the author of the *Nighaṇṭu*: "The wealth that is to be given to the bride and groom who are joined together is considered *yautaka*, based on the etymological derivation *yutayoḥ idam* (this belongs to the two who are united). However, Deva Svāmin says: "'Yautaka' or 'maternal wealth' (*mātṛdhana*) is that which is obtained from the father's house; it is the mother's property belonging to the mother alone, distinguished as separate from what is obtained from the husband's house. This is to be considered doubtful, as both positions are merely speculative. When there are several unmarried daughters, the division of the *yautaka* should be made equally, according to the maxim "it should be equal, as no specific rule is heard," since no specific allotment of shares is recorded. Thus, Gautama states that this threefold maternal inheritance, distinct from the aforementioned types, belongs only to the unmarried daughters—even those who are not established—but not to all daughters: "The woman’s property (*strīdhana*) belongs to the daughters who are unmarried and not established" [GDh 28.24]. The meaning is that the woman’s property, such as *adhyagni* and so forth, belongs only to the unmarried and unestablished daughters. Consequently, the intention is that those daughters alone shall divide that wealth. "Unestablished" (*apratiṣṭhitāḥ*) means childless, penniless, unfortunate, or widowed. In this manner, the statement of Gautama has been explained according to Aparārka. The commentary on this by Vijñāneśvara is to be rejected, as it involves supplying ellipses and other elements based on his own intellect alone. Regarding this very subject, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule: "The daughters [inherit] the remainder after the mother's debts. The meaning is that after the mother's death, the daughters who are unmarried and unestablished shall divide the mother's inheritance remaining after the discharge of her debts equally. He further states that even in the absence of such daughters: "In their absence, the lineage (*anvaya*). Nārada clarifies this very point: "In the absence of daughters, their lineage. Since a lineage cannot exist among unmarried daughters, it is understood by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*) to mean the lineage of married daughters. Because the property goes to women, it is understood as a female lineage. It is stated generally as "their lineage" so that, in the absence of a female lineage among the married daughters, it may belong to the grandsons (*dauhitra*). But in the absence of grandsons as well—
After the death of their parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.

From this statement of Yājñavalkya, it is understood that after the mother's death, her inherited property (*mātṛka-riktha*) and debts incurred by the mother shall be divided equally among the sons; thus, the sons' status as the agents of partitioning the mother’s debts and assets is established. Otherwise, the elliptical expression (*ekaśeṣa*) "the sons shall divide [the estate] of both parents" would be meaningless. In the absence of sons, the grandsons (*pautra*) are the enjoyers of their grandmother’s debts and assets. This is because grandsons also possess the right to discharge debts contracted by their grandmother, according to the rule: "A debt is to be paid by the son and the grandson," and because of the traditional law (*smṛti*): "Those who inherit the estate shall discharge the debt. When there is a gathering of grandsons with different fathers in unequal numbers, the division of the grandmother’s debts and assets follows the same principle as the division of the grandfather’s estate: "The allotment of shares is according to the father. Likewise, when there is a gathering of daughters’ sons (*dauhitra*) and daughters’ daughters (*dauhitrī*) with different mothers in unequal numbers, the allotment of shares is according to the mother. This is based on the traditional law of Gautama: "For each mother, there is a specific share within her own group. As for what was stated by Kātyāyana:

"In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall go to the sons"—this refers to unmarried daughters, because in their case, due to the impossibility of the husband approaching them during their fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), there can be no offspring. Thus, it should be understood that what was stated by Kātyāyana concerns the *yautaka* (separate property) of the wife. After the death of the wife, in the absence of offspring, the wife's inheritance goes to the husband;
likewise, the woman's property belongs to the husband even in the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma, provided she leaves no children.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya; and by the use of the word "also," this applies to the Gāndharva form as well. For this very reason, Manu states:
"In the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, and Prājāpatya forms of marriage, whatever wealth [was given] is held to belong to the husband alone when the wife dies without issue."

The meaning is this: among the five types of marriages mentioned, the wealth belonging to a wife who has been consecrated through those rites is intended to go to her husband alone upon his death, provided that there is no lineage of heirs beginning with her daughter and ending with her granddaughter; it does not, however, go to her maternal relatives such as her mother and so forth. As for what was stated by Kātyāyana—"But property given by relatives goes to the relatives in their absence, and then to the husband"—that refers to the property of a woman consecrated through forms of marriage other than the five specified. And thus, he (Kātyāyana) says:
Whatever ancestral property of her father’s a woman has obtained from Asuras and other [forms of marriage],
that is declared to belong to her mother and father in the absence of their offspring.

"Paternal property" is that which has come to her through a gift from her mother and father. This refers to the absence of offspring born of a woman married by the Āsura or other such rites; the mention of "offspring" is intended as an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for all those heirs to a woman's property mentioned previously, beginning with the daughter’s son and ending with the grandson. As for what was stated by Yama: "Whatever wealth is given in marriages such as the Āsura and others, when she dies childless, the father alone shall take that wealth."

Thus, in this context, the word "by the father" (*pitṛ*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the previously cited statement. In this manner, it should be understood that regarding property given by paternal uncles, brothers, maternal uncles, and other relatives—such as *strīdhana* (woman’s property)—it belongs to those paternal uncles and relatives when they exist; otherwise, it belongs to the husband alone. This applies to the *āsura* and other such forms of marriage. Regarding certain gifts from relatives that do not belong to the giver, Gautama says: "The dowry (*śulka*) of a sister belongs to her uterine brothers after the mother. The *strīdhana* known as *śulka* was defined in the preceding section; its givers are the bridegroom and others. Even though they are the givers, that wealth does not belong to them; rather, the ownership of the wealth belongs to the uterine brothers, and in their absence, it belongs to the mother—this is the meaning. Furthermore, following the phrase "deserves," Śaṅkha states: "And the bridegroom [receives] his own *śulka*. This should be understood to apply when the bride dies before the marriage is completed. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Yājñavalkya: "If she dies, he should take what was given. The remainder of the sentence is: "the bridegroom should take the *śulka* given or the ornaments and so forth. Regarding the maiden's property (*kanyādhana*), Bodhāyana says:
The uterine brothers themselves shall take the inheritance of a deceased maiden;
in their absence, it shall belong to her mother, and in her absence, it shall belong to her father.
Bṛhaspati states, after enumerating the secondary mothers, those who take the inheritance:
"A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal uncle’s wife,
a father’s sister, a mother-in-law, and the wife of an elder brother are declared to be equal to a mother."
"If these [women] have no son born of their own body, nor a daughter's son, nor the son of such a daughter, then their wealth shall be inherited by the sister's son and the others."

The sister’s son (svasrīya) of the female owner of wealth—the nephew (bhāgineya)—shall obtain the property of his maternal grandmother. Those included by the word “and so forth” (evam-ādi) shall likewise obtain the wealth of their respective mothers’ equals, according to the order of succession. In the same manner, the offspring of a co-wife (sapatnī-saṃtāna) shall also obtain the wealth of that stepmother upon the absence of her own offspring, her husband, and others. Manu states that even when a husband or others are present, a specific type of offspring of co-wives is entitled to share in the stepmother’s wealth: "Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father..."
The Brāhmaṇī wife shall take that [property], or it shall belong to her daughter or to her offspring.

By stating "given by the father," he indicates that this applies even when the previously mentioned heirs—the husband, father, and so forth—are present. The meaning is that the property of a wife of a different caste from her husband shall be inherited, in the absence of her offspring, by a daughter who is of the same caste as the husband, or by her offspring. Furthermore, among several wives of the same caste as the husband, if one dies without offspring, neither another wife nor her offspring shall inherit her property; rather, it should be understood that in the case of marriages such as the *brāhma* and others, the husband alone inherits, while in the remaining cases, the giver of the wealth inherits. This summary of the stated matter was provided by Kātyāyana.
"This is the law regarding a woman's property, and its division has been prescribed.
Thus, the meaning is that this law has been defined and the division of a woman's property has been determined.
This concludes the section on the division of wealth acquired through a woman in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the division of wealth acquired through a secondary father (gauṇapitṛ): on this point, Manu says:
"Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs to the estate of the father."
But surely,
the legitimate son alone is the master of his father's wealth?

Since this has been stated by that very [author], there is no possibility of brothers or others inheriting the father’s estate; therefore, how can their exclusion be appropriate? Nor should it be argued that this applies to the case of one whose sons have perished, for such an interpretation would contradict the injunction that “sons are the inheritors of the father’s estate. It is replied: in the statement “sons are the inheritors of the father’s estate,” the words *pitṛ* (father) and *putra* (son) are used in a figurative sense. Thus, the meaning is as follows: sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and others inherit the estate of the father who owns the field and so forth, but not his brothers and the like. Furthermore, sons such as the *kṣetraja* have also been indicated by him [in this context].
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or has become an outcast,
to a wife duly appointed according to her own dharma, is known as a *kṣetraja* (field-born) son.
If the mother or the father should give a son with water in times of distress—
one who is similar and given with affection— he is to be known as a *dattrima* (given) son.
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the "artificial" (kṛtrima) son.
He who is born in a house but is not recognized by anyone is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him from whose wife he was begotten.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is known as an *apaviddha* (cast-off) son.
The son whom an unmarried girl may bear in secret within her father’s house, one should call him by the name Kānīna; he is born from the maiden, not from her husband.
If a woman who is pregnant is married— whether her condition be known or unknown—
that child belongs to the husband and is called *sahoḍha* (one wedded while pregnant).
If one should purchase from a mother and father a son for the sake of offspring,
he is his "bought" son (krītaka), whether he be similar or dissimilar [to them].
He whom a woman, whether abandoned by her husband or being a widow, bears after marrying again by her own will,
is called *paunarbhava*.
One who is bereft of parents, or has been abandoned by them without cause,
and who offers himself to someone— that person is known as one "given by himself" (svayamdatta).
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is indeed a corpse even while still alive;
therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava.
"The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* as described above, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites. [669]

The phrase "with water" (*adbhiḥ*) is intended as an illustration for the procedure of giving away a son; that procedure has been demonstrated by us under the section on *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what has been given). "In times of distress" (*āpadi*) means during a famine or the like, or otherwise when the recipient is in distress and lacks a son. "Similar" (*sadṛśam*) means of the same caste (*savarṇa*) as both the giver and the recipient. "Endowed with affection" (*prītisaṃyuktam*) means not motivated by greed or other such factors. "One should perform" (*prakuryāt*) means one should adopt a childless person as a son. Regarding the statement "whether similar or dissimilar," the word "in terms of qualities" (*guṇāpekṣayā*) is to be supplied. "Abandoned in the house by the wife" means discarded due to reasons such as being born at an inauspicious moment, and not because of a loss of caste (*pātitya*). "A living corpse" (*jīvann eva śavaḥ*) refers to one who is alive but like a corpse. The connection is as follows: fearing the "loss of rites" (*kriyālopa*)—that is, the omission of rites such as the *śrāddha* performed by him in the absence of a biological son (*aurasa*)—the wise have said that one should adopt these secondary sons (*gauṇaputra*). Thus, while the adoption of all these aforementioned secondary sons as sons was permitted in other ages, in the Kali age, it applies only to the *datta* (given) son.
But for those other than the son given (datta) and the son of the breast (aurasa), there is the formal acceptance as a son.

Thus, at the beginning of the Kali age, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, high-souled beings prohibited the adoption of sons other than the *aurasa* (legitimate) and *datta* (given) types. From this very statement, the practice of appointing a daughter (*putrikā*) is also prohibited in the Kali age, because a daughter is distinct from the *datta* and *aurasa* categories. Consequently, it should be understood that in the Kali age, in the absence of an *aurasa* son or grandson, only the *dattaka* son is considered a secondary (*gauṇa*) son, and no other. Furthermore, even the primary son does not exist in the Kali age as one born of a wife of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), due to the prohibition against marrying girls of a different caste. And so says a legal text (*dharmavākya*).
"And the marriage of daughters of different castes by the twice-born.

Here too, the ellipsis of the sentence must be understood as: "this was prohibited at the beginning of the Kali age by the great-souled ones for the sake of protecting the Dharma. For this very reason, we do not record the rules for the partition of the property of sons born of women of different castes, nor of secondary sons other than the *datta* (given) son, nor of the *putrikā* (appointed daughter) or her son; since these are not to be practiced nowadays, their inclusion would result in a useless prolixity of the text. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu: "Of brothers born of one father, if even one should have a son..."
Manu declared that all those [ancestors] become possessed of sons through that son.

Thus, that [statement] does not, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), declare that even another brother possesses the status of a son by virtue of that very same [adopted] son; for even when a brother’s son exists, it is understood that the other brother is not a son [in that sense]. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya, in the passage beginning with “the wife, the daughters,” etc., states “of one who has gone to heaven without a son” even when a brother’s son exists. And for this same reason, it is stated therein that a brother’s son inherits the wealth of one who lacks sons only in the absence of a wife, a daughter, or a father. If this is so, what is the status of Manu’s statement? We have already explained in the section defining the eligibility for *śrāddha* that the declaration of other brothers as sons is for the purpose of praising the legitimate son (*aurasa*), just like the expression “the father of the village. As for what was said by the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
If there are many uterine brothers born of one father,
then when a son is born to even one of them, they are all considered to have sons.
This same rule is prescribed for many wives who have a single husband;
if one among them has sons, he alone is the giver of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) for all of them.

Thus, in order to avoid contradiction with what was stated previously, Devasvāmin has explained the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) through this passage: "In both cases, no other substitute (*pratinidhi*) should be made. The meaning is that the intended sense of both statements—namely, the two passages beginning with "if they are born of one [mother]" (*yady ekajātāḥ*)—is that when a brother’s son or a son by a co-wife can somehow be employed as a substitute for a son, no other substitute should be made; this is how the intended meaning is to be understood. And thus, the acquisition of wealth through a secondary father (*gauṇapitṛ*) in the Kali age occurs only in relation to the son known as the *dattaka* (adopted son). On this point, Manu says:
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.

By the force of the word *api* (also/even), it is understood that this applies even when [the son] has been obtained from one of the same lineage (*sagotra*). Here, the meaning of the third quarter of the verse has been explained by Devasvāmin: "He shall indeed take all of his [the adoptive father's] inheritance and his lineage. Thus, it should be understood that through the very act that establishes the status of a son, the adopted son acquires ownership in the wealth of the adoptive father as well as his lineage. Furthermore, it should be understood that in the case of the donor’s wealth, through the very act of giving—which effects the cessation of the status of a son—there occurs the cessation of the adopted son’s ownership and the cessation of the donor’s lineage. It is with this very intention that it was stated:

"The adopted son shall not take the lineage or the inheritance of his biological father. Thus it is said. Even regarding the taking of the adoptive father's inheritance, he shall not take everything in certain cases. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "If a legitimate son (aurasa) should be born after he has been adopted, [the adopted son] shall be entitled to a fourth share. Viṣṇu states:
"But for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father."
Whatever paternal inheritance belongs to someone, he alone shall take it, and no other.

In a case where one brother has a legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the others have sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and so forth, when they die while their wealth remains undivided, a distribution of the grandfather’s property must then be arranged for those sons—the legitimate and the others—by way of the primary and secondary fathers. Even then, upon the birth of a legitimate son, that son receives only a fourth share, because the logic previously established for the others does not cease to apply. This same principle applies even where some brothers are living and some have perished.
Thus concludes the section on the division of wealth acquired through secondary paternal ancestors in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the division of wealth acquired through sons; regarding this, Manu says:

"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves"—the literal meaning of these words is clear, but the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) remains obscure; it has been shown by the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"The wealth of a deceased wealthy man who is destitute of all sons..."
By whom, then, should this now be received? This is what is stated hereafter.

This is the meaning: when there arises the inquiry as to who should now—immediately after his death—take the wealth of a wealthy man who has died without a primary (mukhya) or secondary (gauṇa) son, the answer is that it should be taken by the father and others. This is now stated by Manu regarding the absence of near relatives who provide manifold assistance, in preference to the father and others. Therefore, having recognized that the secondary sons are closer than the father and others, the author of the *Saṃgraha* explained the intent of the verse "the father shall take the property of one without a son" (*pitā hared aputrasya*) as referring to one who is entirely destitute of offspring; this is indeed faultless. However, just as the secondary sons are more proximate than the father and others because they provide both visible and invisible benefits and thus take precedence over them, so too the wife, upon examining the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other sources, is found to take precedence over the father and others in providing visible and invisible benefits; therefore, she is more proximate than them. Consequently, the intended meaning is understood to be that even in the absence of the wife, it is said by Manu: "the father shall take the property of one without a son. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati, having declared the wife’s proximity relative to others by way of her connection characterized by visible and invisible benefits, has shown that in the absence of secondary sons—even while the father and others, down to the end of the family line, are still living—the wife alone is the heir to the husband's wealth.
In the sacred tradition, in the treatises on law, and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's own body, sharing equally in the fruits of both merit and demerit.
For him whose wife has not passed away, half of his body still lives;
while half of the body lives, how could another take possession of the wealth?
When paternal kinsmen— such as fathers or brothers— are present,
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share.

Here, by the second half [of the verse], it is stated that the wife is more closely related than sons and others in the accomplishment of both visible and invisible benefits. As for the meaning of the individual words: in the *Āmnāya* (the Veda), in such passages as "The wife is indeed half of one's self (*ātman*)," the word "self" means the body. This is what is intended: just as half of the body is beneficial—both visibly and invisibly—so too is the wife. In the *Smṛtitantra*, the treatise on Dharma: "Half of the body falls [with sin] for him whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is prescribed."
In such passages as these; and in worldly conduct (*lokācāra*) and in the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*) which follow worldly custom, such as:

"What wise man would abandon a wife who constitutes half of his own body? [674], and so forth. Because of the joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*) to perform *smārta* rites, which yield the fruits of merit and demerit; and because of the absence of a son—meaning one devoid of both primary and secondary sons—the wife is the one qualified for the sacrifice (*yajña*), being consecrated by the *brāhma* and other praiseworthy forms of marriage that confer the right to participate in sacrifices, according to the Smṛti of Pāṇini: "The word *patnī* [is used] in connection with the husband's sacrifice. It is not the other [concubine], for she is excluded by the term *patnī*, as she lacks the status of being a wife (*patnītva*). And thus another Smṛti states:
But a woman who has been purchased for a price is not called a wife;
she is not [fit] for rites to the gods nor for rites to the ancestors; the wise know her to be a slave.

To demonstrate that in the absence of the status of a wife (*patnītva*), a woman provides only visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*), it is said that "they call a slave-girl a wife" (*dāsīṃ viduḥ*). And thus, even the eligibility for ancestral rites (*pitryādi-karman*) is a factor in the entitlement to a share of the husband's property; this is made known by the inclusion of the term "wife" (*patnī*). For this very reason, Prajāpati stated that the acquisition of the husband’s wealth belongs only to a wife who is eligible for authority—having been protected through her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*)—in the performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites: "If the husband has died, a woman devoted to her husband shall obtain his wealth and his Agnihotra fire; this is the eternal law."

By the term *agnihotra*, the fire that serves as its means (*sādhana*) is indicated. A "faithful wife" (*pativratā*) is one who is well-restrained, either by her own penance or by virtue of being entitled to perform Śrauta and Smārta rites, and thus remains in residence with her husband; this is what is meant. The word "woman" (*nārī*) here refers to the wife (*patnī*), because the mention of obtaining the *agnihotra* implies the status of being a wife. Regarding a woman who is entitled to perform the rites, Bṛhaspati has shown her precedence over brothers and others in ancestral ceremonies (*pitrya-karman*):
"In the absence of a son, the wife shall be the heir; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother. On this point, Vṛddha-Manu says:
A wife who is childless, guarding her husband’s bed and remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall herself offer that funeral oblation (piṇḍa) and receive the entire share.

In the latter half [of the verse], however, the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) is to be understood as being set aside by the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*). Consequently, the meaning is this: the wife, possessing the characteristics already mentioned, shall first receive the husband’s entire share and afterwards offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to him; but not her brother or others while she exists. The phrase "guarding the husband’s bed" means she is well-restrained; that is, even while the husband is alive, she remains devoted to vows and other observances without his permission. This is because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The commencement of vows, fasts, restraints, sacrifices, and so forth, with the husband’s permission, is the duty of a woman. By this, it should be understood that even faithfulness (*āstikatā*) is a factor for obtaining the husband’s share, as indicated by the turn of speech. Although it is established that from the very time of marriage the wife has ownership over the entirety of the husband’s property for as long as she lives—though it is dependent [on him]—nevertheless, the phrase "she shall receive" is stated in order to indicate that she acquires a further form of ownership characterized by independence. The meaning of the words "his" (*tat-*) and "entire" (*kṛtsna-*) in the context of the funeral cake has been elaborated upon by Prajāpati.
Having taken movable and immovable property, gold, base metals, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other periods to be performed.

"One should honor paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, the brother-in-law of one's husband, maternal uncles, as well as elders, the protectorless, and guests, by means of offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and acts of public charity (pūrta). Thus it is said.

Base metals refer to tin, lead, and so forth. *Kavya* refers to food intended for the ancestors. *Pūrta* refers to sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the like that constitute parts of rites known as *pūrta*, such as the digging of wells. This is what is meant: having taken the entire share, even including immovable property, the wife—preceded by her husband’s priests and preceptors—should perform the collection of meritorious acts, such as the *śrāddha* and *pūrta* rites which require wealth, as well as acts of charity, according to the wealth she has received, for the sake of securing the spiritual welfare of both her husband and herself. Thus, the argument put forward by some—that the wealth taken by the wife will go to waste, being neither enjoyed by a suitable husband nor beneficial to the owner, and therefore the wife is not an heir to her husband’s wealth—is to be rejected because its reason is unproven. Furthermore, this ownership of the wife should be understood to apply when the husband is divided (separated). As Bṛhaspati says:
Whatever various property, such as inherited wealth and so forth, is recorded as having been divided,
the wife whose husband has died shall receive it, with the exception of immovable property.

Whatever various wealth, such as property and so forth, consisting of both immovable and movable things, is traditionally held to belong to the husband as its owner—all that he shall obtain in the case of partition; this is the meaning. Because of the mention of "partition," it is understood that in the case of non-partition, those living together—such as the father, brothers, and others—shall obtain the wealth of one who has died without a son. "Jāyā" means the wife. The phrase "excluding immovable property" refers to a wife who has no daughters. However, regarding the case of a wife alone [without other heirs], [the inheritance consists of]: "movable property, immovable property, gold, base metals, grain, liquids, and clothing."
Having taken [the offerings], one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other periods to be performed.

Thus, there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statement. Nor should it be argued that, in order to avoid such a contradiction, this [present] statement must refer to a case where the husband's share has not been divided, or to a wife who is devoid of good conduct (*vṛttahīna*). For he (Yājñavalkya) himself states the following in order to refute such an arrangement:
"Even for a wife who is established in good conduct, even when a share has been allotted, she is entitled to immovable property (*sthāvara*)."

Thus, the entitlement to immovable property—which exists as a function of the continuity of the lineage—depends upon possessing that lineage; therefore, the meaning is that a woman who is devoid of it does not deserve immovable property, even if she is established in her station and even regarding divided assets. Furthermore, it was stated by that same author:
"Upon the death of her husband, a woman of noble family shall receive her husband’s share;
for as long as she lives, her ownership is limited, [consisting only of] the right to give, mortgage, or sell."

Thus, "kulapālikā" means a woman who protects her family lineage, that is to say, one who maintains her conduct. This should be understood as intended to establish the lack of independence for female dancers and others whose gifts serve visible worldly purposes—since the rule for giving prescribes such gifts for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) for the support of the elderly, the helpless, and so forth—whereas she retains full independence in giving for the sake of *dharma* and *artha*. Therefore, she herself stated that the gift for the sake of *dharma* and *artha* must indeed be performed incessantly:
"Devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy, and constantly intent on the gift of *dharma*, even a woman without sons shall go to heaven."

For indeed, the act of giving away [the husband] is not appropriate while he remains under another's authority. Likewise, it should be understood that independence regarding pledging and selling for the purpose of procuring wealth to achieve an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is also not prohibited. Furthermore, as stated by Kātyāyana:
"A sonless widow, remaining with her elders and protecting her husband’s bed, may enjoy [his property] until death; after [her death], the heirs shall take possession."

Thus—"Kṣāntā" means she who endures the obstruction to the disposal of wealth by the heirs. This refers to the case where, during the period of non-separation, the father-in-law and others are either incapable of providing protection and maintenance or are preoccupied with other affairs, and the wife herself has acquired undivided property for the sake of her own livelihood. This applies specifically to undivided property; for if it were to apply to divided property, it would result in a contradiction with the established meaning determined by the statements of Vṛddha-Manu and others. When the father-in-law and others are capable of protection and maintenance, and they have taken possession of the undivided estate upon the death [of the husband], the maintenance must be performed by them alone from the wealth thus received. And so says Nārada:
As many virtuous widows as there may be, they must be maintained with clothing and food by the eldest father-in-law,
or by a kinsman of the same lineage, or by any other [relative].

The term "dhanagrāhin" (the one who takes the wealth) is to be understood as the remainder in all cases, beginning with the eldest [son], because the maintenance [of the wife] is contingent upon the taking of the wealth. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"When the husband has gone to heaven, the wife is entitled to food and clothing;
however, if [the estate] was undivided, she receives a share of the wealth until her death."

The meaning is: "a portion of wealth" refers to that amount of wealth by which an untroubled livelihood is secured, and through which the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, as well as optional vows (*kāmyavrata*) and other acts for which women have authority, can be accomplished. The word *tu* (but) has the sense of *vā* (or); thus, the meaning is that she obtains either a portion of wealth or a portion of land sufficient to produce this much wealth, since the mention of "wealth" is intended to indicate the means of subsistence and so forth. Here, the first position concerns wives other than the [principal] wife, because it speaks of her receiving only a small share of property sufficient for mere maintenance. Nārada states the specific small measure of that which is sufficient for mere maintenance: [Included here would be the citation from Nārada.]
A virtuous woman whose husband has died shall receive twenty-four āḍhakas and forty paṇas every year.

An *āḍhaka* is a heap of grain measuring one hundred and eight minus two *prasṛtis*. A *paṇa* is a *kārṣāpaṇa*; this circulates in some regions in place of the eightieth part of a *vyāvahārika-niṣka*. Therefore, in a region where the *paṇa* does not circulate, the eightieth part of a *vyāvahārika-niṣka* is obtained in its stead. Regarding the phrase "even when a share has been made," Bṛhaspati continues:
"One should indeed give either a *piṇḍa* or a share of the field according to one's own will."

The mention of "lump" (*piṇḍa*) is intended to indicate food and clothing. Thus, the meaning is as follows: he should provide food and clothing in the previously mentioned quantity, or a portion of land that yields the previously mentioned share of wealth, for the sake of livelihood to a widow—other than a wife entitled to a husband’s share—in cases where the property has not been partitioned; this is according to his own will. The particle *eva* (only) serves to indicate the necessity of making this provision. The first alternative here refers to a woman who does not serve her mother-in-law and others. An explanatory authority for this will appear further on. He [the author] states that what has been given must be maintained even by those other than the heirs: [He] says the same: "And what has been given must be protected even by those other than the heirs."
Whatever property for her livelihood was given by her father-in-law to women from immovable assets cannot be taken away by others once the father-in-law has died.

The mention of the "father-in-law" (śvaśura) is intended as an illustration for anyone who provides maintenance; the mention of "immovable property" (sthāvara) is likewise intended as an illustration for all forms of wealth. Therefore, it should be understood that even wealth and other assets given to women for their livelihood cannot be taken away by others. However, Kātyāyana states that in certain cases they may be taken away: "A woman devoted to service to her elders is entitled to enjoy her allotted share; if she does not perform such service, he should employ her in manual labor, such as spinning cotton."

The phrase "having taken away the allotted share" is to be understood as the ellipsis. He states the same regarding women who commit improper acts and so forth, that they must likewise be deprived of their allotted shares:
"A woman who is engaged in misconduct, shameless, a squanderer of wealth, and one who is devoted to infidelity—such a woman does not deserve property. [680]

The meaning is that the four kinds of women mentioned—whether it be wealth consisting of a portion of property set aside for subsistence, or a portion of land set aside for the purpose of livelihood and so forth—are not entitled [to such maintenance]. The mention of "wealth" (dhana) is intended to include food, clothing, and other necessities. For this very reason, Nārada says: "They should provide maintenance for the women until the end of their lives, provided they preserve the bed of their husband; otherwise, they may withhold it from the others."

Regarding the others who are devoted to adultery: "they shall confiscate" means they may seize or take away the provisions—namely, the wealth consisting of grain and the value of clothing—intended for their maintenance, which is to say, for food and clothing. As for what was stated here by Manu:
"One should apply this very same rule even to women who have become outcasts;
however, food and clothing must be given to them, and they should live near the house."

Thus, since it is understood from the first half of the verse itself that this refers to maintenance performed by the husband, there is no contradiction. However, as for a wife who is suspected of infidelity, even though she remains a wife in a divided estate, the rule stated by Hārīta must be followed: "If a widow is in her youth and becomes harsh [in conduct], then a livelihood must be provided for the sake of exhausting her lifespan."

She is harsh, cruel, deserving of rashness, and suspected of infidelity—this is the meaning. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu—"the wife alone shall receive the entire share"—which contradicts what was spoken by Vṛddhamanu:
"If the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his allotted share, or if either of them should die, his portion is not lost."
The uterine brothers, having come together and being united, shall divide it equally;
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.

Thus— "is deprived" (hīyate)— the remainder being "on account of causes such as loss of caste" (pātityādinimitta)— furthermore, after Nārada had stated: "But for those who are reunited, the share belongs to them alone," he said:
If among brothers one should die without offspring or should renounce the world,
the remaining brothers shall divide his property, excluding the woman's property.

Thus, it is quite clear that both of these [statements] refer to the subject of reunited property; therefore, there is no contradiction. And so, the rule stating, "the wife alone shall receive the entire share," should be understood as referring to the case of those who are divided and not reunited. Accordingly, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says: "When brothers have been divided, even if they were later reunited, or when they are deceased, the wife, being appointed by the command of her elders, shall obtain the wealth."

The view of Dhāreśvara—that "those appointed by the command of the guru are entitled to the office"—should be disregarded, as it has been thoroughly refuted by Viśvarūpa and others. Therefore, regarding the subject matter mentioned by the author of the *Saṃgraha*, one should adhere to this very opinion: that the wife, endowed with the qualities mentioned by Vṛddha-Manu, shall obtain the husband's entire property. As for what is stated in the Śruti—"Therefore women are without power and without inheritance"—that too does not contradict the statements of Vṛddha-Manu and others, because it is understood from its association with the term "powerless sons" (*nirindriya-putra*) to refer specifically to women who are offspring. Or, even if it were understood to apply to all women, nevertheless, the scriptural explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning inheritance refers to those other than the wives and so forth specifically named, such as the *patnī*, and thus everything remains consistent. When there are many wives, it is proper that they all share the property of a sonless husband equally. Prajāpati states that those who obstruct the wife’s right to the property—this being determined through the uniformity of all the Smṛtis—must be restrained by the king.
If her sapindas or kinsmen should obstruct her or seize her property, the king shall punish them with the same penalty as for a thief.

Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, regarding the division of wealth acquired through a son, the matters concerning the wife have been concluded; now, some statements concerning daughters and others are written.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"The wife is the one who takes the husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is declared [the heir].

By "in her absence," the meaning is "due to her non-existence. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "The wealth of one who has no son goes to the wife; in her absence, it goes to the daughter. Bṛhaspati states the underlying principle regarding this sequence:
"From every limb of men, the daughter is produced just like a son."
Therefore, how could another man take the paternal wealth?

By virtue of the connection with the constituent parts of the body, a daughter is equal to a son; for while the paternal elements are transmitted in greater quantity to the son, they are transmitted in lesser quantity to the daughter, according to the Smṛti: "A male is born when the male seed is in excess, and a female when that of the female is in excess. Therefore, she is said to be "like a son" due to some degree of commonality. The meaning is: how can another person—other than the son or the wife, such as the father or others—take the son's property while the daughter remains? Thus says Manu: [683]
Just as one’s self, so is one’s son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's own self, how could another take the wealth?

The meaning is: "in oneself" (ātmani) means [in a situation] where there is a son equal to oneself. Now, even so, the logical principle (*nyāya*) regarding the sequence [of inheritance] following the daughter in the absence of both secondary sons (*gauṇaputra*) and a wife has not been stated; for the stated principle establishes only that the daughter inherits upon the mere absence of the legitimate son (*aurasa*). True; however, this was stated with the intention that this very same principle should be inferred (*ūhanīya*) for the sequence following the daughter in the absence of both secondary sons and a wife. For this very reason, Nārada himself, for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect, demonstrated the principle following the sequence by stating that the daughter inherits in the absence of those two as well.
"But in the absence of a son, the daughter [inherits], because she is seen to provide an equivalent lineage. Thus he himself explains the reasoning:
"Both the son and the daughter are equal in producing a lineage."

The meaning is that both are performers of the welfare of their respective fathers and creators of their lineages. For indeed, since there is no equality between a grandson and a daughter’s son—that is, between the lineages of a son and a daughter—in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is intended here that they are equal in terms of their function (*kārya*). Nor is equality possible in terms of the function of discharging a debt, because of the traditional legal text (*smṛti*) stating, "A debt must be paid by sons and grandsons. Likewise, with respect to the property of a grandfather, it is said: "In that regard, the ownership of both the father and the son shall be equal."

Since the superiority of the grandson (*pautra*) is understood from such traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*), it is intended here that they are equal in terms of their unseen effect (*adṛṣṭakārya*). And that [effect] consists in being the giver of the *śrāddha* for the ancestors; for in the utterance of *svadhā*, grandsons are considered to be the same as granddaughters (*dauhitraka*).

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Viṣṇu. And in this way, the daughter’s proximity is established through her connection to the father by means of the invisible benefit (adṛṣṭopakāra) flowing through her own lineage. On account of this much reason, it should be understood that in the statement, “In the absence of a son, however, the daughter,” the mention of the “son” is intended to indicate the wife as well. Now, an objection may be raised: since the father himself provides the invisible benefit in the performance of the Śrāddha, he is more proximate than the daughter; therefore, in the absence of a wife, the occasion for the rule “the father shall take [the estate] of one who has no son” has arrived. How then can the daughter be entitled to the property? Not so.

Since it has been stated by this very [text]: "While she remains in his own self (as his daughter), how could another take the wealth?", it is so; for even though she is separated by a connection of invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭopakāra*), she is nevertheless not separated by a connection of the body (*śārīrasambandha*). Thus, because of this twofold connection, the daughter alone is the foremost. If that were so, then the occasion for the rule "the father shall take [the estate]" would arise only in the absence of a daughter. But even now there is no occasion for that, because even in the absence of a daughter, the grandson (*dauhitra*) belongs to her category and is thus closer than the father and others;
therefore, in the lineage where there is no son or grandson, the grandsons shall obtain the wealth.
But at the offering of *svadhā* for the ancestors, the grandsons and daughters' sons are considered [the ones who perform it].

This is also because of the recollection of Viṣṇu. Thus, by stating with supporting reasoning that the property goes to the daughter in the absence of a wife, the collection of texts which enjoin that the wealth goes to the son of the daughter (*dauhitra*)—as formulated by Bṛhaspati and others—must be understood as referring exclusively to the *putrikā* (appointed daughter), and not to a daughter who is not an appointed daughter. Therefore, the opinion of Dhāreśvara, Devasvāmin, and Devarāta—that such texts apply to daughters other than the *putrikā*—should be known as refuted; it is a fabrication born of the madness of imagining one's own mastery of the *Smṛtitantṛ*. For instance, according to the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*, "The third [type of] son is known as the *putrikā*," the *putrikā* is included within the category of secondary sons (*gauṇaputra*). Consequently, even when a wife exists, just as in the case of the *kṣetraja* and other such sons, [the property goes to the daughter]. [685]

"Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons are heirs to the father's estate"—by such other scriptural statements, the wife’s right to a share of the wealth as the primary heir in the absence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*) is already established by the very logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpa-nyāya*). Why, then, was it necessary for Bṛhaspati and others to initiate further statements to establish her entitlement to the wealth with supporting arguments? Consequently, that view has been refuted by those very [statements]; therefore, enough of our effort in attempting to refute the opinions of Dhāreśvara and others. As for what was stated by Nārada concerning a wife who is childless: [The text continues with the citation of Nārada.]
If, however, she should have a daughter, her paternal share is intended for her maintenance;
until her marriage she may take that portion, but thereafter her husband shall maintain her.

The meaning of this is as follows: if a daughter exists for that wife who is without a son, then, regarding the maintenance of the daughter, the paternal share is intended for her support. Therefore, until the sacrament of marriage, the daughter shall take the father’s portion solely for the purpose of maintenance, and not for the purpose of disposal according to her own will. Thus, it is understood that the general rule (*utsarga*) is that all unmarried daughters have a right to their father’s property. Consequently, one must state that all those texts which constitute exceptions (*apavāda*) to this—establishing a daughter’s right to her father’s property—refer exclusively to the *putrikā* (appointed daughter); for if they applied to daughters in general, they would be redundant, as they would be incapable of constituting exceptions to the general rule. Therefore, one should indeed follow the opinion of Hāreśvara and others, provided that the statement of Nārada pertained to the case of partitioned property. However, through a careful examination of its preceding and following context, it is clearly understood that it actually pertains to the case of reunited coparceners (*saṃsṛṣṭin*). Thus, regarding the case of partition, those texts which establish the daughter's inheritance serve only to grant that right and do not constitute an exception; we find no basis whatsoever for assuming they refer specifically to the *putrikā*. Enough of this prolixity. Even so, those texts do not apply to daughters in general, as Kātyāyana says: [Text of Kātyāyana follows]
"The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall inherit his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall go to the daughter, provided she is unmarried and not established [in a household]."

Thus, the statements of Kātyāyana should be understood as referring either to an unmarried daughter, or else to a married daughter who is destitute. By "destitute" (*nirdhana*) alone, one who is "unestablished" (*apratiṣṭhitā*) is intended here; she is not, however, one who is unestablished due to a lack of progeny through barrenness or similar conditions, for since such a woman lacks a connection to invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) by way of offspring, she cannot logically be an heir to the wealth. By the phrase "in her absence," the absence of the previously mentioned wife—one who is non-deviant—is referred to, and not merely the mere status of being a wife. It should be understood that it is not only in the absence of the wife’s essential nature that the daughter becomes the heir to the wealth, but also in the absence of the qualifying characteristic of being non-deviant. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states:
Even in the absence of such a wife, a daughter is entitled to the wealth.

Thus it has been stated. It is not merely because of the absence of the wife’s essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather for the purpose of defining her as an heir to the wealth; the meaning is that even in the absence of a wife characterized by the aforementioned qualifications, the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is entitled to the wealth. As for the claim that "the appointed daughter is entitled to the wealth," that should be disregarded, as it has already been refuted previously. Therefore, the distinction of subject matter made by some—namely, that when the wife’s essential nature is absent, the property goes to the daughter, but when her qualifications are absent, it goes to the father and others as stated in such texts as "the father shall take"—should also be disregarded. Bṛhaspati, however, states the qualifications for daughters who receive the wealth after the wife, and those who receive the wealth after the primary son. [687]
A virtuous wife, of equal status, wedded to a husband of equal status, who is devoted to service—
whether she has borne sons or not, she shall indeed inherit the wealth of her father.

*Sadṛśī* means of the same caste (*savarṇā*) as the father. Here, the first four qualifiers refer to the daughter who inherits the property after the wife; however, the remaining two apply to the daughter who inherits before the wife. In the phrase *kṛtākṛtā*, the term *putrikā* (appointed daughter) must be supplied as the substantive; in the other case, the term *duhitā* (daughter) must be supplied. The word *vā* (or) is intended to express a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). Thus, the meaning is this: the property of a father who has no legitimate son (*aurasa*) shall first be taken by the appointed daughter, even if she is of two kinds [married or unmarried]; but after the wife, it goes to a daughter endowed with the qualifications of being of the same caste and so forth. Furthermore, when there is a group of daughters after the wife—consisting of those endowed with the qualifications of being of the same caste and so forth, whether they are unmarried or married—the unmarried one alone takes it, because she is to be maintained by the father. In her absence, the unmarried but not yet established (*apratiṣṭhitā*) daughter takes it, for although she is to be maintained by her husband, she is considered "not established" due to the husband's lack of capacity to maintain her. In her absence, the daughter endowed with the qualifications of being of the same caste and so forth, but who is established (*pratiṣṭhitā*), takes it, because she is fit to inherit the property despite being established. In her absence, the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) takes it, as he belongs to that same category. This is how it should be understood. In the absence of the daughter’s son, however, since there is no one else more proximate than the father, and because the occasion arises for what was stated [in Manu 9.185], "The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son," the property goes to the father. At this very stage, since there is no one else more proximate than the mother, [the property goes to her].
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring.

Since this has been stated, the wealth goes to the mother; for this very reason, Yājñavalkya said: "The wife, the daughters, and the parents. By the word *ca* (and), the mother and father are indicated as heirs simultaneously immediately after the daughter's son (*dauhitr*), because there is no logical basis for an internal sequence between them. This is the intention of Yājñavalkya that must be understood. Failing to grasp this intention, some who consider themselves scholars have imagined a certain logic here: namely, that the mother is an exceedingly great benefactor by virtue of conceiving and nourishing the child in the womb.

Furthermore, because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "the mother exceeds the father a thousandfold in terms of dignity," it follows that even while the father is living, the mother alone has the right to take the wealth. However, this reasoning is not sufficient to establish the mother's prior right to take a share, because the father also acts as the provider in many ways, bestows learning, and— since the primacy of the seed is observed— it is the father who is superior even to those two.

And because of this traditional authority (*smaraṇa*). Others, however, have conjectured otherwise: "The father is common to the sons of his co-wives, but the mother is not; thus, there is a superior degree of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). This is like a deception, for there is no gradation in the proximity between the mother and father toward their offspring. Nor does the superiority of proximity—which is based on a direct relationship—depart simply because of many other (indirect) relationships. As for what was said by those same people: "Even when there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*), the priority of the mother is somehow understood," that too is weak. Since there is no perception of order in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) "You two become Sarasvatīs," the order of the two principal acts is shown in the fifth book [of the *Tantravārttika*] according to the order of the *yājyā* verses, rather than the order being established somehow through the single-remainder compound "Sarasvatī and [Sarasvant]" (*sārasvatau*). Thus, the justification for the mother’s priority is entirely without foundation. For this very reason, Śrīkara stated that the parents should divide and take the inheritance separately. That too is incorrect, because from the two texts—"The father shall take the estate of one who dies without a son" and "The mother shall obtain the inheritance of one who has died without a son"—there is a perception of independent ownership, just as rice and barley are independent means [of sacrifice]. Others again propose another way to understand the mother's proximity: "In the rule 'But for a uterine brother, a uterine brother,' since the mention of inheritance in the uterine brother is by way of the mother, the mother's proximity is understood. This is merely clutching at straws (*kāśakuśāvalambana*). For instance, while there is a distinction in proximity between a half-brother and a uterine brother due to having the same mother, we do not know what basis there could be for a distinction in the mother's proximity toward her son compared to the father. Therefore, when the question arises as to the order between the parents when both are present, a specific statement must be made. As for what was said by Śambhu: "Because property is held in common by husband and wife, whatever is taken by either is for the sake of both; thus, no distinction need be stated," that is incorrect. When the property is taken by the mother, it is for the mother alone—just like the woman's property belonging to the fire-altar (*adhyagni*) and so on—and is not for the sake of both; therefore, a distinction must indeed be stated. That is now explained: in the absence of any logical principle (*nyāya*), the scriptural statement itself is the refuge here. And in that statement, the father's right to take the wealth first is established. Thus, following the text "The wealth of one without a son goes to the wife; in her absence, it goes to the daughter," Bṛhad-Viṣṇu says in continuation: "In her absence, it goes to the father; in his absence, it goes to the mother. Although it is stated that the wealth of one without a son goes to the father upon the absence of a daughter, nevertheless, since the going to the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) in the absence of a daughter is established by both logic and scripture, the going to the father should be understood to occur only upon the absence of the daughter's son. It should also be considered that Bṛhad-Viṣṇu did not mention the daughter's son separately because he is included within the category of "daughter. Upon the mother's absence, the going to the uterine brother is obtained by the logic of the superior proximity of the deceased brother due to having the same mother; and upon his absence, the going to the half-brother. This very sequence, rooted in logic, was stated by Yājñavalkya: "The parents, and likewise the brothers. Here, "brothers" refers specifically to uterine brothers, as they are more proximate to the owner of the wealth than half-brothers. Thus, Yājñavalkya has shown the general rule (*utsarga*) that the wealth of one without a son goes to the uterine brother upon the mother's absence. Furthermore, by using the general term "brothers" even when intending to specify the quality of being uterine, he has shown by that same act the rule that half-brothers take it in the absence of uterine brothers. Kātyāyana states the exception (*apavāda*) to this general rule in two cases that will be mentioned later.
When [the estate] has been partitioned and settled, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the father of that [mother], in that order.

The mother of that father—meaning the mother of the father who died after partition—is the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*). The mention of the "son" is for the purpose of indicating those who are more proximate. Therefore, the meaning is that in the absence of those more proximate than the father—starting from the son and ending with the daughter’s son—who are related to the father through visible and invisible services and so forth, the father shall first take the property. The three occurrences of the word "or" (*vā*) here all signify alternatives regarding their absence. Since a thing established as a reality under the name of "ownership" cannot be subject to an option according to the maxim "a thing is not to be optionalized," an equal option is impossible here. Thus, this is what is stated: in the absence of the father, the brother shall take; in his absence, the mother; in her absence, the paternal grandmother—in this order, meaning according to the sequence of the text. And by this very order, in the case of one who has remained separate after partition, Manu also—having used the term "one without a son" (*aputrasya*) as an indicative expression to denote the absence of the more proximate heirs such as the son, wife, daughter, and daughter’s son—states in a half-verse that the father, brother, mother, and paternal grandmother shall take the wealth.
The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, or the brothers themselves;
in the absence of offspring, the mother shall obtain the estate of the deceased son.
"And when the mother has also passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is: "of one who is sonless," that is, one who is devoid of sons, wives, daughters, and grandsons. And thus, the sequence for the succession to wealth among those beginning with the father and ending with the grandfather, as set forth by Kātyāyana and Manu, is based solely on scriptural injunction; therefore, one should not entertain any suspicion here of a conflict with logic, as that would contradict the sequence [established by] the authoritative texts. It is the very statement of Yājñavalkya that is intended to define the order, since its priority is made explicit there by the direct expression: "in the absence of the former, each subsequent one. Consequently, even the interpretation that those statements which appear contradictory to it—such as "the father shall take the property of one who has no son"—are merely concerned with establishing eligibility (*adhikāra*) should be disregarded. This is because the sequence is explicitly remembered in the two statements of Kātyāyana: "or the mother, according to the order of her [own] father," and "and when the mother has also passed away. Regarding the specific point that the brother is the first heir to the mother's wealth, Bṛhaspati states:
"But for one who has died separated from his family, being deprived of wife and sons,
it should be known that the mother is the heir to the estate, or else the brother with her permission."

Regarding that deceased person: the mention of the "wife" (*bhāryā*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the daughter, granddaughter, and father, who are bound by a fixed order according to legal principle. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "one who is devoid of son, wife, daughter, granddaughter, and father. And thus, an exception to the stated order—"the parents, and likewise the brothers"—must be applied in the case of the mother’s authorization and in the case of a living paternal grandmother, following the order prescribed by Kātyāyana and others. By this, the following argument is refuted: "Since the sequence of mother, father, brother, and son is fixed by the statement 'the parents, and likewise the brothers, and their sons,' there can be no insertion in the middle; therefore, after the brother's lineage, the paternal grandmother takes the property, as there is no contradiction since no specific order for her has been stated. For it is not the case that no specific order for the paternal grandmother has been stated, because a specific order for the paternal grandmother was already demonstrated previously through the word *atha* in the reading of Kātyāyana’s text, and by the two words "when the mother has passed away" (*mātari vṛttāyām*) in the Mānava (Manu) text. Furthermore, even though that fixed order is based on legal principle (*nyāyamūla*), there is the possibility of an intermediate insertion based on explicit scriptural statement (*vacanamūlaka*). As for what was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita—"the property of one who has gone to heaven without a son goes to the brothers; in their absence, the parents shall take it"—that stands as an exception to the general rule in cases other than those of separate inheritance, specifically regarding one who has gone to heaven after being reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), and thus there is no contradiction. As for what was stated by Bṛhaspati:
In the absence of a son, however, the wife shall be [the heir]; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the descendant; and after that, the daughter's son shall inherit the wealth.

Thus, that [rule] is intended to exclude the uterine brothers (*sodara*) prior to the wife; it does not, however, intend to establish the priority of the uterine brother over the daughters designated by the term *dāyāda* (heirs). For if that were the case, it would result in a contradiction with his own statement: "A daughter arises from every limb, just like a son. As for what was stated by Devala:
"Thereafter, the uterine brothers shall divide the inheritance of one who has no son;
or the daughters who are equal [in status], or the father, if he is living."
"The brothers, the mother, or the wife, according to their respective order, shall be of the same caste. [693] Thus it is said.

Although a disjointed connection (*vyavahitānvaya*) is perceived here due to the natural flow of the phrasing, nevertheless, for the sake of not contradicting the logic of all the preceding statements, the meaning must be understood precisely through that disjointed connection. To explain: "The wife or the *patnī* shall obtain the inheritance of one who has no son; or else, daughters of equal caste (*savarṇāḥ*) shall divide it; or else, the father, being *dhriyamāṇaḥ*—that is, existing—shall take it.
