From the word *dhriyamāṇaḥ*, which would otherwise be redundant, it is understood that the sequence of connection is: "if the father is not present, the mother [takes it]"; thus, in the absence of the father, the mother shall obtain it. After her, the uterine brothers (*sahodarāḥ*) and brothers of equal caste shall divide it in order—first the uterine brothers, and in their absence, those of equal caste—without deviating from this sequence. This should be understood as applying to cases where there is an absence of both the mother’s authorization and the grandmother. Even regarding this matter, Kātyāyana has shown the sequence for the sake of easy understanding: "First the mother, then the father, then the paternal grandmother; then the uterine brothers, then the half-brothers; then the daughter, then the daughter’s son; then the wife, then the brother-in-law; then the father-in-law, then the maternal uncle; then the paternal uncle, then the sister’s son; then the pupil, then the fellow-student; then the king, then the learned Brāhmaṇa. (Kātyāyana, *Vyavahāranirṇaya*, 651–652) In this context, the term *patnī* refers to the wife who is a co-sharer in the religious rites (*yajñasahabhāryā*), as indicated by the rule: "The wife is called *patnī* because she shares in the sacrifice" (*patyuna yajñasamyoge*). She is the one who obtains the share when the husband dies without sons. The term *duhitaraḥ* refers to unmarried daughters; married daughters do not receive a share, as they have already obtained property through their marriage. The term *pitā* refers to the biological father, not the stepfather, because the latter is not entitled to inherit. The term *bhrātaraḥ* refers to uterine brothers, not half-brothers, because the former are entitled to the entire estate while the latter are entitled only to a portion. The term *bhāryā* refers to the wife who is a co-sharer in the religious rites, not a concubine (*parigrahiṇī*), because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *mātā* refers to the biological mother, not a stepmother, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *pitāmahī* refers to the biological grandmother, not a step-grandmother, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *snuṣā* refers to the daughter-in-law, not a daughter-in-law of another, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *svasā* refers to a sister of the same caste, not a sister of a different caste, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *pautraḥ* refers to a son of a daughter, not a son of a daughter’s daughter, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *pitṛvyaputraḥ* refers to the son of a paternal uncle, not the son of a paternal uncle’s son, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *śiṣyaḥ* refers to a student initiated by the deceased, not a student initiated by another, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *sabrahmacārī* refers to a fellow-student initiated by the same teacher, not a student initiated by the same teacher as the deceased’s teacher, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *rājā* refers to a king of the same caste, not a king of a different caste, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *brāhmaṇaḥ* refers to a learned Brāhmaṇa, not an unlearned one, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *vidvān* refers to one who knows the meaning of the Veda, not one who merely knows the words, because the latter is entitled only to maintenance. The term *kuṭumbinām* refers to householders, not ascetics (*pravrajitānām*), because the latter are entitled only to maintenance. The term *sarveṣām* refers to all these heirs, not to others, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *dāyam* refers to the property of the deceased, not the property of others, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *haret* refers to the taking of the inheritance, not the taking of other property, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *api vā* indicates an alternative, not a conjunction, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *atha vā* indicates a further alternative, not a conjunction, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *tulyāḥ* refers to those of equal caste, not those of different castes, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *savarṇāḥ* refers to those of the same caste, not those of a different caste, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *duhitaraḥ* refers to unmarried daughters, not married daughters, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *vibhajeran* refers to the division of the inheritance, not the division of other property, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *api vā* indicates an alternative, not a conjunction, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *dhriyamāṇaḥ* refers to one who is living, not one who is dead, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *pitā* refers to the biological father, not the stepfather, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *haret* refers to the taking of the inheritance, not the taking of other property, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *anarthaka-* refers to the word *dhriyamāṇa-*, which would be redundant if it did not indicate the sequence of the mother's right. The term *adhyamāṇe* refers to the state of not being present, not the state of being dead, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *pitari* refers to the father, not the grandfather, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *mātā* refers to the biological mother, not the stepmother, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *vāpnuyāt* refers to the obtaining of the inheritance, not the obtaining of other property, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *tataḥ* refers to after the mother, not before her, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *sahodarāḥ* refers to uterine brothers, not half-brothers, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *savarṇāḥ* refers to those of equal caste, not those of different castes, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *ca* refers to a conjunction, not an alternative, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *bhrātaraḥ* refers to brothers, not sisters, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *yathākramam* refers to according to the sequence, not out of order, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *pūrvam* refers to first, not last, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *sahodarāḥ* refers to uterine brothers, not half-brothers, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *tattadabhāve* refers to in the absence of each preceding one, not in the presence of any, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *savarṇāḥ* refers to those of equal caste, not those of different castes, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *iti* refers to the end of the sequence, not the beginning, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *kramānatikrameṇa* refers to without violating the sequence, not by skipping it, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *vibhajeran* refers to the division of the inheritance, not the division of other property, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *mātranujñāyāḥ* refers to the authorization of the mother, not the authorization of others, because others are entitled only to maintenance. The term *pitāmahyāḥ* refers to the grandmother
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters [are entitled];
in their absence, the father, mother, brother, and sons are declared [to be so].

The word *putra* (son), being a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), applies by the logic of the word itself to brothers' sons as well. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya stated: "Brothers, and likewise their sons. As for what was said by the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"Even in the absence of such a daughter, the mother shall obtain the wealth;
even when the father exists, [so shall she] in the presence of a lineage of co-wives' sons."
In the absence of such a mother, the father’s mother shall take the wealth;
even while the father is living, so too in the case of a lineage consisting of sons born of Kṣatriya wives.

"Even in the absence of the paternal grandmother, the father shall obtain the wealth"—in this regard, if the word "provided that there exists" (*vidyamānāyām*) is supplied after the phrase "in the lineage of sons" (*sutasaṃtatau*), the meaning becomes easy to understand. However, since this [interpretation] is based on a legal principle (*nyāya*) conceived by Dhāreśvara, and because Viśvarūpa and others have refuted that principle, it is to be disregarded entirely in the absence of a foundational legal principle. Furthermore, he himself stated:
"If there are brothers, they are of two kinds: uterine and non-uterine."
Even when a non-uterine brother exists, only the uterine brothers are entitled to the inheritance.

Thus, because this is rooted in sound reasoning (*samyag-nyāya*), it is to be respected. This distinction regarding nephews (*bhrātṛ-suta*) should also be understood to apply when there is a combination of sons of uterine and non-uterine brothers. Consequently, in the absence of sons of uterine brothers, the sons of brothers from different mothers (*sapatnī-bhrātṛ-suta*) are the heirs. When the question arises as to who the heirs are in their absence, Yājñavalkya states: "The *gotrajas* (those born of the same lineage). The word "heirs" (*dhanabhājaḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Here, by the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the term *gotraja* refers to those born of the lineage of the grandfather and his descendants, excluding the previously mentioned father, brothers, and their sons. Furthermore, since a singular collective compound (*sarūpaikaśeṣa*) is naturally understood here, it refers to those other than females such as the daughter of the grandfather. Indeed, the understanding of a non-homogeneous collective compound (*virūpaikaśeṣa*) occurs only through another cause, as in the phrase "we shall mate cocks and hens. But no such cause exists here; on the contrary, due to the association with "brothers and their sons," only males are understood as *gotrajas*. Moreover, since the status of heirs for the wife, daughters, and others is established by specific Smṛti texts, and since the Vedic text "therefore women are powerless and not heirs" (*tasmāt striyo nirindriyā adāyādīḥ*) would otherwise have no scope, it was stated that the [Smṛti] refers to those other than them. Therefore, since a homogenous collective compound is possible and consistent with the Smṛti, a non-homogeneous collective compound—which would contradict the Śruti—is cast far aside. For this very reason, while commenting on the Āpastamba Sūtra, "While living, one should divide the inheritance among the sons" (*jīvan putrebhyo dāyaṃ vibhajet*), the commentator stated: "One should divide the inheritance among the sons alone, not among women or daughters. Although it might be argued that, based on the linguistic Smṛti rule "the dual form *bhrātṛputrau* [is used] for brother and sister, son and daughter," one could effect a non-homogeneous collective compound in the Sūtra's "among the sons" (*putrebhyaḥ*) to include daughters as well, nevertheless, the text asserts: "Males are the heirs, not females, because of the Śruti: 'Therefore women are powerless and not heirs. By this, the following view is refuted: some claim that *gotrajas* consist of the grandmother (*pitāmahī*), her *sapindas*, and the *samānodakas*; that among these, the grandmother takes the wealth first; and that although the grandmother’s right to take the wealth after the mother has passed away is established by the text "When the mother has also died, the father’s mother shall take the wealth," she is elevated above the sons and others down to the nephews—because their order is fixed and they cannot intervene—so that she takes the wealth immediately after their sons, as there is no contradiction. However, since the order of the *gotrajas* after the nephews is likewise fixed, the sequence involving the grandmother is sublated here. Because the homogenous collective compound refers only to male *gotrajas* in connection with the nephews, and because the grandmother belongs to a different lineage (*anyagotra*) even if she were deceased, enough of this prolixity. It should be understood that Yājñavalkya’s use of the collective compound *gotrajāḥ* is like the case of "parents" (*pitarau*), as it lacks an intermediate sequence rooted in logic. For there is no logical basis for an intermediate sequence such as "in the absence of nephews, the son of the grandfather is the heir," and so forth. Now, who says that the grandson inherits by skipping over the grandfather? It is Yājñavalkya himself who, having mentioned "brothers and their sons," then mentions the *gotrajas*. Even though the mention of brothers and their sons is already implied by the word *gotraja*, the separate mention of them is intended to indicate that among the *gotrajas*—such as the grandfather and others—the right to inherit belongs specifically to two types of descendants, namely the son and the grandson, just as in the case of the paternal line. This same meaning is also indicated by Manu.
For whoever is the nearest kinsman to the funeral cake-offerer, his shall be the wealth;
after him, the distant relatives (sakulyas) shall inherit, or else the teacher or the pupil.

Dhāreśvara explains this as follows: regarding the phrase "whosoever is immediately next to the *piṇḍa*," the word *piṇḍāt* should be understood in the sense of *sapiṇḍāt* (from the *sapiṇḍa*). But who is this *sapiṇḍa* who serves as the limit? Since the father is the subject under discussion in the rule "the father shall take," it is the father himself. Now, one might object: since the father’s own father and his son are also immediately next to him, when both are present, which one's immediate proximity is logical? We reply: it is that of the sons of the father. Why is this so? Because in the verse, "The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or else the brothers themselves," the word "or else" (*eva*) indicates the absence of a share in the inheritance for the grandfather. Consequently, even though the immediate proximity is equal, by virtue of that very statement, immediate proximity is intended only through the medium of the lineage. Thus, by the phrase "whosoever is immediately next to the *piṇḍa*," in the absence of the father’s lineage, the grandfather’s lineage is designated; in the absence of that too, the great-grandfather’s lineage, and so on, starting from the *sapiṇḍa*. However, in the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, those called *sakulyas* and *samānodakas* are denoted here by the term *sakulya*. In the absence of their nearest lineage, as before, the more remote lineage is entitled to the inheritance. And thus, those who say that after the brother’s son, the grandfather is the heir, and in his absence his lineage, and likewise for the great-grandfather and so on—they do not understand the subtle meaning of the subsequent statements that override the order established by logic. Here is the sequence for obtaining the inheritance: in the absence of the brother’s son, the son of the grandfather obtains the inheritance; in his absence, the son of the great-grandfather; in his absence, the son of the great-great-grandfather; in his absence, the son of the great-great-grandfather’s father; in his absence, the last person of the *sapiṇḍa* line; in his absence, his son; in his absence, the first person of the *samānodaka* line; in his absence, his son; and in this same manner, it should be understood for the six subsequent *samānodaka* lineages. Having all this in mind, Bṛhaspati says: [He provides the following verses: "In the absence of the brother’s son, the son of the grandfather takes the wealth; in his absence, the son of the great-grandfather; in his absence, the son of the great-great-grandfather; in his absence, the son of the great-great-grandfather’s father; in his absence, the last of the *sapiṇḍas*; in his absence, his son; in his absence, the first of the *samānodakas*; in his absence, his son; and so on, up to the sixth degree. Thus ends the section.
Where there are many kinsmen, as well as members of the same lineage and relatives,
he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who has no offspring.

Relatives (*jñāti*) are those of the same *sapinda* lineage, those of the same *sakulya* lineage, and those to whom water is offered (*samānodaka*). However, more proximate kin (*bāndhava*) are shown in another Smṛti text in the following order: "The sons of one's father's sister, the sons of one's mother's sister, and the sons of one's maternal uncle are to be known as one's own kin (*ātmabāndhava*)."
The sons of one's father's paternal aunts, the sons of one's father's maternal aunts,
and the sons of one's father's maternal uncles are to be known as paternal relatives (pitṛbandhu).
"The sons of one's mother's paternal aunts, the sons of one's mother's maternal aunts, and the sons of one's mother's maternal uncles are to be known as maternal kinsmen. Thus it is said.

In the absence of more proximate *jñāti*, *sakulya*, or *bandhu* heirs, one should seek out those who are proximate in any way whatsoever, because of the general rule in the Smṛti of Gautama: "Those connected by funeral offerings (*piṇḍa*), lineage (*gotra*), or *ṛṣi*-ancestry shall divide the inheritance. When the question arises as to who are the heirs in the absence of *bandhus*, Yājñavalkya states: "The student (*śiṣya*) and the fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*). The word "heirs" is to be supplied. A *śiṣya* is one who has been initiated and taught the Veda; a *sabrahmacārin* is one who has had the same teacher. Since the connection to the wealth has already been mentioned for the student through the relationship with the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), the fact that the primary teacher’s claim to the wealth is understood first—by the logic of the "stick and the rice-cake" (*daṇḍāpūpa-nyāya*) when the subordinate is mentioned—is why the teacher is not explicitly named here; this is how it should be understood. When the question arises as to who are the heirs in the absence of a *sabrahmacārin*, Manu says:
But in the absence of all these, Brahmins who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs of the estate; thus the Dharma is not violated.
"The property of a Brāhmaṇa must always be inviolable by the king; such is the established rule.
Regarding the case where no Brāhmaṇa possessing the characteristics described by Manu exists, Nārada says to the king:
"If there is no heir whatsoever for the property of a Brāhmaṇa upon his death..."
It must be given to a Brāhmaṇa alone; otherwise, the king would become a sinner.
"In its loss" means in the loss of the owner of the property. Regarding property other than that belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, Manu says upon its loss:
"But in the case of the other castes, if there is no one [to claim it], the king shall take it.
The "king" is the one who performs the protection of the country, the city, and so forth. Following the principle that "in the absence of all [claimants], the wealth goes to the king," Nārada states:
Except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, however, a king devoted to righteousness shall provide a livelihood for his wives;
this is recorded as the rule for inheritance.

The meaning is: "of their women" refers to the women who are owners of wealth other than that of Brāhmaṇas, and who are themselves ineligible to share in the inheritance. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of all," the author of the *Saṃgraha* states the specific distinctions based on the difference of caste: "Even when the father is absent, the wealth belongs to his paternal lineage; if that [lineage] is absent, it belongs to the paternal grandfather's lineage. [699]
Even in her absence, however, those who are above her in the lineage of the great-grandfather,
being *sapiṇḍas*, are likewise the heirs to the property.
In the absence of those, the kinsmen (sakulyas) shall be the heirs, or the teacher, or even the pupil; likewise, a fellow student—O Brahmins, each subsequent one in the absence of each preceding.
In the absence of a Śūdra’s uterine brother, the king shall receive the property;
likewise, in the absence of a teacher, so too in the case of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.

Thus, because the author of the *Saṃgraha* follows the opinion of Dhāreśvara, he states that even when the father is absent, the wealth belongs to his paternal lineage. However, in this [present] view, it should be understood that when the father is absent, the mother’s wealth [is inherited]; in her absence, that of the paternal grandmother; and in her absence, that of the creditor’s paternal lineage, consisting of the brothers and their sons. All that has been stated regarding the property of one who dies without issue applies, as appropriate, to the case where the owner is a *snātaka* who is outside the stages of life (*āśrama*)—such as the uninitiated, the student (*brahmacārin*), the one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*), or the householder—but not to the property owned by a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*), a forest-dweller (*vanastha*), or an ascetic (*yati*), because other recipients for such property are recorded in the legal tradition. And so says Yājñavalkya:
The heirs of forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students are, in order: the teacher, a virtuous disciple, a spiritual brother, and a fellow student of the same hermitage.

In this context, the term *brahmacārī* is understood to refer to a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*), due to his association with ascetics (*yati*). A "dharma-brother" (*dharmabhrātṛ*) is one who has the same teacher. An "associate of the same sacred site" (*ekatīrthya*) is one who follows the same scripture. The meaning is that, in the absence of each preceding category, each subsequent one is to be approached in order.
Thus ends the section concerning daughters and others in the *Smṛticandrikā* [700].
Now, certain statements concerning reunited brothers (*saṃsṛṣṭabhrātṛ*) and others are recorded as follows:
On this point, Bṛhaspati says: "One who, though previously divided, again comes to live together with his father, a brother,
or an uncle out of affection, is called 'reunited' (saṃsṛṣṭa)."

The meaning is this: when a son or other relative who was previously divided from his father or others, subsequently comes to live together again with that same father or relative—specifically one with whom he was already divided—due to affection or some such cause, he is said to be "reunited" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) with him. Furthermore, it is understood by implication here that there is no such reunion with anyone other than a father, brother, or paternal uncle; that is, not with the sons of brothers or paternal uncles and so forth. Since among men living together there is no physical "reunion" (*saṃsarga*) in the literal sense, reunion must be understood as occurring through the medium of property. It should be understood that reunion does not consist merely of cohabitation, but rather extends to the pooling of assets back into a single mass, thereby removing the defining limitations that served as the basis for the previous transactions regarding distinct shares. For this very reason, Manu, after referring to the division of property being performed once again, describes a specific method for doing so.
If those who were divided but living together should divide again, the division there shall be equal; therein no right of primogeniture exists.

"Living together" means living by means of co-residence; the ellipsis is "they shall divide the commingled property. Since the rule for equal division is already established in that context of dividing commingled property—thereby ensuring that no additional share is taken on account of seniority—this further prohibition against inequality in shares caused by seniority is intended to permit inequality in shares caused by the smallness of the commingled wealth. Therefore, at the time of commingling, the inequality in the division of the commingled property should be determined according to the extent of what was commingled by each person. Thus, it should be understood that the purpose of the commingling is to eliminate uncertainty regarding the identity of the property (*idantā*), and not to eliminate its quantity (*iyattā*). Bṛhaspati states another cause for inequality in shares: *Bṛhaspati*: "One who has been reunited after having separated, or one who is reunited from the beginning, shall receive a share according to his own property. The others shall divide the remainder equally. This means that if a son who had previously separated is reunited with his father, or if he is reunited from the very beginning, he shall take a share proportional to the property he brought into the union. The rest of the estate shall be divided equally among all the sons. This applies even if the reunited son is younger than some of the others. Alternatively, this may be interpreted as referring to a case where the reunited son is the eldest, and the rule serves to exclude the special share (*yautaka*) that would otherwise be due to him by virtue of seniority. Furthermore, Bṛhaspati mentions other causes for inequality: Bṛhaspati: "The eldest son, having given a preferential share (*adhika-bhāga*) to his father, shall take a double share for himself. To the middlemost son, a half-share is ordained; to the youngest, a quarter-share. The meaning is that the eldest son, having provided the father with a preferential share, takes two shares for himself. A half-share is prescribed for the middlemost son, and a quarter-share for the youngest. The term "preferential share" (*adhika-bhāga*) refers to the specific portion traditionally assigned to the eldest. The phrase "having given" (*dattvā*) implies that the eldest son must provide this share to his father before taking his own. If the father is deceased, the eldest son should provide that share to the father's widow or to his brothers. If the father is still living, the eldest son should give it to the father himself. The word *dvayaṃśah* ("double share") indicates that the eldest son receives two shares out of the total remaining estate. The term *ardhabhāk* ("half-sharer") signifies that the middlemost son receives one share and a half. The term *pādabhāk* ("quarter-sharer") signifies that the youngest son receives one share and a quarter. The mention of these specific shares is intended to exclude the special share (*yautaka*) that might otherwise be due to them by virtue of seniority. Alternatively, this may be explained as follows: when the father dies, the eldest son, having given a preferential share to the father's widow or to his brothers, takes two shares for himself. The middlemost son receives one share and a half, and the youngest receives one share and a quarter. The mention of these specific shares is intended to exclude the special share (*yautaka*) that might otherwise be due to them by virtue of seniority. In this context, the term "commingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) refers to the state of being reunited after separation. It does not refer to the mere act of living together, nor to the state of being born of the same parents. The term "commingled" is used here because it denotes a specific relationship between the parties involved. The term "commingled" is also applied to those who have lived together after being separated, as well as to those who were reunited from the beginning. But among those who have lived together, whoever acquires more by means of learning, valor, or other such qualities, to him a double share must be given; the remainder shall have equal shares.

The ellipsis here is "having acquired additional wealth" in that [reunited estate]. This is intended to establish that even property acquired without detriment to the joint estate is subject to partition. Regarding one who has died while among those reunited, provided his sons or other heirs exist, the division must be made according to the rule: "But for those whose fathers have died, the allotment of shares is according to the father," since no other rule is recorded. However, in the absence of sons and others, the principle of the wife and daughter does not apply, because another rule is recorded. And so says Bṛhaspati:
But for brothers who have already divided their inheritance and then live together again out of mutual affection, there is no seniority when they proceed to divide once more.
"When someone dies or somehow renounces the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother."

Just as, prior to the first partition, the share of one who has died without sons or who has renounced the world is lost—because, in the absence of partition, there is no determination of quantity based upon it, and therefore all the inherited property (*riktha*) in that case is taken by all those living together—it is not so here, for there is no absence of a determination of quantity based on partition, since that determination has already been made by the first partition. Nor does that determination disappear through reunion (*saṃsarga*), because reunion merely removes the sense of "this belongs to me" (*idantā*). Therefore, all those reunited need not take the entire inherited property; rather, at the time of partition, each respective share must be set aside separately. And that share, unlike the one belonging to a wife from the very beginning—as in the case of a divided coparcener—is ordained by the scriptural statement for the uterine brother who is reunited. In the phrase "of the uterine brother" (*sodarasya*), the singular number is not intended to be restrictive. For this very reason, Nārada says:
If among brothers one should die childless or renounce the world,
the remaining ones shall divide his property, excluding the woman's separate property.

"The remaining [heirs] are those who have reunited; among them, a uterine brother inherits from a uterine brother. This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Yājñavalkya. The meaning is that the wealth of a brother who has reunited shall be taken by a brother who has also reunited, and not by the wife or others; even in that case, it must be a uterine brother. If it is then asked what becomes of the wives and the unmarried daughters of the deceased in this situation, Nārada says:
They should provide for his maintenance until the end of their lives, provided they preserve the bed of their husband; in the case of others, that [duty] would cease.
"The paternal share of his daughter is considered for her maintenance;

until her marriage, she shall take her portion, but thereafter her husband shall maintain her. The intended meaning of this second verse should be understood as follows: the remaining [heirs] alone shall perform both the marriage of that deceased or renunciant's daughter and her maintenance prior to that event. Furthermore, where there are uterine brothers among the remaining heirs—even if they are not *saṃsṛṣṭa* (united in property)—those uterine brothers who are *saṃsṛṣṭa* shall themselves divide [the estate].

Having introduced the rule, "But the share of those who are reunited belongs to them alone," it is stated that [this applies when] the brothers are childless. However, where all uterine brothers are un-reunited while the half-brothers are reunited, then the uterine brothers alone—even if they are un-reunited—shall divide his wealth, and not the half-brothers even if they are reunited;
for "even though reunited, one shall take [the share] if reunited, but not one born of another mother."

Thus, from the legal tradition (*smaraṇa*) of Yājñavalkya: by the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even one who is not reunited" (*asaṃsṛṣṭy api*), it is understood that there is a prohibition against the taking [of property] by one born of a different mother who is characterized by being a reunited co-heir (*saṃsṛṣṭitva*). However, when among the remaining [heirs] there is no uterine brother, then those born of different mothers who are reunited shall divide [the estate]; for Bṛhaspati states: "Furthermore, two who are reunited through affection are mutual sharers. In this context, it is understood that the term "born of different mothers" (*bhinnamātṛkau*) serves to avoid tautology. As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:

"But one born of the same womb who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall take the wealth, not one born of a different womb"—this is not contradictory, as it refers to a situation where uterine brothers (*sodarya*) exist. If the taking of wealth by those born of different wombs who are *saṃsṛṣṭins* occurs only in the absence of uterine brothers who are themselves *asaṃsṛṣṭas*, then [it applies to the case] where "if the eldest or the youngest among them should perish before the distribution of shares... [and so forth].
Or even if one of them should die, his share is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally;
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.

Thus, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Manu. This is because, by means of the two words *ca* (and), all those mentioned in the verse—the uterine brothers, the sisters, and the half-brothers—are understood to share in the division as mutually associated. Furthermore, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is clearly expressed by the words *sahita* (together) and *sarva* (all), showing that the agency belongs only to those who have assembled, namely: "The reunited half-brothers, together with the uterine brothers, and the uterine sisters, having come together, shall divide that undivided share equally. Thus, the contradiction is evident. Some, for the sake of avoiding this contradiction, explain the verse as follows: "When the uterine brothers are reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), then they alone shall take that undivided share, and not even the non-reunited uterine brothers. In the absence of reunited uterine brothers, all uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally—that is, without deficiency or excess—in a state of equal primacy. In the absence of uterine brothers, the uterine sisters shall divide it. In their absence, the half-brothers shall do so. This interpretation is to be disregarded because it involves numerous unwarranted interpolations (*adhyāhāra*) and is therefore extremely inconsistent. Others, however, for the sake of avoiding the contradiction...
But a uterine brother who is reunited shall take the wealth, not a non-uterine brother;
even one who is not reunited may take it, but one who is reunited shall not take it if he is born of a different mother.

Having cited this statement of Yājñavalkya, they explain that statement as having the same meaning as the *Mānava* (Manu) statement as it is perceived. First, the literal and intended meanings of the portion beginning with "But a half-brother who is reunited shall take the wealth, not a half-brother who is not reunited" have been explained. A half-brother (*anyodarya*) is one born of a different mother; he who is reunited shall take the wealth, but a half-brother who is not reunited shall not take the wealth. By this, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is stated that the state of being reunited for a half-brother is the cause for taking the wealth. Furthermore, by connecting the middle portion "he shall take" with the preceding portion "one who is not reunited," the literal and intended meanings of the phrase "one who is not reunited" have been explained. This term "not reunited" also connects with what follows; thus, even one who is not reunited may take the wealth of one who is reunited. To the question "Who is he?", it says "the reunited one. "Reunited" means one who is reunited in the same womb, that is, a uterine brother (*sodarya*). By this, it is stated that even for one who is not reunited, the state of being a uterine brother is the cause for taking the wealth. Regarding the portion "not born of another mother," the word "only" (*eva*) is supplied and connected with it; the literal meaning of the word "reunited" contained within the middle portion has been explained. This term "reunited" also connects with what follows, where "reunited" means "one who is reunited. In the phrase "not born of another mother," the explanation should be made by supplying the word "only"; thus, even if he is reunited, a half-brother born of another mother, even if accompanied by a uterine brother, shall not take the wealth of the reunited one. In this way, the intended meaning of the entire verse is shown to be identical to the *Mānava* statement. And so, because of the hearing of the word "also" (*api*) in "even one not reunited shall take," and because of the prohibition of restriction in "the reunited one, not born of another mother," it is stated that a division must be made between the uterine brother who is not reunited and the half-brother who is not reunited, since for both there exists only a single cause for taking the wealth. This [explanation] is pleasing only to those commentators themselves, but not to the students, because they have fabricated the meaning of the text by the force of their own intelligence regarding something that is not at all apparent from the words. Therefore, since the statements of Manu and Yājñavalkya here refer to their respective perceived meanings, their non-contradiction must be stated through a distinction of scope (*viṣaya-vyavasthā*), rather than through the laborious effort of asserting identity of meaning. Thus, the statement of Manu [706] refers to the case where both immovable and other types of wealth exist, because Prajāpati has prescribed the division and taking of wealth for those who are reunited and those who are not reunited in that very context.
"And whatever property is hidden shall belong to those who are reunited;
as for land and the house, those not reunited may take them according to their respective shares."

The meaning is as follows: among brothers born of different mothers who are reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), hidden wealth and movable property—consisting of bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth—shall belong [to them] according to their respective shares. However, those not reunited (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*)—namely, uterine brothers and sisters—shall take the house and the field according to their shares. Thus, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), Yājñavalkya’s statement should be understood to apply to cases where there exists only immovable property, or where there exists only property other than immovable. But when only reunited brothers born of different mothers remain, then the father or paternal uncle who was reunited shall take [the property], because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Gautama: "When a reunited person has died, the one who was reunited is the heir to the estate. When, however, no reunited father or paternal uncle exists, then a brother born of a different mother who is not reunited shall take it. In his absence, the father who is not reunited; in his absence, the mother; and in her absence, the wife. Thus says Śaṅkha: "The property of one who has gone to heaven (died) without a son goes to the brothers; in their absence, the parents shall take it, or the eldest wife. The meaning is that for one who has gone to heaven without a son, who was reunited with either a father or a paternal uncle, in the absence of such a reunited kinsman and in the absence of contact with brothers born of different mothers, the property goes to the brothers. And so says Nārada.
But for those who have commingled their property, that share is prescribed as belonging to them alone;
otherwise, they shall be entitled to shares according to their respective portions, while in the case of those who are childless, one should approach others [to provide heirs].

Therefore, otherwise, when those who are reunited exist, those who are not reunited—such as uterine brothers and others—are not entitled to a share. However, when all [the reunited heirs] are without seed (i.e., childless), then he [the non-reunited uterine brother] shall go to the others, meaning he shall obtain the share of the reunited ones. In this regard, the sequence stated in the words of Śaṅkha, "The property goes to the brother," etc., is to be observed. The mention of the "eldest" is for the purpose of describing one who possesses qualities such as being well-restrained, and not for the purpose of excluding the middle or other sons. Furthermore, although it should have been said simply "in his absence," the word *vā* ("or") is employed because the result is the same. For instance, from the word *vā*, an option (*vikalpa*) is understood; yet, in this case, an equal option regarding the actual object consisting of ownership is not possible, since the principle established in the *Nyāya-śāstra* states, "There is no option regarding an existing thing. Therefore, since the option of absence is understood here from the word *vā*, there is indeed equality of result. And thus the sequence is as follows: in the absence of the brother, the father takes; in his absence, the mother; in her absence, the wife. Consequently, because it would contradict the sequence of wife, daughter, and so forth stated for the subject of partition, it is inferred that this [rule] concerns the share of the reunited. The logical sequence of wife, daughter, and so forth stated for the subject of partition is set aside in this matter by the scriptural sequence stated by Śaṅkha. This sequence is indeed scriptural, as there is no underlying logic (*nyāya*) in this specific order. When, according to this reversed order, the wealth has come to the wives and there are still *sapiṇḍa* relatives such as brothers' sons and others present, then Nārada says:
But when the husband has died, the wives who have no brothers, father,
or mother shall all share their own wealth among themselves according to their respective shares, along with all the sapinda relatives.

"Wives" means wives (*patnyaḥ*). "Those who have no brothers, father, or mother" means those who are characterized by the absence of the husband’s brothers, father, and mother; this is the meaning. By composing the compound in this reversed order—thereby abandoning the placement of the word *pitṛ* (father) first, which is more venerable than *bhrātṛ* (brother) in a *dvandva* compound—Nārada demonstrates that the wealth of a deceased reunited coparcener (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) first goes to the brothers; in their absence, to the father; in his absence, to the mother; and in her absence, it goes to all the wives, regardless of their conduct. It should be understood that in the case of reunited coparceners, the wives do not inherit the property upon the absence of secondary sons (*gauṇaputra*), but rather only upon the absence of uterine brothers who were not reunited, as well as the father and mother. The meaning of the verse beginning with "all the sapinda relations" (*sarve sapiṇḍāḥ*) is as follows: those sapinda relations of the deceased reunited coparcener who are distinct from the brothers, father, and mother—namely, the brothers' sons and others—should divide the property previously reunited with their own father and so forth along with the estate of the sonless man, subsequently together with his wives, without exceeding the respective shares: the brothers' sons taking the share of the brother, and the wives taking the share of the husband. However, in the absence of the wives, the deceased's sister receives the share of the reunited coparcener. And so says Bṛhaspati: [The text continues with the citation of Bṛhaspati.]
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father.
Whether she has been given away or not, if a uterine brother dies, she alone shall take his share;
for this is clearly the reason for both cases.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and of one who has neither brother nor mother" serves to include this case as well. In the absence of a sister, however, the *sapiṇḍas* alone shall divide the share of the reunited coparcener according to the sequence already stated—namely, "the wealth of each shall belong to the nearest *sapiṇḍa*"—since those specifically mentioned in the preceding rule are absent. And so says that same author: [709]
If one has died without offspring, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother,
all his *sapiṇḍa* relatives shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares.

This is the inheritance of one who has reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). The meaning of the first half-verse is: "If [the owner] has died childless, being of a different mother, and is devoid of the status of being an expressly designated recipient of wealth by brothers or others. However, in the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, it should be understood that the property of one who has passed away while reunited belongs to the *samānodakas* and others, just like the property of one who lived separately after partition. This is because, regarding the property of one reunited, no specific rule is recorded beyond the *sapiṇḍas*. Thus ends the section on reunited brothers and others in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
now follows the division of separated sons and others.

Regarding this, Viṣṇu says concerning a son born after the division of the estate among the living: “They should give a share to one born after the father’s partition. The meaning of this is as follows: when the father’s wife was not yet clearly pregnant, those sons who were divided by the father should—upon learning of the birth of a son born after their own division—extract from their respective shares the portion that had already entered them and give it to him, since they were unaware of his existence at the time of their own division. However, the father himself need not give a share from his own portion; rather, having taken the portions given by the elder brothers, he should live together with the son born after partition (*vibhaktaja*), because such a son, being of unattained legal capacity (*aprāptavyavahāra*), must be maintained through co-residence. For this very reason, it is said that “the brothers divided by the father should give a share,” and not that “the father and the brothers divided by the father should give a share. As for what Gautama stated: “The son born after partition [takes] only the paternal [share],” the ellipsis is that he “should take a share. This should be understood to apply to a case where the father dies before the brothers divided by the father have given a share to the son born after partition. Accordingly, a share need not be given by the elder brothers, because of the restrictive particle *eva* (only) in the phrase “only the paternal. As for what Bṛhaspati has stated:
Those who have been divided from their father— whether they be stepbrothers or uterine brothers—
and those who are born later, they alone shall take the paternal share.

Thus, in this context, the meaning of the phrase "those who take the paternal share" (*pitṛbhāgaharāḥ*) should be understood as "those who take only the paternal share. This refers specifically to those who, having been conceived in the womb, are born after the partition has already taken place. He himself also states the reason why those born later (*jaghanyajāḥ*) are entitled to take the paternal share alone: "The elder brother is not the owner of the paternal estate; one born after partition [takes] the brother's share."

"Anīśaḥ" means "not the owner. Regarding the statement, "The elder brother is not the owner of the paternal [property]," the intended meaning should be understood as being because he has already been partitioned from the father. However, regarding the statement, "The son born after partition has no right in the share of the brothers," the intended meaning must be determined as being because there is no transfer of wealth from the brothers' shares to him. Having established the lack of ownership of the elder brothers who were previously partitioned over the paternal property according to the first-mentioned intention, that same author states another point by force of that logic: "Whatever was acquired by the father himself after he had been partitioned from his sons..."
It is recorded that all those earlier-born ancestors have no authority over that which has been partitioned.

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of removing the doubt that, because of the subsequent partition, there might still be a share for the sons of the ancestors in property acquired later, even though they did not receive a share previously. Thus, both the elder brothers and the others are, with respect to each other's wealth, as if they were unrelated persons and have no ownership; however, he (the author) states that there is a slight distinction in this regard:

"As it is with wealth, so it is with debt, and in matters of giving, pledging, and buying; they have no mutual authority over one another, except for the rites of impurity and the offering of water. [711]

The meaning is that they have mutual authority only over matters such as impurity (*āśauca*) and water-libations (*udakakriyā*), but not over wealth and the like. *Ādhāna* means a pledge (*ādhi*). He [the author] states that this lack of authority over debts and so forth applies only when there is no association (*saṃsarga*), for he says:
"Furthermore, those two who are associated through affection are heirs to one another.
As for what was stated by Manu:
But one born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide it together with them.

Thus, the phrase "only that which belongs to the father" (*pitryam eva*) is connected also with the latter half of the verse; therefore, it is not in contradiction with what was stated previously. This [rule] is to be understood as applying when the son born after partition (*vibhaktaja*) dies while his father is still living and they are in a state of co-residence. However, regarding a son born after the time of partition from a father who has already died, Yājñavalkya says: "A son born after the [property] has been divided from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share of the partition. Or rather, his share shall be determined from the visible assets, after deducting [the father’s] debts."

When the father has passed away and the mother’s pregnancy is not yet manifest, if sons are born subsequently after the brothers have already divided among themselves, that son is entitled to a share (*vibhāgabhāk*). "Share" (*bhāga*) is the same as "portion" (*vibhāga*); the meaning is that he receives it. That is to say, having set aside a portion from the entire divided wealth; or rather, from the "visible" (*dṛśya*)—that is, from the house, utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, servants, and so forth, which are currently perceived and whose quantity has been determined through income and expenditure, and which are subject to increase and decrease—from that divided property, a portion is extracted for that posthumously born son (*vibhaktaja*). This is the sense. The inclusion of the term "visible" is intended to preclude the calculation of a share by extracting from hidden or secret assets. One should understand that this alternative view was stated by the author because, although there is no difference in the fact that the posthumously born son is still a son, it is reasonable to reduce his share since his existence at the time of partition was difficult to ascertain. However, one should also consider that the difficulty of ascertaining his existence does not constitute a fault in itself; thus, the first position is not entirely improper. Furthermore, in cases where property is acquired after partition due to the fault of the individuals involved, there is only the reduction of the share for the one who acquired it after partition, and no opening for an alternative position of equal shares. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati speaks only of a reduced share in such a case.
Having abandoned the common ancestral property and resorted to another region,
a share must undoubtedly be given to one who has returned from that place, even if only halfway.

The meaning is as follows: having abandoned the common ancestral estate (*gotrasādhāraṇa*) and left the place of residence where all the family members dwell together, one who lives in an extremely distant land and whose existence was unknown to the others, once all the wealth has been divided by those remaining, a share must be given to him upon his later arrival; this share is to be extracted from half of the property already divided. In this case, the fact that the others were unaware of his existence is the basis for that rule, so there is no room for another interpretation. For this very reason, it is stated that "there is no doubt. Thus, he says the same regarding one who returns after a very long period of absence when a division has already been made because his existence was unknown.
Whether it be a debt, a document, a house, or a field that belongs to one's grandfather,
he who returns after having been away for a long time is entitled to his share upon arrival.

"Entitled to a share" (*bhāgabhāk*) means entitled to half a share. "One who has come from partition" (*vibhāgād ūrdhvam āgataḥ*) refers to one who has arrived after the division of property. However, he [the same author] states that a grandson or others who have come from a partition are entitled to a share only in the case of property inherited through succession: "The third, the fifth, or even the seventh—if their births are unknown, they shall receive a share in property acquired through succession. [713]
Regarding the case of someone who arrives as a non-heir (vibhaktāgata), even among those who have inherited by succession, a share must be given in the land itself; thus he [Yājñavalkya] says:
"Land should be given by the kinsmen to one who has arrived as a descendant of that person whom all the original ancestors knew to be their master through tradition."

The phrase "after the division" (*vibhāgād ūrdhvam*) is understood as the remainder [of the context]. He himself states that for one who has arrived after the division—or even for one who arrived earlier—who proceeds to take his own share, there is an entitlement to receive a portion only when he first establishes his ownership over the property dependent on others by means of visible or invisible evidence, and not otherwise: "Whether the division has been performed or not, if an heir proceeds where there is common property and asserts his claim, he alone is the one entitled to receive the share."
Thus concludes the section on the division of property among sons born after partition in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the section on the re-division of property (*avaluptavibhāga*).
Regarding this, Manu says:
When all debts and assets have been divided according to the rule,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be brought into equality.

Whatever debt or wealth is seen at the time of partition, all those sons who inherit their father’s estate shall receive equal shares according to the rule; however, among them, one endowed with learning and virtuous conduct deserves to receive more. [714]

In accordance with such injunctions as these, after the partition has been made, whatever debt of the absent creditor or whatever wealth of the absent depositor and others may be found later at another time in the possession of those nearby, all of that should be brought to equality. The meaning is that it should not be made excessive by being improperly applied to the [other] share. From the fact that the debt seen later is brought to equality, it is understood that there was an inequality in the debt seen earlier, which [inequality] is treated like wealth. Thus, Kātyāyana states that if, upon investigation after the time of partition, an object that had been concealed by some deceitful person through means such as creating the impression that it belonged to another is recognized as indeed belonging to oneself, one should bring that to equality.
If concealed wealth is discovered again, it shall be divided with the brothers once it has been made equal; indeed, in the absence of the father, the sons [shall divide it].

The meaning is that, in the absence of the father, all the sons shall divide whatever has been acquired at that time. Likewise, if among co-residents some property has been misappropriated by one person and is somehow discovered after the partition, they should bring it back to equality. And so says Yājñavalkya: "If any property misappropriated from one another is discovered after partition, they should divide it again into equal shares; such is the settled rule."
The meaning is that all of those [assets] have been divided. Even that which was improperly divided should be brought to equality, as if it were stolen away. And so Kātyāyana says:
"Whatever property may have been mutually withheld or improperly divided, if it is discovered later, Bhr̥gu says it shall be divided into equal shares."

One should bring to equality that which was improperly divided—meaning divided unequally in a manner not prescribed by the scriptures—as well as what has been mutually misappropriated, as if it were an improper division, and what has been taken away by another, and what was lost and then recovered. Furthermore, regarding wealth acquired after the partition, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states that it belongs only to the acquirer and not to the co-heirs: "Whatever wealth is obtained by one who has already partitioned shall belong to him alone; likewise, what was stolen, lost, and recovered, and what was previously mentioned, should be shared again."

That which was previously mentioned as "mutually withheld" (*mitho 'pahṛta*) and "improperly divided" (*durvibhakta*) is cited here again for the sake of illustration. Thus, the meaning is that they should divide [the property] just as previously stated. By this, it should be understood that an equal division of both what was stolen by another and what was recovered after being lost has been prescribed. Since Manu and others have thus ordained the division of only those common assets that are seen *after* the partition, it is understood that the previous partition was correctly executed. Therefore, it should be understood that even if some common property is seen after the partition, the state of the men having already been divided is established from before. As for that which was further stated by Manu:
But when a division has been made and some common property is seen therein, that division is not to be recognized as final; indeed, it must be performed all over again.

Thus, that [rule] regarding those who have been separated should first be understood as applying to the realm of the visible (dṛṣṭaviṣaya), because the management of income, expenditure, and so forth occurs among separated individuals with respect to separated assets; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with all the statements previously mentioned. Furthermore, the purpose of the injunction for subsequent partition is the execution of deductions (*uddhāra*) and other such matters even in the portion seen later.
Thus ends the section on "Partitioned Shares" in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the duties of those who have been partitioned;
regarding this, Nārada says:
If many persons born of one [family] possess separate properties, separate activities,
and are endowed with separate qualities of action, yet they are not in agreement regarding their affairs;
if they should give their respective shares or even sell them— [716] — then [the distribution is valid].
They may do all that as they wish, for they are indeed masters of their own wealth.

The meaning of this is as follows: if many who were born of one [father] are divided in various ways and, being thus separately established, perform Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*—which require wealth—for themselves without mutual consent; or likewise, if they engage in worldly activities such as agriculture, which depend on separate expenditures; or if they possess distinct implements and materials necessary for their tasks; or if brothers are not in agreement regarding their own affairs and may therefore carry out their own business disregarding them; or if those divided individuals give away or sell their own shares, doing all such things as they please—because, being divided, they are independent and, in effect, masters [of their own portions]. As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
for no single person has authority over it in matters of gift, mortgage, or sale.

Thus, *ādhamana* means pledging as security. This refers to a case where, considering the division of immovable property to be extremely difficult due to its nature, heirs—motivated by the intention, "We shall divide the very fruit of that [property] at the time the fruits accrue"—remain undivided from the division of other assets; for in that case, there is no independent ownership (*svatantra-svāmitva*) over the immovable property for each individual. He (Yājñavalkya) also states another legal act concerning one who has been divided: "Whatever share was enjoyed by whom, that he shall not be deprived of.
Likewise, he speaks to the king:

Furthermore, he who, having made a division according to his own will, should subsequently act in contradiction to it, shall be made to stand by the king for his own share and punished for causing such trouble.
"Anubandha" means "nibandha," that is to say, "āgraha" (insistence).
Thus ends the section on duties after partition in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the means for determining the existence of partition and its legal characteristics are stated;
therein, Yājñavalkya says:
When a partition has been denied, the fact of partition should be established by means of kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, written documents,
and separate holdings of houses and fields.
"By means of separate portions set aside. The mention of "division" is intended to indicate the legal rules pertaining to it as well. For this very reason, Nārada states:
"In case of doubt regarding the rules of division among heirs, a decision is reached by kinsmen through a deed of partition, because of the commencement of separate activities."

The meaning is as follows: when there is doubt regarding the existence of a partition and its attendant properties—either by denying the very nature [of the property] through such claims as "there was no partition between us," or by denying the legal attributes through such claims as "there is no partition between us from any divisible object"—the determination is to be known through the testimony of kinsmen and others, or by a written deed of partition, or by logical means such as the separate performance of duties by the heirs. "Separate performance of duties" refers to the heirs' individual engagement in religious acts such as the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, giving alms, and honoring guests. When it is asked how this constitutes a logical means (*yukti*), it has been stated immediately thereafter by that same author: "The separate performance of duties is the carrying out of distinct religious obligations by the heirs individually; for those who have not separated, there is no separate performance of duties. In this context, the term "separate performance of duties" refers to the performance of religious rites such as the Vaiśvadeva, the giving of alms, and the honoring of guests by each heir separately. When it is asked how this serves as a logical criterion, it was stated by him [Vijñāneśvara] immediately following: "Because, in the case of those who have not separated, there is no separate performance of duties. This means that for those who have not divided their estate, there is no independent execution of religious functions; therefore, the observation of such separate performance serves as a logical inference for the existence of a prior partition. Furthermore, he states: "And because there is no commonality in the performance of religious rites, the separation of those who have performed them is established. That is to say, since there is no joint performance of religious duties among those who have separated, the fact that they perform them separately establishes their prior state of division. Thus, the separate performance of duties is a logical means for determining a partition. It should be understood that this applies to cases where there is doubt regarding the partition itself or its characteristics, and not merely to the mere fact of living together or apart. This is because even brothers who live together may perform their duties separately due to differences in age, occupation, or other circumstances, yet remain undivided. Conversely, even those who live together may perform their duties jointly, yet be considered divided if there is a prior agreement on the distribution of assets. Therefore, the separate performance of duties is a decisive factor only when it occurs in conjunction with other evidence, such as the testimony of witnesses or a written document. It is not a standalone proof in every instance. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, he says: "Or, by the separate performance of duties, [partition is inferred]; for those who have not separated, there is no separate performance of duties. This indicates that the separate performance of duties is a logical mark for inferring partition. He further explains: "And because there is no commonality in the performance of religious rites, the separation of those who have performed them is established. This means that since there is no joint performance of religious acts among those who have separated, the fact that they act separately establishes their prior division. Thus, the separate performance of duties is a logical means for determining partition. It must be understood that this applies to cases involving doubt regarding the partition or its attributes, and not simply to cohabitation or non-cohabitation. For even brothers living together may act separately due to differences in age, profession, or other factors while remaining undivided. On the other hand, even those living together may act jointly while being considered divided if there is a prior agreement on the distribution of property. Therefore, the separate performance of duties is a decisive factor only when supported by other evidence, such as witness testimony or a written document. It is not a self-sufficient proof in all cases. This is the sense. For brothers who have not divided their property, a single religious duty (dharma) prevails; once division has occurred, their religious duty also becomes separate for each of them. [718] Religious duty refers here to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and other such rites. And so says Bṛhaspati:
For those living together with a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one;
for those who are divided, that same worship must be performed in every individual household.

Thus, the fact that the performance of rites such as the Vaiśvadeva is carried out separately for each individual—something that does not occur among those who have not divided their property—indicates their state of division. Therefore, it is sound reasoning to state this as a means of determination when a doubt regarding partition exists; this is beyond reproach. To state further arguments, the author himself first sets forth the prohibition against certain acts among undivided brothers, intending to prescribe them for those who are divided, on the grounds that they act as witnesses for one another and so forth: "Brothers who are divided may act as witnesses, stand surety, and engage in giving and receiving [gifts] from one another; those who are undivided may not."

"Receiving" means accepting. And thus, through such arguments as mutual witness-hood and so forth, the understanding of the actual existence of partition is indeed established. For this very reason, it was stated immediately thereafter by that same author:
"Those among whom these transactions proceed regarding their own property in the world—one should understand them to be divided, even in the absence of a written document."

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "they proceed either separately or collectively. Likewise, even the taking of a debt, when occurring among heirs, is an indicator of partition, because it does not occur among those who are unpartitioned. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Suretyship, debt, and witness testimony—these are indeed recorded as not [occurring] among brothers, husband and wife, or father and son, while they remain unpartitioned."

Consequently, it is established that even the debtor is separate from the creditor. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "Those who have separate income, expenditure, and wealth, who engage in lending money to one another, and who carry on trade, are undoubtedly divided."

Lending money for the sake of interest is usury (*kusīda*). Trade is commerce (*vaṇikpatha*). The word "mutually" (*parasparam*) is connected to both [terms]. Thus, he (Yājñavalkya) himself states that a determination based on circumstantial evidence (*hetu*) should be made when there is an absence of superior means of proof (*pramāṇa*) to determine [the matter] directly:
"Ownership of immovable property, forceful seizure (*sāhasa*), prior partition, and the inheritance of heirs—these are to be known through inference (*anumāna*) where there are no witnesses."

"Prior partition" refers to a division that occurred before a dispute over the partition arose. "Inference" means reasoning. For the purpose of demonstrating the reasoning that establishes acts such as *sāhasa* (outrageous acts), that same author states certain proofs: "Evidence of family connection and contradiction constitutes proof of *sāhasa*;
for immovable property, one's own possession is the proof; and for a partition, separate wealth [is the proof]."

*Kulānubandha* is the persistence of enmity from previous generations. *Vyāghāta* is mutual rivalry. *Hoḍha* is the observation of even a small trace of something that was forcibly stolen. *Svasya bhogaḥ* is one's own personal enjoyment; regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"If they live for ten years with separate religious duties and separate activities, those brothers are to be known as divided from the paternal wealth."

In this context, the word "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) is intended as an illustration for any relative connected by inheritance. The mention of "paternal" is intended as an illustration for all types of inherited property. In ultimate reality, even in the absence of a formal act of taking possession, there is loss of land after twenty years of being enjoyed by another while one looks on and says nothing; for wealth, the loss occurs after ten years. [720]

The meaning is that they should be understood as being divided according to the sequence of the forest [categories]. However, for those under ten years of age, the determination is made by the previously mentioned arguments alone. But if there is no determination due to the possibility of their status being established otherwise, and even the arguments prove insufficient, then one should determine it by means of oaths, according to the statement: "Even though an oath is prescribed, nevertheless, a decision should not be made based on an oath. For Yājñavalkya says:

"In cases of doubt regarding the law of partition, the determination of partition should be made by means of relatives, witnesses, and written documents; there shall be no recourse to divine proof (*daivikī kriyā*). When it is asked how a decision is reached when these means of proof are insufficient, Manu says:
Where there is mutual doubt among heirs regarding a partition, a re-partition must be made even by those who are living separately.
The ellipsis "where doubt does not depart through inadequate arguments" is to be understood. Furthermore, it has been stated by that same [author]:
A share of inheritance falls but once; a maiden is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once.
Thus, since that [teaching] has its scope of distinctions free from doubt by means of reasoning and so forth, everything is irreproachable.
Thus concludes the determination of the causes for the existence of the law of partition in the *Smṛticandrikā*,
and the exposition of the rules for the section known as the Partition of Inheritance is finished.

The sequence of topics in this section is as follows: the demonstration of the time, the agent, and the manner of partition; the method of partition during the lifetime of the father; the method of unequal partition; matters concerning the method of partition during the father's lifetime; matters concerning those unworthy of inheritance; the definition of property subject to partition; the definition of property not subject to partition; matters concerning the rules for the partition of property among sons, grandsons, and others; the various types of women’s property (*strīdhana*); the management of women’s property; the division of wealth acquired through a woman; the division of wealth acquired through a secondary father; the division of wealth acquired through a son; matters concerning the wife in the division of wealth acquired through one who has no son; matters concerning daughters and others; matters concerning reunited brothers and others; the partition of property by a son born after partition; the division of property that was lost and recovered; duties following partition; and the means for determining the existence of partition and its legal effects.
Thus ends the sequence of topics within the section on the division of inheritance in the Smṛticandrikā;
the section on the partition of heritage is completed.
Now, the rule regarding the category known as "sāhasa" (heinous offenses) is stated;
therein Bṛhaspati says:
"The killing of a human being, theft, and the violation of another's wife."
Harshness and both [of these] constitute the fourfold *sāhasa* (outrageous act).
Regarding the first two types of violent crimes (*sāhasa*), that same author says, for the purpose of identifying the perpetrator: "Where a person is seen killed but the killer is not seen,
he should be identified by the king through inference based on prior enmity."
A thief is to be recognized by his association with the wicked, by his distinctive marks, and by stolen goods;
this has been declared as the method for identifying murderers and thieves.

"Signs" (cihna) refer to the smearing with blood and so forth. "By means of evidence" (hoḍhena) refers to the wealth and other items held in the hand that have been seized. However, when the aforementioned mental states (*bhāvanā*) are possible, Kātyāyana states: "But when a case known as *sāhasa* (violent crime) proceeds without signs, it should be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies to all legal disputes."
The word "he" refers back to the one accused of committing a rash act (*sāhasa*). Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"One who is cleared by ordeals (*divya*) should be honored; one who is not cleared deserves death. Nārada also says:

"Those who commit such acts should not be punished with fines, but must be executed with diligence. Regarding those who commit such acts—namely, those who commit murder characterized by *sāhasa* (violent crime)—Vyāsa states a specific rule concerning their execution:
"Having correctly identified the killer, along with his associates and kinsmen..."
The king should destroy them by means of various methods of execution that cause terror.
Those who capture bandits, as well as those who steal horses and elephants,
and those who kill by force, the king shall cause such men to be impaled on stakes.
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati: "Those who commit open murder and likewise those who commit secret murder—
having identified them and having confiscated their wealth— they should be executed by various means of capital punishment."

This refers to the case of those who kill a Brahmin, such as Kṣatriyas and others. As Bodhāyana says: "In the case of killing a Brahmin by Kṣatriyas and others, there shall be corporal punishment and the confiscation of all property; for the killing of equals or inferiors among them, one should prescribe appropriate punishments according to their respective strength. To specify the punishment corresponding to the degree of guilt when many people strike a single person, Kātyāyana says: "If many men, acting in concert, should kill a single person, he among them who strikes a vital organ is considered the slayer."
Therefore, he alone is subject to the punishment for the offense of killing. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"But he who strikes their vital parts, one should cause him to pay the fine as previously stated.

The word "him" (*tam*) is to be supplied [as the object], because of the necessary connection between the relative and the demonstrative pronouns (*yad-tad*). Furthermore, the punishment for those other than the strikers of vital parts has also been stated immediately thereafter.
The initiator, the companion, the one who points out the path, the refuge, the giver of weapons, and the giver of food to those who perform evil deeds; [724]
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction,
one who is indifferent, one who is engaged in the task, one who speaks of faults, and one who approves [of them].
Also in another Smṛti:
"Those who are unable to prevent [a crime] shall all be liable for that act;
however, one should impose upon them a punishment according to their respective capacities."

"Anurūpam" means corresponding to the fault (*doṣa*). For this very reason, Manu shows that both [the instigator and the perpetrator] share half of the fault of one who strikes a vital organ (*marmahantr*):
"The one who initiates the act and the accomplice are sharers of the fault, each to half of that amount.

In this way, a reduction in fault for the one who points out the path and so forth should also be inferred. Yājñavalkya, however, states the gradation of the magnitude of the fault based on the gradation of the degree to which one instigates the act of violence, by way of describing the increase in punishment.
He who causes a rash act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
and he who, having said "I will give," causes it to be done, shall pay four times the amount.

The meaning is that if one says, "If you commit this act of violence (*sāhasa*), I shall give you this much wealth," and then causes the violence to be committed, he must be made to pay four times [the value].
