A fault caused by non-human beings occurs when one mutters,
"Do not depart," as well as when [the fault] is caused by wood, clods of earth, arrows, stones, or weapons.

The meaning of this is as follows: a fault such as injury caused by non-humans—such as beasts or birds—arising spontaneously does not accrue to their owners, even though they provide fodder and the like for the purpose of increasing their strength. Likewise, a fault such as injury caused by wood, clods of earth, stones, carts, or draft animals sent by another person does not accrue to the one who repeatedly and loudly utters the command "move aside" (*apasara*). Therefore, the intention here is that there is no punishment in these cases. He himself states an exception to this intended absence of punishment in certain instances:
For a master who is capable, yet fails to restrain fanged or horned animals, shall pay the first amercement; likewise, if he has been called out for help, he shall pay double.

The meaning is that even when one being oppressed cries out "Save me! Save me! and [the official] does not release them, he shall pay two *prathama-sāhasa* fines. Bṛhaspati also states the punishment for an offense equivalent to *sāhasa*: "Those who, displaying themselves as possessing a staff, deerskin, and so forth, cause injury through deception in a secluded place, are to be executed by the king's men."

Yājñavalkya, however, prescribes a punishment for killing a relative: "One who administers poison or sets fire, or one who causes the death of her husband, her guru, or her own child, should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off, and then be caused to die by cows."

However, in the case of an unrelated person, such as in the administration of poison or arson, the death penalty should not be carried out against the accomplices and others, as in the case of a reckless murderer; rather, it should be applied to that person alone. To this effect, Yama says: "Those who administer poison or set fire, thieves, murderers, and those who cause harm—Manu, the Lord of Creatures, has declared that they shall be punished with their own bodies."

Those who cause injury through others are "killers by proxy. Even for one who kills a preceptor (*guru*) or similar superior, the punishment is the same as that for killing a woman, because no distinction is specified and because this is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*). For instance, where even a woman receives a heavy punishment, it is understood that a man would receive an even heavier one. Alternatively, there may be various forms of corporal punishment, since in other cases a greater penalty for a man is observed in comparison to the penalty for a woman. This punishment for killing a relative should be understood to apply to intentional acts (*kāmakṛta*), because it is impossible to conceive of a greater penalty for a mortal sin committed intentionally than what is prescribed for one committed unintentionally. However, regarding the unintentional killing of a relative, a punishment must be devised for one who does not perform the penance ending in exile from the city and involving the forfeiture of all property—a penalty which exceeds the punishment for an unintentional mortal sin. But for one who does perform it, two instances of the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*) should be inferred. Manu also states the punishment for an offense equivalent to a crime of violence (*sāhasa*).
One who destroys a water reservoir should be killed, or else punished by the "pure execution" (śuddhavadha);
furthermore, he should repair that reservoir or pay the highest fine.
In this matter of the alternative punishments, the determination should be made according to the magnitude or smallness of the tank. Likewise:
"But he who diverts the water of a tank already established, or obstructs its inflow, shall be made to pay the first amercement."

"Bringing water" (*āgamam udakasya*) means bringing it toward a tank (*taṭāka*). "He should take it away" implies for the purpose of filling his own tank and so forth; this ellipsis is likewise to be understood in the phrase "he should obstruct it. Kātyāyana also says:
"If one should take away, break, or burn an image of the gods, or should destroy its temple, he shall incur the first amercement."

"But whoever should accomplish a legal matter by means of a false document, or even with a forged seal, shall indeed be made to pay the highest fine. [758] Here, "document" refers to written records and the like. Bṛhaspati also says:
Those who, through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, display some degree of delusion and perform root-rites (mūlakarma) shall be expelled by the king.
Root-rite (*mūlakarman*) is a specific form of subjugation accomplished by means of medicinal roots and the like.
Thus ends the section on punishments for offenses involving violence (*sāhasa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*;
the exposition of the rules pertaining to the incidental category known as *sāhasa* is completed. Now, the rule concerning the category of verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) is stated.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"In cases of verbal abuse between persons of equal caste and qualities,
the punishment prescribed in the treatise is twelve and a half paṇas."

Those for whom the thirteenth is half [of twelve] are so described. Regarding the equality of mere caste, Manu says: "But among all those of equal caste, when there is an offense, the fine is exactly twelve [paṇas]. The words "mutually by speech" are to be supplied as the remainder. Since there is no distinction made by priority or posteriority in an offense committed by speech, when both parties are equally at fault, the punishment is exactly twelve paṇas; it does not mean that the fine for one is less or more than the other. For this very reason, another Smṛti states:

"If no distinction is observed between the two faults of harshness and falsehood when they occur simultaneously, then discipline should be equal for both. But if a distinction is perceived, then punishment must indeed be unequal according to that distinction"—this is the intended meaning. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
In cases of mutual verbal abuse, the punishment for two equals is the same; for the inferior, it is double that amount; and for the superior, it is declared to be half of that.
An unequal punishment [is applied] even when two [parties] have acted simultaneously and are otherwise equal. And so says Nārada:
"He who first brings a charge shall certainly bear the blame;
he who does so later is also a wrongdoer, but the penalty for the former is heavier."

The meaning is that, if the instigation (*ākṣāraṇa*) occurs first as the cause, the punishment resulting from that cause should be greater than the punishment resulting from the subsequent instigation. However, when two people of equal status engage in a dispute and a distinction is observed, there is also gravity of punishment based on that specific cause; thus, the same author says:
"The man who attaches himself equally to both parties involved in a conflict incurs the punishment of one of them—either the first or the latter."

"Of those two who have committed an equal offense"—that is to say, of those two who have brought about an equal incitement. "He receives a punishment equal to theirs" means that he receives as much punishment as the combined punishment of the two who committed the offense together. Furthermore, Uśanas states the manner of determining a reduction in punishment for one who abandons his persistence due to remorse:
"If one says, 'I spoke thus out of delusion, negligence, rivalry, or affection;
I shall not speak so again,' the judge should impose half the punishment upon him."

Thus, although the *smṛtis*—which prescribe various high and low punishments based on the specific distinctions of caste, quality, age, and learning; likewise, the distinctions included within verbal abuse (vākpāruṣya) as expressed in three ways according to whether it is first, middle, or highest degree; likewise, the specific types of verbal abuse such as being harsh, vulgar, or intense; and likewise, the specific types of insults directed at one's learning, lineage, country, occupation, body, father, mother, teacher, and so forth—have been compiled by the authors of the *Vacasamuccaya*, we have not compiled them here. This is because, for the time being, there is no instructor of the people intent upon the practical application of their meaning, and thus we have avoided the fault of a useless proliferation of texts. In some instances, Bṛhaspati states an exception to the punishment for verbal abuse through a particular turn of phrase.
"A Brahmin shall not incur guilt for harshness toward one devoid of merit.
By this phrasing, Nārada states that even when speaking the truth, the punishment for verbal abuse does not disappear:
"Having called an outcast an 'outcast,' or a thief a 'thief' again..."
By speaking thus, one incurs an equal fault; by lying, one incurs a twofold fault.

"From speech" means from truthful speech. And thus that same [text] says: "But he who proclaims the faults of one who is already wicked for the sake of provoking anger, and who speaks by making excuses for others—they know that man to be corrupt in speech."
By saying "on account of anger," he shows that proclaiming the faults [of another] for the purpose of avoiding the wicked does not constitute a fault. And this has been shown by Katyayana:
"Where there may be a proclamation by one who has fallen [from virtue] for the sake of avoidance, there would be no fault on account of the statement, provided one can demonstrate it."

"By statement" means by the proclamation of [the charge of] being an outcast (*patita*) and so forth. The meaning is that even in cases such as a formal accusation where one might prove [the other] to be an outcast and so on, there would be no fault on account of the statement.
Thus concludes the detailed exposition of the section on verbal assault in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the legal procedure for the section known as physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) is stated.
In this regard, Manu says:
"This rule of punishment for verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault."

The meaning is: "From this point forward, I shall declare the determination of punishment for each specific instance of assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). The specific instances of assault have been illustrated by the author of the *Parishishta* (Digest) merely by way of direction:
"That which causes pain, bleeding, a wound, a fracture, or likewise a cutting or piercing of living beings—that indeed is called assault."

The meaning is that *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault) refers to the suffering caused to stationary or moving living beings by other creatures—such as through the tearing of skin with claws and so forth—as well as resulting in blood, wounds, and the like. Vyāsa has also illustrated this in brief:
"Throwing [ashes] and the like, striking with the hand and so forth, and binding with silken cloth and the like is called *daṇḍapāruṣya*."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), substances such as mud, dust, and filth—which cause pain by being thrown upon one from above—are understood. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "with hands etc.," substances such as clubs, stones, bricks, and weapons are meant; by the inclusion of the first term (*ādyagrahaṇena*), substances such as ropes and chains are included. Among the specific instances thus demonstrated, Manu states the legal decision regarding certain cases: "One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow. One who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, but one who breaks a bone shall be banished. [MDh 8.282]

A "flesh-breaker" is one who inflicts a wound; an "bone-breaker" is one who fractures a bone. Kātyāyana also states: "For the cutting off of the ear, lip, nose, foot, eye, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for the breaking [of these], Bṛhaspati says it is the middle fine."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Throwing [ashes] and the like, or striking with the hand and so forth—this constitutes the first degree of assault; in this case, a fine of one *māṣaka* should be imposed."
For striking with bricks, stones, or wood, a fine of two māṣakas shall be imposed; however, the wise should determine the punishment for a wound according to its severity at the time of impact.
"This punishment has been declared for [assaulting] equals and for the wives of others;
it should be understood by the wise as being double or triple, depending on the relative status [of the woman].
Yājñavalkya, however, states the punishment even when the specific forms of assault have not been demonstrated.

For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, or for seizing the hands, one shall pay a fine of ten paṇas; for crushing, dragging, wrapping with a garment, or placing a foot upon [the other], the punishment is a fine of one hundred.

In this context, the wrapping with fine cloth (*aṃśuka*) is illustrated by the examples beginning with "fine cloth" (*aṃśukādi*). However, the remaining [cases] where the specific details are not shown are clearly indicated. Thus, although the compilers have collected the legal rulings (*daṇḍanirṇaya-smṛti*) for each individual case regarding other instances where the specifics are not shown, we have not collected them here for fear of prolixity. Kātyāyana, however, indicates that the legal rulings for each individual case as stated in the section on verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) should be applied here in certain cases where the punishment has not been mentioned:
"Just as they were stated in the section on verbal abuse according to the inverse and direct order [of castes], [so should they be applied here]."
In the same way, punishments for assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) are to be inflicted in due order.

Thus, in this matter, Kātyāyana has recorded that the determination of punishment is made for each individual case, even in cases of inverse intercourse (*prātilomya*) and so forth; therefore, there are no punishments that need not be applied.

Now, one might object: even so, in some instances here, punishments devised according to the specific offense must be applied, because it is impossible to record a determination of punishment for every single individual among infinite individuals.
True. For this very reason it was said by Uśanas:
"In cases where no punishment has been specified by all the great-souled ones due to their infinite number, the wielder of the rod must determine the case and administer the penalty."
The phrase "due to the infinity" refers to the infinite instances of harshness; "effect" refers to the suffering produced for living beings by other living beings. For this very reason, Manu says:
"When a blow is struck against humans or animals, one should impose a punishment in proportion to the extent that great suffering has been caused."

When someone strikes another person out of malice, whether the resulting pain be slight or great, the punishment shall indeed be severe; for it is the ordinance of Manu that whatever limb of a superior man an outcaste may injure,
even that very limb shall be cut off from him.
"Should strike" means he should deal a blow. "A superior twice-born" refers to a *dvija*. "An outcaste" refers to a *śūdra*. And so Bṛhaspati says:
"Whatever limb of the twice-born a *śūdra* strikes with in anger, that very limb of his must be cut off; so it has been declared by Manu."
Manu himself stated the general expression "by whatever limb" in order to specify the particular cases:
"Lifting up his hand or a staff, he deserves the cutting off of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of that foot."
If one spits out of arrogance, the king shall cause both lips to be cut off;
if one urinates upon him, the penis; if one passes wind against him, the anus.
If one seizes him by the hair, he shall have his hands cut off without hesitation.

"On the feet, on the beard, on the neck, and on the testicles"—thus [it is said]. In the phrase "having raised a hand or a staff," the word "striking" is supplied as a complement. Even for one who seizes [another] by the hair with only one hand, the rule for the amputation of both hands is understood from the use of the dual number. The beard is said to be the primary mark of manhood (*liṅga*). By stating "out of anger or pride," he shows that one who strikes or spits [on another] through delusion, negligence, or the like, is not subject to punishment. And this has been shown by Yājñavalkya:
"In cases involving inferior persons, the punishment is half; there is no punishment for those [superior persons] who are intoxicated by delusion or liquor.

This means that when an insult is committed against persons who are inferior—in terms of birth and so forth—compared to the perpetrator of the insult, the punishment for the perpetrator shall be half of that prescribed for equal persons. Regarding the punishment for those who mutually commit insults, Bṛhaspati says:
"When two people strike each other, the punishment for both is declared to be equal."
The instigator and the accomplice shall be made to pay a higher fine.
Regarding the case where there is no equality in number, Yājñavalkya states:

"But for many who strike one person, the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed. This means that each of the many is individually subject to a double fine, and not the group acting together as a single striker, because the gravity of the offense increases for each individual. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: "For many striking one, the aforementioned fine for each individual is doubled. The term *pratyekasya* means "for each individual. Regarding cases where unbearable suffering such as wounds and the like has arisen, Kātyāyana states:
But when there is destruction of the body or the senses, the wise should impose a fine and likewise provide for the restoration and the means of recovery.

"Causing satisfaction" means that which brings relief to an unbearable wound; it should be given by one who has caused the unbearable wound and so forth. "Expenses for recovery" (samutthāna) are those calculated by the wise according to the severity of the wound—this is the implied meaning. And these expenses for recovery should be paid until the wound is healed; he shall pay the expenses for recovery until the wound is healed, because it has been stated by that very same [author]. "Expenses for recovery" refers to the expenditure incurred for the sake of physicians, medicine, diet, drinks, and so on. Bṛhaspati also says:
In cases of pressing a limb, as well as cutting or piercing it,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for its recovery, as well as whatever was seized during the quarrel.
Yājñavalkya states that one who causes suffering by inflicting pain on the limbs and so forth must be made to pay for the expenses incurred in recovery:
"But he who causes suffering shall be made to pay the expenses incurred in recovery... (YDh 2.226).

It causes suffering to human domestic animals—this is the remainder of the sense. And so Viṣṇu says: "All those who cause pain to humans shall be made to pay the expenses arising therefrom, as shall those who cause pain to domestic animals. Regarding the death of an animal due to excessive injury to domestic animals, he (Viṣṇu) himself says: "The killer of a domestic animal shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* and shall pay its value to the owner of the animal. Manu states that the punishment based on the killing of a living being does not apply in certain cases where it is impossible to provide a remedy, because in such instances there is no fault. [766]
When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when it has slipped sideways or become disengaged,
and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or of the chariot wheel;
"Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of a yoke, a harness, or a rein, nor when one cries out 'Get away! Thus it is said.

(*apaihi*), meaning the word "get away" is uttered loudly: [in these cases, there is no punishment]. If a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and shall be fined two hundred panas.

"Of the driver" (*prājaka*) means of one who leads [the vehicle], such as the driver of a cart and so forth. The mention of "two hundred" is intended to indicate the specific punishments prescribed for the injury of various living beings. When the driver is at fault—due to defects such as using only one hand and so on, which have been permitted by the owner for the sake of reducing the wages—the owner is not to be punished; rather, the driver alone is liable. As that same [text] states:
"If the driver is capable, the driver deserves the punishment. (NS 1.295) [767]
"Āptaḥ" means "competent. Nārada also stated that even a master may sometimes be subject to punishment:
"In the case of an offense committed by a son, neither the father nor the owner is liable for the punishment;
nor is the owner of a dog or a monkey liable, unless they were sent by those very individuals."
Manu, however, has declared the punishment for those who cause injury to immobile living beings:
"In the case of injury to any of the forest trees, the fine shall be inflicted in proportion to their utility; such is the settled rule."

The mention of *vanaspati* (trees) is intended to include all species of stationary living beings (*sthāvaraprāṇijāti*). For those trees that serve as sources of great enjoyment, such as the jackfruit tree (*panasa*) and others used for their fruit, the punishment is the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). For those used for their flowers, such as the *campaka* and others which are sources of moderate enjoyment relative to ripe or unripe fruit, the punishment is the middle fine (*madhyamasāhasa*). For stationary beings such as creepers, shrubs, and climbing plants, which are sources of very little enjoyment compared to those used for flowers, the punishment is one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. For grasses, which serve as sources of extremely little enjoyment, the punishment is one *kārṣāpaṇa*. Thus, the penalty is to be understood according to the degree of utility. Accordingly, Viṣṇu states, following the recurring term "punishment": "One who cuts down a tree used for its fruit shall pay the highest fine; one who cuts down [a tree] used for its flowers, the middle fine; one who cuts down a creeper, shrub, or climber, one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*; and one who cuts down grass, one [kārṣāpaṇa]. Furthermore, all these persons shall restore the produce to the owners—that is, the owners of the cut trees—until the time when the trees and other plants have been replanted and are again available for enjoyment. The implication is that all these individuals, from the cutter of fruit-bearing trees onwards, must provide the owners of the cut trees—the owners of the felled trees—with the future yield of those trees until they have grown back and are fit for use.
Thus concludes the exposition of the section titled "Assault" (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the rule regarding the section titled "Gambling and Betting" (*dyūtasamāhvaya*) is stated.
Regarding this, Manu says to the king:
"Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them."
*Tāskarya* means the state of being a thief. One should be diligent; having become diligent, one should restrain those two. And so he [Manu] himself has said:
"The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm.
When the question arises as to what the difference between gambling (*dyūta*) and betting (*samāhvaya*) is, he himself says:
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world;
whereas that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "betting" (samāhvaya).

"By non-living things" refers to dice and the like; "by living things" refers to rams and the like. "Prevention" here means by means of punishment such as banishment, since it is punishment itself that serves to ward off the low-born. For this very reason, he [Yājñavalkya] himself stated that banishment is for the purpose of prevention:
"He should quickly expel from the city actors, gamblers, men belonging to heretical sects, those engaged in forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers."

It should be understood that the mention here of association with various lowly persons, such as actors and musicians, is intended to illustrate the base conduct of gamblers. The word "quickly" (*kṣipram*) is used to indicate that through bad association, people fall into a wrong path without delay. The very purpose of the term "quickly" has been stated by that same author:
"These, existing in the kingdom, are the king's hidden thieves; by their performance of forbidden acts, they constantly afflict the virtuous subjects. [769]
These are the actors and others. Bṛhaspati, however, states both the opinion of Manu and the opinion of others:
"Gambling was prohibited by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth;
yet it has been permitted by others, provided it is conducted under the auspices of the king."
"The business presided over by the *sabhika* is for the purpose of identifying thieves.
Thus [it is said]. One who establishes a gambling hall is a *sabhika*, a gambler. When it is asked how the *sabhika* functions as a gambler, he himself says:
"The *sabhika* shall take the prize-money and give it to the winner and to the king."

The keeper of the gaming house (*sabhika*) shall become the receiver of the stakes from gamblers defeated at dice by means of confinement and other such methods. The meaning is that even before the stakes have been collected, the *sabhika* shall give his own property to the winner and to the king according to their respective shares. Thus says Kātyāyana: "The keeper of the gaming house shall give his own property to the winner; [the stake] should be taken from the gambler after three fortnights, or immediately—of this there is no doubt."

By the phrase "up to three fortnights" (*tripakṣakam*), it is shown that the time for the payment of the stake (*paṇa*) may extend up to three fortnights according to one's capacity. Regarding the interest on one's own property given as a substitute for the stake to both the winner and the king: at the time of receiving the stake, it should be collected by the *sabhika* (the keeper of the gambling hall) together with the stake itself;
however, he should take ten percent (*daśakam*) as interest from the loser.

This is because it has been stated by that same [author]: "He should take ten percent as interest from the defeat. "From the defeat" (*parājayāt*) means "from the defeated person" (*parājitāt*). He [the same author] states that the rule "presided over by the *sabhika*" is not mandatory.

Alternatively, a gambler, having given the king his share as prescribed, may conduct gambling openly; in this way, no fault is found. The "fault" refers either to the characteristic of deceiving the king or the characteristic of acting as a professional gambler. Having introduced the subject of *samāhvaya* (challenging to combat), Bṛhaspati says:
If anyone should suffer defeat in a duel,
the stake that was agreed upon therein must be paid by his master.
In some cases, Nārada states that the stipulation of a wager may be considered either performed or unperformed:
"That which is made in jest, and that which remains unknown, shall not yield the desired result there; nor shall it do so unless it was agreed upon by both parties."

*Kāma* (desire) is that which is desired; it is the stake. The intention is that one should not fail to obtain it, because gambling is for the purpose of dispelling indolence. Regarding those two—the winner and the loser—it follows from the context that the winner may obtain whatever was agreed upon before the game, even if it consists of things done for amusement and the like. In this regard, to prohibit repeated indulgence in eating food and drink obtained through the winning of the stake, the same author says:
"Food, edibles, meals, and drinks, as well as other minor items—these he may enjoy once out of friendship, but he should avoid excessive attachment."

Since the settlement of disputes therein is well known to follow the conventions of the presiding judge and others, we have not collected the statements concerning that subject out of a lack of regard for them.
Thus concludes the exposition of the section titled "Gambling and Betting" in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the rule for the section titled "Miscellaneous" (*prakīrṇaka*) is stated.
In this regard, Bṛhaspati says:
"This judicial procedure (vyavahāra) performed by litigants has been declared in brief; I shall now explain the miscellaneous judicial procedure (prakīrṇaka-vyavahāra) which rests upon the king."

"Caused by litigants" means brought about when a plaintiff and a defendant have reported a mutual disagreement to the king. And that [category] pertains to the entire range of subjects from the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) up to gambling (*dyūta*), not to gambling alone. Here, the word "this" (*eṣa*) refers to the complete group included within the previously mentioned seventeen titles of law, and does not rest solely upon the specific sub-categories mentioned immediately before, namely gambling and betting (*samāhvaya*). The term "in brief" (*samāsataḥ*) is connected to both [the preceding and following clauses]. "Dependent on the king" (*nṛpāśrayam*) means dependent on the king while requiring other bases characterized by wicked conduct. It is called "miscellaneous" (*prakīrṇaka*) because there is no single unified basis for such legal proceedings; and its designation as "miscellaneous" arises from the collection of these scattered matters dependent on the king into one place. Thus says Nārada:
The defiance of the kings' commands, the performance of their duties,
the dimensions of the city, and likewise the discord among the subjects.
The violation of the laws of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies;
disputes between father and son; and the transgression of prescribed penances.
There will be the destruction of the acceptance of gifts and anger even toward those in the stages of life;
there will be the fault of the intermixture of castes as well as the restriction of their livelihoods.
"And whatever was not seen among the previous [texts], all that would be classified as miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka). Thus it is said.

*Pratighāta* (obstruction) means resistance. *Tatkarma* (his duty) refers to royal duties such as ascending the lion-throne and so forth. *Purapramāṇa* (the measurement of the city) refers to the measurement of the records of the conduct of the citizens. *Sambheda* (dissension) is the piercing of the vital points (*marman*) of the subjects and the constituent elements of the kingdom (*rājyāṅga*) by means of well-known vices. Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and others have been explained in various ways previously. The practice of alien religions is the perversion of Dharma. Here, the dispute between father and son is mentioned even though it is not included within the category of "non-payment of debts" (*ṛṇādāna*). The phrase "and that which has not been seen among the previous [categories]" is stated as a supplement to everything mentioned before. Regarding a specific obstruction of the king’s command committed by someone, Yājñavalkya declares the punishment once the matter has been investigated and proven by the king himself: [772] Whoever writes a royal edict with either omissions or additions,
or who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment.

The meaning is that, because violating a document written without deficiency or excess and possessing non-defective characteristics—when such a document has been issued by the king—is an extreme offense due to its nature as a defiance of royal command, the punishment of *uttamasāhasa* (the highest fine) is to be applied here. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that one should bestow honor upon those who carry out orders and inflict extreme harm upon those who act otherwise:
"Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed over the realm, the king should honor the virtuous and cause those who are the opposite to be executed."

Virtuous persons acting in accordance with their appointed positions— “in the kingdom” being used as an illustration— thus says Vyāsa: “Those who, having been appointed to a seat of justice, take a bribe and deliver a verdict, they are indeed corrupters who destroy the king’s wealth.”
"One who lives by bribery should be banished after being deprived of his wealth. [773] Thus it is said. And regarding the punishment for performing such acts, Yājñavalkya states:
"For mounting the king's vehicle or seat, the punishment is the middle amercement."
Kātyāyana also says:
"Those who are addicted to the king's amusements, those who subsist on the king's service,
and he who speaks what is unpleasant to him— for them, the king should carry out the death penalty."

What ought to be done by a king regarding the measurement of cities, the constitution of the state, its division, and so forth, has already been explained by us previously in this section and in the section on *sadācāra* (proper conduct) as part of the context; therefore, we shall now desist. Consequently, only a small portion of what is to be conveyed by the category known as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous matters) has been set forth here. What remains should be understood as having been stated in various places according to the relevant context.

Thus ends the second chapter in the Section on Judicial Procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) of the *Smṛticandrikā*, composed by Yājñika Devaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya Somayājī, son of Śrī Keśavādityabhaṭṭopādhyāya, who was proficient in all branches of knowledge.
And the section is completed.
